lessons.label: What Counts as a Case: Case Definitions

sections.heading: Nothing can be counted until it is defined
sections.body: Before any rate can be computed, an investigator must decide exactly who counts as a 'case.' A case definition specifies clinical criteria (symptoms, lab findings, imaging), and almost always restricts by person (age, exposure group), place (a specific school, county, or facility), and time (onset within a stated window). The CDC's investigation of the 1993 Milwaukee cryptosporidiosis outbreak, for instance, defined a case as watery diarrhea beginning after a specific date among residents served by one water plant — a definition built from all three axes at once. Change any axis and the case count changes, even though the underlying disease has not. The World Health Organization's SARS case definition during the 2003 outbreak went through several formal revisions within months, each one shifting the reported case count even as the actual epidemic curve did not change shape — a reminder that surveillance numbers are as much a product of the definition in force as of the disease itself.

sections.heading: Confirmed, probable, suspected
sections.body: Public health surveillance almost never uses one tier. The CDC's national notifiable disease system sorts cases into confirmed (lab-verified, meeting the reference standard), probable (clinical picture plus a supportive but non-definitive test, or a known epidemiologic link to a confirmed case), and suspected (compatible symptoms with no confirmatory workup yet). This tiering lets surveillance start counting early, when only suspected cases exist, and tighten the estimate as confirmations arrive — visible during COVID-19, where early 2020 U.S. case counts leaned heavily probable and suspected before PCR testing capacity scaled up through March and April of that year, after which the confirmed tier came to dominate reported totals.

sections.heading: The sensitivity-specificity tradeoff in definition-writing
sections.body: A definition is a diagnostic test applied to the whole population, so it inherits the same tradeoff a lab test does. A loose definition (broad symptom list, no lab requirement) is sensitive — it catches nearly every true case — but low-specificity, sweeping in look-alike illnesses and inflating the apparent outbreak size. A tight definition (strict lab confirmation) is specific but misses milder or atypical presentations, understating true burden. Outbreak investigators often deliberately start loose to cast a wide net for hypothesis generation, then tighten the definition for the analytic phase, once a likely source is identified, to avoid diluting a true signal with noise. This staged approach traces back to classic field-epidemiology practice formalized in CDC outbreak-investigation training and textbooks such as Gregg's Field Epidemiology, which teaches investigators to build, then progressively refine, a working case definition as evidence accumulates.

lessons.workedExample: During a suspected norovirus outbreak on a cruise ship, investigators first use a loose definition — any passenger with vomiting or diarrhea in the past 72 hours — and count 340 cases among 3,000 passengers (11.3%). This loose net is used to map the outbreak's timing and rule in food-service exposure. Once stool samples confirm norovirus in 40 of 60 tested passengers, investigators tighten the definition to lab-confirmed or epidemiologically-linked cases sharing the same meal seating, dropping the analytic count to 190 — the number used to calculate a valid attack rate by dining hall.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'how did you decide who counted as a case?' because a shifted case definition can manufacture or erase an entire effect. If a student's case count changed between phases of their project, the judge is checking whether that shift was a deliberate, disclosed sensitivity-for-specificity tradeoff or an undisclosed one that quietly cherry-picked the data toward a hoped-for result.

questions.prompt: An outbreak investigator switches from a loose, symptom-only case definition to a strict, lab-confirmed one partway through an investigation. What is the most likely effect on the case count?

options.text: It rises, because lab confirmation adds cases the symptom list missed
It falls, because some symptomatic people will not be lab-confirmed
It stays the same, since case definitions do not affect counts
It becomes impossible to compare across time

explanations.a: Lab confirmation is a stricter, not looser, filter than a symptom list — it removes cases, not adds them.
explanations.b: Correct: tightening the definition raises specificity at the cost of sensitivity, so genuine but unconfirmed or atypical cases drop out of the count.
explanations.c: Case definitions directly determine who is counted; changing one changes the case count almost by construction.
explanations.d: Comparisons remain possible as long as the definition change and its timing are documented, which is standard outbreak-investigation practice.

questions.prompt: Order the components used to build a case definition, from broadest scope-setting to narrowest confirmation.

items.text: Restrict by place and time (who, where, when the investigation covers)
State clinical/symptom criteria that must be present
Add a laboratory or epidemiologic-link requirement
Classify each candidate as confirmed, probable, or suspected

questions.explanation: Investigators first bound the population and window, then specify symptoms, then layer on confirmatory evidence, and finally sort remaining candidates into surveillance tiers.

questions.prompt: Match each case-definition tier to its evidentiary basis.

right.text: Lab test meeting the reference standard
Compatible symptoms with no confirmatory test yet
Clinical picture plus a supportive test or a link to a confirmed case

questions.explanation: The three tiers move from strongest to weakest evidence: lab-confirmed, then clinical-plus-support, then symptoms alone.

questions.prompt: Why do outbreak investigators often use a loose case definition early and a tight one later?

options.text: Loose definitions are required by law during the first 24 hours
A loose net supports hypothesis generation; a tight net protects the analytic phase from noise
Lab capacity is always unavailable until the outbreak ends
Tight definitions are always more sensitive than loose ones

explanations.a: There is no such legal requirement; the choice is methodological, not regulatory.
explanations.b: Correct: broad criteria maximize sensitivity for spotting patterns early, while narrow criteria maximize specificity so the analytic comparison is not diluted by look-alike illness.
explanations.c: Lab capacity often does become available mid-outbreak, which is exactly what allows the definition to tighten.
explanations.d: Tight definitions trade sensitivity for specificity, not the reverse.

lessons.label: Ratios, Proportions, and Rates

sections.heading: Three formal shapes, three different meanings
sections.body: Epidemiology leans on three measures that get casually swapped in everyday speech but are mathematically distinct. A ratio is a/b where a and b are separate, not-necessarily-related quantities — the numerator is not part of the denominator. The male-to-female ratio of a class of 12 boys and 18 girls is 12:18, or 0.67; it has no upper bound and no units of time. The odds ratio used throughout case-control epidemiology is built the same way — it compares exposure odds in cases to exposure odds in controls, two separate quantities, not a subset relationship. A proportion is a/(a+b): the numerator IS a subset of the denominator, so it is dimensionless and bounded between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%). The fraction of that class that is male, 12/30 = 40%, is a proportion. A true rate measures the occurrence of events per unit of person-time — it has explicit time units built into the denominator and, unlike a ratio or proportion, is not bounded above by 1.

sections.heading: Why 'rate' gets misused constantly
sections.body: News reports and even textbooks routinely say 'mortality rate' or 'attack rate' when they mean a proportion — deaths divided by a headcount, with no time dimension at all. An attack rate (cases divided by the population at risk during an outbreak) is technically a proportion, cumulative over the outbreak period, not a rate in the strict sense; it is grandfathered terminology from before the ratio/proportion/rate distinction was formalized. A genuine rate, like a true incidence rate, divides new cases by person-time at risk (e.g., cases per 1,000 person-years), which lets it exceed 1.0 when events recur or the time window is long, something a proportion structurally cannot do.

sections.heading: Converting and checking dimension
sections.body: The fastest way to tell which of the three you are looking at is to ask two questions: is the numerator contained within the denominator (proportion, not ratio), and does the denominator carry a time unit (rate, not proportion)? A prevalence figure like '8% of the class has asthma' is a proportion. A crude birth rate like '12 births per 1,000 population per year' is a rate — checking the units, 'per 1,000 population per year,' confirms the time dimension. Converting between them requires knowing exactly what was measured; you cannot turn a ratio into a rate without additional person-time data the ratio never captured. This trichotomy is treated as foundational vocabulary in standard epidemiologic methods texts precisely because downstream measures like relative risk and rate ratios inherit whichever structure their inputs have.

lessons.workedExample: A school health office reports three numbers from the same flu season: (1) among 50 sick students, the ratio of students who missed more than 3 days to those who missed 3 or fewer is 20:30, or 0.67 — a ratio, no shared denominator. (2) Of the school's 500 students, 50 got flu, giving a proportion (attack rate) of 50/500 = 10%, dimensionless. (3) Tracking the 500 students across the 20-week semester and summing each student's healthy weeks at risk gives 9,000 person-weeks; 50 cases over 9,000 person-weeks is a true incidence rate of about 5.6 cases per 1,000 person-weeks — the only one of the three with a time unit attached.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this distinction because a student who reports '30% infection rate' when they mean a proportion, or computes a 'rate' with no time denominator, is signaling they copied a formula without understanding what it measures. The tell of real understanding is a student who can name the denominator's units unprompted and explain why a rate, unlike a proportion, is not capped at 100%.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a true rate rather than a proportion?

options.text: 38 out of 200 students report having asthma
12 new cases of injury per 1,000 person-years of athlete exposure
The male-to-female ratio in a clinic's patient roster
An attack rate of 15% during a norovirus outbreak

explanations.a: This is a proportion: 38 is a subset of the 200, and there is no time dimension in the denominator.
explanations.b: Correct: person-years in the denominator gives this an explicit time unit, the hallmark of a true rate, and it is not capped at 100%.
explanations.c: A ratio compares two unrelated quantities (males, females) with no shared numerator/denominator relationship and no time unit.
explanations.d: Despite the name, an 'attack rate' is a cumulative proportion (cases/population at risk) with no time unit; it is grandfathered terminology.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for classifying a measure as ratio, proportion, or rate.

items.text: Check whether the numerator is a subset of the denominator
If yes, check whether the denominator carries an explicit time unit
If it carries a time unit, classify it as a true rate
If not a subset, classify it as a ratio; if a subset with no time unit, classify it as a proportion

questions.explanation: The subset test separates ratios from proportions/rates; the time-unit test then separates proportions from true rates.

questions.prompt: Match each measure to its correct classification.

left.text: 12 boys to 18 girls in a class

right.text: Ratio
Proportion
True rate

questions.explanation: The birth figure has a time unit (rate); the male fraction is a subset of the whole class (proportion); boys-to-girls compares two non-overlapping groups (ratio).

questions.prompt: Why can a true incidence rate exceed 1.0 while a proportion never can?

options.text: Rates are always reported as percentages, which have no upper limit
A proportion's numerator is capped by its own denominator; a rate's denominator is person-time, not a headcount, so events can outnumber people
Rates only apply to rare diseases, which inflates the number
There is no real difference; both are bounded at 1.0

explanations.a: Percentages are still bounded at 100%; that is not the reason rates can exceed 1.0.
explanations.b: Correct: a proportion's numerator cannot exceed its denominator by construction, but person-time denominators let cumulative or recurrent events surpass the number of people observed.
explanations.c: Disease rarity is unrelated to whether the measure is capped at 1.0; the structure of the denominator is what matters.
explanations.d: Proportions are bounded at 1.0 by definition; true rates are not, which is exactly the distinguishing feature.

lessons.label: Prevalence vs Incidence

sections.heading: A snapshot versus a flow
sections.body: Prevalence counts existing cases at a moment or over a defined span: point prevalence is the proportion of a population with disease at one instant (a single survey day), while period prevalence extends that window (all cases present at any point during a year, including ones that started before the window opened). Incidence, by contrast, counts only NEW cases arising in a population initially free of disease. Cumulative incidence — often called risk — is new cases divided by the number initially at risk over a fixed follow-up period, itself a proportion. Confusing the two is the single most common epidemiology error in student projects: a high prevalence does not mean disease is spreading fast; it may mean people survive a long time with it. Prevalence surveys, like the CDC's National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), are relatively cheap because they sample the population once; incidence studies require following an initially disease-free cohort over time, which is far more expensive and slower to yield results.

sections.heading: The steady-state relationship
sections.body: When a disease's incidence rate and average duration are both roughly constant over time (a 'steady state'), prevalence relates to them algebraically: Prevalence is approximately equal to Incidence rate multiplied by average Duration of disease (P ≈ I × D). This steady-state identity is a standard result in epidemiologic textbooks and explains why chronic, slow-killing diseases accumulate high prevalence from modest incidence, while rapidly fatal or rapidly cured diseases keep prevalence low even with substantial incidence.

sections.heading: Why treatment can push prevalence either way
sections.body: A cure shortens duration D, which by P ≈ I × D lowers prevalence even if incidence is unchanged — fewer people are walking around with the disease at any moment because they exit the pool quickly. A life-prolonging but non-curative treatment does the opposite: it extends D, so prevalence RISES even though the treatment is medically beneficial and incidence hasn't budged. This is exactly what happened with HIV after effective antiretroviral therapy arrived in the mid-1990s — U.S. HIV prevalence climbed for years afterward not because more people were being newly infected, but because fewer people with HIV were dying, so the existing pool grew. U.S. surveillance data through the 2000s and 2010s show people living with diagnosed HIV climbing even as annual new-infection estimates from the CDC held roughly flat or declined over the same stretch — the two curves diverging in exactly the direction P ≈ I × D predicts when duration lengthens.

lessons.workedExample: A city's diabetes program tracks two numbers for adults over five years: prevalence and cumulative incidence. On Year 1's survey day, 8,000 of 100,000 adults have diabetes (point prevalence 8%). Over the following year, 1,200 new cases arise among the 92,000 initially disease-free adults, giving a cumulative incidence (risk) of 1,200/92,000 ≈ 1.3%. If average duration of diabetes (time from diagnosis to death or remission) is roughly 20 years and incidence rate is steady at about 1.4 per 100 person-years, P ≈ I × D predicts prevalence near 0.014 × 20 = 28%, far above the 8% observed — signaling the disease is not yet at steady state, likely because incidence has been rising in recent years.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who hears a student claim 'our intervention is working, prevalence dropped' will ask whether incidence or duration changed, because the two have opposite implications: falling incidence means fewer new cases (good and specific to what changed), while falling duration could reflect more deaths, not more cures. Judges probe this to see if a student can decompose a prevalence trend into its two independent drivers rather than reading the number at face value.

questions.prompt: A new drug does not cure a chronic disease but keeps patients alive much longer than before. Assuming incidence stays constant, what happens to the disease's prevalence?

options.text: Prevalence falls, because the drug is beneficial
Prevalence rises, because average duration of disease increases
Prevalence is unaffected, since only incidence drives prevalence
Prevalence and incidence always move together

explanations.a: A beneficial drug is not the same as a curative one; here duration lengthens, which raises prevalence by P ≈ I × D even though outcomes improved.
explanations.b: Correct: extending duration D while incidence I stays fixed raises the product I × D, so more people are living with the disease at any given moment.
explanations.c: Prevalence depends on both incidence and duration, not incidence alone; duration changes alone can move prevalence.
explanations.d: They can move in opposite directions, as in this exact scenario where prevalence rises while incidence is flat.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for computing cumulative incidence (risk) correctly.

items.text: Identify the population initially free of disease at the start of follow-up
Follow that population for a fixed period
Count new cases arising during that period
Divide new cases by the initial disease-free population

questions.explanation: Cumulative incidence requires starting from a disease-free denominator, following it for a defined period, then dividing new cases by that starting count.

questions.prompt: Match each measure to its definition.

right.text: Proportion with disease at one instant in time
Proportion with disease at any time during a defined interval
Proportion of an initially disease-free population that develops new disease over a period

questions.explanation: Point prevalence is a single moment, period prevalence extends over an interval, and cumulative incidence tracks only new cases in a disease-free starting cohort.

questions.prompt: Using P ≈ I × D, why does a slow-killing chronic disease tend to show high prevalence even with modest incidence?

options.text: Because duration D is large, so the product I × D is large even when I is small
Because incidence is always high for chronic diseases
Because prevalence and incidence are the same quantity for chronic disease
Because chronic diseases are always underreported

explanations.a: Correct: long duration multiplies even a modest incidence rate into a large standing prevalence, since people accumulate in the prevalent pool.
explanations.b: Chronic diseases can have low incidence; it is the long duration, not high incidence, that drives up prevalence.
explanations.c: Prevalence and incidence are distinct measures; the relationship is multiplicative (P ≈ I × D), not an identity.
explanations.d: Underreporting is a measurement-quality issue unrelated to the mathematical relationship between prevalence, incidence, and duration.

lessons.label: Person-Time and Incidence Rates

sections.heading: Why person-time exists
sections.body: Cumulative incidence needs every subject followed for the same fixed period, but real cohorts rarely cooperate: people enroll at staggered times, drop out (loss to follow-up), move away, die of unrelated causes, or the study simply ends while they are still healthy (administrative censoring). Person-time solves this by crediting each subject only for the time they were actually observed and at risk. A subject followed for 3 years before being lost contributes 3 person-years, no more, no less; someone followed the full 10-year study contributes 10. Summing every subject's contribution gives total person-time, the denominator for incidence density (also called the incidence rate). This bookkeeping problem is exactly what actuarial life-table methods and the Kaplan-Meier estimator, published by Kaplan and Meier in 1958, were built to handle rigorously, treating censoring as a first-class feature of the data rather than a nuisance to be discarded.

sections.heading: Computing incidence density
sections.body: Incidence density = number of new cases ÷ total person-time at risk, typically expressed as cases per 1,000 or per 100,000 person-years. Once a subject develops the outcome, they stop contributing further at-risk time — a person who gets sick at year 4 of a 10-year study contributes 4 person-years, not 10, because after diagnosis they are no longer 'at risk' of a first case. This is why the denominator is called person-time AT RISK, not simply person-time observed; time after the event, or time someone spends immune or otherwise ineligible (for example, a vaccinated subject in a study of natural-infection risk), is excluded from the denominator entirely, not merely flagged.

sections.heading: The constant-hazard assumption, and when it fails
sections.body: Incidence density implicitly assumes the hazard (instantaneous risk of disease) is roughly constant across the follow-up period, so that 100 person-years from one person followed 100 years is interchangeable with 100 person-years from 100 people followed 1 year each. This assumption breaks when risk changes sharply with time-since-enrollment or calendar time — for example, surgical-site infection risk is heavily concentrated in the first 30 days post-operation, so pooling early and late person-time into one incidence density would understate early risk and overstate late risk. When the constant-hazard assumption fails, epidemiologists split follow-up into time bands and compute a separate incidence density for each — the same logic behind Cox's 1972 proportional-hazards regression, which allows the baseline hazard to vary freely over time while still estimating how covariates shift risk up or down.

lessons.workedExample: A five-person cohort is followed for a planned 5-year study of a chronic disease. Subject A enrolls at year 0 and completes all 5 years disease-free (5 person-years). Subject B develops disease at year 2 (2 person-years, then exits the at-risk pool). Subject C is lost to follow-up after year 3 (3 person-years). Subject D enrolls late, at year 1, and completes the study (4 person-years). Subject E dies of an unrelated cause at year 4 (4 person-years, censored). Total person-time = 5+2+3+4+4 = 18 person-years, with 1 case (Subject B). Incidence density = 1/18 ≈ 0.056 cases per person-year, or about 56 cases per 1,000 person-years.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge checks whether a student summed person-time correctly rather than just dividing cases by headcount, because ignoring staggered entry and censoring silently inflates or deflates the denominator. A student who explains why Subject B stops contributing time after diagnosis, or why loss to follow-up truncates rather than deletes a subject's contribution, is demonstrating they understand incidence density is a rate over exposure time, not a simple proportion.

questions.prompt: In a cohort study, a subject is diagnosed with the outcome disease at year 3 of a planned 8-year follow-up. How many person-years should that subject contribute to the incidence density denominator?

options.text: 8, the full planned follow-up
3, up to the point of diagnosis
0, since they eventually became a case
5, the remaining years after diagnosis

explanations.a: The subject is no longer at risk of a first case after diagnosis, so time beyond year 3 should not be counted toward at-risk person-time.
explanations.b: Correct: person-time at risk stops accumulating once the subject develops the outcome, so they contribute exactly 3 person-years.
explanations.c: Becoming a case does not erase the person-time they contributed while still at risk before diagnosis.
explanations.d: The years after diagnosis are not at-risk time for a first case and should be excluded, not counted as the contribution.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for computing an incidence density for a cohort with staggered entry and censoring.

items.text: Record each subject's entry time into the study
Record each subject's exit time (diagnosis, loss to follow-up, death, or study end)
Sum (exit time − entry time) across all subjects to get total person-time
Divide total new cases by total person-time

questions.explanation: Each subject's at-risk contribution is their individual exit minus entry time; these are summed before dividing case count by the pooled denominator.

questions.prompt: Match each cohort event to how it affects a subject's person-time contribution.

left.text: Subject develops the outcome at year 2 of 6
Subject is lost to follow-up at year 4 of 6

right.text: Contributes 6 full person-years
Contributes 2 person-years, then stops (no longer at risk of a first case)
Contributes 4 person-years, then is censored (true outcome unknown after)

questions.explanation: Diagnosis and loss to follow-up both truncate person-time contribution, but for different reasons: one because risk of a first case ends, the other because observation ends while risk status is unknown.

questions.prompt: Why might pooling all person-time into a single incidence density mislead for a disease like surgical-site infection, where risk is concentrated in the first 30 days after surgery?

options.text: Because person-time cannot be summed across subjects with different follow-up lengths
Because the constant-hazard assumption fails when risk is concentrated early, understating early risk and overstating late risk if pooled
Because incidence density can only be computed for chronic diseases
Because surgical patients cannot be censored

explanations.a: Person-time summation across subjects with different follow-up lengths is exactly how incidence density is meant to be computed; that is not the issue here.
explanations.b: Correct: a single pooled rate assumes hazard is roughly constant over time, which is violated when risk clusters early, so time-banded incidence densities are needed instead.
explanations.c: Incidence density applies to both acute and chronic outcomes; the concern here is about hazard shape over time, not disease chronicity.
explanations.d: Surgical patients can be censored like any other cohort subject (e.g., lost to follow-up, study end); that is unrelated to the constant-hazard problem.

lessons.label: Measures of Mortality and Morbidity

sections.heading: Mortality measures and their denominators
sections.body: The crude mortality rate is total deaths from all causes divided by the total mid-year population, usually expressed per 1,000 or per 100,000 per year — it answers 'how deadly is life here overall' but says nothing about cause. The cause-specific mortality rate narrows the numerator to deaths from one cause (e.g., deaths from heart disease) while keeping the whole population as the denominator. The case-fatality ratio (CFR) is entirely different: it divides deaths from a disease by the number of people WHO HAD that disease (not the whole population), giving the probability that a diagnosed case proves fatal — The World Health Organization has reported CFRs ranging from roughly 25% to 90% across historical Ebola outbreaks depending on strain and access to supportive care, versus a crude mortality rate that stays low in any affected country because Ebola remains rare relative to the whole population.

sections.heading: Proportionate mortality and infant mortality
sections.body: Proportionate mortality is the share of all deaths attributable to a given cause — deaths from cancer divided by ALL deaths, not by the living population — so it can rise even if cancer deaths are flat, simply because other causes of death (like infectious disease) fall. This is why proportionate mortality is easily misread as a trend in cancer risk when it may only reflect success against other causes. Infant mortality rate (IMR) is deaths of infants under age 1 per 1,000 live births in a year — a standard denominator of live births, not total population — and is widely used as a marker of a population's overall health system quality because it is sensitive to prenatal care, nutrition, and sanitation — the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics has tracked U.S. IMR falling from roughly 26 per 1,000 live births in 1960 to under 6 per 1,000 in recent years, a decline widely credited to advances in neonatal intensive care and prenatal screening.

sections.heading: Years of potential life lost, and morbidity versus mortality
sections.body: Years of potential life lost (YPLL) weights each death by how early it occurred relative to a reference age (commonly 75), so a death at 20 contributes 55 YPLL while a death at 74 contributes only 1 — making YPLL sensitive to causes that strike young, like injury or overdose, even when they cause fewer total deaths than diseases of old age. All of these are mortality measures (deaths); morbidity measures disease burden among the living — incidence and prevalence are the core examples — and the two can diverge sharply, as with arthritis, which drives enormous morbidity (pain, disability, health-care use) but contributes almost nothing to mortality statistics. Disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) are not a pure morbidity measure: a DALY is defined as years of life lost to premature death (YLL, a mortality-derived component, related to this lesson's YPLL) plus years lived with disability (YLD, the morbidity component) — so DALYs deliberately fuse both sides of the mortality/morbidity split rather than capturing burden among the living alone.

lessons.workedExample: A country of 10 million records 90,000 total deaths in a year (crude mortality rate 900/100,000 ≈ 0.9%). Of those, 2,000 deaths were from disease X, which had 8,000 diagnosed cases that year — CFR = 2,000/8,000 = 25%, while disease X's cause-specific mortality rate is only 2,000/10,000,000 = 20/100,000, because the disease itself is rare even though it kills a quarter of those who get it. Proportionate mortality from disease X is 2,000/90,000 ≈ 2.2% of all deaths. If the average age at death from X is 30 (versus a 75-year reference), each such death contributes 45 YPLL, so 2,000 deaths contribute 90,000 YPLL — disproportionate to X's 2.2% share of total deaths.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this cluster of measures because each answers a genuinely different question, and picking the wrong one changes the story: CFR tells you how dangerous a disease is once you have it, cause-specific mortality tells you its population-level toll, and YPLL tells you how much of a young-versus-old problem it is. A student who reports a low crude mortality rate as evidence a disease is 'not serious' when its CFR is high is conflating rarity with severity, exactly the confusion judges are trained to catch.

questions.prompt: A disease has a very high case-fatality ratio (60%) but a low cause-specific mortality rate in the general population. What does this combination indicate?

options.text: The disease is not dangerous to those who contract it
The disease is deadly once contracted, but relatively rare in the population
The measures are contradictory and one must be miscalculated
The disease disproportionately affects infants

explanations.a: A 60% CFR means the disease is highly lethal to those who get it; that is the opposite of 'not dangerous.'
explanations.b: Correct: CFR (deaths among cases) can be high while cause-specific mortality (deaths in the whole population) stays low if few people actually contract the disease.
explanations.c: The two measures use different denominators (cases vs. whole population) by design, so they can validly diverge; this is not a contradiction.
explanations.d: Nothing in CFR or cause-specific mortality specifies an age group; that inference is not supported by these two measures alone.

questions.prompt: For one specific year in a region: a disease had 500 diagnosed cases, the region recorded 5,000 live births, 8,000 total deaths from all causes, and a total population of 2,000,000. Order these four mortality-measure denominators from narrowest (smallest count) to broadest (largest count) for this example.

items.text: Case-fatality ratio (denominator: 500 diagnosed cases)
Infant mortality rate (denominator: 5,000 live births)
Cause-specific mortality rate (denominator: 2,000,000 total population)
Proportionate mortality (denominator: 8,000 total deaths)

questions.explanation: Plugging in this year's counts: 500 diagnosed cases is the smallest denominator, then 5,000 live births, then 8,000 total deaths, then the 2,000,000 total population is the largest. This specific ranking of cases, live births, and total deaths is not a fixed epidemiological rule — which of the three is smallest varies by disease and population. Only 'total population is the broadest of the four' holds by definition, since diagnosed cases, live births, and total deaths are each a subset of the total population.

questions.prompt: Match each measure to its denominator.

right.text: Total mid-year population
Diagnosed cases of the disease
Live births in the year
Total deaths from all causes

questions.explanation: Each mortality measure is defined by a distinct denominator, and mixing them up is the most common error in interpreting mortality statistics.

questions.prompt: Why does years of potential life lost (YPLL) rank a cause of death like overdose or injury higher relative to total deaths than a measure like crude mortality would?

options.text: YPLL only counts deaths in people under 18
YPLL weights each death by years short of a reference age, so deaths concentrated in younger people contribute disproportionately more
YPLL and crude mortality are mathematically identical measures
YPLL excludes injury deaths from its calculation entirely

explanations.a: YPLL counts deaths at any age below the reference age (commonly 75), not only those under 18.
explanations.b: Correct: a death at age 20 contributes far more YPLL than a death at 74, so causes that kill younger people show up as larger burdens under YPLL even with fewer total deaths.
explanations.c: Crude mortality counts every death equally regardless of age; YPLL explicitly weights by age at death, so the two measures are structurally different.
explanations.d: Injury deaths are exactly the kind of cause YPLL is designed to highlight, since they often occur at younger ages; they are not excluded.

lessons.label: Comparing Populations: Standardized Rates

sections.heading: Why crude rates mislead across populations
sections.body: A crude mortality rate is a weighted average of age-specific rates, weighted by how many people sit in each age group. Because disease and death risk climb steeply with age for most conditions, a population with more older residents will show a higher crude rate than a younger population even if the older population is, age-for-age, actually healthier. This is Florida-versus-Alaska logic: Florida's large retiree population gives it a higher crude death rate than Alaska's much younger population, even in years when Alaska has higher age-specific mortality at every single age band. Comparing crude rates across differently-aged populations compares apples partly made of demographics, not just health. This confounding-by-age problem is why national vital-statistics agencies, including the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics, publish both crude and age-adjusted rates side by side for mortality trends, since the crude U.S. death rate has risen in recent decades partly because the population itself has aged, not solely because underlying risk has worsened.

sections.heading: Direct standardization
sections.body: Direct standardization removes the age-mix distortion by applying each population's own age-specific rates to one shared 'standard' population (commonly the year-2000 U.S. standard population used by the CDC). For each age band, multiply that band's rate from the population being studied by the standard population's count in that band, sum across bands, and divide by the total standard population — producing an age-adjusted rate that answers 'what would this population's rate be if it had the standard age structure.' Because both populations being compared are forced onto the same age structure, differences in the adjusted rate reflect true differences in age-specific risk, not demographic composition.

sections.heading: Indirect standardization and the SMR
sections.body: Indirect standardization is used when a population's own age-specific rates are unstable or unknown (small sample) but a reliable standard population's age-specific rates ARE known. It applies the standard's age-specific rates to the STUDY population's age structure to get an 'expected' number of deaths, then compares that to the OBSERVED number of deaths via the standardized mortality ratio, SMR = observed/expected. An SMR above 1.0 means the study population had more deaths than expected given its age structure and the standard rates; occupational cohort studies (comparing factory workers to the general population) rely heavily on SMR because worker cohorts are often too small for stable direct age-specific rates — this is the same logic behind the 'healthy worker effect,' where employed cohorts show SMRs below 1.0 relative to the general population simply because people healthy enough to hold a job are, on average, healthier than the general population that includes the disabled and chronically ill.

lessons.workedExample: Town A (older population) has a crude death rate of 14 per 1,000; Town B (younger) has 8 per 1,000 — Town A looks worse. But age-specific rates show Town B actually has higher risk at every age band (e.g., 60-69: Town A 20/1,000, Town B 25/1,000; 70-79: Town A 45/1,000, Town B 55/1,000). Restricting to just these two older bands for illustration (a full standardization would use weights across every age band summing to 100% of the standard population), applying both towns' age-specific rates to a shared standard population age structure of 40% aged 60-69 and 20% aged 70-79 gives Town A a partial weighted rate of about 17/1,000 and Town B about 21/1,000 from those two bands alone — the comparison reverses: even on this partial two-band slice, Town B already comes out higher-risk than Town A, exactly opposite the crude-rate impression, and a complete adjustment across all bands would only sharpen that reversal.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees two crude rates compared across groups with visibly different age structures — comparing a retirement community's disease rate to a college town's, say — will ask whether the student age-adjusted before concluding one group is riskier. The tell of understanding is recognizing that a reversed conclusion after standardization (as in the worked example) is not a contradiction but the entire point of the method: the crude comparison was confounded by age all along.

questions.prompt: Two towns are compared on crude mortality rate. Town A's rate is higher, but Town A also has an older population. What should a careful analyst do before concluding Town A is riskier?

options.text: Accept the crude comparison, since crude rates reflect real mortality
Age-standardize both towns' rates to a common standard population before comparing
Simply exclude everyone over 65 from both populations
Report only Town A's rate, since it is factually higher

explanations.a: Crude rates are real, but they mix age structure with underlying risk, which can mislead when comparing differently-aged populations.
explanations.b: Correct: applying a shared standard population's weights removes the age-mix distortion, isolating true differences in age-specific risk.
explanations.c: Excluding an entire age group discards data and does not correctly adjust for age differences across the remaining structure; standardization uses all age bands.
explanations.d: Reporting the crude rate alone omits the confounding effect of age structure, which is precisely what a careful comparison must address.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of direct standardization.

items.text: Obtain age-specific rates for the population being studied
Choose a standard population with a known age distribution
Apply the study population's age-specific rates to the standard population's counts in each age band
Sum expected events across bands and divide by the total standard population to get the adjusted rate

questions.explanation: Direct standardization keeps the study population's own rates but substitutes in a shared age structure, then recomputes the overall rate under that shared structure.

questions.prompt: Match each standardization concept to its description.

right.text: Applies the study population's own age-specific rates to a standard population's age structure
Applies a standard population's age-specific rates to the study population's age structure to get expected events
Observed events divided by expected events

questions.explanation: Direct and indirect standardization swap which population supplies the rates versus the age-structure weights; SMR is the summary ratio indirect standardization produces.

questions.prompt: Why do occupational cohort studies (e.g., comparing factory workers to the general population) typically use indirect standardization (SMR) rather than direct standardization?

options.text: Because SMR does not require any age data at all
Because worker cohorts are often too small to yield stable age-specific rates of their own, so the standard population's rates are borrowed instead
Because direct standardization is illegal to use in occupational studies
Because SMR always gives a lower estimate than direct standardization

explanations.a: SMR still requires age data — the study population's age structure is needed to compute the expected count.
explanations.b: Correct: when the study cohort is small, its own age-specific rates are unstable, so indirect standardization borrows the standard population's more reliable age-specific rates instead.
explanations.c: There is no such legal restriction; the choice between direct and indirect standardization is a methodological one based on data availability.
explanations.d: SMR is not systematically biased lower than direct standardization; which is higher depends entirely on the data, not the method itself.

lessons.label: The Design Landscape

sections.heading: Two axes, four families
sections.body: Every epidemiologic study can be placed on two axes. The first is descriptive versus analytic: descriptive studies (case reports, case series, cross-sectional surveys) describe who, what, when, and where without a comparison group built to test a hypothesis, while analytic studies (cohort, case-control, randomized controlled trial) compare groups to estimate the effect of an exposure on an outcome. The second axis is experimental versus observational: in an experimental design the investigator assigns exposure — as in a randomized controlled trial (RCT), where a coin flip (or a random-number table) decides who gets the drug and who gets placebo — while in an observational design nature, circumstance, or personal choice assigns exposure, and the investigator only measures what already happened. Cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional studies are all observational; only the RCT is experimental outside of rare field trials.

sections.heading: Time direction is the organizing axis
sections.body: Beneath both axes sits a question that predicts what a design can actually measure: which way does time run relative to the data collection? A cohort study starts with exposure status and moves forward to outcome, so it can measure incidence — new cases arising over a defined period — and can establish that exposure preceded disease, the minimum bar for causal inference. A case-control study starts with outcome (cases who have the disease, controls who do not) and looks backward at prior exposure, trading the ability to compute incidence for speed and efficiency in rare diseases. A cross-sectional study collapses time entirely, measuring exposure and outcome at a single instant, which is why it yields prevalence rather than incidence and cannot, by itself, establish which came first. The RCT is a special forward-moving design where randomization additionally severs the link between exposure and any confounder, observed or not — the one design tool that controls for confounding by design rather than by statistical adjustment.

sections.heading: Why the taxonomy matters before the numbers
sections.body: Textbooks often present relative risk, odds ratio, and prevalence ratio as interchangeable, but each is manufacturable only from the design that fits its time direction: relative risk needs incidence, which needs a cohort or trial; odds ratio is what a case-control study can honestly estimate; prevalence ratio comes from a cross-sectional snapshot. Picking the wrong statistic for a design — computing a 'relative risk' from case-control data without a rare-disease justification, for instance — is a recurring, gradeable error, which is why the taxonomy is worth memorizing before any single design is studied in depth.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher wants to know whether night-shift work causes hypertension. Design A enrolls 2,000 night-shift and 2,000 day-shift nurses free of hypertension in 2015 and tracks new diagnoses through 2025 — a prospective cohort, yielding incidence and relative risk. Design B identifies 500 nurses newly diagnosed with hypertension in 2025 and 500 disease-free nurses, then asks both groups about past shift history — a case-control study, yielding an odds ratio. Design C surveys 3,000 currently employed nurses in one week in 2025 for both shift status and hypertension status simultaneously — a cross-sectional study, yielding prevalence, and unable to rule out that hypertension caused someone to leave night shifts rather than the reverse.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'what design did you use and why' before looking at any number, because the taxonomy predicts and constrains every statistic that follows. A student who answers 'cohort' but then reports an odds ratio, or calls a same-day survey a 'study of causation,' reveals they picked a label without understanding what the time direction of their data collection actually permits them to claim.

questions.prompt: What is the defining feature that makes an RCT 'experimental' rather than 'observational'?

options.text: It uses a larger sample size than observational studies
The investigator assigns exposure rather than measuring exposure that already occurred
It always yields a lower p-value
It is conducted in a laboratory rather than a population

explanations.a: Sample size varies independently of design type and does not define the experimental/observational distinction.
explanations.b: Correct: experimental designs have the investigator control who receives the exposure; observational designs only measure exposure assignment made by nature or choice.
explanations.c: Statistical significance depends on sample size and effect size, not on design category.
explanations.d: Many RCTs (including field trials) are conducted in real populations, not laboratories; the assignment mechanism, not the setting, defines 'experimental.'

questions.prompt: Order these designs by time direction, from data collected entirely in the present, to data that moves forward from exposure, to data that starts at outcome and looks backward.

items.text: Cross-sectional study (exposure and outcome measured simultaneously)
Cohort study (exposure measured first, outcome followed forward)
Case-control study (outcome identified first, exposure history collected backward)

questions.explanation: Cross-sectional collapses time into one instant; cohort moves forward from exposure to outcome; case-control moves backward from outcome to exposure — three distinct time directions, not a strict chronological sequence, but each is defined by which variable is known first relative to data collection.

questions.prompt: Match each study design to the statistic it can validly produce.

right.text: Odds ratio
Relative risk (from incidence)
Prevalence ratio

questions.explanation: Relative risk requires incidence data only a forward-moving cohort can supply; case-control data structurally yields an odds ratio; cross-sectional snapshots yield prevalence, hence prevalence ratios.

lessons.label: Cohort Studies

sections.heading: Following exposed and unexposed forward
sections.body: A cohort study identifies a group free of the outcome at baseline, splits it by exposure status, and follows both groups forward in time to count who develops the outcome. Because the design tracks a defined population through calendar time, it can compute incidence directly — the rate of new cases per person-time at risk — and from incidence in the exposed versus unexposed groups, relative risk (RR = incidence in exposed / incidence in unexposed) falls out naturally. This is the one thing case-control and cross-sectional designs cannot honestly do: a cohort's forward time direction means exposure is always documented before outcome, satisfying temporality, the first and least negotiable of the Bradford Hill criteria for causation.

sections.heading: Prospective versus retrospective (historical) cohorts
sections.body: A prospective cohort enrolls people now and follows them into the future — the investigator waits for outcomes to accrue. A retrospective (historical) cohort instead uses records that already span the follow-up period: the investigator picks a past starting point (say, employment records from 1980), classifies exposure using those old records, and uses existing outcome data (death certificates, disease registries) up to the present. Both are still cohort studies by structure — exposure precedes outcome in calendar time — the only difference is whether the investigator is watching time pass or reconstructing it from archives after the fact, which trades years of waiting for reliance on the completeness of old records.

sections.heading: Strengths, costs, and the Framingham model
sections.body: Cohort studies can track multiple outcomes from a single exposure (useful when a substance is suspected of causing several diseases) and are the design of choice for rare exposures, since investigators can deliberately enroll enough exposed people. Their price is high cost and long duration, and their central threat to validity is loss to follow-up: if participants who drop out differ systematically from those who stay (sicker, or healthier, or simply harder to reach), the remaining sample no longer represents the original cohort. As a working threshold, investigators start to worry once loss to follow-up differs by 20% or more between the exposed and unexposed arms — a gap that size is large enough to manufacture or erase an apparent association on its own, with no true causal effect involved. The Framingham Heart Study, launched in Framingham, Massachusetts in 1948 with roughly 5,200 adult residents, is the archetype: it prospectively followed participants across decades and is where the term 'risk factor' for cardiovascular disease was effectively established, linking hypertension, cholesterol, and smoking to heart disease through sustained, repeated follow-up exams rather than a single measurement.

lessons.workedExample: Framingham enrolled about 5,200 adults aged 30-62 in 1948, none with cardiovascular disease at baseline, and re-examined the cohort roughly every two years. By tracking who among the untreated-hypertension group versus the normotensive group developed coronary heart disease over subsequent follow-up, investigators computed incidence in each group directly and derived relative risk — establishing hypertension as a cardiovascular risk factor decades before a randomized trial could ethically test withholding treatment. A retrospective version of the same logic: a 1990s study using 1960s factory employment and exposure records, matched to a mortality registry through the 2000s, could similarly compute incidence without waiting 40 years in real time.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe cohort projects on loss to follow-up specifically, because a 20% or more differential dropout between exposed and unexposed arms can manufacture or erase an association without any true causal signal — the student who reports a clean relative risk but cannot say what fraction of each arm was lost, and whether losses were balanced, has not actually protected the study's validity.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a retrospective (historical) cohort from a prospective cohort?

options.text: Retrospective cohorts cannot compute relative risk
Retrospective cohorts use existing past records to reconstruct exposure and outcome instead of enrolling and waiting in real time
Retrospective cohorts start from outcome and look backward at exposure, like a case-control study
Retrospective cohorts only work for rare exposures

explanations.a: Both prospective and retrospective cohorts follow exposure forward to outcome in calendar time, so both can compute incidence and relative risk.
explanations.b: Correct: the structure is identical to a prospective cohort — exposure still precedes outcome in time — but the investigator uses archival records already spanning that period instead of watching it unfold.
explanations.c: That backward structure describes a case-control study; a retrospective cohort still moves from exposure to outcome, just using historical rather than newly collected data.
explanations.d: Rare-exposure suitability applies to cohort studies generally (both prospective and retrospective), not specifically to the retrospective variant.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of running a prospective cohort study.

items.text: Enroll a population free of the outcome and classify baseline exposure status
Follow exposed and unexposed groups forward through calendar time
Record new outcome cases as they arise in each group
Compute incidence in each group and derive relative risk

questions.explanation: The cohort's defining logic is baseline exposure classification first, forward follow-up second, outcome accrual third, and the incidence-based relative risk calculation only possible once follow-up data exists.

questions.prompt: Match each cohort study feature to its description.

right.text: 1948 prospective cohort of ~5,200 adults that established cardiovascular risk factors
Threat to validity when dropouts differ systematically between exposure groups
Incidence in exposed divided by incidence in unexposed

questions.explanation: Loss to follow-up is a bias mechanism, Framingham is the historical exemplar cohort, and relative risk is the incidence-ratio statistic cohorts uniquely enable.

lessons.label: Case-Control Studies

sections.heading: Starting from outcome, looking backward
sections.body: A case-control study inverts the cohort's time direction: it starts by identifying cases (people who already have the disease) and controls (comparable people who do not), then looks backward to compare each group's history of exposure. Because the population is selected on outcome rather than followed until outcome occurs, the study cannot compute incidence — there is no defined population followed over person-time — so it cannot yield a true relative risk. What it can compute is an odds ratio: the odds of exposure among cases divided by the odds of exposure among controls, which approximates relative risk only when the disease is rare in the source population (the rare-disease assumption).

sections.heading: Why case-control is chosen: efficiency for rare and slow disease
sections.body: The design's advantage is efficiency. A cohort study of a disease with an incidence of 1 in 10,000 per year would need an enormous sample and years of follow-up to accumulate enough cases to say anything; a case-control study instead deliberately recruits cases who already exist (from a cancer registry, a hospital ward), so the rarer the disease, the more this design's efficiency advantage grows. The same logic applies to diseases with long latency between exposure and diagnosis — decades for many cancers — where a cohort would require waiting out that entire latency period, while a case-control study can be completed in a year or two by interviewing people already diagnosed.

sections.heading: Control selection is the central difficulty
sections.body: The odds ratio is only valid if controls represent the exposure distribution of the same source population that produced the cases — get this wrong and the whole study is biased regardless of sample size. Population controls (randomly sampled from the general population that gave rise to the cases) are the theoretical ideal but are hard and expensive to recruit. Hospital controls (patients admitted for other conditions) are convenient and tend to respond and recall similarly to cases, but risk being systematically unrepresentative if their admitting diagnosis is itself related to the exposure under study (Berkson's bias). Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill's 1950 study is the field's canonical exemplar: they interviewed lung cancer patients across London hospitals and compared their smoking histories to hospital control patients admitted for other diseases, finding heavy smokers dramatically overrepresented among the lung cancer cases — a result robust enough, and later replicated across other case-control and cohort designs, to become foundational evidence in the smoking-cancer causal case.

lessons.workedExample: Doll and Hill (1950) enrolled patients newly diagnosed with lung cancer at London hospitals as cases, and, for each case, a control patient of the same sex and similar age admitted to the same hospital for a non-cancer condition. Interviewers (who did not know which patients were cases) asked both groups about smoking history. Almost all lung cancer patients turned out to be smokers, and heavy smokers were markedly overrepresented among cases compared to hospital controls, producing a large odds ratio for lung cancer among smokers versus non-smokers. Because lung cancer was rare in the underlying population, that odds ratio was a reasonable stand-in for relative risk — but it took later cohort confirmation (including Doll and Hill's own subsequent prospective study of British doctors) to nail down the incidence-based risk directly.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe case-control projects on control selection before anything else, because a mis-selected control group (say, hospital controls whose admitting diagnosis shares a cause with the exposure) can generate a spurious odds ratio in either direction that no amount of statistical adjustment fixes; a student who can explain why their controls represent the same source population as their cases, and who correctly labels their result an odds ratio rather than a relative risk, has understood the design's core vulnerability.

questions.prompt: Why can a case-control study not directly compute relative risk?

options.text: Because it uses hospital records instead of interviews
Because cases and controls are selected based on outcome status, not followed as a defined population over time, so there is no incidence to compute
Because it only studies rare diseases
Because odds ratios are always larger than relative risks

explanations.a: The data source (records vs. interviews) does not determine whether incidence can be computed; the sampling structure does.
explanations.b: Correct: without a population followed forward over person-time, there is no incidence denominator, so relative risk cannot be directly calculated — only the odds ratio can.
explanations.c: Case-control studies are well suited to rare diseases but are not restricted to them; the incidence limitation applies regardless of disease frequency.
explanations.d: The odds ratio approximates but is not systematically larger than relative risk; the relationship depends on the rare-disease assumption, not a fixed inequality.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a case-control study as Doll and Hill (1950) conducted it.

items.text: Identify lung cancer patients (cases) newly diagnosed at hospitals
Select hospital patients with other diagnoses as controls
Interview both groups about past smoking history
Compare the odds of smoking exposure between cases and controls

questions.explanation: Case-control logic requires defining cases and controls first, then collecting exposure history backward, then comparing exposure odds between the two groups.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in case-control design.

right.text: Condition under which the odds ratio approximates relative risk
Convenient control source that risks bias if admitting diagnosis relates to the exposure
The statistic case-control data structurally yields

questions.explanation: The odds ratio is the native case-control statistic; hospital controls are a practical but bias-prone source; the rare-disease assumption is what licenses reading that odds ratio as an approximate relative risk.

lessons.label: Cross-Sectional Studies

sections.heading: A snapshot, not a film
sections.body: A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome in the same group of people at the same point in time — a single interview, exam, or survey wave captures both variables simultaneously, with no follow-up period and no look backward at history beyond what a single questionnaire can ask. This makes it the fastest and cheapest analytic-adjacent design: no years of follow-up, no need to trace old records, just one coordinated data-collection effort across a sample. The statistic it produces is prevalence — the proportion of the sampled population who currently have the outcome (or exposure) at that instant — and, when two groups are compared, a prevalence ratio (or prevalence odds ratio) rather than a relative risk or incidence-based measure.

sections.heading: The temporal-ambiguity problem
sections.body: Because exposure and outcome are captured at the same moment, a cross-sectional study structurally cannot establish which came first. If a survey finds that people with depression report less physical activity, it cannot distinguish 'inactivity contributes to depression' from 'depression causes inactivity' from a third variable driving both — the data are compatible with all three stories and the design has no tool to adjudicate between them. This is the design's core limitation and the reason cross-sectional findings are routinely described as 'associations' rather than causal claims, no matter how strong the statistical relationship measured.

sections.heading: Surveys and hypothesis generation
sections.body: Despite the temporal limit, cross-sectional design is the workhorse of public health surveillance because prevalence — not incidence — is exactly what health systems need to plan capacity, and because a single well-designed sampling wave can measure dozens of exposures and outcomes at once, cheaply. The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), run continuously by the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics since 1999 (with earlier discrete cycles dating to the 1960s-70s), combines interviews, physical exams, and lab tests on a nationally representative sample to track prevalence of obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and nutrient status across the U.S. population over time. NHANES cycles show that concretely: age-adjusted obesity prevalence among U.S. adults climbed from about 30.5% in the 1999-2000 cycle to about 41.9% in the 2017-March 2020 cycle, a trend visible only because each wave repeats the same simultaneous-measurement snapshot on a fresh representative sample. Its cross-sectional waves cannot prove that a given diet pattern causes a given condition, but they are exactly the kind of broad, cheap scan that generates hypotheses a cohort or trial can later test with proper time direction.

lessons.workedExample: An NHANES cycle samples about 5,000 U.S. residents per year, measuring blood pressure and self-reported sodium intake in the same clinic visit. Suppose 32% of high-sodium-intake respondents have hypertension versus 18% of low-sodium respondents — a prevalence ratio of about 1.8. This is a legitimate, useful finding for public health surveillance, but it cannot say whether high sodium intake caused the hypertension, whether people already diagnosed with hypertension changed their diet in response to medical advice (reverse causation), or whether an unmeasured factor like age or kidney function drives both. A follow-up cohort study, tracking sodium intake in currently normotensive people forward to new hypertension diagnoses, would be needed to resolve the direction.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes cross-sectional projects specifically on causal language, because the single biggest scoring error in this design is a student's discussion section quietly upgrading 'associated with' into 'leads to' or 'causes' — the design cannot support that upgrade, and a judge who asks 'how do you know the exposure came first' is testing whether the student recognizes their own design's temporal-ambiguity ceiling.

questions.prompt: Why can a cross-sectional study not resolve whether an exposure preceded an outcome?

options.text: Because the sample size is always too small
Because exposure and outcome are measured at the same single point in time, so their temporal order is unknown
Because it uses self-report instead of medical records
Because it only measures prevalence, which is always inaccurate

explanations.a: Sample size affects precision, not the ability to establish temporal order between exposure and outcome.
explanations.b: Correct: with a single simultaneous measurement, there is no data point establishing which variable existed first, which is the design's structural limitation regardless of sample size or precision.
explanations.c: Self-report versus records is a data-quality issue distinct from the temporal-ambiguity problem, which persists even with perfectly accurate simultaneous measurement.
explanations.d: Prevalence is not inherently inaccurate; it is simply a different quantity from incidence, and the temporal problem exists independent of measurement accuracy.

questions.prompt: Order these steps as they occur in a single NHANES-style cross-sectional survey wave.

items.text: Recruit a representative sample of the population
Measure exposure (e.g., sodium intake) and outcome (e.g., hypertension) in the same visit
Compute prevalence of the outcome overall and within exposure groups
Report a prevalence ratio as an association, not a causal claim

questions.explanation: A cross-sectional wave recruits its sample, takes simultaneous measurements, computes prevalence, and reports the resulting ratio with appropriately cautious causal language.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its cross-sectional role.

right.text: Continuous CDC survey combining interviews, exams, and labs since 1999
Proportion of a sampled population with a condition at one point in time
Inability to determine whether exposure or outcome came first

questions.explanation: Prevalence is the cross-sectional design's native output, NHANES is its major real-world example, and temporal ambiguity is its defining limitation.

lessons.label: Ecological Studies and the Ecological Fallacy

sections.heading: The group, not the person, is the unit of analysis
sections.body: Every design covered so far measures exposure and outcome in individuals. An ecological study instead measures both at the level of a group — a country, a state, a hospital, a birth cohort — using aggregate statistics like per-capita consumption, national disease rates, or regional average income. A researcher might correlate national per-capita fat intake with national breast cancer mortality rates across dozens of countries, or state-level vaccination coverage with state-level outbreak size. No individual is ever linked to their own exposure and outcome; the entire analysis runs on population summaries.

sections.heading: Why it's cheap and where it's used first
sections.body: Ecological studies are attractive because they are often free to run: national health statistics, census figures, and vital registration data already exist for most countries, so a researcher can build a dataset from published tables without recruiting a single new participant or measuring anyone directly. This makes ecological analysis a common first pass — a cheap way to spot a pattern worth investigating with an individual-level design — and it remains the only feasible approach for some exposures, like ambient air pollution or national policy changes, that are inherently defined at the population level rather than the person level.

sections.heading: The ecological fallacy and its mirror, the atomistic fallacy
sections.body: The ecological fallacy is the error of assuming a relationship observed at the group level must hold for individuals within those groups. The classic demonstration is sociologist Robinson's 1950 analysis of U.S. census data: across states, the correlation between percentage foreign-born and literacy rate was positive and fairly strong (ecological r ≈ +0.53) — states with more foreign-born residents had higher average literacy — yet at the individual level the same relationship was weak and negative (r ≈ -0.11): foreign-born residents were actually slightly less literate than native-born residents. The state-level pattern reversed, and reversed by a wide margin, because foreign-born immigrants settled disproportionately in states that were already more literate overall, a confound invisible at the aggregate level. The mirror-image error, the atomistic (or individualistic) fallacy, runs the other way: assuming a relationship established from individual-level data must also describe how groups or populations behave, ignoring that group-level dynamics (social context, policy, herd effects) can differ from the sum of individual behaviors.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a researcher plots per-capita chocolate consumption against national Nobel laureate counts for 20 countries and finds a strong positive correlation — a real, published pattern. The ecological fallacy would be concluding that eating more chocolate raises an individual person's odds of winning a Nobel Prize; the true driver is very likely national wealth, which independently predicts both chocolate consumption and research funding. Applied to health: a country-level correlation between dietary fat and breast cancer mortality might reflect fat intake's genuine individual-level effect, or might reflect that wealthier countries have both higher fat consumption and better cancer detection and reporting — the aggregate correlation alone cannot distinguish the two without individual-level data.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe ecological-design projects hardest on this single question: 'does your group-level finding hold at the individual level, and how would you know?' A student who presents a country-level correlation as if it directly describes personal risk has committed the ecological fallacy in front of the judge; naming the fallacy by name and proposing the individual-level design needed to confirm it (a cohort or case-control) is the signal of real understanding.

questions.prompt: In Robinson's 1950 analysis, why did the positive state-level correlation between percent foreign-born and literacy NOT hold for individuals?

options.text: Because the census data contained recording errors
Because foreign-born immigrants settled disproportionately in states that were already more literate overall, confounding the aggregate pattern
Because literacy cannot be measured at the individual level
Because sample sizes at the state level were too small to be reliable

explanations.a: The reversal is a structural statistical phenomenon (the ecological fallacy), not a data quality or recording problem.
explanations.b: Correct: the state-level aggregate pattern reflected where foreign-born immigrants settled, not how literate they individually were, illustrating how a group-level confound can invert the individual-level relationship.
explanations.c: Literacy is straightforwardly measurable at the individual level, and Robinson's point relied on comparing individual-level data to the aggregate pattern.
explanations.d: State-level counts in a full census are large; the discrepancy is about aggregation logic, not sample size.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of building and interpreting an ecological study correctly.

items.text: Gather group-level exposure and outcome statistics (e.g., national averages)
Compute a correlation or association across the groups
Recognize the association describes groups, not individuals
Design or seek an individual-level study to confirm the pattern before drawing personal-risk conclusions

questions.explanation: Sound ecological reasoning proceeds from aggregate data, to an aggregate association, to an explicit caveat about its level, to individual-level confirmation before any personal-risk claim.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

right.text: Assuming individual-level relationships describe group-level dynamics
Assuming a group-level association holds for individuals within the group
A design measuring exposure and outcome at the population or region level

questions.explanation: The ecological fallacy runs group-to-individual, the atomistic fallacy runs individual-to-group, and the ecological study is the design that produces the group-level data both fallacies misuse.

lessons.label: Nested and Hybrid Designs

sections.heading: Case-control nested inside a cohort
sections.body: A nested case-control study starts with an established cohort that has already been followed forward, with exposure data and often banked biological specimens collected at baseline before anyone got sick. Instead of analyzing every cohort member, the investigator identifies all the cases that developed during follow-up, then samples a matched set of controls from cohort members still at risk at the time each case occurred (risk-set sampling). Because exposure was measured at baseline — before outcome — for the whole original cohort, this design preserves the cohort's clean forward time direction, while gaining case-control's efficiency: expensive assays (say, measuring a biomarker in frozen blood) only need to be run on the cases and the sampled controls, not the entire cohort of thousands.

sections.heading: Case-cohort: one subcohort, reusable across outcomes
sections.body: A case-cohort design is a close cousin with one structural difference: instead of sampling a fresh set of controls for each case (or each outcome being studied), the investigator selects a single random subcohort at baseline, before any outcomes have occurred, and that same subcohort serves as the comparison group for every case that later arises — potentially across several different diseases studied from the same parent cohort. This makes case-cohort designs efficient when a cohort will be mined for multiple outcomes over time, since the subcohort's expensive baseline measurements need to be made only once and reused, rather than re-sampling and re-measuring controls separately for each new question.

sections.heading: Case-crossover: each case as their own control
sections.body: Case-crossover designs solve a different problem: transient exposures that trigger acute events, where a person's stable characteristics (genetics, chronic disease, baseline habits) would confound a between-person comparison. Each case serves as their own control by comparing their exposure status in a brief hazard period immediately before the event to their own exposure in a separate control period, eliminating confounding by anything that does not change over that short span. Malcolm Maclure introduced the design in 1991, and one of its best-known applications is Mittleman and colleagues' 1993 study of heavy physical exertion as a trigger for acute myocardial infarction, which compared each patient's activity in the hour before their heart attack to their own usual activity level over the prior year, finding transiently elevated risk during and shortly after heavy exertion.

lessons.workedExample: A cohort of 50,000 adults enrolled in 2005 gave blood samples at baseline. By 2025, 400 developed pancreatic cancer. A nested case-control study assays a novel biomarker only in those 400 cases plus 1,600 controls sampled from cohort members still cancer-free at each case's diagnosis date — 2,000 assays instead of 50,000, at a fraction of the cost, while still using pre-diagnosis blood, so exposure clearly precedes outcome. A case-cohort version of that same 50,000-person cohort instead draws one random subcohort of about 2,000 people (4% of the parent cohort) at baseline, before any outcomes occur, and reuses that identical 2,000-person subcohort as the comparison group not only for the 400 pancreatic cancer cases but also for a separate later analysis of, say, 250 diabetes cases arising from the same cohort — one subcohort, measured once, doing double duty across two unrelated outcome studies. Contrast both with Mittleman's case-crossover logic: a patient who has a heart attack at 2pm after shoveling snow is compared to their own exertion level during a matched control period (say, the same hour the day before), asking whether the hazard window itself carried elevated risk — not whether snow-shovelers differ from non-shovelers as people.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe hybrid-design projects on why the hybrid was chosen over a plain cohort or case-control, because each hybrid solves a specific cost or confounding problem: nested case-control and case-cohort exist to avoid assaying an entire cohort, while case-crossover exists to remove stable between-person confounding for transient triggers. A student who cannot say which specific problem their hybrid solves has likely chosen the fancier-sounding design rather than the right one.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of a nested case-control study over analyzing an entire parent cohort directly?
