options.text: It allows the study to use outcome-based sampling for controls while cutting the cost of measuring exposure or biomarkers to only cases and a sampled control set
It eliminates the need for a defined cohort altogether
It removes the need for any control group
It allows exposure to be measured after the outcome has occurred

explanations.a: Correct: by sampling controls from the risk set rather than measuring everyone, expensive baseline assays are limited to cases and a manageable control sample while temporality from the parent cohort is preserved.
explanations.b: A nested case-control study depends entirely on an already-established cohort; it does not replace the need for one.
explanations.c: Nested case-control studies still require a control group, just a sampled subset rather than the full cohort.
explanations.d: The design's key strength is that exposure was measured at baseline, before outcome, using the parent cohort's data — reversing that order would destroy its main advantage.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of Mittleman's 1993 case-crossover study of exertion and heart attack.

items.text: Identify cases who just had a myocardial infarction
Assess each patient's own physical exertion in the hazard period just before the event
Compare that hazard-period exposure to the same patient's exertion during a separate control period
Estimate the transient risk associated with the triggering exposure

questions.explanation: Case-crossover logic identifies cases, measures their own exposure just before the event, compares it to their own baseline control period, and derives risk from that within-person contrast.

questions.prompt: Match each hybrid design to the specific problem it is built to solve.

right.text: Avoids repeatedly re-sampling controls when a cohort will be studied for multiple outcomes over time
Removes confounding by stable individual traits for transient exposure triggers
Cuts the cost of assaying an entire cohort by sampling controls only for the cases that occur

questions.explanation: Nested case-control samples controls per case-set to save cost, case-cohort reuses one subcohort across outcomes, and case-crossover uses each case as their own control to remove stable confounding.

lessons.label: Design-Specific Traps

sections.heading: Case-control's trap: recall bias
sections.body: Because a case-control study asks people to report past exposure from memory, recall bias arises when cases and controls remember or report that history differently — most commonly, people who already have a disease search their memory harder for a cause, over-reporting past exposures compared to healthy controls who have no such motivation. A mother of a child born with a birth defect, asked about medication use during pregnancy, may recall and report a minor drug exposure that a control mother of a healthy child simply forgets. This differential recall can manufacture an association even when true exposure rates were identical, and it is largely specific to designs that depend on retrospective self-report.

sections.heading: Cohort's traps: loss to follow-up and the healthy-worker effect
sections.body: A cohort study's long duration creates its own vulnerability: participants who drop out before the study ends are lost, and if dropout is related to both exposure and outcome, the remaining sample is biased. A related but distinct problem specific to occupational cohorts is the healthy-worker effect — people who are employed are, on average, healthier than the general population, because illness that would prevent someone from working also prevents them from being hired or staying employed. An occupational cohort comparing factory workers' mortality to general-population mortality rates can therefore underestimate the true risk of a workplace exposure, since the worker cohort's baseline health advantage partially masks the harm.

sections.heading: Cross-sectional's traps: survivorship and prevalence-incidence (Neyman) bias
sections.body: A cross-sectional study captures only the prevalent cases who are alive and have the disease at the moment of the survey — anyone who died quickly after onset, or who recovered quickly, is systematically absent from that snapshot. This is prevalence-incidence bias, also called Neyman bias after Jerzy Neyman, who formally described it in 1955: because the survey only sees survivors of a selection process (surviving long enough with the disease to still have it at the survey date), the exposure-disease relationship measured among prevalent cases can look weaker, stronger, or even reversed compared to the true relationship among everyone who ever developed the disease, including those who died or recovered before the snapshot was taken.

sections.heading: Matching the trap to the question
sections.body: Choosing a design means choosing which trap you are willing to manage. A study of a rapidly fatal exposure-outcome pair is especially vulnerable to Neyman bias if done cross-sectionally, since the sickest cases vanish before any survey catches them — a cohort avoids this by catching outcomes as they happen. A study relying on decades-old self-reported exposure is especially vulnerable to recall bias if done as case-control — a nested case-control using pre-collected cohort data avoids this by fixing exposure data before diagnosis. There is no trap-free design; the discipline is naming the trap that most threatens a specific question and picking the structure built to dodge it.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher studying whether a pesticide causes a fast-progressing, often-fatal lung disease chooses a cross-sectional survey of currently living farmworkers. Because the disease kills quickly, most people who developed it after heavy exposure are already dead and absent from the survey, while people with mild or no disease dominate the sample — Neyman bias will likely understate the true pesticide-disease association. A cohort study following farmworkers forward from enrollment, capturing every case (fatal or not) as it occurs, avoids this trap entirely, at the cost of the years and expense a cohort requires — illustrating that the 'correct' design depends on which specific trap threatens the specific question.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'what is the single biggest threat to your study's validity, and how does your design specifically address it' is testing whether a student picked their design deliberately or by habit. The strongest answers name the trap by its mechanism — differential recall between cases and controls, healthy-worker selection into an occupational cohort, or survivors-only sampling in a snapshot — rather than gesturing vaguely at 'bias.'

questions.prompt: Why does the healthy-worker effect tend to make an occupational cohort UNDERestimate the true risk of a workplace exposure?

options.text: Because workers are randomly assigned to exposure levels
Because people healthy enough to be employed are, on average, healthier than the general population used as the comparison group
Because workers always under-report their exposure history
Because occupational cohorts are always too small to detect real risk

explanations.a: Occupational cohorts are observational; exposure (the job itself) is not randomly assigned, which is unrelated to the healthy-worker effect.
explanations.b: Correct: the employed comparison group starts healthier than the general population by virtue of being well enough to work, which masks part of any true excess risk from the workplace exposure.
explanations.c: The healthy-worker effect is a selection bias about who becomes and stays employed, not a reporting or recall problem.
explanations.d: Sample size affects statistical precision, not the direction of the healthy-worker effect, which is a systematic bias present regardless of size.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning that leads to Neyman (prevalence-incidence) bias in a cross-sectional study of a fast-fatal disease.

items.text: Disease causes rapid death or rapid recovery in many affected people
Only people who still have the disease and are alive at the survey moment are captured
The captured prevalent cases are an unrepresentative subset of everyone who ever developed the disease
The measured exposure-disease association is distorted relative to the true relationship

questions.explanation: Neyman bias flows from rapid disease resolution (death or recovery), to survivors-only capture at the survey moment, to an unrepresentative case sample, to a distorted measured association.

questions.prompt: Match each design to the trap it is most specifically vulnerable to.

right.text: Recall bias from differential memory of past exposure
Loss to follow-up and the healthy-worker effect
Neyman (prevalence-incidence) bias from missing fast-resolving cases

questions.explanation: Each design's structural weak point follows from how it collects data: retrospective report for case-control, extended follow-up for cohort, single-moment snapshot for cross-sectional.

lessons.label: The 2x2 Table

sections.heading: Four cells, one shared skeleton
sections.body: Every classic measure of association in epidemiology starts from the same 2x2 table: exposure (yes/no) crossed with outcome (yes/no). By convention the cells are labeled a (exposed, diseased), b (exposed, not diseased), c (unexposed, diseased), and d (unexposed, not diseased). Rows are exposure groups; columns are outcome groups. Almost every ratio you will meet later — risk ratio, odds ratio, rate ratio — is just a different arithmetic combination of a, b, c, and d, so misreading which cell is which is the single most common source of a flipped or inverted answer on a science-fair poster.

sections.heading: What the study design fixes for you
sections.body: The table looks identical across designs, but what a researcher was allowed to control differs, and that controls what the table can honestly tell you. In a cohort study, investigators enroll people by exposure status and follow them forward, so the row totals (a+b and c+d) are fixed by the sampling design — the researcher chose, say, 500 exposed and 500 unexposed workers before any disease occurred. Because the row totals are fixed at the true group sizes, a/(a+b) and c/(c+d) are genuine cumulative risks, and their ratio is a true risk ratio. In a case-control study, investigators instead enroll by outcome status — a fixed number of cases and a fixed number of controls — so the column totals (a+c and b+d) are fixed by design, not by nature. Row proportions like a/(a+b) are meaningless here because the number of exposed and unexposed people was never sampled to reflect the source population; only the odds within each column (a/c versus b/d) are valid, which is why case-control data yield an odds ratio rather than a risk ratio. This distinction — which margin the design fixes — is the reason the same four numbers support different math depending on how the study was built, and it is the first thing to identify before touching a calculator.

sections.heading: An early exposure table, before the formalism existed
sections.body: The logic of the 2x2 table predates its modern name by a century. John Snow's 1854 investigation of a London cholera outbreak compared death rates between households supplied by two water companies, Southwark and Vauxhall versus Lambeth, after Lambeth had moved its intake upstream of London's sewage discharge. Snow's 1855 report tabulated deaths against water-company exposure much like a modern cohort table's rows, and the stark gap in death rates between the two supplies became one of the first exposure-outcome comparisons to influence public policy, well before Ronald Fisher and Jerzy Neyman formalized the statistical theory such tables now rest on.

lessons.workedExample: A cohort of 1,000 smokers and 1,000 nonsmokers is followed 10 years for lung cancer. Results: a=95 (smokers, cancer), b=905 (smokers, no cancer), c=10 (nonsmokers, cancer), d=990 (nonsmokers, no cancer). Because row totals (1,000 and 1,000) were fixed by enrollment, risk in the exposed is a/(a+b)=95/1000=9.5%, and risk in the unexposed is c/(c+d)=10/1000=1.0% — real cumulative risks, ready for a risk ratio of 9.5.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'was this cohort or case-control?' before accepting any risk percentage on a poster, because a case-control table cannot produce a valid risk even though the four cells look the same. A student who computes 'risk' from a case-control table (e.g., dividing cases by cases+controls) is dividing by a number the researcher chose, not a population — a red flag that signals the student built the table without understanding what the sampling design actually fixed.

questions.prompt: In a case-control study of 200 cases and 400 controls, why can't you compute a/(a+b) as a valid 'risk in the exposed'?

options.text: Because a+b is not a real population size, only a total controlled by the outcome-based sampling
Because case-control studies never record exposure status
Because odds ratios cannot be computed from a 2x2 table
Because a is always smaller than b in case-control data

explanations.a: Correct: rows in a case-control table mix an arbitrary number of cases and controls, so a/(a+b) is not a rate in any real population — it depends on the study's case:control ratio, not on disease frequency.
explanations.b: Case-control studies do record exposure status for both cases and controls; that's precisely how the table's cells are filled.
explanations.c: Odds ratios are exactly what a case-control 2x2 table is built to produce; the problem is with risk, not odds.
explanations.d: There's no rule that a is smaller than b; cell sizes depend on exposure prevalence among the cases sampled.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to correctly decide what a 2x2 table can compute.

items.text: Identify how subjects were sampled: by exposure (cohort) or by outcome (case-control)
Determine which margin (rows or columns) that sampling scheme fixed
If rows are fixed, compute row-wise risks and a risk ratio
If columns are fixed, compute odds within columns and an odds ratio

questions.explanation: You must know the sampling scheme before trusting any proportion computed from the table; the fixed margin determines whether risk or only odds is valid.

questions.prompt: Match each cell label to its definition in the standard 2x2 table.

right.text: Exposed, diseased
Exposed, not diseased
Unexposed, diseased
Unexposed, not diseased

questions.explanation: a-b-c-d is the standard epidemiology convention: rows are exposure status, columns are outcome status, read exposed-then-unexposed and diseased-then-not.

lessons.label: Risk, Relative Risk, and Risk Difference

sections.heading: Cumulative incidence as risk
sections.body: Risk in epidemiology has a precise meaning: the proportion of a defined, disease-free population that develops the outcome over a stated follow-up period. This is also called cumulative incidence. Using the 2x2 table from a cohort design, risk in the exposed group is R_e = a/(a+b) and risk in the unexposed group is R_u = c/(c+d). Both are plain proportions between 0 and 1, and both require the row totals to represent real population counts — which is exactly what cohort sampling guarantees and case-control sampling does not.

sections.heading: Two ways to compare two risks
sections.body: Once you have R_e and R_u, there are two legitimate ways to compare them, and they answer different questions. Relative risk (RR), also called the risk ratio, is R_e/R_u — how many times higher (or lower) the exposed group's risk is, multiplicatively. RR = 1 means no association (the null value); RR > 1 means the exposure is associated with higher risk; RR < 1 means the exposure looks protective. Risk difference (RD) is R_e minus R_u — the absolute gap in risk, expressed in the same units as risk itself (a proportion, or per 1,000, per 100,000, etc.). RD = 0 is the null value here. The two measures can tell very different stories from the same data: a RR of 2.0 sounds dramatic, but if R_u is 0.0001, the RD is only 0.0001 — a doubling of an already-tiny risk. This is precisely why public-health decisions and clinical decisions increasingly report both figures side by side rather than relative risk alone; the RR captures strength of association (useful for causal reasoning), while the RD captures the actual burden a person or population experiences (useful for deciding whether to act).

sections.heading: A landmark cohort built for exactly this arithmetic
sections.body: The Framingham Heart Study, begun in 1948 in Framingham, Massachusetts, and still ongoing across three generations of enrolled residents, is the textbook example of a cohort designed so that R_e and R_u are real cumulative risks rather than approximations. The original cohort enrolled 5,209 disease-free men and women aged 30 to 62, all free of cardiovascular disease at baseline, and followed them with repeated exams every two years — exactly the fixed-denominator, fixed-follow-up structure the 2x2 table's row totals assume. Because Framingham tracked cardiovascular events over those fixed follow-up windows, it could report both RR and RD for exposures like high blood pressure or elevated cholesterol directly from the 2x2 arithmetic in the previous lesson — no rare-disease assumption or odds-based workaround needed, unlike a case-control design.

lessons.workedExample: In a cohort of 2,000 daily aspirin users and 2,000 non-users followed 5 years for GI bleeding: users have 40 bleeds (R_e = 40/2000 = 0.020 = 2.0%), non-users have 20 bleeds (R_u = 20/2000 = 0.010 = 1.0%). RR = 0.020/0.010 = 2.0 — aspirin users have twice the risk. RD = 0.020 - 0.010 = 0.010, or 1.0 extra bleed per 100 users over 5 years. The RR of 2.0 sounds alarming in isolation; the RD shows the absolute excess is modest at this baseline risk.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will ask a student to state both the RR and the RD for their headline finding, because reporting only 'a 2x2-fold increase' without the absolute numbers is a classic way results get overstated — it is the same rhetorical move used in some misleading health journalism. A student who can explain why the same data give a big RR but a small RD (or vice versa) demonstrates they understand risk is baseline-dependent, not just that they can plug numbers into a formula.

questions.prompt: A study reports RR = 3.0 for a rare exposure-outcome pair where R_u = 0.0002. What can you conclude about the risk difference?

options.text: RD is very small (about 0.0004) even though the RR looks large
RD must also be large, since RR is large
RD cannot be calculated from RR and R_u alone
RD equals RR minus 1

explanations.a: Correct: R_e = RR x R_u = 3.0 x 0.0002 = 0.0006, so RD = 0.0006 - 0.0002 = 0.0004 — tiny in absolute terms despite the tripled relative risk.
explanations.b: RR and RD can diverge sharply; a large multiplicative increase on a tiny baseline still yields a tiny absolute increase.
explanations.c: RD = R_e - R_u = (RR x R_u) - R_u, so it is fully computable once RR and R_u are both known.
explanations.d: That formula does not correspond to any standard measure; RD is an absolute difference in risks, not derived by subtracting 1 from RR.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to compute RR and RD from cohort data.

items.text: Compute R_e = a/(a+b) from the exposed row
Compute R_u = c/(c+d) from the unexposed row
Divide R_e by R_u to get RR
Subtract R_u from R_e to get RD

questions.explanation: Both group-specific risks must be computed first; RR and RD are then two independent summaries of the same pair of risks.

questions.prompt: Match each RR value to its interpretation.

right.text: No association (null value)
Exposure associated with higher risk
Exposure appears protective

questions.explanation: RR is centered on 1: values above 1 indicate the exposed group's risk exceeds the unexposed group's, values below 1 indicate the reverse.

lessons.label: The Odds Ratio

sections.heading: Odds is not risk
sections.body: Risk is the probability of an event: (number with the event) / (total number at risk). Odds is a different ratio: (number with the event) / (number without the event). If 20 out of 100 people develop disease, risk = 20/100 = 0.20, but odds = 20/80 = 0.25. The two converge toward each other only when the event is rare, because then the denominator of risk (total) and the denominator of odds (non-events) are nearly the same number. As the event becomes common, odds increasingly overstates risk, since dividing by a shrinking non-event pool inflates the ratio.

sections.heading: Why case-control designs give you an odds ratio
sections.body: The odds ratio (OR) from a 2x2 table is the cross-product ratio: OR = (a x d)/(b x c), equivalently (a/c)/(b/d) — the odds of exposure among cases divided by the odds of exposure among controls, which algebraically equals the odds of disease among exposed divided by the odds of disease among unexposed. This symmetry is what makes the OR computable in a case-control study: even though the row totals (a+b, c+d) are not real population sizes, the odds of exposure within each column (cases, controls) are valid, and the cross-product ratio recovers the same OR you would get by working the other direction. A cohort or cross-sectional study could also report an OR, but only case-control designs are forced to, since they cannot report a true RR.

sections.heading: The rare-disease approximation and its limits
sections.body: When the outcome is rare (a common rule of thumb is under about 10% cumulative incidence in both groups), b is close to a+b and d is close to c+d, so OR ≈ RR — this is the rare-disease assumption that let mid-20th-century case-control studies (including Doll and Hill's 1950 lung-cancer study) speak informally about relative risk despite computing an OR. When the outcome is common, the approximation breaks badly: OR is always farther from 1 than RR in the same direction, so a common-outcome OR systematically overstates the strength of a real risk-ratio effect, sometimes by several-fold. The approximation itself was put on rigorous footing by biostatistician Jerome Cornfield in a 1951 paper in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute, which proved that under a rare-disease condition the case-control odds ratio is a valid estimator of the cohort relative risk — the theoretical result that legitimized using case-control designs to study rare cancers at all.

lessons.workedExample: A case-control study of 100 lung-cancer cases and 100 controls finds 90 cases were smokers (a=90, c=10 non-smoking cases) and 50 controls were smokers (b=50, d=50 non-smoking controls). OR = (a x d)/(b x c) = (90 x 50)/(50 x 10) = 4500/500 = 9.0. Because lung cancer is not rare within this heavily-diseased sample construction, this OR should not be casually read as 'smokers have 9 times the risk' without checking baseline population incidence — the true population RR is typically smaller than an OR computed this way suggests.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can state, from memory of the math (not just the label), why a case-control study cannot produce a risk ratio, and whether the student flags when the rare-disease approximation is being stretched. A student who reports 'OR = 9, so smokers have 9x the risk' without qualification, when the underlying outcome prevalence is not rare, is the single most common overreach seen on posters using case-control data.

questions.prompt: Why does the rare-disease assumption let OR approximate RR?

options.text: Because when the outcome is rare, the non-event count is close to the total count in each group, making odds close to risk
Because rare diseases always have an OR of exactly 1
Because case-control studies only exist for rare diseases
Because odds and risk are mathematically identical for any disease frequency

explanations.a: Correct: odds = events/non-events and risk = events/total; when events are rare, non-events ≈ total, so the two ratios nearly coincide.
explanations.b: Rarity affects how closely OR tracks RR, not the value of OR itself, which reflects the strength of the exposure-disease association.
explanations.c: Case-control designs can study common outcomes too; the approximation to RR simply becomes less accurate in that case.
explanations.d: Odds and risk are identical only in the limiting case of a very rare event; for common events they diverge substantially.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to compute an odds ratio from a case-control 2x2 table.

items.text: Tabulate exposure status separately among cases and among controls
Compute the odds of exposure among cases as a/c
Compute the odds of exposure among controls as b/d
Divide to get OR = (a/c)/(b/d) = (a x d)/(b x c)

questions.explanation: The OR is built from within-column odds because only columns (case status, control status) are fixed by case-control sampling design.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to its effect on the OR-vs-RR relationship.

left.text: Outcome incidence under about 10% in both groups
Outcome incidence around 40-50% in both groups
Cohort study reporting a true risk ratio directly

right.text: OR closely approximates RR
OR substantially overstates RR
No OR-vs-RR approximation needed

questions.explanation: The rare-disease approximation only holds at low incidence; cohort studies with real row totals can report RR directly and skip the approximation issue.

lessons.label: Rate Ratios and Hazard Ratios

sections.heading: Incidence rates use person-time, not head counts
sections.body: Cumulative incidence (risk) assumes everyone is followed for the same length of time, which real studies rarely achieve — people enroll at different points, drop out, die of other causes, or the study ends mid-follow-up. The incidence rate instead uses person-time as the denominator: total new cases divided by the sum of time each person was actually at risk, expressed as, for example, cases per 1,000 person-years. The incidence-rate ratio (IRR) compares two such rates, exposed versus unexposed: IRR = (cases_e/persontime_e) / (cases_u/persontime_u). Unlike RR, the IRR properly credits someone followed for 2 years with twice the at-risk time of someone followed for 1 year, which matters whenever follow-up length varies across subjects.

sections.heading: The hazard ratio: an instantaneous version
sections.body: The hazard ratio (HR) extends this idea further: instead of one rate averaged over the whole study, it compares the instantaneous risk of the event at every moment during follow-up, conditional on having survived event-free up to that moment. HRs come out of time-to-event (survival) analysis, most commonly the Cox proportional-hazards model, introduced by David Cox in 1972. The central assumption, proportional hazards, is that the ratio of the two groups' hazards stays constant over the entire follow-up period — the exposed group's instantaneous risk is always some fixed multiple k of the unexposed group's risk, even though both groups' absolute risk may rise or fall over calendar time or age. This assumption is checkable (e.g., via Schoenfeld residuals) and is routinely violated in real data, which is why papers using Cox models are expected to report whether they tested it.

sections.heading: How HR differs from RR and OR
sections.body: RR and OR are both single-timepoint or fixed-follow-up summaries; they say nothing about when events happened, only whether they happened by the study's end. HR uses every subject's exact event or censoring time, which makes it more statistically efficient and lets it handle censoring (subjects who leave a study without the event) properly — RR and OR mishandle censored subjects by either dropping them or misclassifying them as non-events. This is why time-to-event outcomes (death, relapse, disease onset with variable follow-up) are analyzed with hazard ratios in essentially all modern clinical trials, while RR and OR remain the tools for outcomes measured at one fixed point. Cox's original 1972 paper, published in the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, deliberately avoided specifying the shape of the underlying hazard function over time — the 'semi-parametric' trick that made the model usable without knowing the true baseline hazard, and the reason it remains the default choice for survival analysis in medical journals today.

lessons.workedExample: A trial follows a treatment group for a cumulative 950 person-years with 38 events and a control group for 900 person-years with 54 events. IRR = (38/950)/(54/900) = 0.0400/0.0600 = 0.67 — the treatment group's rate is two-thirds the control's. If instead a Cox model is fit on the same data using each subject's exact time-to-event, it might report HR = 0.65 (95% CI 0.44-0.96) — close to the IRR here because event rates were fairly steady over time, illustrating that IRR and HR often agree when hazards genuinely are proportional.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student picked the right measure for their outcome type: if follow-up time varied across subjects or the analysis is 'time to X,' a plain risk ratio without accounting for person-time or censoring is a design flaw, not just a stylistic choice. A student who explains why they chose an IRR or HR over an RR — and can state the proportional-hazards assumption in their own words — signals real understanding of longitudinal data, not just formula recall.

questions.prompt: Why is the incidence-rate ratio preferred over a simple risk ratio when subjects have unequal follow-up time?

options.text: Because it weights each subject's contribution by their actual at-risk time rather than treating everyone as followed equally
Because rate ratios ignore how many events occurred
Because risk ratios cannot be computed unless everyone has identical exposure
Because the IRR does not require any denominator

explanations.a: Correct: person-time denominators credit longer-followed subjects with more at-risk time, which a head-count risk denominator cannot do.
explanations.b: IRR still uses the case counts in its numerator; it changes the denominator, not whether events are counted.
explanations.c: RR can be computed with unequal follow-up, it's just biased or misleading in that situation, not undefined.
explanations.d: IRR's denominator is total person-time, summed across all subjects' at-risk periods.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to compute an incidence-rate ratio.

items.text: Sum person-time at risk separately in the exposed and unexposed groups
Count new cases in each group over the same follow-up
Divide cases by person-time in each group to get two incidence rates
Divide the exposed rate by the unexposed rate to get IRR

questions.explanation: Person-time must be tallied before rates can be computed; the IRR is the ratio of the two resulting rates.

questions.prompt: Match each measure to the situation it is best suited for.

right.text: Cohort study with equal, fixed follow-up for all subjects
Case-control study sampled by outcome status
Time-to-event data with variable follow-up and censoring

questions.explanation: Each measure matches the data structure it was built for: fixed-time cohorts, outcome-sampled case-control studies, and censored time-to-event data respectively.

lessons.label: Attributable Risk and Population Impact

sections.heading: Attributable risk: the excess owed to exposure
sections.body: Attributable risk (AR), also called the risk difference, isolates how much of the exposed group's risk is actually caused by the exposure rather than by background causes shared with the unexposed: AR = R_e - R_u. The attributable fraction (AF), also called the attributable proportion, converts this into a share of the exposed group's total risk: AF = (R_e - R_u)/R_e = AR/R_e, often expressed as a percent. AF answers 'of all the disease that occurs among exposed people, what fraction would disappear if the exposure were removed?' — a different and more actionable question than the risk ratio, which only says how much higher exposed risk is, multiplicatively, without saying how much disease that translates to.

sections.heading: Scaling up: population attributable risk
sections.body: Attributable risk describes one exposed individual's excess burden; population attributable risk (PAR) scales this to the whole population, exposed and unexposed combined: PAR = R_total - R_u, where R_total is the risk in the entire population regardless of exposure status. The population attributable fraction (PAF) is PAR/R_total, and it depends on two things multiplied together: the strength of the association (via RR) and how common the exposure is in the population. A weak exposure that is nearly universal (like a mildly elevated dietary risk factor) can carry a larger PAF than a strong exposure that is rare, because PAF scales with exposure prevalence. This is the lever public-health interventions actually pull: reducing how many people are exposed lowers PAF even if you cannot change RR itself, which is why campaigns target prevalence (smoking rates, vaccination gaps) rather than trying to alter individual susceptibility.

sections.heading: Where the concept came from
sections.body: The attributable-risk framework was introduced by Morton Levin in 1953 in a paper estimating the share of lung-cancer occurrence in the population attributable to smoking, work that predates the more famous Doll and Hill cohort results and helped establish that a strong individual-level association (a high RR) does not by itself tell you how much disease a public-health program could actually prevent — that translation step is exactly what PAR and PAF were built to supply. This same reasoning underpinned the 1964 US Surgeon General's report on smoking and health, which moved beyond citing relative risk alone to estimate the absolute national mortality burden attributable to cigarette smoking — the argument that ultimately drove policy, because a population-level number, not an individual relative risk, is what a regulator needs to justify an intervention.

lessons.workedExample: Say lung-cancer risk among smokers is 17% (R_e = 0.17) over a lifetime and among nonsmokers is 1% (R_u = 0.01) — figures broadly consistent with mid-to-late-20th-century US cohort estimates. AR = 0.17 - 0.01 = 0.16, so a smoker's excess lifetime risk attributable to smoking is 16 percentage points, and AF = 0.16/0.17 ≈ 94% of a smoker's lung-cancer risk is attributable to smoking. If 20% of the population smokes, R_total ≈ (0.20 x 0.17) + (0.80 x 0.01) = 0.034 + 0.008 = 0.042, so PAR = 0.042 - 0.01 = 0.032 and PAF = 0.032/0.042 ≈ 76% of all lung cancer in this population is attributable to smoking.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can distinguish 'risk to one exposed person' from 'burden to the whole population,' because these numbers support very different claims: AF tells a smoker their personal excess risk, while PAF tells a health department how much disease a smoking-cessation program could plausibly prevent. A student who reports only RR and calls it 'the impact' has skipped the step that actually connects the statistic to a policy or an individual decision, which is exactly what a judge's follow-up question probes.

questions.prompt: Two exposures have identical RR = 3.0. Exposure X is present in 5% of the population; exposure Y is present in 60%. Which has the larger population attributable fraction (PAF), all else equal?

options.text: Exposure Y, because PAF increases with exposure prevalence even at equal RR
Exposure X, because rarer exposures always have larger PAF
They must have equal PAF since RR is identical
PAF cannot be determined without knowing the outcome's total incidence

explanations.a: Correct: at equal RR, PAF rises with how common the exposure is, since more of the population's total risk is then attributable to it.
explanations.b: The opposite is true; rarer exposures contribute less to population-level risk at a given RR, not more.
explanations.c: RR alone does not determine PAF; exposure prevalence is the other required input and differs sharply here (5% vs 60%).
explanations.d: PAF can be determined from RR and exposure prevalence alone via the standard formula; total incidence is not required as a separate input here.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to move from individual attributable risk to population attributable fraction.

items.text: Compute R_e and R_u to get attributable risk (AR = R_e - R_u)
Divide AR by R_e to get the attributable fraction among the exposed
Weight R_e and R_u by exposure prevalence to get R_total for the whole population
Compute PAF = (R_total - R_u)/R_total

questions.explanation: Individual-level AR and AF come first from the two group risks; population-level PAR and PAF require folding in exposure prevalence to reconstruct the total population's risk.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its formula or defining input.

right.text: R_e - R_u
(R_e - R_u)/R_e
Depends on both RR and exposure prevalence

questions.explanation: AR and AF are individual-level, computed purely from the two group risks; PAF is population-level and additionally requires knowing how common the exposure is.

lessons.label: Number Needed to Treat and Harm

sections.heading: Turning absolute risk change into a headcount
sections.body: Number needed to treat (NNT) converts an absolute risk reduction (ARR) into a more tangible clinical quantity: the number of patients who must receive a treatment for one additional patient to benefit, compared to receiving the control. NNT = 1/ARR, where ARR = R_control - R_treatment (the same quantity as attributable risk, just labeled from a treatment-benefit angle). Number needed to harm (NNH) is the mirror image, used when a treatment or exposure increases risk of an adverse outcome: NNH = 1/ARI, where ARI = R_exposed - R_unexposed is the absolute risk increase. Both concepts were formalized by Laupacis, Sackett, and Roberts in a widely cited 1988 New England Journal of Medicine paper, and both are now standard in clinical-trial reporting and evidence-based-medicine teaching.

sections.heading: Why baseline risk drives NNT, not just relative benefit
sections.body: Because NNT is 1 divided by an absolute difference, and absolute difference depends on baseline risk, the same relative risk reduction produces wildly different NNTs depending on how common the outcome already is. A drug that cuts relative risk by 25% in a population with 40% baseline risk yields ARR = 0.40 x 0.25 = 0.10, so NNT = 1/0.10 = 10 — treat 10 people to prevent one event. The identical 25% relative reduction in a population with 2% baseline risk yields ARR = 0.02 x 0.25 = 0.005, so NNT = 1/0.005 = 200 — treat 200 people for the same one prevented event. This is precisely why press coverage of 'cuts risk by 25%' without stating baseline risk can mislead: the relative number stays constant while the practical NNT swings by a factor of 20, and a low-baseline-risk population may not be worth treating at all once side effects and cost are weighed against a NNT of 200.

sections.heading: NNT as a common language across trials
sections.body: Because NNT is expressed as a plain headcount rather than a percentage or ratio, it became a standard summary statistic in evidence-based medicine after Laupacis, Sackett, and Roberts proposed it, and it is now reported routinely in Cochrane systematic reviews so that clinicians can compare treatments for entirely different conditions on the same intuitive scale — a vaccine with NNT=200 to prevent one hospitalization and a surgery with NNT=8 to prevent one recurrence can be weighed against their respective NNH and cost in the same sentence, something a bare relative risk reduction cannot support.

lessons.workedExample: A statin trial reports 5-year cardiovascular event risk of 12% in placebo and 9% in treatment (RR = 0.75, a 25% relative reduction). ARR = 0.12 - 0.09 = 0.03, so NNT = 1/0.03 ≈ 33 — about 33 patients need 5 years of statin therapy to prevent one cardiovascular event. If the same drug causes a rare muscle-damage side effect (myopathy) in 0.2% of treated patients versus 0.05% in placebo, ARI = 0.0015, so NNH = 1/0.0015 ≈ 667 — one myopathy case per 667 treated patients, letting a clinician weigh NNT=33 for benefit against NNH=667 for harm on the same numeric scale.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student reporting a treatment effect can produce the NNT alongside the relative risk reduction, because NNT is the number that translates a statistic into a real-world resource and side-effect tradeoff question: is treating 33 people to help one worth it given cost and NNH? A student who only cites 'a 25% relative risk reduction' without baseline risk or NNT has presented a number that sounds impressive but cannot actually be evaluated for practical significance.

questions.prompt: Two trials both report a 30% relative risk reduction from a drug. Trial A has 50% baseline event risk; Trial B has 3% baseline event risk. Which trial has the lower (better) NNT?

options.text: Trial A, because its higher baseline risk produces a larger absolute risk reduction for the same relative reduction
Trial B, because lower baseline risk always improves NNT
They are equal, since NNT depends only on relative risk reduction
NNT cannot be computed without knowing sample size

explanations.a: Correct: ARR = baseline risk x relative reduction, so Trial A's ARR = 0.50 x 0.30 = 0.15 (NNT ≈ 7) versus Trial B's ARR = 0.03 x 0.30 = 0.009 (NNT ≈ 111) — Trial A's higher baseline gives a far better NNT.
explanations.b: Lower baseline risk shrinks the absolute risk reduction for a fixed relative reduction, which makes NNT worse (larger), not better.
explanations.c: NNT depends on the absolute risk reduction, which itself depends on baseline risk, not on relative risk reduction alone.
explanations.d: NNT is computed from ARR (a proportion), not from sample size; sample size affects the precision/confidence interval around NNT, not the point estimate.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to compute NNT from two group risks.

items.text: Determine R_control and R_treatment from trial data
Compute ARR = R_control - R_treatment
Take the reciprocal: NNT = 1/ARR
Round up to a whole number of patients for practical reporting

questions.explanation: NNT requires the absolute risk reduction first; the reciprocal converts a proportion into a headcount, which is conventionally rounded up since a fractional patient cannot be treated.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its formula.

right.text: 1/ARR
1/ARI
R_control - R_treatment

questions.explanation: NNT and NNH are reciprocals of absolute risk change in the beneficial and harmful directions respectively; ARR is the underlying absolute difference that feeds NNT.

lessons.label: Confidence Intervals for Effect Measures

sections.heading: Why ratio measures need the log scale
sections.body: Every effect measure computed so far — RR, OR, IRR, HR — is a point estimate from one sample, and a different sample from the same population would give a slightly different number. A confidence interval (CI) quantifies that sampling variability: a 95% CI is the range that would contain the true population value in 95% of repeated samples, under standard frequentist interpretation. For ratio measures, the raw ratio's sampling distribution is skewed (it cannot go below 0 but has no upper bound), so statisticians compute the CI on the natural-log scale, where ln(RR) is approximately normally distributed, then exponentiate the endpoints back to the ratio scale. This is why published CIs for OR or RR are asymmetric around the point estimate — for example an OR of 2.0 might have a 95% CI of (1.3, 3.1), not (1.5, 2.5) — reflecting the log-scale symmetry, not an error.

sections.heading: Reading whether the interval crosses the null
sections.body: Every ratio measure has a null value of 1 (no association); every difference measure — RD, AR, NNT's underlying ARR — has a null value of 0. If a 95% CI for an RR or OR excludes 1 entirely (e.g., 1.3 to 3.1), the association is conventionally called statistically significant at the 0.05 level; this is mathematically equivalent to a two-sided p-value below 0.05 for that same comparison. If the CI includes 1 (e.g., 0.8 to 2.4), the study cannot rule out no association at that confidence level.

sections.heading: Width is precision, not effect size — and absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence
sections.body: Two studies can report the same point estimate (say RR = 1.5) with very different CI widths: a huge study might report (1.4, 1.6), a small pilot might report (0.6, 3.8). The width reflects sample size and event count, not how strong the effect is. A wide CI that happens to cross 1, especially from an underpowered study, means the data are simply too sparse to distinguish a real effect from chance — it does not mean the null hypothesis has been confirmed. Treating 'CI crosses 1, therefore no effect exists' as equivalent to 'we have positive evidence of no effect' is one of the most common statistical misreadings in both press coverage and student posters; the correct reading is 'inconclusive; a larger study is needed.' The confidence interval itself, as a formal concept distinct from a standard error or a p-value, was introduced by Jerzy Neyman in a 1937 paper on statistical estimation, and the log-scale transformation for ratio measures became standard epidemiological practice decades later as case-control and cohort methods matured through the mid-20th century.

lessons.workedExample: A pilot cohort study of a workplace exposure computes RR = 1.8 based on only 12 exposed cases, with 95% CI (0.9, 3.6) — the interval crosses 1, so the result is not statistically significant at the 0.05 level, even though 1.8 sounds like a meaningful elevation. A follow-up study with 20x the sample size finds the same RR = 1.8 but with 95% CI (1.5, 2.2), now excluding 1. Both studies estimated the identical point effect; only the precision (driven by sample size and case count) changed, which is why the pilot's 'non-significant' result should have been reported as inconclusive, not as evidence of safety.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges specifically listen for whether a student says 'not significant' means 'no effect' versus 'insufficient data to detect an effect' — conflating the two is the single most common statistical error at science fairs, and it directly follows from misunderstanding that CI width tracks sample size, not truth. A student who can point to their own CI width and connect it to their sample size demonstrates they understand the interval is a precision statement, which is exactly the follow-up question judges ask after seeing any ratio measure on a poster.

questions.prompt: A small study reports OR = 2.2 with 95% CI (0.7, 6.9). What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: The data are consistent with both a substantial protective-to-harmful range of true effects and cannot rule out no association; a larger study is needed
The study proves there is no association, since the interval crosses 1
The study proves a strong association, since the point estimate is 2.2
The CI is invalid because it is not symmetric around 2.2

explanations.a: Correct: a wide CI crossing the null reflects insufficient precision, not evidence of no effect; the honest conclusion is that this study alone cannot distinguish a real elevated risk from chance.
explanations.b: A CI crossing 1 means the result is not statistically significant, which is different from proving the null is true — that requires a well-powered study with a narrow CI centered near 1.
explanations.c: A point estimate alone, without regard to its CI, cannot establish that an association is real or strong; the wide interval here shows substantial uncertainty.
explanations.d: Asymmetric CIs around a ratio point estimate are expected and correct, a direct consequence of computing the interval on the log scale before exponentiating back.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to construct a 95% confidence interval for an odds ratio.

items.text: Compute the point estimate OR from the 2x2 table
Take the natural log of the OR and compute its standard error on the log scale
Add and subtract 1.96 standard errors to get the log-scale interval bounds
Exponentiate both bounds to return to the OR scale

questions.explanation: The interval is built on the log scale because that is where the sampling distribution is approximately normal, then converted back to the interpretable ratio scale at the end.

questions.prompt: Match each CI scenario to its correct interpretation.

right.text: Statistically significant elevated risk, estimated precisely
Inconclusive: too little precision to detect an effect either way
Statistically significant protective association, estimated precisely

questions.explanation: Whether the interval excludes 1 determines statistical significance; how narrow it is separately determines how precisely the effect (if real) has been pinned down.

lessons.label: Sensitivity and Specificity

sections.heading: Reading the 2x2 in two directions
sections.body: Every diagnostic test can be scored against a reference standard (biopsy, culture, gold-standard imaging) in a 2x2 table with four cells: true positives (TP), false negatives (FN), false positives (FP), and true negatives (TN). Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) asks a question conditioned on people who are truly diseased: of everyone who actually has the condition, what fraction did the test catch? Specificity = TN/(TN+FP) asks the mirror question conditioned on people who are truly healthy: what fraction did the test correctly clear? Both denominators are defined by TRUE disease status, never by the test result, which is the detail students most often get backwards.

sections.heading: Why they don't move with prevalence
sections.body: Because sensitivity is computed only within the diseased row and specificity only within the healthy row, neither depends on how many diseased versus healthy people are in the sample. Run the same test on a high-prevalence hospital ward or a low-prevalence community screen and, aside from sampling noise, sensitivity and specificity stay put with respect to prevalence — the ratio of diseased to healthy people in the sample. This is what makes them the right numbers to report in a validation study, and it's the property predictive values (PPV, NPV) conspicuously lack. Prevalence-invariance is not the same as population-invariance, though. Sensitivity and specificity can still shift when the case-mix within the diseased or healthy group changes shape, even at identical prevalence — the classic example being spectrum bias (Ransohoff & Feinstein, NEJM, 1978). A test validated on a hospital ward full of advanced, symptomatic cases will often measure higher sensitivity than the same test applied to a population skewed toward early-stage or borderline disease, because early disease produces weaker signal regardless of how many diseased people are in the sample. So a reported sensitivity travels safely across settings that differ only in prevalence, but not across settings that differ in how severe or advanced the typical case is.

sections.heading: The tradeoff and the SnNout/SpPin shortcut
sections.body: For most tests, sensitivity and specificity trade off against each other at a single fixed cutoff: loosen the cutoff to catch more true cases and you also let in more false positives, raising sensitivity while lowering specificity, and vice versa. Clinicians popularized in evidence-based-medicine teaching (associated with Sackett's Clinical Epidemiology texts) use SnNout and SpPin as bedside shortcuts: with a highly SeNsitive test, a Negative result rules OUT disease (few false negatives to worry about); with a highly SPecific test, a Positive result rules IN disease (few false positives). Neither shortcut works well when the test's sensitivity and specificity are both mediocre.

lessons.workedExample: A rapid strep test has 85% sensitivity and 95% specificity. Among 200 kids with confirmed strep (by culture), the test correctly flags about 170 (TP) and misses 30 (FN) — sensitivity = 170/200 = 85%. Among 200 kids without strep, it correctly clears about 190 (TN) and falsely flags 10 (FP) — specificity = 190/200 = 95%. Because specificity is high, a positive rapid test is a fairly trustworthy SpPin rule-in; because sensitivity is only 85%, a negative rapid test still leaves real doubt, so clinics often culture-confirm negatives before ruling strep out.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge hearing 'our sensor detected 90% of contaminated samples' wants the paired specificity, not just one number, because a project can trivially hit near-100% sensitivity by flagging almost everything positive while specificity collapses. The tell of real understanding is stating both numbers, knowing they came from the diseased and healthy rows respectively, and being able to say whether the project's cutoff was chosen to favor SnNout or SpPin behavior and why that fits the use case.

questions.prompt: Sensitivity is calculated using which group as the denominator?

options.text: Everyone who tested positive
Everyone who is truly diseased
Everyone who is truly healthy
The entire sample regardless of status

explanations.a: That group (TP+FP) is the denominator for PPV, not sensitivity.
explanations.b: Correct: sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN), and TP+FN is exactly everyone with true disease.
explanations.c: That group (TN+FP) is the denominator for specificity, the mirror statistic.
explanations.d: Sensitivity conditions on true disease status only, not the whole sample.

questions.prompt: A test is moved from a hospital ward (high prevalence) to a community health fair (low prevalence). What happens to its sensitivity and specificity, aside from sampling noise?

options.text: Both rise substantially
Both fall substantially
Neither changes, because both are intrinsic to the test
Sensitivity falls while specificity rises

explanations.a: Sensitivity and specificity are not prevalence-dependent, so no systematic rise occurs.
explanations.b: Sensitivity and specificity are not prevalence-dependent, so no systematic fall occurs.
explanations.c: Correct: because each is computed within one true-status row, prevalence (the mix of rows) does not change either value.
explanations.d: There is no mechanism linking prevalence to a sensitivity/specificity split like this; predictive values, not these, move with prevalence.

questions.prompt: Match each mnemonic to what it lets you conclude.

right.text: A negative result on a highly sensitive test rules disease out
A positive result on a highly specific test rules disease in

questions.explanation: SnNout pairs high Sensitivity with a Negative result ruling disease out; SpPin pairs high Specificity with a Positive result ruling disease in.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to compute sensitivity and specificity from raw test results against a reference standard.

items.text: Classify every subject by the reference (gold) standard as truly diseased or truly healthy
Within the truly-diseased group, count how many tested positive (TP) versus negative (FN)
Within the truly-healthy group, count how many tested negative (TN) versus positive (FP)
Divide TP by (TP+FN) for sensitivity and TN by (TN+FP) for specificity

questions.explanation: You must fix true status first, then split each true-status group by test result, before the two ratios can be formed.

lessons.label: Predictive Values and Prevalence

sections.heading: The question a patient actually asks
sections.body: Sensitivity and specificity answer the researcher's question — given true status, what does the test show? A patient holding a positive result wants the reverse: given this result, what is my true status? That's positive predictive value, PPV = TP/(TP+FP), the share of all positive tests that are real. Negative predictive value, NPV = TN/(TN+FN), is its mirror: the share of all negative tests that are real. Unlike sensitivity and specificity, both denominators here are defined by the TEST result, not true status — which is exactly why prevalence enters the picture.

sections.heading: Bayes' theorem in disguise
sections.body: PPV is a Bayesian quantity: it's the posterior probability of disease given a positive test, and Bayes' theorem says a posterior always depends on the prior. The prior here is prevalence — the pre-test probability of disease in the population being tested. Holding sensitivity and specificity fixed, lowering prevalence shrinks the true-positive pool (fewer diseased people to catch) while the false-positive pool, drawn from a large healthy majority, barely shrinks — so PPV falls even though the test itself hasn't changed at all. This is the base-rate effect, and it is the single most common source of confusion when reading screening statistics.

sections.heading: Why the same test behaves differently in two settings
sections.body: A cardiologist ordering a troponin test on a patient already presenting with crushing chest pain is working at high pre-test probability; a positive result there is highly believable. Screen the same troponin test across a general asymptomatic population at near-zero prevalence and most positives will be false, even though sensitivity and specificity are identical in both settings. This is why population screening programs (mammography, PSA, newborn metabolic panels) build in confirmatory second-line testing before treatment — a positive screen is a prompt to investigate further, not a diagnosis. Population screening mammography is the standard teaching example: individual screens report sensitivity and specificity numbers in the 85-95% range, yet because breast cancer prevalence in the screened age range is low, the PPV of a single positive screening mammogram is commonly cited at only around 10% — meaning roughly nine out of ten women called back after an abnormal screen do not have cancer. That gap between a near-90% specificity headline and a roughly 10% PPV is exactly the base-rate effect in action, and it is precisely why an abnormal mammogram triggers diagnostic imaging and biopsy rather than immediate treatment: the screen narrows the population worth investigating further, it does not itself establish disease.

lessons.workedExample: Take a test with 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity applied to 10,000 people. At 1% prevalence: 100 truly diseased, 9,900 healthy. TP = 99, FN = 1; FP = 99, TN = 9,801. PPV = 99/(99+99) = 50%. Now raise prevalence to 10% (1,000 diseased, 9,000 healthy): TP = 990, FP = 90, so PPV = 990/1,080 ≈ 92%. Same test, same sensitivity and specificity, but PPV swings from a coin flip to near-certain purely because the pre-test prevalence changed tenfold.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student reports 'our test is 99% accurate' without ever stating the prevalence it was validated against — that phrase is close to meaningless without a base rate attached. The tell of real understanding is recomputing PPV at the prevalence relevant to the actual deployment population, not just quoting the manufacturer's sensitivity and specificity, and being able to explain why a rare-disease screen needs a confirmatory second test even when the screening test itself is excellent.

questions.prompt: A test with 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity is applied to a population at 1% prevalence. Roughly what is the PPV?

options.text: About 99%
About 50%
About 10%
About 1%

explanations.a: 99% is the specificity/sensitivity, not the PPV; at 1% prevalence the false positives roughly equal the true positives.
explanations.b: Correct, as shown in the worked example: TP=99 and FP=99 give PPV=50%.
explanations.c: 10% understates PPV here; at this sensitivity/specificity/prevalence combination the true and false positives are roughly equal, giving 50%, not 10%.
explanations.d: 1% would imply almost all positives are false, but the worked 2x2 table gives a 50/50 split, not this extreme.

questions.prompt: Why does PPV depend on prevalence while sensitivity and specificity do not?

options.text: Because PPV's denominator (all test positives) mixes true and false positives, whose relative sizes shift with how many diseased people exist
Because prevalence changes how accurately the test can detect disease at the molecular level
Because PPV is always computed from a different, smaller sample than sensitivity
Because sensitivity and specificity are estimated using different reference standards than PPV

explanations.a: Correct: PPV's denominator (TP+FP) is a test-result-defined mix whose composition changes as prevalence changes, unlike sensitivity/specificity's true-status-defined denominators.
explanations.b: Prevalence is a population property; it does not alter the test's intrinsic detection mechanism.
explanations.c: All four statistics can be computed from the same 2x2 table and the same sample.
explanations.d: The reference standard used to establish true status is the same one underlying every cell of the table, including PPV's.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning for why a highly accurate test can still have a low PPV in a rare disease.

items.text: Prevalence is very low, so the diseased group is small relative to the healthy group
Even with high specificity, applying a small false-positive rate to a very large healthy group yields many false positives in absolute terms
The small diseased group, even with high sensitivity, yields relatively few true positives in absolute terms
False positives end up comparable to or larger than true positives, dragging PPV down

questions.explanation: The base-rate effect works by comparing absolute counts: a rare disease means few true positives but the large healthy majority still yields a comparable number of false positives, together pulling PPV down.

questions.prompt: Match each predictive value to its formula.

right.text: TP / (TP + FP)
TN / (TN + FN)

questions.explanation: PPV conditions on all test positives; NPV conditions on all test negatives — both denominators are defined by test result, unlike sensitivity/specificity.

lessons.label: Likelihood Ratios and Post-Test Probability

sections.heading: A single number that stays constant across populations
sections.body: Likelihood ratios fix the awkward property of PPV: they combine sensitivity and specificity into a number that, like those two, is intrinsic to the test and does not shift with prevalence — yet it directly updates a patient's individual probability of disease. The positive likelihood ratio LR+ = sensitivity/(1−specificity) asks: how much more likely is a positive result in a diseased person than in a healthy one? The negative likelihood ratio LR− = (1−sensitivity)/specificity asks the mirror question for a negative result. LR+ values well above 1 (roughly 10+) and LR− values well below 1 (roughly 0.1 or less) are considered clinically powerful; an LR of 1 means the test result changed nothing. Most real tests land between these extremes, and the commonly taught scale (Jaeschke, Guyatt & Sackett, 'Users' Guides to the Medical Literature III,' JAMA, 1994) fills in that middle ground: LR+ of 5-10 or LR− of 0.1-0.2 produces a moderate, often clinically decisive shift in probability; LR+ of 2-5 or LR− of 0.2-0.5 produces a small shift that can still matter when combined with other findings; and LR+ or LR− within roughly 0.5-2 of 1 is treated as rarely important on its own. Reading a test's LR against this scale, rather than only checking whether it clears the 'powerful' bar, is what lets a clinician judge how much a middling test result is actually worth.

sections.heading: Turning ratios into probabilities: odds form of Bayes
sections.body: Likelihood ratios plug directly into Bayes' theorem written in odds form: post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR. Pre-test odds are converted from pre-test probability (prevalence, or clinical judgment) via odds = probability/(1−probability), and the resulting post-test odds convert back with probability = odds/(1+odds). Because this is a straight multiplication, LRs make it easy to see exactly how much a test result moved a clinician's belief, in a way a bare PPV number — computed only for one fixed prevalence — cannot.

sections.heading: The Fagan nomogram and chaining tests
sections.body: Fagan (1975) published a graphical shortcut — a nomogram with three parallel scales for pre-test probability, likelihood ratio, and post-test probability — so a clinician can draw one straight line and read off the answer without doing the odds arithmetic by hand; it remains a staple of bedside teaching. LRs also chain: because sequential, reasonably independent tests each multiply the running odds by their own LR, a clinician can combine a history finding, an exam sign, and a lab result into one cumulative post-test probability — something PPV, being tied to a single fixed prevalence, cannot do without being recomputed from scratch at every step.

lessons.workedExample: A test has sensitivity 90% and specificity 80%, so LR+ = 0.90/0.20 = 4.5 and LR− = 0.10/0.80 = 0.125. A patient's pre-test probability is 20% (pre-test odds = 0.2/0.8 = 0.25). A positive result gives post-test odds = 0.25 × 4.5 = 1.125, which converts to probability = 1.125/2.125 ≈ 53%. A negative result instead gives post-test odds = 0.25 × 0.125 = 0.03, or about 3% probability — the same test result pushes belief in opposite directions by very different amounts depending on the LR used.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'how much did this test result actually change your confidence?' is testing whether a student can move past a single PPV snapshot to the general Bayesian update — computing an LR, applying it to whatever pre-test probability the project's real subjects had, and reporting a post-test probability rather than reusing the validation-study PPV as if it applied unchanged to a different population.

questions.prompt: Why do researchers prefer likelihood ratios over PPV when describing a test's diagnostic value in general?

options.text: LRs are always larger numbers and easier to report
LRs, like sensitivity and specificity, do not depend on prevalence, so one LR value applies across populations
LRs eliminate the need for a reference standard
LRs measure something unrelated to sensitivity and specificity

explanations.a: LR size has no bearing on why they are preferred; some LRs are less than 1.
explanations.b: Correct: LRs are built entirely from sensitivity and specificity, so they stay constant as prevalence changes, unlike PPV.
explanations.c: A reference standard is still required to establish sensitivity and specificity, which LRs are built from.
explanations.d: LR+ and LR− are direct algebraic combinations of sensitivity and specificity, not something separate.

questions.prompt: A test result yields a likelihood ratio of exactly 1. What does this mean?

options.text: The test is perfectly accurate
The result does not change the pre-test probability at all
The test has 100% specificity
The disease is certain regardless of the result

explanations.a: An LR of 1 signals a useless result, the opposite of high accuracy.
explanations.b: Correct: multiplying pre-test odds by 1 leaves post-test odds, and therefore post-test probability, unchanged.
explanations.c: An LR of 1 could arise from many sensitivity/specificity combinations; it does not imply perfect specificity.
explanations.d: An LR of 1 means the result carries no diagnostic information, not that disease is certain.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to go from pre-test probability to post-test probability using a likelihood ratio.

items.text: Convert pre-test probability to pre-test odds: odds = p/(1-p)
Multiply pre-test odds by the likelihood ratio (LR+ or LR-) for the observed result
This product is the post-test odds
Convert post-test odds back to probability: p = odds/(1+odds)

questions.explanation: Bayes' theorem in odds form requires converting to odds first, applying the LR as a multiplier, then converting the result back to a probability.

questions.prompt: Match each likelihood ratio formula to its definition.

right.text: sensitivity / (1 - specificity)
(1 - sensitivity) / specificity

questions.explanation: LR+ compares the chance of a positive result in diseased vs. healthy people; LR- compares the chance of a negative result in diseased vs. healthy people.

lessons.label: ROC Curves and Cutoff Choice

sections.heading: One test, many possible cutoffs
sections.body: Any test that reports a continuous number (a biomarker level, a risk score, a pixel-intensity threshold) isn't really one test — it's a family of possible tests, one for every choice of cutoff separating 'positive' from 'negative.' Lower the cutoff and sensitivity rises (you catch more true cases) while specificity falls (you also flag more healthy people); raise it and the reverse happens. A receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plots this whole family at once: sensitivity on the y-axis against 1−specificity (the false-positive rate) on the x-axis, one point per cutoff, traced from the most lenient cutoff to the most strict.

sections.heading: Area under the curve as overall discrimination
sections.body: The area under the ROC curve (AUC) summarizes how well the test separates diseased from healthy people across every possible cutoff, independent of which one you'd actually use. AUC has a clean probabilistic meaning: it equals the probability that a randomly chosen diseased person's test value is ranked higher than a randomly chosen healthy person's. An AUC of 0.5 traces the diagonal line — pure chance, no better than a coin flip — while 1.0 is perfect separation; AUCs in the 0.7–0.9 range are typical for genuinely useful clinical biomarkers, and values much above 0.9 are unusual outside near-diagnostic tests. A single AUC value on its own doesn't say whether one test meaningfully outperforms another, though — that requires a confidence interval or a formal comparison. The standard approach for two ROC curves measured on the same patients (correlated data, since both tests were run on the same people) is the method of DeLong et al. (1988), which accounts for that correlation when testing whether the difference in AUC is statistically significant; treating the two curves as independent samples would overstate the uncertainty and risk missing a real difference. Reporting an AUC with its confidence interval, rather than as a bare point estimate, is what lets a reader judge whether 0.82 versus 0.78 reflects a real improvement or just noise.

sections.heading: Picking one point: the Youden index
sections.body: AUC compares whole tests to each other but doesn't tell you where to actually set the cutoff for use. The Youden index, J = sensitivity + specificity − 1, is maximized at the ROC point farthest above the diagonal (chance) line, and picking the cutoff that maximizes J is a common default when false positives and false negatives are considered equally costly. But that default is often wrong in practice: a screen for a disease with harmless false positives but catastrophic missed cases (an aggressive cancer) should deliberately choose a more lenient cutoff than the Youden-optimal one, trading some specificity for higher sensitivity, and vice versa when false positives trigger risky confirmatory procedures.

lessons.workedExample: A biomarker test evaluated at five cutoffs gives these (1-specificity, sensitivity) points: (0.05, 0.40), (0.15, 0.70), (0.30, 0.85), (0.50, 0.92), (0.80, 0.98). Youden's J at each is 0.35, 0.55, 0.55, 0.42, and 0.18 respectively — the two middle cutoffs tie for the highest J, both trading roughly 15-30% false positives for 70-85% sensitivity. Trapezoidal AUC across these points and the endpoints (0,0) and (1,1) comes out around 0.84, indicating a genuinely useful but imperfect test, well above the 0.5 chance diagonal.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe ROC/AUC claims because 'our model has 95% accuracy' is often reported at a single, arbitrarily chosen cutoff, hiding how the model performs everywhere else and what the cutoff decision actually cost in false positives or false negatives. The strong answer states the AUC as an overall discrimination summary, explains why the working cutoff was NOT simply the Youden-maximizing point if the false-positive and false-negative costs were asymmetric, and justifies that tradeoff explicitly.

questions.prompt: What does an AUC of 0.5 on an ROC curve indicate?

options.text: The test perfectly separates diseased from healthy people
The test performs no better than random chance at ranking diseased above healthy
The test has 50% sensitivity at every cutoff
The test's specificity equals its sensitivity

explanations.a: Perfect separation corresponds to an AUC of 1.0, not 0.5.
explanations.b: Correct: an AUC of 0.5 traces the diagonal chance line, meaning a diseased person's value is no more likely to rank above a healthy person's than a coin flip.
explanations.c: AUC is a probability across all cutoffs, not a statement about sensitivity at any single cutoff.
explanations.d: An AUC of 0.5 says nothing specific about where sensitivity equals specificity; that can happen at any AUC.

questions.prompt: A disease screen has cheap, harmless false positives but a very costly consequence for false negatives (a missed aggressive cancer). Relative to the Youden-optimal cutoff, the chosen operating cutoff should generally be:

options.text: More lenient, accepting lower specificity for higher sensitivity
More strict, accepting lower sensitivity for higher specificity
Exactly at the Youden-optimal point regardless of costs
Chosen to maximize AUC directly

explanations.a: Correct: when missed cases are far costlier than false alarms, sensitivity should be favored, which means a more lenient cutoff than the cost-neutral Youden point.
explanations.b: This would increase missed cases, the opposite of what the cost asymmetry calls for.
explanations.c: The Youden index assumes equal costs for false positives and false negatives; asymmetric costs justify moving off that point.
explanations.d: AUC is a whole-curve summary and is not something a single cutoff choice can 'maximize' — it's fixed once the test is fixed.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to build an ROC curve and pick a Youden-optimal cutoff.

items.text: Compute sensitivity and 1-specificity at many possible cutoffs of the continuous test score
Plot sensitivity against 1-specificity for each cutoff to trace the ROC curve
Compute Youden's J = sensitivity + specificity - 1 at each cutoff
Select the cutoff with the maximum J as the Youden-optimal operating point

questions.explanation: The curve is built from per-cutoff sensitivity/specificity pairs, plotted, then J is computed per cutoff to locate the point farthest from the chance diagonal.

questions.prompt: Match each ROC-related quantity to what it represents.

right.text: Overall discrimination across all cutoffs
sensitivity + specificity - 1, maximized at one cutoff
The false-positive rate plotted on the x-axis

questions.explanation: AUC summarizes the whole curve, Youden's J locates a single best-tradeoff cutoff on it, and 1-specificity is the x-axis quantity the curve is plotted against.

lessons.label: Screening Program Biases

sections.heading: Lead-time bias: moving the clock, not the outcome
sections.body: Screening finds disease earlier than it would present clinically, so the interval between diagnosis and death — the number typically reported as '5-year survival' — stretches even if the actual date of death never moves. A cancer diagnosed by screening five years before it would otherwise have caused symptoms, and that still kills the patient on schedule, shows a five-year survival improvement that reflects nothing but an earlier diagnosis. This is lead-time bias, and it means survival-time comparisons between screened and unscreened patients are unreliable evidence of benefit; only trials that track mortality from a fixed starting point (like randomization), not diagnosis, can separate a real benefit from a lead-time artifact.

sections.heading: Length-time bias and the slow-tumor problem
sections.body: Screening tests sample the population at intervals, so they are far more likely to catch a slow-growing tumor, which sits in a long detectable-but-asymptomatic window, than a fast, aggressive one that appears and causes symptoms between two scheduled screens (an 'interval cancer'). This skews the population of screen-detected cases toward the more indolent, better-prognosis disease, making screening look more effective than it is even without any lead-time effect. The extreme version of length-time bias is overdiagnosis: detecting a real tumor that was never going to progress, grow, or cause harm in the patient's remaining lifetime. Autopsy studies have long found undiagnosed, clinically silent prostate cancer in a substantial share of older men who died of unrelated causes — those tumors, had they been screen-detected and treated, would count as a 'cure' with zero actual lives saved.

sections.heading: The healthy-screenee effect and deciding whether to screen at all
sections.body: People who volunteer for optional screening tend to be more health-conscious, better resourced, and generally healthier at baseline than non-participants, so comparing screened volunteers to the general population — instead of to a randomized control group — biases outcomes favorably regardless of whether the test does anything. Because all three biases can manufacture the appearance of benefit from a program that does nothing, or even harms via overdiagnosis and overtreatment, Wilson and Jungner (1968), in a WHO monograph, laid out roughly ten criteria for whether a disease is worth screening at all: it must be an important health problem with a well-understood natural history and a detectable latent stage, an acceptable and accurate test must exist, an effective treatment for early-detected disease must exist, and treating early must be shown advantageous over treating at usual clinical presentation — a criterion overdiagnosis and lead-time bias make deceptively hard to actually demonstrate.

lessons.workedExample: Disease X is always fatal exactly 10 years after the first detectable cell exists, regardless of when treatment starts (a worst-case, purely illustrative scenario). Unscreened, symptoms appear at year 8 and death at year 10 — 2-year survival from diagnosis. A screening program detects it at year 3 instead; death still occurs at year 10, but survival from diagnosis is now reported as 7 years. Five-year survival statistics would show a dramatic 'improvement' from screening even though not a single day of life was actually extended — pure lead-time bias, only unmasked by comparing mortality rates (deaths per person-year in the population) between randomized screened and unscreened arms, not survival time among the diagnosed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A project claiming a diagnostic tool 'improves survival' is making one of the most commonly misused claims in screening research, and a judge who asks 'survival from what starting point, and compared to what control?' is checking whether the student can distinguish a real mortality reduction from lead-time or length-time artifacts, and whether they know overdiagnosis is a real harm, not just a hypothetical, that any new early-detection tool must be evaluated against.
