questions.prompt: A new screening test increases the reported 5-year survival rate for a cancer, but a randomized trial shows no change in the disease's mortality rate. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The test is highly effective but survival statistics undercount its benefit
Lead-time and/or length-time bias inflated the survival statistic without any real mortality benefit
The randomized trial must have been underpowered
Survival rate and mortality rate always move together, so this pattern is impossible

explanations.a: If a real benefit existed, the randomized mortality comparison — the more reliable measure — would be expected to show it too.
explanations.b: Correct: this exact mismatch (survival up, mortality flat) is the classic signature of lead-time and length-time bias distorting the survival statistic.
explanations.c: An underpowered trial would more likely show an uncertain result, not a clean flat mortality line contradicted by a clear survival rise.
explanations.d: This pattern is exactly what these biases are known to produce, so it is not impossible; that's the whole point of using mortality trials as the standard.

questions.prompt: Length-time bias causes screening programs to preferentially detect which kind of tumor?

options.text: Fast-growing, aggressive tumors that would present clinically between screens
Slow-growing, indolent tumors with a long detectable asymptomatic window
Tumors of a specific tissue type unrelated to growth rate
Only tumors that have already caused symptoms

explanations.a: Fast tumors are more likely to be missed by periodic screening and instead show up as interval cancers between scheduled screens.
explanations.b: Correct: a slow-growing tumor spends more calendar time in the detectable-but-asymptomatic window that a periodic screen can catch, so screening over-represents these.
explanations.c: Length-time bias is specifically about growth rate and time-in-detectable-window, not tissue type.
explanations.d: Screening targets asymptomatic, not already-symptomatic, disease by definition.

questions.prompt: Order these from the concept about DIAGNOSIS TIMING, to the concept about TUMOR GROWTH RATE, to the concept about WHO VOLUNTEERS, to the criteria for whether to screen at all.

items.text: Lead-time bias
Length-time bias / overdiagnosis
Healthy-screenee (volunteer) effect
Wilson and Jungner (1968) screening criteria

questions.explanation: Lead-time bias is about when diagnosis happens; length-time bias/overdiagnosis is about which tumors get caught given growth rate; the healthy-screenee effect is about who chooses to participate; the Wilson and Jungner criteria are the overarching framework for judging whether a screening program is worthwhile at all.

questions.prompt: Match each bias or effect to its description.

right.text: Diagnosis moves earlier but the death date is unchanged, inflating apparent survival
A detected tumor was never going to cause symptoms or death in the patient's lifetime
Screening volunteers are healthier at baseline than the general population, biasing outcome comparisons

questions.explanation: All three inflate the apparent benefit of screening through a different mechanism: timing, tumor biology, and participant selection respectively.

lessons.label: Method Agreement: Bland-Altman and Kappa

sections.heading: Why a high correlation is not agreement
sections.body: When comparing a new measurement method against an established one (a cheap home blood-pressure cuff versus an arterial line, a new assay versus a reference lab test), a strong Pearson correlation coefficient feels like proof they agree — but correlation only measures whether two methods move together in the same direction, not whether they give the same VALUE. A new device that reads consistently 20 mmHg higher than the reference at every level will still correlate at r near 1.0, because the relationship is still perfectly linear; correlation is blind to a constant or scaling offset that would make the new device clinically useless. Bland and Altman (1986), in a widely cited Lancet paper, argued correlation is the wrong tool for method-comparison studies entirely.

sections.heading: The Bland-Altman plot and limits of agreement
sections.body: Their alternative plots, for each subject, the difference between the two methods (method A minus method B) on the y-axis against the mean of the two methods on the x-axis. The average difference across all subjects is the bias — a systematic offset between methods — and the spread of points around that average is scored with limits of agreement, set at the mean difference ± 1.96 times the standard deviation of the differences, which should contain about 95% of the differences if they're roughly normally distributed. A clinician (or protocol) then judges whether that spread is small enough to use the two methods interchangeably — a judgment call with no universal cutoff, unlike a hypothesis test's p-value.

sections.heading: Cohen's kappa for categorical agreement
sections.body: When the measurement is categorical rather than continuous — two radiologists each calling a scan 'positive' or 'negative,' two raters each staging a tumor — plain percent agreement is misleading because two raters can agree often purely by chance, especially when one category is common. Cohen (1960) proposed kappa = (observed agreement − expected agreement by chance) / (1 − expected agreement by chance), which corrects for exactly that chance component; kappa = 0 means agreement is no better than chance, kappa = 1 means perfect agreement, and negative values mean agreement is worse than chance. Landis and Koch's commonly cited (though somewhat arbitrary) benchmarks label 0.61–0.80 as 'substantial' agreement and above 0.80 as 'almost perfect,' with anything below 0.40 flagged as poor enough to question the rating protocol itself.

lessons.workedExample: Two raters classify 100 chest X-rays as pneumonia-present or -absent. They agree on 85 (percent agreement 85%), but by chance alone, given each rater calls 'present' on 40% and 50% of scans respectively, expected chance agreement works out to about 0.4×0.5 + 0.6×0.5 = 0.50, or 50%. Kappa = (0.85 − 0.50) / (1 − 0.50) = 0.70 — 'substantial' agreement by the Landis-Koch labels, meaningfully lower than the raw 85% figure suggested because a sizable share of that raw agreement was chance-driven given how common 'present' calls were for both raters.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge seeing 'our new low-cost sensor correlates with the lab reference at r=0.97' should ask for a Bland-Altman plot, because that correlation alone cannot rule out a systematic offset that would make every reading clinically wrong in the same direction; for categorical calls, a judge asking 'what's your kappa, not just percent agreement' is checking whether the student knows raw agreement inflates apparent reliability whenever one category dominates.

questions.prompt: Two measurement methods have a Pearson correlation of r=0.98, but one method reads consistently 15 units higher than the other at every level. What does the correlation coefficient fail to detect?

options.text: That the two methods are unrelated
The systematic offset (bias) between the two methods
That the sample size was too small
That the data is not normally distributed

explanations.a: High correlation actually shows they are strongly linearly related, which is why it can mislead about agreement.
explanations.b: Correct: correlation captures whether values move together, not whether they are numerically equal, so a constant offset can coexist with a near-perfect correlation.
explanations.c: Sample size affects the precision of the correlation estimate, not this specific offset blind spot.
explanations.d: Distributional shape is a separate issue from the offset problem correlation ignores.

questions.prompt: In a Bland-Altman plot, the limits of agreement are typically calculated as:

options.text: The mean difference plus or minus 1.96 standard deviations of the differences
The Pearson correlation coefficient plus or minus its standard error
The range from the minimum to the maximum observed difference
The mean of method A plus or minus the mean of method B

explanations.a: Correct: mean difference ± 1.96 SD of the differences is the standard limits-of-agreement formula, capturing about 95% of differences under normality.
explanations.b: Bland-Altman analysis deliberately avoids relying on the correlation coefficient at all.
explanations.c: The min/max range is not the standard limits-of-agreement calculation, which is based on the mean and SD of differences.
explanations.d: This mixes the two methods' means rather than using the differences between paired measurements, which is what the plot is built from.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to compute Cohen's kappa for two raters' categorical calls.

items.text: Tabulate the raters' calls in a 2x2 (or larger) agreement table
Compute observed agreement as the proportion of cases both raters agreed on
Compute expected chance agreement from each rater's marginal category rates
Compute kappa = (observed - expected) / (1 - expected)

questions.explanation: Kappa requires the raw agreement table first, then observed agreement, then the chance-expected agreement from the marginals, before the correction formula can be applied.

questions.prompt: Match each method-agreement tool to the data type and question it is built for.

right.text: Continuous measurements: is there a systematic bias or excessive spread between two methods?
Categorical calls: do two raters agree more than chance alone would predict?

questions.explanation: Bland-Altman handles paired continuous measurements via differences and limits of agreement; kappa handles categorical ratings via chance-corrected agreement.

lessons.label: Selection Bias

sections.heading: Berkson's Bias: When the Sample Itself Distorts Cause and Effect
sections.body: In 1946, biostatistician Joseph Berkson showed that studies drawing both cases and controls from hospitalized patients can manufacture an association between two diseases that are unrelated in the general population. Hospitalization depends on more than one condition -- a person is more likely to be admitted if they have either disease A or disease B, and more likely still if they have both. Restricting the sample to hospitalized patients conditions on hospitalization, a variable influenced by both diseases. In causal-graph terms, hospitalization is a collider on the path between disease A and disease B; conditioning on a collider opens a spurious statistical path between its two causes even though neither causes the other. The result: a case-control study built entirely from inpatients can report an odds ratio linking two diseases that would vanish if community-based controls were used instead.

sections.heading: The Healthy-Worker Effect
sections.body: Occupational cohort studies routinely compare disease or mortality rates among workers to rates in the general population, but people who are employed and remain employed are, on average, healthier than the general population, which includes the disabled, chronically ill, and those unemployed for health reasons. This 'healthy-worker effect' biases occupational mortality comparisons toward showing workers as healthier than the public even when their jobs involve genuine hazards -- asbestos and radiation cohorts have shown lower all-cause mortality than the general population despite documented excess cancer risk, because the healthy-worker effect and the hazard's true effect point in opposite directions and partly cancel. The standard fix is to compare exposed workers to unexposed workers from the same industry, not to the general population, removing the built-in health advantage of simply holding a job.

sections.heading: Volunteer Bias and Differential Loss to Follow-Up
sections.body: People who volunteer for research differ systematically from those who do not -- typically healthier, more educated, and more health-conscious -- so studies built on volunteers can show falsely protective associations. Observational cohorts of hormone replacement therapy in the 1980s-90s found lower heart disease among users, partly because health-conscious volunteers were more likely to both take hormones and adopt other protective behaviors; the randomized Women's Health Initiative trial (2002) reversed this, finding increased cardiovascular risk once randomization removed the selection. Differential loss to follow-up causes a related distortion after enrollment: if a drug's side effects cause sicker exposed participants to drop out at a higher rate than unexposed participants, the exposed group remaining at study's end is a healthier, biased subset, understating the drug's true harm.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose diabetes and gallbladder disease are causally unrelated in the community, each carried by 5% of people, giving a true odds ratio of 1.0. But a hospital admits patients more readily if they have either condition: baseline admission risk is 2%, rising to 10% with diabetes alone, 10% with gallbladder disease alone, and 40% with both, since either condition can trigger admission and having both raises the chance further. In a population of 10,000, that yields 10 hospitalized with both conditions, 47.5 hospitalized with gallbladder disease alone, 47.5 hospitalized with diabetes alone, and 180.5 hospitalized with neither. A case-control study restricted to hospitalized patients -- using hospitalized non-gallbladder patients as controls for gallbladder cases -- gives OR = (10x180.5)/(47.5x47.5) = 0.80, deflating the apparent diabetes-gallbladder odds ratio to well below 1.0, an apparent protective association where none exists, purely from conditioning on admission: Berkson's original 1946 point, where hospital-based diabetes and cholecystitis patients showed a spurious negative association.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who spots 'all our subjects came from the pediatric oncology ward' or 'we recruited by asking gym members' is testing whether the presenter can name why that sampling frame threatens the causal claim, not just gesture at 'a limitation.' The tell of understanding is naming the mechanism -- a collider like hospitalization, or a selection factor like employment or volunteering -- and stating which direction it pushes the estimate, then naming a fix: population-based controls, or an internal unexposed comparison group instead of the general population.

questions.prompt: Why does restricting a case-control study to hospitalized patients risk creating a spurious association between two unrelated diseases?

options.text: Hospitalization is a collider: conditioning on it opens a statistical path between its independent causes
Hospitals measure diseases less accurately than community clinics
Hospitalized patients are randomly assigned to disease categories
Hospital records are smaller samples, so the effect is just low statistical power

explanations.a: Correct: Berkson showed hospitalization is influenced by both diseases, and conditioning on this shared effect (a collider) induces an association between them that need not exist in the population.
explanations.b: This is a bias of sample selection, not a measurement-accuracy problem; the diseases can be diagnosed perfectly and the bias still appears.
explanations.c: The problem is exactly that hospitalization is NOT independent of disease status -- patients with either disease are admitted more often.
explanations.d: Small samples cause imprecision, not a systematic, directional bias like Berkson's.

questions.prompt: An occupational cohort study finds lower all-cause mortality among asbestos-exposed factory workers than in the general population, despite known excess cancer risk from asbestos. What best explains this?

options.text: Asbestos exposure is protective against most other causes of death
The healthy-worker effect: employed people are inherently healthier than the general population, masking the hazard's true effect
The general population comparison group had differential loss to follow-up
Volunteer bias inflated the workers' reported health status

explanations.a: Asbestos is a documented carcinogen; the lower overall mortality is a sampling artifact, not a real protective effect.
explanations.b: Correct: people who hold jobs are selected for baseline health, so worker cohorts start out healthier than a general population that includes the disabled and chronically ill, partly canceling the true excess risk.
explanations.c: Differential loss to follow-up refers to biased dropout during the study, not the baseline selection of who becomes a worker in the first place.
explanations.d: Volunteer bias concerns self-selection into a study, distinct from the structural selection built into having employment.

questions.prompt: Order the steps by which Berkson's bias produces a spurious hospital-based association.

items.text: Two diseases are causally unrelated in the community
Each disease independently raises the chance of hospital admission
A study samples only hospitalized patients, conditioning on admission
An association between the two diseases appears in the sample that is absent in the community

questions.explanation: The bias starts from true independence, requires each disease to influence admission, is triggered by restricting the sample to the admitted, and manifests as a spurious association only inside that restricted sample.

questions.prompt: Match each selection bias to the scenario that illustrates it.

right.text: Hospital-based controls create a spurious link between two unrelated diseases
Sicker drug-treated participants drop out of a trial more often than untreated participants
Occupational cohorts appear healthier than the general population regardless of workplace hazards
Early hormone-therapy cohorts of health-conscious enrollees showed falsely protective results later reversed by a randomized trial

questions.explanation: Each bias has a distinct entry point into the study: Berkson's bias at the sampling frame (hospitalization), the healthy-worker effect at baseline employment status, volunteer bias at enrollment, and differential loss to follow-up during the study itself.

lessons.label: Information and Misclassification Bias

sections.heading: Recall Bias and Interviewer Bias
sections.body: In case-control studies, people who already have a diagnosis often search their memory more thoroughly for a cause than healthy controls do -- a mother of a child born with a birth defect is more likely to recall a viral illness or medication taken early in pregnancy than a mother of a healthy child, even if true exposure rates were identical. This recall bias is a form of differential misclassification driven by the outcome itself. A related distortion, interviewer bias, arises when interviewers who know a subject's case or control status probe cases more persistently or record ambiguous answers differently. Both are minimized by blinding interviewers to case status and by using pre-existing records, such as pharmacy or medical charts, instead of self-report wherever those records exist.

sections.heading: Measurement Error and the Gold-Standard Problem
sections.body: Beyond memory, exposure and outcome measures carry ordinary measurement error: self-reported diet, activity questionnaires, and even blood-pressure cuffs vary from a true 'gold standard' value. Because every classification tool has some error, epidemiologists assess the sensitivity and specificity of the exposure or outcome measure itself, not just of a diagnostic test. A concrete case: a single clinic blood-pressure reading, validated against 24-hour ambulatory monitoring (the gold standard for true hypertensive status), typically shows sensitivity around 75% and specificity around 85% -- meaning roughly one in four truly hypertensive patients is missed by the clinic reading alone, and about one in seven normotensive patients is wrongly flagged as hypertensive. A hypertension-outcome study that classifies exposure status from single clinic readings therefore starts with a meaningful, quantifiable measurement-error problem before any confounding or selection issue even enters the analysis. Repeated measurements, objective biomarkers such as urinary sodium in place of self-reported salt intake, and validation substudies that compare an instrument against a gold standard let researchers estimate, and sometimes statistically correct for, this error rather than simply assume it away.

sections.heading: Non-Differential vs Differential Misclassification
sections.body: Misclassification is non-differential when the error rate in classifying exposure or outcome is the same across the comparison groups -- for example, a diet questionnaire that misclassifies true low-fat and high-fat eaters equally often regardless of disease status. For a binary exposure and binary outcome, non-differential misclassification predictably biases the measure of association toward the null (a risk ratio or odds ratio closer to 1.0), diluting a real effect rather than fabricating one. Misclassification is differential when the error rate depends on the other variable -- recall bias is the canonical example, since cases and controls report past exposure with different accuracy. Differential misclassification can push the estimate in either direction, toward or away from the null, and is harder to predict or correct after the fact.

lessons.workedExample: Take 200 cases and 200 controls with a true exposure-disease odds ratio of 3.0: 100 of 200 cases truly exposed, 50 of 200 controls truly exposed (OR = (100x150)/(100x50) = 3.0). Now apply a non-differential exposure questionnaire with 80% sensitivity and 80% specificity, equally inaccurate in both groups. Observed exposed cases = (100x0.8)+(100x0.2) = 100; observed exposed controls = (50x0.8)+(150x0.2) = 70. The observed OR = (100x130)/(100x70) = 1.86 -- diluted from the true 3.0 toward the null of 1.0, purely from equal-rate measurement error, with no change to who was actually exposed.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe how exposure data was collected -- self-report versus objective record -- and whether the presenter assessed whether resulting error was likely differential (a real recall-bias risk in a case-control design comparing cases to controls) or non-differential (the same instrument applied blind to outcome status everywhere). The tell of understanding is stating the predicted direction of bias -- non-differential error dilutes toward the null, so a genuinely null result is less reassuring, while differential error could go either way and cannot be assumed away.

questions.prompt: A study uses the same imperfect exposure questionnaire for both cases and controls, with equal accuracy in each group. What is the expected effect on a true binary exposure-disease odds ratio of 3.0?

options.text: The observed OR is biased toward the null, landing somewhere between 1.0 and 3.0
The observed OR is biased away from the null, landing above 3.0
The observed OR is unaffected, since the questionnaire is applied equally
The direction of bias cannot be predicted without knowing which group had more errors

explanations.a: Correct: non-differential misclassification of a binary exposure predictably dilutes the association toward 1.0, as shown when the true OR of 3.0 fell to 1.86 under equal 80%/80% sensitivity and specificity.
explanations.b: Non-differential error dilutes associations; it does not exaggerate them.
explanations.c: Equal error rates still shift some truly exposed and unexposed subjects into the wrong category in both groups, changing the observed cell counts and the OR.
explanations.d: The direction is predictable precisely because the error rate is equal (non-differential) in both groups -- differential error is the case where direction becomes unpredictable.

questions.prompt: Mothers of children with birth defects recall prenatal illnesses and medications more thoroughly than mothers of healthy children, even when true exposure rates are equal. This is best classified as:

options.text: Non-differential misclassification, since both groups answer the same questionnaire
Differential misclassification (recall bias), since accuracy depends on case status
Confounding, since a third variable explains the association
Selection bias, since it concerns who enters the study

explanations.a: Using the same questionnaire does not make misclassification non-differential; what matters is whether the resulting accuracy differs by case status, and here it does.
explanations.b: Correct: recall accuracy differs between cases and controls because the diagnosis itself prompts more thorough memory search, making this differential misclassification.
explanations.c: Confounding involves a third variable associated with exposure and outcome; recall bias is an information-collection problem, not a third-variable problem.
explanations.d: Selection bias concerns who is sampled into the study; recall bias concerns the accuracy of information collected from subjects already in the study.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to show how non-differential exposure misclassification dilutes an odds ratio.

items.text: Start from true exposure counts in cases and controls and compute the true OR
Apply the same sensitivity and specificity of the exposure measure to both groups
Recompute the observed exposed and unexposed counts in each group
Compute the observed OR and compare it to the true OR

questions.explanation: Demonstrating dilution requires a true baseline OR, applying an equal error rate to both groups, recomputing the resulting misclassified counts, and only then comparing observed to true.

questions.prompt: Match each information-bias concept to its description.

right.text: Cases remember past exposures more thoroughly than controls because of their diagnosis
An interviewer who knows case status probes cases more persistently than controls
Error rate is equal across comparison groups and typically biases toward the null
Error rate differs across comparison groups and can bias in either direction

questions.explanation: Recall bias and interviewer bias are specific mechanisms that produce differential misclassification; the last two rows define the general categories those mechanisms fall under.

lessons.label: Confounding: The Third Variable

sections.heading: The Three Criteria for a Confounder
sections.body: A variable is a confounder of an exposure-outcome relationship only if it satisfies three conditions simultaneously. First, it must be statistically associated with the exposure in the source population -- not necessarily causing the exposure, just co-occurring with it. Second, it must be an independent risk factor for the outcome among people who are unexposed -- its effect on the outcome cannot come solely through the exposure itself. Third, it must not lie on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome -- it cannot be a consequence of the exposure that then goes on to cause the disease. All three must hold; a variable associated with exposure but unrelated to outcome, or one that is itself caused by the exposure, does not qualify, even if adjusting for it happens to change a risk estimate.

sections.heading: Confounding vs. Mediation: the Third Criterion is the Hard One
sections.body: The first two criteria are usually easy to check with data; the third -- not on the causal pathway -- requires substantive, non-statistical knowledge of biology or mechanism, and is where confounding is most often confused with mediation. A mediator sits between exposure and outcome on the same causal chain: smoking causes tar and carcinogen deposition in lung tissue, which causes the DNA damage that becomes lung cancer, so lung tar deposits are a mediator of the smoking-lung cancer effect, not a confounder. Adjusting for a mediator statistically blocks part of the very pathway being studied, producing over-adjustment bias -- shrinking or erasing a real effect rather than correcting a spurious one. Deciding whether a third variable is a confounder to remove or a mediator to leave alone requires a causal model of the disease process, not just a low p-value.

sections.heading: Worked Case: Alcohol, Smoking, and Lung Cancer
sections.body: Heavy alcohol drinkers show a higher crude rate of lung cancer than light drinkers, but heavy drinkers are also disproportionately smokers, and smoking is a well-established independent cause of lung cancer even among nondrinkers. Smoking meets all three confounding criteria for the alcohol-lung cancer association: it is associated with alcohol use (criterion 1), it independently raises lung cancer risk regardless of drinking (criterion 2), and it is not a downstream consequence of alcohol nor a step alcohol must pass through to reach the lungs (criterion 3). Alcohol itself largely fails criterion 2 for lung cancer once smoking is accounted for, meaning the original crude association was substantially confounded rather than causal -- a textbook illustration of why 'associated with the outcome' is meaningless without asking whether a third variable produced the whole story.

lessons.workedExample: Among 1,000 heavy drinkers, lung cancer incidence is 32 per 1,000; among 1,000 light drinkers, it is 14 per 1,000, giving a crude relative risk of 2.29. But 60% of heavy drinkers smoke versus only 20% of light drinkers. Stratifying by smoking status: among smokers, lung cancer incidence is 50 per 1,000 regardless of drinking level; among nonsmokers, it is 5 per 1,000 regardless of drinking level -- so heavy drinkers' crude rate is (600x50 + 400x5)/1,000 = 32 per 1,000, and light drinkers' crude rate is (200x50 + 800x5)/1,000 = 14 per 1,000. The stratum-specific relative risk for heavy versus light drinking is 1.0 within smokers and 1.0 within nonsmokers -- the entire crude RR of 2.29 is explained by heavy drinkers being more often smokers, unmasking smoking, not alcohol, as the true cause.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a presenter checked their claimed exposure-outcome link for a lurking third variable that tracks with both -- a science-fair project linking screen time to poor grades must rule out household income, which is associated with screen time and independently predicts grades regardless of screen time. The tell of understanding is naming a specific, plausible confounder, showing it meets the three criteria rather than just asserting 'there could be confounders,' and describing how it was measured or adjusted for in the analysis.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the three required criteria for a variable to be a confounder?

options.text: It is associated with the exposure in the source population
It is an independent risk factor for the outcome among the unexposed
It produces a large, statistically significant change in the risk estimate when added to a model
It does not lie on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome

explanations.a: This is the first criterion: association with the exposure.
explanations.b: This is the second criterion: an independent effect on the outcome, not mediated through the exposure.
explanations.c: Correct: a large numeric change in the estimate is a common informal heuristic, but it is not one of the three defining criteria and can flag mediators or colliders too, not just confounders.
explanations.d: This is the third criterion: the variable must not be a downstream consequence of the exposure.

questions.prompt: In the smoking-lung cancer relationship, tar deposition in lung tissue lies between smoking and the DNA damage that becomes cancer. Tar deposition should be treated as a:

options.text: Confounder, and should be adjusted for to isolate smoking's true effect
Mediator, and adjusting for it would mask part of smoking's real causal effect
Effect modifier, since its impact varies by smoking amount
Selection factor, since it determines who is diagnosed

explanations.a: Tar deposition fails the third confounding criterion because it sits ON the causal pathway from smoking to cancer, so adjusting for it is not the same as controlling confounding.
explanations.b: Correct: tar deposition is a step in the causal chain from exposure to outcome, so statistically adjusting for it would block part of the very effect being measured, producing over-adjustment bias.
explanations.c: Effect modification concerns whether an effect's size differs across strata of a third variable, not whether that variable sits on the causal path.
explanations.d: Selection factors affect who enters or remains in a study sample, which is unrelated to a biological step on a causal pathway.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for evaluating whether a candidate variable is a true confounder of an exposure-outcome association.

items.text: Check whether the candidate variable is associated with the exposure
Check whether it independently predicts the outcome among the unexposed
Determine, using subject-matter knowledge, whether it lies on the causal pathway
If it passes all three checks, adjust for it; if it is a mediator, leave it unadjusted

questions.explanation: The two statistical association checks come first, the causal-pathway judgment requires mechanistic knowledge and comes third, and only after all three is it appropriate to decide whether to adjust.

questions.prompt: In the alcohol-smoking-lung cancer example, match each role to the variable that plays it.

left.text: Variable whose crude association was fully explained away by stratification

right.text: Alcohol consumption
Lung cancer
Smoking status
Alcohol's stratum-specific relative risk of 1.0

questions.explanation: Alcohol is the exposure under study and lung cancer the outcome, while smoking meets all three confounding criteria; stratifying by smoking drove alcohol's own relative risk down to 1.0, showing the crude association was confounding, not a real alcohol effect.

lessons.label: Controlling Confounding

sections.heading: Design-Stage Control: Randomization, Restriction, Matching
sections.body: Randomization in a controlled trial distributes both known and unknown confounders evenly across arms by chance alone -- it is the only tool that controls confounders a researcher never thought to measure, which is why randomized trials remain the strongest design for causal claims. Restriction limits eligibility to a single level of the confounder, such as enrolling only nonsmokers, which eliminates confounding by that variable entirely but shrinks the sample and limits how far results generalize. Matching pairs exposed and unexposed subjects, or cases and controls, on confounder values at enrollment, forcing balance the same way restriction does but across multiple strata at once. Matching on a variable that actually sits on the causal pathway, or so tightly that it also matches the exposure itself, causes overmatching -- wasting statistical power on a variable that was never a true confounder.

sections.heading: Analysis-Stage Control: Stratification, Mantel-Haenszel, Standardization, Regression
sections.body: When confounders cannot be handled at the design stage, or additional ones are found afterward, analysis-stage tools adjust for them statistically. Stratification splits the analysis into strata of the confounder and reports a stratum-specific estimate within each. The Mantel-Haenszel method, introduced by Nathan Mantel and William Haenszel in 1959, pools those stratum-specific estimates into a single weighted summary, still one of the most widely used ways to combine 2x2 tables across strata. Standardization applies a common reference weighting -- age-standardized mortality rates, for instance -- so populations with different confounder distributions become comparable. Multivariable regression, such as logistic or Cox regression, adjusts for several confounders simultaneously in one model, which becomes necessary once stratification would slice the data into too many small, sparse cells to estimate reliably.

sections.heading: Simpson's Paradox and the Limits of Adjustment
sections.body: Simpson's paradox occurs when a crude association reverses direction once a confounder is stratified out, and it is the sharpest demonstration that adjustment is not optional. The classic case is the 1973 UC Berkeley graduate admissions data, analyzed by Bickel, Hammel, and O'Connell (1975): men were admitted overall at a higher rate than women, but within most individual departments women were admitted at an equal or higher rate, because women disproportionately applied to more competitive departments. No adjustment tool, however, reaches a confounder that was never measured or was measured with error; residual confounding is the gap left over after imperfect adjustment, and it is why even a heavily adjusted observational study cannot claim the certainty of a well-run randomized trial.

lessons.workedExample: Charig and colleagues' 1986 comparison of two kidney-stone treatments, reanalyzed by Julious and Mullee (1994), is a classic Simpson's-paradox case. Overall, open surgery succeeded in 78% of cases (273/350) versus 83% (289/350) for the newer percutaneous technique, appearing to favor the newer method. But stone size confounded the comparison: surgeons preferentially used open surgery on harder, larger stones. Stratified by size, open surgery actually won in both groups -- 93% versus 87% for small stones, and 73% versus 69% for large stones. The technique that looked superior overall was worse within every stratum, purely because it was disproportionately used on the easier cases; only stratifying by stone size revealed the reversal.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a presenter checked a crude, overall comparison against a stratified or adjusted one before claiming a causal difference between two groups or treatments -- the kidney-stone reversal is exactly the trap a science-fair project comparing 'treatment A vs B' or 'group X vs Y' can fall into unnoticed. The tell of understanding is showing both the crude and adjusted estimates side by side, naming the confounder that stratification or matching controlled for, and naming at least one plausible unmeasured confounder that adjustment could not reach.

questions.prompt: Why is randomization considered uniquely powerful among confounding-control methods?

options.text: It guarantees a statistically significant result
It balances both measured and unmeasured confounders across groups by chance
It eliminates the need for a control group
It removes the need to define the exposure precisely

explanations.a: Randomization affects internal validity, not whether a result reaches statistical significance.
explanations.b: Correct: unlike restriction, matching, stratification, or regression, which only control confounders the researcher identifies and measures, randomization balances confounders whether or not anyone thought to measure them.
explanations.c: Randomized trials still require a comparison arm; randomization determines how subjects are assigned to arms, not whether a control group exists.
explanations.d: Precise exposure definition remains necessary regardless of allocation method.

questions.prompt: In the kidney-stone treatment example, open surgery had a lower overall success rate than the percutaneous technique but a higher success rate within both the small-stone and large-stone strata. What does this pattern demonstrate?

options.text: Measurement error in recording surgical outcomes
Simpson's paradox: stone size, unevenly distributed between treatments, reversed the crude comparison
Effect modification, since stone size changed which treatment worked better
Selection bias from differential loss to follow-up

explanations.a: The outcomes themselves were recorded correctly; the distortion comes from how stone size was distributed across treatments, not from measurement error.
explanations.b: Correct: stone size was associated with which treatment was chosen and independently predicted success, so its uneven distribution reversed the crude comparison -- the defining pattern of Simpson's paradox.
explanations.c: Effect modification would mean each treatment's advantage differs by stratum; here open surgery wins in every stratum, so the direction is consistent, not modified -- only the crude summary was reversed.
explanations.d: This scenario describes complete treatment outcomes in existing patients, not bias from subjects dropping out of the study.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a Mantel-Haenszel stratified analysis.

items.text: Define strata based on levels of the suspected confounder
Compute a stratum-specific effect estimate within each stratum
Weight and pool the stratum-specific estimates into one Mantel-Haenszel summary estimate
Compare the pooled estimate to the crude, unstratified estimate

questions.explanation: Mantel-Haenszel pooling requires strata to be defined first, an estimate computed inside each stratum, those estimates combined by weighting, and only then compared against the unadjusted crude estimate to see how much confounding was present.

questions.prompt: Match each confounding-control method to its description.

right.text: Distributes confounders, known or unknown, by chance across trial arms
Limits eligibility to one level of the confounder, at the cost of sample size and generalizability
Pairs subjects on confounder values at enrollment
Combines stratum-specific estimates into one weighted summary estimate

questions.explanation: Randomization and restriction and matching act at the design stage before data collection, while Mantel-Haenszel pooling is an analysis-stage tool applied after stratifying the collected data.

lessons.label: Effect Modification vs Confounding

sections.heading: Two Different Questions Stratification Can Answer
sections.body: Splitting an analysis by a third variable can reveal two very different things, and confusing them is a common error. Confounding is a nuisance: it distorts a single true effect into an incorrect crude number, and stratification is used to remove it, then pool the strata back into one corrected estimate. Effect modification, also called interaction, is a scientific finding: the exposure's effect on the outcome genuinely differs depending on the level of a third variable, and no single pooled number should paper over that difference -- it belongs in the results, not the adjustment. The diagnostic tell is how the stratum-specific estimates behave. For confounding, they are similar to each other but both differ from the confounded crude estimate. For effect modification, the stratum-specific estimates differ meaningfully from each other, which is exactly the pattern worth reporting rather than collapsing away.

sections.heading: Additive vs Multiplicative Scale
sections.body: Whether an interaction shows up at all can depend on which scale is used to measure it. A risk factor can have a constant relative risk across strata of a third variable -- no multiplicative-scale interaction -- while still producing very different absolute risk differences if baseline risk varies by stratum, which counts as additive-scale interaction. Kenneth Rothman argued that additive-scale interaction is usually the more public-health-relevant measure, since risk differences map directly onto how many cases an intervention would actually prevent in each stratum, while standard logistic regression, by testing a multiplicative product term, defaults to the multiplicative scale. A factor combination -- smoking and asbestos exposure on lung cancer risk is the textbook case -- can be far from additive even when it looks close to multiplicative, so checking only one scale can miss a real interaction on the other.

sections.heading: Worked Case: Smoking, Asbestos, and Lung Cancer Incidence
sections.body: Take lung cancer incidence per 100,000 person-years: 10 among people with neither exposure, 50 among asbestos-exposed nonsmokers (RR = 5.0), and 100 among smoking non-asbestos-workers (RR = 10.0). On the multiplicative scale, the expected joint relative risk if the two factors act independently is 5.0 x 10.0 = 50.0, predicting a joint incidence of 10 x 50 = 500 per 100,000 among people with both exposures -- and if the observed joint incidence is in fact close to 500, there is essentially no multiplicative-scale interaction; the risk ratios simply multiply. On the additive scale, the expected joint risk difference under no interaction is (50-10) + (100-10) = 130, predicting a joint incidence of only 10 + 130 = 140 per 100,000. An observed joint incidence of 500 is more than three times the additive prediction of 140, revealing a large additive-scale interaction -- excess risk far beyond what the two individual risk differences would predict -- even though the multiplicative scale showed none. This is exactly why Rothman treated the additive scale as the one that should drive public-health decisions: it is the scale on which this combination's true synergy becomes visible.

lessons.workedExample: Scenario A tests sex as a candidate variable for a drug-outcome association: the crude relative risk is 3.0, but stratifying by sex gives RR = 1.2 in men and RR = 1.3 in women -- close to each other, both far from the crude 3.0. This pattern is confounding; the stratum estimates should be pooled, for example with a Mantel-Haenszel summary near 1.25. Scenario B tests age for the same association: stratifying gives RR = 1.1 in younger patients and RR = 4.5 in older patients -- the stratum estimates differ sharply from each other. This pattern is effect modification; reporting a single pooled RR would hide that the drug's effect is roughly four times stronger (~4.1x) in the older stratum.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a presenter can tell 'the drug works far better in an unexpected subgroup' -- a reportable finding -- apart from 'the crude number was wrong because of an unbalanced third variable' -- a bias to fix before reporting anything. A student who checked only the multiplicative scale (a constant risk ratio) can still miss a real additive-scale interaction driven by different baseline risks. The tell of understanding is presenting stratum-specific and pooled estimates side by side with a stated decision rule for which pattern justifies which choice, not silently pooling every stratified table into one number.

questions.prompt: A crude odds ratio of 3.0 splits into stratum-specific odds ratios of 1.2 and 1.3 when stratified by sex. What does this pattern indicate, and what should be done?

options.text: Effect modification by sex; report the two odds ratios separately
Confounding by sex; pool the stratum-specific estimates into one summary
Selection bias; the sample must be re-collected
No third-variable problem; the crude estimate should be reported as is

explanations.a: Effect modification would require the stratum-specific estimates to differ meaningfully from each other; here 1.2 and 1.3 are close.
explanations.b: Correct: similar stratum-specific estimates that both differ sharply from the crude estimate is the signature of confounding, so the strata should be pooled, for example via Mantel-Haenszel, rather than reported separately.
explanations.c: Nothing about this pattern implicates who was sampled into the study; it concerns how a third variable distorts the crude estimate.
explanations.d: The large gap between the crude estimate (3.0) and both stratum-specific estimates (1.2, 1.3) shows the crude number is distorted and should not be reported alone.

questions.prompt: A drug shows the same relative risk of 2.0 in both a high-baseline-risk and a low-baseline-risk stratum, but the absolute risk difference is far larger in the high-baseline stratum. This scenario shows:

options.text: No interaction on either scale, since the relative risk is constant
Multiplicative-scale homogeneity with an additive-scale interaction
Confounding by baseline risk, requiring pooling
Additive-scale homogeneity with a multiplicative-scale interaction

explanations.a: A constant relative risk means no interaction on the multiplicative scale specifically, but the differing risk difference shows interaction is still present on the additive scale.
explanations.b: Correct: a constant risk ratio across strata is multiplicative-scale homogeneity, while a risk difference that varies with baseline risk is additive-scale interaction -- exactly the asymmetry Rothman highlighted as more relevant to public-health impact.
explanations.c: Baseline risk here is the stratifying variable revealing a scale-dependent interaction, not a nuisance variable distorting a single true crude estimate.
explanations.d: The relative risk is constant (multiplicative homogeneity) while the risk difference varies (additive interaction) -- the reverse of what this option states.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for deciding whether a stratified third variable represents confounding or effect modification.

items.text: Compute the crude, unstratified effect estimate
Stratify the analysis by the candidate third variable
Compare the stratum-specific estimates to each other
If they are similar to each other but differ from the crude estimate, treat it as confounding and pool; if they differ from each other, treat it as effect modification and report separately

questions.explanation: The comparison that distinguishes confounding from effect modification requires a crude estimate first, then stratification, then comparing the strata to each other before applying the decision rule.

questions.prompt: Match each stratified-analysis pattern to its correct interpretation.

left.text: Stratum estimates similar to each other, but both differ from the crude estimate
Stratum estimates differ substantially from each other
Constant risk ratio but differing risk difference across strata
Constant risk difference but differing risk ratio across strata

right.text: Confounding: pool the strata into one summary estimate
Effect modification: report the stratum-specific estimates separately
Interaction present on the additive scale only
Interaction present on the multiplicative scale only

questions.explanation: The first two rows distinguish confounding from effect modification by whether stratum estimates agree with each other; the last two rows show that whether an interaction appears at all can depend on the additive or multiplicative scale used to measure it.

lessons.label: Bradford Hill and the Causal Criteria

sections.heading: The 1964 Surgeon General Report and Hill's 1965 Address
sections.body: By the early 1960s, epidemiologists faced a problem no randomized trial could ethically solve: was smoking a cause of lung cancer? The 1964 US Surgeon General's Advisory Committee report on smoking and health argued yes, without a trial, by weighing several criteria including the consistency, strength, specificity, temporal relationship, and coherence of the accumulated evidence. A year later, Austin Bradford Hill formalized and expanded this reasoning in his 1965 presidential address to the Royal Society of Medicine, 'The Environment and Disease: Association or Causation?', proposing nine 'viewpoints': strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment, and analogy. Hill was explicit that these were considerations to weigh in judgment, not boxes to check off or a formal statistical test -- no fixed number of them needs to be satisfied before a causal claim is justified.

sections.heading: The Load-Bearing Viewpoints
sections.body: Temporality -- the cause must precede the effect -- is the one viewpoint Hill treated as truly indispensable; every other viewpoint is a matter of degree. Strength refers to the size of the association: a large relative risk is less plausibly explained away entirely by unmeasured confounding than a weak one. Biological gradient, or dose-response, asks whether increasing exposure tracks with increasing risk, as pack-years of smoking track with lung cancer risk. Consistency asks whether different populations, study designs, and researchers reach the same finding, and coherence asks whether the claim fits with what is already known about the disease's natural history. Plausibility asks whether a credible biological mechanism exists, and experiment asks whether removing the exposure reduces the outcome, as declining lung cancer rates followed population-level drops in smoking.

sections.heading: Specificity and Analogy: the Criticized Viewpoints
sections.body: Two of Hill's nine viewpoints have aged the worst. Specificity holds that a cause should produce one effect and an effect should have one cause, an idea borrowed from infectious-disease thinking. But Hill himself acknowledged its weakness: smoking causes lung cancer, heart disease, emphysema, and several other conditions at once, so demanding one-to-one specificity would wrongly disqualify a genuinely causal exposure. Analogy asks whether a proposed cause-effect pattern resembles an already-accepted one -- for instance, if one drug is known to cause birth defects, a chemically similar drug might too. Critics consider analogy the weakest and most subjective viewpoint, since it can be invoked to support almost any prior belief and offers no independent evidence of its own. Modern epidemiologists generally treat both as the least reliable of the nine.

lessons.workedExample: Applying several viewpoints to smoking and lung cancer: strength comes from Doll and Hill's British Doctors Study (begun 1951), which found lung cancer mortality roughly ten to twenty times higher in heavy smokers than nonsmokers. Biological gradient appears as risk rising with pack-years smoked. Consistency holds because case-control and cohort studies across many countries and decades reproduced the finding. Temporality is satisfied because prospective cohorts showed smoking preceded diagnosis by years. Experiment is supported by falling lung cancer incidence following population-level declines in smoking after the 1964 report. Specificity fails outright, since smoking also causes heart disease and emphysema -- exactly why Hill flagged that viewpoint as unreliable rather than disqualifying.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a presenter treats Hill's viewpoints as a rigid checklist ('we satisfied 6 of 9, so it's causal') or understands them as weighted judgment with one near-requirement -- temporality -- and several viewpoints, especially specificity and analogy, that carry little independent weight. The tell of understanding is applying the strong viewpoints (strength, dose-response, consistency, temporality) to the student's own data and explicitly declining to lean on specificity or analogy, rather than listing all nine as if each counted equally.

questions.prompt: Which of Bradford Hill's nine viewpoints did he treat as the one true requirement for a causal claim, rather than a matter of degree?

options.text: Specificity
Analogy
Temporality
Coherence

explanations.a: Specificity is one of the viewpoints Hill himself flagged as weak, not a requirement.
explanations.b: Analogy is widely considered the weakest and most subjective of the nine, not a requirement.
explanations.c: Correct: the cause must precede the effect, which Hill treated as indispensable while the other eight viewpoints are matters of degree to be weighed.
explanations.d: Coherence -- fitting with existing knowledge of the disease -- strengthens a causal case but is not the one viewpoint Hill singled out as necessary.

questions.prompt: Why has the specificity viewpoint been criticized as unreliable, using smoking as the example?

options.text: Smoking's relative risk for lung cancer is too small to demonstrate specificity
Smoking causes multiple diseases at once, violating the one-cause-one-effect idea specificity assumes
Smoking's effect appears only after a long latency period
Smoking rates vary too much between countries to assess specificity

explanations.a: Strength is a separate viewpoint concerned with the size of the relative risk, not with specificity.
explanations.b: Correct: specificity holds that one cause should produce one effect, but smoking causes lung cancer, heart disease, and emphysema simultaneously, so a genuinely causal exposure fails a strict specificity test.
explanations.c: Long latency relates to temporality and study design, not to why specificity fails for smoking.
explanations.d: Cross-country variation in smoking rates is a consistency consideration, not the reason specificity is unreliable.

questions.prompt: Place these events in the smoking-lung cancer causal debate in chronological order.

items.text: Doll and Hill publish a case-control study linking smoking to lung cancer (1950)
The British Doctors Study begins prospective follow-up of physician smokers and nonsmokers (1951)
The US Surgeon General's Advisory Committee report on smoking and health applies several causal criteria (1964)
Bradford Hill's presidential address proposes nine viewpoints for causal judgment (1965)

questions.explanation: The case-control finding came first, the prospective cohort that confirmed and quantified it began the following year, the Surgeon General's report drew a causal conclusion from the accumulated evidence in 1964, and Hill generalized the underlying reasoning into nine viewpoints the next year.

questions.prompt: Match each Bradford Hill viewpoint to what it asks.

right.text: Is the size of the association large enough to resist being fully explained by confounding?
Does increasing exposure track with increasing risk?
Does removing the exposure reduce the outcome?
Does the pattern resemble an already-accepted cause-effect relationship?

questions.explanation: Strength, biological gradient, and experiment are among the viewpoints considered more evidentially load-bearing, while analogy -- resemblance to an already-accepted relationship -- is considered the weakest and most subjective of the nine.

lessons.label: Modern Causal Inference

sections.heading: Counterfactuals and the Fundamental Problem
sections.body: The potential-outcomes framework, formalized by Donald Rubin in 1974, defines an individual's causal effect as the difference between two outcomes for that same person: what would happen if they were exposed, and what would happen if they were not. Only one of these two potential outcomes is ever observed for any given person -- a person is either exposed or not -- which statistician Paul Holland's 1986 paper named the 'fundamental problem of causal inference': individual causal effects are, strictly speaking, unobservable. Epidemiology works around this by estimating an average treatment effect across groups instead of an individual one. Randomization is powerful precisely because it makes the exposed and unexposed groups exchangeable, so the unexposed group's average outcome can stand in for what the exposed group's outcome would have been had they not been exposed.

sections.heading: Rothman's Sufficient-Component Cause Model (1976)
sections.body: Kenneth Rothman's 1976 'causal pie' model reframes how multiple causes combine. Each 'sufficient cause' is a full pie made of several 'component causes,' or pie slices, and any one complete pie is enough on its own to produce disease. A single component -- a genetic susceptibility, say -- can be a slice in several different pies, which is how the model explains multicausality: the same disease can arise through several distinct causal pathways, each sufficient but none individually necessary except a component present in every pie. Two component causes sitting in the same pie represent biological interaction, sometimes called causal co-action, because neither slice alone completes that pathway -- both are required together. The model reduces Hill-style single-cause thinking to a special case: a 'necessary cause' is a component that appears in every pie, and a cause that is 'sufficient' on its own is a one-slice pie.

sections.heading: DAGs, Confounders vs. Colliders, and a Rigorous 'Correlation Is Not Causation'
sections.body: Directed acyclic graphs, central to the causal-inference tradition built by Judea Pearl and applied to epidemiology by researchers including Sander Greenland and James Robins, represent variables as nodes and causal assumptions as arrows between them. A DAG lets an analyst formally identify a 'backdoor path' -- an indirect route from exposure to outcome through a common cause -- and Pearl's backdoor criterion specifies exactly which variables must be adjusted for to block that path, and which must not be adjusted for because they are colliders, common effects of two other variables. This turns 'correlation is not causation' from a slogan into a graphical, checkable criterion: given a DAG encoding the analyst's assumptions, the adjustment set that removes confounding without opening collider bias is mathematically determined, and the DAG makes explicit exactly which untestable assumptions the causal claim depends on.

lessons.workedExample: Draw a DAG for coffee drinking and pancreatic cancer. Age has arrows into both coffee drinking and pancreatic cancer risk, forming a backdoor path from coffee to cancer through age -- the backdoor criterion says age must be adjusted for. Now add hospital admission, which receives arrows from both pancreatic cancer and the unrelated gastrointestinal conditions that heavy coffee drinking can also worsen: hospital admission is a collider, not a confounder, so restricting the study to hospitalized controls and effectively 'adjusting' for admission opens a new spurious path rather than closing one. The same DAG and the same backdoor rule that says 'adjust for age' also says 'never condition on hospital admission.'
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a presenter's causal language is disciplined enough to survive a follow-up question like 'how do you know that's a confounder and not a collider?' The tell of understanding is sketching a simple DAG for the student's own claim, naming which node sits on a backdoor path and must be adjusted for versus which node is a collider that must be left alone, and stating the individual-level counterfactual their group-level estimate is standing in for -- rather than reaching for 'correlation isn't causation' as an unexplained disclaimer.

questions.prompt: Under the potential-outcomes framework, why is an individual's causal effect described as fundamentally unobservable?

options.text: Measurement instruments are never precise enough to detect it
A person can only be observed in either the exposed or unexposed state, never both
Individual effects do not exist; only group averages are meaningful
Ethical constraints prevent exposing any individual to the study condition

explanations.a: The issue is not measurement precision; it is that one of the two required states never occurs for that person at all.
explanations.b: Correct: Holland's 'fundamental problem of causal inference' is that a person's individual causal effect requires comparing their exposed and unexposed outcomes, but only one of those two potential outcomes is ever realized.
explanations.c: Individual effects are considered real but unobservable, not nonexistent; group averages are an estimation workaround, not a redefinition of what a causal effect is.
explanations.d: The unobservability holds even for exposures with no ethical barrier at all, such as naturally occurring genetic variation.

questions.prompt: In Rothman's causal pie model, what does it mean when two component causes appear as slices in the same sufficient-cause pie?

options.text: The two components are mutually exclusive and cannot occur in the same person
One of the two components must be a confounder of the other
The two components exhibit biological interaction, since that pathway to disease requires both together
The pie is disqualified as a sufficient cause once it contains more than one component

explanations.a: Components in the same pie can and must co-occur; the pie is only completed when all its slices are present in one person.
explanations.b: Confounding is a separate concept about a third variable distorting an association; it is not what co-occurrence within a single pie represents.
explanations.c: Correct: neither slice alone completes that particular sufficient cause, so their joint presence is what Rothman's model treats as biological interaction, or causal co-action, along that pathway.
explanations.d: A sufficient cause is typically made of several component causes; a pie is disqualified only if it is missing a required slice, not by having more than one.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for using a DAG and the backdoor criterion to choose an adjustment set.

items.text: Draw a DAG encoding the analyst's causal assumptions among exposure, outcome, and other relevant variables
Identify all backdoor paths connecting exposure to outcome through common causes
Select variables that block those backdoor paths while excluding any colliders
Adjust for exactly that selected set in the statistical analysis

questions.explanation: The backdoor criterion is only applicable once the causal assumptions are drawn as a DAG; backdoor paths must then be identified before a valid adjustment set, which must exclude colliders, can be selected and finally applied.

questions.prompt: Match each modern causal-inference term to its definition.

right.text: What would happen to a given individual under a specific exposure state
A complete set of component causes that together guarantee disease
One slice of a sufficient-cause pie, not by itself enough to produce disease
A variable that is a common effect of two other variables, which must not be adjusted for

questions.explanation: Potential outcomes belong to Rubin's individual-level framework, sufficient and component causes belong to Rothman's pie model, and colliders belong to the DAG-based tradition that formalizes which variables to adjust for.

lessons.label: Reading the Epidemic Curve

sections.heading: A histogram that tells a story
sections.body: An epidemic curve (epi curve) is a histogram of case counts plotted against time of illness onset, usually binned by day or week. It is the first chart any outbreak investigator builds, because its overall shape narrows down how the pathogen is spreading before a single lab result comes back. The x-axis is onset date, not report date or diagnosis date, since reporting lags distort the true epidemiology; the y-axis is case count, often stacked or color-coded by variables like location or exposure group to reveal sub-clusters.

sections.heading: Three shapes, three mechanisms
sections.body: A point-source outbreak, where everyone is exposed to a single contaminated source over a short interval (a wedding buffet, one contaminated well), produces a single narrow peak whose width roughly equals the range of the pathogen's incubation period — the worked example below, a banquet-linked norovirus outbreak, is a textbook case. A continuous common-source outbreak, where the source keeps releasing exposure over an extended period (a persistently contaminated water system), produces a plateau or a peak with a long flattened tail rather than a sharp single spike, because new people are exposed on a rolling basis rather than all at once — the classic example is the 1993 Milwaukee Cryptosporidium outbreak, where a Lake Michigan water-treatment plant kept releasing contaminated drinking water for roughly two to three weeks in March-April 1993 before the problem was identified and the plant shut down, producing a broad, gradually rising curve rather than one sharp spike. A propagated (person-to-person) outbreak, like measles or Ebola, produces a series of peaks each roughly one serial interval apart, and each successive peak tends to be taller as the number of infectious people grows — the visual signature of exponential chains of transmission rather than one shared exposure. The serial interval is the average time between symptom onset in one case and symptom onset in the people that case goes on to infect: for measles it's about 11 to 12 days, so a growing chain shows new peaks roughly a week and a half to two weeks apart, while for Ebola it's longer, averaging around 15 days, versus an incubation period that itself ranges roughly 2 to 21 days. Because each peak reflects a fresh generation of infections seeded by the previous one, the growing height directly visualizes the reproduction number driving the outbreak.

sections.heading: Back-calculating the exposure window
sections.body: For a point-source curve, investigators can work backward: if the peak spans from day 3 to day 6 after presumed exposure and the pathogen's known incubation period is 1 to 3 days (as with Salmonella), the true exposure event likely happened in a narrow window that, when the incubation range is added, reproduces the observed spread of onset dates. This back-calculation is how field epidemiologists narrow an interview window to 'what did you eat between Tuesday and Thursday' instead of asking about an entire month, and it only works because incubation period is a roughly known, pathogen-specific quantity.

lessons.workedExample: An investigator plots 40 gastroenteritis cases from a conference: onsets cluster tightly between 18 and 30 hours after the opening banquet, with a single sharp peak around 24 hours and nothing before or after. This one-peak, narrow-window shape is classic point-source. Because the pathogen (later confirmed as norovirus, incubation 12-48 hours) matches that window, the investigator concludes a single shared meal is the likely source and focuses interviews on banquet food items rather than the whole three-day conference, dramatically shrinking the hypothesis space for the case-control study that follows.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge handed an epi curve as supporting evidence checks whether the student can name the mechanism the shape implies, not just describe 'a peak.' Confusing a continuous common-source plateau with a propagated outbreak's multiple growing peaks leads to the wrong control strategy — you shut off a water source for a common-source event, but you'd need contact tracing and isolation for propagated spread. Judges probe whether the student used the curve to generate a testable hypothesis (a specific exposure window) rather than just describing the picture.

questions.prompt: An epi curve shows several peaks, each roughly one serial interval apart and each taller than the last. This shape most strongly suggests:

options.text: A point-source exposure with a long incubation period
A propagated, person-to-person outbreak
A continuous common-source outbreak
A reporting artifact from delayed lab confirmation

explanations.a: A point-source outbreak produces one peak, not a series of growing peaks spaced by a serial interval.
explanations.b: Correct: successive peaks one serial interval apart, growing in height, are the signature of chains of person-to-person transmission.
explanations.c: A continuous common-source outbreak produces a plateau or a broad single peak with a flattened tail, not distinct growing peaks.
explanations.d: Reporting lag would smear or shift the curve unpredictably, not produce a regular series of growing peaks tied to a serial interval.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in back-calculating a likely exposure window from a point-source epi curve.

items.text: Plot case counts by onset date to confirm a single narrow peak
Look up the pathogen's known incubation period range
Subtract the incubation range from the observed onset dates
Focus exposure interviews on the narrowed candidate window

questions.explanation: You must first confirm the point-source shape, then apply the pathogen's incubation period to the observed onsets to back-calculate when exposure likely occurred, before interviewing.

questions.prompt: Match each epi curve shape to its outbreak type.

left.text: Single narrow peak, width matches incubation range
Plateau or broad peak with a flattened tail
Successive growing peaks one serial interval apart

right.text: Point-source
Continuous common-source
Propagated

questions.explanation: Each shape reflects a distinct exposure mechanism: one-time shared exposure, ongoing shared exposure, and chains of person-to-person spread.

lessons.label: Survival and Kaplan-Meier Curves

sections.heading: The censoring problem
sections.body: A survival curve tracks the probability of remaining event-free (alive, relapse-free, disease-free) over time. The complication that ordinary summary statistics can't handle is censoring: a participant who drops out, is lost to follow-up, or is still event-free when the study ends has an unknown true survival time — you only know it exceeds their last observed time point. Simply excluding censored participants throws away real information (they did survive at least that long) and biases the estimate, since people who drop out are rarely a random subset. Right-censoring, where the true event lies somewhere after the last known observation, is the dominant case in clinical trials.

sections.heading: The Kaplan-Meier estimator
sections.body: Kaplan and Meier's 1958 paper introduced the product-limit estimator, which handles censoring correctly by recomputing survival probability only at each moment an event actually occurs. At every event time, the estimator multiplies the running survival probability by (number still at risk minus number of events) divided by (number at risk), and censored participants are dropped from the risk set at their last known time without counting as an event. The result is plotted as a step function: a flat line between events, a vertical drop at each event, and small tick marks (or plus signs) marking censored observations where no drop occurs. Because it is a step function rather than a smooth curve, the KM plot directly reflects the discrete times events were observed.

sections.heading: Reading median survival and comparing curves
sections.body: Median survival is read directly off the plot: trace horizontally from 0.50 on the y-axis until it meets the curve, then drop straight down to the x-axis. If the curve never crosses 0.50, median survival is undefined ('not reached') and only reported as a lower bound. To compare two KM curves (say, treatment vs. control), the log-rank test asks whether the two step functions differ more than chance would predict, pooling the comparison across every event time rather than just comparing one snapshot. The hazard ratio (HR) summarizes the same comparison as a single number — the instantaneous event rate in one group relative to the other — and an HR consistently below 1 across follow-up corresponds visually to one curve staying persistently above the other; a log-rank p-value tests significance, while the HR (with its own confidence interval) gives the magnitude.

lessons.workedExample: In a 200-patient trial, 90 patients relapse at known times, 30 drop out early (censored), and 80 finish the trial relapse-free (censored at study end). A naive analysis dropping the 110 censored patients would badly overestimate the relapse rate since it only counts confirmed events. The KM estimator instead recalculates survival at each of the 90 relapse times, shrinking the risk set correctly as people are censored without treating them as events. The resulting curve crosses 0.50 at 14 months, so median relapse-free survival is reported as 14 months; the treatment arm's curve stays above the control arm's throughout, consistent with a log-rank p=0.01 and reported HR of 0.62.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student understands censoring is not missing data to discard but partial information to use correctly — a common poster error is a survival curve or table that silently drops censored patients, inflating apparent event rates. A second common probe is whether the student can read median survival off their own KM plot and explain why an HR and a log-rank p-value are answering different questions (magnitude vs. whether the difference is due to chance), since posters often report only one.

questions.prompt: A patient is lost to follow-up at 8 months without having relapsed. In the Kaplan-Meier framework, this patient is:

options.text: Excluded entirely from the analysis
Counted as an event at 8 months
Censored: kept in the risk set through 8 months, then removed without counting as an event
Imputed to have relapsed at the study's median survival time

explanations.a: Excluding them entirely wastes the real information that they were event-free through month 8, and biases the estimate.
explanations.b: They did not have a confirmed event; treating them as one would overstate the event rate.
explanations.c: Correct: censoring keeps the participant's known event-free time in the risk set, then removes them from later calculations without counting a false event.
explanations.d: The Kaplan-Meier method does not impute event times for censored participants; it uses the actual censoring time to adjust the risk set.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to read median survival off a Kaplan-Meier plot.

items.text: Locate 0.50 on the survival-probability y-axis
Trace horizontally until the line meets the step function
Drop straight down to the x-axis at that intersection
Read the corresponding time value as median survival

questions.explanation: Median survival is the time at which the step function crosses 50% survival probability, found by tracing across then down.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it does in survival analysis.

right.text: Produces the step-function survival curve accounting for censoring
Tests whether two survival curves differ more than chance predicts
Summarizes the relative event rate between two groups as one number
Removes censored patients from the dataset before analysis

questions.explanation: The KM estimator builds the curve, the log-rank test evaluates significance of the difference between curves, and the hazard ratio gives its magnitude; none of them discard censored patients.

lessons.label: Forest Plots and Meta-Analysis

sections.heading: Anatomy of a forest plot
sections.body: A forest plot stacks the results of every study included in a meta-analysis as one row apiece, letting a reader compare them at a glance. Each row shows a point estimate (a square or circle marking that study's effect — an odds ratio, risk ratio, or mean difference) sitting on a horizontal line, the confidence interval, that stretches from the lower to the upper bound of the study's own uncertainty. A vertical line marks the value of no effect (1.0 for ratio measures, 0 for differences); a study whose CI crosses that line did not reach statistical significance on its own. The size of each square is scaled to that study's weight in the pooled analysis — bigger studies with narrower CIs get bigger squares and pull the pooled result toward themselves. At the bottom, a diamond represents the pooled effect across all studies, its width equal to the pooled confidence interval, and its horizontal position is the meta-analysis's single best estimate.

sections.heading: Fixed-effect vs. random-effects pooling
sections.body: A fixed-effect model assumes every included study is estimating the exact same true effect, so it pools estimates and weights purely by within-study statistical precision (small variance = more weight).
