A random-effects model instead assumes each study estimates its own true effect drawn from a distribution of related-but-different true effects (different populations, doses, follow-up), so it adds a between-study variance term to every weight, which shrinks weight differences between big and small studies and tends to widen the pooled CI. The practical rule of thumb: use random-effects whenever there's reason to expect real clinical or methodological differences across studies, which is most of the time in observational epidemiology.

sections.heading: Heterogeneity and I-squared
sections.body: Before trusting a diamond, a reader has to ask whether it even makes sense to combine these studies at all — this is the question of heterogeneity. The I-squared statistic (Higgins and Thompson, 2002) answers it quantitatively: it estimates the percentage of total variability across studies that is due to real differences between them rather than to chance alone, ranging from 0% (all variation explainable by sampling error) to values near 100% (almost all variation reflects true between-study differences). Rough conventional bands are roughly 25% = low, 50% = moderate, 75%+ = substantial, though these are heuristics, not hard cutoffs. High I-squared is a flag to consider subgroup analysis, a random-effects model, or in the worst case, not pooling the studies into a single number at all.

lessons.workedExample: A meta-analysis pools 8 trials of a drug for reducing hospital readmission. Two large trials (n>1000) show risk ratios near 0.75 with tight CIs and large squares; four small trials (n<100) scatter widely between 0.4 and 1.3 with CIs crossing 1.0 and tiny squares; two mid-size trials sit around 0.85. The pooled diamond under a random-effects model lands at RR 0.78 (95% CI 0.65-0.94), narrower than any single small study but wider than the two big trials alone would give, and I-squared is calculated at 62%, flagging moderate-to-substantial heterogeneity — enough that the poster should mention exploring why the small trials scattered before treating 0.78 as a settled number.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who spots a forest plot on a poster is checking whether the student can explain why the diamond, not any single study, is the headline result, and whether they can name box size as weight rather than just importance. The sharper probe is heterogeneity: if I-squared is high, a student who still presents the pooled estimate as if all the underlying studies agreed is overclaiming certainty the data don't support, and a judge will ask exactly that question.

questions.prompt: On a forest plot, why do large trials get bigger squares than small trials?

options.text: Larger trials are always methodologically superior
Square size reflects each study's weight in the pooled estimate, driven by precision
Square size is proportional to sample size alone, unrelated to the CI
Larger squares indicate the study crossed the line of no effect

explanations.a: Trial size affects precision and weight but does not by itself guarantee better methodology (bias, design flaws can still affect a large trial).
explanations.b: Correct: square size represents statistical weight in the pooled estimate, which is driven mainly by precision (narrower CI, larger weight).
explanations.c: Weight is driven by precision (inverse of variance), which correlates with but is not identical to raw sample size.
explanations.d: Whether a CI crosses the null line is shown by the horizontal line's position, not by square size.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in interpreting a forest plot before trusting its pooled diamond.

items.text: Read each study's point estimate and confidence interval
Note which studies individually cross the line of no effect
Check the I-squared statistic for heterogeneity
Interpret the pooled diamond's position and width as the meta-analysis result

questions.explanation: You read individual studies first, then assess whether combining them is justified via heterogeneity, before trusting the pooled diamond.

questions.prompt: Match each forest plot element to what it represents.

right.text: That study's confidence interval
The pooled effect estimate and CI across all studies
That study's weight in the pooled analysis
Percent of variability due to true between-study differences

questions.explanation: Each visual element maps to a distinct piece of meta-analytic information: individual precision, individual uncertainty, pooled result, and cross-study consistency.

lessons.label: Funnel Plots and Publication Bias

sections.heading: Effect size against precision
sections.body: A funnel plot is a scatterplot built from the same set of studies as a meta-analysis's forest plot, but arranged differently: each study's effect size sits on the x-axis, and a measure of its precision (typically standard error, plotted with the axis inverted so more precise studies sit higher) sits on the y-axis. Small studies, which estimate effects imprecisely, scatter widely near the bottom; large studies, which estimate effects tightly, cluster narrowly near the top. If there is no bias and no true heterogeneity beyond chance, this scatter should form a roughly symmetric inverted funnel or triangle centered on the true pooled effect, wide at the bottom and narrowing to a point at the top.

sections.heading: Reading asymmetry as missing studies
sections.body: The diagnostic use of a funnel plot is spotting asymmetry: a gap in the lower corner of the funnel on one side, most often the side representing small studies with null or negative results. This pattern signals the file-drawer problem — small studies that failed to find a significant effect are less likely to be submitted, accepted, or published at all, so they are simply missing from the plot and from the pooled literature, while small studies that happened to find a large effect (often by chance, given their imprecision) do get published and sit alone in the opposite lower corner. Because large studies are more likely to be published regardless of their result, the top of the funnel usually stays symmetric even when publication bias is severe; asymmetry concentrates at the bottom where sample sizes are small.

sections.heading: Egger's test and the consequence for pooled effects
sections.body: Because eyeballing a funnel plot for asymmetry is subjective, Egger and colleagues (1997) proposed a formal regression-based test — Egger's test — that regresses each study's standardized effect against its precision and checks whether the regression intercept differs significantly from zero; a nonzero intercept quantifies the asymmetry a symmetric funnel should not have. The consequence of undetected publication bias is not neutral: because the missing studies are disproportionately the small null or negative ones, their absence systematically pulls the pooled estimate in a meta-analysis toward showing a larger effect than truly exists, meaning a forest plot's diamond can look more impressive than reality simply because inconvenient small studies never made it into the funnel in the first place.

lessons.workedExample: A funnel plot of 20 studies on a supplement's effect on blood pressure shows large trials clustered tightly near the top around a modest effect, but the lower-left quadrant (small studies showing no benefit or harm) is nearly empty while the lower-right quadrant (small studies showing large benefit) has 6 scattered points. Egger's test returns a significant nonzero intercept (p=0.02), confirming visual asymmetry statistically. Because the missing small-null studies would have pulled the pooled effect toward zero, the reported pooled benefit is likely inflated by publication bias, and a careful poster would flag the pooled estimate as an upper bound rather than a settled effect size.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe funnel plots to see whether a student understands publication bias as a structural feature of how science gets published, not a vague warning label — the tell is being able to say specifically which corner of the plot should be empty and why it's the small, null-result studies that go missing rather than the large ones. A student who cites a meta-analysis's impressive pooled effect without checking (or at least mentioning) whether the underlying funnel plot was symmetric is treating a possibly biased number as settled fact.

questions.prompt: In a funnel plot showing signs of publication bias, which studies are most likely missing from the lower corner of the funnel?

options.text: Large studies with statistically significant positive results
Small studies with null or negative results
Large studies with null results
Small studies with large, striking positive results

explanations.a: Large significant studies are exactly the kind of result likely to be published, not missing.
explanations.b: Correct: small studies with unexciting null or negative findings are the least likely to be written up, accepted, or published, leaving a gap in that corner.
explanations.c: Large studies tend to be published regardless of their result because of the resources invested in running them; they aren't the typical missing group.
explanations.d: Small studies with striking positive results are attractive to publish and typically appear in the opposite corner, not the missing one.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in using a funnel plot to assess publication bias in a meta-analysis.

items.text: Plot each study's effect size against its precision
Visually check whether the scatter forms a symmetric inverted funnel
Run Egger's test to formally test for asymmetry
If asymmetric, treat the pooled effect as a possible overestimate

questions.explanation: You build the plot, inspect it visually, confirm with a formal test, and only then adjust your interpretation of the pooled estimate.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in assessing publication bias.

right.text: Formal regression test for funnel plot asymmetry
The phenomenon of null results going unpublished
Scatter of effect size vs. precision used to visualize bias

questions.explanation: The funnel plot is the visualization, Egger's test is the formal statistical check on it, and the file-drawer problem is the underlying mechanism that creates the asymmetry.

lessons.label: Statistical vs Clinical Significance

sections.heading: What a p-value actually answers
sections.body: A p-value is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as what was collected, if the null hypothesis were exactly true — formally P(data | null), the probability of the data given no true effect. It is not, despite near-universal misreading, P(null true | data), the probability that the null hypothesis is actually correct given what was observed; that would require Bayesian machinery and a prior probability that classical significance testing never supplies. A p-value of 0.03 does not mean there's a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true — it means that if there truly were no effect, data this extreme (or more so) would occur about 3% of the time by chance alone.

sections.heading: Sample size distorts the picture in both directions
sections.body: Because statistical power grows with sample size, a large enough study can detect a genuinely trivial effect — a 0.5 mmHg blood pressure difference, a 1-point IQ shift — as 'statistically significant' at p<0.05, even though no clinician or patient would ever act on a difference that small. The flip side is equally dangerous: a small, underpowered study can fail to reach p<0.05 for a real and clinically important effect simply because it doesn't have enough participants to distinguish signal from noise, and a poster that reports 'no significant difference' from such a study is easily misread as evidence of no effect, when it is really evidence of not enough data. Statistical significance is a statement about sampling noise, not about whether an effect matters.

sections.heading: Why 0.05 and what the ASA said about it
sections.body: The 0.05 threshold traces to Ronald Fisher's early-20th-century convention of convenience, not to any principled cutoff where 'real' effects begin — an effect at p=0.049 is not meaningfully different from one at p=0.051. In 2016 the American Statistical Association issued a formal statement (Wasserstein and Lazar, 2016) explicitly warning against treating p<0.05 as a bright line for scientific conclusions, business decisions, or publication, and urging researchers toward reporting effect sizes, confidence intervals, and study context instead of a single pass/fail number. The practical standard for reading evidence, and for presenting it on a poster, is to report the effect size with its confidence interval alongside clinical or practical relevance — a small p-value with a trivial effect size is far weaker evidence for action than a modest p-value attached to a large, clinically meaningful effect with a tight CI.

lessons.workedExample: A trial of 50,000 patients finds a new drug lowers LDL cholesterol by 1.2 mg/dL more than placebo, with p=0.001 — highly statistically significant because the huge sample makes even a tiny difference detectable. But 1.2 mg/dL is far below any threshold cardiologists consider clinically meaningful (typically 30-40 mg/dL matters for outcomes), so despite the small p-value, the effect size and its practical relevance argue against changing prescribing behavior. Meanwhile a 40-patient pilot study of a different drug finds a 25 mg/dL LDL reduction with p=0.08 — not 'significant' by convention, but the effect size is large and clinically important, and the honest conclusion is that the study is underpowered to confirm it, not that the drug doesn't work.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges deliberately ask 'was that difference significant, and does it matter?' as two separate questions, because a very common poster error is reporting a p-value as if it were the whole finding. The tell of real understanding is a student who volunteers the effect size and CI unprompted and can explain, in their own study's numbers, why a small p-value from a huge sample or a large-but-underpowered null result needs a second sentence about clinical relevance before it means anything.

questions.prompt: A p-value of 0.02 from a hypothesis test means:

options.text: There is a 2% chance the null hypothesis is true
There is a 98% chance the observed effect is real
If the null hypothesis were true, data this extreme would occur about 2% of the time by chance
The effect size is small but clinically meaningful

explanations.a: This is the classic misreading: a p-value is not the probability the null hypothesis is true; that requires Bayesian priors it doesn't supply.
explanations.b: A p-value says nothing directly about the probability the alternative hypothesis or effect is real.
explanations.c: Correct: the p-value is the probability of data this extreme (or more) occurring under the assumption the null hypothesis is true.
explanations.d: A p-value carries no information about effect size or clinical meaning on its own; those must be reported separately.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in properly interpreting a study's statistical result before claiming it matters.

items.text: Note the p-value and whether it crosses the chosen threshold
Report the effect size and its confidence interval
Consider the sample size and whether it could distort significance either way
Judge clinical or practical relevance of the effect size

questions.explanation: A full interpretation moves from the raw significance test to the magnitude and precision of the effect, accounts for how sample size could mislead, and finally asks whether the effect is practically meaningful.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to the correct interpretation.

right.text: Study likely underpowered; absence of significance is not evidence of no effect
Statistically significant but may not be clinically meaningful
Report effect sizes and CIs rather than relying on a p<0.05 bright line

questions.explanation: Large samples can make trivial effects significant, small samples can hide real effects, and the ASA statement pushes researchers toward richer reporting than a single threshold.

lessons.label: The Evidence Hierarchy and Critical Appraisal

sections.heading: The pyramid and its logic
sections.body: The evidence hierarchy is usually drawn as a pyramid, with study designs ranked by how well they control bias and confounding rather than by how interesting or large they are. At the top sit systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (RCTs), which pool multiple randomized trials; just below sit individual RCTs, where random allocation to exposure balances both known and unknown confounders between groups. Below that come cohort studies (following exposed and unexposed groups forward for outcomes) and case-control studies (comparing people with and without an outcome for past exposures), both observational and therefore vulnerable to confounding despite statistical adjustment. Near the bottom sit case series and case reports, which describe a handful of patients with no comparison group at all, and expert opinion or editorials, which carry no primary data and rest on judgment alone.

sections.heading: The pyramid's real limits
sections.body: The hierarchy is a starting heuristic, not an absolute ranking of every individual study: a poorly designed or underpowered RCT can be less trustworthy than a large, carefully adjusted cohort study, and for questions where randomization is unethical or impossible (does smoking cause lung cancer, does a rare exposure cause a rare birth defect), cohort and case-control designs are the best evidence that can exist, not a consolation prize. This is why GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation), developed by an international working group starting in the early 2000s, does not simply rank by design type but rates the certainty of a body of evidence on factors including risk of bias, inconsistency across studies, indirectness to the actual question, imprecision, and publication bias — allowing a well-conducted set of observational studies to be rated with higher certainty than a poorly conducted RCT.

sections.heading: PICO/PECO and a judge's checklist
sections.body: Before appraising any single study, a clear question has to specify Population, Intervention (or Exposure, giving PECO for observational designs), Comparison, and Outcome — a poster claim like 'vitamin D reduces illness' is unusable until PICO turns it into something checkable, such as 'in adults over 65 (P), does daily vitamin D supplementation (I) versus placebo (C) reduce respiratory infection incidence over 12 months (O)?' A judge applying a critical-appraisal checklist to a poster's cited evidence works through a similar short list: what study design produced this claim, where does that design sit on the hierarchy and does that placement even fit the question being asked, how large and how was the comparison group chosen, and is the cited source itself a primary study, a systematic review, or someone's unsupported opinion dressed up as a citation.

lessons.workedExample: A poster claims 'social media use causes anxiety in teens,' citing a single case series of 12 clinic patients. A judge applying PECO reframes the claim as: in teenagers (P), does high social media exposure (E) versus low exposure (C) affect anxiety diagnosis rates (O)? Against that question, a 12-patient case series with no comparison group sits near the bottom of the hierarchy and cannot support a causal claim at all — it can only generate the hypothesis. The judge would expect the strongest available evidence instead: ideally a systematic review of prospective cohort studies (RCTs being impractical here), and would flag the mismatch between the sweeping causal claim and the weak, uncontrolled source actually cited.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use the hierarchy as their default lens for probing any cited source on a poster, because it is the fastest way to catch a mismatch between how strong a claim sounds and how strong its evidence actually is. The sharper probe is whether a student can explain the hierarchy's limits — that a big well-run cohort study can beat a small flawed RCT, and that GRADE exists precisely because design type alone is an incomplete certainty rating — rather than reciting the pyramid as an unbreakable rule.

questions.prompt: Why can a large, carefully conducted cohort study sometimes be rated as more certain evidence than a small, poorly conducted RCT?

options.text: Cohort studies are always ranked above RCTs on the evidence hierarchy
GRADE rates certainty using factors like risk of bias and precision, not design type alone
Randomization never actually balances confounders in practice
Case-control and cohort studies are immune to confounding
Peer review guarantees RCTs are always well-conducted

explanations.a: The hierarchy generally ranks RCTs above cohort studies as a class; this option reverses the standard ranking incorrectly.
explanations.b: Correct: GRADE evaluates risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias, so a flawed RCT can be rated lower than a strong cohort study.
explanations.c: Randomization does balance confounders on average when properly executed; the issue here is a specific RCT being small and poorly conducted, not randomization failing in general.
explanations.d: Observational designs remain vulnerable to confounding despite statistical adjustment; this option is false on its face.
explanations.e: Peer review does not guarantee sound conduct or adequate sample size for any individual RCT.

questions.prompt: Order the study design tiers from strongest to weakest on the standard evidence hierarchy.

items.text: Systematic review/meta-analysis of RCTs
Individual randomized controlled trial
Cohort or case-control study
Case series or case report
Expert opinion

questions.explanation: The pyramid ranks pooled RCT evidence highest, then single RCTs, then observational comparative studies, then uncontrolled case descriptions, then opinion with no primary data.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its definition in evidence appraisal.

right.text: Framework for structuring a checkable research question
System for rating certainty of a body of evidence beyond design type alone
Description of a handful of patients with no comparison group

questions.explanation: PICO/PECO structures the question being asked, GRADE rates how certain the resulting evidence is, and a case series is a low-hierarchy design lacking a comparison group.

lessons.label: Snow and the Birth of Field Epidemiology

sections.heading: A map, a pump, and no idea what a germ was
sections.body: In late August 1854, cholera tore through Soho, London, killing roughly 616 people within about ten days in a few blocks around Broad Street. John Snow, a physician skeptical of the prevailing 'miasma' theory that disease spread through foul air, plotted each death's address on a street map. The deaths clustered tightly around the Broad Street pump. Snow interviewed households, found exceptions that strengthened rather than broke the pattern (a workhouse and a brewery near the pump had almost no deaths because their inmates and workers drank from other supplies), and persuaded the local council to remove the pump handle on September 8, 1854. The outbreak was already fading by then, so the handle removal was more symbolic than curative, but Snow had already identified the mechanism: contaminated water, not bad air. This was more than two decades before Robert Koch's germ-theory postulates and Louis Pasteur's germ-theory experiments, so Snow built his case entirely on the pattern of who got sick and where, not on any visible organism.

sections.heading: The natural experiment: two companies, one river
sections.body: Snow's stronger evidence came from a citywide comparison he called his 'grand experiment.' Two water companies, Southwark & Vauxhall and Lambeth, drew drinking water from the Thames and piped it to interspersed, socioeconomically similar households across London. Critically, Lambeth had moved its intake upstream of London's sewage discharge in 1852, while Southwark & Vauxhall still drew water downstream, near the sewage outflow. Because customers of each company were mixed street by street, Snow had an unplanned but nearly randomized comparison. He tabulated cholera deaths per 10,000 houses by supplier: about 315 for Southwark & Vauxhall versus about 37 for Lambeth, an eightfold difference in a population that differed by almost nothing except which pipe reached their tap. This is why Snow is credited with founding both spatial epidemiology (the map) and analytic epidemiology (the water-company comparison): he used naturally occurring variation in exposure to test a causal hypothesis, the same logic that underlies today's natural-experiment and instrumental-variable designs. Acceptance of Snow's theory was far from immediate: the General Board of Health's own committee of inquiry into the 1854 outbreak favored the prevailing miasma explanation over Snow's water-source account, and the Broad Street pump handle was quietly restored not long after the outbreak had already subsided, a sign that Snow's contemporaries remained unconvinced. Wider acceptance built gradually over the following decade, helped by the registrar-general's statistician William Farr, who had initially favored miasma theory himself but increasingly credited environmental exposure routes as more outbreak data accumulated, and it gained further corroboration from the 1866 East London outbreak, when investigators traced illness to a reservoir contaminated by sewage in the East London Water Company's supply. Firm confirmation of the underlying mechanism had to wait until 1883, when Robert Koch isolated the cholera bacterium, Vibrio cholerae, in Egypt and India.

lessons.workedExample: Snow's water-company table, reconstructed: Southwark & Vauxhall supplied roughly 40,000 houses and recorded about 1,263 cholera deaths in the 1854 outbreak, a rate near 315 per 10,000 houses. Lambeth supplied about 26,000 houses and recorded about 98 deaths, near 37 per 10,000 houses. The rest of London, on mixed or other supplies, ran about 59 per 10,000. Because the two companies' customers were interleaved on the same streets, differing mainly by which underground pipe served their house, Snow could attribute the eightfold mortality gap to water source rather than to wealth, occupation, or neighborhood sanitation, which is exactly the confounding a critic of the time would have raised.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this case because it is the cleanest historical example of establishing causation without a mechanism in hand: Snow could not see the cholera vibrio, so he had to argue from exposure-outcome pattern alone, anticipating Bradford Hill's later criteria by decades. A student who can explain WHY the water-company comparison is more convincing than the pump map alone, because it controls for confounding by using naturally interspersed exposure, demonstrates real grasp of analytic versus descriptive epidemiology rather than just knowing the story's plot.

questions.prompt: Why is the Southwark & Vauxhall vs. Lambeth water-company comparison considered stronger evidence than the Broad Street pump map alone?

options.text: It showed a larger raw number of deaths
It compared interspersed households differing mainly by water source, reducing confounding
It was conducted after germ theory confirmed the mechanism
It relied on laboratory identification of the cholera organism
It used a larger map

explanations.a: Raw death counts alone don't establish causation; the strength comes from the comparison structure, not the tally.
explanations.b: Correct: because customers of the two companies lived on the same streets and differed mainly by which pipe served them, other causes of cholera were roughly balanced across the comparison, isolating water source as the likely cause.
explanations.c: Snow's work in 1854 preceded confirmed germ theory by decades; it did not rely on it.
explanations.d: Snow had no laboratory confirmation of the cholera organism; his argument was purely epidemiological.
explanations.e: Map size is irrelevant to the strength of a causal argument.

questions.prompt: Order Snow's investigative steps during the Broad Street outbreak.

items.text: Plot cholera deaths by address on a street map
Interview households, including exceptions like the workhouse and brewery
Identify the Broad Street pump as the shared exposure
Persuade the council to remove the pump handle

questions.explanation: Snow first mapped the pattern, then explained apparent exceptions through interviews, which pointed to the pump as the common exposure, and only then acted on that conclusion.

questions.prompt: Match each element of Snow's investigation to what it demonstrates.

left.text: The death map around Broad Street
The workhouse and brewery with almost no deaths
The Southwark & Vauxhall vs. Lambeth comparison

right.text: Spatial clustering suggesting a point source
An exception that, once explained, strengthens the causal pattern
A natural experiment controlling for confounding

questions.explanation: Each piece of evidence plays a distinct epidemiological role, from descriptive clustering to explained exceptions to a near-randomized comparison.

questions.prompt: Snow's Broad Street and water-company investigations preceded confirmed germ theory. What does this imply about his method?

options.text: His conclusions were unreliable without a known mechanism
Causal inference in epidemiology can precede identification of a biological mechanism
He accidentally discovered the cholera bacterium
His method only worked because miasma theory was later proven correct

explanations.a: His conclusions held up and directed effective public health action despite the missing mechanism, showing pattern-based inference can be reliable.
explanations.b: Correct: Snow demonstrates that exposure-outcome patterns, rigorously compared, can establish causation before the underlying biology is understood.
explanations.c: Snow never isolated or observed the organism; that came later with Robert Koch's and others' bacteriological work.
explanations.d: Miasma theory was the theory Snow's evidence argued against, and it was later rejected, not confirmed.

lessons.label: Doll, Hill, and Proving Smoking Causes Cancer

sections.heading: A case-control study and a cohort to check it
sections.body: In 1950, Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill published a case-control study in the BMJ comparing lung cancer patients admitted to London hospitals against matched patients with other diseases, asking each about smoking history. Smokers were dramatically overrepresented among the lung cancer cases. Case-control studies can be distorted by recall bias or by how controls are chosen, so Doll and Hill immediately moved to a stronger design: starting in 1951, they mailed a smoking questionnaire to about 59,600 British doctors on the UK medical register, of whom roughly 40,700 provided usable responses, and then simply watched who died of what over the following years, a prospective cohort with no retrospective recall involved. Because doctors' deaths and causes were reliably recorded, this British Doctors Study could track dose-response (heavy smokers dying of lung cancer at higher rates than light smokers) and show that mortality dropped in doctors who quit during the study, evidence a single case-control snapshot could not provide.

sections.heading: Hill's causal reasoning and Fisher's dissent
sections.body: Bradford Hill later formalized the kind of reasoning this work required into what became known as the Bradford Hill criteria: considerations like strength of association, consistency across studies, a biological dose-response gradient, temporality, and coherence with existing knowledge, used to judge whether an association is likely causal rather than proof by any single test. The most serious contemporary pushback came from Ronald Fisher, the statistician who had helped found modern experimental design and who was himself a pipe smoker. Fisher argued the association could reflect reverse causation or, more pointedly, a shared genetic or constitutional factor that predisposed some people both to crave tobacco and to develop lung cancer, meaning smoking would be a correlate rather than a cause. This was a genuinely serious objection, not a fringe one, since observational data alone cannot rule out an unmeasured common cause. It was rebutted over the following decade by the dose-response and quitting evidence from the British Doctors Study, animal experiments showing tar from cigarette smoke caused tumors, and the sheer consistency of the association across many countries and study designs. In 1964, the U.S. Surgeon General's Advisory Committee report concluded smoking causes lung cancer, formally closing the debate at the policy level. The dose-response criterion was not just a theoretical checkbox: by the mid-1950s the British Doctors Study showed doctors smoking 25 or more cigarettes a day dying of lung cancer at roughly twenty times the rate of doctors who had never smoked, with lighter smokers falling at intermediate rates in between, a gradient orderly enough that it was hard to attribute to a fixed constitutional trait rather than to the smoking itself.

lessons.workedExample: By the mid-1950s the British Doctors Study showed a clear dose-response gradient: doctors smoking 25 or more cigarettes a day had a lung cancer death rate roughly twenty times that of nonsmoking doctors, while light smokers fell in between, and doctors who quit during follow-up saw their risk decline toward that of never-smokers over subsequent years. Fisher's genetic-confounding hypothesis predicts no such change with quitting, since a fixed constitutional trait would not shift just because someone stopped smoking. The observed drop in risk after cessation, unexplained by Fisher's model, was one of the strongest pieces of evidence against it and for a direct causal effect of smoking itself.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this case because Fisher's objection is the textbook illustration of the 'third variable' problem, and a student who can only say 'Fisher was wrong' hasn't understood why. What actually resolved the debate was not a single killer study but converging evidence: dose-response, change in risk after quitting, and biological plausibility from lab work, exactly the pattern behind Hill's later criteria. A judge wants to see a student reason about what evidence would distinguish causation from Fisher's shared-cause hypothesis, not just cite the 1964 report as a verdict from authority.

questions.prompt: Why did Doll and Hill follow their 1950 case-control study with the British Doctors cohort starting in 1951?

options.text: Case-control studies are always fraudulent
A prospective cohort avoids recall bias and can show dose-response and the effect of quitting
The BMJ required a second study before publishing
Cohort studies are cheaper to run than case-control studies

explanations.a: Case-control studies are a legitimate design; the issue is their vulnerability to specific biases, not fraud.
explanations.b: Correct: following smokers and nonsmokers forward avoids relying on patients' memory of past habits and lets researchers observe dose-response and risk change after quitting, which a single retrospective comparison cannot.
explanations.c: There was no such publication requirement; the follow-up cohort was a scientific choice, not an editorial one.
explanations.d: Large prospective cohorts are typically more expensive and slower than case-control studies, not cheaper.

questions.prompt: What was the core of Ronald Fisher's objection to the smoking-cancer link?

options.text: That lung cancer rates were not actually rising
That a shared genetic or constitutional factor might cause both the urge to smoke and susceptibility to lung cancer
That Doll and Hill had fabricated their doctor survey data
That smoking could only cause heart disease, not cancer

explanations.a: Fisher did not dispute the rise in lung cancer rates; his objection concerned interpretation of the association, not the underlying trend.
explanations.b: Correct: Fisher proposed an unmeasured common cause, a genuine confounding hypothesis that observational association alone could not rule out.
explanations.c: Fisher's critique was a scientific and statistical argument about confounding, not an accusation of fabrication.
explanations.d: Fisher's constitutional hypothesis was offered as an alternative explanation for the lung cancer association specifically.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the smoking-and-cancer timeline.

items.text: Doll and Hill's case-control study published in the BMJ
British Doctors Study questionnaire mailed to doctors
Fisher publishes his genetic-confounding objection
US Surgeon General's report concludes smoking causes lung cancer

questions.explanation: The 1950 case-control study came first, the 1951 cohort followed to test it further, Fisher's dissent came as the evidence accumulated in the mid-to-late 1950s, and the 1964 Surgeon General report closed the debate at the policy level.

questions.prompt: Match each piece of evidence to what it established against Fisher's constitutional hypothesis.

left.text: Dose-response gradient by cigarettes per day
Falling risk in doctors who quit smoking

right.text: A fixed genetic trait would not explain risk changing after behavior changed
Biological plausibility for a causal mechanism
Heavier exposure predicting heavier harm, as expected under direct causation

questions.explanation: Each strand of evidence attacked a different weak point in the confounding hypothesis: dose-response fit direct causation, quitting behavior contradicted a fixed genetic cause, and lab work supplied a mechanism.

lessons.label: Framingham and the Chronic-Disease Cohort

sections.heading: Watching a whole town age
sections.body: In 1948, the newly formed National Heart Institute enrolled 5,209 residents of Framingham, Massachusetts, aged 30 to 62 and free of heart disease at baseline, into what became the Framingham Heart Study. Rather than chasing an outbreak like Snow or comparing exposed groups retrospectively like Doll and Hill, the design was simple and expensive: bring the same people back every two years for physical exams, blood tests, and interviews, indefinitely, and see who developed cardiovascular disease and why. Chronic diseases like heart attack and stroke unfold over decades, so a study built to catch a short epidemic couldn't answer questions about slow-building risk; Framingham was built for exactly that timescale. It is still running: the Offspring Cohort of participants' children began in 1971, an Omni cohort recruiting racially and ethnically diverse Framingham residents was added starting in 1994, and a Third Generation cohort of grandchildren began in 2002, making it a multi-generational natural laboratory for how cardiovascular risk runs in families over time. Framingham the town was not a random pick: it already had a stable, trackable population near Boston and a two-decade history of organized community health surveillance, dating to a 1917-1923 tuberculosis health demonstration project run with the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company, so residents and local institutions were accustomed to cooperating with population-wide health studies before the heart study ever began.

sections.heading: Coining 'risk factor' and its limits
sections.body: Framingham investigators are widely credited with introducing the term 'risk factor' into medical language, notably in a 1961 paper by William Kannel and colleagues that used six years of Framingham follow-up to show that high cholesterol, elevated blood pressure, and cigarette smoking each independently predicted future coronary heart disease. Before this kind of prospective analysis, clinicians associated these traits with heart disease anecdotally; Framingham quantified them and showed they combined additively so that a person with several elevated risk factors faced compounding, not merely additive, risk. This became the template for essentially all cardiovascular risk-factor epidemiology since, including tools like the later Framingham Risk Score used in clinics. The lasting critique is that the founding cohort was drawn from one middle-class, overwhelmingly white New England town in the 1940s, so risk equations built on it can miscalibrate for other populations with different genetic backgrounds, diets, and access to care; the Omni cohort and comparable studies elsewhere were direct responses to that generalizability gap.

lessons.workedExample: Kannel and colleagues' 1961 analysis followed the Framingham cohort for six years and reported that men with serum cholesterol in the highest range developed coronary heart disease at several times the rate of men in the lowest range, and that this cholesterol effect persisted after separately accounting for blood pressure and smoking status, meaning each factor added risk on its own rather than one fully explaining the others. A hypothetical 50-year-old man with high cholesterol, high blood pressure, and a smoking habit therefore carried substantially higher risk than the sum of any single factor's effect alone would suggest, which is the compounding pattern that made multivariable risk scoring, rather than single-factor screening, the clinical standard that followed.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe Framingham because it is the clearest example of a study design chosen to match the disease's timescale: chronic, slow-developing conditions require decades of prospective follow-up that a case-control or short cohort cannot provide. A strong answer explains why the multi-generational extension (Offspring, Omni, Third Generation) exists, that it is not scope creep but a direct fix for the founding cohort's narrow demographics, and can articulate concretely how a risk equation trained on 1948 Framingham, Massachusetts might misestimate risk in a population with different ancestry, diet, or healthcare access today.

questions.prompt: Why did the Framingham Heart Study use a decades-long prospective cohort design rather than a short case-control study?

options.text: Cardiovascular disease develops over decades, requiring long-term follow-up to observe risk factors preceding outcomes
Case-control studies were not yet invented in 1948
The National Heart Institute lacked funding for a shorter study
Framingham residents refused to participate in a shorter study

explanations.a: Correct: chronic diseases like heart disease unfold slowly, so researchers needed to track the same people over years to see which baseline traits preceded later disease.
explanations.b: Case-control methodology existed by the 1940s and was used elsewhere, including contemporaneously in cancer research; it simply doesn't fit questions about slow-developing risk over time as well.
explanations.c: The long design was a scientific choice matched to the disease's timescale, not primarily a funding constraint.
explanations.d: Participation was a design choice by researchers, not a constraint imposed by resident refusal of alternatives.

questions.prompt: Match each Framingham cohort extension to what it added.

right.text: Participants' children, enabling study of familial risk
Grandchildren of the original cohort
Racially and ethnically diverse Framingham residents

questions.explanation: Each extension addressed a different gap: the Offspring cohort added a second generation for familial analysis, the Omni cohort addressed the founding cohort's lack of diversity, and the Third Generation cohort extended the family design further.

questions.prompt: What is the main critique of applying Framingham-derived risk equations to other populations today?

options.text: The original cohort was too large to analyze accurately
The founding cohort was demographically narrow, so risk estimates may miscalibrate elsewhere
Framingham never measured blood pressure
The study stopped following participants after six years

explanations.a: Cohort size was not the issue; roughly 5,200 participants was workable for the statistical methods used.
explanations.b: Correct: a cohort drawn from one 1940s New England town may not generalize to populations differing in ancestry, diet, or healthcare access, which is exactly why later cohorts diversified.
explanations.c: Blood pressure was one of the three core risk factors Framingham established, alongside cholesterol and smoking.
explanations.d: Framingham is still an ongoing, multi-generational study; the 1961 six-year analysis was one report from within a much longer follow-up.

questions.prompt: Order these Framingham milestones chronologically.

items.text: Original cohort of 5,209 residents enrolled
Kannel et al. publish the six-year risk-factor analysis
Offspring Cohort begins
Omni Cohort begins

questions.explanation: Enrollment began in 1948, the landmark risk-factor paper followed in 1961 after six years of data, the Offspring Cohort started in 1971, and the Omni Cohort was added in 1994.

lessons.label: Streptomycin and the Randomized Trial

sections.heading: Why historical controls weren't good enough
sections.body: Before 1948, drug evaluation typically compared treated patients to 'historical controls,' earlier patients with the same disease treated before the new drug existed. This let two eras of medical care differ in every way except the drug under study, including diagnostic standards, nursing quality, nutrition, and which patients happened to be sick that decade, so any apparent benefit could really be secular improvement in care rather than the drug. When streptomycin, the first antibiotic to show activity against tuberculosis, became available in Britain after WWII, Austin Bradford Hill designed a Medical Research Council trial to test it properly: patients diagnosed with active pulmonary tuberculosis were assigned, using a table of random numbers, to receive either streptomycin plus bed rest or bed rest alone. The assignment itself was concealed inside numbered, opaque sealed envelopes prepared in advance by Hill's statistical office; a patient's envelope was opened only after a physician had already decided the patient was eligible and accepted them into the trial, so no clinician could see or influence which arm a given patient would land in before committing to enroll them, with both groups treated and followed concurrently in the same hospitals over the same months. Concurrent, randomly allocated controls meant the only planned difference between groups was the drug itself, which is what makes this trial, published in the BMJ in 1948, widely regarded as the first properly randomized controlled trial in medicine.

sections.heading: Why randomize a scarce, life-or-death drug
sections.body: The trial enrolled 107 patients, 55 assigned to streptomycin and 52 to the control arm; by six months, four patients in the streptomycin group had died compared to 14 in the control group, and X-ray improvement was far more common with treatment. The ethical question of withholding a promising drug from sick patients was blunted by a real-world fact: in 1946-47 Britain, streptomycin was in genuinely short supply and could not have been given to every tuberculosis patient regardless of the trial, so allocating the limited supply by random assignment inside a rigorous study was, if anything, a fairer and more informative use of scarcity than allocating it by clinical favoritism or waiting lists. Randomization also served a second, non-ethical purpose Hill cared about deeply: concealing the allocation from the physicians deciding whether a patient was eligible prevented them from consciously or unconsciously steering sicker or healthier patients toward one arm, a bias that had undermined earlier, non-randomized comparisons of tuberculosis treatments. That combination, randomization for unbiased allocation plus a concurrent control group for a fair comparison, became the template every modern RCT still follows.

lessons.workedExample: Picture a tuberculosis ward in 1947 with only enough streptomycin for half the eligible patients. A non-randomized approach might give the drug to whichever patients seemed most likely to benefit or whose physicians requested it first, systematically enriching the treated group with less-sick patients and making streptomycin look better than it truly was even if it did nothing. Hill's design instead used sealed, random-number-based allocation unknown to admitting physicians, so a patient's illness severity had no bearing on which arm they entered. When the treated group still showed a clear mortality advantage (4 deaths versus 14 in 55 versus 52 patients) despite that allocation being unbiased, the result could be attributed to the drug rather than to who happened to get it.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this trial because it is the origin point of the logic underlying every RCT a student will cite elsewhere in their project: randomization isn't about fairness for its own sake, it is a specific tool for preventing allocation bias, and concurrent controls prevent confounding by era. A strong answer explains why scarcity made randomization more ethically defensible here, not less, since someone had to be denied the drug regardless, and distinguishes clearly between what randomization fixes (selection into groups) and what a concurrent control group fixes (secular trends over time), rather than treating 'randomized controlled trial' as one indivisible buzzword.

questions.prompt: What specific problem does comparing treated patients to historical controls risk?

options.text: Historical controls are always sicker than new patients
Care standards and patient populations can differ across eras, confounding any apparent drug effect
Historical records are never kept in hospitals
Historical controls require more patients than randomized trials

explanations.a: There's no general rule that historical patients are sicker; the problem is that many things besides severity can differ between eras.
explanations.b: Correct: nutrition, diagnostic criteria, nursing care, and which patients happened to be ill can all shift over time, so a difference in outcomes may reflect the era, not the drug.
explanations.c: Hospitals did keep records; the issue is comparability of what those records represent, not their existence.
explanations.d: Sample size requirements depend on effect size and design, not specifically on whether controls are historical or concurrent.

questions.prompt: Why was randomizing scarce streptomycin considered more, not less, ethically defensible?

options.text: Because randomization guaranteed every patient would eventually receive the drug
Because the drug's scarcity meant not everyone could receive it regardless, so random, allocation-concealed assignment avoided favoritism-driven bias
Because patients in the control arm were told they were receiving streptomycin
Because randomization made the trial run faster than usual

explanations.a: Randomization did not guarantee eventual access for all participants; scarcity meant real rationing was happening either way.
explanations.b: Correct: since supply couldn't cover every eligible patient, allocating it by unbiased random process within a trial that would generate knowledge was more defensible than ad hoc clinical favoritism.
explanations.c: Deceiving control patients about their treatment was not part of this trial's design.
explanations.d: Trial speed was not the ethical justification for randomization here; unbiased, informative allocation of a scarce resource was.

questions.prompt: Order the design steps of the 1948 MRC streptomycin trial.

items.text: Diagnose patients with active pulmonary tuberculosis
Assign patients to streptomycin-plus-bed-rest or bed-rest-alone using a sealed random-number allocation
Treat and follow both groups concurrently in the same hospitals
Compare six-month mortality and X-ray improvement between groups

questions.explanation: Diagnosis established eligibility, concealed randomization prevented allocation bias, concurrent treatment controlled for era effects, and the outcome comparison at six months produced the trial's result.

questions.prompt: Match each trial feature to the specific bias it addresses.

right.text: Prevents clinicians from steering certain patients toward one arm
Prevents differences in care standards over time from being mistaken for a drug effect

questions.explanation: Randomization with concealment targets selection bias at assignment; running both arms in the same period targets secular-trend confounding that historical controls cannot rule out.

lessons.label: When Epidemiology Got It Wrong: HRT

sections.heading: Decades of observational data pointed one way
sections.body: Starting in 1976, the Nurses' Health Study, a large prospective cohort of American nurses founded by Frank Speizer, tracked hormone use alongside health outcomes for tens of thousands of postmenopausal women. Through the 1980s and into the early 1990s, this and other observational cohorts consistently found that women taking hormone-replacement therapy (HRT), typically estrogen with or without progestin, had substantially lower rates of coronary heart disease than non-users; a widely cited 1991 pooled analysis by Stampfer and Colditz estimated roughly a 50% reduction in coronary risk among HRT users (a pooled relative risk near 0.50), and broader observational summaries across the 1990s converged on a similar 35-50% reduction range across studies. The proposed biology was plausible too: estrogen improves cholesterol profiles and has favorable effects on blood vessels in laboratory studies. By the 1990s, HRT was being promoted, including by some professional guidelines, partly as cardioprotective, and tens of millions of women worldwide were prescribed it with heart-health benefit as part of the rationale.

sections.heading: The Women's Health Initiative reversed the story
sections.body: The Women's Health Initiative (WHI) was a large randomized controlled trial designed to test HRT properly rather than infer from observational cohorts. In its estrogen-plus-progestin arm of roughly 16,600 postmenopausal women, the study was halted early in July 2002, after about 5.2 years of average follow-up, because the data safety monitoring board found increased risk rather than benefit: a hazard ratio near 1.29 for coronary heart disease, along with increased breast cancer, stroke, and blood clot risk, though with some reduced risk of colorectal cancer and hip fracture. Randomization meant treatment groups didn't differ systematically at baseline, so this result could not be explained away by the confounding that likely biased the cohorts. The leading explanation is healthy-user bias combined with confounding by indication: women who chose or were prescribed HRT tended to be healthier, wealthier, and more engaged with preventive healthcare to begin with, and physicians may have been less likely to prescribe it to women already showing signs of cardiovascular disease, both of which would make HRT look protective in observational data even if it did nothing or caused harm. Later reanalyses also raised a timing hypothesis, that starting HRT soon after menopause may differ from starting it years later as WHI participants often did, but the core lesson, that observational association reversed under randomization, stands as the field's most cited cautionary tale. The WHI also ran a separate estrogen-only arm, for roughly 10,700 women who had already had a hysterectomy and so did not need progestin to protect the uterine lining, and its results diverged from the combined estrogen-plus-progestin arm: no statistically significant increase in coronary heart disease overall, and some analyses even suggested a possible reduction in younger women who started estrogen soon after menopause, underscoring that the reversal was specific to the hormone combination and timing tested rather than a uniform verdict against all HRT regimens.

lessons.workedExample: Compare the two study types directly: the Nurses' Health Study and similar cohorts observed that HRT users had roughly 35-50% lower coronary heart disease rates than non-users, a strong protective association. The WHI randomized trial, removing the self-selection into HRT use, found instead a roughly 29% higher rate of coronary heart disease in the hormone arm (hazard ratio about 1.29). If the true causal effect were protective, randomization should have reproduced or exceeded the observational benefit, not reversed its direction; the flip is the signature of confounding, specifically healthy-user bias, where the kind of woman who requests and receives HRT was already lower-risk for reasons unrelated to the hormones themselves.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this case because it is the strongest available demonstration that a well-powered, long-running observational literature can get a causal direction backward, not just the magnitude wrong. A strong answer names healthy-user bias and confounding by indication specifically, rather than just saying 'confounding,' and can explain why randomization neutralizes exactly that kind of bias by breaking the link between a woman's underlying health and her likelihood of treatment. Judges also want to see this used to argue FOR triangulating observational and experimental evidence, not as a blanket dismissal of all observational epidemiology.

questions.prompt: What did observational cohorts like the Nurses' Health Study find regarding HRT and coronary heart disease before 2002?

options.text: HRT users had substantially higher coronary heart disease rates
HRT users had substantially lower coronary heart disease rates
No association was found either way
HRT was linked only to reduced fracture risk, not heart disease

explanations.a: This is the WHI's later finding under randomization, not what the earlier observational cohorts reported.
explanations.b: Correct: observational data through the 1980s-90s, including analyses like Stampfer and Colditz's 1991 pooled estimate, found HRT users had markedly lower coronary risk.
explanations.c: The observational literature found a strong, not null, protective association, which is precisely why the WHI reversal was so notable.
explanations.d: The observational cardioprotective claim specifically concerned coronary heart disease, not just fracture outcomes.

questions.prompt: Why did the Women's Health Initiative's randomized design change the conclusion about HRT and heart disease?

options.text: It used a much larger sample than any cohort study
Randomization removed the self-selection that made healthier, lower-risk women more likely to use HRT in observational data
It only enrolled women who already had heart disease
It measured cholesterol instead of clinical heart disease events

explanations.a: Sample size alone doesn't resolve confounding; several observational cohorts were themselves very large.
explanations.b: Correct: by randomly assigning HRT versus placebo, the WHI balanced known and unknown risk factors across arms, eliminating the healthy-user bias that likely inflated the observational benefit.
explanations.c: WHI enrolled postmenopausal women broadly, not a group pre-selected for existing heart disease.
explanations.d: WHI tracked clinical events like heart attacks and strokes, not merely a cholesterol surrogate.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the HRT and heart disease story.

items.text: Nurses' Health Study begins tracking hormone use and health outcomes
Stampfer and Colditz publish a pooled analysis estimating reduced coronary risk with HRT
WHI randomizes women to estrogen-plus-progestin or placebo
WHI's estrogen-plus-progestin arm is halted early after showing increased risk

questions.explanation: The Nurses' Health Study (1976) generated decades of observational data, the 1991 pooled analysis summarized the apparent benefit, the WHI trial then tested it directly, and its 2002 early halt reversed the conclusion.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in explaining the HRT reversal.

right.text: Women who choose preventive treatments tend to be healthier for unrelated reasons
Physicians' prescribing choices track patients' underlying risk
Breaks the link between treatment assignment and prior health status

questions.explanation: Healthy-user bias and confounding by indication are two related mechanisms that can make an observational treatment look protective; randomization is the design tool that neutralizes both.

lessons.label: Live Debates in Modern Epidemiology

sections.heading: The reproducibility crisis and nutritional epidemiology's credibility problem
sections.body: In 2005, John Ioannidis published 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False' in PLoS Medicine, arguing that small sample sizes, flexible analysis choices, and publication bias toward positive results mean a large share of statistically significant findings in biomedicine, epidemiology included, fail to replicate. This fed a broader reckoning: the American Statistical Association issued a formal 2016 statement warning against treating p<0.05 as a bright line for truth, and in 2019 a Nature comment by Amrhein, Greenland, and McShane, signed by hundreds of scientists, called to 'retire statistical significance' as a threshold entirely, arguing it encourages researchers to chase a cutoff rather than report effect sizes and uncertainty honestly. Nutritional epidemiology has taken particularly sharp criticism within this crisis: most diet studies rely on food-frequency questionnaires asking people to recall what they ate over weeks or months, a method with substantial measurement error, and the field has produced a long history of associations that flip direction across studies, most visibly dietary fat: national guidelines from the late 1970s through the 2000s urged Americans to cut total and saturated fat to protect the heart, largely on observational grounds, only for larger trials and re-analyses in the 2010s to find little to no coronary benefit from that specific substitution and to instead implicate refined carbohydrates and added sugar, a reversal serious enough that the U.S. dietary guidelines dropped their long-standing numeric cap on total fat intake in 2015. Critics, Ioannidis prominent among them, argue the field needs larger, better-measured studies and more caution before headlines claim a food 'causes' or 'prevents' disease from observational data alone.

sections.heading: Target trials and the ethics of watching everyone
sections.body: A methodological response to weak observational designs is the 'target trial emulation' framework, formalized by Miguel Hernán and James Robins in a 2016 paper, which asks researchers to first specify the randomized trial they would ideally run, then explicitly map each design element (eligibility, treatment strategies, follow-up start) onto available observational data, exposing biases like immortal time bias that looser analyses hide. This represents a shift from classical single-risk-factor epidemiology toward causal-inference methods borrowed from statistics and economics, and it is not universally embraced; some traditional epidemiologists argue the framework adds formal overhead without new data, while proponents argue it prevents the kind of confounded, poorly specified comparisons that produced the HRT reversal. A separate live debate concerns big-data surveillance: tools like mobile-phone contact tracing and exposure-notification apps deployed during COVID-19 gave epidemiologists unprecedented real-time population data, but raised unresolved questions about consent, data retention, and whether public-health emergency powers used to justify surveillance quietly become permanent, a tension between epidemiological power and individual privacy that remains actively contested rather than settled.

lessons.workedExample: A nutritional epidemiology example: an observational study using food-frequency questionnaires might find that people who report eating more of a given food have lower rates of a disease years later, generating a headline claim. A critic applying Ioannidis-style scrutiny would ask whether the questionnaire's recall error is large enough to distort the estimate, whether the finding survived multiple-comparisons correction given how many foods and outcomes were tested, and whether it replicates in an independent cohort. A target-trial-emulation response would go further, specifying the hypothetical RCT (who would be eligible, what exact dietary change would be assigned, when follow-up would start) and checking whether the observational analysis actually maps onto that trial design or silently include biases like counting person-time before the exposure was even measured.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe these live debates because they test whether a student can distinguish 'this finding is uncertain' from 'this entire field is fake,' a distinction lost in a lot of pop-science coverage of the reproducibility crisis. A strong answer can name a specific mechanism, recall error in food-frequency questionnaires, p-hacking through flexible analysis choices, or immortal time bias in observational cohort designs, rather than gesturing vaguely at 'bad science,' and can explain what methodological fix (target trial emulation, preregistration, larger sample sizes) is actually being proposed and why it addresses that specific failure mode.

questions.prompt: What was the central argument of Ioannidis's 2005 paper 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False'?

options.text: That researchers routinely commit outright fraud
That small samples, flexible analyses, and publication bias make many statistically significant findings fail to replicate
That epidemiology should be replaced entirely by randomized trials
That p-values below 0.05 are always correct

explanations.a: The paper's argument is about structural statistical and publication incentives, not deliberate fraud by researchers.
explanations.b: Correct: Ioannidis argued that a combination of low power, analytic flexibility, and bias toward publishing positive results systematically inflates the share of false positive findings in the literature.
explanations.c: The paper argues for more rigor and caution in interpreting findings, not for eliminating observational epidemiology.
explanations.d: The paper's point is nearly the opposite: passing a p<0.05 threshold does not guarantee a finding is true.

questions.prompt: What problem does the target trial emulation framework (Hernán and Robins, 2016) primarily address?

options.text: It eliminates the need for any observational data
It forces explicit mapping of an observational analysis onto a hypothetical randomized trial design, exposing biases like immortal time bias
It replaces statistical significance testing with big-data surveillance
It only applies to nutritional epidemiology

explanations.a: The framework works with observational data; it structures how that data is analyzed rather than replacing it.
explanations.b: Correct: by specifying the target trial first, researchers must align eligibility, treatment timing, and follow-up start with observational data, revealing subtle design flaws that looser analyses can hide.
explanations.c: Target trial emulation is a causal-inference design framework, not a surveillance or statistics-replacement tool.
explanations.d: The framework is general to observational causal inference and has been applied well beyond nutrition, including drug-effectiveness studies.

questions.prompt: Match each modern debate to its central tension.

right.text: Flexible analysis and publication bias inflating false-positive findings
Measurement error in self-reported diet producing unstable associations
Population-level data power versus consent and privacy

questions.explanation: Each modern debate centers on a distinct tension: statistical incentive structures, measurement error specific to diet research, and the ethics of population surveillance tools.

questions.prompt: Order these developments in the reproducibility and statistical-significance debate.

items.text: Ioannidis publishes 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False'
American Statistical Association issues its formal statement on p-values
Amrhein, Greenland, and McShane's Nature comment calls to retire statistical significance

questions.explanation: Ioannidis's 2005 paper raised the alarm, the ASA's 2016 statement formally cautioned against p-value misuse, and the 2019 Nature comment pushed further to argue for abandoning the significance threshold altogether.

units.label: Applied Epidemiology: Designing and Critiquing a Study

lessons.label: From Question to Design

sections.heading: PICO becomes PECO for observational exposures
sections.body: Every rigorous epidemiological study starts by forcing a fuzzy question into a structured one. Evidence-based medicine's PICO framework (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) assumes someone assigns the intervention, as in a trial. Most science-fair projects instead observe an exposure nobody assigned, so epidemiologists substitute Exposure for Intervention: PECO. A vague question like 'do energy drinks cause heart problems in teens' becomes: Population = adolescents aged 13-18; Exposure = regular energy drink consumption (e.g., at least one can/day); Comparison = non-consumers; Outcome = physician-diagnosed arrhythmia within a defined follow-up window. Each element must be answerable from data you can actually collect, not just conceptually true.

sections.heading: Matching design to how common the outcome is
sections.body: The three classic observational designs trade off against outcome frequency and feasibility. A cohort study enrolls people by exposure status and follows them forward; it directly yields relative risk and can track multiple outcomes at once, but needs a large sample and years of follow-up when the outcome is rare. The Framingham Heart Study, begun in 1948 with 5,209 Massachusetts residents, could afford this because cardiovascular disease is common enough to accumulate cases within a feasible cohort. A case-control study instead samples by outcome status and looks backward for exposure history, making it efficient for rare outcomes. Doll and Hill's 1950 British Medical Journal case-control study compared roughly 650 lung cancer patients against hospital controls and found the smoking association within about a year, at the price of yielding only an odds ratio and being more vulnerable to recall bias. A cross-sectional design measures exposure and outcome at a single moment, which is fast and cheap (NHANES surveys thousands of Americans this way each cycle) but gives prevalence, not incidence, and cannot establish which came first.

sections.heading: Operational definitions and the effect measure come before data collection
sections.body: A design choice is wasted if exposure and outcome stay vague. 'High sugar intake' must become a measurable cutoff, such as grams per day from a validated food log, and 'depression' must become a specific screening-instrument threshold, not a self-report of feeling sad. Equally important: decide the primary effect measure before looking at any data. Cohort designs naturally support relative risk; case-control designs are restricted to odds ratios, which approximate risk ratios only when the outcome is rare (the rare-disease assumption). Choosing the measure in advance, alongside the design, prevents switching to whichever measure looks most impressive after the numbers are in.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to study whether social-media use affects anxiety in her high school. Anxiety is common, not rare, but she has only one semester, ruling out a multi-year cohort. She frames it as PECO: Population = students grades 9-12; Exposure = more than 3 hours/day self-reported social media use; Comparison = 3 hours/day or less; Outcome = score above the clinical cutoff on the GAD-7 anxiety screener, administered once. This forces a cross-sectional design, so she pre-commits to reporting a prevalence odds ratio, not a risk ratio, and states in her plan that the design cannot determine whether high use preceded anxiety or followed it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge's first design question is often 'why this design and not another,' because mismatched designs are the most common flaw in fair projects: cross-sectional data reported with causal language, or a cohort attempted for a disease too rare to accrue cases in a semester. A student who can state the outcome's approximate frequency, name the feasibility constraint that ruled out the alternatives, and show the effect measure was chosen before seeing results demonstrates the design was reasoned, not just whatever was easiest to run in a school hallway.

questions.prompt: A student wants to study a rare pediatric cancer (roughly 1 in 20,000 children) and has one school year to finish the project. Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: A cohort study, because it directly yields relative risk
A case-control study, because it samples by outcome status and can find enough cases without waiting years
A cross-sectional study, because it is the fastest design available
A randomized controlled trial, because it eliminates confounding

explanations.a: A cohort would need an enormous sample followed for years to accrue even a handful of cases of a 1-in-20,000 outcome — infeasible in one school year.
explanations.b: Correct: sampling by outcome status lets you gather enough cases immediately, which is exactly why Doll and Hill used this design for rare lung cancer in 1950.
explanations.c: A single snapshot would capture almost no cases of a disease this rare, so it cannot detect a meaningful pattern.
explanations.d: You cannot ethically or practically randomize children to a suspected cancer exposure.

questions.prompt: PECO framing replaces PICO's 'Intervention' with 'Exposure.' Why is this substitution necessary for most epidemiological science-fair projects?

options.text: Because exposures are always harmful while interventions are always beneficial
Because in observational research nobody assigns the exposure to participants, unlike a trial where researchers assign the intervention
Because PECO only applies to environmental pollution studies
Because comparison groups only exist in observational studies

explanations.a: Exposures are not inherently harmful and interventions are not inherently beneficial; the distinction is about assignment, not value.
explanations.b: Correct: PICO assumes a researcher-assigned intervention as in a trial; PECO fits observational designs where the exposure occurs naturally.
explanations.c: PECO applies to any observational exposure question, not just environmental ones.
explanations.d: Comparison groups exist in both trial and observational designs; that is not what distinguishes PICO from PECO.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for turning a vague research idea into a chosen study design.

items.text: State a vague research question
Translate it into PECO with measurable Population, Exposure, Comparison, Outcome
Estimate how common the outcome is and what time and resources are feasible
Select cohort, case-control, or cross-sectional design accordingly
Pre-specify the primary effect measure before collecting data

questions.explanation: Design choice and effect-measure selection only make sense once the question is operationalized and the outcome's frequency and feasibility constraints are known.

questions.prompt: Match each design to its defining feature.

right.text: Follows exposure groups forward in time; yields relative risk; needs large n for rare outcomes
Samples by outcome status and looks backward for exposure; yields odds ratio; efficient for rare outcomes
Measures exposure and outcome at one time point; yields prevalence; cannot establish temporality

questions.explanation: Each design's sampling direction (by exposure, by outcome, or simultaneous) determines both which effect measure it can produce and what outcome frequency it handles efficiently.

lessons.label: Writing the Case Definition and Analysis Plan

sections.heading: Turning a fuzzy 'case' into a reproducible rule
sections.body: Outbreak investigators do not ask 'does this person seem sick?' They apply a written case definition, often tiered the way CDC and the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists tier surveillance definitions: a confirmed case meets a definitive diagnostic standard (for the 2009 H1N1 influenza investigation, that meant a positive RT-PCR test), while a probable case meets clinical and epidemiologic criteria without lab confirmation. The tiers matter because two different people applying a vague definition ('flu-like illness') will classify the same patient differently, and that misclassification quietly biases results. A science-fair project needs the same discipline: write the inclusion and exclusion criteria for 'case' and 'exposed' before touching any data, in language specific enough that a stranger could apply it and get the same classification you would.

sections.heading: Laying out the 2x2 or stratified analysis before collecting data
sections.body: Sketch the primary analysis table before data collection: exposed/unexposed crossed with case/non-case. If a confounder is likely (age, weather, baseline health), pre-specify a stratified analysis rather than deciding after the fact. The Mantel-Haenszel method, introduced by Mantel and Haenszel in 1959, pools odds ratios across strata of a confounder into one adjusted estimate, correcting for the confounding a single crude table can hide or exaggerate (a version of Simpson's paradox). A classic real case: in a 1986 BMJ study of two kidney-stone treatments, open surgery (A) beat percutaneous removal (B) within both the small-stone group (93% vs. 87% success) and the large-stone group (73% vs. 69%) — yet the crude, un-stratified table showed B winning overall (83% vs. 78%), because surgeons had preferentially used A on the harder large-stone cases. Stone size was the confounder: it drove both which treatment a patient received and how likely treatment was to succeed, so pooling without stratifying flipped the apparent winner. Splitting the analysis by stone size, the way Mantel-Haenszel splits by confounder strata before pooling, recovers the true direction that the crude table hid. Naming the confounders to adjust for in advance, based on prior knowledge rather than which adjustment produces the largest effect, prevents 'confounder-shopping' — the analysis-side twin of p-hacking.

sections.heading: Locking the primary measure and pre-registering the plan
sections.body: Decide the single primary effect measure and how its confidence interval will be computed before running any test. Then timestamp the whole plan publicly, the way trial registries require: the FDA Amendments Act of 2007 made prospective registration mandatory for many US trials specifically to stop outcomes from shifting after results come in. That the requirement is routinely violated even by professionals is documented by Ben Goldacre's COMPare project, which in 2016 audited 67 published trials against their registered protocols.
