A school project doesn't need a formal registry — a locked document dated and shared with a mentor before pulling data serves the same purpose.

lessons.workedExample: A student studies whether a school's new recess policy reduces playground injuries. Case definition: a documented case is any incident logged by the school nurse requiring first aid during school hours; a self-report with no nurse visit is excluded to avoid misclassification. Before pulling any logs, she writes an analysis plan: primary table is policy-period vs. pre-policy-period crossed with injury/no-injury per 100 recess-days; the pre-specified confounder is weather, analyzed via Mantel-Haenszel stratified by wet vs. dry days; the primary measure is a risk ratio with a 95% confidence interval. She emails this plan to her teacher-mentor before requesting the nurse's records, so she cannot later narrow the outcome to 'twisted ankles only' if the overall injury rate looks unimpressive.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'did you decide this before or after you saw the data?' because post-hoc confounder or outcome selection leaves no fingerprint in a results section — it just quietly moves the answer toward what the student hoped to find. Goldacre's 2016 audit shows this happens routinely even in professionally registered trials, so a student who can produce a dated plan naming the case definition, confounders, and primary measure in advance demonstrates the result was not reverse-engineered from whichever comparison came out significant.

questions.prompt: Why do surveillance case definitions like CDC/CSTE's tier cases into 'confirmed' and 'probable'?

options.text: To inflate the total case count for public attention
To give investigators a reproducible rule so the same patient is classified the same way regardless of who applies it, reducing misclassification
To let researchers pick whichever tier best supports their hypothesis after reviewing the data
To make classification a subjective judgment call for each local doctor

explanations.a: Tiered definitions constrain classification; they are not designed to inflate counts.
explanations.b: Correct: a written, specific rule applied consistently prevents different investigators from classifying the same patient differently, which would otherwise bias results.
explanations.c: Choosing a tier after seeing the data is exactly the kind of post-hoc flexibility a fixed case definition is meant to prevent.
explanations.d: The point of a formal case definition is to remove subjective, doctor-by-doctor judgment, not enable it.

questions.prompt: What problem does a Mantel-Haenszel stratified analysis solve that a single crude 2x2 table cannot?

options.text: It removes the need for a comparison group entirely
It pools odds ratios across strata of a confounder into one adjusted estimate, correcting for confounding a crude table would miss
It eliminates the need to write a case definition
It automatically converts an odds ratio into an absolute risk

explanations.a: A comparison group is still required; Mantel-Haenszel adjusts the comparison, it does not remove it.
explanations.b: Correct: by combining stratum-specific odds ratios (e.g., across age or weather categories), Mantel-Haenszel produces an estimate adjusted for that confounder, unlike a single pooled crude table.
explanations.c: A case definition is still necessary before any table, crude or stratified, can be built.
explanations.d: The odds ratio stays an odds ratio; Mantel-Haenszel does not convert it into a risk measure.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for writing an analysis plan before collecting data.

items.text: Write precise case and exposure criteria (e.g., confirmed vs. probable)
List the confounders to adjust for, based on prior knowledge
Specify the primary 2x2 or stratified analysis and how the confidence interval will be computed
Lock and timestamp the plan (e.g., share it with a mentor) before touching the data
Collect the data and run only the pre-specified analysis

questions.explanation: Every planning decision — definitions, confounders, measure, and CI method — has to be fixed and timestamped before the data is collected, or the analysis can be silently reshaped to fit the results.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

right.text: Meets the case definition via a definitive diagnostic standard, such as a positive lab test
Meets clinical or epidemiologic criteria but lacks laboratory confirmation
A timestamped, shared description of the case definition, confounders, and primary measure, fixed before data collection

questions.explanation: Confirmed and probable are tiers of diagnostic certainty within a case definition; pre-registration is a separate safeguard that fixes the whole analysis plan in time.

questions.prompt: Ben Goldacre's COMPare project audited 67 published trials against their registered protocols in 2016. What did it find?

options.text: All 67 trials matched their pre-registered outcomes exactly
Only 9 trials fully matched their registration; across the rest, 301 pre-specified outcomes went unreported and 357 new ones were silently added
The trials had too few outcomes listed to make any comparison possible
Pre-registration made no measurable difference because journals do not check registries

explanations.a: Only 9 of the 67 trials were fully consistent with their registered protocol.
explanations.b: Correct: this is the headline finding of the 2016 COMPare audit, showing outcome switching was the norm rather than the exception even in registered trials.
explanations.c: The audit compared each trial's registered outcomes against its published outcomes in detail; the issue was mismatch, not insufficient data to compare.
explanations.d: The project's entire point was that registries let outsiders detect switching after the fact, which is exactly what it demonstrated.

lessons.label: Sampling, Sample Size, and Power in Practice

sections.heading: A biased sampling frame beats any sample size
sections.body: In 1936, the magazine Literary Digest mailed 10 million ballots drawn from telephone directories, car registrations, and club rosters, got 2.4 million back, and predicted Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt 57% to 43%. Roosevelt won roughly 62% to 38% — a sampling error near 19 points, the largest in a major poll's history at the time. The frame was the problem: in 1936, phones and cars were luxuries, so the list systematically excluded poorer voters, who leaned heavily toward Roosevelt. George Gallup, sampling only about 50,000 people but drawing a frame meant to represent the whole electorate, correctly called a Roosevelt win. No amount of n fixes a frame that structurally excludes part of the population — selection bias comes from who can even be sampled, and non-response bias from who bothers to reply, and both survive a bigger n untouched.

sections.heading: Why more n narrows the interval and raises power
sections.body: For a proportion, the standard error is roughly the square root of p(1-p)/n, so the confidence interval's width shrinks with the square root of n: quadrupling the sample roughly halves the interval. Statistical power — the probability of detecting a true effect if one exists — rises with n for the same reason: a bigger sample lets the real signal stand out further above sampling noise, which is why underpowered studies routinely miss real effects, not just avoid false ones. Epidemiology conventionally targets 80% power at a 0.05 significance level, meaning the study is designed to catch a true effect of the assumed size four times out of five.

sections.heading: A back-of-envelope estimate, plus the consent basics
sections.body: A rough sample-size formula for estimating a proportion within margin of error E at confidence level Z is n = Z-squared times p(1-p), divided by E-squared; using p = 0.5 (the most conservative, largest-variance assumption) when no prior estimate exists. This gives a defensible target n before recruiting, rather than 'however many people I could reach.' Recruiting itself must respect human-subjects basics: the 1979 Belmont Report established respect for persons, beneficence, and justice as the governing principles, enforced in practice by Institutional Review Board (IRB) review before a study proceeds. For minors, US federal regulation (45 CFR 46, Subpart D) requires both parental permission and the child's own assent — two separate agreements, not one.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to estimate what share of her school skips breakfast, aiming for a 5% margin of error at 95% confidence (Z = 1.96). With p = 0.5: n = 1.96-squared times 0.5 times 0.5, divided by 0.05-squared, which is 0.9604 divided by 0.0025, about 384. She needs roughly 384 respondents. She recruits via a random draw of homerooms rather than handing surveys to friends in the hallway — the convenience-sample trap that doomed the Literary Digest — and collects both a parental consent form and each student's own written assent before any survey goes out, since her participants are minors.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether the sample size was calculated or just whatever was convenient, and whether consent was handled correctly for minors, because both failures are common and both are disqualifying at most fairs. 'I surveyed 40 people' invites the follow-up 'why 40, and what margin of error does that buy you?' — a student who can show n = 384 was derived from a target precision, and that parental consent plus student assent were both obtained, has done the two things a design with no sample-size logic and no ethics review cannot fake.

questions.prompt: Despite collecting 2.4 million responses, the 1936 Literary Digest poll missed the election result by about 19 points. What was the primary cause?

options.text: The sample size was too small to be reliable
Selection bias: the sampling frame (phone books, car registrations, club rosters) systematically excluded poorer voters, who leaned Roosevelt
The poll question itself was worded misleadingly
Random chance — a 19-point error is expected noise at that sample size

explanations.a: 2.4 million responses is enormous; the error came from who was in the frame, not how many replied.
explanations.b: Correct: the mailing list itself under-represented poorer, pro-Roosevelt voters because phones and cars were disproportionately owned by wealthier households in 1936.
explanations.c: The failure was in sampling, not question wording; this is the textbook example of frame-driven selection bias.
explanations.d: A 19-point error at that sample size is far too large to be random noise; it reflects a systematic bias in who was sampled.

questions.prompt: Holding everything else constant, if a study quadruples its sample size, what happens to the width of its confidence interval for a proportion?

options.text: It roughly halves, since standard error scales with the square root of n
It roughly quarters
It stays about the same
It roughly doubles

explanations.a: Correct: standard error is proportional to 1 over the square root of n, so quadrupling n halves the standard error and roughly halves the CI width.
explanations.b: Quartering the interval would require a 16-fold increase in n, not a 4-fold one.
explanations.c: CI width is directly tied to n through the square-root relationship; it does not stay constant.
explanations.d: Larger n narrows the interval; it does not widen it.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for a back-of-envelope precision estimate and the ethics steps that follow it.

items.text: Choose the desired margin of error E and confidence level (Z)
Assume the conservative p = 0.5 if no prior estimate of the proportion exists
Compute n = Z-squared times p(1-p), divided by E-squared
Plan a sampling frame that can reach that n without excluding part of the population
Obtain parental consent and participant assent before collecting any data

questions.explanation: The precision target and its assumptions come first because they determine the required n; only then can a frame be planned to reach that n, and consent must be secured before data collection begins, not after.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in protecting human subjects.

right.text: Established respect for persons, beneficence, and justice as the governing principles for human-subjects research
The body that reviews a study against those principles before it is allowed to proceed
A minor participant's own agreement to take part, required in addition to parental consent

questions.explanation: The Belmont Report set the principles, IRBs enforce them procedurally, and assent is the specific additional safeguard required when participants are minors.

lessons.label: Critically Appraising a Published Paper

sections.heading: Two checklists for two kinds of study
sections.body: Before appraising a paper's claims, identify whether it is observational or a trial, because different reporting standards apply to each. STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology), published in 2007, is a 22-item checklist for cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional studies, covering how the sample was selected, how bias and confounding were addressed, and how missing data was handled. CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials), first published in 1996 and most recently updated in 2010, does the equivalent job for randomized trials, including its signature participant flow diagram tracking how many people were assessed, randomized, and actually analyzed. Neither checklist certifies that a finding is true; both simply require the paper to report enough methodological detail that a reader can judge validity independently.

sections.heading: Extracting design, effect measure, and CI before reading the discussion
sections.body: Before reading what the authors concluded, pull out: the exact design, the effect measure and its point estimate, the confidence interval, and which biases or confounders the methods section says were addressed. The hormone-replacement-therapy story is the classic teaching case: the Nurses' Health Study, an observational cohort begun in 1976, reported substantially lower coronary heart disease risk among women using HRT. The Women's Health Initiative, a randomized controlled trial published by Rossouw and colleagues in JAMA in 2002, found instead an increased hazard ratio for coronary heart disease with combined estrogen-progestin, and that trial arm was stopped early. Same exposure, same broad outcome, opposite direction, because the cohort could not fully separate HRT's effect from the 'healthy-user' pattern of women who chose to take it — more health-conscious, more affluent, more likely to see a doctor regularly — a confounding-by-indication problem that randomization directly removes.

sections.heading: Separating what the data show from what authors claim
sections.body: A limitations paragraph naming an unhandled bias is a sign of honest reporting, not proof the whole study is flawed. A discussion section can also overreach: language like 'these results demonstrate' attached to an observational odds ratio claims more than the design supports on its own. The appraiser's job is to check the abstract's headline claim against the actual confidence interval in the results table — a CI that crosses 1.0 for a ratio measure means the result is statistically compatible with no effect, regardless of how confidently the discussion is written.

lessons.workedExample: Appraising Rossouw et al.'s 2002 JAMA paper: design = randomized controlled trial, so CONSORT applies rather than STROBE. Effect measure = hazard ratio for coronary heart disease, reported as 1.29 with a 95% CI of 1.02 to 1.63 for combined HRT versus placebo. Confounding was controlled by randomization itself, verified by a baseline-characteristics table showing the groups were balanced; outcome assessors were blinded. The authors' own limitations note that only postmenopausal women aged 50 to 79 were studied, so results may not generalize to women just entering menopause. A careful reader notes the CI barely excludes 1.0 — a real but modest effect — rather than repeating the flatter 'HRT causes heart attacks' headline many outlets ran.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use appraisal questions to test whether a student can separate a paper's actual result from its abstract's spin, since abstracts and news coverage are both known to overstate findings. A student who names the exact design, states the point estimate with its CI, and can cite one bias the authors handled and one they left as a stated limitation demonstrates they read the methods and results, not just the abstract — the specific tell that separates genuine appraisal from repeating a press release.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a reporting checklist like STROBE or CONSORT?

options.text: To guarantee that the study's conclusion is true
To ensure the paper reports enough methodological detail — sample selection, bias handling, missing data or participant flow — that a reader can judge validity independently
To retroactively require the study to have been pre-registered
To replace peer review entirely

explanations.a: Neither checklist evaluates truth; a fully STROBE- or CONSORT-compliant paper can still report a wrong or biased finding if the underlying study was poorly designed.
explanations.b: Correct: both checklists exist to make sure enough methodological detail is disclosed for an independent reader to assess the study's validity.
explanations.c: The checklists govern reporting completeness at publication, not pre-registration status.
explanations.d: They supplement peer review by giving reviewers and readers a structured completeness check; they do not replace it.

questions.prompt: The observational Nurses' Health Study found lower coronary heart disease risk with HRT, while the randomized Women's Health Initiative (2002) found a higher hazard ratio. What best explains the reversal?

options.text: WHI simply had a larger sample, so it was more precise but should have found the same direction of effect
Randomization in WHI balanced the 'healthy-user' pattern — more health-conscious, affluent women choosing HRT — that had confounded the observational cohort
The two studies measured entirely different outcomes, so the results are not actually comparable
WHI's confidence interval crossed 1.0, meaning it found no real effect at all

explanations.a: Sample size affects precision, not the direction of a confounded estimate; the reversal is about confounding, not power.
explanations.b: Correct: randomization removes confounding by indication, including the healthy-user effect that biased the cohort's estimate toward apparent benefit.
explanations.c: Both studies examined coronary heart disease risk associated with HRT use; the outcome was the same broad endpoint.
explanations.d: The reported CI of 1.02 to 1.63 excludes 1.0, so WHI did find a statistically real, if modest, increased risk.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of critically appraising a published epidemiological paper.

items.text: Identify whether the design is observational or a randomized trial
Extract the effect measure and its point estimate
Extract the confidence interval
Note which biases or confounders the methods section says were, and were not, addressed
Compare the abstract's headline claim against the actual CI before accepting the conclusion

questions.explanation: Design identifies which reporting checklist applies, which frames how to read the effect measure, CI, and bias handling — only then can the headline claim be checked against what the data actually support.

questions.prompt: Match each item to its role in paper appraisal.

left.text: A CI that crosses 1.0 for a ratio measure

right.text: 22-item checklist (2007) for cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional study reporting
Checklist (1996, updated 2010) for randomized trial reporting, including a participant flow diagram
Signals the result is statistically compatible with no effect, regardless of how confidently the discussion is worded

questions.explanation: STROBE and CONSORT are reporting-completeness checklists for different designs, while a CI crossing 1.0 is a statistical signal independent of either checklist.

lessons.label: Presenting Epidemiological Evidence to Judges

sections.heading: Choosing the honest figure for the design
sections.body: The figure should match the design, not just look impressive. A forest plot — a column of point estimates with horizontal confidence-interval lines against a vertical null line — is for combining multiple studies or subgroup estimates, not a single comparison. A raw 2x2 table suits a single case-control or cross-sectional result, because it lets a judge recompute the effect measure themselves from the actual counts rather than trusting a summary bar. A Kaplan-Meier survival curve, the method Kaplan and Meier introduced in 1958, fits a cohort with time-to-event data: it plots the cumulative probability of the outcome across time separately for each group, ideally with a number-at-risk table beneath it showing how many participants remained under observation at each time point. Presenting the wrong figure for the design is itself a tell that the student may not fully understand what the design can and cannot show.

sections.heading: Report effect size, CI, and absolute impact — not a bare p-value
sections.body: A p-value alone says nothing about magnitude. Report the point estimate for the pre-registered effect measure together with its 95% confidence interval, then translate it into an absolute term a judge intuits directly: absolute risk difference, or numbers needed to treat or harm. A relative risk of 2.0 sounds dramatic on its own, but if it moves absolute risk from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000, that context changes how the finding should be weighed — and a judge will expect the student to volunteer that distinction, not wait to be asked for it.

sections.heading: Name your biases first, then argue causation with Bradford Hill
sections.body: State at least one specific bias inherent to the design — selection, recall, or confounding — in the student's own words during the results discussion, rather than letting a judge surface it first; naming it signals it was understood, not missed. To argue for a causal, rather than merely associational, claim, draw on the considerations Austin Bradford Hill laid out in 1965: strength and consistency of the association across settings, temporality (exposure clearly preceding outcome), a dose-response gradient, biological plausibility, and analogous experimental evidence. Hill never proposed these as a rigid checklist that proves causation when satisfied, and no single one is decisive — but walking two or three of them against the specific finding turns a bare assertion of causation into a defended one.

lessons.workedExample: A student studying cafeteria seating noise and reported stress presents a 2x2 table, since her design is cross-sectional: a prevalence odds ratio of 2.2 (95% CI 1.3 to 3.4) for high stress among students in loud seating versus quiet seating. She translates this to absolute terms — 35% high-stress prevalence in loud seating versus 20% in quiet, a 15-percentage-point absolute difference — and states on her results slide that a cross-sectional design cannot establish temporality, since stressed students may have chosen loud seating rather than the reverse. In Q&A, she cites consistency (two other classroom surveys that semester found the same direction) but concedes she collected no dose-response data, and explicitly frames her claim as associational, not causal.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges expect a strong evidence presentation to read like an honest brief, not a sales pitch: reporting only 'p less than 0.05' with no effect size, or a bar chart with no confidence interval, reads as either not knowing better or hiding something. A student who leads with the CI, states the absolute impact next to the relative one, names the design's own weak point before being asked, and can say plainly 'this is associational, not causal, because temporality is missing' demonstrates the quantitative honesty and epistemic humility that judging rubrics are built to reward.

questions.prompt: A cohort study follows two exposure groups over several years to see who develops an outcome. Which figure best matches this design, and why?

options.text: A bar chart of final outcome proportions in each group
A Kaplan-Meier survival curve, because it shows the cumulative probability of the outcome over time for each group, with a number-at-risk table
A forest plot, because it is the standard figure for any epidemiological result
A 2x2 table of final counts only

explanations.a: A single end-of-study bar chart discards all the time-course information the cohort design collected.
explanations.b: Correct: Kaplan-Meier curves are built for exactly this — time-to-event data followed across a cohort — and preserve the timing information a bar chart or table loses.
explanations.c: Forest plots combine point estimates across multiple studies or subgroups; a single cohort's own time-to-event result is not what they are for.
explanations.d: A 2x2 table collapses the entire follow-up period into one endpoint count, throwing away when events occurred.

questions.prompt: Why should a results section report an absolute measure (like absolute risk difference or NNT) alongside a relative measure like relative risk?

options.text: Because absolute measures are always numerically larger and therefore more persuasive
Because a large relative risk can correspond to a tiny absolute impact when the baseline risk is very low, and both numbers are needed to judge real-world importance
Because reporting relative risk alone is not statistically valid
Because absolute measures make reporting a confidence interval unnecessary

explanations.a: Absolute measures are often much smaller than relative ones, not larger; that is precisely why they provide necessary context.
explanations.b: Correct: a relative risk of 2.0 means very different things depending on whether baseline risk is 1% or 0.01%, so both figures are needed to convey real-world magnitude.
explanations.c: Relative risk is a valid measure on its own; the issue is incompleteness, not invalidity.
explanations.d: A confidence interval is still required around whichever measure is reported, absolute or relative.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for presenting epidemiological evidence to a science-fair judge.

items.text: Choose the figure that matches the study design (2x2, forest plot, or Kaplan-Meier curve)
Report the point estimate for the primary effect measure with its confidence interval
Convert the relative measure into an absolute-impact statement
State at least one specific bias inherent to the design in your own words
Use Bradford Hill's considerations to argue for association versus causation appropriately

questions.explanation: The figure and numbers come first so the audience has the evidence in front of them, then the bias is named proactively, and only then is the association-versus-causation argument made on top of that honestly presented base.

questions.prompt: Match each Bradford Hill consideration to its meaning.

right.text: The exposure demonstrably preceded the outcome in time
Higher exposure doses are associated with higher outcome risk (a dose-response pattern)
The association is observed repeatedly across different populations or studies

questions.explanation: Hill's 1965 considerations each probe a different angle on an association; temporality and dose-response are about the exposure-outcome relationship itself, while consistency is about replication across settings.

units.label: Detecting Outbreaks and the Investigation Framework

lessons.label: Outbreak, Cluster, Epidemic: Defining the Signal

sections.heading: Endemic baseline, epidemic excess
sections.body: Epidemiologists define an epidemic not by an absolute number of cases but by comparison to an expected baseline. A disease is endemic when it holds at a roughly constant, predictable level in a population over time — that steady level is the "expected" count. An epidemic (used interchangeably with outbreak, though outbreak conventionally implies a smaller geographic scope, such as a school or ward) is the occurrence of cases clearly in excess of that expectation for the given place, population, and season. The expected count itself is disease- and context-specific: it is usually built from several years of prior surveillance data, adjusted for known seasonal cycles, so that a December rise in respiratory illness is not mistaken for an epidemic the way the identical case count would be in July.

sections.heading: Cluster, outbreak, epidemic, pandemic
sections.body: Cluster is the loosest term: an aggregation of cases grouped in time and place that has drawn attention but has not yet been confirmed to exceed the expected number — a hypothesis to test, not a confirmed diagnosis. Outbreak and epidemic are technically synonyms, both meaning a confirmed excess, but outbreak is conventionally used for a localized event and epidemic for something wider, often national. Pandemic describes geographic scope, not severity: an epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents and affects a large number of people. The World Health Organization's March 11, 2020 pandemic declaration for COVID-19 reflected sustained transmission across every continent, not a sudden change in how dangerous the virus had become.

sections.heading: When the expected count is zero
sections.body: For some diseases, one case is itself the outbreak, because the expected baseline is zero. A country that has eliminated a disease — the U.S. declared measles eliminated in 2000, meaning no continuous domestic transmission chain for twelve or more months — treats any locally acquired case as evidence a transmission chain still exists, triggering full contact tracing before a second case can appear. Foodborne botulism is investigated on a single case because it usually signals a contaminated food lot that could reach many more people. Cholera works the same way in a country with no recent transmission: when cholera reappeared in Haiti in October 2010 after decades of absence, the first cluster of severe watery diarrhea was investigated as an outbreak immediately, because Haiti's expected cholera count was zero.

lessons.workedExample: In spring 1993, waterborne Cryptosporidium illness in Milwaukee was ordinarily rare enough that no meaningful baseline existed — the expected count was essentially zero. After a contaminated water-treatment intake let the parasite through, an estimated 403,000 residents developed watery diarrhea and about 4,400 were hospitalized, according to MacKenzie and colleagues' 1994 New England Journal of Medicine investigation. Because the observed count so vastly exceeded the near-zero expected baseline for this pathogen, officials did not need weeks of surveillance data to call it an epidemic; pharmacies reporting anti-diarrheal medication shortages were an informal signal within days, well before formal case counts caught up.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'how many cases makes something an outbreak?' is testing whether a student conflates outbreak status with a fixed number. The defensible answer names the comparison — observed versus expected, for that disease, place, and season — and explains why one measles case can matter more than fifty flu cases in flu season. A student who can also explain the single-case exception (elimination status, botulism, novel introduction) shows they understand that 'expected' is sometimes legitimately zero, which separates a memorized definition from an applied one.

questions.prompt: A country with no domestic cholera transmission for decades confirms one severe watery-diarrhea case as cholera. Why is this single case treated as an outbreak requiring investigation?

options.text: Because cholera is always fatal without treatment
Because the expected baseline count of cholera in that country is zero, so even one case is a clear excess
Because national law requires investigating exactly one case of any disease
Because cholera has an unusually short incubation period

explanations.a: Cholera is treatable, and most cases are not fatal with prompt rehydration; severity alone is not why one case triggers investigation.
explanations.b: Correct: with an expected count of zero, a single case is already a complete excess over baseline, which is what defines an outbreak.
explanations.c: There is no such blanket one-case law; the threshold is context-dependent (an expected count of zero), not a universal rule.
explanations.d: Incubation period affects how fast a chain of transmission unfolds, not whether a single case counts as an outbreak.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

right.text: An aggregation of cases in time and place not yet confirmed to exceed the expected number
A confirmed excess over expected, conventionally used for a localized event
Technically synonymous with outbreak, conventionally used for a wider, often national, event
An epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents

questions.explanation: The four terms differ mainly in confirmation status (cluster vs. the rest) and geographic scope (outbreak/epidemic vs. pandemic), not in the underlying biology.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of applying the epidemic-threshold idea to a rise in reported cases.

items.text: Establish the expected case count from historical surveillance data for that disease, place, and season
Count the observed cases in the current period
Compare the observed count to the expected count
If observed clearly exceeds expected (or is any count above a zero baseline), call it an outbreak

questions.explanation: The threshold comparison requires an expected count before it means anything to count the current cases; only after both numbers exist can they be compared and a call made.

questions.prompt: Which best distinguishes 'epidemic' from 'pandemic'?

options.text: Pandemic means more people have died
Pandemic means the disease has spread across multiple countries or continents
Epidemic only applies to viral diseases
Pandemic is simply an older, interchangeable term for epidemic

explanations.a: Pandemic describes geographic spread, not severity or death toll.
explanations.b: Correct: pandemic specifically denotes an epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents.
explanations.c: Epidemic applies to any disease, bacterial or parasitic included, not only viral ones.
explanations.d: The terms are related but not interchangeable; pandemic adds a specific geographic-scope claim that epidemic does not make.

lessons.label: Why Investigate — and When Not To

sections.heading: The standard reasons to investigate
sections.body: Field epidemiology lists several reasons a health department launches a full investigation rather than just logging the case counts: disease control and prevention (stopping ongoing transmission or a continuing common-source exposure); severity (even a handful of cases of something highly lethal justifies disproportionate resources); the research opportunity, since many established facts came out of investigations pursued because they were scientifically informative, not because caseloads demanded it; training value, since field investigations are how epidemiologists in training, such as CDC's Epidemic Intelligence Service officers, learn the discipline; and public, legal, or political concern, where media attention or a legislator's inquiry can force an investigation even when the epidemiologic signal is weak on its own.

sections.heading: A resource decision, not a reflex
sections.body: Every investigation consumes staff time, laboratory capacity, and travel budget that could go toward a different problem, so health departments weigh opportunity cost before committing a team. A modest, plausible-seasonal uptick in gastroenteritis reports from a single nursing home might be fully explained by normal winter norovirus circulation and resolve with routine infection-control reinforcement rather than a formal case-control study; sending a full field team would not change the outcome and would pull staff away from an investigation that could. The decision runs on the same observed-versus-expected logic used to detect the outbreak in the first place, plus a judgment about whether investigating would actually change what happens next.

sections.heading: When the calculus argues against investigating
sections.body: Sometimes the right call is to decline a full field investigation: a cluster that is small, mild, and already resolving on its own; a signal a quick chart review shows is fully explained by a change in testing volume rather than true disease; or a suspected cluster spread across independent locations with no plausible common source, where descriptive review answers the question without full case-finding. A concrete example of the second case: a lab reports a jump in positive strep tests at a clinic, but a quick chart review shows the clinic switched to a faster rapid-antigen test the same week the jump appeared, with no matching rise in patients actually presenting with sore throat and fever — the same artifact-checking logic taught for pseudo-outbreaks elsewhere in this unit, applied here to decide whether a field team is even worth dispatching. This judgment is real and reversible — health departments often start with a light-touch review and escalate to a full investigation only if that review turns up evidence of a true excess.

lessons.workedExample: By 1980, cumulative U.S. toxic shock syndrome (TSS) case counts since 1970 were still only in the hundreds — 941 confirmed cases and 73 deaths, not enough volume to strain a health system. CDC investigated aggressively anyway, because TSS was a newly recognized, sometimes-fatal syndrome in previously healthy young women with an unclear cause: a research and severity case, not a caseload case. Shands and colleagues' 1980 case-control study phoned 52 confirmed cases and 52 matched controls and found tampon use over-represented among cases; a follow-up case-control study by Schlech and colleagues (1982) narrowed the association to a single tampon brand, Rely. Neither study happened because volume demanded it — it happened because the etiology was unknown and worth chasing.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student treats 'investigate' as automatic once any threshold is crossed. The stronger answer frames it as a cost-benefit call: severity, unknown etiology, transmissibility, and public concern can justify investigating a handful of cases, as with early toxic shock syndrome, while a mild, self-limited, plausibly seasonal cluster may not justify a full field team even at an elevated case count. A student who can name a scenario where declining to investigate was the correct call demonstrates they understand opportunity cost, not just the checklist of reasons to launch one.

questions.prompt: In 1980, cumulative U.S. toxic shock syndrome case counts were still only in the hundreds. Why did CDC invest in a formal case-control study on a comparatively rare condition?

options.text: Case-control studies are legally required once exactly 52 cases are reported
It was a novel, sometimes-fatal syndrome of unknown cause in healthy young women, so research value and severity outweighed the modest count
Tampon manufacturers funded and requested the investigation
State law mandated investigation once deaths exceeded 50

explanations.a: There is no such numeric legal trigger; 52 was simply the number of confirmed cases available to interview in that study.
explanations.b: Correct: research opportunity and severity are reasons to investigate even when absolute case counts are modest.
explanations.c: Nothing in the record supports manufacturer funding as the reason; the driver was the unknown, severe etiology.
explanations.d: No such fixed death-count law is described; the decision followed the severity and research-value reasoning, not a numeric statute.

questions.prompt: A nursing home reports a mild, self-limited uptick in gastroenteritis matching expected winter norovirus circulation. What does the opportunity-cost logic in this lesson suggest?

options.text: Always send a full field team regardless of severity or cause
A full investigation may not be justified if routine infection control will resolve it and resources are better used elsewhere
Investigation is prohibited without a court order
Case counts must exceed 100 before any response is required

explanations.a: This ignores opportunity cost; the lesson explicitly argues against reflexive full investigation for a mild, seasonal, self-limited signal.
explanations.b: Correct: this is the light-touch, resource-aware response the lesson describes for a plausible seasonal explanation.
explanations.c: No such legal requirement exists in this context.
explanations.d: No fixed numeric threshold like this is described; the decision is judgment-based, not a hard count rule.

questions.prompt: Match each reason to investigate with its description.

right.text: Even a few cases justify disproportionate resources because outcomes are serious
Cases with unknown etiology teach investigators something the next study can test, regardless of volume
Field investigations are how officers in training, such as CDC's Epidemic Intelligence Service, learn the discipline
Media attention or a legislator's inquiry can force an investigation even with a weak epidemiologic signal

questions.explanation: These four reasons operate independently of raw case count, which is why investigation decisions cannot be reduced to a single numeric threshold.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning steps a health department follows before committing a full field team.

items.text: Check whether the apparent excess could be explained by a benign, resolving cause such as normal seasonal circulation
Weigh the severity and transmissibility of the suspected agent
Weigh whether investigating would actually change what happens next
Commit or decline the field investigation

questions.explanation: Ruling out benign explanations comes first because it can end the question quickly; severity and expected impact are weighed next, and only then is the resource commitment decided.

lessons.label: The Steps of an Outbreak Investigation

sections.heading: The ordered checklist
sections.body: Field epidemiology teaches a standard sequence: prepare for fieldwork (logistics, equipment, coordination with local authorities); establish the outbreak's existence by comparing observed to expected cases; verify the diagnosis with clinical and laboratory review; construct a working case definition; find and count cases systematically; perform descriptive epidemiology by characterizing cases across time, place, and person; generate hypotheses about the source or mode of spread; evaluate those hypotheses with an analytic study that compares exposure between cases and a comparison group; refine hypotheses and run additional studies if the first result is ambiguous; implement control and prevention measures; communicate findings to stakeholders; and maintain ongoing surveillance to confirm the intervention worked and catch a resurgence.

sections.heading: Why the order is a guideline, not a law
sections.body: In real fieldwork these steps iterate rather than run once each in strict sequence. Hypothesis testing often reveals gaps that send investigators back to refine the case definition or find more cases. Control measures are frequently implemented as soon as a likely source is identified, well before the analytic study is finished, because delaying intervention to preserve methodological purity would let more people get sick — protecting people takes priority over procedural tidiness. Surveillance and communication also run throughout, not just at the end, since interim findings often need to reach clinicians or the public before the investigation formally closes.

sections.heading: How descriptive epidemiology turns into a testable hypothesis
sections.body: Descriptive epidemiology means plotting every counted case by time, place, and person and reading the resulting picture. Plotting onset dates as an epidemic curve reveals the outbreak's shape: a single sharp peak with cases clustered tightly around one incubation period after a shared moment points to a common-source exposure, like a contaminated event or meal, while a curve with a slow rise and multiple smaller peaks spaced roughly one incubation period apart points to person-to-person spread. Plotting cases on a map or by subgroup does the same work for place and person: a spot map that clusters cases around one building, ward, or water source narrows the field of plausible exposures the same way a sharp epidemic-curve peak narrows the field of plausible dates. Together, the curve's shape and the map's clustering are what let investigators generate a specific, testable hypothesis, such as 'exposure to the hotel's cooling-tower mist between July 21 and 24' rather than a vague 'something at the hotel,' and that specific hypothesis is what the analytic study is then designed to test.

lessons.workedExample: In the 1976 Legionnaires' investigation, a CDC team was dispatched within days of reports from the American Legion convention at Philadelphia's Bellevue-Stratford Hotel (July 21–24, 1976). Establishing the outbreak's existence was straightforward given 221 total illnesses and 34 deaths among conventiongoers and others in the hotel's vicinity, far above any expected pneumonia baseline. Verifying the diagnosis took months, since the causative organism, later named Legionella pneumophila, was not isolated until months after the convention. Investigators still built a working case definition and used it to find and count cases while descriptive epidemiology by time (an epidemic curve peaking days after the convention) and place (proximity to the hotel lobby) pointed toward an airborne, common-source exposure well before the bacterium had a name — showing several steps proceeding in parallel, not strict sequence.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student treats these steps as a rigid checklist completed once each. The strong answer explains iteration: hypotheses get revised, the case definition tightens as data accumulate, and control measures often start before the analytic study is finished because protecting people takes priority over methodological completeness. A project write-up that shows a case definition changing mid-investigation, or control measures implemented before the final analytic study, demonstrates a realistic understanding of fieldwork rather than a memorized sequence recited from a slide.

questions.prompt: Put the standard field-epidemiology steps in their canonical order.

items.text: Prepare for fieldwork
Establish the outbreak's existence
Verify the diagnosis
Construct a working case definition
Find and count cases
Perform descriptive epidemiology (time, place, person)
Generate hypotheses
Evaluate hypotheses with an analytic study
Implement control and prevention, then communicate and maintain surveillance

questions.explanation: This is the canonical sequence taught in field epidemiology, though the lesson stresses that real investigations frequently loop back to earlier steps rather than completing each exactly once.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes how these steps actually run in a real field investigation?

options.text: Strictly sequential; no step is ever repeated
Iterative — hypotheses and even the case definition are commonly revisited as more data comes in
Control measures are always implemented last, only after a final publication
Communication happens exactly once, at the very end

explanations.a: The lesson explicitly describes looping back to refine earlier steps, contradicting a strict one-pass sequence.
explanations.b: Correct: field investigations iterate, revising hypotheses and case definitions as evidence accumulates.
explanations.c: Control measures are often implemented early, as soon as a likely source is identified, not held until publication.
explanations.d: Interim findings are often communicated before the investigation formally closes, not only at the very end.

questions.prompt: Match each step to what it accomplishes.

right.text: Confirms reported illnesses are truly the suspected disease
Creates objective criteria for consistently counting cases
Characterizes cases by time, place, and person to generate hypotheses
Tests hypotheses statistically against a comparison group

questions.explanation: Each step has a distinct function; descriptive epidemiology generates hypotheses, while the analytic study is what actually tests them.

questions.prompt: In the Legionnaires' worked example, why did investigators build a case definition and begin descriptive epidemiology before the causative bacterium had even been identified?

options.text: Because clinical and epidemiologic criteria alone can define and count cases while lab work to identify the organism continues
Because CDC regulation required a case definition before any lab testing could legally begin
Because the bacterium was theoretically impossible to identify
Because case definitions can only be based on confirmed laboratory etiology

explanations.a: Correct: a case definition built on clinical criteria plus person/place/time restrictions does not require the pathogen to be known yet.
explanations.b: No such regulatory sequencing requirement is described; the parallel work reflected practical necessity, not law.
explanations.c: The bacterium was in fact identified later, so it was not theoretically impossible.
explanations.d: This contradicts the very case shown: the definition and case-finding proceeded before lab confirmation of the organism existed.

lessons.label: Establishing That an Outbreak Is Real

sections.heading: Artifacts that mimic a real increase
sections.body: Before committing resources, investigators must rule out several mundane explanations for an apparent rise in reported cases. A change in reporting practice — a new mandatory-reporting rule, a reminder to clinicians, or a new electronic lab-reporting feed — can double reported counts overnight with no change in true disease frequency. A newly available or more sensitive diagnostic test means a facility switching from slow culture to PCR will detect more true cases, and sometimes more false ones, than the old method ever could. A new clinician, lab, or clinic opening in an area finds more cases simply because there is more testing capacity, not more disease. Population growth or an influx of visitors raises the raw case count without raising the underlying rate. And seasonal or cyclical variation means a disease that always spikes in a particular month is not, by itself, evidence of an outbreak of that expected spike.

sections.heading: Pseudo-outbreaks: the lab itself is the outbreak
sections.body: A pseudo-outbreak is an apparent cluster caused by contamination or an artifact in specimen collection, handling, or testing rather than true illness in patients — the exposure never happened, or the organism was never really present. Common causes include contaminated reagents, a colonized reused instrument, or a diagnostic assay that cross-reacts with related but harmless organisms, generating positive results in people who were never truly infected. Investigators catch a pseudo-outbreak by sending a sample of the positive specimens for confirmatory testing with a different, gold-standard method — typically an older but more specific technique, such as bacterial culture, rather than a faster or more sensitive one, such as PCR — and comparing the two result sets. If the new test's positives collapse under the gold-standard method, the excess lived in the assay, not in the patients; if most of the positives hold up under confirmatory testing, the excess is real disease.

sections.heading: Comparing observed against a real baseline
sections.body: The only way to distinguish a true excess from any of these artifacts is to compare the observed count against an expected count computed the same way, over the same population, for the same season, using several years of historical surveillance data so a single unusual year does not set the bar. If the artifact explanations are ruled out and the observed count still clearly exceeds that historical expected range, the outbreak is real.

lessons.workedExample: In spring 2006, Dartmouth-Hitchcock Medical Center in Lebanon, New Hampshire, appeared to have a major pertussis outbreak: 142 PCR tests came back positive, prompting the hospital to furlough or quarantine roughly 1,000 employees, give 3,599 Tdap vaccinations, and distribute 1,364 courses of azithromycin. But the 27 specimens sent for traditional bacterial culture all came back negative, and CDC's own retesting confirmed only a single true case. The PCR assay used was non-standardized and cross-reacted with other, mostly viral, respiratory pathogens circulating that spring, turning ordinary colds into apparent pertussis positives. CDC's 2007 MMWR report on this event and two related ones in Massachusetts and Tennessee (2004–2006) formally classified all three as pseudo-outbreaks: the excess was in the laboratory, not in the population.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student's claimed 'increase' in cases has been checked against boring explanations first — a new test, a new reporting rule, more testing capacity — before being presented as a real biological signal. The Dartmouth-Hitchcock case is instructive because every visible signal, positive tests, symptomatic patients, a plausible respiratory illness, looked real; only comparing PCR results to gold-standard culture exposed the artifact. A judge who asks 'could this be a testing or reporting artifact instead' is testing exactly this discipline.

questions.prompt: At Dartmouth-Hitchcock in 2006, 142 PCR tests came back positive for pertussis, but cultures from the same patients were negative and CDC confirmed only one true case. What does this best illustrate?

options.text: A true epidemic with unusually mild cases
A pseudo-outbreak, where a non-specific or cross-reactive lab test created an apparent cluster that was not really pertussis
Population growth inflating the case count
A new mandatory-reporting law that increased detection

explanations.a: Mild cases would still be culture-positive for the true pathogen; the negative cultures point to an assay artifact, not mild true disease.
explanations.b: Correct: the PCR assay's cross-reactivity generated positives without true infection, the defining feature of a pseudo-outbreak.
explanations.c: Nothing in this scenario involves a change in population size; the issue was the diagnostic test.
explanations.d: No reporting-law change is described; the mechanism was cross-reactive lab testing, not a reporting policy shift.

questions.prompt: Match each artifact type to its example.

right.text: A new mandatory-reporting rule increases counts with no change in true disease frequency
A hospital adopts PCR and detects more cases, true and false, than the prior culture method did
A cross-reactive assay creates positive results with no true infection present, as at Dartmouth-Hitchcock in 2006
A disease predictably spikes every year in the same month, which is not itself evidence of an outbreak

questions.explanation: Each artifact inflates apparent case counts through a different mechanism, which is why ruling them out requires different checks.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to determine whether an apparent case increase is a true outbreak.

items.text: Check whether reporting practices, testing volume, or population changed recently
Confirm positive results with a second, independent testing method where possible
Compute the expected count from several years of historical surveillance data for the same season
Compare the confirmed observed count to that expected range to decide if a true excess exists

questions.explanation: Ruling out obvious artifacts comes first, followed by confirming results independently, before the comparison against a historical baseline can be trusted.

questions.prompt: A city's flu case reports rise every December compared to summer. Is this rise, by itself, evidence of an outbreak?

options.text: Yes, any rise in absolute case counts is evidence of an outbreak
No — expected counts must be adjusted for known seasonal cycles before comparing to the current count
Yes, but only if the rise exceeds 50 percent
No, seasonal diseases can never have true outbreaks

explanations.a: This ignores the seasonal-baseline point made in the lesson; a predictable seasonal rise is not automatically an excess.
explanations.b: Correct: the expected baseline must already account for the normal seasonal cycle before any comparison is meaningful.
explanations.c: No such fixed percentage threshold is described in this lesson.
explanations.d: Seasonal diseases can absolutely have true outbreaks; the point is that the expected baseline must be seasonally adjusted first, not that outbreaks are impossible.

lessons.label: Verifying the Diagnosis

sections.heading: Confirming the illness is what it appears to be
sections.body: Verifying the diagnosis means confirming that reported cases genuinely have the disease under investigation, not something else that merely looks similar clinically. This involves reviewing clinical findings and laboratory results for a sample of cases, ideally examining or interviewing several patients directly rather than relying only on secondhand chart summaries, and actively ruling out laboratory error — a mislabeled specimen, a contaminated reagent batch, or a test with known cross-reactivity, any of which can manufacture 'cases' that never had the disease at all. In practice this means sorting each reported case into one of two tiers before trusting it: 'clinically compatible,' meaning the symptoms and exposure history fit but no lab test has confirmed the specific pathogen, versus 'laboratory confirmed,' meaning an independent lab result — a positive culture, a paired serology showing a rising antibody titer, or a second lab's retest of the same specimen — backs up the clinical picture. A cluster built mostly of clinically-compatible cases with few or no lab-confirmed ones is a weaker claim than one where an independent lab has verified even a handful of specimens, which is why investigators push to get at least some cases lab-confirmed before treating the whole cluster as verified.

sections.heading: Why verification and confirming existence happen together
sections.body: Field epidemiologists usually verify the diagnosis at the same time they establish that an outbreak exists, rather than as two strictly sequential steps, because each check informs the other: if reported cases turn out not to share a true diagnosis, there may be no single outbreak at all, or two smaller unrelated ones, and conversely a real excess of correctly diagnosed cases is what makes the verification effort worthwhile in the first place. Doing both together also means the same site visits, chart reviews, and specimen requests serve both purposes rather than duplicating fieldwork.

sections.heading: The cost of getting this step wrong
sections.body: Skipping verification risks two costly errors: chasing a false lead if the presumed diagnosis is wrong, wasting time on an intervention aimed at the wrong pathogen or exposure, or, just as damaging, dismissing a genuinely new and dangerous disease because it doesn't fit an already-assumed diagnosis. Systematically ruling out the familiar, expected explanation is often exactly what clears the way to recognize something the investigators have never seen before. The 1999 New York City encephalitis outbreak illustrates the first failure mode. Cases were initially attributed to St. Louis encephalitis based on a cross-reactive serologic test, and the city's response, syndrome-specific surveillance and public messaging built around mosquito species associated with that virus, was organized around that presumed diagnosis for weeks. Only when a Bronx Zoo pathologist's report of dying crows prompted a second look, and more specific viral testing was run, did investigators recognize the true cause was West Nile virus, a pathogen never before documented in the Western Hemisphere; the SLE-focused response had to be reworked around the corrected diagnosis.

lessons.workedExample: In spring 1993, a young couple in the Four Corners region died within days of each other after a sudden respiratory illness with fever and pulmonary edema. Because plague (Yersinia pestis) is endemic to rodent populations there, investigators' first working diagnosis was pneumonic plague, and autopsies were ordered specifically to confirm or rule it out; the plague tests came back negative. The differential was widened to leptospirosis, inhalational anthrax, tularemia, rickettsial infection, and legionellosis, all ruled out for lack of supporting lab evidence, before a CDC-led team identified a previously unrecognized hantavirus, reported in the MMWR on June 11, 1993. By the end of that year, 33 confirmed Four Corners-region cases and 17 deaths were attributed to what became known as Sin Nombre virus. Had investigators stopped at the plague hypothesis, the true pathogen would have gone unidentified.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a project's claimed 'outbreak' has been verified beyond the presenting symptom description. The Four Corners case shows why this matters: the initial, most plausible diagnosis (plague, given local ecology) was wrong, and only systematically ruling it out with lab confirmation, not clinical impression alone, cleared the way to find a genuinely new pathogen. A judge asking 'how do you know this is the disease you think it is, and not something that just looks like it' is testing whether verification happened before the rest of the investigation was built on an assumed diagnosis.

questions.prompt: In the 1993 Four Corners outbreak, why did investigators order autopsies specifically testing for plague before considering other causes?

options.text: Plague is the only disease that can cause respiratory failure
Plague is endemic to the region's rodent population, making it the most clinically plausible initial diagnosis given the symptoms and location
CDC regulations require testing for plague before any hantavirus test
The patients had recently traveled to a plague-endemic country

explanations.a: Many conditions cause respiratory failure; plague was suspected for ecological, not exclusivity, reasons.
explanations.b: Correct: regional disease ecology made plague the most plausible working diagnosis to test and rule out first.
explanations.c: No such testing-order regulation is described; the sequence reflected clinical judgment, not a fixed rule.
explanations.d: Travel history is not part of this scenario; the concern was local endemic disease ecology, not travel exposure.

questions.prompt: Why do field epidemiologists typically verify the diagnosis and establish the outbreak's existence in the same phase of work rather than sequentially?

options.text: Regulation requires simultaneous sign-off from two separate officials
Each check informs the other — if cases don't share a true diagnosis there may be no single outbreak, and a real excess is what justifies the verification effort
Verifying the diagnosis becomes unnecessary once an excess is confirmed
Establishing existence always takes far longer, so it is simply done first out of necessity

explanations.a: No such dual sign-off requirement is described in this lesson.
explanations.b: Correct: this mutual dependency is exactly why the two checks run together rather than in strict sequence.
explanations.c: This contradicts the lesson directly; a confirmed excess of a wrong diagnosis is not a validated outbreak.
explanations.d: No claim about relative duration is made; the reason for doing both together is informational overlap, not timing.

questions.prompt: Order the diagnostic-verification process in the Four Corners case.

items.text: Notice a cluster of unexplained deaths with a specific clinical presentation
Test the most clinically plausible known diagnosis given local disease ecology (plague)
Rule out that diagnosis via lab evidence and widen the differential to other known pathogens
Rule out the widened differential for lack of supporting evidence
Identify a previously unrecognized pathogen through further lab work

questions.explanation: Verification proceeded from the most plausible known cause outward through less likely known causes before landing on a genuinely novel pathogen.

questions.prompt: Match each verification activity to what it protects against.

left.text: Reviewing lab results for a sample of cases directly
Interviewing or examining patients directly rather than relying on secondhand summaries
Ruling out cross-reactive or contaminated test results

right.text: Catches whether a lab error or contamination created false cases
Catches details lost or altered in chart summaries or hearsay
Prevents a pseudo-outbreak from being investigated as if it were a real one

questions.explanation: Each verification activity guards against a distinct source of error, from lab artifacts to secondhand documentation gaps.

lessons.label: Constructing an Outbreak Case Definition

sections.heading: The four components
sections.body: A working case definition combines clinical criteria — the signs, symptoms, or lab findings that must be present, such as fever plus radiographically confirmed pneumonia — with three restrictions that bound who counts: person (demographic or exposure-neutral characteristics such as age or occupation, but never the specific exposure under suspicion), place (a defined geographic or institutional boundary, such as attendees of a specific hotel or convention), and time (a defined window, such as onset within a stated number of days of a suspected event). Together these four pieces make the definition objective and reproducible: any two investigators applying it to the same patient should reach the same yes-or-no answer.

sections.heading: Confirmed, probable, suspect
sections.body: Case definitions are commonly graded into tiers of certainty rather than a single yes-or-no. A confirmed case meets the clinical criteria and has definitive laboratory confirmation, such as a positive culture. A probable case has the clinical picture plus a supportive but non-definitive lab result, or a clear epidemiologic link to a confirmed case without its own lab confirmation. A suspect case meets only the clinical picture, with no supporting lab result or link. Investigators often count all three tiers early to keep case-finding sensitive, then focus analysis on confirmed and probable cases once resources allow tighter follow-up. In the 1976 Legionnaires' outbreak, only a minority of the 221 total illnesses ever became lab-confirmed, since the causative organism was not isolated until months later; most of the 221 were counted as clinical or epidemiologically-linked cases at the time, illustrating why investigators lean on the probable and suspect tiers during the early weeks of a novel outbreak rather than waiting on lab confirmation to start counting.

sections.heading: Keep the definition independent of the exposure
sections.body: A case definition must never build in the exposure being investigated, such as 'attended the picnic,' because doing so makes it circular, guaranteeing a spuriously perfect association between exposure and disease that reflects the definition rather than reality. A definition drawn too tight, using highly specific lab criteria only, undercounts true cases and can miss the outbreak's real size or shape; one drawn too loose, using vague clinical criteria with no time or place bound, sweeps in unrelated illness and dilutes any true signal. Investigators typically start looser to find the full universe of possible cases, then tighten for the analytic phase.

lessons.workedExample: For the 1976 Legionnaires' investigation, CDC investigators built a case definition with clinical criteria (fever, cough, and chest-X-ray-confirmed pneumonia), a place restriction (attendance at the Bellevue-Stratford Hotel or the American Legion convention held there July 21–24, 1976, or presence in the hotel's vicinity), and a time restriction (onset within a set window of the convention). The definition said nothing about air conditioning, cooling towers, or any specific exposure investigators suspected; that independence let the later analytic study test air-conditioning proximity as a hypothesis without the case definition already assuming the answer. Applying this definition, investigators counted 221 total cases and 34 deaths among conventiongoers and others in the hotel's vicinity.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether the definition used to count cases in a science-fair project accidentally includes the hypothesis being tested. A definition that partly defines cases by the suspected exposure, such as 'anyone who ate the suspect food and got sick,' manufactures a perfect but meaningless association. A judge who asks a student to state their case definition's four components, clinical criteria plus person, place, and time, and confirm none of them names the exposure under study, is testing exactly this discipline, along with whether the student can defend why the definition isn't too tight or too loose for the current stage of investigation.

questions.prompt: A case definition for a suspected foodborne outbreak reads: 'vomiting or diarrhea, AND ate the potato salad at the church picnic.' What is the problem?

options.text: Nothing; this maximizes sensitivity, which is always the priority
It builds the suspected exposure into the case definition, guaranteeing a spuriously perfect association between potato salad and illness
It is missing laboratory confirmation, which every case definition must always require
It is too loose because it lacks a place restriction

explanations.a: Sensitivity is not always the priority, and this specific flaw is circularity, not an appropriate sensitivity choice.
explanations.b: Correct: naming the exposure inside the case definition makes the exposure-disease association true by construction, not by evidence.
explanations.c: Suspect and probable tiers exist precisely because lab confirmation is not always required or available.
explanations.d: The definition does include a place restriction (the picnic); the flaw is the embedded exposure, not a missing place bound.

questions.prompt: Match each case tier to its definition.

right.text: Meets clinical criteria and has definitive laboratory confirmation
Meets clinical criteria plus a supportive but non-definitive lab result, or a link to a confirmed case
Meets only the clinical picture, with no supporting lab result or epidemiologic link

questions.explanation: The three tiers grade certainty from strongest (lab-confirmed) to weakest (clinical picture alone), letting investigators track both sensitivity and confidence.

questions.prompt: Order how a case definition is typically used across the phases of an investigation.

items.text: Start case-finding with a looser definition to find the full range of possible cases
Classify found cases into confirmed, probable, and suspect tiers
Tighten the definition heading into the analytic phase
Apply the tightened definition and compare exposures or attack rates across groups

questions.explanation: Sensitivity is prioritized early to avoid missing true cases, and specificity is prioritized later to keep the analytic comparison accurate.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the four standard components of a case definition?

options.text: Clinical criteria
Person restriction
Place restriction
Exposure history to the specific suspected source

explanations.a: Clinical criteria are one of the four standard components.
explanations.b: Person restriction is one of the four standard components.
explanations.c: Place restriction is one of the four standard components.
explanations.d: Correct: exposure to the specific suspected source must not be built into the case definition, since it is the hypothesis being tested, not a definitional component.

lessons.label: Sensitivity, Specificity, and Evolving the Case Definition

sections.heading: Two definitions for two jobs
sections.body: Early in an investigation, a sensitive, loose case definition — broad clinical criteria, wide time and place bounds — is used deliberately to cast a wide net and find as many true cases as possible, even at the cost of catching some false positives, people who look sick from something else. Once hypothesis testing begins, a specific, tight definition is preferred, often restricted to confirmed and probable tiers with more precise clinical or lab criteria, because the analytic study needs classification to be as accurate as possible: every misclassified person distorts the comparison being measured. This tradeoff has a concrete consequence for how a positive result should be read: a case definition's positive predictive value, the chance that someone meeting it truly has the disease, depends not just on the definition's sensitivity and specificity but on how common the disease actually is in the population being screened. When true prevalence is low, even a definition that is 90 percent specific can still produce more false positives than true positives in absolute terms, because the large pool of truly unaffected people generates more false matches than the small pool of truly affected people generates true ones. That is why a loose definition tuned for sensitivity is deliberately not trusted for classification once the investigation moves from finding cases to counting them accurately.

sections.heading: Why misclassification biases toward the null
sections.body: When a case definition is too loose and case status is misclassified without regard to true exposure status — non-differential misclassification, where the error rate is the same whether or not someone was exposed — the measured association between exposure and disease is mathematically pulled toward showing no association, a relative risk or odds ratio closer to 1, even when a true association exists. Misclassified 'cases' dilute the truly exposed group's excess risk and dilute the unexposed group's baseline risk in the same direction, shrinking the gap between them. This is counterintuitive: sloppy case definitions during the analytic phase don't just add random noise, they systematically understate the true strength of an association.

sections.heading: Re-counting when the definition changes
sections.body: A change to the case definition mid-investigation is not a failure; it is expected practice, and every prior case must be re-evaluated against the new criteria, since some earlier 'cases' may now fail to qualify if the definition tightened, or new candidates may now qualify if the clinical criteria were broadened based on what investigators learned. Attack rates and any completed comparisons must be recalculated using the revised counts before conclusions are drawn. Skipping this step carries forward exactly the dilution mechanism shown in the worked example above: a comparison run on the old, looser case list still contains the same non-differentially misclassified cases, so the measured relative risk stays pulled toward 1.0 even after the definition on paper has been tightened. Tightening the definition only sharpens the analytic result once the case list itself is re-applied and every attack rate is recomputed from that revised list — the definitional change does nothing on its own.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a picnic's true illness rate is 40 percent among 100 exposed attendees who ate the potato salad (40 true cases) and 10 percent among 100 unexposed attendees who did not (10 true cases), a true relative risk of 4.0. Now apply a loose case definition that is only 80 percent sensitive and 80 percent specific, applied equally in both groups (non-differential). Among the exposed: 32 true cases are correctly captured, plus 20 percent of the 60 truly well (12) are misclassified in, for 44 counted cases, or 44 percent. Among the unexposed: 8 true cases are correctly captured, plus 20 percent of the 90 truly well (18) are misclassified in, for 26 counted cases, or 26 percent. The measured relative risk falls from a true 4.0 to about 1.7 (44/26), still elevated, but the loose definition has hidden most of the real effect.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student who reports a modest or null association understands it might be a case-definition artifact rather than proof of no real effect. Non-differential misclassification is unintuitive: it doesn't add noise in unpredictable directions, it specifically and predictably shrinks a measured relative risk or odds ratio toward 1.0. A student who can explain why their attack-rate comparison might be an underestimate, and that tightening the case definition, trading some sensitivity for specificity, would sharpen rather than distort the true signal, shows they understand classification error as a mechanism, not just a caveat to mention in a limitations slide.

questions.prompt: A loose case definition misclassifies people non-differentially, at the same error rate regardless of true exposure status. What happens to the measured relative risk compared to the true relative risk?

options.text: It is biased away from the null, appearing stronger than the truth
It is biased toward the null, appearing weaker than the truth, closer to 1.0
It is biased in an unpredictable, random direction
It is unaffected as long as the sample size is large enough

explanations.a: Non-differential misclassification does not inflate the measured association; it does the opposite.
explanations.b: Correct: non-differential misclassification predictably dilutes the observed association toward no effect.
explanations.c: The direction is predictable, not random, precisely because the misclassification is non-differential.
explanations.d: A larger sample reduces random error but does not remove this systematic dilution bias.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, the true relative risk was 4.0 (40 percent vs. 10 percent). After applying a case definition with 80 percent sensitivity and 80 percent specificity, applied equally to both groups, what happened to the measured relative risk?

options.text: It stayed at 4.0
It fell to about 1.7 (44 percent vs. 26 percent)
It rose to about 8.0
It fell all the way to about 1.0, erasing the association entirely

explanations.a: Misclassification changed the measured rates in both groups, so the ratio did not stay at the true value.
explanations.b: Correct: this matches the worked calculation of 44 percent among exposed versus 26 percent among unexposed.
explanations.c: The bias direction is toward the null, not away from it, so the measured risk could not rise above the true value this way.
explanations.d: The association shrank substantially but did not vanish entirely; 1.7 still reflects an elevated, detectable risk.

questions.prompt: Order the case-definition strategy across the phases of an investigation.
