items.text: Use a loose, sensitive definition during case-finding to identify the full range of possible cases
Classify found cases into confirmed, probable, and suspect tiers
Tighten the definition toward specificity before the analytic phase
Recalculate attack rates and exposure comparisons using the tightened, re-applied definition

questions.explanation: Sensitivity matters most while still finding cases; specificity matters most once the definition is used to measure an association, which requires re-counting under the new criteria.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in an outbreak investigation.

right.text: Used early, for case-finding, to avoid missing true cases even at the cost of some false positives
Used for the analytic phase, to minimize misclassification that would bias the exposure-disease comparison
Same error rate in exposed and unexposed groups; biases the measured association toward the null

questions.explanation: The loose and tight definitions serve different phases of the same investigation, and non-differential misclassification is the specific statistical consequence of using a loose definition during the analytic phase.

units.label: Descriptive Epidemiology and the Line List

lessons.label: Building the Line List

sections.heading: One row per case, one column per fact worth comparing
sections.body: The line list is the single spreadsheet that an outbreak investigation runs on: each row is one case, each column is a fact the team will later need to sort, filter, or count. A working line list carries a unique case identifier, name or initials for follow-up, age and sex, address or workplace, date and time of symptom onset, the specific signs and symptoms present, relevant exposures (foods eaten, events attended, water source), lab specimen status and result, and case classification (confirmed, probable, suspect). CDC's Field Epidemiology Manual and the classic Gregg's Field Epidemiology text both treat the line list as the first deliverable of any field investigation, built within hours of the first report and updated continuously, not assembled retrospectively once the outbreak is over.

sections.heading: It feeds everything downstream
sections.body: Every later analytic step is a view onto the line list. The epidemic curve is a histogram of the onset-date column. The spot map plots the address column. The person tables cross-tabulate age and sex against attack rates. The 2x2 tables in a case-control or cohort analysis are built by filtering the exposure and outcome columns. If a column is missing or inconsistently coded at intake, that gap resurfaces as a hole in the curve, an unmappable case, or an unanalyzable stratum weeks later. This is why investigators standardize categories (e.g., a fixed symptom checklist rather than free text) before the second wave of interviews, and why the case identifier is assigned once and never reused, so records merged later from lab reports or hospital charts can be matched without ambiguity.

sections.heading: Keeping it current under a rising case count
sections.body: Outbreaks are dynamic: cases are still being reported while the list is being analyzed, so the line list must be a living document, not a snapshot. Investigators re-run the case count, redraw the curve, and recheck the map each time a batch of new reports arrives, watching in particular whether new cases keep the same exposure and onset pattern as earlier ones or start to diverge, which can signal a second source or ongoing transmission. Duplicate-checking (same person reported by two clinics) and classification review (upgrading a suspect case to confirmed once labs return) are routine maintenance tasks, not one-time cleanup, and a stale line list is one of the most common reasons a field team misreads the shape of an outbreak in progress.

lessons.workedExample: A norovirus outbreak line list starts with 12 rows after day one: columns for case ID, age, sex, onset date/time, vomiting (Y/N), diarrhea (Y/N), fever (Y/N), banquet attendance (Y/N), and lab specimen status. By day three the list has grown to 47 rows as more cases self-report; two entries turn out to be the same person reported once by a clinic and once by the venue, caught only because both share a phone number in the identifier column. Recomputing the epidemic curve after the merge shifts the apparent peak by several hours and removes a false second bump the duplicate had created.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'how did you organize your case data' expecting to hear a specific column structure, not 'we kept notes.' A fair project that can produce its actual line-list columns (and explain why age, onset time, and exposure are separate fields rather than one free-text note) demonstrates the data was structured for analysis from the start; a project that reconstructed a curve or map from scratch notes after the fact is a signal the underlying data collection was not rigorous.

questions.prompt: Why does a line list include a unique case identifier column separate from the person's name?

options.text: To allow records from different sources (clinic, lab, venue) to be matched and deduplicated without relying on name spelling
Because names are considered private and cannot appear in outbreak data at all
To satisfy a legal requirement that has nothing to do with the analysis
Because case identifiers are what get plotted on the epidemic curve

explanations.a: Correct: a stable ID lets a case reported by two different sources be recognized as one person and merged, preventing double-counting.
explanations.b: Line lists do carry identifying information for follow-up; the ID column serves matching, not anonymization.
explanations.c: The ID column is an analytic tool, not a compliance checkbox, though privacy handling is a separate real concern.
explanations.d: The epidemic curve is built from the onset-date column, not the identifier column.

questions.prompt: Order these events in maintaining a line list during an active outbreak.

items.text: Assign a unique case ID and record onset date/time and exposures at intake
New reports arrive and are added as additional rows
Check new and existing rows for duplicate persons across sources
Recompute the epidemic curve and case counts from the updated list

questions.explanation: Cases are entered with a stable structure first, new reports keep accumulating, duplicates must be resolved before recount, and only then do downstream analyses like the curve reflect accurate numbers.

questions.prompt: Match each line-list column to the downstream analysis it primarily feeds.

right.text: Epidemic curve
Spot map
Person tables / attack rates by group
2x2 analytic tables

questions.explanation: Each descriptive or analytic output is essentially a filtered or cross-tabulated view of one or more line-list columns.

lessons.label: Case Finding and the Hypothesis-Generating Interview

sections.heading: Passive versus active case finding
sections.body: Passive case finding relies on the existing reporting system: clinicians and labs send reports to health departments as part of routine notifiable-disease surveillance, at whatever pace and completeness that system normally runs. Active case finding is the investigation team going out to look: calling every emergency department and clinic in the affected area, faxing or emailing an alert describing the case definition and asking providers to report matching patients, reviewing lab logs directly for a specific organism, or going door to door in a defined population. Active case finding is more sensitive but costs far more staff time, so field teams typically start passive, then switch to active once an outbreak is suspected, because passive reporting alone systematically undercounts mild or unrecognized cases and can miss the true extent of an outbreak: in the 2015 multistate Blue Bell listeriosis investigation, CDC's active follow-up on isolates already sitting in state lab collections, matched by whole-genome sequencing, linked the outbreak back to illnesses from 2010 to 2015 that routine passive surveillance alone had never connected to a common source.

sections.heading: Stimulating reporting from clinicians and labs
sections.body: Because passive systems undercount, investigators often explicitly stimulate reporting: sending a health advisory to hospitals and labs describing the syndrome, providing a working case definition, and asking staff to actively watch for and report matching patients going forward. This is distinct from a retrospective active search of existing records; it recruits the clinical system itself as an ongoing sensor for new cases as the outbreak unfolds.

sections.heading: The hypothesis-generating interview: cast the net wide first
sections.body: Once a handful of early cases are identified, investigators do NOT jump straight to a structured, hypothesis-testing questionnaire. Instead they conduct open-ended, wide-net interviews with the first several cases, sometimes called the hypothesis-generating or 'shotgun' interview, asking about every food eaten, every place visited, every person contacted, and every product used over the exposure period, without presupposing which one matters. This deliberately unfocused approach exists because the investigators do not yet know what to ask about narrowly; a premature focus on one suspected exposure (say, only asking about restaurant meals) can miss the actual source entirely. Only after this open interview generates one or a few candidate hypotheses does the team write a focused, structured analytic questionnaire with fixed response categories, standardized wording, and a denominator-appropriate comparison group, ready to test the hypothesis formally in a cohort or case-control study.

lessons.workedExample: In an early Salmonella cluster of 6 cases, investigators first run 45-to-60-minute open-ended interviews asking each patient to recall everything eaten and everywhere visited in the prior week, with no prompted list. Five of six mention a specific grocery chain's pre-cut cantaloupe; the sixth cannot recall food details clearly. That single recurring detail becomes the hypothesis. The team then drafts a structured questionnaire asking every subsequent case and control the same fixed question, 'Did you eat pre-cut cantaloupe from Store X in the past 7 days: yes/no/unsure,' rather than the earlier open-ended prompt, so responses can be tabulated into a 2x2 table.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student understands that hypothesis-generating and hypothesis-testing interviews are different instruments with different goals, not the same questionnaire used loosely. A project that jumped straight to a structured survey without first asking open-ended questions of early cases risks having anchored on the wrong exposure before knowing what to ask about; judges want to hear which candidate exposure(s) emerged from open interviews and why that shaped the later structured questions.

questions.prompt: Why do investigators use an open-ended, wide-net interview with the earliest cases before writing a structured questionnaire?

options.text: Because the source of the outbreak is not yet known, and a narrow question list could miss it entirely
Because open-ended interviews are faster to conduct than structured ones
Because structured questionnaires cannot legally be used until a case-control study begins
Because early cases are less reliable narrators than later cases

explanations.a: Correct: at this stage investigators do not know which exposure to focus on, so a broad, unprompted interview avoids prematurely excluding the true source.
explanations.b: Open-ended interviews typically take longer per case, not less, since there is no fixed checklist to move through quickly.
explanations.c: There is no such legal restriction; the sequencing is a methodological choice, not a compliance rule.
explanations.d: Reliability of recall is not the reason for the open approach; the goal is not to bias which exposures get asked about.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in case finding and hypothesis generation.

items.text: Rely on passive/routine reporting to first detect a possible cluster
Stimulate reporting or actively search records to find more cases
Conduct open-ended hypothesis-generating interviews with early cases
Draft a focused, structured analytic questionnaire to test the leading hypothesis

questions.explanation: Detection typically starts with existing passive surveillance, is expanded by active case finding, informs broad open interviews, and only then narrows to a structured, testable questionnaire.

questions.prompt: Match each case-finding or interview approach to its description.

right.text: Relies on the routine reporting system without extra outreach
Investigators directly search records or contact providers to find cases
Open-ended, unprompted questions asked of the earliest cases
Structured, fixed-category questions used to formally test a hypothesis

questions.explanation: Each term names a distinct stage or tool in moving from detecting an outbreak to testing a specific cause.

lessons.label: Time: Onset Data Before the Curve

sections.heading: Time is the richest of the three descriptive axes
sections.body: Descriptive epidemiology organizes cases along person, place, and time, but time is usually the richest signal because it is recorded for every case, is rarely missing the way an exposure detail might be, and its shape alone can suggest whether an outbreak is a single point-source event, a continuing common source, or person-to-person spread before any other analysis is done. Getting the raw time data right at intake, before anyone draws a single bar of a curve, determines whether that later shape is trustworthy or an artifact of sloppy collection.

sections.heading: Choosing date versus time-of-day resolution
sections.body: The line list must record onset with a resolution matched to the disease's incubation period. For an illness with an incubation period measured in days to weeks, such as hepatitis A (average about 28 days) or a slow-building foodborne illness, date of onset is sufficient resolution; a curve binned by date will still show clean structure. For a short-incubation illness, such as Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning (onset commonly 1 to 6 hours) or Norovirus (typically 12 to 48 hours), date-only resolution can collapse an entire outbreak into one or two bars and hide the very compact clustering that reveals a point-source event; investigators need onset time-of-day, sometimes down to the hour, to see that structure. The rule of thumb taught in CDC field epidemiology training is to bin the curve at roughly one-quarter of the incubation period, which is precisely why onset time, not just date, must be captured on the line list from the first interview.

sections.heading: Reporting lags distort the recent tail
sections.body: The most recent days of any onset-time series are artificially low, not because fewer people are truly getting sick, but because of reporting lag: the delay between a person falling ill, seeking care, a lab confirming a diagnosis, and that result reaching the line list. This delay, sometimes called the reporting or right-censoring effect, means the last several days of a line list always undercount true recent onsets, and a naive read of a downward-sloping recent tail as 'the outbreak is ending' is one of the most common misreadings in field epidemiology. Investigators account for this by tracking the typical lag length for their reporting system and treating the most recent period as provisional and likely to rise as more reports arrive, rather than as a settled count.

lessons.workedExample: A norovirus outbreak at a wedding reception is investigated by date of onset only, producing two flat bars covering 'day 1' and 'day 2' with no visible peak. Re-interviewing all 30 cases for onset time-of-day shows 24 of them fell ill between 6pm and midnight the following day, a tight 6-hour cluster roughly 24 to 30 hours after the shared reception meal and consistent with norovirus's 12-to-48-hour incubation period; only the finer time resolution reveals the point-source shape that date alone had hidden.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask what resolution the onset data was collected at and why, because a curve built on date-only data for a short-incubation pathogen can look artificially smeared or continuous, leading a student to misclassify a point-source outbreak as ongoing transmission. A judge also probes whether the student flagged the last few days as provisional due to reporting lag rather than reading a falling recent tail as proof the outbreak was already over.

questions.prompt: For an outbreak of Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning, with onset typically 1 to 6 hours after exposure, why is date-only onset resolution likely to be a problem?

options.text: It can collapse the whole outbreak into one or two date bars, hiding the compact clustering that reveals a point source
Staphylococcus aureus cases are never reported to health departments
Date-only resolution makes case identifiers impossible to assign
It has no effect since the epidemic curve is always drawn using dates regardless of incubation period

explanations.a: Correct: with a 1-to-6-hour incubation period, nearly all cases could fall on the same one or two calendar dates, so date-only bins would obscure the tight time clustering that time-of-day data would reveal.
explanations.b: Staphylococcal food poisoning is a reportable/investigable illness in outbreak settings; this option is unrelated to resolution.
explanations.c: Case identifiers are independent of onset-time resolution.
explanations.d: Bin width should match the incubation period; using date-only bins for a short-incubation illness is a real distortion, not a neutral default.

questions.prompt: Why does the most recent portion of an outbreak's onset-time series typically appear to dip, even while the outbreak is still active?

options.text: Reporting lag means recent illnesses have not yet worked through care-seeking, lab confirmation, and reporting to appear on the line list
The pathogen loses infectiousness over the course of an outbreak
Health departments deliberately exclude the most recent week of cases from all analyses
Later cases are less severe and therefore go uncounted entirely

explanations.a: Correct: the delay between falling ill and appearing on the line list means the most recent days are systematically undercounted, not truly lower.
explanations.b: Pathogen infectiousness dynamics are a separate biological question, not the cause of the recent-tail dip in reported counts.
explanations.c: Recent cases are not deliberately excluded; they are simply not yet reported due to the pipeline delay.
explanations.d: Severity does not determine whether a case is eventually reported; the dip is a timing artifact, not a severity filter.

questions.prompt: Match each situation to the correct time-data practice.

left.text: Most recent days of the curve

right.text: Date-of-onset resolution is usually sufficient
Record onset time-of-day, not just date
Treat counts as provisional due to reporting lag

questions.explanation: Bin width should track incubation period, and the most recent tail of any series needs a reporting-lag caveat regardless of disease.

lessons.label: Place: Spot Maps and Area Maps

sections.heading: The spot map: one dot, one case, no denominator needed
sections.body: A spot map places one mark per case at the location most relevant to the exposure question, usually residence, workplace, or the specific site where exposure is suspected (a ward, a restaurant, a well). It requires no population data at all, only the case addresses already sitting in the line list, which makes it the fastest place-based tool available and often the first map an investigation produces. John Snow's 1854 map of cholera deaths clustered around the Broad Street pump in London's Soho district is the founding example: each death was marked as a bar near its residence, and the visual clustering around one pump, rather than an even spread across the neighborhood, was itself the evidence that pointed to contaminated water from that single source, famously reinforced when Snow had the pump handle removed.

sections.heading: The limits of dots: population density confounds a spot map
sections.body: A spot map's central weakness is that it shows raw counts, not rates, so a dense cluster of dots can simply reflect a densely populated area rather than a truly elevated risk. Ten cases in a crowded apartment block is a very different finding from ten cases spread across a similarly sized area with one house per acre, yet a plain spot map cannot distinguish the two without additional context. Investigators reading a spot map have to consciously ask what the underlying population distribution looks like before concluding that a visual cluster means a shared exposure.

sections.heading: The area (choropleth) map: rates instead of counts
sections.body: An area map, often a choropleth map shaded by rate, solves this by dividing the region into defined units (census tract, school zone, water district) and computing an attack rate per unit: cases in that unit divided by the population living, working, or served there, then shading each unit by that rate. This is more work, since it requires a real denominator for every area, often from census data or facility rosters, but it directly answers the question a spot map cannot: is this area's risk actually elevated relative to its population, or does it just look busy because more people live there? A water-supply-zone map is a common outbreak application, shading each distribution zone by cases per 1,000 residents served, which can reveal that risk tracks a specific water main or treatment zone rather than simple population density.

lessons.workedExample: A hospital-ward outbreak produces a spot map with dots clustered in the east wing, but the east wing also has twice the bed count of the west wing. A plain dot count could wrongly suggest the east wing carries double the risk. Converting to an area map using each wing's patient-days as the denominator instead shows an attack rate of 4 cases per 100 patient-days in the west wing versus 2.5 per 100 in the east wing — the true elevated-risk area was the smaller west wing, invisible on the raw dot count because it had fewer beds to begin with.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student defaulted to a spot map when an area map with real denominators was actually needed, because a dot cluster in a high-population area is a classic false lead a judge will test for by asking 'what's the population in that area versus the comparison area?' A student who chose the map type deliberately, and can state why counts alone would have misled in their specific setting, demonstrates the analysis was reasoned rather than just visually plotted.

questions.prompt: What is the key limitation of a spot map that an area (choropleth) map is designed to fix?

options.text: A spot map shows raw case counts, which can look clustered simply due to population density rather than elevated risk
A spot map cannot show case locations at all, only case counts by date
A spot map requires a population denominator that is often unavailable
A spot map can only be used for waterborne disease outbreaks

explanations.a: Correct: because a spot map plots raw counts without a denominator, a dense-looking dot cluster may just reflect a densely populated area rather than true elevated risk.
explanations.b: Spot maps do show case locations directly, one dot per case; that is their core feature.
explanations.c: It is the area map, not the spot map, that requires a population denominator; the spot map needs none.
explanations.d: Spot maps have been used across many outbreak types (John Snow's cholera map, hospital ward clusters, restaurant-linked outbreaks), not only water-related ones.

questions.prompt: In John Snow's 1854 investigation, what made the clustering of cholera deaths around the Broad Street pump meaningful evidence?

options.text: The deaths clustered visually around one specific pump rather than spreading evenly across the neighborhood
Snow had already confirmed cholera's bacterial cause in a laboratory before mapping the deaths
The map showed rates per capita rather than raw counts
Government health officials had already identified the pump as contaminated before the map was made

explanations.a: Correct: the spatial clustering of raw case counts around the Broad Street pump, rather than an even spread, was the visual evidence pointing to a single common source.
explanations.b: The germ theory understanding of cholera's causative agent came later; Snow's map preceded confirmed bacteriological proof.
explanations.c: Snow's map was a spot map of raw death locations, not a rate-based choropleth map.
explanations.d: The map itself was the tool that helped identify the pump as the likely source, not a confirmation of a prior official finding.

questions.prompt: Match each map type to its defining requirement.

right.text: Needs only case locations, no population denominator
Needs a population denominator per area to compute a rate

questions.explanation: The spot map is fast because it plots raw case locations; the area map is slower but more valid because it converts counts to rates using real denominators.

lessons.label: Person: Who Is Affected

sections.heading: Beyond counting cases: characterizing who they are
sections.body: The person axis of descriptive epidemiology asks a different question than time or place: not when or where did people get sick, but who got sick, characterized by age, sex, occupation, race/ethnicity, underlying health status, and any other host attribute recorded on the line list. Simple counts by these categories, and better yet attack rates (cases divided by the population at risk in that category), turn a flat case list into a picture of which group carries disproportionate risk, which is often the fastest route to a testable hypothesis about exposure.

sections.heading: Occupation and age as exposure proxies
sections.body: A person characteristic is rarely interesting for its own sake in an outbreak; it matters because it proxies for an exposure. An outbreak concentrated among poultry-processing plant workers points investigators toward a specific occupational exposure (as seen repeatedly in avian influenza spillover investigations, where case clusters track workers with direct bird contact rather than the general public). An outbreak skewed toward children under five versus adults can point toward a daycare, school, or playground water feature rather than a citywide exposure, since young children's behaviors and contact patterns differ sharply from adults'. The 1993 Milwaukee Cryptosporidium outbreak, one of the largest documented waterborne outbreaks in U.S. history with an estimated 403,000 people affected, illustrates the limit of person data alone: it was geography, not age, that localized the source. Attack rates were elevated among residents in the zip codes served by the city's Howard Avenue treatment plant compared with those served by the Linnwood plant, and that place-based pattern, not an age-skewed one, is what combined with the area map to point investigators at the single failing plant rather than the water system as a whole; a follow-up survey actually found the elderly (over 70) had the lowest attack rate of watery diarrhea of any age group studied, the opposite of what an age-driven explanation would predict.

sections.heading: Person data narrows, it does not confirm
sections.body: A person-based pattern is a hypothesis generator, not proof of cause. Finding that cases skew toward one age group or occupation tells investigators where to look harder, which structured questions to prioritize in the analytic questionnaire, and which comparison group makes sense for a case-control study, but it does not by itself establish that age or occupation caused the illness; age and occupation are almost always proxies for an underlying exposure that a formal analytic study still has to test directly. Treating a demographic pattern as a final answer, rather than a lead, is a common overreach in early outbreak reporting. Concretely, if cases skew toward ages 20-29, investigators use that skew to build an age-matched comparison group rather than to declare age itself causal: for every case aged 20-29 they select controls from that same age band and source population, so an exposure difference the study later finds cannot simply reflect age-related differences in diet, work, or contact patterns. Thirty cases matched against sixty same-band controls, rather than controls drawn from the population's full age spread, is what lets a finding such as 'cases were three times more likely to have used the salad bar' be attributed to the salad bar, not to some other trait that just travels with being 20-29.

lessons.workedExample: An outbreak of gastrointestinal illness at a summer camp shows an attack rate of 62% among campers aged 8-12 who used the climbing wall's water station, versus 8% among staff of the same age range who did not use that station and 4% among campers under 8 who were too short to reach it. The age- and activity-linked pattern (not age alone, but age combined with station access) immediately narrows the hypothesis to the water station rather than the camp's shared dining hall, which all age groups used equally and which the person data therefore helps rule out.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'why did you look at age/occupation specifically' expecting the answer to name what exposure that variable stands in for, not just that it's a standard demographic field. A project that reports 'cases were mostly ages 20-30' without connecting that to a plausible shared setting or activity for that age group has stopped at description instead of using person data to generate a testable hypothesis, which is the actual point of the person axis.

questions.prompt: Why is a person characteristic like occupation or age usually informative in an outbreak investigation?

options.text: It typically proxies for a specific exposure or setting shared by that group, narrowing where to look for the cause
It directly proves the biological cause of the illness without further study
It is required by law to be reported regardless of relevance
It replaces the need to collect time or place data entirely

explanations.a: Correct: age, occupation, and similar traits usually matter because they stand in for a shared exposure or setting, which helps generate a focused hypothesis.
explanations.b: A demographic pattern generates a hypothesis; it does not itself prove causation, which still requires analytic testing.
explanations.c: Person data collection is a methodological choice tied to its analytic value, not merely a legal formality.
explanations.d: Person, place, and time are complementary; person data does not substitute for the other two axes.

questions.prompt: In the 1993 Milwaukee Cryptosporidium outbreak, what actually localized the failure to one water treatment plant, and what did age-specific attack-rate data show?

options.text: Geographic data, attack rates by zip code served by the Howard Avenue versus Linnwood plant, localized the source; age data showed the elderly actually had the lowest attack rate, not an elevated one
Age data alone, showing elevated attack rates in older residents, identified the Howard Avenue plant without any geographic analysis
Person data was not collected in this outbreak since it relied only on the area map
Occupation data alone, without any age or geographic analysis, identified the treatment plant

explanations.a: Correct: it was place data, attack rates by treatment-plant service area, combined with the area map that pinpointed the failing plant; the age-stratified data actually ran the other way, with the elderly showing the lowest rate.
explanations.b: Age data did not identify the plant, and it did not show elevated rates in older residents; geography did the localizing, and the elderly subgroup had the lowest rate of any age group studied.
explanations.c: Person-level attack rate data (by age) was collected; it just was not what localized the source, geography was.
explanations.d: It was the combination of place (area map and service-area attack rates) that narrowed the source, not occupation data.

questions.prompt: Match each person-based finding to what it most plausibly points toward as an exposure proxy.

left.text: Cases concentrated among children under five, not adults
Cases spread evenly across all ages and occupations

right.text: An occupational exposure specific to that workplace
A setting or product used mainly by young children
A widely shared exposure not tied to a specific group

questions.explanation: A skewed demographic pattern points to a group-specific exposure, while an even spread suggests something broadly shared, such as a general water supply.

lessons.label: The Population Pyramid and Comparing to Background

sections.heading: What a population pyramid shows
sections.body: A population pyramid is a back-to-back horizontal bar chart with age groups stacked on the vertical axis (typically 5-year bands from 0-4 up through 80+) and sex split left-right, males conventionally on the left and females on the right, each bar's length showing that group's share of the total population. Demographers use the overall shape to read a population's history and trajectory: a wide base narrowing quickly to a point resembles a true pyramid and marks a young, high-fertility population, while a column-like shape with a bulge in the middle marks an aging population with historically lower birth rates, the shape most industrialized countries including the United States show today.

sections.heading: Overlaying cases reveals over-representation
sections.body: In outbreak work, the pyramid becomes an analytic tool once the case distribution is overlaid on the source population's own pyramid, either as a second pyramid drawn beside it or as case counts converted to age-sex-specific attack rates plotted against the same bands. If cases were simply a random draw from the population, the case pyramid would echo the shape of the source pyramid. Where a bar bulges out disproportionately relative to that population's underlying share, that age-sex stratum is over-represented among cases, which is exactly the signal that a specific group carries elevated risk rather than the whole population being affected equally.

sections.heading: Why comparing to background, not raw counts, matters
sections.body: Raw case counts by age or sex can mislead in the same way raw spot-map dots can: an age band with more cases might simply be a larger band in the underlying population, not a genuinely higher-risk group. Comparing the case pyramid's shape to the source population's pyramid, or better, computing an attack rate per age-sex stratum, corrects for this the same way an area map corrects a spot map. Consider a hypothetical respiratory outbreak in a retirement community where cases might look concentrated in the 65-74 band simply because that band dominates the community's population; only comparing case share to that band's population share reveals whether 65-74-year-olds are truly overrepresented among cases or just overrepresented in the community to begin with. The same correction applies at finer resolution: converting each age-sex band's case count and population count into a standardized attack-rate ratio (that band's attack rate divided by the whole population's overall attack rate) turns the visual bulge on the pyramid into a single comparable number, so a ratio above 1.0 flags real over-representation and a ratio near 1.0 flags a band that only looks large because it is large.

lessons.workedExample: A source population of 10,000 is 20% aged 60-69 (2,000 people) and 10% aged 20-29 (1,000 people). An outbreak produces 40 cases in the 60-69 band and 30 cases in the 20-29 band. Raw counts make 60-69 look like the bigger problem, but attack rates tell the opposite story: 40/2,000 = 2.0% for the older band versus 30/1,000 = 3.0% for the younger band. Overlaying case share against population share on the pyramid shows the 20-29 bar bulging out relative to its population slice, while the 60-69 bar is roughly proportionate, correctly flagging the younger group as the truly over-represented, higher-risk stratum.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student compared case demographics to the correct background population, not just to their own case list, because concluding 'most cases were age X' without stating age X's share of the source population confuses raw counts with risk, the same error a spot map makes without a denominator. A judge will ask for the source population's age-sex breakdown alongside the case breakdown; a student who can only produce the case side has not actually completed the person analysis.

questions.prompt: An outbreak has more raw cases in the 60-69 age band than the 20-29 band. What must be true before concluding 60-69-year-olds carry higher risk?

options.text: The comparison must account for each band's share of the source population, since a larger band can produce more raw cases without a higher rate
Nothing further is needed; more raw cases always means higher risk
The case pyramid must always match the shape of a young, high-fertility population
Sex must be ignored entirely when comparing age bands

explanations.a: Correct: raw counts conflate population size with risk; only comparing case share to population share (or computing attack rates) per band reveals true relative risk.
explanations.b: This is the exact error the lesson describes: a larger population band can generate more raw cases with a lower true rate, as the worked example shows.
explanations.c: There is no requirement that a case pyramid resemble any particular population shape; the comparison is against that specific source population's actual pyramid.
explanations.d: Sex is one of the two axes of a population pyramid and is not something to discard from the comparison.

questions.prompt: In the worked example (2,000 people aged 60-69 with 40 cases; 1,000 people aged 20-29 with 30 cases), which band has the higher attack rate?

options.text: 60-69, at 2.0% versus 3.0% for 20-29, so 60-69 is correctly identified as higher-risk by raw counts
Both bands have identical attack rates once population size is considered
Attack rate cannot be computed without knowing the sex breakdown of each band

explanations.a: Correct: 30/1,000 = 3.0% for 20-29 versus 40/2,000 = 2.0% for 60-69, so the younger band has the higher true attack rate despite fewer raw cases.
explanations.b: This reverses the correct comparison; 60-69 has the lower rate (2.0%) despite having more raw cases, precisely because its population band is larger.
explanations.c: The rates are different (3.0% vs 2.0%), not identical, once each band's population size is used as the denominator.
explanations.d: Attack rate only requires cases divided by population at risk for that stratum; sex breakdown is not required to compute the age-specific rate given here.

questions.prompt: Match each pyramid-related concept to its correct description.

left.text: Case pyramid matching source pyramid shape
Case pyramid bulging in one band relative to source

right.text: A back-to-back age-by-sex bar chart of a population's structure
Consistent with cases being roughly proportionate to population share
Signals that age-sex stratum is over-represented among cases

questions.explanation: The pyramid itself is a structural chart; comparing a case pyramid to it distinguishes proportionate representation from a genuinely elevated-risk stratum.

lessons.label: Constructing the Epi Curve

sections.heading: A histogram of onset times, not a line chart
sections.body: An epidemic curve (epi curve) is a histogram: the x-axis is time of illness onset, the y-axis is the count of cases in each time interval. Investigators build it directly from the line list compiled during case finding, plotting each case as one unit — often a stacked square or a dot — so the eye can read both the total case count and the outbreak's shape at once. Unlike a smoothed line graph, the blocky histogram preserves the raw case-by-case texture that reveals whether a wave is single or double-peaked, an artifact a smoothed curve can hide.

sections.heading: Choosing the interval: roughly a quarter to a third of the incubation period
sections.body: The single most consequential design choice is the width of each x-axis bar. CDC's field epidemiology guidance (as taught in the agency's Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice training series) recommends an interval of about one-quarter to one-third of the disease's average incubation period. Too wide an interval — say, weekly bars for norovirus, whose incubation runs roughly 12 to 48 hours — smears a sharp point-source spike into a shapeless mound and destroys the very information the curve exists to show. Too narrow an interval — hourly bars over a multi-week outbreak — fragments the data into noisy, sparse bars where random fluctuation swamps the signal, making a real second wave indistinguishable from sampling noise.

sections.heading: Annotating the frame
sections.body: A usable epi curve marks known exposure events (a banquet date, a facility opening, a boil-water notice) as vertical reference lines, and labels the axes with actual dates or times, not just relative day numbers, so the curve can be cross-referenced against a line list or exposure roster. Investigators typically build several versions at different intervals during an active investigation, because the 'right' interval is diagnostic in itself — the width that makes the curve look most like a single tight peak, versus a plateau, versus successive waves, is a clue to the transmission pattern investigated in later lessons of this unit. A curve drawn during an active investigation also needs a specific caveat: its most recent bars are always artificially low, a phenomenon called right-censoring, because cases still incubating or not yet reported haven't appeared on the line list yet. Investigators reading a live curve treat the last incubation period or two of bars as provisional and expect them to grow as more reports arrive, rather than reading a downward tick at the very right edge as the outbreak already tapering off.

lessons.workedExample: An investigator plots 40 gastroenteritis cases from a wedding reception. At a 1-day interval, the curve looks like a single lumpy 4-day mound. At an 8-hour interval — about one-quarter of norovirus's roughly 33-hour median incubation — the same data resolve into one sharp peak 30-36 hours after the reception, consistent with a single point-source exposure at the meal. The 1-day bars had visually merged the rise and fall into noise; the finer interval revealed the peak's actual timing, which is what the team needed to identify the implicated dish.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why did you choose that bin width?' is testing whether the student understands the curve as a measurement instrument with a resolution, not just a chart. A rehearsed answer that cites 'a quarter to a third of the incubation period' and ties it to the specific pathogen's known incubation range shows the student chose the interval deliberately rather than accepting a spreadsheet default — the same scrutiny a judge would apply to a bin width in any histogram-based measurement.

questions.prompt: Why does CDC guidance recommend an epi curve interval of about one-quarter to one-third of the incubation period, rather than a fixed unit like 'one day'?

options.text: Because that interval scales with the disease, keeping the curve's shape informative regardless of whether the pathogen incubates in hours or weeks
Because public health agencies standardized on it for regulatory reporting, independent of any statistical reasoning
Because narrower bars always look more precise on a printed report
Because it matches the typical duration of a case interview

explanations.a: Correct: a fixed interval like one day would smear a norovirus point-source spike or fragment a hepatitis A curve; scaling the bin to the incubation period keeps resolution appropriate to the disease.
explanations.b: The rule is a statistical/visual-resolution guideline from field epidemiology training, not a reporting mandate unrelated to the data.
explanations.c: Precision is not the goal — an interval too narrow relative to incubation period creates noisy, uninterpretable bars.
explanations.d: Interview duration has no bearing on how the histogram bins onset times.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in constructing a usable epi curve during an active outbreak investigation.

items.text: Compile a line list with each case's onset date/time
Select a bar interval of roughly one-quarter to one-third of the known or suspected incubation period
Plot each case as a stacked unit on the onset-time histogram
Annotate known exposure events as reference lines on the time axis

questions.explanation: The line list is the raw data source; the interval choice must come before plotting since it defines the bins; annotation is a final step layered onto the completed histogram.

questions.prompt: A team plots a known point-source outbreak using weekly bars instead of an 8-hour interval appropriate to the pathogen's incubation period. What is the most likely visual consequence?

options.text: The sharp single peak is smeared into a broad, shapeless mound that looks like a plateau
The total case count displayed will be mathematically incorrect
The curve will show extra false peaks from random noise
The exposure date annotation becomes impossible to place

explanations.a: Correct: an interval far wider than the incubation period compresses a tight rise-and-fall into what visually resembles a sustained plateau, obscuring the point-source signature.
explanations.b: Total case count is preserved regardless of bin width; only the shape resolution is affected.
explanations.c: Noise-driven false peaks are a risk of intervals that are too narrow, not too wide.
explanations.d: Exposure annotations are independent of bar width and can be placed at any interval.

questions.prompt: Match each epi curve design choice to its main risk if done incorrectly.

left.text: Interval far wider than the incubation period
Interval far narrower than the incubation period
No exposure event annotated on the axis

right.text: Sharp peaks smear into an uninformative mound
Random case-to-case variation looks like a real secondary wave
The curve cannot be cross-referenced against a suspected source

questions.explanation: Bin width errors distort shape in opposite directions depending on whether the interval is too coarse or too fine, while missing annotations remove the curve's link back to specific suspected exposures.

lessons.label: The Point-Source (Common-Source) Curve

sections.heading: One brief exposure, one tight curve
sections.body: A point-source (or common-source) outbreak happens when a group of people share a single, brief exposure to the same contaminated source — a dish at a banquet, a batch of a recalled product, an aerosol at one event. Because everyone was exposed at essentially the same moment, every case's onset time is separated from the others only by variation in individual incubation period, not by any staggering in exposure timing. The result is a curve compressed into roughly the width of the pathogen's incubation-period range: a norovirus point source resolves in a day or two, a hepatitis A point source can still span several weeks, because hepatitis A's incubation period itself spans weeks.

sections.heading: Steep rise, slower fall — the log-normal signature
sections.body: The classic point-source curve is not symmetric. It rises steeply as the bulk of cases cluster near the median incubation period, then falls more gradually as a long right tail of slower-incubating cases trickles in. This right-skewed shape reflects the underlying biology: incubation periods across a population are well approximated by a log-normal distribution, a finding formalized by Sartwell (1950) in an analysis of incubation-period data across multiple diseases showing that the logarithm of incubation time, not incubation time itself, is approximately normally distributed. That skew is why the curve's peak (mode) sits earlier than its mean, and why a small number of very late-onset cases are expected biology, not necessarily evidence of a second source.

sections.heading: The archetype: the shared-meal outbreak
sections.body: The textbook silhouette for teaching this pattern is a church-supper or banquet outbreak: a defined guest list, a single shared meal, and a case count that rises within hours of the meal and tapers off over the following day or two. A widely used field-epidemiology training case is a 1940 church supper outbreak in Oswego County, New York, still taught because it demonstrates the pattern cleanly — nearly all cases cluster within a narrow window after the identified meal, and the attack rate by dish, not just the curve shape, ultimately pinpoints the vehicle: in the Oswego investigation, guests who ate the vanilla ice cream fell ill at a far higher rate than those who didn't, identifying it as the vehicle even though several other dishes were served at the same shared meal. A single sharp point-source peak is itself evidence: it argues against ongoing transmission and against a contaminated ongoing source, and it points investigators toward one shared event to interview about.

lessons.workedExample: At a 200-guest banquet, 60 guests develop acute gastroenteritis. Onset times cluster tightly: 3 cases by hour 12 after the meal, 40 cases between hours 18 and 30, tapering to the last case at hour 50. Plotted at a 4-hour interval, the curve shows a steep rise to a peak around hour 24 and a longer, gentler decline through hour 50 — the right-skewed log-normal shape. The roughly 12-to-50-hour span is consistent with a Salmonella-like agent, and because the whole outbreak resolves within one incubation-period range with no second bump, investigators focus entirely on the one shared meal rather than searching for an ongoing source.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can read a single tight, right-skewed peak as a specific epidemiological claim — a single brief shared exposure — rather than just describing the shape. A strong answer explains why the rise is steeper than the fall (clustering near the median incubation period, then a log-normal tail) and connects the curve's total width to the pathogen's known incubation range, rather than treating 'peak' and 'shape' as purely descriptive vocabulary.

questions.prompt: Why is a classic point-source epi curve right-skewed rather than symmetric?

options.text: Because incubation periods across a population approximate a log-normal distribution, clustering near the median with a long tail of later cases
Because case reporting is always delayed for people who fall ill later in an outbreak
Because the exposure itself was staggered over several days
Because public health investigators round late onset times down to the nearest day

explanations.a: Correct: Sartwell (1950) showed incubation periods follow an approximately log-normal distribution, producing a steep rise near the median incubation time and a gradual, extended fall.
explanations.b: Reporting delay is a data-quality issue, not the biological reason the underlying incubation-period distribution itself is skewed.
explanations.c: A staggered exposure describes a continuous or intermittent source, not a point source, and would produce a plateau rather than a single skewed peak.
explanations.d: Rounding practice does not create a systematic skew in incubation-period distributions.

questions.prompt: A single, sharp, right-skewed peak spanning roughly one incubation-period range is best interpreted as evidence for:

options.text: A single brief shared exposure, arguing against an ongoing source or person-to-person spread
A contaminated water supply still actively serving the community
Person-to-person transmission through several generations of cases
Chronic low-level exposure to a persistent environmental source

explanations.a: Correct: a single peak confined to one incubation-period range is the signature of one brief shared exposure, not ongoing or repeated exposure.
explanations.b: An actively serving contaminated water supply would produce a plateau spanning well beyond one incubation-period range, the continuous-source pattern covered in the next lesson.
explanations.c: Person-to-person spread produces successive waves separated by roughly a serial interval, not one compressed peak.
explanations.d: Chronic low-level exposure would not compress into a single tight peak matching one incubation-period range.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning steps used to identify a point-source pattern from a curve and confirm the vehicle.

items.text: Observe a single tight, right-skewed peak on the epi curve
Check that the curve's total width roughly matches the pathogen's known incubation-period range
Identify a single shared exposure event common to the case group
Compare attack rates by specific food or exposure item to pinpoint the vehicle

questions.explanation: The curve shape first suggests a point source, the width check confirms consistency with the suspected pathogen, a shared event is then identified, and attack-rate analysis by item narrows down the specific vehicle.

questions.prompt: Match each feature of the point-source curve to its explanation.

left.text: Gradual, extended fall after the peak
Total curve width close to one incubation-period range

right.text: Most cases cluster near the median incubation period
A long right tail of slower-incubating cases, per the log-normal distribution
All cases stem from one exposure moment, not staggered exposures

questions.explanation: Each visual feature of the point-source curve traces back to the same underlying fact: everyone was exposed once, at the same time, and individual biological variation in incubation period does the rest.

lessons.label: Continuous and Intermittent Common-Source Curves

sections.heading: When the source keeps giving: the plateau
sections.body: Not every common-source outbreak comes from one brief exposure. A continuous common-source outbreak arises when a contaminated source keeps exposing new people over an extended period — a contaminated well that the community keeps drinking from, or a food product that stays on shelves and keeps being sold. Because new people are exposed on different days throughout that window, the epi curve does not resolve into the point source's single tight peak; instead it rises and then flattens into a plateau that can span many incubation-period ranges, with a relatively sharp cutoff only once the source is identified and removed. The 1993 Milwaukee Cryptosporidium outbreak, described by MacKenzie and colleagues (1994) in the New England Journal of Medicine, is the canonical large-scale example: contamination of the public water supply produced an outbreak that built and then sustained a broad plateau over roughly a month, with an estimated 400,000-plus residents affected, until the water treatment problem was corrected.

sections.heading: When the source is sporadic: irregular peaks
sections.body: An intermittent common-source outbreak sits between the point source and the continuous source. Exposure recurs, but not steadily — a caterer contaminates food only on days a particular ingredient is used, or a food product is contaminated only in scattered production batches or shipments. The curve reflects that irregularity directly: instead of one smooth peak or a steady plateau, it shows multiple separated peaks of uneven height, each corresponding to a distinct exposure episode, with case-free or low-case gaps between them roughly matching the incubation period. This is the pattern behind produce-linked outbreaks where contaminated shipments arrive only periodically, such as the mid-1990s multistate Cyclospora outbreaks tied to imported raspberries, where case counts rose and fell in bursts tracking shipment timing rather than forming one continuous curve.

sections.heading: Why the distinction matters for the response
sections.body: Reading plateau versus irregular-peaks versus single-peak is not just descriptive; it changes what investigators do next. A plateau argues for hunting a persistent, still-active source that needs to be shut off — a well to close, a product to recall — and the outbreak should end abruptly once that happens. Irregular peaks argue for a source that is only sometimes contaminated, pushing investigators toward supply-chain or batch-level tracing rather than a single fixed location. Confusing either pattern with a point source risks investigators searching for one meal or one moment of exposure when the real answer is a source still operating in the present. Investigators do not have to wait for the full curve to shape up before telling an accumulating point-source tail from a genuine continuous-source plateau: they check whether the new cases report a fresh, recent exposure to the suspected source, which points to an ongoing continuous source, or whether they are simply late-incubating members of the original exposed cohort with no new contact, which points to an ordinary point-source tail instead.

lessons.workedExample: A rural water system serves 5,000 residents. Gastrointestinal illness reports climb steadily over three weeks rather than spiking once, holding at 15-25 new cases per day — a plateau, not a peak. Investigators test the well and find persistent fecal contamination from a failed septic system uphill. Case counts drop sharply within days of chlorinating the supply and issuing a boil-water notice, confirming the source was continuously active the entire time, exactly as the flattened three-week plateau on the epi curve had suggested before the well was even tested.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this concept by asking what a plateau or a cluster of uneven peaks rules in or out before any lab result comes back. A strong answer states that a plateau implies an ongoing, currently active source that must be found and stopped, while irregular multiple peaks imply sporadic contamination worth tracing to specific batches or shipments — showing the student treats curve shape as an investigative lead, not just a picture to describe after the fact.

questions.prompt: An epi curve for a suspected waterborne outbreak shows cases rising then holding at a steady elevated level for three weeks before dropping sharply after the water supply is treated. This shape is best classified as:

options.text: A continuous common-source pattern, implying an ongoing active source
A point-source pattern, implying a single brief shared exposure
A propagated pattern, implying person-to-person spread
Random noise with no interpretable pattern

explanations.a: Correct: a sustained plateau that only drops once the source is removed is the signature of a continuous common source, as in the Milwaukee Cryptosporidium outbreak.
explanations.b: A point source resolves within roughly one incubation-period range as a single peak, not a multi-week plateau.
explanations.c: A propagated pattern shows successive rising waves separated by a serial interval, not a flat sustained plateau.
explanations.d: The steady elevation and its sharp drop after intervention are a clear, interpretable continuous-source signature, not noise.

questions.prompt: An epi curve shows several separated peaks of uneven height over two months, each followed by a case-free gap, with no single sustained plateau. This pattern most strongly suggests:

options.text: An intermittent common source, such as sporadically contaminated batches or shipments
A single point-source exposure at one event
A source that has been continuously active the entire two months
A laboratory error in case classification

explanations.a: Correct: irregular, separated peaks with gaps between them match sporadic exposure episodes, the hallmark of an intermittent common source like periodically contaminated shipments.
explanations.b: A single point-source event produces one peak, not several separated peaks over two months.
explanations.c: A continuously active source produces a sustained plateau, not distinct peaks separated by case-free gaps.
explanations.d: The pattern is consistent with a known real-world exposure mechanism, not a data artifact.

questions.prompt: Match each common-source pattern to its epi curve shape.

right.text: One sharp, right-skewed peak within about one incubation-period range
A sustained plateau spanning many incubation-period ranges
Multiple separated peaks of uneven height with case-free gaps

questions.explanation: Each pattern reflects how exposure was distributed over time: once, continuously, or sporadically, and the curve shape mirrors that exposure timing directly.

questions.prompt: Order the investigative response appropriate to identifying a continuous common-source outbreak from its epi curve.

items.text: Notice case counts rise and then hold at a sustained elevated plateau
Infer an ongoing, still-active source rather than a single past exposure
Search for and test a persistent source such as a water supply or shelf-stable product
Confirm the source by observing case counts drop sharply after the source is removed or treated

questions.explanation: The plateau shape first suggests an active ongoing source, prompting a targeted search, and the outbreak's sharp end after intervention confirms the source was correctly identified.

lessons.label: The Propagated (Person-to-Person) Curve

sections.heading: Waves, not a single peak
sections.body: A propagated outbreak spreads through direct person-to-person transmission rather than from a shared external source: an infected person passes the agent to close contacts, those contacts become infectious after their own incubation period, and pass it on again. The epi curve for this pattern does not look like one point-source peak or a common-source plateau; it shows a series of successive waves, each cresting roughly one incubation period (more precisely, one serial interval — the time from one case's onset to their contacts' onset) after the previous wave. Reading a propagated curve means counting waves and measuring the gap between their peaks, not just describing a single high point.

sections.heading: Why later waves are often taller and messier
sections.body: Early in a propagated outbreak, few people are infectious, so the first wave is often small. As each generation of cases infects its own contacts, the pool of currently infectious people can grow, and later waves are frequently taller and less cleanly separated than the first — overlapping tails from one generation bleed into the rise of the next as transmission continues across multiple settings (a household, then a classroom, then a workplace) rather than one bounded group. This growth is not indefinite: as the outbreak burns through the pool of susceptible contacts — people who are unvaccinated or otherwise not immune — each successive generation finds fewer new people left to infect, a dynamic called susceptible depletion. Waves therefore tend to grow while susceptible contacts are still plentiful and then shrink once immune or already-infected people dominate the exposed population, which is why real propagated curves are often described as growing-then-shrinking rather than endlessly escalating. This progressive blurring, where distinct waves become harder to tell apart as the outbreak matures, is itself a signature that distinguishes propagated spread from the clean, bounded shapes of common-source outbreaks.

sections.heading: Two textbook archetypes: measles and hepatitis A
sections.body: Measles is the classic fast propagated curve: its incubation period averages about 11 to 12 days to first symptoms (prodrome), but runs about 14 days (range 7 to 21) to rash onset — the milestone actually used to plot cases on an epi curve — so successive generations of cases stack up roughly two weeks apart. The 2014-2015 Disneyland-linked measles outbreak, first documented in a CDC report by Zipprich and colleagues (2015) as it was unfolding, grew to a final U.S. total of 147 cases by the time CDC closed out the investigation months later, and showed exactly this generational spacing as the virus moved from the initial park exposure into households, schools, and healthcare settings. Hepatitis A shows the same wave structure but stretched out, because its incubation period averages about 28 days: person-to-person hepatitis A outbreaks among socially connected groups, such as the multistate outbreaks tied to injection drug use and homelessness reported by CDC starting in 2017, unfold over many months, with successive waves separated by roughly a month rather than two weeks — the same propagated shape, just running on a slower clock.

lessons.workedExample: A daycare measles exposure produces 4 cases in week 1 (the initial generation). Roughly 14 days later, in week 3, a second wave of 11 cases appears among siblings and classmates who were infected by the first group. Another 14 days on, a third wave of 9 cases appears among contacts of the second group, this time in a different school. The gap between each wave's peak is close to measles's roughly 14-day incubation period to rash onset, and the growing-then-shrinking wave sizes track how many people were infectious in each generation — a textbook propagated curve rather than a single point-source peak.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can distinguish 'multiple peaks' from a common-source intermittent pattern by checking the spacing: propagated waves sit apart by roughly one serial interval tied to the agent's biology, while intermittent common-source peaks track external exposure events like shipment dates instead. A strong answer names the expected wave spacing for the specific pathogen and explains why later waves often blur together, rather than simply pointing at bumps on the curve.

questions.prompt: What primarily explains why successive waves in a propagated epi curve are spaced roughly one incubation period (serial interval) apart?

options.text: Each new wave consists of people infected by the previous wave's cases, so the gap reflects the time needed for infection to take hold and become symptomatic again
Public health agencies report cases in fixed reporting cycles that create artificial gaps
The source of contamination is replenished on a fixed external schedule
Laboratory confirmation delays are consistent across all cases

explanations.a: Correct: propagated spread is chained transmission, so each generation's onset lags the prior generation's onset by about one incubation period, producing evenly spaced waves.
explanations.b: Reporting cycles are an artifact of surveillance systems, not the biological mechanism producing wave spacing tied to incubation periods.
explanations.c: A fixed external replenishment schedule describes an intermittent common source, not person-to-person propagated spread.
explanations.d: Consistent lab delays would shift the whole curve later but would not create the specific spacing tied to incubation period.

questions.prompt: Why do later waves in a propagated outbreak often appear taller and less cleanly separated than the first wave?

options.text: As transmission spreads into more settings, more people become infectious simultaneously and generational tails begin to overlap
Case definitions become less strict as the outbreak continues
Later cases always have shorter incubation periods than earlier cases
Testing capacity improves over the course of the outbreak

explanations.a: Correct: as spread moves from one setting into households, schools, or workplaces, more people are infectious at once, and their overlapping incubation periods blur wave boundaries.
explanations.b: Loosening case definitions is not the mechanism behind taller, blurrier later waves; it would be a surveillance artifact unrelated to transmission dynamics.
explanations.c: Incubation period is a property of the pathogen and host biology, not something that systematically shortens as an outbreak progresses.
explanations.d: Improved testing could increase detected case counts but does not explain the specific wave-blurring pattern caused by overlapping generations.

questions.prompt: Order the mechanism by which a propagated outbreak's epi curve develops successive waves.

items.text: An initial small group of cases becomes infectious after exposure
Those cases transmit the agent to close contacts during their infectious period
New contacts pass through their own incubation period before becoming symptomatic
A second wave of onsets appears roughly one serial interval after the first wave's peak

questions.explanation: Propagated spread is a chain: each generation must become infectious, transmit, and let the next generation incubate before that generation's onset wave appears on the curve.

questions.prompt: Match each pathogen to its approximate wave-spacing behavior on a propagated epi curve.

right.text: Successive waves roughly 14 days apart
Successive waves roughly a month apart

questions.explanation: Measles's shorter incubation period produces tightly spaced waves, as seen in the 2014-2015 Disneyland-linked outbreak, while hepatitis A's longer incubation period stretches the same wave structure over months.

lessons.label: Incubation Periods and What the Curve Reveals

sections.heading: The curve's width is a clue, not just a shape
sections.body: Before any stool sample or blood test comes back from the lab, the epi curve already carries information about which pathogen is plausible, because the total time span over which cases appear is bounded by the causal agent's incubation period. A point-source outbreak that resolves entirely within about a day is not consistent with an agent whose incubation period is measured in weeks, and one that stretches across a month is not consistent with a fast-acting toxin. Investigators routinely work this comparison in both directions: known incubation-period ranges narrow the list of plausible agents given an observed curve, and a suspected agent from clinical symptoms predicts what curve width to expect.

sections.heading: Four reference windows worth memorizing
sections.body: At the very short end sit preformed-toxin illnesses like Staphylococcus aureus or Bacillus cereus food poisoning, roughly 1 to 6 hours, because the toxin is already made before the food is eaten and no bacterial incubation is needed — a curve that resolves almost entirely within a single afternoon points here, not toward an infectious agent at all. Norovirus has one of the shortest incubation periods among common infectious outbreak agents, roughly 12 to 48 hours, which is why norovirus point-source outbreaks — the classic cruise-ship or banquet scenario — resolve almost entirely within two days of the shared exposure. Salmonella sits in a wider, overlapping band of roughly 6 to 72 hours, so a curve spanning two to three days after a suspected meal is equally consistent with either agent on timing alone, and symptom pattern (norovirus favors vomiting as a dominant symptom, Salmonella favors fever and diarrhea) has to help distinguish them. Hepatitis A sits in an entirely different regime, averaging around 28 days with a range that can run from about 15 to 50 days, so a point-source hepatitis A curve can still be unfolding a month after the exposure even though every case stems from the same single event.

sections.heading: Using the window as a filter, not a verdict
sections.body: None of these windows are diagnostic on their own — norovirus and Salmonella overlap substantially in the 12-to-48-hour range, so curve timing alone cannot separate them. What the incubation window does reliably do is rule agents out: a curve resolving in 36 hours effectively excludes hepatitis A regardless of symptoms, and a curve still generating new cases after three weeks effectively excludes norovirus or Salmonella as the sole explanation. Investigators use the curve's timing to prioritize which lab tests to run first and which agents to stop chasing, treating incubation period as a fast, free filter that narrows the field before the more expensive confirmatory testing begins.

lessons.workedExample: An outbreak at a catered event produces its first case 14 hours after the meal and its last case 44 hours after the meal, a roughly 30-hour total span. Norovirus (12-48 hours) fits comfortably within that span; Salmonella (6-72 hours) also fits; hepatitis A (about 28 days on average) is essentially ruled out by timing alone, since the entire outbreak is over before hepatitis A's typical incubation period would even begin producing symptoms. Investigators prioritize norovirus and Salmonella testing and do not request hepatitis A serology, saving a test that the curve's timing had already made very unlikely to be useful.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this concept by asking a student to defend a testing decision using the curve alone, before mentioning any lab result. A strong answer states the specific incubation-period window for the pathogens under consideration and explains which agents the observed curve span rules out, showing that the student treats the epi curve as active evidence that shapes the investigation, not merely a retrospective chart drawn after the pathogen is already known.

questions.prompt: An epi curve for a point-source outbreak spans only about 30 hours from first case to last case. Based on incubation period alone, which agent is most strongly ruled out?

options.text: Hepatitis A, whose incubation period averages around 28 days
Norovirus, whose incubation period is roughly 12 to 48 hours
Salmonella, whose incubation period is roughly 6 to 72 hours
No agent can be ruled out from curve span alone

explanations.a: Correct: a curve resolving in about 30 hours is far shorter than hepatitis A's roughly 15-to-50-day range, effectively excluding it on timing alone.
explanations.b: A 30-hour span sits comfortably within norovirus's 12-to-48-hour incubation window, so norovirus is not ruled out.
explanations.c: A 30-hour span also sits within Salmonella's 6-to-72-hour window, so Salmonella is not ruled out.
explanations.d: Curve span is a real, usable filter; it directly excludes agents whose incubation-period range does not overlap the observed span.

questions.prompt: Norovirus (roughly 12-48 hours) and Salmonella (roughly 6-72 hours) both fit a 40-hour outbreak span. What does this overlap imply about using curve timing alone?

options.text: Timing alone cannot distinguish between the two agents in this range; other evidence like symptom pattern is needed
The curve definitively points to Salmonella because its range is wider
The curve definitively points to norovirus because its range is narrower
The overlap means neither agent should be tested for

explanations.a: Correct: when incubation windows overlap, curve timing narrows but does not resolve the choice between agents; symptom pattern or lab testing is needed to distinguish them.
explanations.b: A wider range does not make an agent more likely; overlap only means both remain plausible on timing grounds.
explanations.c: A narrower range does not make an agent more likely by itself; both agents remain consistent with the observed span.
explanations.d: Overlap means both remain plausible and worth testing, not that testing should be abandoned.

questions.prompt: Order the incubation-period windows from shortest to longest.

items.text: Norovirus: roughly 12-48 hours
Salmonella: roughly 6-72 hours
Hepatitis A: roughly 15-50 days, averaging about 28 days

questions.explanation: Norovirus's window is the shortest, Salmonella's overlaps but extends further, and hepatitis A's window is measured in weeks rather than hours, making it the longest by a wide margin.

questions.prompt: Match each observed epi curve span to the agent it most strongly rules out on incubation-period grounds alone.

left.text: Earliest case appears just 8 hours after the suspected exposure
Outbreak still generating new cases 45 days after exposure

right.text: Hepatitis A is ruled out (span far shorter than its ~15-50 day range)
Norovirus is ruled out (8 hours is faster than its 12-hour minimum incubation period)
Norovirus and Salmonella are both ruled out (span exceeds both of their upper bounds)

questions.explanation: Matching an observed span against each agent's known window is exactly how investigators use incubation period as a fast filter before lab confirmation: an earliest case at 8 hours is faster than norovirus's 12-hour minimum, so norovirus is excluded even though the slower-minimum Salmonella (6 hours) and the preformed toxins are not.

lessons.label: Back-Calculating the Time of Exposure

sections.heading: Running the incubation period backward from the peak
sections.body: Once a point-source epi curve is drawn, investigators can run the logic of incubation period in reverse: instead of predicting when symptoms should appear after a known exposure, they subtract the pathogen's median incubation period from the curve's peak or median onset time to estimate when exposure actually happened. Because the log-normal incubation-period distribution clusters most cases near the median, the peak onset time is the single most information-dense point on the curve for this calculation — it represents the modal incubation period acting on the true exposure time, so subtracting the median incubation period from it gives a reasonable point estimate of the exposure moment even before any interview data narrows down a specific meal or event.

sections.heading: Bracketing with the minimum and maximum, not just the median
sections.body: A single point estimate is fragile, so investigators pair it with a bracket built from the two ends of the curve. Subtracting the pathogen's minimum known incubation period from the earliest case's onset time gives the latest possible exposure time — exposure cannot have happened after this, or even the fastest-incubating case couldn't have gotten sick that early. Subtracting the pathogen's maximum known incubation period from the latest case's onset time gives the earliest possible exposure time — exposure cannot have happened before this, or the slowest-incubating case would already have shown symptoms sooner than it did. Together, these two bounds define a window, and any candidate meal, product lot, or event that falls outside that window can be excluded immediately, often before lab confirmation returns. Both bounds matter because they fail in different directions: relying only on the latest-possible-exposure bound risks accepting an implausibly early candidate event that the earliest-possible-exposure bound would have ruled out, while relying only on the earliest-possible-exposure bound risks missing a genuine late-window event that the latest-possible-exposure bound would have flagged as too late to explain the fastest-incubating case.

sections.heading: From a time window to one implicated event
