sections.body: The back-calculated window becomes operationally useful when it's checked against a roster of candidate exposures — a schedule of meals served at a conference, a list of shifts a food handler worked, or a set of delivery dates for a suspected product. If only one plausible event falls inside the calculated window, that event becomes the leading hypothesis for targeted interviews and environmental sampling, well before waiting on stool or blood culture results. If several events fall inside the window, the back-calculation has still done its job by shrinking a long list of candidates down to a short, testable one.

lessons.workedExample: A norovirus outbreak (incubation roughly 12-48 hours, median about 33 hours) has its peak onset at 2:00 PM on day 2 and its earliest case onset at 8:00 PM on day 1. Subtracting the ~33-hour median from the peak gives an estimated exposure around 5:00 AM on day 1 — implausible for a meal, flagging that the true exposure is likely later than the point estimate suggests once real event timing is checked. Subtracting the 12-hour minimum from the earliest case (8:00 PM day 1) gives a latest-possible-exposure bound of 8:00 AM day 1. The outbreak's latest case has onset at 4:00 AM on day 3; subtracting the 48-hour maximum incubation period from that gives an earliest-possible-exposure bound of 4:00 AM on day 1, meaning exposure could not have happened before that time either. Checking a conference's meal schedule against that full window (4:00 AM to 8:00 AM on day 1), only the day-1 breakfast service falls inside it, immediately narrowing the search to one meal.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this concept by asking a student to justify a claimed exposure time using the curve's numbers, not intuition. A strong answer shows the subtraction explicitly — peak or median onset minus median incubation period for the point estimate, plus the minimum- and maximum-incubation brackets from the earliest and latest cases — and explains why the bracket, not just the point estimate, is what should be checked against a roster of candidate exposure events.

questions.prompt: To estimate the latest possible time that exposure could have occurred, an investigator should:

options.text: Subtract the pathogen's minimum known incubation period from the earliest case's onset time
Subtract the pathogen's maximum known incubation period from the latest case's onset time
Subtract the median incubation period from the peak onset time
Add the maximum incubation period to the latest case's onset time

explanations.a: Correct: the earliest case sets the tightest constraint on how late exposure could have been, since even the fastest possible incubation period had to have already elapsed by that case's onset.
explanations.b: That calculation gives the earliest possible exposure time (the other bound of the bracket), not the latest possible time.
explanations.c: That gives a single point estimate of exposure, not the bound defining the latest possible exposure time.
explanations.d: Adding rather than subtracting incubation period moves forward in time from onset, which does not correspond to estimating a past exposure time.

questions.prompt: Why do investigators use the peak or median onset time, rather than a randomly chosen case, to compute the point-estimate of exposure time?

options.text: Because the peak reflects the modal incubation period, clustering the most information-dense set of cases in a log-normal distribution
Because the peak case is always the index case who was first exposed
Because peak cases are more reliably interviewed than other cases
Because the peak onset time is always exactly equal to the true exposure time

explanations.a: Correct: since incubation periods cluster near the median in a log-normal distribution, the peak represents the modal, most typical incubation period acting on the true exposure time.
explanations.b: The peak reflects the most common incubation period among many people exposed together, not any single index case.
explanations.c: Interview reliability has no systematic relationship to where a case falls on the curve.
explanations.d: The peak onset time minus the median incubation period only approximates exposure time; it is a point estimate, not an exact equality.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for back-calculating a bracketed exposure window from an epi curve.

items.text: Identify the earliest case onset time and the latest case onset time on the curve
Subtract the pathogen's minimum incubation period from the earliest onset to bound the latest possible exposure
Subtract the pathogen's maximum incubation period from the latest onset to bound the earliest possible exposure
Check which candidate exposure events fall inside the resulting time window

questions.explanation: The bracket requires both the earliest and latest case onset times before either bound can be calculated, and only once both bounds are set can candidate events be checked against the window.

questions.prompt: Match each back-calculation input to what it produces.

left.text: Peak onset time minus median incubation period
Earliest onset time minus minimum incubation period
Latest onset time minus maximum incubation period

right.text: A single point estimate of exposure time
The latest possible exposure time (bracket's upper bound)
The earliest possible exposure time (bracket's lower bound)

questions.explanation: The point estimate uses the median incubation period on the peak, while the two bracket bounds use the extreme incubation periods on the extreme case onset times.

lessons.label: Outliers, Secondary Cases, and Reading the Tail

sections.heading: Early outliers: the case before the crowd
sections.body: A case whose onset falls well before the main cluster of a point-source curve is not noise to discard; it is frequently the most informative single data point on the whole chart. An early outlier can be the index case — the person originally infected elsewhere who then became the source for everyone else, for instance an infected food handler who contaminated a dish before the event the rest of the group attended. Investigators specifically interview early outliers about exposures the rest of the group did not share: did this person eat something before the shared meal, work in food preparation, or have contact with an animal or environmental source the others didn't? Dismissing an early case as an unrelated illness can mean missing the actual origin of the contamination.

sections.heading: Late outliers: two very different explanations
sections.body: A case trailing well after the main peak on a point-source curve is ambiguous and needs to be interpreted carefully, because it has at least three distinct explanations that call for different responses. First, it may simply be a slow-incubating case sitting in the long right tail of the pathogen's log-normal incubation-period distribution — expected biology, not a new event. Second, it may be a secondary case, someone infected not by the original source but by person-to-person contact with an earlier case, which is common with highly infectious agents like norovirus, where household secondary attack rates of roughly 20 to 30 percent are typical even after a genuine point-source origin. Third, it may reflect a second, separate exposure — the same contaminated product served again, or a different meal at the same venue — which would mean the outbreak is not actually over.

sections.heading: Using the tail to judge whether spread continued
sections.body: Distinguishing these explanations changes what the tail implies about the outbreak's classification. A tail that stays within roughly the pathogen's known incubation-period range past the last plausible point-source case is consistent with ordinary biological variation and a contained point source. A tail that extends further, especially when late cases cluster among household members or close contacts of earlier cases rather than the original exposed group, points to secondary transmission layered on top of an otherwise genuine point source — still fundamentally different from a propagated outbreak, but requiring added precautions like isolation or hygiene messaging for contacts. A tail with a genuinely new, separate peak well beyond one incubation-period range instead suggests a second exposure event and should prompt investigators to check for continued availability of the original source.

lessons.workedExample: A 50-person banquet point-source outbreak has its main cluster of 45 cases between hours 18 and 50 after the meal. One case appears at hour 3 — an early outlier who turns out to be a server who had eaten leftovers from the kitchen before the event and had been symptomatic since the prior evening, identifying them as the likely contamination source. Four more cases appear between hours 80 and 96, well past the pathogen's roughly 48-hour upper incubation bound; interviews show all four live with an initial case and had no independent exposure to the banquet food, confirming these are secondary household transmissions rather than evidence the original source is still active.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this concept by pointing at a specific outlier on a curve and asking what it means before the student has case-interview data. A strong answer names the competing explanations for that position on the curve — index case versus expected tail variation versus secondary transmission versus a second exposure — and states what follow-up interview question would distinguish them, rather than treating every outlier as either an error to ignore or automatic proof of ongoing spread.

questions.prompt: A single case appears well before the main cluster on an otherwise clean point-source epi curve. What is the most useful next investigative step?

options.text: Interview that case specifically about exposures the rest of the group did not share, since they may be the index or source case
Exclude the case from the line list as a data error
Assume the case has an unrelated illness and stop investigating them further
Reclassify the entire outbreak as propagated based on this one case

explanations.a: Correct: an early outlier is frequently the index case or source, such as an infected food handler, and targeted interview questions about their distinct exposures can identify the contamination origin.
explanations.b: Discarding the case as an error risks losing the most informative data point on the curve without any evidence it is actually erroneous.
explanations.c: Assuming an unrelated illness without investigation risks missing the actual source of the outbreak.
explanations.d: A single early case does not itself establish person-to-person propagation; it needs to be evaluated for its role as a possible source before any reclassification.

questions.prompt: Several late-onset cases appear beyond a point-source outbreak's expected incubation window, and interviews show they are household members of earlier cases with no independent exposure to the original source. This pattern is best explained as:

options.text: Secondary person-to-person transmission layered on top of an underlying point-source origin
Ordinary biological variation fully explained by the log-normal incubation-period tail
Proof that the original point source is still actively contaminating new victims
Evidence that the initial point-source classification was incorrect and the whole outbreak is propagated

explanations.a: Correct: late cases among close contacts of earlier cases, with no independent exposure to the original source, indicate secondary transmission added on top of a genuine point-source event.
explanations.b: Cases extending beyond the pathogen's known incubation window, tied specifically to contact with earlier cases, go beyond what ordinary tail variation alone would explain.
explanations.c: Household transmission among contacts does not indicate the original source is still active; it indicates person-to-person spread from existing cases instead.
explanations.d: A point source with limited secondary spread is a distinct, common pattern; it does not require reclassifying the entire outbreak as propagated from the start.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning process for interpreting a late-onset outlier on a point-source epi curve.

items.text: Check whether the case's onset still falls within the pathogen's known incubation-period range from the original exposure
If it does, treat it as expected tail variation and take no special action
If it exceeds the range, interview the case for independent exposure to the original source versus contact with an earlier case
Classify the case as secondary transmission or a new exposure event based on that interview

questions.explanation: The incubation-window check comes first because it determines whether further investigation is even needed, and only cases outside the window require the follow-up interview that distinguishes secondary transmission from a new exposure.

questions.prompt: Match each outlier scenario to its most likely interpretation.

left.text: Case onset well before the main cluster, traced to a symptomatic food handler
Late case within the pathogen's known incubation-period range of the original exposure
Late cases among household contacts of earlier cases, no independent exposure to the original source

right.text: Likely the index or source case
Expected biological variation in the incubation-period tail
Secondary person-to-person transmission

questions.explanation: Each outlier position and its supporting interview evidence points to a distinct role in the outbreak: originating source, ordinary tail variation, or downstream secondary spread.

units.label: Attack Rates and the Analytic Investigation

lessons.label: The Attack Rate

sections.heading: Cumulative incidence over the outbreak
sections.body: The attack rate is field epidemiology's term for cumulative incidence during a defined outbreak period: the number of people who become ill divided by the number who were at risk of becoming ill, almost always expressed as a percentage rather than a rate in the strict per-person-time sense. It is a proportion, a risk over one specific window, not an ongoing rate. Investigators define "at risk" carefully to mean the population that could plausibly have been exposed, not the surrounding town or county. A church supper with 75 known attendees uses 75 as the denominator, not the population of the county the church sits in. Choosing the wrong denominator is the single most common way an attack rate gets misreported, because it silently changes what the numerator is being compared against and can make an outbreak look larger or smaller than it is.

sections.heading: Overall versus group-specific rates
sections.body: The overall attack rate is one summary number for the whole event, but it hides variation. Group-specific attack rates split the same population by food eaten, by table or seating section, by age band, or by sex, and compute a separate rate for each subgroup. This comparison is the entire engine of an analytic outbreak investigation: a food-specific attack-rate table, covered in the next lesson, is nothing more than a set of group-specific attack rates lined up side by side. An overall attack rate with little variation across the obvious risk groups is itself informative, since it suggests the true exposure has not yet been captured on the questionnaire; a genuine point-source event should show a sharp split between an exposed group and an unexposed one.

sections.heading: The secondary attack rate and transmissibility
sections.body: A distinct measure, the secondary attack rate, asks a different question: among the susceptible close contacts of a primary case, such as household members, what fraction go on to become ill within one incubation period? Its denominator excludes people already immune or already infected, since only susceptible contacts can convert to new cases. Because it isolates person-to-person spread from the original shared exposure, the secondary attack rate is the standard measure epidemiologists use to compare how transmissible different pathogens are: among susceptible household contacts, measles runs as high as roughly 90%, one of the highest secondary attack rates known for any human pathogen, while a pooled meta-analysis of early studies put the household secondary attack rate for SARS-CoV-2 at about 16.6% (Madewell et al., 2020). A single outbreak can report both figures: a point-source attack rate for the original event, and a secondary attack rate for whether the pathogen kept spreading afterward.

lessons.workedExample: At a 75-person church supper, the line list shows 46 people ill within 48 hours: overall attack rate = 46/75 = 61%. Splitting by age shows 74% among the 43 attendees under 60 versus 42% among the 32 attendees 60 and older, a group-specific gap worth flagging before any single food is examined. Two weeks later, one ill attendee's household is followed forward: of 4 household members, 1 was already immune from a prior infection, leaving 3 susceptible contacts. One of the 3 becomes ill within the pathogen's incubation window, a secondary attack rate of 1/3 = 33%, built from a completely different denominator than the church-supper attack rate.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "attack rate of what, among whom" because a bare percentage without a stated denominator is unfalsifiable. A judge expects a student to state whether a reported figure is overall or group-specific, name the exact population at risk used as the denominator, and explain why the secondary attack rate is a fundamentally different calculation, restricted to susceptible contacts, rather than a follow-up statistic on the same denominator. Using a countywide population as the denominator for an event with a known guest list, or quoting a secondary attack rate without excluding already-immune contacts, is the error judges are primed to catch first.

questions.prompt: An outbreak's "attack rate" is best described as:

options.text: Cumulative incidence over the defined outbreak period, expressed as a percentage
An incidence rate measured in cases per person-time
The prevalence of illness at a single point in time
The case-fatality ratio among confirmed cases

explanations.a: Correct: it is a proportion (ill / at risk) over one bounded window, not a true rate with a time unit in the denominator.
explanations.b: A rate in the strict sense divides events by person-time at risk; the attack rate divides events by people at risk, with no time dimension.
explanations.c: Prevalence describes existing cases at one moment; the attack rate accumulates new cases over the whole outbreak period.
explanations.d: Case-fatality ratio divides deaths by cases, an entirely different numerator and question.

questions.prompt: Why does the secondary attack rate exclude household contacts who were already immune before the primary case became ill?

options.text: Because only susceptible contacts can convert to a new case, so including immune people would understate transmissibility
Because immune contacts are not legally required to be counted in outbreak reports
Because immune contacts always develop mild, unreported illness
Because the primary case's own immunity status determines who counts as a contact

explanations.a: Correct: the secondary attack rate measures transmissibility, so its denominator must be restricted to people who could actually become new cases.
explanations.b: There is no such legal rule; the exclusion is a methodological requirement of the measure, not a reporting law.
explanations.c: Immune contacts are excluded because they cannot become cases at all, not because their illness goes unreported.
explanations.d: Contact status depends on exposure to the primary case, not on the primary case's own immune history.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in moving from an overall attack rate to a secondary attack rate.

items.text: Compute the overall attack rate using the total population at risk of the event as denominator
Split the population into subgroups and compute group-specific attack rates
Compare group-specific rates to look for one exposure with a much higher rate
Follow ill cases' household contacts forward to compute a secondary attack rate

questions.explanation: Overall attack rate establishes the outbreak's scope, group-specific rates narrow toward a candidate exposure, comparison flags the likely vehicle, and the secondary attack rate is a separate, later calculation testing onward person-to-person spread.

questions.prompt: Match each attack-rate term to its correct denominator.

right.text: Total population at risk of the original event
People in one exposure or demographic subgroup
Susceptible close contacts of a primary case

questions.explanation: Each measure answers a different question, so each is defined by a different denominator population.

lessons.label: The Food-Specific Attack-Rate Table

sections.heading: One row per food, four counts per row
sections.body: The food-specific attack-rate table is the standard next step after a line list, taught in CDC field epidemiology training as the workhorse of a foodborne outbreak investigation. Each row is one food item served at the event; each row carries four counts: ill among those who ate it, well among those who ate it, ill among those who did not eat it, and well among those who did not eat it. From those four counts, two attack rates are computed per row, one for eaters and one for non-eaters, and the rows are stacked so every item served can be scanned at once. Because the same 2x2 structure repeats for every food, the table turns a long, messy set of individual food histories into a single comparable summary an investigator can read down in minutes. Investigators build one such row for every distinct food and beverage on the menu, often a dozen or more items from a single banquet, so the table is typically the largest single exhibit in an outbreak report.

sections.heading: What the suspect vehicle looks like in the table
sections.body: The true vehicle produces a distinctive pattern: a high attack rate among the people who ate it, a low attack rate among the people who did not, and, critically, the eaters' case count accounts for nearly all of the outbreak's total cases, not merely a large fraction relative to non-eaters. A food eaten by only a few attendees can show a dramatic-looking gap between its two attack rates while explaining only a handful of the total cases, which makes it a poor candidate even though its row looks striking. The classic teaching case is the 1940 Oswego County church supper: New York State investigators interviewed 75 of the attendees, the population an infectious cause was thought to have moved through in a single evening, and found 46 ill overall, a 61% attack rate; homemade vanilla ice cream stood out with roughly 80% attack rate among the people who ate it versus roughly 14% among those who did not, and it was the one item whose eaters accounted for nearly the full case count.

sections.heading: Foods that fail the test
sections.body: Most rows in a real table fail one half of the pattern: a food eaten by almost everyone at the event, like bread or coffee, will show similar attack rates among eaters and non-eaters simply because there are too few non-eaters to compare against meaningfully, and a food eaten by very few people can show a large gap by chance alone. Reading the whole table together, rather than picking the single highest attack rate in isolation, is what separates a supportable conclusion from a coincidence; the next lesson formalizes that comparison as a risk ratio.

lessons.workedExample: In the Oswego supper table, cakes shows 27 ill of 40 eaters (68%) versus 19 ill of 35 non-eaters (54%), a modest gap that covers most of the total but not sharply enough to stand out. Vanilla ice cream shows roughly 43 ill of 54 eaters (80%) versus 3 ill of 21 non-eaters (14%): a much wider gap, and those 43 eater-cases alone account for 43 of the 46 total cases, essentially the whole outbreak. Chocolate ice cream, eaten by far fewer people, shows little difference between eaters and non-eaters. Reading all three rows together, not just the single highest percentage, points to vanilla ice cream as the vehicle.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who hears a single "80% attack rate" claim will ask what it was 80% of, and whether the investigator also checked the non-eaters' rate and the food's share of total cases before naming a vehicle. The tell of real understanding is presenting the whole table, not one cherry-picked row, and being able to explain why a food eaten by nearly everyone at the event cannot produce a useful comparison even if its point estimate looks elevated, since its non-eater group is too small to compare against.

questions.prompt: A table row for a food eaten by only 8 of 75 attendees shows 87.5% ill among those 8 eaters (7 of 8) and 58% ill among the 67 non-eaters (39 of 67), in an outbreak with 46 total ill. Why is this food a poor candidate vehicle despite the high eater attack rate?

options.text: Because only 8 people ate it, so its eater-cases cannot account for most of the 46 total cases
Because an 87.5% attack rate is not mathematically possible in a real outbreak
Because the non-eater attack rate of 58% is too low to be a valid comparison
Because attack-rate tables cannot be used for foods eaten by a minority of attendees

explanations.a: Correct: even a striking eater/non-eater gap is unconvincing if so few people ate the item that it cannot explain most of the outbreak's cases.
explanations.b: Attack rates of 87.5% or higher are unusual but entirely possible in a small, heavily exposed group.
explanations.c: 58% is a real, meaningful non-eater attack rate; the problem is the tiny size of the eater group, not this number.
explanations.d: The table can include foods eaten by a minority; the issue here is that this particular minority is too small to explain the outbreak's case count.

questions.prompt: In the Oswego church supper table, why does vanilla ice cream outrank cakes as the likely vehicle even though cakes also shows a higher attack rate among eaters?

options.text: Vanilla ice cream shows a much wider eater/non-eater gap and its eaters account for nearly all 46 cases
Cakes was not included in the food-specific table
Vanilla ice cream was eaten by every attendee, leaving no non-eaters to compare
Cakes' non-eater attack rate of 54% proves it caused no illness

explanations.a: Correct: roughly 80% versus 14% is a far sharper split than cakes' 68% versus 54%, and vanilla ice cream's eaters cover nearly the full case count.
explanations.b: Cakes appears in the table with its own row and counts; it was considered and compared, not excluded.
explanations.c: 21 of the 75 attendees did not eat the vanilla ice cream, so a non-eater comparison group existed.
explanations.d: A 54% non-eater rate does not prove cakes caused no illness; it simply produces a much smaller gap than ice cream's.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in building and reading a food-specific attack-rate table.

items.text: For each food, count ill and well among those who ate it and among those who did not
Compute an attack rate for eaters and for non-eaters for each food
Scan all rows for the widest eater/non-eater gap
Check that the leading item's eaters account for nearly all total cases before naming it the vehicle

questions.explanation: The four counts come first, rates are derived from them, the gap across rows narrows the candidates, and the case-count check confirms the leading candidate actually explains the outbreak.

questions.prompt: Match each pattern in a food-specific attack-rate table to what it suggests.

left.text: High eater rate, low non-eater rate, eaters cover nearly all cases
Similar eater and non-eater rates for a food nearly everyone ate
Large eater/non-eater gap, but very few people ate the item

right.text: Strong candidate for the outbreak vehicle
Uninformative row; too few non-eaters for a real comparison
Gap may be due to chance given the small exposed group

questions.explanation: A convincing vehicle needs both a sharp rate gap and enough eaters to plausibly account for the case count; either missing ingredient weakens the row as evidence.

lessons.label: Choosing the Study: Retrospective Cohort vs Case-Control

sections.heading: The deciding question: can you define a denominator?
sections.body: Before any 2x2 table gets built, an outbreak investigator has to answer one design question: is the population that was at risk enumerable, meaning every member can be identified and contacted, or is it an open community with no roster at all? A wedding reception, a cruise ship, a church supper, or a scout troop's overnight trip all have a guest list, a boarding manifest, or a permission-slip roster; everyone who could have been exposed is, at least in principle, nameable. A statewide cluster of Salmonella cases linked to a grocery-store product, or a multistate outbreak tied to a restaurant chain visited by an unknown number of unrecorded customers, has no such list; nobody knows how many people ate at that chain last month, let alone their names. That single fact, whether a denominator can be defined, is what decides which analytic design is used.

sections.heading: Closed, enumerable population: retrospective cohort
sections.body: When the population is closed and enumerable, investigators run a retrospective cohort study: interview everyone on the list (or as many as can be reached) about what they ate and whether they became ill, then compute an attack rate directly for each exposure group, because the true denominator, everyone who was there, is known. Risk and risk ratios, covered in the next lesson, are computed directly from these real attack rates. This is the strongest design available in an outbreak, but it only works when the roster exists; trying to force it onto an open community means guessing at a denominator that cannot actually be counted. In practice a roster is rarely reached at 100%: the 1940 Oswego County church supper investigation, the classic teaching cohort for this design, interviewed 75 of the 80 known attendees, and investigators still had to consider whether the 5 uninterviewed guests differed systematically from the rest before treating 75 as an adequate stand-in for the full roster.

sections.heading: Open community: case-control
sections.body: When no roster exists, investigators instead run a case-control study: they identify confirmed or probable cases directly, from surveillance reports, clinic referrals, or active case finding, then recruit a separate comparison group of controls from the same source population who did not become ill, matched loosely on factors like neighborhood or time period. Because the true population at risk was never counted, an attack rate cannot be computed; instead, investigators compare the odds of exposure between cases and controls, yielding an odds ratio rather than a risk ratio, the subject of the odds-ratio lesson later in this unit. The tradeoff is real: case-control studies are more prone to control-selection bias and recall bias than cohorts, precisely because there is no fixed list to sample controls from cleanly, and both design families require the investigator to justify their choice explicitly rather than default to whichever is more familiar.

lessons.workedExample: A 120-guest wedding reception reports 68 guests ill. Because the caterer's guest list gives an exact roster, investigators run a retrospective cohort, interview all 120 by phone, and compute attack rates directly: 85% among guests who ate the seafood tower versus 20% among those who did not. Three months later, a separate cluster of 30 Salmonella cases is reported across four counties, all linked by genomic fingerprinting to the same strain, with no shared event or guest list; investigators instead run a case-control study, interviewing the 30 cases and 90 randomly selected, healthy telephone-survey controls from the same counties about food exposures in the two weeks before onset.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this choice because picking the wrong design is a flaw a judge can spot before looking at a single result: a student who ran a case-control study for an event with a known guest list wasted the chance to compute a real attack rate and risk ratio, while a student who tried to compute an "attack rate" for an open community with no roster is reporting a number with an undefined denominator. The tell of understanding is stating explicitly why the population was or was not enumerable before describing which design was used.

questions.prompt: What single fact about the at-risk population determines whether an outbreak investigation runs as a retrospective cohort or a case-control study?

options.text: Whether the total population at risk can be enumerated (a roster exists) or not
Whether the outbreak is caused by a bacterium or a virus
Whether the outbreak has already been reported to a health department
Whether more than 50 people are estimated to be involved

explanations.a: Correct: an enumerable, closed population supports computing real attack rates directly, which is impossible without a defined denominator.
explanations.b: Pathogen type affects clinical case definition and lab confirmation, not which analytic design fits the population structure.
explanations.c: Reporting status affects how cases are found, not whether a denominator can be defined for the population at risk.
explanations.d: Outbreak size alone does not determine enumerability; a 500-person cruise ship manifest is still a closed, countable roster.

questions.prompt: Why can't investigators compute a true attack rate for an open-community outbreak with no guest list or roster?

options.text: Because the total number of people who were actually at risk of exposure is unknown, so there is no valid denominator
Because open-community outbreaks never produce enough cases to calculate a rate
Because attack rates can only be computed for foodborne, not waterborne, outbreaks
Because case-control studies are statistically forbidden from reporting percentages

explanations.a: Correct: an attack rate requires knowing everyone who was at risk, which an open community with no roster cannot provide.
explanations.b: Case count is unrelated to whether a denominator exists; large open-community outbreaks still lack a countable at-risk population.
explanations.c: The exposure route, food or water or person-to-person, does not determine whether a population is enumerable.
explanations.d: Case-control studies can report percentages of exposure among cases and controls; they simply cannot report a population attack rate.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning an investigator uses to choose between a retrospective cohort and a case-control design.

items.text: Ask whether everyone at risk can be identified from a roster or list
If yes, interview the whole enumerable population and compute attack rates by exposure group
If no, identify cases directly and recruit controls from the same source population
Compute the measure of association appropriate to whichever design was used

questions.explanation: Enumerability is checked first because it branches the entire design; only after that branch is chosen does the appropriate measure (risk ratio or odds ratio) get computed.

questions.prompt: Match each outbreak setting to the design it calls for.

left.text: Cruise ship with a full passenger manifest
Statewide cluster linked by lab fingerprinting, no shared event
Wedding reception with a caterer's guest list
Restaurant-chain cluster with unknown total customers

right.text: Retrospective cohort
Case-control
Retrospective cohort
Case-control

questions.explanation: A defined roster supports a cohort in each case; an open, uncounted population forces a case-control design instead.

lessons.label: Relative Risk in the Outbreak Cohort

sections.heading: Building the 2x2 table per food
sections.body: With a retrospective cohort's full roster in hand, each food gets its own 2x2 table: rows for ate/did not eat, columns for ill/well. From that table, risk among the exposed is ill-exposed divided by all exposed (eaters), and risk among the unexposed is ill-unexposed divided by all unexposed (non-eaters); each of these is simply that food's group-specific attack rate. The risk ratio, also called relative risk, is risk-among-exposed divided by risk-among-unexposed. A risk ratio of 1 means the food made no difference; well above 1 means eating it raised the risk of illness; near or below 1 means it did not, or was even mildly protective, most often because it was a garnish so widely eaten it barely separates cases from non-cases. A related but distinct measure, the risk difference (risk among exposed minus risk among unexposed), reports the same comparison as a subtracted percentage rather than a ratio; it is useful for sizing the excess burden directly, while the ratio is what gets compared across foods to rank candidates.

sections.heading: Attributable cases: how much of the outbreak the item explains
sections.body: The risk ratio alone can mislead if read without the case counts behind it. Attributable cases among the exposed, roughly the excess ill count beyond what the unexposed group's baseline risk would predict, shows how much of the total outbreak a given item actually explains. The attributable fraction among the exposed, (RR minus 1) divided by RR and expressed as a percentage, answers a related question: of the illness seen among people who ate the item, what share is attributable to that exposure rather than to whatever baseline risk the unexposed group already carried. A food with an enormous risk ratio but only a handful of eaters can still account for very few of the total cases, which is why investigators report the risk ratio, the attributable fraction, and the share of total cases among eaters together, not the ratio alone, before naming a vehicle.

sections.heading: Reading across all the tables at once
sections.body: The true vehicle is the item whose risk ratio is both large and consistent with nearly explaining the total case count, not merely the item with the single highest ratio in the set. A food eaten by only 3 people, 2 of whom happened to be ill, can produce a risk ratio far above a genuine vehicle's simply from small numbers; a 95% confidence interval around that ratio would typically be extremely wide and might still include 1, a sign of statistical instability that the point estimate alone hides. Investigators cross-check each candidate's risk ratio and confidence interval against its share of total cases and against the food-specific table from the previous lesson before settling on one item.

lessons.workedExample: In the Oswego church supper cohort of 75, vanilla ice cream's 2x2 table gives risk among the 54 eaters of 43/54 = 80% and risk among the 21 non-eaters of 3/21 = 14%; risk ratio = 0.80/0.14 = 5.7. Chicken salad's table gives risk among 40 eaters of 27/40 = 68% and risk among 35 non-eaters of 19/35 = 54%; risk ratio = 0.68/0.54 = 1.3. Vanilla ice cream's risk ratio is over four times chicken salad's, and its 43 eater-cases cover 43 of the 46 total cases (93%) versus chicken salad's 27 (59%), so ice cream is the far stronger candidate on both counts, not just the ratio.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "what was the risk ratio for your suspected exposure" is testing whether a student can compute relative risk from a real 2x2 table, not just eyeball a percentage gap. The stronger tell is a student who volunteers the attributable case count alongside the ratio, showing they checked that the leading candidate explains most of the outbreak rather than just having the flashiest single number, which guards against a small, noisy exposed group masquerading as the vehicle.

questions.prompt: For a food with risk among eaters of 80% and risk among non-eaters of 14%, the risk ratio is closest to:

explanations.a: Correct: 0.80 divided by 0.14 is approximately 5.7, meaning eaters were about 5.7 times as likely to become ill as non-eaters.
explanations.b: 0.66 is the difference between the two risks (80% minus 14%), not their ratio.
explanations.c: 66 would result from treating the risks as raw percentage points subtracted then misplaced, not from dividing 0.80 by 0.14.
explanations.d: 1.14 does not correspond to dividing either risk by the other; it is not a value produced by this calculation.

questions.prompt: A food eaten by only 3 of 75 attendees, 2 of whom were ill, produces a very high risk ratio. Why should this alone not be enough to name it the outbreak vehicle?

options.text: With so few eaters, the ratio can be driven by chance and the item cannot explain most of the outbreak's total cases
Risk ratios below 10 are never considered meaningful in field epidemiology
Foods eaten by very few people are always contaminated intentionally
A risk ratio can only be trusted if the food was also tested in a laboratory first

explanations.a: Correct: a tiny exposed group can produce an extreme ratio from very few cases, and even a huge ratio there explains only a small share of the outbreak.
explanations.b: There is no fixed cutoff like 10 for meaningfulness; the concern here is small-group instability and low case coverage, not the ratio's size alone.
explanations.c: Rarity of consumption says nothing about intent or contamination; it only affects the statistical stability of the estimate.
explanations.d: Risk ratios are computed from questionnaire and case data alone; lab confirmation is a separate, later step, not a precondition for calculating one.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in using relative risk to identify an outbreak vehicle across several candidate foods.

items.text: Build a 2x2 table (ate/did not eat by ill/well) for each candidate food
Compute risk among eaters and risk among non-eaters for each food
Compute the risk ratio for each food from those two risks
Check each food's share of total outbreak cases before naming the vehicle

questions.explanation: The ratio is only meaningful once it is checked against how much of the actual outbreak the candidate item's eaters cover, not treated as the final word on its own.

questions.prompt: Match each risk ratio value to what it indicates about a candidate food.

left.text: Risk ratio well above 1, high case coverage
Risk ratio well above 1, tiny eater group

right.text: Food made little or no difference to illness risk
Strong candidate vehicle
Possibly unstable estimate; check case counts before concluding

questions.explanation: The ratio's size only supports a conclusion once it is paired with how many people were actually exposed and how much of the outbreak they account for.

lessons.label: Odds Ratios in the Case-Control Outbreak

sections.heading: Selecting controls from the source population
sections.body: A case-control study's validity rests on one requirement: controls must be a fair sample of the same source population that produced the cases, people who could have become a case had they been exposed and ill, just as the actual cases were, but who happen not to be ill. In a community outbreak with no roster, investigators commonly draw controls by random-digit-dial telephone survey within the same counties and time period, or from the same clinic system for unrelated conditions, matched loosely on age group or neighborhood. The control group is not meant to represent "healthy people" in general; it is meant to represent the exposure pattern of the population the cases came from, so that comparing exposure between the two groups isolates the food or product's effect rather than some unrelated difference between where cases and controls were drawn from. Outbreak case-control studies commonly enroll more controls than cases, often 2 to 4 per case, since the case count is fixed by how many people actually became ill while the control pool can be expanded to sharpen the precision of the resulting odds ratio.

sections.heading: Exposure odds and the odds ratio
sections.body: Because there is no enumerable denominator, investigators cannot compute a risk; instead they compute odds of exposure within each group and compare them. Among cases, the odds of having eaten the suspect item is (cases exposed) divided by (cases unexposed); among controls, the odds of exposure is (controls exposed) divided by (controls unexposed). The odds ratio is the first odds divided by the second, and, like relative risk, a value near 1 means no association, well above 1 means the item is linked to illness. When cases and controls are individually matched, for example by neighborhood or age band, the odds ratio is instead calculated from the discordant pairs, pairs where the case and control differ on exposure, rather than from the simple cross-product of group totals.

sections.heading: Why the odds ratio approximates the risk ratio here, and where controls go wrong
sections.body: The odds ratio approximates the risk ratio when the outcome, being a case in this outbreak, is rare within the broader source population, which holds in nearly every community outbreak since only a small fraction of everyone exposed to a common food or product actually becomes an identified case; this rare-outcome condition is why case-control results can be read almost like a risk ratio despite using odds. Control selection is where community outbreaks most often go wrong: drawing controls only from hospitalized patients with a different diagnosis can introduce Berkson's bias if hospitalization itself relates to the exposure, and drawing controls from cases' own friends or family can bias the odds ratio toward the null if friends share exposures with the case, since exposure prevalence in the control group is pulled toward that of the cases, narrowing the gap the odds ratio depends on.

lessons.workedExample: In the 1994 multistate Salmonella enteritidis outbreak traced to a nationally distributed ice-cream brand, Hennessy and colleagues (1996) ran a matched case-control study: 11 of 15 cases (73%) had eaten the brand's ice cream versus 2 of 15 matched controls (13%). A simple cross-product of the group totals, (11/4) / (2/13) = 17.9, is not the right calculation here: because the controls were individually matched to cases, the true odds ratio has to come from the discordant pairs rather than from group totals. Using that matched-pairs method, the study reported a matched odds ratio of 10.0 (95% CI 1.4-434, P = 0.007), large and statistically significant despite the wide interval from the small matched sample, and traceback confirmed contaminated tanker trailers had carried the ice-cream premix after previously hauling unpasteurized liquid eggs.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe control selection specifically because it is where a well-computed odds ratio can still be wrong: a judge who hears "we compared cases to their neighbors" or "we used hospital patients as controls" will ask whether that control source could be systematically more or less exposed than the true source population, independent of illness. A project that explains why its controls represent the same population that could have produced the cases, and names the specific bias it tried to avoid, shows real command of the design; one that treats "any healthy person" as an acceptable control does not.

questions.prompt: Why must case-control study controls be drawn from the same source population as the cases, rather than from any conveniently available healthy people?

options.text: So that the comparison of exposure isolates the suspect item's effect rather than an unrelated difference in who was sampled
Because health departments require controls to live on the same street as a matched case
Because controls must have the exact same age as their matched case to be valid
Because odds ratios cannot be calculated unless controls are also mildly ill

explanations.a: Correct: if controls come from a differently exposed population, the odds ratio reflects that mismatch as much as, or instead of, the true exposure effect.
explanations.b: Matching can involve neighborhood as one factor among several, but there is no rule requiring the same street; the underlying goal is a shared source population.
explanations.c: Exact age matching is one possible matching strategy, not a universal requirement for a valid control.
explanations.d: Controls are, by definition, people without the outcome being studied; the odds ratio compares exposure, not illness severity, between cases and controls.

questions.prompt: The odds ratio approximates the risk ratio in an outbreak case-control study primarily because:

options.text: Becoming an identified case is rare within the broader source population that produced both cases and controls
Odds and risk are mathematically identical formulas at any disease frequency
Case-control studies always enroll more controls than cases
The suspect exposure itself is rare among both cases and controls

explanations.a: Correct: when the outcome is rare, the odds of exposure and the risk of exposure converge numerically, which is the standard rare-outcome justification for reading an odds ratio like a risk ratio.
explanations.b: Odds and risk diverge as an outcome becomes common; they are only approximately equal when the outcome is rare, not identical in general.
explanations.c: The control-to-case ratio can be 1:1, 2:1, or otherwise; it does not drive the odds-ratio-to-risk-ratio approximation.
explanations.d: It is the rarity of the outcome (being a case), not the rarity of the exposure, that underlies this approximation.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in computing and interpreting an odds ratio from a case-control outbreak study.

items.text: Identify cases and recruit controls from the same source population
Ask both groups about exposure to the suspect item using the same structured questions
Compute the odds of exposure separately among cases and among controls
Divide the cases' odds of exposure by the controls' odds of exposure

questions.explanation: Valid group selection and identical questioning must come before the odds are calculated, and the odds ratio itself is the final ratio of those two odds.

questions.prompt: Match each control-selection problem to its consequence.

left.text: Controls drawn only from hospitalized patients with a different diagnosis
Controls drawn from cases' own friends and family
Controls drawn by random-digit-dial from the same counties and period as cases

right.text: Risk of Berkson's bias if hospitalization relates to the exposure
Risk of an odds ratio biased toward the null if friends share the case's exposures
Reasonable approximation of the community source population

questions.explanation: Each control source carries a different risk of misrepresenting the true source population's exposure pattern. Friend and family controls tend to share the case's exposures, an overmatching problem that pulls the control group's exposure prevalence toward the cases' and biases the odds ratio toward the null.

lessons.label: Dose-Response and Strengthening the Link

sections.heading: Beyond a single 2x2 table
sections.body: A risk ratio or odds ratio near or above the others in a food-specific table is suggestive, but a single comparison of eaters versus non-eaters cannot fully rule out coincidence or a confounded food eaten alongside the true vehicle. Dose-response is a second, independent line of evidence: if attack rate rises step by step as the amount or number of servings of an item increases, from none, to one serving, to two or more, that gradient is much harder to explain by chance or by a confound than a single yes/no comparison, because it would require the confound to also track serving size in exactly the same graded way. Dose-response reasoning appears directly in Bradford Hill's widely used 1965 criteria for judging causation, where a demonstrable gradient is treated as one of the stronger pieces of supporting evidence for a causal, not merely associated, relationship. Hill listed it alongside strength of association, consistency across studies, and temporality as one of nine considerations for judging whether an observed link reflects cause and effect rather than coincidence, and it is the one an outbreak's own questionnaire data can usually speak to directly, without needing outside studies to corroborate it.

sections.heading: Building the gradient from the questionnaire
sections.body: To capture dose, the structured questionnaire covered in the earlier hypothesis-generating lesson must ask not just "did you eat X" but "how much" or "how many servings," recorded in ordered categories: none, one serving, two servings, three or more. Investigators then compute a separate attack rate for each category and lay them in order, watching for a rate that climbs steadily rather than jumping around unpredictably. A gradient that is monotonic, each step at least as high as the one before, is stronger evidence than one that rises then falls, since a real biological dose effect should not reverse itself at higher exposure.

sections.heading: What a gradient does and does not prove
sections.body: A clean dose-response gradient strengthens confidence in a candidate vehicle considerably, but it is still an epidemiologic pattern, not proof; it needs to be read alongside the food-specific table and risk ratio from earlier lessons, not as a replacement for them. A comparable, real dose-response finding appears in the 1994 multistate Salmonella enteritidis ice-cream outbreak, where investigators found that the more of a production batch's premix had been hauled in tanker trailers immediately after a raw-egg load, the more likely that batch was to be linked to illness (Hennessy et al., 1996), a genuine graded relationship between contamination dose and outcome rather than a single exposed/unexposed split.

lessons.workedExample: At a 60-person banquet, investigators ask each guest how many servings of a suspect casserole they ate. Attack rate by serving count: 0 servings, 4 of 15 ill (27%); 1 serving, 9 of 20 ill (45%); 2 servings, 12 of 16 ill (75%); 3 or more servings, 8 of 9 ill (89%). The rate climbs at every step with no reversal, a monotonic gradient. Combined with a risk ratio of roughly 2.4 for any exposure versus none, the gradient makes the casserole a far stronger candidate than a single eaters-versus-non-eaters comparison alone would have shown, since a confound eaten alongside it would need to track serving count this precisely by coincidence.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe dose-response because it distinguishes a student who understands strength of evidence from one who stopped at a single comparison. A project that asked only "did you eat it" cannot show a gradient even if the food truly is the vehicle, so a judge hearing "we also asked how many servings and the rate rose at each level" is hearing evidence of a more rigorous questionnaire design, not just a stronger result; a judge will also ask whether the gradient was monotonic or noisy, since a reversal at the highest exposure level weakens the causal argument.

questions.prompt: Why is a monotonic dose-response gradient considered stronger evidence for a vehicle than a single eaters-versus-non-eaters attack rate comparison?

options.text: A steadily rising attack rate across serving amounts is harder to explain by chance or by a confounded food than one binary comparison
Dose-response gradients are required by law before an outbreak can be officially closed
A gradient replaces the need to compute a risk ratio or odds ratio at all
Serving-size data is always more accurate than yes/no exposure data

explanations.a: Correct: for a confound to fake a graded pattern, it would have to track serving size in exactly the same stepwise way, which is a much less likely coincidence than a single elevated ratio.
explanations.b: There is no legal requirement of this kind; dose-response is a strength-of-evidence consideration, not a procedural mandate.
explanations.c: A gradient supplements the risk ratio or odds ratio from a single 2x2 table; it does not substitute for computing one.
explanations.d: Serving-size recall can be less reliable than a simple yes/no, since guests estimate quantities imprecisely; its value comes from the pattern it reveals, not inherent accuracy.

questions.prompt: An investigator finds attack rates of 20%, 55%, 40%, and 70% across increasing serving categories of a suspect food (0, 1, 2, 3+ servings). What weakens this as dose-response evidence?

options.text: The gradient is not monotonic; it dips at 2 servings before rising again
The rates were not converted into a single relative risk
Four serving categories are too many to analyze meaningfully
The 0-serving category should have been excluded from the table

explanations.a: Correct: a real dose-response relationship is expected to rise (or fall) steadily; a mid-sequence reversal undercuts the argument that the pattern reflects an actual dose effect.
explanations.b: A relative risk can still be computed from any-exposure versus none; the weakness here is specifically the reversal in the trend, not the absence of a single ratio.
explanations.c: More categories generally give a finer picture of the gradient; the count of categories is not the problem.
explanations.d: The 0-serving group is the necessary baseline for comparison and should stay in the table.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in building and interpreting a dose-response analysis for a suspect food.

items.text: Ask each respondent how many servings of the suspect item they consumed, in ordered categories
Compute a separate attack rate for each serving-count category
Arrange the categories in order and check whether the rate rises steadily
Weigh the gradient alongside the food-specific table and risk ratio, not as a replacement for them

questions.explanation: Dose data must be collected in ordered form before rates can be computed and compared, and the resulting gradient is integrated with, not substituted for, the earlier analysis.

questions.prompt: Match each dose-response pattern to what it implies for the investigation.

left.text: Attack rate rises steadily at every higher serving category
Attack rate rises then reverses at the highest category
Attack rate is flat across all serving categories

right.text: Strong supporting evidence for this item as the vehicle
Weakened evidence; the gradient is not monotonic
No dose-response support for this item

questions.explanation: A clean, monotonic gradient strengthens the causal argument, a reversal weakens it, and a flat pattern provides no dose-response support at all.

lessons.label: When the Table Lies: Confounded Foods and Multiple Vehicles

sections.heading: Foods served together produce parallel tables
sections.body: When two items are almost always eaten together, a sauce ladled over every serving of roast beef, for instance, both items' rows in the food-specific table will show nearly identical attack rates and nearly identical risk ratios, because the people who ate one almost always ate the other. The table alone cannot tell which item, the meat or the sauce, is the actual vehicle; both look equally implicated by the raw comparison. Investigators resolve this with stratified analysis: split the people who ate the meat into those who also had the sauce and those who did not, and compute the sauce's attack rate separately within each stratum. If the sauce's association disappears once the meat is held constant, the meat was the real vehicle and the sauce was simply confounded through co-service; if the meat's association disappears instead, the reverse is true.

sections.heading: Stratification as the general tool for confounding
sections.body: This approach, computing an association within fixed levels of a second variable and comparing the stratum-specific results to the crude, unstratified result, is the same stratified-analysis logic formalized more broadly by Mantel and Haenszel (1959) for combining and comparing results across strata. In an outbreak, the "strata" are just exposure categories for the confounding food; the same idea used in the earlier dose-response lesson to order servings is used here to isolate one exposure from another. Where dose-response ordered a single food into graded categories, confounding-control stratification splits the population by a second food entirely, but both techniques rest on the same principle: hold one variable fixed and see whether the association of interest survives.

sections.heading: More than one contaminated item, and where the association ends
sections.body: Stratification assumes one true vehicle is hiding behind a correlated one, but some outbreaks genuinely have more than one contaminated item, most often because a single infected food handler cross-contaminated several dishes during preparation, or because two separate ingredients from the same contaminated supplier ended up in different foods on the same menu. In those cases, more than one row in the table will retain a real, independent association even after stratification, and investigators report multiple implicated items rather than forcing a single answer. In every case, though, a statistical association from a food-specific table, however clean, is not itself proof: it is a hypothesis strong enough to justify the confirmatory work covered in the next unit, laboratory culture or genetic fingerprinting of the food and of patient specimens, and environmental inspection of where and how the item was prepared, before a vehicle is named with confidence.

lessons.workedExample: At a banquet, 50 of 60 guests ate roast beef and 48 of those 50 also had the gravy poured over it. Crude analysis shows both roast beef (risk ratio 4.1) and gravy (risk ratio 3.9) strongly associated with illness, nearly identical because they were served together. Stratifying by roast beef: among the 50 who ate beef, comparing the 48 who also had gravy to the 2 who did not shows almost no difference in attack rate (82% versus 80%), so gravy adds nothing once beef is held constant. Among the 10 who skipped beef, the few who still had gravy on a side dish show no elevated attack rate either. Beef, not gravy, is the vehicle.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe confounded-food scenarios because naming the wrong item from two nearly identical rows is the most common analytic error in a food-specific table, and a judge who asks "were any two of your top foods eaten together" is checking whether the student stratified before concluding. A project that reports a single vehicle from a crude table without checking co-service, or one that reports two implicated items without explaining why stratification did not resolve them to one, both signal the same gap: the table's raw numbers were read as final rather than as a starting hypothesis still needing lab and environmental confirmation.

questions.prompt: Two foods, meat and a sauce served over it, show nearly identical risk ratios in the food-specific table. What technique separates which one is the true vehicle?

options.text: Stratify by one food (e.g., meat eaten or not) and check whether the other food's association persists within each stratum
Discard both foods from the table since neither can be trusted
Assume the food with the alphabetically earlier name is the true vehicle
Report only the risk ratio for whichever food was eaten by more people

explanations.a: Correct: holding one exposure constant and checking whether the second exposure's association survives is exactly how stratified analysis separates a real vehicle from a confounded co-served item.
explanations.b: Discarding both throws away real evidence; stratification, not exclusion, is the standard way to resolve the ambiguity.
explanations.c: Food naming has no bearing on which is biologically or statistically the vehicle.
explanations.d: The number of eaters affects statistical stability but does not by itself distinguish a true vehicle from a confounded one.

questions.prompt: Why might a genuine outbreak implicate more than one food item even after stratification?

options.text: An infected food handler or a shared contaminated supplier can independently contaminate more than one dish
Stratified analysis always produces two implicated items regardless of the true cause
Food-specific tables cannot distinguish more than one item under any circumstances
Two implicated items always means the food-specific table was built incorrectly

explanations.a: Correct: real cross-contamination pathways, like one handler touching multiple dishes or one contaminated supplier feeding two menu items, can produce two genuinely independent associations.
explanations.b: Stratification is a tool for resolving confounding, not a procedure that mechanically outputs two results; a single true vehicle typically leaves only one association standing.
explanations.c: The table plus stratification can and does distinguish one item from a correlated one in the typical single-vehicle case.
explanations.d: A correctly built table can legitimately show two real, independently supported vehicles when the underlying contamination pathway supports it.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for resolving two foods with nearly identical risk ratios in a food-specific table.

items.text: Notice that two foods, usually served together, show nearly identical risk ratios
Stratify by one food and recompute the other food's association within each stratum
Identify which food's association persists and which disappears once the other is held constant
Pursue lab or environmental confirmation for the surviving candidate before naming it the vehicle

questions.explanation: The confound is first noticed as parallel rows, then resolved by stratification, then confirmed statistically, and only then handed off for lab and environmental verification.

questions.prompt: Match each situation to the correct next analytic step.

left.text: Two co-served foods show nearly identical risk ratios
After stratifying by food A, food B's association vanishes
After stratifying, both foods retain independent associations
A stratified analysis has identified one strong statistical vehicle

right.text: Suspect confounding through co-service; stratify to separate them
Food A is the true vehicle; food B was confounded
Consider that the outbreak may have more than one contaminated item
Seek laboratory and environmental confirmation before concluding

questions.explanation: Each stage of resolving a confounded food-specific table calls for a different next action, ending with confirmation beyond the statistical association alone.

lessons.label: John Snow and the Broad Street Pump (1854)

sections.heading: The spot map and the pump handle
sections.body: In August-September 1854, a violent cholera outbreak hit the Golden Square area of Soho, London, killing 616 people in about ten days. Physician John Snow, who had argued since his 1849 pamphlet On the Mode of Communication of Cholera that cholera spread through contaminated water rather than foul air (miasma theory, the dominant view), plotted each death as a bar on a street map centered on Broad Street. The bars piled into a dense cluster around a single public pump. Snow also chased anomalies that strengthened his case rather than weakening it: workhouse inmates and brewery workers near Broad Street, who drank from their own well or drank beer instead of pump water, were largely spared. On September 7 he presented the map to the St James parish Board of Guardians; they had the Broad Street pump handle removed on September 8. The outbreak was already subsiding by then, so the removal cannot be credited alone with ending it - but it became the enduring symbol of evidence-driven public health action.

sections.heading: The Grand Experiment
sections.body: Snow's stronger evidence came from a natural experiment assembled before Broad Street. Two water companies, Southwark & Vauxhall and Lambeth, piped drinking water to intermingled households across south London, sometimes on the same street. In 1852 Lambeth had relocated its intake upstream of London's sewage discharge into the Thames, while Southwark & Vauxhall's intake stayed downstream in sewage-contaminated water. Because residents had no say in which company's pipes reached their house, Snow treated the comparison as close to a randomized trial. Tabulating deaths per 10,000 houses during the 1853-54 epidemic, he found 315 cholera deaths per 10,000 Southwark & Vauxhall houses versus 37 per 10,000 Lambeth houses, published in the 1855 second edition of his pamphlet.

sections.heading: Whitehead and the source
sections.body: The piece Snow lacked was a specific origin point. Rev. Henry Whitehead, a local curate initially unconvinced by Snow's waterborne theory, ran his own house-to-house canvass and traced the outbreak's onset to 40 Broad Street, where five-month-old Frances Lewis fell ill with diarrhea on August 28 and died on September 2. Her mother had rinsed the soiled diapers into a leaking cesspool three feet from the pump's well, whose decayed brickwork let sewage seep directly into the water. Whitehead's fieldwork supplied the mechanism Snow's map could only imply, and together the two accounts became the founding narrative of field epidemiology.

lessons.workedExample: Snow's 1855 table for Southwark & Vauxhall versus Lambeth: among houses supplied by Southwark & Vauxhall, cholera killed at 315 per 10,000 houses; among Lambeth-supplied houses, only 37 per 10,000 died - roughly an eightfold difference. Because the two companies' pipes ran down the same streets to houses that differed only in which company's water reached the tap, the gap could not be explained by neighborhood, income, or air quality, the confounders miasma theory would invoke. The comparison behaved like a randomized trial: which company served a given rented house depended on pipe-laying decisions made years earlier, before Lambeth moved its intake in 1852, not on anything about the household itself.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows only the pump-handle story often assumes Snow proved his case by removing a handle and watching the outbreak stop. Pressed further, that claim weakens: deaths were already declining before September 8. The stronger evidence is the Southwark & Vauxhall/Lambeth comparison, a natural experiment where exposure was effectively unrelated to any confounder, letting Snow demonstrate causation from tabulated deaths per household years before germ theory existed. A judge assessing a student's own causal claim will ask whether the compared groups differ only in the exposure of interest - exactly the standard Snow's water-company comparison meets and a raw before/after pump story does not.

questions.prompt: What made the Southwark & Vauxhall vs. Lambeth water comparison closer to a natural experiment than the pump-handle removal?

options.text: Households had no control over which company's pipes served them, so exposure was effectively independent of other risk factors
Snow randomly assigned each household to a water company himself
It only counted brewery workers, who never got cholera
It measured air quality instead of water source

explanations.a: Correct: residents couldn't choose their water company, so the comparison groups differed in exposure but not in the confounders miasma theory pointed to, mimicking randomization.
explanations.b: Snow observed an existing arrangement of competing pipes; he didn't assign households to companies.
explanations.c: The brewery workers were a separate anomaly within the Broad Street cluster, unrelated to the water-company comparison.
explanations.d: The comparison measured cholera deaths per household by water company, not air quality.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the Broad Street investigation.

items.text: Frances Lewis's diarrhea begins at 40 Broad Street (Aug 28)
Frances Lewis dies (Sept 2)
Snow presents the spot map to the parish Board of Guardians (Sept 7)
The Broad Street pump handle is removed (Sept 8)

questions.explanation: The index case's illness and death preceded Snow's map presentation, which in turn preceded the handle's removal the next day.

questions.prompt: Match each person to their role in the investigation.

right.text: Mapped deaths and ran the Southwark & Vauxhall/Lambeth comparison
Traced the leaking cesspool to the outbreak's source
The five-month-old whose illness marked the outbreak's start

questions.explanation: Snow supplied the map and the water-company comparison; Whitehead's canvass found the mechanism; Frances Lewis was the index case.

questions.prompt: In Snow's 1853-54 tabulation, roughly what were the cholera deaths per 10,000 houses for Southwark & Vauxhall versus Lambeth customers?

options.text: 315 versus 37
37 versus 315
616 versus 29
100 versus 100

explanations.a: Correct: 315 per 10,000 for Southwark & Vauxhall, the company drawing sewage-contaminated water, versus 37 per 10,000 for Lambeth, which had moved its intake upstream.
explanations.b: This reverses the two companies; Southwark & Vauxhall, not Lambeth, had the higher rate.
explanations.c: 616 was the Golden Square death toll over ten days, not a per-10,000-houses rate, and 29 is unrelated to this comparison.
explanations.d: Equal rates would mean water source made no difference, which contradicts the whole point of the comparison.

lessons.label: William Budd, Snow, and the Priority Debate

sections.heading: A parallel discovery in Bristol
sections.body: John Snow was not alone in arguing cholera traveled through water. Physician William Budd, working independently in Bristol, published his own pamphlet, Malignant Cholera, about a month after Snow's 1849 On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, reaching a similar contagion-based conclusion from his own local outbreak investigation - and Budd himself explicitly credited Snow with priority. Budd's more lasting contribution was typhoid fever. Starting with a July 1839 outbreak he treated at North Tawton, Devon, that grew to more than 80 cases by November, Budd traced how the illness spread household to household and concluded the disease's cause multiplied inside a patient's intestines and was cast off in their excretions, a fecal-oral contagion model built decades before any organism was seen under a microscope. Building on that case and decades of subsequent Bristol case work, he argued typhoid spread through fecal-contaminated water and soiled linens, culminating in his 1873 monograph Typhoid Fever. Bristol's cholera deaths fell from roughly 2,000 in the 1849 epidemic to 29 by 1866, a decline Budd attributed to the disinfection and sanitary measures his fecal-oral model prescribed.

sections.heading: Miasma held the institutional high ground
sections.body: Despite two independent contagion-based cases, the General Board of Health rejected Snow's conclusions after its own 1854 investigation - even though one of its own investigators had observed comma-shaped 'vibriones' under the microscope in cholera patients' stool, evidence that supported a living waterborne agent but was dismissed rather than pursued. Miasma theory, that disease spread through foul air, remained the dominant medical orthodoxy for decades more. The organism itself was identified twice before anyone believed it mattered: Filippo Pacini described and named Vibrio cholerae from Florence autopsy specimens in 1854, the same year as Broad Street, but his paper went essentially unread; Robert Koch's independent 1883-84 isolation in Egypt and India is what the medical establishment credits with settling the question. Modern taxonomy has since restored Pacini's 1854 priority in the species name.

sections.heading: What the founding myth simplifies
sections.body: The popular telling makes Snow a lone genius who single-handedly proved waterborne transmission by pulling a pump handle. That compresses several separate contributions into one dramatic act: Budd's near-simultaneous, independently derived argument; Rev. Henry Whitehead's fieldwork that actually located the contamination source; and the decades-long gap before institutions accepted the theory at all. The myth also obscures how contested the science remained - officials who saw microscope evidence for a living waterborne agent still favored miasma, showing that data alone rarely defeats an entrenched theoretical framework without institutional buy-in.

lessons.workedExample: In 1849, Snow published On the Mode of Communication of Cholera arguing waterborne transmission; about a month later, working independently in Bristol, Budd published Malignant Cholera reaching a similar conclusion from his own outbreak. Both theories sat unaccepted for decades: the General Board of Health's 1854 report on Broad Street favored miasma despite an investigator's own microscope observations of vibrio-shaped organisms in patients' stool. It took Robert Koch's 1883-84 isolation of Vibrio cholerae in Egypt and India - three decades after Pacini's overlooked 1854 identification of the same organism in Florence - for germ theory to gain institutional acceptance. A century later, taxonomy now credits Pacini's 1854 name, Vibrio cholerae Pacini 1854, over Koch's.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this history because it separates 'who first observed the correct pattern' from 'who gets remembered as the founder' - a distinction that matters when a student claims a novel finding. Budd matched Snow's conclusion almost simultaneously and the Board of Health's own microscopist saw the organism, yet institutional acceptance took another three decades. A judge wants to know whether a student understands that good evidence does not automatically win against an entrenched framework, and can name who actually did what rather than reciting the simplified pump-handle legend as the whole story.

questions.prompt: What is the accurate relationship between Budd's and Snow's 1849 cholera pamphlets?

options.text: Budd published Malignant Cholera about a month after Snow's pamphlet, reaching a similar conclusion independently, and credited Snow with priority
Budd's typhoid monograph appeared years before Snow's cholera pamphlet
Snow and Budd co-authored a single 1849 pamphlet on cholera
Budd publicly disputed Snow's claim to priority for decades

explanations.a: Correct: Budd's pamphlet followed Snow's by about a month, was developed independently in Bristol, and Budd himself acknowledged Snow's priority.
explanations.b: Budd's typhoid monograph came in 1873, decades after both 1849 cholera pamphlets.
explanations.c: The two men worked independently and published separate pamphlets, not a joint one.
explanations.d: Budd credited rather than disputed Snow's priority on the waterborne-cholera claim.

questions.prompt: Order these milestones in the acceptance of waterborne cholera transmission.

items.text: Snow publishes On the Mode of Communication of Cholera (1849)
Budd publishes Malignant Cholera about a month later (1849)
Pacini identifies and names Vibrio cholerae in Florence (1854)
Koch independently isolates the organism in Egypt and India (1883-84)

questions.explanation: Snow's pamphlet came first, Budd's followed within a month, Pacini's identification came five years later, and Koch's isolation, credited with institutional acceptance, came three decades after that.
