questions.prompt: Match each figure or body to their role in this history.

right.text: Named Vibrio cholerae in 1854 from Florence specimens, but was ignored
Independently isolated the organism in 1883-84, credited with acceptance
Reached a parallel contagion theory in 1849, later built the fecal-oral case for typhoid
Rejected Snow's conclusion despite an investigator's own supporting microscope evidence

questions.explanation: Each figure or body played a distinct and separately documented role in the decades-long path to accepting waterborne cholera transmission.

questions.prompt: What evidence did the General Board of Health's own 1854 investigation have that supported Snow's theory, yet still rejected?

options.text: An investigator's microscope observation of comma-shaped 'vibriones' in cholera patients' stool
A signed statement from Budd endorsing Snow's conclusion
Chemical analysis proving the Broad Street well contained no sewage
A census showing brewery workers had higher cholera rates than pump-water drinkers

explanations.a: Correct: a Board investigator saw vibrio-shaped organisms in stool samples, a finding consistent with a living waterborne agent, but the Board still favored miasma explanations.
explanations.b: Budd's endorsement concerned Snow's priority, not a formal statement submitted to the Board of Health's investigation.
explanations.c: The well's contamination was demonstrated, not disproven; this option reverses the actual finding.
explanations.d: Brewery workers had lower cholera rates, since they drank beer instead of pump water, the opposite of this option's claim.

lessons.label: Typhoid Mary and the Healthy Carrier (1906)

sections.heading: Soper traces a common cook
sections.body: In August 1906, six of the eleven people in a rented summer household in Oyster Bay, Long Island, belonging to banker Charles Henry Warren, came down with typhoid fever within about three weeks of a new cook's arrival. Sanitary engineer George Soper was hired to find the source, and instead of testing the water or food directly, he investigated the cook's own work history. Tracing her employment back to 1900, Soper found that Mary Mallon had cooked for seven families and that typhoid had followed her from house to house: at least 22 people fell ill and one died in households she had worked in before Oyster Bay, even though Mallon herself had never once shown a symptom of the disease.

sections.heading: The asymptomatic carrier state
sections.body: Soper's hypothesis, that a perfectly healthy person could shed a pathogen and infect others without ever getting sick herself, was a hard sell to a medical establishment that equated infection with visible illness, and Mallon herself found it just as implausible. When Soper first confronted her directly at her Oyster Bay kitchen and asked for stool, urine, and blood samples, she refused and, by his own account, chased him off with a carving fork. When she continued to refuse testing, the New York City Health Department, with inspector S. Josephine Baker, physically apprehended her in 1907. Laboratory testing found persistent Salmonella typhi colonizing her gallbladder, which intermittently shed bacteria into her stool; because shedding was inconsistent rather than continuous, some households she cooked for stayed healthy while others fell ill. She was the first culture-confirmed healthy typhoid carrier identified in the United States, a case that forced public health surveillance to look past whoever felt sick.

sections.heading: Detention, relapse, and the liberty question
sections.body: The Health Department confined Mallon on North Brother Island in the East River from 1907 to 1910, then released her on condition that she never work as a cook again. Distrustful of a diagnosis she never felt the effects of, she broke that condition, cooked under the alias Mary Brown, and in 1915 seeded an outbreak at Sloane Maternity Hospital that infected 25 people and killed 2. The city then quarantined her permanently; she remained on North Brother Island until her death in 1938, with at least 51 cases and 3 deaths across her career attributed to a woman who was never sick a day herself. Her case is still the reference point for weighing an individual's liberty against a public-health authority's power to detain someone whose only offense is carrying a risk that symptoms can't reveal.

lessons.workedExample: Soper's case-finding worked backward from illness to a common exposure: he listed the seven households Mallon had cooked for since 1900, checked each for a typhoid cluster near her start date, and found 22 illnesses and 1 death scattered across them before Oyster Bay's 6 cases even happened. That pattern, an unexplained cluster following one person across unrelated households, is what flagged her as a carrier rather than a coincidence. Later lab work explained the inconsistency: because gallbladder shedding is intermittent, not every household she cooked for got sick, which is exactly why simple contact tracing without the lab confirmation could not have proven the case Soper's employment-history method did.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this case because it separates two questions students often conflate: whether someone is a transmission risk, and whether that risk justifies overriding their consent. Mallon never exhibited a symptom, never agreed she was contagious, and was detained for years on lab evidence she didn't accept. A judge wants a student proposing any surveillance or quarantine measure to state explicitly whose liberty is being traded for whose safety, and to justify that trade with evidence, not just intuition, exactly the standard Soper's carrier theory had to meet before New York City would act on it.

questions.prompt: How did George Soper identify Mary Mallon as the outbreak's source, rather than testing water or food at the Oyster Bay house?

options.text: He traced her employment history and found typhoid clusters following her across prior households
He tested her blood before she had ever worked as a cook
He relied on a report that she had once been visibly sick with typhoid
He surveyed the Oyster Bay water supply and found contamination

explanations.a: Correct: Soper's method was occupational contact tracing, checking each of Mallon's seven prior households for a typhoid cluster tied to her start date.
explanations.b: Soper investigated her employment history after the Oyster Bay outbreak, not before she began cooking.
explanations.c: Mallon never showed symptoms; her case is notable precisely because she was an asymptomatic carrier.
explanations.d: Soper's method centered on the cook's history, not a water-supply survey, which is why it succeeded where testing the house alone would not have.

questions.prompt: Order these events in Mary Mallon's case.

items.text: Soper traces prior households and finds 22 illnesses linked to her cooking
Health Department detains her on North Brother Island (1907)
She is released in 1910 on condition she not cook
She causes the Sloane Maternity Hospital outbreak under an alias (1915)

questions.explanation: Soper's tracing preceded her 1907 detention, which preceded her 1910 conditional release, which preceded her 1915 relapse under an alias.

questions.prompt: Match each person or place to their role in the case.

right.text: Sanitary engineer who traced the outbreak to Mallon's work history
NYC health inspector involved in Mallon's 1907 apprehension
Site of Mallon's detention, first temporary then permanent
Site of her 1915 outbreak under the alias Mary Brown

questions.explanation: Each figure or place played a distinct, separately documented part in the investigation, detention, and relapse.

questions.prompt: Why did some households Mallon cooked for stay healthy while others fell ill?

options.text: Her gallbladder shed Salmonella typhi intermittently, not continuously
She only became contagious after her 1907 detention
Typhoid only spreads through direct blood contact, which varied by household
She deliberately contaminated only some households
Households with more children were immune to typhoid

explanations.a: Correct: intermittent gallbladder shedding meant her stool carried the bacterium inconsistently, so exposure risk varied across households and over time.
explanations.b: She was shedding the bacterium before 1907 too, as shown by the 22 illnesses Soper traced to earlier households.
explanations.c: Typhoid spreads via the fecal-oral route, typically through contaminated food or water, not blood contact.
explanations.d: There's no evidence of deliberate contamination; the pattern is explained by intermittent, unintentional shedding.
explanations.e: Typhoid susceptibility isn't explained by household size or child count; the variability traces to her shedding pattern.

lessons.label: The 1976 Philadelphia Legionnaires' Outbreak

sections.heading: A convention, a hotel, and a mystery pneumonia
sections.body: On July 21-24, 1976, more than 2,000 American Legion members gathered at the Bellevue-Stratford Hotel in Philadelphia for the organization's annual convention, timed to the U.S. bicentennial. Within days, veterans began falling ill with a severe pneumonia; ultimately 182 people were diagnosed, 147 were hospitalized, and 29 died. Public alarm was intense partly because investigators could find nothing: standard bacteriology, virology, and toxicology testing of blood, tissue, and hotel samples for every known pathogen and poison came back negative, month after month, while the press speculated about sabotage and novel toxins.

sections.heading: A rickettsiologist's unconventional culture
sections.body: CDC epidemiologists, initially led by David Fraser, mapped cases and found the strongest statistical association with time spent in or near the Bellevue-Stratford's lobby, consistent with an airborne source rather than person-to-person spread: cases clustered by exposure to the hotel and its immediate sidewalk, not by later contact with other sick Legionnaires, and no secondary wave of illness followed among people who had only been exposed to patients rather than the hotel itself. Still, no organism turned up under standard lab methods. The breakthrough came from a scientist working outside the main effort: Joseph McDade, in CDC's Rickettsia branch, had set aside slides of lung tissue from guinea pigs that sickened after being injected with ground patient lung samples, a technique that worked in guinea pigs after mice had shown nothing. Returning to the unexplained slides after Christmas 1976, McDade applied a culturing method built for the fastidious rickettsia he normally studied, growing the organism in antibiotic-free fertilized eggs. It worked: a previously unknown bacterium emerged in pure culture. CDC announced the discovery, Legionella pneumophila, on January 18, 1977, six months after the convention.

sections.heading: Tracing it to the cooling tower
sections.body: Once the organism was identified, investigators confirmed it in samples from the hotel's rooftop cooling tower, whose evaporative water had aerosolized bacteria into an outdoor air intake feeding the lobby, exactly the exposure pattern the epidemiological mapping had already pointed to. The case established Legionella pneumophila as a genuinely new human pathogen, showed that building water systems, cooling towers, plumbing, decorative fountains, can incubate and aerosolize it, and became the template for pairing shoe-leather epidemiology's exposure mapping with a laboratory culture technique borrowed from an unrelated specialty. The disease's name comes directly from its first recognized victims, and the reputational damage was severe enough that negative publicity forced the Bellevue-Stratford itself to close in November 1976, reopening only after a $25 million renovation in 1979.

lessons.workedExample: Standard bacteriology missed Legionella because it doesn't grow on the routine culture media in common use in 1976. McDade's workaround: inoculate guinea pigs with ground patient lung tissue (they sickened; mice hadn't), harvest the guinea pigs' spleens and lungs, and grow whatever organism was inside using antibiotic-free fertilized chicken eggs, a technique standard for culturing rickettsia, the tick-borne pathogens McDade's branch actually studied, not for pneumonia bacteria. Applying an unrelated specialty's culture method to lung tissue that had sat unexplained since summer is what finally isolated Legionella pneumophila by December 1976, confirmed and announced on January 18, 1977.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this case because it shows two things students conflate: months of negative standard testing is not proof that no pathogen exists, and the epidemiological picture (lobby-time association, airborne pattern) can be solid well before the lab confirms a mechanism. McDade's fix came from applying a technique built for an entirely different pathogen family, not from a bigger version of the same failed tests. A judge wants a student whose own investigation hits a dead end to explain what alternative method or adjacent field's technique they'd try next, not just repeat the same negative test.

questions.prompt: Why did standard 1976 laboratory testing fail to identify the pathogen for months?

options.text: Legionella doesn't grow on the routine culture media used at the time
The outbreak was later found to be non-infectious food poisoning
CDC had not yet been established as an agency in 1976
Investigators never collected any patient tissue samples

explanations.a: Correct: Legionella is a fastidious organism that does not grow on the routine media 1976 labs used, which is why standard bacteriology repeatedly came back negative.
explanations.b: The cause was a novel bacterium, Legionella pneumophila, not food poisoning; toxicology testing had already ruled out poisons.
explanations.c: CDC was long-established by 1976 and led the investigation from the start.
explanations.d: Investigators did collect tissue samples; McDade's breakthrough came from lung tissue collected during the initial investigation.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the Legionnaires' investigation.

items.text: American Legion convention at the Bellevue-Stratford (July 1976)
Months of negative standard bacteriology and toxicology testing
McDade returns to unexplained guinea pig lung slides after Christmas 1976
CDC announces Legionella pneumophila (January 18, 1977)

questions.explanation: The convention triggered the outbreak, standard testing failed for months, McDade's post-holiday re-examination produced the isolate, and the announcement followed.

questions.prompt: Match each person, group, or place to their role in the investigation.

right.text: Isolated the organism using a rickettsia-culturing technique
Led the epidemiological mapping of cases to lobby exposure
Sickened after lung-tissue inoculation when mice had not
Aerosolized the bacteria into the hotel's air intake

questions.explanation: Each figure, animal model, or site played a distinct, separately documented part in identifying both the organism and its source.

questions.prompt: Of the 182 people diagnosed with Legionnaires' disease in the 1976 Philadelphia outbreak, how many died?

explanations.a: Correct: 29 of the 182 diagnosed cases died, a case-fatality rate of roughly 16 percent.
explanations.b: 147 is the number hospitalized, not the number who died.
explanations.c: 182 is the total number diagnosed, not the death toll.
explanations.d: 2,000 is roughly the number of convention attendees, not the number diagnosed or the death toll.

lessons.label: Minamata and Environmental Outbreak Epidemiology

sections.heading: A strange disease emerges
sections.body: On May 1, 1956, a physician at the Chisso Corporation's own factory hospital in Minamata, on Japan's Kyushu island, formally reported an unexplained cluster of neurological illness, staggering gait, slurred speech, numbness, tremor, narrowing vision, and in severe cases coma and death, concentrated among fishing families around Minamata Bay. Chisso, whose acetaldehyde plant had been discharging wastewater into the bay since 1932, was simultaneously the polluter, a major local employer, and the hospital that first documented the disease its own effluent caused, a conflict of interest that shaped years of denial. Cats in the fishing villages had shown similar staggering and convulsions even earlier, a warning sign dismissed at the time.

sections.heading: Finding methylmercury, and the fight to ignore it
sections.body: Kumamoto University researchers worked through competing hypotheses, manganese, thallium, an infectious agent, before identifying organic mercury compounds as the cause by 1959, tracing them to methylmercury generated as a byproduct of Chisso's acetaldehyde manufacturing process and discharged directly into the bay, where it bioaccumulated up the food chain into the fish and shellfish that were a dietary staple. Chisso disputed the university's finding, funded a rival researcher who blamed dumped wartime explosives instead, and kept discharging the same effluent for nearly a decade after the mechanism was known, until the Japanese government finally recognized methylmercury as the official cause and Chisso halted acetaldehyde production, both in 1968.

sections.heading: Congenital Minamata disease and a new kind of case
sections.body: Physicians eventually identified a distinct and more troubling pattern: infants born with severe cerebral-palsy-like symptoms to mothers who had eaten contaminated seafood during pregnancy but who themselves showed only mild or no symptoms. Methylmercury crosses the placenta readily, so a fetus could be devastated by an exposure the mother barely felt, reframing Minamata as a story about a vulnerable subpopulation invisible to symptom-based surveillance of the exposed population as a whole. By March 2001, Japan had officially certified 2,265 Minamata disease victims, of whom 1,784 had died, while more than 10,000 additional people had received compensation from Chisso without full certification, a gap that itself became a decades-long legal and political fight over how strict the causal criteria for a slow environmental exposure should be. The disease's name eventually became shorthand for industrial mercury poisoning worldwide: in 2013, over 140 countries adopted the Minamata Convention on Mercury, a treaty restricting mercury use and emissions, at a diplomatic conference held in nearby Kumamoto, with a symbolic signing ceremony held in Minamata itself.

lessons.workedExample: Methylmercury discharged from Chisso's plant entered Minamata Bay at low absolute concentration in the water itself, but bioaccumulated at each trophic step: plankton absorbed it from the water, small fish ate plankton and concentrated it further, and the larger predatory fish and shellfish that were the base of the local fishing diet could carry far higher mercury concentrations than the water they lived in. A family eating bay fish and shellfish daily could ingest a meaningful mercury dose from water that, tested directly, looked unremarkable, which is why the first real evidence was the pattern of illness by diet and geography, families clustered around the bay who ate fish daily, not a water sample.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe environmental cases like Minamata because chronic, low-dose exposure breaks the tools built for acute infectious outbreaks: there is no single case-defining lab test, latency runs years, and the polluter can fund its own counter-explanation, as Chisso did with the wartime-explosives theory. Congenital Minamata disease adds a harder point, that exposure timing (fetal versus adult) can matter more than symptom severity in the person who was actually exposed. A judge wants a student to recognize when their own project's exposure is chronic rather than acute, and to explain why that changes what counts as sufficient evidence of causation.

questions.prompt: What was the mechanism that carried methylmercury from Chisso's factory discharge into the bodies of Minamata Bay residents?

options.text: Bioaccumulation up the marine food chain, from bay water into fish and shellfish that were a dietary staple
Airborne dispersal of mercury vapor from factory smokestacks
Direct mercury injections given at the Chisso factory hospital
Contamination of a single shared drinking well, as at Broad Street

explanations.a: Correct: methylmercury discharged into the bay concentrated at each step of the marine food chain, reaching residents through the fish and shellfish that were a daily dietary staple.
explanations.b: The pathway was dietary, through contaminated seafood, not airborne mercury vapor from smokestacks.
explanations.c: There is no such mechanism; the hospital documented illness caused by dietary exposure, it did not cause the exposure.
explanations.d: Minamata's exposure was through food, not a shared well; that mechanism describes the 1854 Broad Street outbreak, not this one.

questions.prompt: Order these milestones in the Minamata disease investigation.

items.text: Chisso begins discharging acetaldehyde plant wastewater into Minamata Bay (1932)
A factory-hospital physician officially reports the unexplained neurological illness (May 1956)
Kumamoto University identifies methylmercury as the causal agent (by 1959)
Japanese government officially recognizes methylmercury as the cause; Chisso halts acetaldehyde production (1968)

questions.explanation: Discharge began decades before the disease was reported, the report preceded the university's causal identification, and official government recognition came nearly a decade after that.

questions.prompt: Match each entity or term to its role in the Minamata case.

right.text: The polluter, and also the hospital that first reported the disease
Identified methylmercury as the causal agent by 1959
Fetal cases more severe than the exposed mother's own symptoms
Year of official government recognition and the end of Chisso's discharge

questions.explanation: Each entity or date marks a distinct, separately documented step between the first discharge and official recognition of the cause.

questions.prompt: By March 2001, roughly how many officially certified Minamata disease victims had died?

explanations.a: Correct: of the 2,265 officially certified victims, 1,784 had died by March 2001.
explanations.b: 2,265 is the total number of officially certified victims, not the number who had died among them.
explanations.c: Over 10,000 is the number who received compensation from Chisso without full certification, a separate and larger figure.
explanations.d: 29 is the death toll from the unrelated 1976 Philadelphia Legionnaires' outbreak, not Minamata.

lessons.label: 1993 Jack in the Box and the E. coli O157:H7 Reckoning

sections.heading: The outbreak
sections.body: In January 1993, physician Phil Tarr reported a cluster of children with bloody diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome to the Washington State Department of Health; State Epidemiologist John Kobayashi's team traced the cases back to undercooked hamburger patties served at Jack in the Box restaurants. The outbreak ultimately sickened 732 people linked to 73 restaurants across Washington, California, Idaho, and Nevada, hospitalized 171, left 178 with permanent injury such as kidney and brain damage, and killed 4 children. The regulatory gap behind it was already documented before a single patty was served: effective May 1, 1992, Washington State had required restaurants to cook hamburgers to an internal temperature of 155 degrees Fahrenheit specifically to kill E. coli O157:H7, fifteen degrees above the older federal guideline of 140 degrees. Jack in the Box kept cooking to 140 degrees, later explaining that patties cooked longer became tough, a business judgment that left a Shiga-toxin-producing strain capable of causing severe illness from a very small dose alive inside the meat.

sections.heading: Confirming the link and racing the clock
sections.body: The multistate spread posed a new problem: how do investigators prove that E. coli isolates from sick children in four different states came from the same contaminated batch of meat, rather than four coincidental, unrelated infections? The outbreak became the first major real-world use of pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE), a DNA fingerprinting method that cuts bacterial DNA at specific sites with a restriction enzyme and compares the resulting fragment patterns. Matching band patterns across the four states confirmed a single common source and let investigators move from suspicion to proof fast enough to still matter for the recall, while separately, Washington's existing 155-degree rule became the case study cited nationwide for why a safety standard is worthless if it isn't enforced.

sections.heading: Rewriting food-safety policy
sections.body: The regulatory response went beyond one company's compliance: USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service formally declared E. coli O157:H7 an adulterant in raw ground beef, meaning any detectable presence made the product illegal to sell rather than merely undesirable, a major shift in enforcement power, and the 155-degree cooking standard Washington had already required spread into routine practice at chains nationwide. Three years later, in 1996, CDC and partner agencies built PFGE into permanent national infrastructure by launching PulseNet, a molecular subtyping network letting public health labs across the country compare bacterial DNA fingerprints in near real time, catching multistate foodborne clusters far faster than case counts and phone calls ever could, a direct descendant of the technique this outbreak forced into use.

lessons.workedExample: Before PFGE, if a child in California and a child in Idaho both grew E. coli O157:H7 from stool samples, investigators had no fast way to know whether it was the same strain from a shared source or two unrelated infections; they could compare symptom timing and food history, but not the bacteria's own genetic fingerprint. PFGE cut each isolate's DNA into fragments and ran them through a gel, producing a band pattern like a barcode. When 1993 investigators ran isolates from the four affected states, the patterns matched, confirming a single common source, the contaminated meat supply, fast enough to support a recall while cases were still emerging.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing a multistate or multi-site claim will ask how the student proved separate observations share one cause rather than assuming it because the timing lines up. This outbreak is the concrete answer: descriptive epidemiology, case reports, cooking-temperature history, generated the hypothesis, but a molecular fingerprinting method, not another round of interviews, is what converted 732 scattered illnesses in four states into a single provable event fast enough to still matter for the recall. A judge wants to hear that same distinction from a student: what actually confirmed a shared cause, not just consistent symptoms.

questions.prompt: What method first confirmed that E. coli O157:H7 cases across Washington, California, Idaho, and Nevada shared a single contaminated source?

options.text: Pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE) matching DNA band patterns across isolates
Matching blood types among the affected children
Comparing symptom-onset timing alone, without any lab testing
A shared restaurant loyalty-card database

explanations.a: Correct: PFGE fragmented each isolate's DNA and compared the resulting band patterns, confirming the isolates from all four states matched a single source.
explanations.b: Blood type has no bearing on identifying a shared bacterial source; the confirmation came from DNA fingerprinting.
explanations.c: Symptom timing alone generated the hypothesis but couldn't prove a shared source; PFGE supplied the proof.
explanations.d: No such database confirmed the outbreak; PFGE laboratory matching did.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the Jack in the Box investigation and its aftermath.

items.text: Phil Tarr reports the HUS cluster to Washington State (Jan 1993)
Kobayashi's team traces cases to undercooked hamburger patties
PFGE confirms a shared source across the four affected states
USDA/FSIS declares E. coli O157:H7 an adulterant in raw ground beef

questions.explanation: The initial clinical report preceded the epidemiological trace-back, which preceded the lab confirmation, which preceded the regulatory declaration.

questions.prompt: Match each person, method, or system to its role in this case.

right.text: Physician who reported the initial HUS cluster
Washington State Epidemiologist who traced the source
DNA fingerprinting method that confirmed the shared source
Permanent national network built on that method for ongoing surveillance

questions.explanation: Each person, method, or system played a distinct, separately documented part in detecting, confirming, and institutionalizing the response to this outbreak.

questions.prompt: How many US states had confirmed cases linked to the 1993 Jack in the Box outbreak?

explanations.a: Correct: confirmed cases spanned four states, Washington, California, Idaho, and Nevada.
explanations.b: The outbreak was multistate, not confined to a single state, which is precisely what made PFGE confirmation necessary.
explanations.c: 73 is the number of implicated Jack in the Box restaurants, not the number of states.
explanations.d: 178 is the number of victims left with permanent injury, not the number of states.

lessons.label: Live Debates in Field Epidemiology

sections.heading: Shoe-leather judgment vs. formal hypothesis testing
sections.body: Field epidemiology has always split investigators between two temperaments. Snow's Broad Street work is shoe-leather epidemiology: rapid, descriptive, pattern-first, acting on a spot map and interviews before any formal statistical test. The competing tradition insists on structured case-control or cohort designs, with calculated odds ratios and confidence intervals, before accepting a hypothesis, the approach that eventually confirmed E. coli O157:H7 in undercooked ground beef and, decades later, fenugreek sprouts as an outbreak source in Germany. The debate isn't settled: descriptive methods generate hypotheses fast enough to guide an active outbreak, but a compelling-looking pattern on a map can also mislead, which is why formal case-control studies remain the standard for confirming, not just suggesting, a cause.

sections.heading: How fast to act on incomplete evidence
sections.body: An investigator who waits for full statistical certainty lets an active outbreak keep infecting people; one who acts early on an incomplete hunch risks a costly, reputation-destroying mistake if the hypothesis turns out wrong. Snow's pump-handle removal is the celebrated case for acting early: the intervention cost almost nothing, the outbreak was already ebbing, and the underlying theory later proved correct, so a wrong call would have cost little either way. That calculus, sometimes called act-then-confirm, changes completely when the candidate intervention is expensive, hard to reverse, or when naming a suspected source publicly damages an identifiable party before the evidence is solid. A removed pump handle can be put back with no lasting harm if Snow had been wrong; a nationally broadcast accusation against a named farm or company cannot be un-said even once corrected, exactly the asymmetry German officials misjudged in 2011.

sections.heading: Source attribution can go wrong publicly
sections.body: In the 2011 German Escherichia coli O104:H4 outbreak, nearly 4,000 people fell ill and 53 died, with roughly 800 developing hemolytic uremic syndrome, an unusually severe complication rate. In late May, Hamburg health authorities publicly named Spanish cucumbers as the likely source based on preliminary trace-back interviews; Spanish growers reported losses near $200 million a week as Russia and other markets closed their borders to EU produce, before Germany's Robert Koch Institute and EU food safety agencies confirmed in late June that the true source was fenugreek sprouts grown from Egyptian seed at a single German producer, a completely different food category. Whole-genome sequencing of the outbreak strain helped confirm and characterize the source and is now displacing slower classical fingerprinting methods, like the PFGE that solved the Jack in the Box outbreak in 1993, as the default tool for real-time attribution, precisely because a wrong public accusation has its own real cost.

lessons.workedExample: German officials announced Spanish cucumbers as a likely source around late May 2011, based on early interviews. Spanish growers reported losses near $200 million a week as EU nations pulled Spanish produce from shelves and Russia banned all EU fresh-produce imports. By late June, formal case-control studies plus trace-back of a specific fenugreek seed shipment imported from Egypt in 2009 pointed instead to sprouts grown by one German producer, confirmed by the Robert Koch Institute and EU agencies. The roughly month-long gap between the premature public accusation and the confirmed source is the visible cost of naming a suspected source before a formal case-control result, rather than after.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this debate because a science-fair project that names a suspected cause faces the same speed-versus-certainty trade-off the Hamburg health authorities faced: naming a source before a formal case-control study confirms it can look decisive but cause real, sometimes irreversible harm if wrong. A judge wants to know whether a student's causal claim rests on a plausible early correlation or on the harder standard, a controlled comparison, or now a molecular fingerprint, that actually separates the true source from a coincidental one. Naming a suspect is cheap; being right about which one is not.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many people died in the 2011 German E. coli O104:H4 outbreak?

explanations.a: Correct: the 2011 German outbreak killed roughly 53 people among nearly 4,000 cases.
explanations.b: 29 was the death toll of the unrelated 1976 Philadelphia Legionnaires' outbreak.
explanations.c: 4 was the death toll of the unrelated 1993 Jack in the Box E. coli outbreak.
explanations.d: 616 was the ten-day Golden Square cholera death toll in the unrelated 1854 Broad Street outbreak.

Spanish growers report roughly $200 million a week in losses
Robert Koch Institute and EU agencies confirm fenugreek sprouts as the true source (late June 2011)
Whole-genome sequencing helps confirm and further characterize the outbreak strain

questions.explanation: The premature cucumber accusation came first, its economic fallout followed quickly, the sprout source was confirmed weeks later, and genomic characterization of the strain continued afterward.

Structured design using calculated odds ratios to confirm a cause

questions.prompt: Which severe complication developed in roughly 800 of the 2011 German outbreak's cases?

Typhoid fever

explanations.a: Correct: roughly 800 of the outbreak's cases developed hemolytic uremic syndrome, an unusually high complication rate that made this outbreak notable.
explanations.b: Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella typhi, unrelated to this Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli outbreak.

explanations.d: Congenital Minamata disease results from prenatal methylmercury exposure, unrelated to this foodborne E. coli outbreak.

units.label: Advanced Field Methods: Molecular and Statistical Detection

lessons.label: The Laboratory Arm: Confirming Agent and Vehicle

sections.heading: Two specimen streams, one investigation
sections.body: A field investigation runs two parallel tracks that must eventually meet: the epidemiologic track, which uses case interviews and a case-control or cohort study to statistically implicate a food or exposure, and the laboratory track, which tries to isolate the same pathogen from patients AND from the suspected vehicle. Clinical specimens (usually stool for enteric pathogens, blood for invasive disease like Listeria) go to culture, PCR, or increasingly culture-independent diagnostic tests (CIDTs) — typically PCR-based panels that confirm which pathogen is present directly from the specimen without ever growing a live isolate. CIDTs are fast and sensitive for diagnosis, but strain-level subtyping (PFGE or whole-genome sequencing) requires an actual isolate, so a CIDT-positive specimen usually triggers a lab 'reflex culture' attempt before that case can be molecularly linked to others. Food, water, or environmental swabs go to a food-testing lab for enrichment culture. An outbreak is not truly confirmed until the same organism, at the strain level, shows up on both sides.

sections.heading: Timing determines whether the organism is still there
sections.body: Shedding windows are short and pathogen-specific: Salmonella is typically detectable in stool for one to four weeks after symptom onset but peaks early, norovirus sheds heavily for about a week then declines but can be detected by PCR for weeks, and Shiga toxin-producing E. coli sheds for roughly one to three weeks. Interview-to-specimen lag matters enormously — a patient interviewed on day 10 of a 21-day illness window may already be past peak shedding, producing a false negative that has nothing to do with whether they were truly infected. Specimens also need a validated cold chain (typically 2-8°C, sometimes frozen for later strain typing) because temperature abuse in transit degrades organisms before the lab ever plates them.

sections.heading: Why a negative food culture never clears a vehicle
sections.body: By the time an outbreak is recognized — often two to four weeks after the last exposure, given incubation periods plus diagnosis and reporting lag — the implicated lot of food is frequently gone: eaten, discarded, or past its shelf life. Even food a lab can test may culture negative because contamination is patchy (a single case of romaine can have one contaminated head among dozens), pathogen loads are often below the culture's limit of detection, or the specific lot sampled was not the contaminated one even though the product category was. This is why the CDC and FDA explicitly treat epidemiologic and laboratory evidence as complementary, not substitutable: the 2018 romaine lettuce E. coli O157:H7 outbreak was declared over and the vehicle confirmed from epidemiologic linkage and environmental water testing well before any retail lettuce sample cultured positive.

lessons.workedExample: In a suspected Salmonella outbreak linked to a catered event, 40 of 120 attendees develop diarrhea. Stool specimens collected from 15 cases within 5 days of onset yield Salmonella Enteritidis in 12 (80% positive). Of 5 late-interviewed cases (specimen collected 12+ days after onset), only 1 cultures positive. Meanwhile, the leftover chicken salad was discarded the night of the event; a swab of the prep table cultures negative for Salmonella. Investigators still name chicken salad as the vehicle because the case-control study shows a strong dose-response with servings eaten, and 12 of the 13 confirmed human isolates share an indistinguishable molecular fingerprint (the 13th, from a late-collected specimen, was not typed in time to include in the comparison) — the environmental swab's negative result reflects surface cleaning and time elapsed, not innocence of the food.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student conflates 'no positive food sample' with 'source unproven.' The correct answer is that vehicle attribution rests on the epidemiologic association (usually a case-control odds ratio) plus, when available, laboratory confirmation linking human and source isolates — and that a negative food culture is expected, not exculpatory, given specimen timing, patchy contamination, and detection limits. A project that treats a negative environmental sample as disproving its own hypothesis, or that never explains why specimens were collected when they were, reads as lab-naive.

questions.prompt: A suspected food vehicle in an outbreak culture-tests negative. What is the most defensible conclusion?

options.text: The food is definitively cleared as the vehicle
The food may still be the vehicle; a negative culture is expected given timing, patchy contamination, and detection limits
The outbreak must have a different, unidentified cause
The epidemiologic study should be discarded since lab evidence disagrees

explanations.a: A single negative culture does not clear a vehicle; by the time testing occurs the contaminated lot is often gone or the pathogen has fallen below detectable levels.
explanations.b: Correct: negative food cultures are common and expected because of specimen timing lag, patchy/uneven contamination, and limits of detection, not evidence of innocence.
explanations.c: A negative food culture alone does not point to a different cause; the epidemiologic association may still strongly implicate this food.
explanations.d: Epidemiologic and laboratory evidence are complementary; a negative lab result does not override a statistically strong case-control finding.

questions.prompt: Order the events from exposure to a food-culture result during a typical outbreak investigation.

items.text: Patient consumes contaminated food
Symptom onset after the incubation period
Case reported and interviewed, implicated food identified
Investigators attempt to locate and culture a sample of that food

questions.explanation: Exposure precedes illness by the incubation period, illness precedes reporting and interview, and only after a food is implicated do investigators attempt to sample it — by which point it is frequently gone.

questions.prompt: Match each specimen type to its typical collection target.

right.text: Stool culture
Blood culture
Environmental swab

questions.explanation: Enteric pathogens are recovered from stool, invasive pathogens like Listeria are recovered from blood (or CSF), and suspected environmental sources are sampled by swab.

lessons.label: Molecular Subtyping: From Serotype to Fingerprint

sections.heading: Same species name, different bug
sections.body: 'Salmonella' is not one organism for surveillance purposes — it is a genus with over 2,500 serotypes, distinguished historically by the Kauffmann-White scheme, which classifies strains by their surface O antigen and flagellar H antigen combinations. Two patients both diagnosed with 'Salmonella' could be infected with Enteritidis and Typhimurium respectively — as unrelated as two different diseases sharing a genus name. Serotyping was the first layer of resolution public health labs used to decide whether cases might belong to the same outbreak, and it remains useful as a fast first pass, but it is far too coarse on its own: serotype Enteritidis alone causes well over ten thousand sporadic, unrelated U.S. infections a year, so matching serotype cannot distinguish a true cluster from background noise.

sections.heading: PFGE: cutting the genome into a barcode
sections.body: Pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE), adopted by public health labs starting in the 1990s, resolves this by cutting a bacterium's whole genome with a rare-cutting restriction enzyme (for example XbaI for Salmonella and E. coli) into a set of large DNA fragments, then separating those fragments by size using an electric field that periodically switches direction — ordinary electrophoresis cannot resolve fragments this large, hence the 'pulsed field.' The result is a pattern of bands, a DNA fingerprint, unique to closely related strains. Isolates with indistinguishable PFGE patterns are far more likely to share a common source than isolates that merely share a serotype, because the pattern reflects thousands of base pairs of real genomic similarity, not just two surface antigens. PulseNet, the national laboratory network that standardizes this work, assigns each distinct pattern a code (organism prefix, enzyme, and a sequential pattern number, as in JEGX01.0032) so labs anywhere in the country can compare results on a shared naming system; 'indistinguishable' has a strict technical meaning here — the two patterns show the same number of bands at the same positions, not merely a similar overall look.

sections.heading: Closing the loop: human isolate to food isolate
sections.body: The decisive move in a cluster investigation is running PFGE (or its modern successor, whole-genome sequencing) on an isolate recovered from the suspected food or environmental sample and comparing its fingerprint directly to the human case isolates. An indistinguishable match converts a plausible epidemiologic hypothesis into strong microbiological evidence: it means the strain circulating in patients and the strain found in the product are, as far as this method can tell, the same clone. This match does not by itself prove that food caused the illness — cross-contamination or coincidence remain formally possible — but combined with a case-control association it is the strongest single piece of evidence an outbreak investigation can produce.

lessons.workedExample: An investigation identifies 30 Salmonella Enteritidis cases across four states. Serotyping alone cannot separate them from the roughly 15,000 sporadic Enteritidis infections reported nationally that year. PFGE on all 30 isolates shows 22 share an indistinguishable pattern (call it pattern JEGX01.0032); the other 8 have related but distinguishable patterns and are dropped from the cluster. Investigators then culture Salmonella from an unopened package of the suspected product and find it also matches JEGX01.0032. That single matching isolate — one food sample out of dozens tested — is what converts 'egg-associated illness cluster' into a confirmed source.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student understands that subtyping resolution is what defines a 'cluster' in the first place — without it, any two Salmonella cases in the same week could be wrongly lumped together, or a real cluster could be missed by relying on serotype alone. A project that says 'the strains matched' without specifying which method (serotype vs. PFGE vs. sequence-level) is not making a falsifiable claim; a project that explains why serotype match is necessary but not sufficient shows it understands how outbreak clusters are actually defined in practice.

questions.prompt: Why is matching Salmonella serotype alone insufficient to declare two cases part of the same outbreak?

options.text: Serotyping is not a real laboratory method
A single serotype like Enteritidis includes thousands of unrelated sporadic infections nationally, so serotype match does not imply a shared source
Serotype cannot be determined from human specimens
Serotyping requires whole-genome sequencing equipment most labs lack

explanations.a: Serotyping (the Kauffmann-White scheme, based on O and H antigens) is a real and long-used method; the issue is its resolution, not its validity.
explanations.b: Correct: with well over ten thousand sporadic Enteritidis cases nationally, serotype match alone cannot distinguish a true point-source cluster from coincidental background cases.
explanations.c: Serotyping is routinely performed on human clinical isolates; that is not the limitation.
explanations.d: Serotyping predates and does not require sequencing; it is based on antigen typing, which is the opposite of the problem described.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in the PFGE process, from raw bacterial isolate to comparable fingerprint.

items.text: Grow pure bacterial isolate and extract whole-genome DNA
Digest the DNA with a rare-cutting restriction enzyme
Separate fragments using a periodically switching electric field
Compare the resulting band pattern to other isolates' patterns

questions.explanation: PFGE requires isolating DNA first, cutting it into large fragments with a restriction enzyme, then using the pulsed-field technique (not standard electrophoresis) to resolve those large fragments by size before patterns can be compared.

questions.prompt: Match each subtyping method to what it primarily distinguishes.

left.text: Matching a human isolate to a food isolate

right.text: Broad classification by surface O and flagellar H antigens
A genome-wide restriction fragment fingerprint
Direct microbiological evidence linking a case to a specific source

questions.explanation: Serotyping is the coarsest layer, PFGE gives a finer genome-based fingerprint used to define a cluster, and matching a human isolate to a food isolate is the strongest source-confirming evidence.

lessons.label: PulseNet and Whole-Genome Sequencing

sections.heading: A network, not just a technique
sections.body: PulseNet is the innovation that made molecular subtyping useful at national scale: it is a CDC-coordinated network, launched in 1996 with the Association of Public Health Laboratories and founding state labs in Massachusetts, Minnesota, Texas, and Washington, that standardizes subtyping protocols and pools the resulting fingerprints into a shared national database. Before PulseNet, a PFGE pattern generated in one state lab was not directly comparable to a pattern from another state's lab, because equipment, enzymes, and gel-running conditions varied. PulseNet fixed this by requiring every participating lab to run the identical standardized protocol, so a pattern uploaded from Oregon can be matched against one uploaded from Florida the same week — which is precisely how multistate clusters, invisible to any single state working alone, get detected.

sections.heading: Why PFGE eventually ran out of resolution
sections.body: PFGE was a major upgrade over serotyping, but it has a real ceiling: it only reads differences in fragment size at a handful of large restriction sites, so genetically distinct strains can occasionally produce indistinguishable band patterns, and closely related strains can occasionally look different due to a single mutation at a cut site. Listeria monocytogenes exposed this ceiling starkly, since it has comparatively low genetic diversity, making PFGE patterns cluster together even across epidemiologically unrelated strains. In September 2013, CDC and its state and FDA partners launched a pilot in which every clinical Listeria isolate nationally was whole-genome sequenced, with food and environmental isolates sequenced by state labs and deposited into GenomeTrakr, the FDA's public sequence database built for this purpose.

sections.heading: From band patterns to SNP and allele distances
sections.body: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) reads essentially the entire bacterial genome rather than a handful of fragment sizes, so comparisons are made by counting actual differences between genomes: single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) distance, or allele-based schemes like core-genome multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST), which count differing gene alleles across a defined set of core genes. A cluster is now typically defined as isolates within some small SNP or allele distance of each other — often on the order of a handful of differences — rather than a visually 'indistinguishable' band pattern, giving investigators a quantitative, reproducible threshold instead of a qualitative match. Following the Listeria pilot's success, PulseNet transitioned its entire network from PFGE to WGS as the primary subtyping method by 2019, and GenomeTrakr's growing library of food and environmental sequences lets a new human case be compared not just against other patients but directly against thousands of previously sequenced product and facility isolates.

lessons.workedExample: During the 2013 Listeria pilot, CDC sequences a clinical isolate from a patient with listeriosis. Its genome differs from a food isolate sequenced two years earlier from a stone-fruit processing facility, uploaded to GenomeTrakr, by only 4 SNPs across the whole genome — well within the small-distance threshold used to call a match. That close genomic link, impossible to make with PFGE alone since Listeria's low diversity often produced identical-looking PFGE patterns across unrelated strains, lets investigators connect the current human case to a specific, previously characterized environmental source years after the original sample was taken.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can explain WHY WGS replaced PFGE, not just that it did — the real driver was PFGE's resolution ceiling being exposed by low-diversity organisms like Listeria, producing false matches and false non-matches. A project that says 'we used genetic fingerprinting' without naming SNP or allele distance, or without knowing that PulseNet is a coordinating network rather than a lab technique, has not engaged with how modern cluster detection actually draws its boundary between 'same outbreak' and 'coincidence.'

questions.prompt: Why did the Listeria WGS pilot specifically expose a weakness of PFGE?

options.text: Listeria cannot be cultured, so PFGE was never possible for it
Listeria's comparatively low genetic diversity meant PFGE often produced indistinguishable patterns even for epidemiologically unrelated strains
PFGE requires a live vaccine strain that Listeria lacks
Listeria genomes are too large for any restriction enzyme to cut

explanations.a: Listeria monocytogenes is routinely cultured from clinical, food, and environmental specimens; culturability was not the issue.
explanations.b: Correct: Listeria's low genetic diversity meant PFGE's limited resolution often could not distinguish unrelated strains, motivating the shift to whole-genome comparison.
explanations.c: PFGE is a fingerprinting method applied to bacterial DNA directly; it has nothing to do with vaccine strains.
explanations.d: Restriction enzymes cut bacterial genomes of all common foodborne pathogens, including Listeria; genome size was not the limiting factor.

questions.prompt: Order these PulseNet/WGS milestones chronologically.

items.text: PulseNet launched by CDC and partner state labs
CDC and partners begin the Listeria whole-genome sequencing pilot, uploading isolates to GenomeTrakr
PulseNet completes its network-wide transition from PFGE to WGS as the primary subtyping method

questions.explanation: PulseNet began in 1996 using PFGE; the Listeria WGS pilot started in September 2013; the full network transition to WGS followed by 2019.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it represents.

right.text: CDC-coordinated national network standardizing subtyping across labs
FDA's database of sequenced food and environmental pathogen isolates
Quantitative measure used to define a WGS-based cluster

questions.explanation: PulseNet is the coordinating network, GenomeTrakr is the FDA sequence database populated by food and environmental isolates, and SNP or allele distance is the quantitative threshold that replaced visual PFGE pattern matching.

lessons.label: Detecting Clusters in Surveillance Data

sections.heading: Automating the question 'is this normal?'
sections.body: Before molecular matching can even begin, someone has to notice that an unusual number of cases is happening. Historically that was an alert clinician or lab noticing a pattern; today it is increasingly a statistical algorithm running continuously over case report time series, because human pattern recognition does not scale to the volume of routine surveillance data and is bad at detecting subtle, slow-building signals. Aberration detection algorithms compare the observed count of cases (or syndrome reports, or lab test orders) in a recent time window against a baseline expectation built from historical data, and flag the window when the observed count exceeds that expectation by more than chance would explain.

sections.heading: CUSUM and the EARS moving-average family
sections.body: The cumulative sum (CUSUM) method, originally developed for industrial quality control by E.S. Page in the 1950s, sums the deviations of each day's count from the expected baseline and flags an alert when that running sum crosses a threshold — its strength is catching a small, sustained shift that no single day's count would trigger on its own. CDC's Early Aberration Reporting System (EARS) adapts this logic for syndromic surveillance with a family of algorithms (commonly labeled C1, C2, and C3) that compare a recent count to a short moving average and standard deviation of a trailing baseline period, flagging when the recent count is several standard deviations above that rolling average. EARS was built to work with limited historical data, since many syndromic feeds have only weeks of history rather than years, unlike more data-hungry regression-based methods.

sections.heading: Adding space: Kulldorff's scan statistic
sections.body: Time series methods answer 'is there too much disease right now,' but they say nothing about where. Martin Kulldorff's spatial scan statistic, published in 1997, answers both at once by scanning a moving window — implemented in his SaTScan software as a cylinder whose circular base sweeps across geography and whose height sweeps across time — across many candidate space-time windows, computing a likelihood ratio comparing observed to expected cases inside versus outside each window, and identifying the most statistically unlikely cluster while correcting for the many comparisons being tested. This is what lets an investigator ask not just 'are cases elevated this week' but 'are cases elevated in this particular set of neighboring zip codes this week,' which is exactly the resolution needed to catch a localized outbreak sitting inside noisy statewide numbers.

sections.heading: The sensitivity-versus-noise dial
sections.body: Every one of these methods has a tunable alarm threshold, and every choice trades sensitivity for false alarms: a loose threshold catches real outbreaks earlier but buries investigators in false signals they must chase down and dismiss, while a tight threshold reduces false alarms at the cost of missing small or slow-building clusters, or catching them only after belated confirmation from other sources. Public health agencies tune these thresholds empirically against known past outbreaks and their operational capacity to investigate alerts, which is why the same algorithm can run with different sensitivity settings in a jurisdiction with ample epidemiologist staffing versus one running lean.

lessons.workedExample: A state health department's EARS C2 algorithm monitors daily emergency-department visits for gastrointestinal illness. The trailing 7-day baseline average is 40 visits with a standard deviation of 6. On a given day, 61 visits are logged — roughly 3.5 standard deviations above baseline — triggering an alert. Simultaneously, SaTScan run weekly on the same case-level data with home addresses flags a cylindrical cluster covering three adjacent zip codes and a 4-day window, with an observed-to-expected case ratio of 2.8 and a statistically significant p-value after adjusting for the many windows scanned. The time-series alert said 'something is happening now'; the spatial scan said 'and it is concentrated here' — together they point investigators toward a specific neighborhood rather than an entire county.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student understands that outbreak detection is itself a statistical decision problem with a real cost function, not just 'noticing.' The tell of depth is naming a specific method (CUSUM's cumulative deviation, EARS's moving-average threshold, or Kulldorff's likelihood-ratio scan) and explaining the sensitivity-versus-false-alarm trade-off in that method's own terms, rather than asserting an algorithm 'detects outbreaks' as if detection threshold were not a deliberate, tunable choice with real operational cost on both sides.

questions.prompt: What advantage does Kulldorff's spatial scan statistic add beyond a pure time-series method like CUSUM?

options.text: It eliminates the need for a baseline expectation
It identifies where a cluster is concentrated geographically, not just whether counts are elevated overall
It requires no statistical threshold or significance testing
It only works for exactly one disease, unlike CUSUM

explanations.a: The scan statistic still compares observed to expected counts within a window; it does not remove the need for a baseline.
explanations.b: Correct: by scanning a moving space-time window (a cylinder in SaTScan), it locates which geographic area and time window is statistically unlikely, not just whether totals are elevated.
explanations.c: SaTScan explicitly uses a likelihood ratio test and corrects for the many windows scanned; it is built on significance testing.
explanations.d: Neither method is disease-specific; both are general statistical approaches applied to whatever case time series or location data is fed in.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of running a spatial scan statistic like SaTScan on outbreak surveillance data.

items.text: Define candidate space-time windows (varying location and size) to scan across the study area
Compute observed vs. expected case counts inside and outside each window
Calculate a likelihood ratio for each candidate window
Identify the most statistically unlikely cluster, correcting for the number of windows tested

questions.explanation: The scan statistic sweeps many candidate windows, compares observed to expected counts in each, ranks them by likelihood ratio, and then corrects for multiple testing to report the single most significant cluster.

questions.prompt: Match each surveillance method to its core mechanism.

right.text: Sums daily deviations from baseline, alerting when the running total crosses a threshold
Compares recent counts to a short trailing moving average and standard deviation
Scans a moving space-time cylinder, comparing observed to expected counts per window

questions.explanation: CUSUM tracks cumulative deviation over time, EARS uses a short rolling baseline suited to limited historical data, and SaTScan adds the spatial dimension via a scanning cylinder.

lessons.label: Trace-Back and the Supply Chain

sections.heading: Following the food backward through the chain
sections.body: Once epidemiologic and laboratory evidence converge on a food item, a separate investigative process — traceback — starts at the point of purchase or consumption and works backward through each link of the supply chain: retailer, distributor, processor, and ultimately grower or producer. Each link is documented by records the food industry is required to keep, such as invoices, bills of lading, and lot or batch codes, so investigators can reconstruct exactly which shipments moved where and when. This is slow, labor-intensive work, because supply chains for a single product often braid together multiple growers, packers, and distribution centers before reaching a store shelf, and records are not always complete, standardized, or quickly accessible across every business in the chain.

sections.heading: Point of convergence: many patients, one shared point upstream
sections.body: Traceback becomes far more powerful when investigators can trace multiple independent cases' food purchases back simultaneously and look for the point where all of their separate supply chains converge on a common upstream source — a single grower, packing facility, or even a specific field. This point-of-convergence approach does not require every case to have bought from the same store; it requires enough independent chains, traced back far enough, to overlap at one node. It was central to identifying the source of the 2018 E. coli O157:H7 outbreak linked to romaine lettuce, where traceback and environmental assessment converged on irrigation canal water near Yuma, Arizona, contaminated near a large cattle feedlot operation, even though the sick people across many states had bought lettuce from many different stores and brands.

sections.heading: The regulatory handoff: recall and jurisdiction
sections.body: Once a source is identified with enough confidence, the investigation shifts from epidemiology to regulatory action, and jurisdiction depends on the food category: the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service (USDA-FSIS) regulates meat, poultry, and processed egg products, while the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulates essentially everything else, including produce, seafood, and packaged foods. A recall can be voluntary, where the company withdraws product after being informed of the findings, or in narrower circumstances the agency can mandate one. Because recalls are disruptive and costly and rest on evidence that may still be probabilistic rather than absolute, agencies weigh the strength of traceback and lab evidence carefully before initiating one, which is part of why some outbreaks end with public advice to avoid an entire product category rather than a narrow, product-specific recall.

lessons.workedExample: Twenty E. coli cases across eight states report eating bagged romaine salad in the two weeks before illness, but each bought a different brand from a different store. Investigators collect purchase records and lot codes from all 20 patients and trace each bag backward through its distributor to its processing facility, then to the field where it was harvested. Despite the different retail brands, all 20 traces converge on farms in a single growing region during a narrow harvest window. Environmental assessment of that region finds E. coli-contaminated irrigation water in a canal near a cattle operation upstream of several of the implicated fields — matching the human outbreak strain — closing the loop from plate back to field.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student understands that traceback is a converging, not a single-chain, process — the power comes from multiple independent cases pointing to the same upstream node, not from following one patient's grocery receipt. They also check whether a student knows that regulatory jurisdiction is split (USDA-FSIS for meat, poultry, and eggs; FDA for nearly everything else) and that a recall is a distinct, costly, and evidence-gated action taken only after the epidemiologic, laboratory, and traceback lines converge — not an automatic response to any suspected link.

questions.prompt: Why is 'point of convergence' analysis more powerful than tracing a single patient's purchase back one step?

options.text: It only requires records from a single retailer
It finds the common upstream node where many independent patients' separate supply chains overlap, even if their retail purchases differed
It replaces the need for any laboratory confirmation
It is faster because it skips distributor and processor records

explanations.a: Convergence analysis typically spans many different retailers; its value comes from tracing several independent chains, not limiting to one.
explanations.b: Correct: by tracing many independent patients' purchases backward and looking for where those separate chains overlap, investigators can identify a shared upstream source even without a single common retail purchase.
explanations.c: Traceback is complementary to, not a replacement for, laboratory confirmation; both lines of evidence are used together.
explanations.d: Convergence analysis still requires working through distributor and processor records for each chain; it does not skip steps, it just compares many full chains.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a traceback investigation from a confirmed illness to a regulatory recall.

items.text: Collect purchase records and lot codes from multiple independent cases
Trace each case's supply chain backward through retailer, distributor, and processor
Identify the point of convergence where chains overlap on a common upstream source
Regulatory agency (FDA or USDA-FSIS) acts on the finding, potentially issuing a recall

questions.explanation: Traceback starts with gathering purchase and lot records from cases, follows each chain backward, looks for convergence on a shared source, and only then moves to regulatory action.

questions.prompt: Match each food category to its regulating U.S. agency.

left.text: Meat, poultry, and processed egg products
Produce, seafood, and most packaged foods

right.text: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS)
Food and Drug Administration (FDA)

questions.explanation: USDA-FSIS has jurisdiction over meat, poultry, and processed egg products; the FDA regulates essentially all other foods, including produce and seafood.

lessons.label: Source Attribution and Environmental Assessment

sections.heading: From one outbreak to the whole burden of disease
sections.body: A single outbreak investigation answers 'what caused these particular cases,' but public health agencies also need a broader answer: of all the Salmonella or E. coli illness in the country every year, most of which is sporadic and never tied to a named outbreak, what share comes from poultry versus produce versus dairy? This is the source attribution question, and the Interagency Food Safety Analytics Collaboration (IFSAC) — formed in 2011 by CDC, FDA, and USDA-FSIS specifically to harmonize this work across agencies — tackles it primarily by pooling data from over a thousand solved outbreaks and using the food vehicles identified in those outbreaks as a proxy for what is driving illness generally, publishing annual attribution percentages by food category for Salmonella, E. coli O157, Listeria monocytogenes, and Campylobacter.

sections.heading: Expert elicitation as a complementary method
sections.body: Outbreak-based attribution has a structural weakness: solved, multi-case outbreaks are not a random sample of all illness, since foods more likely to cause large recognizable clusters (like leafy greens sold nationally) are overrepresented relative to foods that mostly cause sporadic, hard-to-link cases. Hoffmann and colleagues' 2007 study addressed this gap with expert elicitation, formally surveying food safety experts to estimate, pathogen by pathogen, what share of illness likely traces to each food category, then combining those judgments statistically. Expert elicitation captures knowledge outbreak data misses but trades a different kind of uncertainty for it — it depends on expert judgment rather than case counts, so IFSAC's modern approach treats outbreak-based and elicitation-based estimates as complementary cross-checks rather than substitutes for each other.

sections.heading: Environmental assessment: how, not just where
sections.body: Attribution answers which food category causes illness in aggregate; environmental health assessment answers how contamination happened at one specific implicated facility once an outbreak has already pointed there. Investigators walk the facility — a farm, packing house, or processing plant — examining water sources, sanitation practices, employee illness policies, wildlife intrusion, and equipment cleaning logs, often collecting environmental swabs to culture alongside the review. This is where the 2018 romaine investigation's canal water finding came from: an on-site environmental assessment following traceback, not the traceback itself. The output is usually a set of contributing factors rather than one single smoking gun, since real contamination events typically involve multiple simultaneous failures — for example, contaminated irrigation water plus inadequate buffer distance from livestock plus no water treatment step before harvest.

lessons.workedExample: IFSAC's annual report estimates that a given year's Salmonella illnesses attribute roughly 20% to chicken (with a published credible interval spanning roughly 15%-25%), a smaller share to seeds/vegetable row crops, and smaller shares still to several other categories, based on food vehicles identified across the outbreaks in its dataset; a companion expert-elicitation estimate for the same pathogen, drawn from surveyed specialists' judgment rather than outbreak case counts, lands in a broadly similar range for poultry but differs somewhat on categories with few solved outbreaks. Separately, when a specific multistate Salmonella outbreak is traced to one poultry processing plant, an environmental assessment there might find inadequate cooler sanitation and a wastewater drainage issue near a receiving dock — two contributing factors, not stated as the singular cause, that plausibly explain contamination at that one facility.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can distinguish population-level attribution (which food category drives illness overall, an inherently uncertain estimate built from a biased sample of solved outbreaks) from single-facility environmental assessment (how contamination happened at one already-implicated site). A project that quotes an attribution percentage as if it were an exact, uncontested fact — without acknowledging that outbreak-based data overrepresents foods prone to large recognizable clusters, and that expert elicitation is used precisely because of that gap — misses the central limitation judges expect a strong project to name.

questions.prompt: Why does outbreak-based source attribution risk overestimating some food categories' share of overall illness?

options.text: Outbreak data is never used in attribution estimates
Foods more likely to cause large, recognizable, multi-case clusters are overrepresented relative to foods that mostly cause sporadic, hard-to-link illness
IFSAC only studies foodborne illness caused by viruses, not bacteria
Outbreak investigations never identify a food vehicle

explanations.a: IFSAC's outbreak-based method is built directly on data from solved outbreaks; the issue is a sampling bias within that data, not its absence.
explanations.b: Correct: large, widely distributed products are more likely to produce a recognizable multistate cluster that gets solved and counted, while foods causing scattered sporadic illness are underrepresented in outbreak data.
explanations.c: IFSAC's core pathogens are bacterial: Salmonella, E. coli O157, Listeria monocytogenes, and Campylobacter.
explanations.d: Many outbreak investigations do successfully identify a food vehicle; attribution work relies on the ones that do, which is exactly why that subset is a biased sample.

questions.prompt: Order these steps from a single outbreak's traceback finding to an environmental assessment's conclusion.

items.text: Traceback and point-of-convergence analysis implicate a specific facility
Environmental health investigators visit and examine the facility's water, sanitation, and practices
Environmental swabs are collected and cultured, sometimes matching the outbreak strain
Investigators report contributing factors that plausibly explain how contamination occurred

questions.explanation: Environmental assessment follows traceback: only after a facility is implicated do investigators walk the site, sample it, and synthesize findings into contributing factors.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its correct description.

right.text: CDC/FDA/USDA-FSIS collaboration producing outbreak-based attribution estimates by food category
Survey-based method estimating attribution from expert judgment rather than outbreak counts
On-site review of a single implicated facility to find contributing contamination factors

questions.explanation: IFSAC produces population-level, outbreak-based attribution; expert elicitation is a complementary judgment-based method addressing outbreak data's sampling bias; environmental assessment is a facility-specific investigation of how contamination occurred.

lessons.label: A Foodborne Salmonella Investigation, End to End

sections.heading: A slow-building point-source signal
sections.body: In spring 2008, PulseNet — the CDC network that matches bacterial DNA fingerprints across state labs — flagged a cluster of Salmonella enterica serotype Saintpaul infections sharing an unusual pulsed-field gel electrophoresis pattern. By the time CDC declared the outbreak over that August, 1,442 people across 43 states, the District of Columbia, and Canada were confirmed infected; about 21% were hospitalized and two died. Recognizing the cluster was step one of the standard sequence: confirm the diagnosis and case definition, verify a true increase over baseline, then interview cases about foods eaten in the days before onset and compare exposures against healthy controls in a case-control study to see which item's odds ratio stood out.

sections.heading: The tomato trace-back and its cost
sections.body: Early case-control results pointed toward raw tomatoes, and in June the FDA issued a nationwide warning advising consumers to avoid raw red plum, roma, and round tomatoes from unimplicated regions. Growers estimated losses near $100 million as tomato sales collapsed and unsold produce was destroyed, yet trace-back teams following tomato supply chains from restaurants backward to farms kept dead-ending — no single farm or packing shed connected enough case-patients. Part of that failure was structural, not just slow legwork: tomatoes from many different growers are commingled at packing sheds and distribution centers before they ever reach a restaurant, where lots are combined, repacked, and resold as generic 'tomatoes' with no lot-level record of which farm grew which fruit. A restaurant's tomato supply in a given week could blend produce from a dozen farms across several states or countries, so even a complete list of every restaurant a case-patient visited could not, by itself, resolve to one origin — the traceability broke at the packing shed, not in the interview room. The tomato lead was plausible, not proven, and it consumed weeks of investigative capacity and public trust before it fully unraveled.

sections.heading: Peppers, trace-forward, and the source
sections.body: Investigators broadened food-history questions to include jalapeño and serrano peppers, common in the same salsa and pico de gallo dishes as tomatoes, and a second round of case-control analysis showed jalapeños carrying a strong, statistically significant association. Trace-back this time worked forward from restaurant purchase records and backward from a Texas distribution point, converging on a single farm in Nuevo León, Mexico. There, the outbreak strain was isolated directly from irrigation water and from a serrano pepper sample — genetic proof, not just statistical association, closing the case in late July.

lessons.workedExample: The case-control study that broke the outbreak compared 100+ ill case-patients against matched well controls on dozens of food items. Raw tomato showed a modest, inconsistent odds ratio across sites early on — enough to justify a warning but not to explain all clusters. When investigators added jalapeño pepper to the questionnaire, the odds ratio for illness among jalapeño-eaters was far higher and consistent across states, and it held up under multivariable analysis controlling for tomato co-exposure (since tomatoes and peppers are often eaten together in salsa). That statistical signal, combined with the later isolation of Salmonella Saintpaul from a Nuevo León farm's irrigation water, converted an association into a confirmed, mechanistically explained source.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks how you distinguish a real vehicle from a food that merely correlates with it because people eat it alongside the true culprit.
