sections.body: Adding births (rate μ, entering S) and deaths (rate μ, leaving every compartment, keeping N constant) turns the equations into dS/dt = μN - βSI/N - μS, dE/dt = βSI/N - (σ+μ)E, dI/dt = σE - (γ+μ)I, dR/dt = γI - μR. New susceptibles are born continuously, so even after a large outbreak burns through most of S, the population slowly refills and R0(S/N) can climb back above 1, producing another wave. This system has a stable endemic equilibrium where S settles at S* = N/R0 (equivalently S*/N = 1/R0) and disease incidence holds at a steady low level rather than dying to zero — the classic case is pre-vaccine measles, endemic in cities for generations with a roughly two-year epidemic cycle in some settings before oscillations dampen. This same S* = N/R0 condition is where herd-immunity targets come from: vaccinating (or otherwise immunizing) a fraction pc of the population removes those people from S, so transmission can no longer sustain R0(S/N) above 1 once pc ≥ 1 - 1/R0 — the critical vaccination coverage threshold. For measles at R0 = 15, that puts pc at roughly 93%, which is why measles elimination programs target coverage in the mid-90s rather than the 80-90% that suffices for lower-R0 diseases.

sections.heading: The mean age at infection reveals R0
sections.body: At equilibrium, a strikingly useful relation falls out of the model: the average age A at which someone gets infected relates to life expectancy L and R0 by A ≈ L/(R0 - 1). The intuition: high R0 means transmission is intense, so susceptibles get infected quickly after losing maternal immunity, pushing A down; low R0 means transmission is sluggish, so people go longer before being caught, pushing A up. This is a real epidemiological tool — Anderson and May's work in the 1980s used exactly this relation to back out R0 for measles, mumps, and rubella from age-stratified serosurveys and case-report data, since R0 is hard to measure directly but the average age of infection can be read straight from surveillance records.

lessons.workedExample: In a population with life expectancy L = 70 years and measles R0 = 15 (typical range 12-18 in dense pre-vaccine settings), the model predicts A ≈ 70/(15-1) = 5 years — matching the historical observation that measles was overwhelmingly a disease of young children before vaccination. Contrast a lower-R0 pathogen like rubella at R0 = 6 in the same population: A ≈ 70/(6-1) = 14 years, pushing infections into adolescence — which matters clinically because rubella infection during pregnancy causes congenital rubella syndrome, so a lower R0 that delays infection into reproductive years can, paradoxically, worsen outcomes.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student understands that R0 is not directly observable but can be inferred from something that IS observable — the age distribution of cases. A student who can derive or apply A ≈ L/(R0-1) demonstrates they grasp both the demographic mechanics of endemicity and a real historical method (Anderson and May) rather than just quoting the formula. It also tests whether they see that raising vaccination coverage (lowering effective R0) predictably raises the age at infection, a fact with direct clinical consequences for diseases like rubella.

questions.prompt: Why does a closed-population SIR model (no births or deaths) always fail to sustain a disease indefinitely?

options.text: Because γ eventually reaches zero
Because the susceptible pool is finite and never replenished, so it eventually can't sustain R0(S/N) > 1
Because β increases without bound over time
Because R stops being infectious

explanations.a: γ is a fixed recovery rate parameter; it doesn't drift to zero over the course of the epidemic.
explanations.b: Correct: with no new susceptibles entering, S/N keeps falling until effective transmission can no longer be sustained.
explanations.c: β is treated as a fixed transmission parameter in the basic model, not something that grows.
explanations.d: R (Recovered) isn't infectious in this model at all; that's not the mechanism limiting the epidemic.

questions.prompt: At the endemic equilibrium of an SIR model with vital dynamics, S* satisfies:

options.text: S*/N = R0
S*/N = μ/γ

explanations.a: Correct: at equilibrium the effective reproduction number R0(S*/N) equals exactly 1, which requires S*/N = 1/R0.
explanations.b: This is inverted; R0 is typically greater than 1, which would make S* exceed N.
explanations.c: S* = 0 would mean no susceptibles remain, which is inconsistent with a nonzero steady incidence being sustained.
explanations.d: μ/γ isn't the equilibrium condition; the birth/death rate μ determines how fast the system approaches S*, not its value.

questions.prompt: A vaccination campaign lowers a pathogen's effective R0 in a population. What does the model predict happens to the mean age at infection among remaining unvaccinated cases?

options.text: It falls, since fewer people are infected overall
It rises, since lower R0 means transmission is slower and susceptibles take longer to be infected
It is unaffected by R0
It becomes undefined once R0 drops below 1

explanations.a: Overall case counts falling doesn't determine the age distribution among those still infected; the relevant driver is transmission intensity.
explanations.b: Correct: A ≈ L/(R0-1) increases as R0 falls, which is why lower vaccination coverage against rubella specifically raises congenital rubella syndrome risk by shifting cases into childbearing years.
explanations.c: A is explicitly a function of R0 in this model.
explanations.d: Below R0 = 1 the disease isn't endemic at all, but that's a different regime, not a claim that A is undefined near the threshold from above.

questions.prompt: Match each modification to its consequence in the demographic SIR/SEIR model.

right.text: Continuously replenishes the susceptible pool
Keeps total population N constant over time
Lowers the mean age at infection A

questions.explanation: Births refill S, matched deaths hold N steady so a true equilibrium exists, and A ≈ L/(R0-1) falls as R0 rises.

lessons.label: Waning Immunity: SIRS and SEIRS

sections.heading: The lifelong-immunity assumption breaks for many pathogens
sections.body: Basic SIR and SEIR treat R as a terminal state: once recovered, always immune, forever. That's a reasonable approximation for measles, where natural infection confers immunity that is durable for decades. It is a poor approximation for coronaviruses, many bacterial respiratory pathogens, and malaria, where protective antibody titers decline and reinfection is documented within a year or two. SIRS (and its latent-period cousin SEIRS) fixes this by adding a flow ω from R back to S: dS/dt = -βSI/N + ωR, dR/dt = γI - ωR, where 1/ω is the mean duration of immunity. Once immunity wanes, a recovered person becomes susceptible again, exactly as if they'd never been infected.

sections.heading: Why waning immunity sustains recurrent waves even without births
sections.body: This matters because SIRS can sustain endemic transmission through a completely different mechanism than the birth-driven endemicity of demographic SIR: instead of new susceptibles being born, old susceptibles are recycled. On a timescale much shorter than a human lifespan — months to a few years rather than decades — the R-to-S flow alone can keep R0(S/N) oscillating above and below 1, producing recurrent epidemic waves. Common cold coronaviruses (e.g., HCoV-OC43, HCoV-229E) are the textbook case: reinfection studies (including a well-cited 1990 human-challenge study by Callow and colleagues, in which most volunteers rechallenged with the same 229E strain a year later shed virus again, though noticeably fewer developed cold symptoms and those illnesses ran milder and shorter than the first infection) found susceptibility returning within about a year, consistent with the seasonal, recurring pattern these viruses show every winter rather than a single depleting outbreak.

sections.heading: When the SIRS/SEIRS extension is unavoidable, not optional
sections.body: The decision of whether to add ω isn't cosmetic — it changes what the model can even represent. A plain SIR or SEIR model, run long enough, will always predict eventual extinction of transmission (in a closed population) because R only grows. If the real data show multiple documented waves within an immunologically short window — as seasonal coronaviruses, pertussis (where acellular-vaccine-derived immunity wanes over roughly 4-12 years, faster than the longer protection natural infection tends to confer), and rotavirus all do — a model without R-to-S is structurally incapable of reproducing that pattern no matter how the other parameters are tuned. Modelers reach for SIRS specifically when reinfection data (rising IgG-negative fractions, repeat PCR-confirmed infections) show waning is happening on a timescale comparable to the outbreak dynamics being studied, not just as a generic embellishment.

lessons.workedExample: Consider a coronavirus with R0 = 3, γ = 1/5 per day, and immunity lasting 1/ω = 300 days on average. Starting from a fully susceptible population, the first wave depletes S sharply and case counts crash — but because ω = 1/300 per day steadily returns recovered individuals to S, within roughly a year S/N climbs back enough to push R0(S/N) above 1 again, triggering a second wave without any births needed and without reintroducing the pathogen from outside. Set ω = 0 (SIR) and the same model predicts a single outbreak that never recurs, which is the wrong qualitative behavior for this pathogen.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes whether a student chose SIRS/SEIRS because the pathogen's actual reinfection biology demands it, or bolted it on reflexively. The tell of real understanding is citing evidence for waning — a reinfection study, declining titers, repeat-positive PCR — and connecting the timescale of ω to the observed inter-wave spacing in the data, rather than treating 'immunity fades' as a vague truism applied to every disease regardless of whether measles-like lifelong immunity actually fits better.

questions.prompt: What does the added flow in SIRS, from R back to S, represent biologically?

options.text: Recovered individuals dying and being replaced by births
Protective immunity declining over time, making recovered individuals susceptible again
A second, distinct pathogen strain infecting recovered individuals
Recovered individuals becoming asymptomatic carriers

explanations.a: That describes demographic turnover (births/deaths), a separate mechanism from waning immunity and not what ω represents.
explanations.b: Correct: ω is the rate at which immune protection fades, returning people to a susceptible state without any new infection or birth.
explanations.c: SIRS as described doesn't model strain diversity; it's the same pathogen and the same immune state cycling.
explanations.d: Asymptomatic carriage is a different compartment concept (see the asymptomatic/pre-symptomatic lesson), not what R-to-S represents.

questions.prompt: A model shows a single outbreak that dies out and never returns, but real surveillance data show the disease recurring every winter for years. What does this mismatch most directly suggest about the model?

options.text: β was set too high
The model likely needs an R-to-S (waning immunity) flow, since plain SIR/SEIR cannot reproduce recurring waves on a short timescale
γ was set too low
The population size N was set incorrectly

explanations.a: A higher β changes the size and speed of a single wave but doesn't create recurrence after S is depleted.
explanations.b: Correct: without an R-to-S flow (or births, which act on a much slower timescale), the model is structurally unable to generate a second wave shortly after the first.
explanations.c: γ affects wave duration and peak height, not whether a second wave can occur at all.
explanations.d: N sets the scale of the population, not whether susceptibles are replenished over time.

questions.prompt: Order the transitions a single individual cycles through in the SIRS model (starting susceptible, assuming they get infected and immunity later wanes).

items.text: Susceptible (S)
Infectious (I)
Recovered/immune (R)
Susceptible again (S), after immunity wanes

questions.explanation: SIRS closes the loop that basic SIR leaves open: after recovery and temporary immunity, the ω flow returns the individual to S.

questions.prompt: Match each model to whether it can represent lifelong immunity or requires an explicit immunity-duration parameter.

right.text: Assumes lifelong immunity once recovered (no ω)
Has an R-to-S flow with rate ω but no separate latent (E) stage
Has both a latent stage and a waning-immunity flow

questions.explanation: SIR has no waning term at all; SIRS adds ω without an E compartment; SEIRS combines the latent-period structure of SEIR with the waning-immunity flow of SIRS.

lessons.label: Asymptomatic and Pre-symptomatic Compartments

sections.heading: One infectious class is too coarse
sections.body: Plain SEIR treats everyone in I as equally infectious for the same duration, but real infectiousness is rarely uniform or tied cleanly to symptom onset. Splitting I into sub-classes lets a model capture this: Ip (pre-symptomatic, infectious before symptoms appear), Isym (symptomatic, typically more cautious or isolated once recognized), and Iasym (asymptomatic, infectious for the full course but never showing symptoms at all). Each sub-class gets its own duration and its own relative infectiousness parameter, e.g. dIp/dt = σE - (γp + fraction-to-symptomatic-rate)Ip, feeding separately into Isym and Iasym, with each contributing βpIp, βsymIsym, or βasymIasym to the force of infection rather than a single shared β.

sections.heading: Why this split mattered acutely for COVID-19
sections.body: For COVID-19, estimates from contact-tracing and viral-load studies (including Moghadas et al., 2020, and He et al., 2020) put a substantial share of transmission — often cited around 40-50% — as occurring before symptom onset or from people who never developed symptoms at all. He et al. 2020's inferred infectiousness profile put the onset of pre-symptomatic infectiousness at roughly 2.3 days before symptom onset on average, with infectiousness peaking about 0.7 days before symptoms appeared — transmission was already ramping up well before, and peaking just ahead of, the point a symptom check would catch it. That timing is structurally different from SARS-CoV-1 in 2003, where infectiousness tracked symptom severity closely and peaked after symptom onset, which is a large part of why fever screening and symptom-based isolation worked reasonably well for SARS-1 containment but performed far worse against COVID-19.

sections.heading: Why silent transmission defeats symptom-triggered control
sections.body: Any intervention that triggers on symptoms — fever checks at an airport, 'stay home if you feel sick' guidance, symptom-based contact tracing — implicitly assumes the Ip and Iasym fractions are small. When they're not, a large share of transmission chains are invisible to that control lever entirely: an Ip individual spreads the pathogen for days before there's any symptom to notice, and an Iasym individual never presents a trigger at all. Modeling these as separate compartments isn't just more granular bookkeeping — it changes the qualitative conclusion a model gives about whether a given intervention can plausibly control spread, which is why outbreak modelers immediately began estimating asymptomatic-fraction and pre-symptomatic-window parameters as a first priority once COVID-19 case data emerged in early 2020.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose contact-tracing data show 30% of confirmed COVID-19 cases were fully asymptomatic and, among symptomatic cases, infectiousness began on average about 2.3 days before symptom onset (peaking roughly 0.7 days before onset, per He et al. 2020) with that pre-symptomatic window accounting for about 40% of a case's total transmission. A model lumping everyone into one I compartment triggered by symptoms would miss the asymptomatic 30% entirely and undercount the pre-symptomatic 40% of transmission from the remaining 70% — meaning a policy of 'isolate on symptom report' addresses well under half of total transmission even under generous compliance, a conclusion invisible without the Ip/Iasym split.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this concept wants to see whether a student can name the actual mechanism by which silent transmission undermines control — not just assert 'some people don't have symptoms.' The strong answer distinguishes pre-symptomatic from asymptomatic (different biology, same policy problem), cites a rough fraction of transmission attributable to each from real COVID-19 estimates, and connects it to why testing-based or exposure-based strategies (rather than symptom-based ones) became necessary once that fraction was recognized to be large.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a pre-symptomatic infectious individual from an asymptomatic one?

options.text: Pre-symptomatic individuals are not infectious; asymptomatic individuals are
Pre-symptomatic individuals will later develop symptoms; asymptomatic individuals complete infection without ever developing symptoms
They are two names for the same compartment
Pre-symptomatic individuals have already recovered

explanations.a: Both are infectious; the distinction is about eventual symptom status, not about whether transmission occurs.
explanations.b: Correct: pre-symptomatic is a transient stage before symptoms appear, while asymptomatic describes a full infectious course with no symptoms ever.
explanations.c: They require separate compartments precisely because they have different durations and different downstream paths.
explanations.d: Both terms describe stages of active infection, not recovery.

questions.prompt: Why did symptom-based screening work better for SARS-CoV-1 (2003) than for COVID-19?

options.text: SARS-CoV-1 had a lower R0
SARS-CoV-1 infectiousness peaked after symptom onset, giving symptom checks something to catch, unlike COVID-19's substantial pre-/asymptomatic transmission
SARS-CoV-1 had no incubation period
COVID-19 had a much longer infectious period

explanations.a: R0 differences don't explain why symptom-timing-based screening specifically succeeded or failed; the timing of infectiousness relative to symptoms does.
explanations.b: Correct: because SARS-1 infectiousness tracked and peaked with symptom severity, symptom-triggered isolation caught cases before much transmission occurred — the opposite of COVID-19's pre-symptomatic peak.
explanations.c: SARS-CoV-1 had a defined incubation period like other coronaviruses; that's not the distinguishing factor here.
explanations.d: Infectious period length isn't the mechanism described in this lesson; timing of infectiousness relative to symptoms is.

questions.prompt: Order the sub-stages an eventually-symptomatic COVID-19 case passes through, from infection to isolation-eligibility.

items.text: Exposed (E) — infected, not yet infectious
Pre-symptomatic infectious (Ip) — infectious, no symptoms yet
Symptomatic infectious (Isym) — symptoms present, now detectable by screening

questions.explanation: The pre-symptomatic window sits between becoming infectious and becoming detectable by symptom-based screening, which is exactly the gap that undermines that control strategy.

questions.prompt: Match each infectious sub-compartment to what makes it distinct from a single lumped I class.

right.text: Transitions to a symptomatic stage after a defined window, contributing to silent transmission until then
Never triggers symptom-based detection at all for the full infectious course
The stage symptom-based screening and self-isolation guidance actually target

questions.explanation: Ip is a transient invisible window, Iasym is permanently invisible to symptom screening, and Isym is the only stage that symptom-triggered interventions can actually catch.

lessons.label: Compartments for Severity and Outcomes

sections.heading: Infections aren't the deliverable — capacity and deaths are
sections.body: A basic SEIR model answers 'how many people got infected and when,' but the questions that actually drive public-health decisions are downstream of that: how many will need a hospital bed, how many will need an ICU bed, and how many will die. Chaining new compartments onto I — Hospitalized (H), Intensive Care (ICU or C), and Dead (D) — lets a model answer those questions directly rather than forcing someone to guess at a fixed ratio applied after the fact. A typical chain looks like dH/dt = pIH·γI − (γH + pHC·δH)H, where pIH is the probability a symptomatic case is hospitalized and γH governs how fast people leave H (to recovery or to ICU).

sections.heading: Branching probabilities and time lags, not just extra boxes
sections.body: The key modeling ideas are branching (a person leaves each compartment down one of several possible paths, each with its own probability) and lags (each transition takes real time, not zero time). From H, some fraction pHC proceeds to ICU after a delay of roughly 3-7 days from hospitalization in influenza and COVID-19 modeling literature, while the rest recover directly. From ICU, a further fraction pCD proceeds to death, typically after another multi-day to multi-week stay, while the remainder step back down to a general ward or recover. Each of these branch probabilities is age- and risk-stratified in serious models — CDC and academic COVID-19 models (e.g., the CDC COVID-19 Forecast Hub ensemble efforts from 2020 onward) used age-banded hospitalization and fatality probabilities because a flat population-average badly misrepresents both a 25-year-old's risk and an 80-year-old's.

sections.heading: Why capacity, not just death count, drives the modeling
sections.body: The H and ICU compartments exist for a reason beyond counting bodies: hospital and ICU bed counts are hard, finite numbers, and when demand (the size of H or ICU at a given time) exceeds supply, outcomes worsen for everyone in the system, not just the marginal patient — a dynamic sometimes modeled with an elevated case-fatality probability once occupancy crosses a capacity threshold. This is precisely the mechanism behind 'flatten the curve' messaging in 2020: the goal wasn't to reduce total infections to zero, it was to keep the peak of H+ICU under the region's bed capacity, a statement that is meaningless in a plain SEIR model with no H or ICU compartment to compare against a capacity line at all.

lessons.workedExample: A region has 500 ICU beds. A model projects an unmitigated outbreak with peak I of 200,000 concurrent infections, of which 5% are hospitalized (pIH = 0.05, so 10,000 concurrent H) and 20% of hospitalized reach ICU (pHC = 0.20, so 2,000 concurrent ICU) — four times the region's capacity. The same model with a transmission-reducing intervention that cuts peak I to 80,000 brings peak ICU demand to about 800, still over capacity but far closer, showing why modelers report projected peak H and ICU occupancy against the fixed 500-bed line rather than just total infections, which alone can't say whether the health system holds.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge evaluating a severity-chain model wants to see the student separate two questions that get blurred in casual reporting: how many people get infected, and how many need scarce medical resources. The strong answer explains why pIH and pHC are branching probabilities (not everyone follows every path), why the H-to-ICU and ICU-to-D transitions take real time (lags matter for forecasting when a capacity crunch hits, not just whether), and why age-stratifying those probabilities is necessary rather than optional given how sharply risk varies by age.

questions.prompt: In a chained I→H→ICU→D model, what does the parameter pIH represent?

options.text: The overall case fatality rate
The probability that a symptomatic infectious case is hospitalized
The rate at which hospitalized patients recover
The total number of ICU beds available

explanations.a: Case fatality rate would depend on the full chain (pIH, pHC, pCD together), not on pIH alone.
explanations.b: Correct: pIH is the branching probability governing what fraction of I flows into H rather than recovering directly.
explanations.c: That would be governed by a recovery rate parameter like γH, not by the branching probability pIH.
explanations.d: Bed capacity is an external constraint compared against model output, not a model parameter like pIH.

questions.prompt: Why do serious COVID-19 and influenza models age-stratify the H, ICU, and D branching probabilities rather than using one population-wide value?

options.text: Because age doesn't actually affect these probabilities, it's just convention
Because hospitalization, ICU, and death risk vary sharply by age, and a flat average misrepresents both low-risk and high-risk groups
Because age-stratification simplifies the equations
Because β varies by age but the outcome probabilities do not

explanations.a: Age strongly affects these probabilities in the pathogens discussed; that's exactly why stratification is used.
explanations.b: Correct: a flat average badly misstates risk at both ends of the age distribution, which matters for both individual guidance and capacity forecasting.
explanations.c: Age-stratification adds parameters and complexity; it isn't done for simplicity.
explanations.d: Outcome probabilities (hospitalization, ICU, death) are exactly the parameters that are age-stratified in real models.

questions.prompt: Order the compartments in a typical severity chain for a case that ultimately dies.

items.text: Infectious (I)
Hospitalized (H)
Intensive Care (ICU)
Dead (D)

questions.explanation: The chain models progressively more severe stages, each reached only by a branching subset of the previous compartment after a time lag.

questions.prompt: Match each modeling concept to its role in the severity chain.

left.text: Time lag (e.g., H to ICU delay)

right.text: Determines what fraction takes a given path rather than another
Determines when a transition's effect shows up in the projection, not just whether it happens
An external constraint compared against projected occupancy to judge whether the system holds

questions.explanation: Branching sets the split, lags set the timing, and capacity is the fixed line severity projections are measured against.

lessons.label: Vaccination and Intervention Compartments

sections.heading: Adding a Vaccinated compartment
sections.body: Modeling a vaccination program means adding a V compartment that susceptibles flow into at some vaccination rate ν, typically dS/dt = -βSI/N - νS and dV/dt = νS - (leak or waning terms). The critical modeling choice is how V behaves once someone is in it, because 'vaccinated' does not mean 'as unreachable as Recovered' for most real vaccines — it means partially protected, and how that partial protection is represented changes the model's conclusions substantially.

sections.heading: All-or-nothing versus leaky vaccine models
sections.body: There are two standard ways to represent imperfect vaccine efficacy VE. An all-or-nothing (also called 'take') model assumes a fraction VE of vaccinated people become fully immune (functionally moved to R, unreachable by infection) while the remaining 1-VE get no protection at all and remain as susceptible as anyone in S. A leaky model instead assumes every vaccinated person gets partial protection: their per-contact susceptibility is reduced by a factor (1-VE), so the force of infection acting on V is (1-VE)βI/N rather than the full βI/N — nobody is fully immune, but everybody in V is harder to infect. These are mathematically distinct even at the same headline VE, and clinical trials (which report VE as a reduction in infection risk over a trial period) generally cannot distinguish the two mechanisms from the topline number alone — Halloran, Struchiner, and colleagues developed much of the statistical framework in the 1990s specifically because these two failure modes have different implications for who bears infection risk when a vaccine 'doesn't fully work.'

sections.heading: Why leaky vaccines shrink but don't empty the effective susceptible pool
sections.body: The practical difference matters enormously for herd-immunity calculations. Under all-or-nothing, a VE = 0.7 vaccine effectively removes 70% of vaccinated people from the susceptible pool entirely, just like natural immunity. Under leaky, 100% of vaccinated people remain infectable, just less easily — meaning breakthrough infections are expected and routine even at high coverage, and the effective reproduction number falls by a smaller amount for the same VE and coverage than the all-or-nothing case predicts, because a leaky vaccine reduces transmission risk per contact rather than removing contacts from the susceptible pool. This is a large part of why widespread, real breakthrough infections after COVID-19 vaccination were expected under a leaky-vaccine framing (consistent with vaccine efficacy against infection being well below efficacy against severe disease) rather than being evidence the vaccines 'weren't working.'

lessons.workedExample: A population of 100,000 has R0 = 4 and 80% vaccine coverage at VE = 75%. Under all-or-nothing: 80,000 vaccinated x 75% take = 60,000 fully immune, leaving 40,000 effectively susceptible out of 100,000 (40%), and effective R0(S/N) ≈ 4 x 0.40 = 1.6, still above 1. Under leaky: all 80,000 vaccinated remain infectable but with transmission risk cut 75%, so their contribution to force of infection is 80,000 x 0.25 = 20,000 'susceptible-equivalents,' plus the 20,000 unvaccinated at full weight, giving 40,000 susceptible-equivalents out of 100,000 — the same 1.6 in this simplified case, but the leaky model predicts breakthrough infections spread across nearly all 80,000 vaccinated people rather than concentrated in the unprotected 20,000, a very different real-world pattern of who gets infected.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing vaccination modeling wants to know whether a student understands that VE alone is not enough information to build a model — the mechanism (all-or-nothing vs. leaky) has to be specified too, because it changes who is predicted to get infected even when the aggregate reproduction-number math comes out similar. The strong answer explains why breakthrough infections are the expected signature of a leaky vaccine rather than a failure, and cites that real vaccine trials generally can't tell the two mechanisms apart from the topline efficacy number alone.

questions.prompt: Under an all-or-nothing vaccine model with VE = 0.6, what happens to a vaccinated individual who is among the 60% for whom the vaccine 'took'?

options.text: They remain 60% as susceptible as an unvaccinated person
They become fully immune, functionally equivalent to Recovered
Their infectiousness to others is reduced by 60%, but their own susceptibility is unchanged
They are removed from the population entirely

explanations.a: That partial-reduction description is the leaky model's mechanism, not all-or-nothing.
explanations.b: Correct: in the all-or-nothing framing, the fraction for whom the vaccine 'took' becomes fully immune, just like a recovered individual.
explanations.c: All-or-nothing concerns the vaccinated person's own susceptibility to infection, not a separate infectiousness-to-others parameter.
explanations.d: Vaccinated individuals with a successful take remain in the population; they simply cannot be infected.

questions.prompt: Widespread breakthrough infections occurring even among fully vaccinated people, spread broadly rather than concentrated in a small unprotected subgroup, is the expected signature of which vaccine model?

options.text: All-or-nothing
Leaky
Neither model predicts breakthrough infections
Both models predict identical infection patterns

explanations.a: All-or-nothing predicts breakthroughs are concentrated among the fraction for whom the vaccine didn't take, not spread broadly.
explanations.b: Correct: leaky vaccination leaves everyone partially susceptible, so breakthrough infections are expected to occur broadly across the vaccinated population.
explanations.c: Both models predict some breakthrough infection at VE < 1; the difference is in the pattern, not whether it occurs.
explanations.d: The two models predict different distributions of who gets infected even at matched headline VE, which is the core point of this lesson.

questions.prompt: Match each vaccine model to how it modifies the force of infection acting on vaccinated individuals.

right.text: A fraction VE face zero force of infection (fully immune); the rest face the full force
Every vaccinated individual faces a force of infection reduced by a factor (1-VE)

questions.explanation: All-or-nothing splits the vaccinated population into two fully-different-risk groups; leaky applies a uniform partial reduction to everyone vaccinated.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in building a vaccination-extended SEIR model's V compartment.

items.text: Choose a vaccination rate ν governing the flow from S into V
Choose a vaccine efficacy VE from trial or observational data
Choose a mechanism (all-or-nothing vs. leaky) for how VE translates into reduced risk
Compute the resulting effective reproduction number and compare to the herd-immunity threshold

questions.explanation: VE alone is insufficient; the mechanism choice is a distinct modeling decision that must be made before the effective reproduction number can be computed correctly.

lessons.label: Sojourn-Time Structure and Its Consequences

sections.heading: The hidden assumption in every dI/dt = -γI term
sections.body: Writing dI/dt = σE - γI implicitly assumes that the time a person spends infectious follows an exponential distribution with mean 1/γ. The exponential distribution is memoryless: someone who has already been infectious for 6 days has exactly the same probability of recovering in the next hour as someone who just became infectious. Real infectious periods don't behave like that — a person who just became infectious yesterday is very unlikely to recover tomorrow, and one who's been sick for a typical duration is much more likely to recover soon. The single-compartment exponential 'sojourn time' (time spent in a compartment) is a mathematical convenience baked into standard ODE compartmental models, not a biological finding.

sections.heading: The linear-chain (Erlang) fix
sections.body: The standard fix, sometimes called the linear chain trick, replaces one I compartment with k sequential sub-compartments I1, I2, ..., Ik, each with exponential exit rate kγ, so people must pass through all k stages before recovering: dI1/dt = σE - kγI1, dI2/dt = kγI1 - kγI2, and so on. The total time spent across all k stages follows an Erlang (gamma) distribution with mean still 1/γ but with a peaked, more realistic shape — as k increases, the distribution becomes progressively less spread out and less memoryless, converging toward something closer to a fixed duration as k grows large. k=1 recovers plain exponential SEIR exactly; larger k (often k=2 to k=10 in practice) is used when real duration data (from viral shedding studies, symptom-duration cohorts) show a distribution tightly clustered around a mean rather than exponentially spread with many very-short and some very-long durations.

sections.heading: Why the choice biases timing and R0 estimates, not just aesthetics
sections.body: This isn't a cosmetic refinement: sojourn-time shape measurably affects both epidemic growth trajectories and inferred parameters. An exponential (k=1) infectious period generates a wider spread of individual infectious durations than an Erlang with the same mean, which changes how quickly the epidemic can grow because some individuals recover very fast (contributing little) while others linger very long (contributing disproportionately to the tail). Wearing and colleagues (2005) and subsequent work in the mathematical epidemiology literature showed that fitting an exponential-stage model to outbreak data generated from a more realistic gamma-distributed process systematically biases the inferred growth rate and R0 estimate, and shifts predicted peak timing — because the exponential assumption gets the variance of the generation interval wrong even when it matches the mean, and R0 estimation from early growth-rate data is sensitive to that variance, not just the mean.

lessons.workedExample: Two models share γ = 1/6 per day (mean 6-day infectious period) and the same β. Model A uses k=1 (plain exponential): individual infectious durations range widely, with a substantial share recovering in 1-2 days and a longer tail extending past 15 days. Model B uses k=4 sub-stages (mean still 6 days, Erlang-4 shape): durations cluster much more tightly around 6 days, with very few people recovering before day 3 or lingering past day 12. Fed the same initial conditions, Model A's epidemic grows measurably faster in the early phase because its high-variance duration distribution generates more short, fast-succession transmission events, and a modeler who used Model A to back out R0 from early case-count growth would infer a higher R0 than actually generated the data if the true process looked more like Model B.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who understands sojourn structure will ask whether a student picked k=1 out of default habit or because the pathogen's real duration data support the memoryless assumption. The strong answer names the linear-chain/Erlang trick by name, explains that it's the variance (not just the mean) of the infectious-period distribution that matters for growth-rate and R0 inference, and can say what real duration data (viral shedding curves, symptom-duration studies) would justify choosing a larger k over plain exponential for their specific pathogen.

questions.prompt: What does 'memoryless' mean for the exponential infectious-period assumption in standard SIR/SEIR?

options.text: The probability of recovering in the next instant is the same regardless of how long someone has already been infectious
Infected individuals forget they are infected
The model has no memory of past epidemic waves
Recovery probability increases the longer someone has been infectious

explanations.a: Correct: this is the defining property of the exponential distribution — the hazard of recovery doesn't depend on elapsed time.
explanations.b: Memorylessness is a mathematical property of the duration distribution, not a statement about patient awareness.
explanations.c: That describes something unrelated to sojourn-time distributions; memorylessness is about the compartment's exit-time distribution.
explanations.d: That describes the opposite: a distribution where hazard increases with elapsed time is not memoryless, which is exactly what makes real infectious periods different from the exponential assumption.

questions.prompt: In the linear-chain (Erlang) trick, what happens to the sojourn-time distribution's shape as k increases, holding the mean 1/γ fixed?

options.text: It becomes more spread out and more exponential-like
It becomes more tightly clustered around the mean, less memoryless, as k grows
The mean duration increases with k
k has no effect on the distribution's shape, only on computation speed

explanations.a: Increasing k moves away from the exponential (k=1) case toward a tighter distribution, not a more spread-out one.
explanations.b: Correct: larger k concentrates the Erlang distribution more tightly around its mean, better approximating a realistic, less-memoryless duration.
explanations.c: The construction explicitly holds the mean at 1/γ regardless of k; only the shape/variance changes.
explanations.d: k directly changes the statistical shape (variance) of the sojourn time, which is the entire point of the trick, not merely a computational detail.

questions.prompt: Why can using an exponential (k=1) infectious-period assumption bias an R0 estimate fit to real early-outbreak growth data, even if the mean infectious period is correctly specified?

options.text: Because R0 estimation from growth-rate data is sensitive to the variance of the generation interval, not just its mean, and exponential and Erlang distributions with the same mean have different variances
Because γ cannot be estimated from data at all
Because exponential distributions always overestimate the mean duration
Because R0 is unrelated to the infectious-period distribution

explanations.a: Correct: matching the mean isn't sufficient — the growth-rate-to-R0 conversion depends on the full shape (including variance) of the generation-interval distribution.
explanations.b: γ is routinely estimated from duration data; that's not the source of the bias described here.
explanations.c: The mean can be matched exactly (both structures set to 1/γ); the bias comes from variance mismatch, not a mean error.
explanations.d: R0 estimation from growth-rate data explicitly depends on the generation-interval distribution, which is directly tied to the infectious-period structure.

questions.prompt: Match each value of k in the linear-chain trick to the resulting sojourn-time behavior.

right.text: Plain exponential distribution; fully memoryless
Tightly clustered near the mean duration; much less memoryless

questions.explanation: k=1 is exactly the standard exponential SEIR case; increasing k progressively narrows the distribution around its mean.

lessons.label: R0 as the Epidemic Threshold

sections.heading: One case, one fully susceptible population
sections.body: The basic reproduction number, R0, is the expected number of secondary infections produced by a single infected individual introduced into a population where everyone else is susceptible. It is a per-generation count, not a rate over clock time: R0 = 3 means one case begets three cases on average across the next generation of infection, whatever that generation happens to take in days or weeks for a given pathogen. Two diseases can share the same R0 while spreading at wildly different speeds if their generation intervals differ, and conflating R0 with a growth rate is one of the most common errors students make when reading outbreak reports.

sections.heading: The threshold and why it is sharp
sections.body: R0 > 1 means each case produces more than one successor on average, so a chain of transmission can sustain and grow into an epidemic; R0 < 1 means each generation shrinks and the chain dies out even without intervention. R0 = 1 is the knife-edge threshold value separating these regimes, which is why so much of outbreak control -- vaccination coverage, distancing, isolation -- is framed as pushing the effective reproduction number below 1 rather than to zero. This sharp threshold is not merely a modern convention: Kermack and McKendrick proved it mathematically in 1927 in what is now called the epidemic threshold theorem, showing within the SIR framework they were developing that an epidemic can only take off if the initial density of susceptibles in the population exceeds a specific critical value. Below that critical density, an introduced infection fades out on its own; above it, case counts initially grow before susceptible depletion turns the curve back down. Their 1927 result is the historical origin of the R0 = 1 threshold used throughout epidemiology today, translating a density condition on susceptibles into the reproduction-number language taught in modern courses.

sections.heading: The SIR special case: R0 = beta/gamma
sections.body: In the simplest compartmental model, the SIR model, the population is split into Susceptible, Infected, and Recovered compartments. New infections arise at rate beta per contact between an infected and susceptible person, and infected people recover (or are removed) at rate gamma, so 1/gamma is the mean infectious period. In this model R0 = beta/gamma: the transmission rate per unit time multiplied by how long, on average, a person stays infectious. Doubling the infectious period doubles R0 with beta held fixed, which is exactly why isolating cases faster -- shrinking the effective duration of infectiousness -- is a lever on R0 even when transmissibility itself is unchanged.

lessons.workedExample: A novel respiratory virus has an estimated transmission rate beta = 0.4 per day and a mean infectious period of 5 days, so gamma = 1/5 = 0.2 per day. R0 = beta/gamma = 0.4/0.2 = 2: each case infects two others on average in a fully susceptible population, and since R0 > 1 the outbreak can grow. If a public-health intervention shortens the infectious period to 2.5 days by isolating cases after symptom onset, gamma rises to 0.4 and R0 falls to 0.4/0.4 = 1, sitting exactly at the epidemic threshold -- illustrating why case isolation, not just reducing contact, is a legitimate R0 lever.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can state what R0 is actually counting -- secondary cases per generation, in a fully susceptible population -- rather than reciting it as a vague 'contagiousness score.' A common tell of shallow understanding is treating R0 as if it were a speed (like doubling time) or as a fixed property of the pathogen alone; a strong answer separates R0's per-generation definition from Rt's time-varying, population-dependent value, and can derive R0 = beta/gamma conceptually rather than just quoting the formula.

questions.prompt: In the SIR model, if the mean infectious period doubles while the transmission rate beta stays fixed, R0:

options.text: Doubles, because R0 = beta/gamma and gamma is halved when the infectious period doubles
Halves, because a longer infectious period means gamma increases
Stays the same, since R0 depends only on beta
Becomes undefined, since gamma is no longer meaningful

explanations.a: Correct: gamma = 1/(infectious period), so doubling the infectious period halves gamma, and R0 = beta/gamma doubles when beta is unchanged.
explanations.b: This reverses the relationship: gamma is the recovery RATE, so a longer infectious period means a SMALLER gamma, not larger.
explanations.c: R0 depends on both beta and gamma in the SIR model; ignoring gamma misses half the formula.
explanations.d: Gamma remains well-defined as the reciprocal of the (now longer) infectious period; the formula still applies.

questions.prompt: Two pathogens both have R0 = 2, but pathogen A has a generation interval of 4 days and pathogen B has a generation interval of 20 days. What can you conclude?

options.text: Pathogen A will produce epidemic growth roughly five times faster in real time despite the identical R0
Both pathogens spread at the same real-time speed, since R0 is identical
Pathogen B has a higher true reproduction number than reported
R0 cannot be equal unless the generation intervals are also equal

explanations.a: Correct: R0 is a per-generation count, not a per-time-unit rate, so the pathogen completing generations five times faster reaches the same per-generation multiplication five times sooner in calendar time.
explanations.b: This is the classic error the lesson warns against -- equal R0 does not imply equal real-time speed when generation intervals differ.
explanations.c: R0 as reported is per-generation and is unaffected by how long a generation takes; there is no hidden adjustment needed.
explanations.d: R0 and generation interval are independent quantities; two pathogens can share an R0 while differing completely in generation time.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning steps that show why R0 = 1 is called the epidemic threshold.

items.text: Define R0 as expected secondary cases per generation in a fully susceptible population
Note that if R0 > 1, each generation produces more cases than the last, so the chain grows
Note that if R0 < 1, each generation produces fewer cases than the last, so the chain shrinks toward extinction
Conclude that R0 = 1 is the exact boundary between sustained spread and self-limiting extinction

questions.explanation: The threshold logic starts from the per-generation definition, examines both directions away from 1, and only then names 1 as the boundary.

questions.prompt: Match each SIR quantity to what it represents.

right.text: Transmission rate per contact, per unit time
Recovery (removal) rate per unit time
Mean duration of the infectious period
R0 in the SIR model

questions.explanation: Beta and gamma are rates; their ratio beta/gamma combines them into the dimensionless R0, and 1/gamma converts the recovery rate into a mean duration.

lessons.label: Computing R0: The Next-Generation Matrix

sections.heading: Beyond beta/gamma: heterogeneous populations
sections.body: R0 = beta/gamma works for a single homogeneous compartment, but real populations split into age groups, risk groups, or disease stages with different contact patterns and different disease dynamics, and a single scalar ratio cannot capture that. Diekmann, Heesterbeek and Metz formalized the fix in 1990 with the next-generation operator: build a matrix K where entry K_ij is the expected number of new infections in group i produced by one infected individual in group j over their full infectious period, accounting for who contacts whom and at what rate. R0 is then defined as the dominant eigenvalue -- the spectral radius -- of this next-generation matrix, which reduces to the familiar beta/gamma when there is only one group. This definition is only well-posed because of a guarantee from linear algebra: since K's entries are expected counts of new infections, they are all non-negative by construction, and the Perron-Frobenius theorem states that any matrix with non-negative entries has a real, non-negative dominant eigenvalue. That is what lets modelers call the spectral radius of K 'the' R0 with a single unambiguous number, rather than having to worry about complex or negative eigenvalues dominating the calculation.

sections.heading: The F and V matrices: van den Driessche and Watmough (2002)
sections.body: For compartmental ODE models with several infected stages -- exposed, mildly infected, severely infected, hospitalized -- van den Driessche and Watmough gave a general recipe for building the next-generation matrix directly from the model equations. Linearize the infected-compartment equations near the disease-free equilibrium and split the result into F, the matrix of rates at which new infections are generated, and V, the matrix of rates at which individuals move between infected compartments or exit them (progression, recovery, death). R0 is then the spectral radius of the matrix FV^-1: F captures 'in-flow' of new cases, V^-1 captures how long individuals spend, and in what states, before leaving the infected class, so FV^-1 tallies secondary cases exactly the way the simple beta/gamma ratio does, but for arbitrarily many compartments and groups.

sections.heading: Why the recipe matters for real models
sections.body: This F/V machinery is what lets modelers report a single R0 for an SEIR model with age-stratified contact matrices, or for a disease with both symptomatic and asymptomatic infectious stages carrying different transmission rates -- cases that a hand-derived beta/gamma cannot handle. It is now the standard method cited whenever a paper reports R0 for a model with more than one infected compartment, and the 2002 paper is among the most-cited works in mathematical epidemiology precisely because it turned a case-by-case derivation into a mechanical, reproducible calculation.

lessons.workedExample: Consider a two-group model splitting a population into children and adults, where children contact each other more than they contact adults. Suppose the next-generation matrix (new infections per group, per one initial case) is K = [[4, 1], [1, 2]]: a child case causes 4 new child infections and 1 adult infection; an adult case causes 1 child infection and 2 adult infections. The dominant eigenvalue of K -- found by solving the characteristic equation lambda^2 - 6*lambda + 7 = 0 -- is 3 + sqrt(2), approximately 4.41, so R0 approx 4.41, noticeably higher than either diagonal entry alone because the two groups reinforce each other's transmission. Reporting only 'the child R0 is 4' or 'the adult R0 is 2' would understate the true threshold value for the mixed population.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because many student models informally add an age-structured or multi-stage compartment (exposed vs. infectious, or vaccinated vs. unvaccinated) without updating how they compute R0, and then misapply beta/gamma to a model it no longer fits. A strong answer recognizes that R0 for a multi-compartment model requires an eigenvalue of a next-generation matrix, can name the F and V matrices from van den Driessche and Watmough (2002), and can explain in words what F and V represent even without walking through the full linear algebra.

questions.prompt: In the van den Driessche and Watmough (2002) framework, what do the F and V matrices represent?

options.text: F is the rate of new-infection generation; V is the rate of transitions between infected compartments (progression, recovery, death)
F is the total population size; V is the vaccination coverage
F is the force of infection in adults; V is the force of infection in children
F and V are both transmission rates, one for symptomatic and one for asymptomatic cases

explanations.a: Correct: F captures new infections entering the infected compartments, V captures movement out of and between those compartments; R0 is the spectral radius of FV^-1.
explanations.b: Neither matrix represents population size or coverage; both are built from the linearized infected-compartment dynamics.
explanations.c: F and V are not split by age group in this framework; that structure belongs to the next-generation matrix K itself, not the F/V decomposition.
explanations.d: F and V are general rate matrices for any compartment structure, not specifically a symptomatic/asymptomatic split.

questions.prompt: Why is R0 defined as the SPECTRAL RADIUS (dominant eigenvalue) of the next-generation matrix rather than, say, its trace or average entry?

options.text: The dominant eigenvalue describes the long-run per-generation growth factor of the total infected population across all groups
The trace is undefined for non-square next-generation matrices
Eigenvalues are easier to compute by hand than sums
The spectral radius is always equal to beta/gamma regardless of group structure

explanations.a: Correct: the dominant eigenvalue governs how the vector of infections in each group scales generation to generation once the group proportions settle into their stable mix, exactly generalizing the single-group growth factor.
explanations.b: Next-generation matrices from this framework are square by construction (groups by groups), so this is not the reason.
explanations.c: Eigenvalues of anything beyond 2x2 matrices are generally harder, not easier, to compute by hand than a simple average.
explanations.d: The spectral radius only reduces to beta/gamma in the single-group special case; with multiple groups it is generally a different, larger value, as the worked example shows.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the van den Driessche and Watmough (2002) recipe for computing R0.

items.text: Identify the disease-free equilibrium of the compartmental model
Linearize the infected-compartment equations near that equilibrium
Split the linearization into F (new infections) and V (transitions between/out of infected compartments)
Compute the spectral radius of FV^-1 as R0

questions.explanation: The recipe proceeds from finding the equilibrium, to linearizing around it, to decomposing into F and V, to the final eigenvalue calculation.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its role in next-generation-matrix R0 calculations.

right.text: Introduced the next-generation operator for heterogeneous populations
Gave the F, V matrix recipe for compartmental ODE models
The dominant eigenvalue of the next-generation matrix, defined as R0
Reduces the matrix formula to R0 = beta/gamma

questions.explanation: The 1990 paper set up the general operator; the 2002 paper made it computable from ODEs; the eigenvalue is the actual quantity called R0; and the one-group case collapses back to the simple ratio.

lessons.label: Generation Time versus Serial Interval

sections.heading: Two clocks that are not the same clock
sections.body: The generation time (or generation interval) is the time between when an infector was infected and when they infect someone else -- an infection-to-infection interval. The serial interval is the time between symptom onset in an infector and symptom onset in the person they infect -- an onset-to-onset interval. They sound interchangeable but are not: infection times are almost never directly observed in a real outbreak (you rarely know the exact moment of exposure), while symptom-onset dates are routinely collected through case interviews, so the serial interval is the quantity epidemiologists can actually measure, and the generation time is the quantity the mathematics of R0 actually needs.

sections.heading: Why they diverge: Svensson (2007)
sections.body: Svensson's 2007 analysis showed the two intervals share the same mean under reasonable assumptions but differ in variance and shape: the serial interval is built from the difference of two incubation periods (infector's and infectee's) plus the generation interval, so its distribution is effectively 'noisier' and can even take negative values in principle -- an infectee showing symptoms before their infector does, which happens in real contact-tracing data when the infectee has a short incubation period and the infector a long one. Svensson also stressed that because generation time is unobservable, models routinely substitute the serial interval as a practical proxy, which is valid for estimating R0's mean but can distort variance-sensitive calculations if the substitution is not made carefully.

sections.heading: From growth rate to R0: Wallinga and Lipsitch (2007)
sections.body: An emerging outbreak's exponential growth rate r is often the first quantity available -- read straight off a rising epidemic curve -- while R0 is what policymakers want. Wallinga and Lipsitch connected the two through the Euler-Lotka equation from demography: R0 = 1/M(-r), where M is the moment generating function of the generation-interval distribution. For a generation interval that is simply a fixed constant T, this collapses to the familiar-looking R0 = exp(rT); for a more realistic gamma-distributed generation interval with shape k and scale theta it gives R0 = (1 + r*theta)^k. The key insight is that the SAME observed growth rate r implies a different R0 depending on the assumed shape of the generation-interval distribution, not just its mean -- so misjudging generation-interval variance, not just its average, biases R0 estimates from growth-rate data.

lessons.workedExample: An outbreak's case counts are doubling every 5 days, giving an exponential growth rate r = ln(2)/5 approx 0.139 per day. If the mean generation interval is treated as a fixed constant T = 6 days, the Wallinga-Lipsitch formula gives R0 = exp(0.139 x 6) = exp(0.83) approx 2.3. But if the generation interval instead follows a gamma distribution with the same mean of 6 days and considerable spread (shape k=2, scale theta=3), the formula R0 = (1 + r*theta)^k gives R0 = (1 + 0.139x3)^2 approx (1.417)^2 approx 2.0 -- a visibly different R0 from the same growth-rate data, purely because the two calculations assumed different generation-interval shapes around the identical mean.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because student projects that estimate R0 from a rising case count almost always plug in a single point-estimate 'generation time' pulled from a paper without checking whether that paper reported generation time or serial interval, and without acknowledging that the shape of the distribution, not just its mean, changes the answer. A strong answer states plainly that generation time is infection-to-infection and unobservable, serial interval is onset-to-onset and observable, and that converting a growth rate to R0 via Wallinga and Lipsitch (2007) requires committing to a full distribution, not just a mean.

questions.prompt: Why do epidemiologists typically use the serial interval rather than the generation time when analyzing real contact-tracing data?

options.text: Serial interval is based on symptom-onset dates, which are observable, while generation time requires infection dates, which usually are not
Serial interval is always larger and therefore more conservative
Generation time and serial interval are mathematically identical, so the choice makes no difference
Generation time can only be computed for vector-borne diseases

explanations.a: Correct: infection times are rarely known precisely, but symptom-onset dates are routinely collected in case interviews, making the serial interval the practically measurable stand-in.
explanations.b: There is no general rule that serial interval is always larger; Svensson (2007) shows they share roughly the same mean but differ in variance and shape.
explanations.c: They share a similar mean under reasonable assumptions but differ in variance and can even differ in sign (a negative serial interval is possible), so they are not identical.
explanations.d: Generation time is a general concept for any transmissible infection, not restricted to vector-borne disease.

questions.prompt: In the Wallinga and Lipsitch (2007) approach, why does assuming a different SHAPE for the generation-interval distribution (while keeping the same mean) change the R0 estimated from a fixed growth rate r?

options.text: Because R0 = 1/M(-r) depends on the full moment generating function of the distribution, not just its mean
Because the growth rate r itself changes when the distribution shape changes
It does not change; only the mean generation interval affects R0
Because shape only matters for serial interval, not generation interval

explanations.a: Correct: the moment generating function M evaluated at -r encodes the whole distribution's shape, so two distributions with equal means but different variances/shapes generally give different R0 for the same r, exactly as the worked example shows (2.3 vs. 2.0).
explanations.b: r is the observed epidemic growth rate, an input to the formula; it does not depend on which generation-interval distribution the analyst later assumes.
explanations.c: This is the misconception the lesson warns against -- the mean alone is not sufficient; the worked example shows two different R0 values from the same mean.
explanations.d: The formula concerns the generation-interval distribution specifically; shape sensitivity is not restricted to serial interval.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps in converting an observed epidemic growth rate into an R0 estimate via Wallinga and Lipsitch (2007).

items.text: Observe the exponential growth rate r from the rising epidemic curve
Choose a generation-interval distribution (mean and shape) for the pathogen
Compute the moment generating function of that distribution evaluated at -r
Compute R0 as 1 divided by that moment-generating-function value

questions.explanation: The Euler-Lotka-based method starts from the observed growth rate, requires a full generation-interval distribution as input, evaluates the Laplace/moment-generating transform, and only then produces R0.

questions.prompt: Match each interval concept to its correct description.

right.text: Infection-to-infection interval; not directly observable
Symptom-onset-to-symptom-onset interval; observable via case interviews
Showed the two intervals share a mean but differ in variance and can even go negative
Gave the formula converting growth rate r into R0 via the generation-interval distribution

questions.explanation: Generation time is the theoretical infection-to-infection quantity; serial interval is its observable onset-based proxy; Svensson formalized their relationship; Wallinga and Lipsitch built the growth-rate-to-R0 conversion on top of it.

lessons.label: The Effective Reproduction Number Rt

sections.heading: R0 only applies once: to a fully susceptible population
sections.body: R0 describes the very first case in a population with zero immunity and zero behavior change. Once an epidemic runs, susceptibles are depleted, some people gain immunity from infection or vaccination, and behavior often shifts (masking, distancing, closures) -- so the actual number of secondary cases per infector falls over time even if the pathogen's intrinsic transmissibility is unchanged. The effective reproduction number, Rt (sometimes written R_e), captures this real, time-varying value. In the simplest depletion-only case, Rt = R0 x S(t)/N, where S(t)/N is the fraction of the population still susceptible at time t: as S(t)/N shrinks from 1 toward 0, Rt shrinks proportionally from R0 toward 0, crossing the epidemic threshold of 1 exactly at the herd-immunity point.

sections.heading: Two ways to estimate Rt from real data: case vs. instantaneous
sections.body: Rt cannot usually be computed from first principles during a real outbreak because S(t)/N, contact rates, and control-measure effects are not directly known; instead it is estimated backward from case counts. Wallinga and Teunis (2004) defined the case reproduction number: for each case, look forward at everyone infected by them (in expectation, via the generation-interval distribution) and average across cases infected around the same time. This method is retrospective by nature -- it needs data from AFTER the time point of interest to know who those cases infected -- so it estimates the transmission conditions in effect when today's cases were infected, but only once enough future data has accumulated, which delays real-time reporting.

sections.heading: The instantaneous reproduction number and EpiEstim: Cori et al. (2013)
sections.body: Cori and colleagues instead defined the instantaneous reproduction number: for a given day t, divide the number of new cases on day t by the sum of past cases weighted by the generation-interval distribution, capturing the reproduction number implied by transmission conditions AT time t using only data up to time t. Written out, their estimator is Rt = I_t / sum_s(I_{t-s} x w_s), where I_t is the number of new cases on day t, I_{t-s} is the number of new cases s days earlier, and w_s is the probability the generation-interval distribution assigns to a lag of s days -- the numerator is today's incidence, the denominator is a weighted sum of past incidence standing in for how much of today's cases each earlier day could plausibly have generated. Because it needs no future data, this instantaneous approach is what powers real-time Rt dashboards, implemented in the widely used EpiEstim R package, which became one of the standard tools for near-real-time Rt tracking during COVID-19. The case and instantaneous definitions can diverge noticeably right after a sudden change in transmission (like a lockdown), since one is forward-looking and the other backward-looking by construction.

lessons.workedExample: A pathogen has R0 = 3 in a fully susceptible city of 1,000,000. Partway through the outbreak, 600,000 people have been infected and recovered (assume permanent immunity, no vaccination), so S(t)/N = 400,000/1,000,000 = 0.4. Depletion alone gives Rt = R0 x S(t)/N = 3 x 0.4 = 1.2 -- still above the threshold of 1, so cases are still growing, just more slowly than at the start. Herd immunity in this simple model is reached when Rt = 1, i.e., S(t)/N = 1/R0 = 1/3, meaning roughly 67% of the population needs to have been infected (or vaccinated) before case counts begin to decline on their own.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe Rt because it is the number that actually matters for real-time decisions -- 'is R0 = 3' is a historical or intrinsic fact, while 'is Rt currently above or below 1' is what determines whether a policy is working right now. A strong answer distinguishes the simple S(t)/N depletion formula (useful for herd-immunity reasoning) from the real-data estimation methods, and can explain WHY Wallinga and Teunis (2004)'s case reproduction number needs future data (it looks at who each case infected) while Cori et al. (2013)'s instantaneous number does not (it looks backward at incidence weighted by the generation interval).

questions.prompt: Why does the case reproduction number of Wallinga and Teunis (2004) require data from AFTER the time point being estimated?

options.text: Because it is computed by counting, for cases infected around that time, how many people they went on to infect
Because generation intervals cannot be measured until an outbreak ends
Because it requires knowing S(t)/N, which is only available retrospectively
It does not require future data; that is a property of the instantaneous method instead

explanations.a: Correct: the case reproduction number is a forward-looking average of secondary infections caused by cases at time t, so it can only be finalized once enough of those secondary infections have actually occurred and been observed.
explanations.b: Generation intervals are estimated from paired infector-infectee data generally and are not the reason this specific method needs future data; the reason is the forward-looking definition itself.
explanations.c: The case reproduction number as defined by Wallinga and Teunis does not require directly knowing S(t)/N; it works from observed transmission pairs/incidence data.
explanations.d: This reverses the two methods: the instantaneous number (Cori et al., 2013) is the one that uses only past data; the case reproduction number is the forward-looking one.

questions.prompt: In the simple depletion model Rt = R0 x S(t)/N, at what value of S(t)/N does Rt cross the epidemic threshold of 1?

options.text: S(t)/N = R0

explanations.a: Correct: setting R0 x S(t)/N = 1 and solving gives S(t)/N = 1/R0, which is exactly the herd-immunity threshold condition (e.g., 1/3 for R0=3, matching the worked example).
explanations.b: S(t)/N is a fraction between 0 and 1; setting it equal to R0 (which is 3 in the worked example) is not a valid fraction and does not solve the threshold equation.
explanations.c: This does not satisfy R0 x S(t)/N = 1 in general; it is not the algebraic solution to the threshold condition.
explanations.d: This is not the solution to R0 x S(t)/N = 1; dividing R0 by 2 has no basis in the depletion formula.

questions.prompt: Order the events in an outbreak's trajectory under the simple depletion model, from earliest to latest.

items.text: S(t)/N = 1 (fully susceptible population); Rt = R0
S(t)/N falls below 1 as cases accumulate; Rt falls below R0 but remains above 1
S(t)/N reaches 1/R0; Rt crosses down through the threshold value of 1
S(t)/N continues falling; Rt drops below 1 and case counts decline

questions.explanation: Rt tracks S(t)/N proportionally, starting at R0 when everyone is susceptible and falling monotonically as immunity accumulates, crossing 1 at the herd-immunity threshold and continuing to fall thereafter.

questions.prompt: Match each Rt estimation approach to its defining feature.

right.text: Rt = R0 x S(t)/N, ignoring behavior change and control measures
Wallinga and Teunis (2004); forward-looking, needs future case data
Cori et al. (2013); backward-looking, usable in real time
Widely used software implementing the instantaneous-Rt method

questions.explanation: The depletion formula is the textbook simplification; Wallinga-Teunis and Cori et al. are the two dominant real-data estimation approaches, and EpiEstim is the software built on the latter.

lessons.label: R0 Across Pathogens

sections.heading: The canonical comparison table
sections.body: Textbooks and public-health briefings routinely list R0 ranges to give intuition for how contagious different diseases are relative to each other: measles is the standard extreme example at roughly R0 = 12-18, driven by its airborne spread and long infectious period; smallpox, also airborne but less efficiently transmitted, sits around R0 = 5-7; pandemic influenza strains (including the 1918 and 2009 pandemics) are typically estimated around R0 = 1.3-2; SARS in the 2002-2003 outbreak is usually placed around R0 = 2-3; and early estimates of COVID-19 in Wuhan before interventions were also around R0 = 2-3. The ordering broadly tracks route of transmission (airborne aerosol diseases like measles transmit far more readily than diseases requiring closer or more limited contact) and duration of infectiousness, though the table compresses a great deal of underlying variability into single numbers.

sections.heading: Why these numbers are estimated, not measured directly
sections.body: None of these values were read off an instrument; each is inferred from models fit to case data, serological surveys, or contact-tracing chains, using methods including SIR/SEIR model fitting, final-size equations applied to serosurveys, and the growth-rate-to-R0 conversion from generation intervals covered earlier in this unit. Different studies of the SAME pathogen commonly use different methods, different populations (dense urban vs. rural, different age structures, different baseline contact patterns), and different time windows, and each of those choices can shift the estimate substantially -- which is why any single R0 range should be read as a summary of a body of estimates, not a physical constant of the pathogen.

sections.heading: The comparison pitfall
sections.body: Because the underlying estimation methods and populations differ study to study, directly comparing a headline R0 for one disease against a headline R0 for another -- 'measles is roughly six times as transmissible as pandemic flu' -- silently assumes the estimates were produced comparably, which they usually were not. A measles R0 estimated from a densely mixing 19th-century island population and a flu R0 estimated from a 21st-century contact-tracing study differ not just because the pathogens differ, but because the contact structures, susceptibility profiles, and estimation techniques differ too. This comparison pitfall is the subject of the next lesson in this unit, which examines how a systematic review reopened the specific case of the measles 12-18 figure.

lessons.workedExample: A science-fair project claims 'our modeled pathogen has R0 = 2.5, making it roughly as transmissible as SARS and about half as transmissible as smallpox.' A judge should recognize this as a reasonable, appropriately hedged comparison, since it places the value within a commonly cited range (SARS approx 2-3) rather than asserting false precision. It would be a red flag, by contrast, to claim 'our pathogen is exactly 0.15 more transmissible than the 2009 flu pandemic (R0=1.35 vs 1.2)' as if both figures were exact physical measurements taken by the same method in the same population -- the headline ranges (pandemic flu approx 1.3-2) are summaries across heterogeneous studies, not single precise numbers to be subtracted from each other.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the comparison table because it is genuinely useful for building intuition (measles really is far more transmissible than seasonal flu) but is routinely over-interpreted by students who treat a rough historical range as a precise, universally comparable constant. A strong answer can recite the canonical ranges roughly (measles highest, smallpox next, SARS and early COVID-19 similar mid-range, pandemic flu lowest of the group) while also flagging that these ranges come from different methods and populations, so fine-grained cross-disease comparisons need the same caution as fine-grained cross-study comparisons within one disease.

questions.prompt: Which pathogen in the canonical comparison table has the highest commonly cited R0 range?

options.text: Measles, at roughly 12-18
Smallpox, at roughly 5-7
SARS, at roughly 2-3
Pandemic influenza, at roughly 1.3-2

explanations.a: Correct: measles is the standard highest example in this table, commonly cited around 12-18, reflecting efficient airborne spread and a long infectious period.
explanations.b: Smallpox at roughly 5-7 is lower than measles in the canonical table, not the highest.
explanations.c: SARS at roughly 2-3 sits in the middle of this comparison group, well below measles.
explanations.d: Pandemic influenza at roughly 1.3-2 is the lowest of the four pathogens listed in this table.

questions.prompt: Two published studies report different R0 values for the same pathogen. What is the most likely explanation according to this lesson?

options.text: The studies plausibly used different estimation methods, populations, or time windows, all of which can shift the estimate
One of the two studies must have made an arithmetic error, since R0 is a fixed biological constant
R0 cannot legitimately vary between studies of the same pathogen
The difference can only be explained by a mutation in the pathogen between the two studies

explanations.a: Correct: this lesson stresses that R0 estimates depend on estimation method, population contact structure, and time window, so legitimate variation across studies of the same pathogen is expected, not necessarily an error.
explanations.b: Differing R0 estimates do not imply an error; R0 is not a fixed biological constant independent of context, as this lesson and the next lesson in this unit both emphasize.
explanations.c: Variation between studies is expected and documented, not a sign that something is illegitimate.
explanations.d: A pathogen mutation is one possible but not the most general or likely explanation; method and population differences are far more commonly the driver.

questions.prompt: Order these pathogens from LOWEST to HIGHEST commonly cited R0 range, per the canonical comparison table in this lesson.

items.text: Pandemic influenza (approx 1.3-2)
SARS / early COVID-19 (approx 2-3)
Smallpox (approx 5-7)
Measles (approx 12-18)

questions.explanation: The canonical table orders pandemic influenza lowest, SARS and early COVID-19 next, smallpox higher still, and measles as the highest commonly cited range.

questions.prompt: Match each pathogen to its commonly cited R0 range from this lesson.

right.text: Approximately 12-18
Approximately 5-7
Approximately 2-3 (SARS, based on early outbreak contact-tracing studies)
Approximately 2-3 (early Wuhan COVID-19 estimates)

questions.explanation: Measles and smallpox each have distinct canonical ranges; SARS and early COVID-19 share a similar mid-range estimate of roughly 2-3 in this table.

lessons.label: The Limits and Misuses of R0

sections.heading: R0 is a function of context, not a fixed property of a pathogen
sections.body: Delamater and colleagues' 2019 review, 'Complexity of the Basic Reproduction Number (R0),' laid out why R0 is frequently misunderstood as an intrinsic biological constant when it is actually a function of contact rates, infectious duration, and population structure -- quantities that depend on host behavior and setting, not on the pathogen genome alone.
