The same virus produces a different R0 in a dense urban household with many contacts than in a sparse rural community with few; a different R0 in a population with pre-existing partial immunity from related pathogens than in an immunologically naive one; and a different R0 depending on the estimation method applied to the same underlying data, since different models make different assumptions about mixing patterns and generation intervals.

sections.heading: The measles 12-18 figure, reopened: Guerra et al. (2017)
sections.body: The 12-18 range for measles, repeated across textbooks for decades, was systematically re-examined by Guerra and colleagues in 2017. Reviewing 18 studies that together produced 58 distinct R0 estimates meeting their inclusion criteria, they found feasible measles R0 values spanning roughly 3.7 to 203.3 -- a far wider spread than the familiar range suggests, driven by differences in the populations studied (varying density, age structure, and contact patterns), the time periods (pre- versus post-vaccination era social mixing), and the estimation methods used across studies. The 12-18 figure is not wrong so much as it is an average-of-averages that discards the real variability documented in the underlying literature.

sections.heading: Why a single headline number misleads
sections.body: Collapsing a distribution of context-dependent estimates into one repeated number creates two failure modes: it invites false precision (treating '12-18' as if it applies unchanged to any population, when the Guerra review shows measles R0 in a specific setting could plausibly sit well outside that range), and it obscures the actionable levers -- since R0 is built from contact rate and infectious duration, a policy that cuts contacts (school closure) or shortens infectious duration (early isolation) measurably changes the real R0 in that setting, which a single 'the R0 of measles is 15' framing does not communicate. Roberts and Heesterbeek (2003) built a tool specifically for this problem: the type-reproduction number, T, which asks how many secondary cases a single case in one target sub-population would generate if transmission into every OTHER sub-population were fully controlled. Where a single R0 forces an intervention to average its effect across the whole population, T lets a modeler target reduction at the sub-population actually driving spread -- a school-age group for measles, say -- and ask how much control effort in that group alone would push transmission below threshold. For a science-fair project, citing a headline R0 without naming the population and method it came from repeats exactly the error these reviews were written to correct.

lessons.workedExample: A project reports 'we modeled measles with R0=15, matching the textbook value.' A judge asks: 15 for what population and time period? If the model represents a modern, moderately dense suburban school district, citing an unqualified 12-18 range (drawn largely from historical, densely mixing populations) may overstate transmissibility for that setting -- and Guerra et al. (2017)'s finding of a 3.7-to-203.3 feasible range across 58 estimates shows the 'right' figure is highly context-dependent. A stronger project either cites a study whose population resembles its modeled setting, or explicitly states R0 was chosen as a mid-range illustrative assumption rather than a precisely sourced figure.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because it is the single most common overreach in student epidemiology projects: quoting a headline R0 as though it were a fixed constant of the pathogen, rather than the output of a specific model applied to a specific population. A strong answer can name Delamater et al. (2019) for the general claim that R0 depends on contact rate, infectious duration, and population structure, and can name Guerra et al. (2017) for the concrete case showing the celebrated measles 12-18 figure understates the true documented range (3.7 to 203.3 across 58 estimates) once population and method differences are accounted for.

questions.prompt: According to Delamater et al. (2019), R0 varies primarily because of differences in:

options.text: Contact rates, infectious duration, and population structure across settings
Random measurement noise that averages out with enough studies
The pathogen's genome mutating between every study
Which continent the study was conducted on, independent of any other factor

explanations.a: Correct: Delamater et al. (2019) identify contact rates, infectious duration, and population structure as the drivers of R0 variability, framing R0 as context-dependent rather than a fixed biological constant.
explanations.b: The review frames the variability as real and structural (driven by contact patterns and population differences), not as noise that would simply average away.
explanations.c: Genomic mutation is not the mechanism identified in this review; the same pathogen genotype can still show different R0 across different contact and population contexts.
explanations.d: Continent alone is not the driver identified; it is contact rate, infectious duration, and population structure, which can vary within or across any geography.

questions.prompt: Guerra et al. (2017) reviewed measles R0 estimates and found a feasible range of approximately:

options.text: 3.7 to 203.3, drawn from 58 estimates across 18 studies
12 to 18, confirming the traditional textbook figure exactly
1 to 2, similar to pandemic influenza
exactly 15, with no meaningful variation across studies

explanations.a: Correct: the systematic review found 58 R0 estimates across 18 qualifying studies spanning roughly 3.7 to 203.3, far wider than the commonly cited 12-18 range.
explanations.b: The review's point is precisely that the true documented range is much wider than 12-18, not a confirmation of that narrower figure.
explanations.c: This range belongs to pandemic influenza in the earlier comparison table, not to the measles estimates Guerra et al. reviewed.
explanations.d: The review found substantial variation across studies, not a single confirmed value with no spread.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the argument this lesson makes against treating R0 as a fixed constant.

items.text: Note that R0 is built from contact rate, infectious duration, and population structure (Delamater et al., 2019)
Observe that these inputs vary by setting, time period, and estimation method
Show the measles 12-18 figure understates the true documented range once this variability is accounted for (Guerra et al., 2017)
Conclude that a headline R0 number should be reported with its population and method, not quoted as a universal constant

questions.explanation: The argument builds from R0's structural dependence on contact/duration/population, to the resulting variability across studies, to the concrete measles case, to the practical reporting conclusion.

questions.prompt: Match each source to its specific contribution regarding the limits of R0.

right.text: General review arguing R0 depends on contact rates, infectious duration, and population structure, not fixed biology
Systematic review of measles R0 finding a feasible range of roughly 3.7-203.3 across 58 estimates

questions.explanation: Delamater et al. make the general conceptual argument; Guerra et al. supply the concrete measles case study that demonstrates it.

units.label: Reading Epidemic Curves and Model Output

lessons.label: The Anatomy of an Epidemic Curve

sections.heading: Exponential Growth and Doubling Time
sections.body: In the earliest days of an outbreak, almost the entire population is susceptible, so each infectious person passes the pathogen to roughly R0 others per generation interval Tg. Case counts therefore compound: C(t) ≈ C0 * e^(rt), where r is the exponential growth rate. Plotting log(cases) against time turns this curve into a straight line, and a linear regression on that log-scale plot gives r directly from surveillance data — no transmission model required. The doubling time, Td = ln(2)/r, converts r into something actionable: how many days until case counts double. Because r is read straight off the counts, it is one of the first quantitative signals available in a new outbreak, well before contact-tracing data exists to estimate R0 directly.

sections.heading: Converting r into R0
sections.body: r is a property of the data; R0 is a property of a transmission model, and the two connect only through an assumption about the generation interval Tg, the time between when one person is infected and when they infect the next. In the simple SIR model with constant recovery rate gamma, the early exponential rate is r = gamma(R0 - 1), so R0 = 1 + r/gamma = 1 + r*Tg. Wallinga and Lipsitch (2007) generalized this to arbitrary generation-interval distributions using the discretized Euler-Lotka equation borrowed from demography, where a population's age structure grows at a rate set by its birth-timing distribution in the same way a case count grows at a rate set by its transmission-timing distribution. Their key result is that the same measured r implies a larger R0 when the generation interval is longer, or more variable — a slower or more dispersed per-generation process needs a bigger per-generation multiplier to reproduce an identical daily growth rate. This is why independent groups analyzing an identical case curve can publish visibly different R0 values in the same week of an outbreak: they assumed different generation-interval distributions, not different underlying case data.

sections.heading: The Peak and the Decline
sections.body: Growth continues only while the effective reproduction number Rt = R0 * (S/N) exceeds 1. As infections accumulate, susceptibles S deplete, Rt falls, and incidence peaks at the instant S/N = 1/R0 — the threshold reached from below, not the epidemic's end. Past the peak, incidence declines because Rt < 1, but the decline is usually slower and messier than the rise: susceptible depletion near the peak is gradual rather than abrupt, behavioral changes and seasonal forcing shift transmission independent of the model's fixed beta, and reporting delays smear the tail of the observed curve well after true transmission has fallen. The 1918 influenza pandemic's Philadelphia curve is a textbook case of the reverse problem: after the city allowed a large Liberty Loan parade on September 28, the growth phase was so explosive that daily deaths roughly doubled within days, a rate of rise the decline phase weeks later never came close to matching.

lessons.workedExample: Li et al. (2020) fit the early Wuhan case-count curve and reported a doubling time near 7.4 days, implying r ≈ ln(2)/7.4 ≈ 0.094/day. Using their mean serial-interval estimate of about 7.5 days as a proxy for Tg, the simple relation R0 = 1 + r*Tg gives R0 ≈ 1 + 0.094 × 7.5 ≈ 1.7 — lower than their own reported R0 ≈ 2.2, because their full renewal-equation calculation used the entire generation-interval distribution, not just its mean, and the distribution's variance also pushes the R0 estimate upward for a fixed r.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees 'R0 = 2.4' on a poster will ask how that number was obtained, and the correct answer is never 'read directly off the case curve' — r comes from the curve, R0 comes from r plus an assumed generation-interval distribution. Students who cannot state that assumption, or who treat r and R0 as interchangeable, have not understood what their own model measured. This also explains why independent teams analyzing the same epidemic curve report different R0 values: a signature of differing generation-interval assumptions, not of bad data.

questions.prompt: A researcher fits C(t) ≈ C0 e^(rt) to early outbreak case counts using linear regression on log-transformed data. What does the resulting r represent?

options.text: A quantity read directly off the case data, independent of any transmission-model assumption
The basic reproduction number R0
The mean generation interval Tg
The herd-immunity threshold 1/R0

explanations.a: Correct: r is the slope of log(cases) vs. time, obtainable by regression alone, with no model of transmission needed.
explanations.b: R0 requires r plus an assumed generation-interval distribution; it is not read off the curve directly.
explanations.c: Tg is a separate, independently assumed or estimated quantity used to convert r into R0, not r itself.
explanations.d: The herd-immunity threshold 1/R0 is a susceptible-fraction condition, unrelated to the growth-rate slope.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to convert a measured growth rate r into an R0 estimate.

items.text: Fit log(cases) vs. time to obtain r
Choose or estimate a generation-interval distribution Tg
Apply R0 = 1 + r*Tg (or the Euler-Lotka generalization)
Report R0 with the caveat that a longer assumed Tg raises the estimate for the same r

questions.explanation: r comes first from data alone; only after assuming a generation interval can it be converted to R0, and that assumption must be stated because it drives the final number.

questions.prompt: At the exact instant an epidemic curve peaks in the simple SIR model, which condition holds?

options.text: S/N = 0
I = N

explanations.a: Correct: the peak occurs when Rt = R0*(S/N) = 1, i.e., S/N has fallen to exactly 1/R0.
explanations.b: S/N reaching 0 would mean total depletion of susceptibles, which does not happen exactly and is not the peak condition.
explanations.c: The entire population is never simultaneously infectious in a standard SIR outbreak; this describes no realistic state.
explanations.d: R0 is a fixed model parameter, not a time-varying quantity that reaches 1; it is Rt that crosses 1 at the peak.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its definition.

right.text: ln(2)/r
Slope of log(cases) vs. time
Mean time between successive infections in a transmission chain

questions.explanation: Td is derived algebraically from r; r is measured directly from the log-linear case curve; Tg is a property of the transmission chain needed to convert r into R0.

lessons.label: The Phase Plane and Trajectories

sections.heading: Building the S-I Phase Plane
sections.body: The basic SIR model is two coupled equations, dS/dt = -beta*S*I/N and dI/dt = beta*S*I/N - gamma*I. Dividing one by the other eliminates time entirely: dI/dS = -1 + (gamma*N)/(beta*S) = -1 + 1/(R0 * S/N), using R0 = beta/gamma. This gives a single curve in the S-I plane — the phase-plane trajectory — that traces the epidemic's path independent of how fast time is actually passing, which is exactly the trick that lets the equation be solved by direct integration rather than numerically stepping through time. Kermack and McKendrick (1927) integrated this relation to get I + S - (N/R0)*ln(S) = constant, the conserved quantity that defines the trajectory's exact shape for any starting point, and this single algebraic relation is what the S-I phase plane displays as one continuous curve running from the starting point down toward the eventual final state.

sections.heading: Why There Is No Closed Orbit
sections.body: Predator-prey systems like Lotka-Volterra produce closed orbits in their phase plane: both populations rise and fall cyclically, returning to the same point forever, because both populations can independently increase and decrease. The basic SIR model, without births or deaths, cannot do this, because dS/dt = -beta*S*I/N is never positive — S only decreases, no matter how I behaves. A trajectory that can only move leftward in S can never return to a state it already passed through, so it cannot close into a loop; instead it traces one continuous, non-repeating arc from (S0, I0) toward a final resting point on the S-axis. This single sign constraint is the qualitative fact that separates an epidemic's one-shot burnout from an oscillatory predator-prey cycle, and it is the first thing a phase-plane sketch should make visible before any numbers are computed.

sections.heading: The Turning Point at S = N/R0
sections.body: Because S falls monotonically, the trajectory crosses any given value of S exactly once. dI/dt = 0 exactly where beta*S*I/N = gamma*I, i.e., S/N = 1/R0. Since S is strictly decreasing, this crossing happens at a single, unique moment: before it, dI/dt > 0 and I is climbing; after it, dI/dt < 0 and I is falling. That single crossing is the peak — a geometric feature of the trajectory's shape in the S-I plane, not merely a fact you get from calculus on I(t) alone. It also explains, without any reference to clock time, why every basic-SIR epidemic has exactly one peak: the S-I plane has exactly one point where the trajectory's slope dI/dS switches from positive to negative, because S/N = 1/R0 is crossed only once.

lessons.workedExample: Take R0 = 2.5, N = 1000, with S0 ≈ 1000 and I0 ≈ 0. The conserved quantity gives C ≈ 1000 - 400*ln(1000) ≈ 1000 - 2763.1 = -1763.1 (since N/R0 = 400). The peak occurs at S = 400: I_peak = C - 400 + 400*ln(400) ≈ -1763.1 - 400 + 2396.6 ≈ 233.5. So about 23.4% of the population is infectious simultaneously at the peak — a number obtained purely from the phase-plane conservation relation, without ever solving for I(t) as a function of time.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges who ask a team to 'show me the phase plane' are testing whether the model was actually understood as a dynamical system, not just simulated and plotted. A student who can explain why S can only decrease — and therefore why the trajectory cannot loop like a predator-prey cycle — has grasped the structural difference between SIR and other classic ODE systems. Being able to locate the peak geometrically, at S = N/R0, rather than only by eyeballing where I(t) stops rising, signals real command of the model.

questions.prompt: In the basic SIR model without births or deaths, why doesn't the S-I trajectory form a closed orbit like a Lotka-Volterra predator-prey cycle?

options.text: Because S(t) is monotonically non-increasing, so the trajectory can never return to a previous state
Because I(t) is monotonically increasing throughout the epidemic
Because R0 changes value over the course of the epidemic
Because beta and gamma are not held constant

explanations.a: Correct: dS/dt ≤ 0 always in the basic model, so S never increases, and a trajectory that can only move one direction along S cannot close into a loop.
explanations.b: I(t) rises then falls; it is not monotonic, and this is not the reason orbits fail to close.
explanations.c: R0 = beta/gamma is a fixed model parameter in the basic SIR model; it does not change during the epidemic.
explanations.d: beta and gamma are held constant in the basic SIR model; their constancy is assumed, not the cause of the open trajectory.

questions.prompt: Order these states as they occur along the S-I trajectory during a single epidemic.

items.text: S near N, I small, dI/dt > 0
S falling, I rising
S = N/R0, dI/dt = 0 (the peak)
S < N/R0, I declining toward 0

questions.explanation: S decreases monotonically throughout, so the trajectory passes through these states in exactly this order: initial rise, continued climb, the single peak crossing at S = N/R0, then decline.

questions.prompt: Match each phase-plane quantity to its meaning.

right.text: Always ≤ 0 in the basic SIR model (no births)
Occurs at S = N/R0, the epidemic peak
The trajectory's slope in the S-I plane, found by dividing dI/dt by dS/dt

questions.explanation: dS/dt's fixed sign is what forbids closed orbits; dI/dt = 0 marks the peak at S = N/R0; dI/dS is the time-free trajectory slope obtained by eliminating dt.

questions.prompt: In the worked example (R0 = 2.5, N = 1000), why does the trajectory cross S = 400 exactly once?

options.text: Because S decreases monotonically, so the trajectory crosses any given threshold value at most once
Because I decreases monotonically throughout the epidemic
Because R0 = 2.5 mathematically forces exactly two crossings of any threshold
Because beta equals gamma at that particular point in the trajectory

explanations.a: Correct: since dS/dt ≤ 0 always, S only moves in one direction, so it passes through 400 exactly once on its way from N down toward its final value.
explanations.b: I is not monotonic — it rises before the peak and falls after — so this cannot explain a single crossing of a fixed S value.
explanations.c: R0's numeric value does not determine how many times a threshold is crossed; monotonicity of S is what guarantees a single crossing.
explanations.d: beta and gamma are constants throughout the model; they do not become equal at any particular point on the trajectory.

lessons.label: Peak Timing, Peak Height, and Flattening the Curve

sections.heading: What Sets Peak Height
sections.body: Starting from Kermack and McKendrick's (1927) conserved phase-plane relation with S0 ≈ N and I0 ≈ 0, the peak prevalence works out to I_peak/N = 1 - 1/R0 - ln(R0)/R0. Every term is set by R0 alone: a higher R0 means susceptibles are burned through faster and more of the population is simultaneously infectious when the peak hits. A lower R0 — whether biologically low to begin with, or driven down by interventions that cut beta, such as masking, distancing, or school closures — produces a smaller, later peak, because Rt = R0*(S/N) takes longer to fall to 1 when R0 starts closer to that threshold. Peak timing and peak height move together: whatever slows the approach to S/N = 1/R0 also delays and flattens the peak simultaneously, they are not independent levers.

sections.heading: The Duration-Height Trade-off
sections.body: Reducing beta lowers I_peak/N but also slows how fast S depletes, stretching the epidemic over more calendar time — the classic peak-height-versus-duration trade-off. The final attack rate is governed separately by the implicit final-size equation 1 - S_inf/N = 1 - e^(-R0*(1 - S_inf/N)); near the herd-immunity threshold, a modest reduction in R0 mostly redistributes the same total burden over more days rather than eliminating it, while a larger reduction that pushes R0 below or close to 1 shrinks the total attack rate as well, not just the peak. This is the distinction between 'flattening' the curve, which mainly stretches a similar total burden across more time, and 'bending' it below the epidemic threshold entirely, which shrinks the total burden itself — two related but distinct intervention goals that are frequently conflated in public communication.

sections.heading: Flattening the Curve as Health-System Logic
sections.body: The 'flatten the curve' framing, widely popularized by public-health agencies including the CDC in early 2020, is not primarily about stopping an epidemic — it is about keeping I(t) under a fixed horizontal capacity line, such as the number of available ICU beds or ventilators in a region. Even when total infections stay similar, spreading them over a longer window keeps simultaneous demand from exceeding what a health system can treat at once, which is why the intervention target in this framing is peak height and timing specifically, not only R0's absolute value or the eventual total case count. A model that only reports a total attack rate misses this entirely; the poster needs I(t) plotted against a capacity line to show why the timing of the peak, not just its eventual total, is the quantity interventions are aimed at.

lessons.workedExample: Comparing two scenarios with the peak-height formula: at R0 = 2.5, I_peak/N = 1 - 1/2.5 - ln(2.5)/2.5 = 1 - 0.4 - 0.9163/2.5 ≈ 0.234, so about 23.4% of the population is infectious at once. At R0 = 1.5 (representing interventions that cut transmission), I_peak/N = 1 - 1/1.5 - ln(1.5)/1.5 = 1 - 0.667 - 0.4055/1.5 ≈ 0.063, about 6.3%. Cutting R0 from 2.5 to 1.5 nearly quarters the simultaneous infected fraction — the quantitative content behind a 'flatten the curve' poster.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can quantify 'flattening' rather than just gesture at the famous graphic — can they compute I_peak/N from R0 and show that even a partial reduction in transmission produces a dramatic drop in peak prevalence? They also expect students to distinguish flattening (spreading a similar burden over more time to protect health-system capacity) from actually ending the epidemic (pushing R0 below 1), since conflating the two is a common and telling misunderstanding.

questions.prompt: According to I_peak/N = 1 - 1/R0 - ln(R0)/R0, what happens to peak prevalence as R0 increases?

options.text: It increases, since a larger R0 depletes susceptibles faster before the peak
It decreases, since a larger R0 makes the epidemic end sooner
It stays constant regardless of R0
It becomes undefined for R0 greater than 2

explanations.a: Correct: the worked example shows I_peak/N rising from about 6.3% at R0=1.5 to about 23.4% at R0=2.5, confirming the formula's increasing relationship with R0.
explanations.b: A faster epidemic still infects a larger simultaneous fraction at its peak; ending sooner does not mean a smaller peak.
explanations.c: The formula depends explicitly on R0 through both the 1/R0 and ln(R0)/R0 terms, so peak prevalence is not constant.
explanations.d: The formula is well defined for any R0 greater than 1; there is no singularity at R0 = 2.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps behind how flattening the curve protects a health system.

items.text: Interventions reduce beta, lowering the effective reproduction number
Peak height I_peak/N = 1 - 1/R0 - ln(R0)/R0 falls
Susceptible depletion slows, stretching the epidemic over more days
Peak incidence stays under a fixed health-system capacity line

questions.explanation: Lowering beta is the intervention; it mechanically lowers the peak-height formula's value; the slower depletion this causes is what stretches the timeline; the combined effect is what keeps demand under capacity.

questions.prompt: Match each R0 value from the worked example to its approximate peak prevalence.

right.text: ≈23% of the population infectious simultaneously at peak
≈6% of the population infectious simultaneously at peak

questions.explanation: Plugging each R0 into I_peak/N = 1 - 1/R0 - ln(R0)/R0 gives approximately 23.4% for R0=2.5 and 6.3% for R0=1.5.

questions.prompt: Flattening the curve without pushing R0 below 1 primarily achieves what?

options.text: Spreads a similar total burden over more time, keeping peak demand under a fixed health-system capacity line
Immediately drives Rt below 1 and ends the epidemic within days
Increases the peak height while shortening the epidemic
Has no effect on either peak height or epidemic duration

explanations.a: Correct: as the trade-off section explains, a partial reduction in R0 mainly redistributes similar total burden over a longer window rather than eliminating the epidemic.
explanations.b: If R0 stays above 1, Rt does not drop below 1 from the reduction alone, so the epidemic continues rather than ending within days.
explanations.c: The peak-height formula shows the opposite: lowering R0 decreases peak height, and the epidemic lengthens rather than shortens.
explanations.d: The worked example shows a clear, large effect on peak height (23.4% to 6.3%), so this option contradicts the model's output.

lessons.label: Endemic Equilibria and Oscillations

sections.heading: Adding Demography: Births Refill Susceptibles
sections.body: Without births, the SIR model always burns out to I = 0, as the phase-plane trajectory in an earlier lesson shows: S can only fall, so eventually too few susceptibles remain to sustain transmission. Adding a birth rate mu (balanced by an equal death rate, keeping total population N constant) continuously replenishes S. Now the system can settle at a nontrivial endemic equilibrium (S*, I*), where new infections exactly balance recoveries and where new susceptibles entering by birth exactly balance those removed by infection: S* = N/R0, the same threshold fraction that marked the epidemic peak in the no-demography model, and I* = mu*N*(R0 - 1)/beta, a small but permanently nonzero infectious fraction rather than a transient peak that eventually disappears. This equilibrium exists only because inflow and outflow of susceptibles now balance continuously, a mechanism entirely absent from the closed-population, no-demography model of earlier lessons.

sections.heading: Damped Oscillations Toward Equilibrium
sections.body: Linearizing the SIR-with-demography equations around (S*, I*) produces complex eigenvalues with negative real parts — a stable spiral rather than a stable node, the qualitative signature that distinguishes this system from the simple no-demography case. Practically, this means the system does not settle smoothly: it overshoots the equilibrium, undershoots on the rebound, and rings through several shrinking cycles before flattening out, much like a damped pendulum settling after being pushed. Anderson and May (1991), in their reference text Infectious Diseases of Humans, showed the natural period of this damped ringing is approximately T ≈ 2*pi*sqrt(A*D), where A ≈ 1/(mu*(R0-1)) is the mean age at infection — younger on average for pathogens with higher R0, since faster transmission catches people sooner in life — and D is the mean infectious period.

sections.heading: Linking the Model to Real Childhood-Disease Cycles
sections.body: The deterministic model predicts this ringing damps out over time, leaving a flat endemic level with no further oscillation. Real pre-vaccination measles data does not flatten this way — London and Yorke (1973) documented persistent, roughly biennial (about two-year) recurrent outbreaks in large U.S. cities including New York and Baltimore, cycles that kept recurring for decades rather than damping away. The natural damped period computed from the demographic model lands close to that observed cycle length for realistic measles parameters, but sustaining the ringing indefinitely, rather than letting it damp away as the bare model predicts, requires an external driver: seasonal forcing from school-term contact patterns pumps transmission back up each autumn, re-exciting the oscillation that demography alone would let decay to a flat line.

lessons.workedExample: For pre-vaccine measles with a mean age at infection A ≈ 5 years (1825 days) and a mean infectious period D ≈ 6.5 days, T ≈ 2*pi*sqrt(A*D) = 2*pi*sqrt(1825 × 6.5) = 2*pi*sqrt(11862.5) ≈ 2*pi*108.9 ≈ 684 days, or about 1.9 years — strikingly close to the roughly two-year cycle London and Yorke (1973) documented in large-city measles records before vaccination, even though the bare demographic model alone would only predict this as a damping transient, not a sustained cycle.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks why real measles data shows sustained multi-year cycles is testing whether a student conflates the model's transient ringing with the observed, seemingly permanent oscillation. The correct answer names both halves: the demographic model's natural period explains why the cycle length is close to two years, but only an added seasonal driver (school terms) explains why the ringing does not damp away in reality. A student who cites only demography, or only seasonality, has half the mechanism.

questions.prompt: Why does the SIR model with demography reach a nonzero endemic equilibrium instead of burning out to I=0 like the closed SIR model?

options.text: Births continuously replenish the susceptible pool, allowing new infections to balance ongoing recoveries indefinitely
Because R0 automatically drops to exactly 1 once births are added
Because the infectious period D becomes infinite with demography
Because adding births removes the recovery term gamma*I from the model

explanations.a: Correct: without births S only falls and the epidemic burns out; with births, new susceptibles keep arriving, which is what makes a nonzero (S*, I*) equilibrium possible.
explanations.b: R0 = beta/gamma is unaffected by adding a birth/death rate; it does not change to 1.
explanations.c: The infectious period D is set by the recovery rate gamma and is unrelated to whether births are included.
explanations.d: The recovery term gamma*I remains in the model with demography; only a birth term is added, not a removal of recovery.

questions.prompt: Order these stages as the system rings its way toward the endemic equilibrium (S*, I*).

items.text: An initial epidemic peak overshoots the equilibrium level I*
Susceptible depletion drives incidence to crash well below I*
Births slowly replenish S, triggering a smaller secondary peak
Oscillation amplitude decays toward the endemic equilibrium (S*, I*)

questions.explanation: The stable-spiral dynamics produce an overshoot, an undershoot, a smaller rebound, and progressively shrinking cycles that converge on equilibrium rather than a smooth, direct approach.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its formula or definition.

right.text: ≈ 2*pi*sqrt(A*D)
N/R0

questions.explanation: A depends on the birth rate and R0; T combines A with the infectious period D via Anderson and May's (1991) formula; S* mirrors the same N/R0 threshold seen in the epidemic-peak condition.

questions.prompt: London and Yorke (1973) documented roughly two-year cycles in pre-vaccination measles incidence in large U.S. cities. What does the SIR-with-demography model say about this observation?

options.text: The model's natural damped-oscillation period is close to two years for realistic measles parameters, but sustaining the cycle indefinitely also requires an external driver like seasonal school-term forcing
The model predicts the two-year cycle continues forever with no need for any seasonal forcing, since demography alone fully explains it
The model predicts no oscillation at all for measles-like parameters, under any assumptions
The two-year period is coincidental and unrelated to anything the demographic model predicts

explanations.a: Correct: the worked example's ≈1.9-year natural period matches the observed cycle length, but the bare demographic model damps this ringing away, so a sustaining driver like seasonal forcing is still required.
explanations.b: The demographic model alone predicts the oscillation damps to a flat equilibrium; it does not predict an indefinitely sustained cycle without an added driver.
explanations.c: The worked calculation shows a clear damped oscillation with a period near two years, so this option contradicts the model's own output.
explanations.d: The close numerical match between the computed natural period and the observed cycle length shows a real, non-coincidental connection.

lessons.label: Calibrating Models to Data

sections.heading: Three Ways to Fit a Curve to Data
sections.body: Least squares chooses beta, gamma, and initial conditions that minimize the summed squared differences between the model's predicted case counts and the observed ones — simple to implement with a standard optimizer, and reasonable when observation noise is roughly symmetric and Gaussian-like, but it silently assumes constant-variance noise that real case-count data rarely has. Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) instead picks the parameters that maximize the probability of the observed counts under an explicit noise model, typically a Poisson or, since real case counts are usually overdispersed relative to Poisson because of clustering in transmission, a negative-binomial observation model that adds a dispersion parameter to absorb that extra variance. Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) goes further: it places prior distributions on the parameters, reflecting what is already known or plausible before seeing the current outbreak's data, and samples the full joint posterior distribution using algorithms like Metropolis-Hastings or Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, returning not a single best guess but an entire distribution of plausible parameter combinations along with their combined uncertainty.

sections.heading: The Identifiability Problem
sections.body: A fitted curve that visually matches the data is not the same as a uniquely determined parameter set. During the early exponential-growth phase, case counts constrain only the combination gamma*(R0-1) — the growth rate r — not beta and gamma individually, echoing the same limitation seen when converting r to R0 in an earlier lesson. Many different (beta, gamma) pairs, or different assumed initial conditions, can reproduce an indistinguishable early curve while implying very different R0 values and very different projected peaks weeks later. Raue and colleagues (2009) termed this practical non-identifiability, distinguishing it from structural non-identifiability, which persists even with infinite noiseless data because of the model's algebraic form; practical non-identifiability is instead a consequence of the finite, noisy, limited-time-window data actually available in a live outbreak, and it can shrink or disappear once more data — especially data spanning the peak — comes in.

sections.heading: Why This Matters for a Science Fair Board
sections.body: Presenting a single best-fit curve without checking whether meaningfully different parameter sets fit nearly as well overstates precision. A defensible calibration reports the spread — a confidence interval from repeated least-squares fits, an MLE profile-likelihood curve, or the width of a Bayesian posterior — and states plainly which parameters remain poorly constrained by the available data window, rather than presenting one number as though it were exact when the underlying data could not have pinned it down that tightly.

lessons.workedExample: Early in an outbreak, only the exponential-growth phase has been observed, giving r ≈ 0.1/day. Two very different parameter pairs both reproduce this: (beta=0.3, gamma=0.2) gives R0=1.5 and r=beta-gamma=0.1; (beta=0.5, gamma=0.4) gives R0=1.25 and the same r=0.1. From the early case counts alone, these are indistinguishable curves, yet they predict different peak heights and different herd-immunity thresholds. Only data collected past the peak, once susceptible depletion bends the curve, breaks the tie between them.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a team distinguishes a visually good fit from an identifiable set of parameters — can they explain why two different (beta, gamma) pairs might fit their early data equally well, and can they name a way to detect or resolve this, such as a profile-likelihood check or waiting for post-peak data? A single confident point estimate with no discussion of alternative fits that work almost as well is the tell of a team that has not stress-tested its own calibration.

questions.prompt: Which calibration method directly produces a full probability distribution over the parameters, rather than a single point estimate?

options.text: Least squares
Maximum likelihood estimation
Bayesian MCMC
None of these — all three always give a single fixed answer

explanations.a: Least squares returns a single set of parameter values that minimizes squared residuals, not a distribution.
explanations.b: MLE returns a single point estimate that maximizes the likelihood; confidence intervals require additional asymptotic calculations layered on top.
explanations.c: Correct: Bayesian MCMC combines a prior with the likelihood and samples the resulting joint posterior, directly yielding a full distribution over all parameters.
explanations.d: Bayesian MCMC is specifically designed to output a distribution rather than a fixed answer, so this option is incorrect.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a Bayesian MCMC model calibration.

items.text: Specify prior distributions for beta, gamma, and initial conditions
Define a likelihood connecting model output to observed case counts
Run an MCMC sampler (e.g., Metropolis-Hastings) to draw from the posterior
Summarize the posterior distribution for R0 and other parameters, including its spread

questions.explanation: Priors and the likelihood must both be defined before sampling can begin; the sampler then produces draws from the posterior, which are finally summarized.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, (beta=0.3, gamma=0.2) and (beta=0.5, gamma=0.4) both produce r=0.1/day during the exponential phase. What does this illustrate?

options.text: Practical non-identifiability: growth-phase data alone constrains the combination gamma*(R0-1), not beta and gamma individually
A coding error, since two different parameter sets can never produce the same growth rate
That R0 is identical for both parameter sets
That least squares always finds the single, uniquely correct answer

explanations.a: Correct: both pairs give R0*gamma-gamma = r = 0.1, but R0 differs (1.5 vs. 1.25), exactly the practical non-identifiability the lesson describes.
explanations.b: This is expected model behavior during the early growth phase, not a bug — multiple parameter pairs genuinely share the same r.
explanations.c: R0 differs between the two pairs (1.5 vs. 1.25) even though r is identical for both.
explanations.d: The example shows the opposite: least squares fit to early data alone cannot distinguish between these two very different parameter sets.

questions.prompt: Match each calibration method to what it directly outputs.

right.text: Parameter values minimizing summed squared residuals
Parameter values maximizing the likelihood of the observed counts
A full posterior probability distribution over parameters, combining prior and likelihood

questions.explanation: Each method optimizes or samples a different objective: squared error, likelihood, or a full Bayesian posterior.

lessons.label: Sensitivity and Uncertainty Analysis

sections.heading: Latin Hypercube Sampling
sections.body: Blower and Dowlatabadi (1994) introduced a now-standard workflow for exploring epidemic-model uncertainty, applied originally to a model of HIV transmission and intervention. Latin Hypercube Sampling (LHS) divides each parameter's plausible range into N equal-probability intervals, draws exactly one value from each interval per parameter, and then randomly pairs values across parameters to build N full parameter sets, so that every parameter's full range is represented exactly once across the sample rather than clustering randomly. This stratification guarantees each parameter's whole range is represented evenly, achieving good coverage of a k-dimensional parameter space with only N model runs — far cheaper than a full factorial grid, which would need on the order of N^k runs to cover the same space at comparable resolution, making LHS the practical choice once a model has more than two or three uncertain parameters.

sections.heading: Partial Rank Correlation Coefficients
sections.body: After running the model once per LHS-sampled parameter set and recording an output of interest — final epidemic size, say, or cumulative infections at a fixed time horizon — a partial rank correlation coefficient (PRCC) is computed for each parameter. PRCC first rank-transforms all values, replacing each raw number with its rank in the sample, which makes it robust to nonlinear-but-monotonic relationships common in epidemic models where a doubling of a parameter does not double the output. It then measures each parameter's correlation with the output after statistically removing the linear effects of every other parameter, isolating that one parameter's independent contribution. PRCC values range from -1 to 1: magnitude ranks how influential a parameter is relative to the others in the same analysis, and sign shows whether increasing it pushes the output up or down.

sections.heading: Tornado Plots and Communicating Uncertainty
sections.body: A tornado plot displays each parameter's PRCC, sorted by magnitude, as horizontal bars — the widest bar at top names the assumption the conclusion depends on most, letting a reader see at a glance which inputs actually matter and which barely move the output. Honest reporting pairs a central-estimate curve with a shaded uncertainty band drawn from the LHS ensemble or the Bayesian posterior, rather than presenting one deterministic trajectory as settled fact. Early COVID-19 projections from groups such as Imperial College London were paired with explicit uncertainty ranges precisely to avoid the false precision that a single unqualified line would imply to policymakers making decisions under real, unresolved parameter uncertainty.

lessons.workedExample: An epidemic model with parameters beta, contact rate c, and gamma is run N=1000 times using an LHS design, recording cumulative infections at year 5 each time. Computed PRCCs are: beta = 0.82, contact rate c = 0.65, gamma = -0.58. A tornado plot sorted by magnitude places beta's bar longest at the top, then c, then gamma. The signs make sense mechanistically: higher beta or c increases cumulative infections (positive PRCC), while higher gamma — faster recovery — reduces them (negative PRCC), and beta is the single assumption the year-5 projection is most sensitive to.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a team ran a systematic global sensitivity analysis, varying all parameters together across their plausible ranges, versus simply nudging one parameter at a time and eyeballing the change — the latter misses interactions between parameters that LHS/PRCC captures. They also expect the final poster to show an uncertainty band around any projected curve, not a single confident line, since a stated 'we don't know' about a weakly constrained parameter is itself evidence of rigor, not a weakness to hide.

questions.prompt: Why does Latin Hypercube Sampling need far fewer runs than a full factorial grid to explore a k-parameter space?

options.text: It stratifies each parameter's range and pairs strata across parameters, achieving even multidimensional coverage without testing every combination
It only samples the mean value of each parameter, ignoring the rest of the range
It ignores any parameter with a narrow plausible range
It varies only one parameter at a time while holding the others fixed

explanations.a: Correct: stratified, paired sampling covers the space with N runs instead of the N^k a full factorial grid over k parameters would require.
explanations.b: LHS samples across each parameter's full stratified range, not just its mean.
explanations.c: LHS treats every parameter's range with the same stratification regardless of how narrow or wide it is.
explanations.d: Varying one parameter at a time is local (one-at-a-time) sensitivity analysis, the opposite of LHS's simultaneous, global approach.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of an LHS/PRCC global sensitivity analysis.

items.text: Define plausible ranges or distributions for each parameter
Stratify each range and draw a Latin hypercube sample of N parameter sets
Run the model once per sampled parameter set and record the output of interest
Compute PRCC between each parameter and the output, then rank by magnitude

questions.explanation: Ranges must be set before sampling; sampling must happen before the model can be run on each set; PRCC can only be computed once outputs from all runs are in hand.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, beta has PRCC=0.82 and gamma has PRCC=-0.58 against cumulative infections at year 5. What does this indicate?

options.text: Beta is the more influential driver of cumulative infections, and increasing gamma tends to decrease the output while increasing beta tends to increase it
Gamma is more influential than beta because its PRCC is negative
Both parameters are equally influential, since neither PRCC equals exactly 1
Beta has no relationship with the outcome, since 0.82 is less than the maximum possible value of 1

explanations.a: Correct: influence is ranked by magnitude (0.82 > 0.58), and the sign shows direction — negative for gamma means faster recovery lowers cumulative infections.
explanations.b: A negative sign indicates direction, not greater importance; magnitude (|0.82| vs. |-0.58|) determines which parameter is more influential.
explanations.c: The differing magnitudes (0.82 vs. 0.58) show beta is meaningfully more influential than gamma, not equal.
explanations.d: A PRCC of 0.82 out of a maximum of 1 indicates a strong, not absent, relationship with the outcome.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in a sensitivity analysis.

right.text: Efficiently generates a stratified sample covering the multidimensional parameter space
Ranks each parameter's monotonic influence on an output after controlling for the others
Visualizes ranked parameter influence as sorted horizontal bars

questions.explanation: LHS generates the sample, PRCC quantifies each parameter's influence from the resulting runs, and the tornado plot is the visualization of those ranked PRCC values.

lessons.label: Ronald Ross and the Birth of Transmission Modeling

sections.heading: From statistics to mechanism
sections.body: Before Ronald Ross, epidemic science was mostly descriptive: count cases, plot them against time or place, look for correlations. Ross, a British army physician who had already shown in 1897-1898 that Anopheles mosquitoes transmit malaria (work that won him the 1902 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine), pushed further. He wanted to know not just that mosquitoes carried malaria but how the mosquito population's size governed whether an epidemic could sustain itself at all. His 1908 'Report on the Prevention of Malaria in Mauritius' introduced a mathematical argument that became the field's first mechanistic transmission model, applying a differential-equation logic he had sketched as early as 1904-1905 in correspondence and lectures but had not yet formalized in print.

sections.heading: The mosquito-density threshold
sections.body: Ross's key result, refined through his 1911 book 'The Prevention of Malaria', was counterintuitive: malaria transmission does not require eliminating mosquitoes, only reducing their density below a critical threshold. Below that threshold, each infected mosquito fails, on average, to produce enough new infected mosquitoes to sustain transmission, and the parasite dies out even though mosquitoes remain present. This threshold logic — a population-level tipping point set by a ratio of rates, not by driving a vector to zero — is the direct ancestor of the basic reproduction number, R0, used throughout modern epidemic modeling. Ross framed his equations around a small set of measurable quantities — mosquito density per person, biting rate, the fraction of mosquitoes that survive long enough to become infectious, and human recovery rate — and showed algebraically that these combine multiplicatively, so a modest cut to any one factor could tip the whole system below threshold.

sections.heading: A priori pathometry
sections.body: Ross generalized this approach starting in 1916, publishing with mathematician Hilda Hudson a three-part series, 'An Application of the Theory of Probabilities to the Study of a priori Pathometry' (1916-1917). Ross called this method 'a priori pathometry' or 'constructive epidemiology': assume known mechanisms of transmission, write differential equations encoding those mechanisms, derive their logical consequences, and only then test the predictions against observed case data. This inverted the prevailing statistical approach, which fit curves to data without committing to an underlying mechanism, and it set the template every subsequent transmission model — including Kermack and McKendrick's SIR framework a decade later — would follow. Hudson, a Cambridge-trained mathematician and the first woman invited to address the International Congress of Mathematicians, supplied much of the probability-theory rigor behind the later papers, extending Ross's single-equation arguments into a fuller stochastic and deterministic treatment of epidemic curves.

lessons.workedExample: Consider a village where each infected mosquito, over its lifetime, would infect 3 people if mosquito density were unchanged, but observed density is only 40% of that baseline. Applying Ross's threshold logic, the effective transmission ratio scales down to roughly 3 x 0.4 = 1.2 — still above the threshold of 1, so malaria persists. If a drainage campaign cuts mosquito density to 25% of baseline, the ratio falls to 3 x 0.25 = 0.75, below threshold, and Ross's model predicts local malaria elimination without a single mosquito species being wiped out — matching what colonial anti-malaria campaigns in Mauritius and Egypt actually observed when partial larval-source reduction produced disproportionate drops in transmission.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a student cite 'R0 > 1 means an epidemic grows' wants to know whether the student understands this is a 110-year-old mechanistic claim, not a modern statistical convention. Asking a student to trace the threshold idea back to Ross's mosquito-density argument tests whether they grasp that thresholds emerge from population-level ratios of contact and recovery rates, not from any single dramatic intervention — a distinction that matters whenever a project proposes a partial rather than total control measure.

questions.prompt: Ross's mosquito-density threshold result showed that malaria transmission could be stopped by:

options.text: Eliminating every mosquito in the area
Reducing mosquito density below a critical threshold, without eliminating them
Vaccinating the human population
Increasing mosquito lifespan to reduce biting frequency

explanations.a: This was the intuitive assumption Ross's math overturned — total elimination is not required.
explanations.b: Correct: below a critical density, each infected mosquito fails on average to replace itself with a new infected mosquito, and transmission collapses even with mosquitoes still present.
explanations.c: No malaria vaccine existed in this era; Ross's intervention logic centered on the vector, not human immunity.
explanations.d: Ross's model treats biting rate and density as separate parameters; increasing lifespan would generally increase transmission, not reduce it.

questions.prompt: What did Ross mean by 'a priori pathometry'?

options.text: Fitting statistical curves to case data without assuming a mechanism
Assuming known transmission mechanisms, deriving equations from them, then testing predictions against data
Predicting epidemics using only historical average case counts
A purely qualitative theory of disease causation with no mathematics

explanations.a: That describes the older statistical-description approach Ross was explicitly moving away from.
explanations.b: Correct: Ross and Hudson's 1916-1917 papers defined this as starting from assumed causal mechanisms, building differential equations, and testing the logical consequences against observed statistics.
explanations.c: Ross's method was mechanistic and predictive, not a simple historical average.
explanations.d: The Ross-Hudson papers were explicitly mathematical, using probability theory and differential equations.

questions.prompt: Order these milestones in Ross's career chronologically.

items.text: Shows Anopheles mosquitoes transmit malaria (1897-1898)
Awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (1902)
Publishes the Mauritius report introducing the mosquito-density threshold (1908)
Publishes 'a priori Pathometry' series with Hudson (1916-1917)

questions.explanation: Ross's discovery of the transmission vector came first, the Nobel Prize recognized that discovery in 1902, the threshold theorem followed in 1908 as he turned to modeling control, and the general mathematical framework with Hudson came last.

questions.prompt: Match each Ross-era work to what it established.

right.text: Anopheles mosquitoes as the malaria vector
The mosquito-density threshold for transmission
The general 'a priori pathometry' mathematical method

questions.explanation: Each work built on the last: identifying the vector, then finding a population-level threshold for it, then generalizing the underlying method into a formal mathematical framework.

lessons.label: Kermack and McKendrick, 1927

sections.heading: A paper that named the field's core model
sections.body: In 1927, biochemist William Ogilvy Kermack and physician-mathematician Anderson Gray McKendrick published 'A Contribution to the Mathematical Theory of Epidemics' in the Proceedings of the Royal Society A. Working in Edinburgh, they built on Ross's threshold logic but generalized it beyond malaria to any closed population experiencing a single-outbreak epidemic. Their paper introduced what students now call the SIR model: individuals move through Susceptible, Infected, and Removed compartments, governed by a transmission rate and a removal (recovery or death) rate. It was the first of a planned trilogy; Kermack and McKendrick followed with a second and third paper in the early 1930s extending the framework to recurrent epidemics and to populations with ongoing births and deaths.

sections.heading: The threshold theorem
sections.body: Kermack and McKendrick's central mathematical result, the threshold theorem, states that an epidemic can only grow if the initial density of susceptibles exceeds a critical value set by the ratio of the removal rate to the transmission rate — otherwise a small number of introduced cases simply dies out without a major outbreak. This is the same logic as Ross's mosquito threshold, but framed in terms of human susceptibles rather than vector density, and it is mathematically equivalent to the modern statement that an epidemic grows exactly when the effective reproduction number exceeds 1. Their paper further derived a 'final size' relation predicting the total fraction of the population ultimately infected, showing it depends only on the starting susceptible fraction and the threshold ratio — a result still used to estimate cumulative attack rates from a single early growth-rate measurement.

sections.heading: General theory versus the special case everyone teaches
sections.body: Crucially, the 1927 paper did not present the simple SIR differential equations most courses teach today. Its full model was an 'age of infection' formulation, in which infectiousness and removal probability could vary continuously with the time since an individual was infected — a far more general and mathematically demanding framework. The simple constant-rate SIR equations are a special case that Kermack and McKendrick derived only as a tractable illustration. Because the general theory was difficult to apply and its full implications were not widely appreciated, the paper was largely set aside for decades; epidemic modeling only became a mainstream tool after later researchers, especially Anderson and May in the 1980s-90s, rediscovered and popularized the simplified SIR framework as the field's foundation. Kermack himself was completely blinded in a laboratory accident in 1924, three years before the paper appeared, and continued the collaboration with McKendrick largely through dictation — a detail historians of the field cite as a reminder that landmark theory can outlast the immediate circumstances of its authors by decades before its full value is recognized.

lessons.workedExample: Take a closed population of 10,000 fully susceptible people with a removal rate of 0.2/day and a transmission rate per contact such that the reproduction number R0 = 3. The threshold theorem says an epidemic requires the susceptible fraction to exceed 1/R0 = 1/3. Since the population starts 100% susceptible, well above one-third, a single introduced case triggers a major outbreak — Kermack and McKendrick's model predicts the epidemic will grow until susceptibles are driven down near that 1/3 threshold, then decline, leaving a substantial fraction of the population never infected, a 'final size' result their 1927 equations also derive.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student knows the SIR equations they coded are a simplification of the actual 1927 theorem, not the whole of it. A student who can explain that Kermack and McKendrick's true model allowed infectiousness to vary with time-since-infection — the 'age of infection' structure later revived in models for diseases with complex infectious profiles like COVID-19 — signals they understand SIR's constant-rate assumption as a modeling choice, not a law of nature.

questions.prompt: According to Kermack and McKendrick's 1927 threshold theorem, a major epidemic occurs only if:

options.text: The number of initial cases exceeds 100
The initial susceptible density exceeds a critical value set by the removal-to-transmission rate ratio
The population is larger than 250,000
The disease has an incubation period longer than its infectious period

explanations.a: The theorem is about population susceptibility, not the absolute number of index cases.
explanations.b: Correct: this is the threshold condition, mathematically equivalent to today's statement that R-effective must exceed 1.
explanations.c: That population figure describes critical community size for endemic persistence, a different concept from the 1927 outbreak threshold.
explanations.d: The threshold theorem does not depend on comparing incubation to infectious period length.

questions.prompt: The simple constant-rate SIR equations taught in most courses today are:

options.text: The complete model Kermack and McKendrick published in 1927
A special case of their more general 'age of infection' formulation
A post-2000 replacement for their original, now-obsolete equations
Unrelated to the 1927 paper and developed independently by Anderson and May

explanations.a: The 1927 paper's full model let infectiousness vary with time since infection; constant-rate SIR is a simplified illustration within it.
explanations.b: Correct: Kermack and McKendrick derived the constant-rate case as a tractable special case of their broader age-of-infection theory.
explanations.c: The simple equations date to 1927 itself, not a later replacement.
explanations.d: Anderson and May popularized this simplified form decades later, but it originates in the 1927 paper.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the history of the Kermack-McKendrick model.

items.text: Kermack and McKendrick publish the general age-of-infection model and threshold theorem (1927)
The paper's full implications go largely unapplied for decades
Anderson and May popularize the simplified constant-rate SIR framework
SIR becomes the standard entry point for teaching transmission modeling

questions.explanation: The general theory came first but sat underused, was revived in simplified form decades later, and only then became the field's standard teaching model.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it describes in the 1927 paper.

right.text: Condition on susceptible density for an epidemic to grow
General model where infectiousness varies with time since infection
Simplified special case with fixed transmission and removal rates

questions.explanation: The threshold theorem is the growth condition; the age-of-infection model is the general framework it was proven within; constant-rate SIR is the simplified case most commonly taught.

lessons.label: Reed-Frost, Soper, and Bartlett

sections.heading: Reed-Frost: chance enters the model
sections.body: Kermack and McKendrick's SIR equations are deterministic — given a starting state, the epidemic's whole trajectory is fixed. In the 1920s, biostatistician Lowell Reed and epidemiologist Wade Hampton Frost, teaching at Johns Hopkins, developed an alternative they never formally published but taught for years in lectures: the chain-binomial model, now called Reed-Frost. It treats each generation of infection as a random (binomial) draw — every susceptible person has some independent probability of being infected by the current infectious group — so an outbreak can, by chance, fizzle out even when the average trajectory predicts growth. This stochastic lineage became essential for understanding small outbreaks and rare events that deterministic averages miss, and the chain-binomial structure — infections in one generation determining a binomial draw of new infections in the next, discrete generation — is still the basis for modern branching-process outbreak simulations.

sections.heading: Soper and measles periodicity
sections.body: In 1929, Herbert Soper published 'Interpretation of Periodicity in Disease Prevalence', analyzing why measles notifications in cities showed regular biennial or annual epidemic cycles rather than settling to a steady endemic level. Soper showed that the interaction between an accumulating pool of susceptible children (born since the last epidemic) and periodic depletion by outbreaks naturally produces oscillations — a mechanistic explanation for a pattern that had previously been treated as a puzzling empirical regularity in vital-statistics records. Each epidemic burns through most of the accumulated susceptible pool; births then slowly rebuild that pool until it again crosses the epidemic threshold, producing the next wave roughly one to three years later depending on local birth rates.

sections.heading: Bartlett and the critical community size
sections.body: Maurice Bartlett's 1957 paper 'Measles Periodicity and Community Size' pushed the stochastic question further: how large does a population need to be for measles to persist endemically at all, rather than dying out between epidemics and requiring reintroduction from elsewhere? Using UK and US city-level notification data, Bartlett estimated this critical community size at roughly 250,000-300,000 people — below that threshold, chance fadeout (the small-number randomness Reed-Frost had formalized) eventually extinguishes local transmission during the trough between epidemics, even though the deterministic SIR threshold condition would predict indefinite persistence. Bartlett defined the threshold operationally as the population size at which measles had roughly even odds of surviving versus fading out between epidemic peaks, and later re-analyses using longer US city time series arrived at comparable figures in the 250,000-500,000 range. Bartlett's finding gave measles a distinct claim to fame among childhood infections: unlike diseases with lower R0 or shorter infectious periods, its threshold population was large enough that, before global eradication efforts, only a relatively small number of major cities were big enough to sustain it without reintroduction.

lessons.workedExample: Consider two towns, both above the deterministic epidemic threshold for measles. Town A has 150,000 residents; Town B has 400,000. In Town A, after a big epidemic burns through most susceptibles, the pool of infectious individuals in the trough can shrink to single digits — Reed-Frost's binomial chance means there is a real probability that in some week, zero of those few infectious people transmit, and the chain goes extinct locally, matching Bartlett's finding that cities below roughly 300,000 saw measles fade out and reappear only after reintroduction. Town B's larger susceptible pool keeps enough infectious individuals circulating that the chain almost never hits zero, so measles persists continuously — the qualitative difference Bartlett's critical community size threshold predicts.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing a fadeout claim wants to see the student distinguish stochastic extinction from deterministic decline: a population can be above the SIR threshold and still lose an infection by chance if absolute case counts get small, which is exactly the mechanism Reed-Frost formalizes and Bartlett's critical community size quantifies. Citing a specific population figure (roughly 250,000-300,000 for measles) instead of a vague 'small towns lose diseases, big cities keep them' shows the student engaged with the actual empirical result, not an intuition.

questions.prompt: What does the Reed-Frost chain-binomial model add that deterministic SIR equations lack?

options.text: A term for vaccination coverage
Random chance in whether each susceptible person is infected each generation
A correction for underreporting of cases
Seasonal forcing of the transmission rate

explanations.a: Reed-Frost is about the probabilistic structure of transmission, not about adding a vaccination compartment.
explanations.b: Correct: Reed-Frost models each generation as a binomial draw, so an outbreak can go extinct by chance even when average dynamics predict growth.
explanations.c: Reporting error correction is a separate statistical issue, not what distinguishes Reed-Frost from deterministic SIR.
explanations.d: Seasonal forcing was Soper's later addition to explain periodicity, not the core Reed-Frost innovation.

questions.prompt: Bartlett's 1957 critical community size result for measles found that populations below roughly 250,000-300,000 tended to:

options.text: Never experience a measles epidemic at all
Experience epidemics but then lose the infection to chance extinction until it was reintroduced
Show no periodicity in case counts
Have a lower deterministic R0 than larger cities

explanations.a: Small populations could still have epidemics; the issue was whether measles persisted continuously afterward.
explanations.b: Correct: below the critical community size, the infectious pool shrinks small enough between epidemics that chance fadeout ends local transmission, requiring reintroduction from outside.
explanations.c: Soper had already shown periodicity itself arises from susceptible accumulation and depletion, independent of population size.
explanations.d: R0 depends on transmission and recovery rates, not directly on population size in this framework.

questions.prompt: Order these developments in the stochastic/periodicity lineage of transmission modeling.

items.text: Reed and Frost teach the chain-binomial model at Johns Hopkins (1920s)
Soper explains measles periodicity via susceptible accumulation and depletion (1929)
Bartlett estimates the critical community size for measles persistence (1957)

questions.explanation: The stochastic chain-binomial framework came first, was applied to explain observed periodic cycles next, and was extended to the question of population-size thresholds for persistence last.

questions.prompt: Match each contributor to their central result.

right.text: Chain-binomial model treating each transmission generation as a random draw
Mechanistic explanation of biennial/annual measles cycles
Critical community size threshold (~250,000-300,000) for measles persistence

questions.explanation: Each built on the last: a stochastic transmission model, an application explaining periodic cycles, and a population-size threshold for whether the disease persists at all.

lessons.label: Anderson and May and the R0 Synthesis

sections.heading: From scattered mathematics to a public-health toolkit
sections.body: For roughly fifty years after Kermack and McKendrick's 1927 paper, transmission modeling remained a fairly specialized mathematical pursuit, applied unevenly across malaria, measles, and a handful of other diseases without a unifying framework accessible to working epidemiologists. Roy Anderson, a parasitologist, and Robert May, a theoretical ecologist, changed that. Through a series of papers in the late 1970s and 1980s — including a widely cited pair in Nature in 1979 applying the framework to helminth and viral infections — and then their 1991 book 'Infectious Diseases of Humans: Dynamics and Control', they systematized the mathematics into a coherent toolkit built around a single organizing quantity: the basic reproduction number, R0, the expected number of secondary infections one infectious individual produces in an entirely susceptible population.

sections.heading: Making the herd-immunity threshold usable
sections.body: Anderson and May's most consequential practical contribution was deriving and popularizing a simple, general formula connecting R0 to the vaccination coverage needed to stop transmission: the herd-immunity threshold, roughly 1 - 1/R0 (in the simplest homogeneous-mixing case). This let public-health planners translate an abstract epidemiological parameter directly into a vaccination-coverage target — for a disease with R0 around 15, roughly 93% coverage is needed, while a disease with R0 around 3 needs only about 67%. Before their synthesis, this logic existed in scattered mathematical papers; after it, it became a standard planning tool taught in public-health training worldwide, and it directly informed WHO guidance on the coverage levels required for measles, rubella, and pertussis elimination campaigns.

sections.heading: Extending the framework across diseases and structure
sections.body: 'Infectious Diseases of Humans' extended R0-based reasoning well beyond the simple SIR case that Kermack and McKendrick had used as an illustration: Anderson and May incorporated age structure (since contact patterns and susceptibility vary strongly with age), heterogeneous mixing between subgroups, and macroparasite dynamics for helminths and other diseases with more complex life cycles. This breadth is why the book became the field's standard reference — it demonstrated that the same core reproduction-number logic Ross and Kermack-McKendrick had developed for single diseases could be generalized into a systematic discipline applicable across pathogens, moving transmission modeling from a mathematical curiosity into mainstream public-health infrastructure. Anderson, a parasitologist by training, brought firsthand experience with helminth life cycles, while May, who had moved into ecology from theoretical physics, brought population-dynamics tools from predator-prey theory — a cross-disciplinary pairing credited for the book's unusually broad reach across both microparasitic and macroparasitic disease systems.

lessons.workedExample: A health ministry is planning a measles vaccination campaign and knows from surveillance that R0 is approximately 15 in the local population. Using the Anderson-May herd-immunity threshold formula, 1 - 1/R0 = 1 - 1/15 ≈ 0.933, so at least about 93% of the population needs immunity to interrupt transmission. If the same ministry were instead planning for a pathogen with R0 = 5, the target drops to 1 - 1/5 = 80%. This single formula, popularized through Anderson and May's synthesis, is why measles campaigns are held to a stricter coverage bar than campaigns against lower-R0 diseases.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student treats R0 as a fixed biological constant or, correctly, as a modeling output that depends on population contact structure — and whether they can derive a concrete policy number (a vaccination-coverage target) from it rather than just quoting 'R0 is the average number of secondary cases.' A student who can compute 1 - 1/R0 for their own project's pathogen and explain what assumption (homogeneous mixing) the formula rests on is demonstrating the actual Anderson-May contribution, not just a memorized phrase.

questions.prompt: What was Anderson and May's central organizing contribution to transmission modeling?

options.text: Discovering that mosquitoes transmit malaria
Systematizing R0-based reasoning into a general toolkit connecting transmission dynamics to vaccination policy
Proving the first stochastic chain-binomial model
Explaining biennial cycles in measles notifications

explanations.a: That was Ross's late-1890s fieldwork, decades before Anderson and May.
explanations.b: Correct: their 1991 book systematized R0 across diseases and derived the herd-immunity threshold formula that made the mathematics usable for public-health planning.
explanations.c: That stochastic lineage traces to Reed and Frost in the 1920s, not Anderson and May.
explanations.d: Explaining measles periodicity was Soper's 1929 contribution.

questions.prompt: Using the herd-immunity threshold formula 1 - 1/R0, what vaccination coverage is needed for a pathogen with R0 = 5?

explanations.a: 20% is 1/R0 itself, not 1 minus that fraction.
explanations.b: 50% would correspond to R0 = 2, not R0 = 5.
explanations.c: Correct: 1 - 1/5 = 0.8, so 80% coverage is the herd-immunity threshold.
explanations.d: 95% coverage corresponds to a much higher R0, around 20, not 5.

questions.prompt: Order these developments in the path from Kermack-McKendrick to public-health practice.

items.text: Kermack and McKendrick publish the general SIR threshold theorem (1927)
The mathematics remains a specialized pursuit applied unevenly for decades
Anderson and May publish 'Infectious Diseases of Humans', systematizing R0 and the herd-immunity threshold (1991)
R0-based vaccination-coverage targets become standard public-health planning tools

questions.explanation: The foundational mathematics came first, sat underused for decades, was systematized by Anderson and May, and only then became routine public-health practice.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to what Anderson and May's synthesis did with it.

right.text: Made the central organizing quantity of the whole toolkit
Translated abstract transmission math into a vaccination-coverage target
Extended the framework beyond simple homogeneous-mixing SIR

questions.explanation: Anderson and May centered the whole framework on R0, derived a usable policy formula from it, and generalized the underlying model to reflect realistic population structure.

lessons.label: SARS 2003: Modeling in a Real-Time Emergency

sections.heading: Estimating R0 while the outbreak was still moving
sections.body: SARS (severe acute respiratory syndrome) emerged in late 2002 and spread internationally by early 2003, giving epidemiologists their first major test of transmission modeling under real-time outbreak pressure since the mathematics had matured. Steven Riley and colleagues, in a paper published in Science in 2003, fit a stochastic transmission model to 1,512 SARS cases in Hong Kong and estimated that, excluding superspreading events, each case generated about 2.7 secondary infections on average in the outbreak's early stage — a moderate R0, well above the epidemic threshold of 1 but far below diseases like measles. A companion Science paper by Marc Lipsitch and colleagues, published the same week using different data and methods, arrived at a similar range, giving public-health officials rare early convergence between two independent modeling teams during a live emergency.

sections.heading: Superspreading breaks the average
sections.body: That average masked something the Hong Kong data made impossible to ignore: a small number of infected individuals, later called superspreaders, generated enormous numbers of secondary cases (one Amoy Gardens housing-estate cluster alone produced over 300 cases from what appeared to trace to very few source infections), while most infected people transmitted to few or nobody. In 2005, James Lloyd-Smith and colleagues formalized this pattern in Nature, showing that a negative binomial distribution with a dispersion parameter k fit real outbreak data far better than assuming every case transmits similarly. For SARS, they estimated k around 0.16, a very low value indicating extreme heterogeneity — most transmission was driven by a minority of cases, a pattern the 80/20-style 'superspreading' framing still uses today.

sections.heading: Timing of infectiousness determines controllability
sections.body: A separate 2004 paper by Christophe Fraser, Riley, Roy Anderson, and Neil Ferguson in PNAS asked a more strategic question: what makes an outbreak controllable using isolation and contact tracing alone?
