Their answer was that the proportion of transmission occurring before symptom onset (pre-symptomatic transmission) mattered as much as R0 itself. SARS was fortunate in this respect — infectiousness peaked after symptoms appeared, so isolating symptomatic cases could interrupt most chains of transmission, which is a major reason SARS was eventually contained by classical public-health measures without a vaccine. Fraser et al. formalized this into a general threshold: they showed the maximum R0 controllable by isolation and contact tracing alone falls sharply as the pre-symptomatic transmission fraction rises, giving public-health planners a way to gauge, from a pathogen's incubation biology, whether case-based control could plausibly work before a single outbreak had run its course.

lessons.workedExample: Hong Kong hospital administrators in spring 2003 needed to decide whether symptom-based isolation alone could contain SARS. Riley et al.'s R0 estimate of about 2.7 meant each case needed to be reduced to under 1 secondary infection to reverse growth — a roughly 63% cut in transmission. Fraser et al.'s finding that SARS infectiousness was concentrated after symptom onset meant isolating symptomatic patients could plausibly deliver that cut, and it did: Hong Kong's epidemic peaked in spring 2003 and was controlled within months. Contrast this with a hypothetical pathogen having the same R0 = 2.7 but most transmission occurring pre-symptomatically — Fraser et al.'s model shows that pathogen would require contact tracing and quarantine of exposed-but-asymptomatic people to achieve the same control, since isolating only symptomatic cases would already be too late for most of the transmission chain.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge assessing a project on outbreak control wants to see the student separate three distinct questions the SARS literature answers separately: how transmissible is it on average (R0 ≈ 2.7, Riley et al. 2003), how unevenly is that transmission distributed across individuals (dispersion k ≈ 0.16, Lloyd-Smith et al. 2005), and when during infection does transmission happen (pre- versus post-symptomatic, Fraser et al. 2004). Conflating these — for example, assuming a low R0 automatically means an outbreak is easy to control by isolation — is the exact mistake this trio of papers was written to correct.

questions.prompt: Riley et al. (2003) estimated SARS's early-outbreak R0 in Hong Kong, excluding superspreading events, at approximately:

explanations.a: A value below 1 would mean the outbreak was already shrinking, which contradicts the observed 2003 growth.
explanations.b: Correct: Riley et al. fit a stochastic model to 1,512 Hong Kong cases and estimated approximately 2.7 secondary infections per case in the early outbreak.
explanations.c: 8.0 is far above published SARS estimates and closer to figures for diseases like smallpox in some settings.
explanations.d: 15 is in the range associated with measles, a far more transmissible disease than SARS.

questions.prompt: Lloyd-Smith et al. (2005) used a low dispersion parameter (k ≈ 0.16) for SARS to show that:

options.text: Transmission was evenly spread across nearly all infected individuals
A small minority of cases (superspreaders) generated a disproportionate share of secondary infections
SARS had no superspreading events at all
R0 for SARS was underestimated by Riley et al.

explanations.a: A low k value specifically indicates the opposite: highly uneven, overdispersed transmission.
explanations.b: Correct: low k means a negative binomial offspring distribution with heavy skew — most cases infect few or none, while a minority drive most transmission.
explanations.c: The Amoy Gardens cluster and the low k estimate together document substantial superspreading in SARS.
explanations.d: Lloyd-Smith et al.'s work is about the distribution of secondary cases around R0, not a re-estimate of R0 itself.

questions.prompt: Order these SARS modeling contributions by publication year.

items.text: Riley et al. estimate R0 ≈ 2.7 in Hong Kong (2003)
Fraser, Riley, Anderson, and Ferguson show pre-symptomatic transmission determines controllability (2004)
Lloyd-Smith et al. formalize superspreading with dispersion parameter k (2005)

questions.explanation: The average transmissibility estimate came first during the outbreak itself, the controllability analysis followed the next year, and the general superspreading framework was published in 2005.

questions.prompt: Match each SARS-era study to its central finding.

right.text: R0 ≈ 2.7 in early Hong Kong outbreak
Dispersion parameter k ≈ 0.16 quantifying superspreading
Pre-symptomatic transmission fraction determines whether isolation alone controls an outbreak

questions.explanation: Each paper answered a different question: how transmissible on average, how unevenly distributed, and when during infection transmission occurs.

lessons.label: COVID-19 and the Modeling That Moved Governments

sections.heading: A single report and a policy pivot
sections.body: On 16 March 2020, a team led by Neil Ferguson at Imperial College London released 'Report 9: Impact of Non-Pharmaceutical Interventions (NPIs) to Reduce COVID-19 Mortality and Healthcare Demand'. Its unmitigated scenario — no behavior change, no government action, roughly 81% of the population eventually infected, with an assumed infection fatality rate near 0.9% — projected approximately 510,000 deaths in Great Britain and 2.2 million in the United States. The report explicitly called this scenario unlikely, but used it as the baseline against which every intervention option was compared, including suppression strategies combining case isolation, household quarantine, and broad social distancing. Within days, the UK government shifted its stated strategy from 'mitigation' (slowing spread) to 'suppression' (actively driving transmission down), and the report is widely credited with helping trigger that shift, along with similar lockdown decisions elsewhere.

sections.heading: Estimating what interventions actually did
sections.body: Once lockdowns were underway, a second question emerged: did they work, and by how much? Seth Flaxman, Samir Bhatt, and a large collaborative team answered this in a 2020 Nature paper, 'Estimating the Effects of Non-Pharmaceutical Interventions on COVID-19 in Europe.' Using a Bayesian model fit across 11 European countries, they estimated that NPIs had driven the effective reproduction number below 1 in every country studied and that these interventions had collectively averted approximately 3.1 million deaths by early May 2020 — a number that became one of the most cited (and most contested) figures of the pandemic's first year.

sections.heading: The attribution dispute
sections.body: Both papers drew sustained methodological criticism. Critics of Report 9 argued its unmitigated scenario overstated infection fatality rates and ignored voluntary behavior change that would have occurred without government mandates, making the 'do-nothing' counterfactual unrealistic. Critics of Flaxman et al., including a published comment arguing the effects were statistical artefacts, contended that the model's structure — which assumed a fixed relationship between each NPI and its effect and could not fully separate the impact of one intervention from another rolled out at nearly the same time — attributed too much of the case-count decline specifically to lockdowns rather than to other simultaneous changes. Both disputes turn on the same underlying issue: distinguishing what a model was designed to project (a scenario's consequences, given stated assumptions) from a claim about what actually would have happened (a genuine counterfactual prediction) — a distinction the next lesson examines directly. Both papers were released as preprints or reports ahead of full peer review, a pattern that became routine across the pandemic; it let policymakers act on the fastest available evidence but also meant contested figures like the 510,000 and 3.1 million estimates entered public debate before the normal cycle of scientific critique and revision had run its course.

lessons.workedExample: A journalist in April 2020 wants to know whether UK lockdown 'worked.' Report 9's unmitigated projection of 510,000 UK deaths was never meant as a forecast of what would happen — it was a scenario input assuming zero behavioral or policy response, a baseline for comparison. Flaxman et al.'s separate analysis, using actual observed case and death data across countries, estimated the interventions had averted about 3.1 million deaths across the 11 countries studied by early May 2020. Reporting 'the model predicted 510,000 deaths and only about 40,000 UK deaths occurred by summer 2020, so the model was wrong' conflates these two different modeling exercises — the first was an explicit worst-case scenario used to justify acting, the second was a retrospective effect-estimate of the actions actually taken.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge evaluating a project that cites pandemic modeling wants to see the student distinguish a scenario projection (Report 9's unmitigated case, built to be avoided) from an effect estimate (Flaxman et al.'s NPI impact, built to explain what happened). Students who treat a stated worst-case scenario as a falsified prediction when reality diverges from it — without noting that policy responded to the scenario precisely to prevent it — are making the single most common public misreading of this modeling episode, and judges probe for it directly.

questions.prompt: Imperial College Report 9's unmitigated scenario (16 March 2020) projected approximately how many deaths in the United States?

options.text: 2.2 million
22 million

explanations.a: This figure is two orders of magnitude too low for the report's stated unmitigated projection.
explanations.b: This is roughly the actual US COVID-19 death toll reported through 2020-2021, not the report's unmitigated projection.
explanations.c: Correct: the report's unmitigated scenario, assuming no behavioral or policy response, projected approximately 2.2 million US deaths.
explanations.d: This figure is an order of magnitude too high relative to the report's stated projection.

questions.prompt: Flaxman et al. (2020) in Nature estimated that non-pharmaceutical interventions across 11 European countries had, by early May 2020:

options.text: Averted approximately 3.1 million deaths
Had no measurable effect on transmission
Increased the effective reproduction number above 1
Averted approximately 3,100 deaths

explanations.a: Correct: the Bayesian model estimated roughly 3.1 million deaths averted across the 11 countries by that point.
explanations.b: The paper's central finding was a substantial, measurable effect driving transmission down, not a null result.
explanations.c: The paper's finding was that NPIs drove the effective reproduction number below 1, not above it.
explanations.d: 3,100 is off by three orders of magnitude from the paper's actual estimate.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the COVID-19 modeling timeline.

items.text: Imperial College Report 9 projects unmitigated death tolls and is released (16 March 2020)
UK government shifts stated strategy from mitigation to suppression
Lockdowns and other NPIs are implemented across European countries
Flaxman et al. publish their retrospective estimate of NPI effects on deaths averted (2020)

questions.explanation: The scenario projection came first and helped trigger the policy shift, interventions followed, and the retrospective effect-estimate was only possible once real intervention data existed to analyze.

questions.prompt: Match each study to what kind of claim it made.

left.text: Flaxman et al. NPI effect estimate

right.text: A hypothetical baseline projection assuming no response, used to justify action
A retrospective estimate of deaths averted by interventions actually taken
An argument that the model overattributed case declines to NPIs specifically

questions.explanation: Report 9 modeled a scenario to be avoided, Flaxman et al. estimated the effect of the response that followed, and critics disputed whether that effect estimate correctly isolated NPIs from other simultaneous changes.

lessons.label: Open Debates: Does R0 Even Mean What We Say?

sections.heading: Measles: a single number that isn't one
sections.body: Measles is the textbook example of a high-R0 disease, but the actual published estimates disagree by an order of magnitude. Fiona Guerra and colleagues, in a 2017 systematic review in The Lancet Infectious Diseases, found published measles R0 estimates spanning roughly 3.7 to 203.3 across different studies, settings, and estimation methods, with commonly cited summary figures around 12-18. Paul Delamater and colleagues, in a 2019 Emerging Infectious Diseases paper, 'Complexity of the Basic Reproduction Number (R0)', reviewed the same kind of wide-ranging published R0 estimates and argued the variation reflects real differences in population contact structure and study method, not just noise — meaning R0 is not a fixed biological property of a pathogen but a quantity that depends on the population it's measured in.

sections.heading: Herd immunity, overshoot, and the 2020 argument
sections.body: The Anderson-May herd-immunity threshold, 1 - 1/R0, describes the immunity level at which an epidemic stops growing — but an unmanaged epidemic does not stop exactly there. Because infections in progress keep transmitting past that point, cumulative infections 'overshoot' the threshold, often substantially, before the epidemic burns out — a mathematical consequence of the SIR equations themselves, not a modeling error. In 2020, this overshoot dynamic became politically charged: some public commentators argued that simply allowing COVID-19 to spread through younger, lower-risk populations would efficiently reach herd immunity, a position public-health epidemiologists rejected because it ignored both overshoot's excess-death cost and the fact that immunity from natural infection (like immunity from many vaccines) can wane, meaning a population can cross the threshold and later fall back below it as immune individuals become susceptible again.

sections.heading: Projection versus prediction
sections.body: Underlying all these disputes is a distinction models communicate poorly to the public: a scenario projection states 'if these assumptions hold, this follows' and is meant to inform decisions that change the assumptions, while a prediction claims 'this is what will happen.' Report 9's unmitigated scenario and the wide range of measles R0 estimates are not failures of accuracy in the way a missed weather forecast is — they are outputs conditioned on stated assumptions about contact patterns and behavior that differ across settings and are supposed to differ. When the public conflates the two, a model performing exactly as designed looks, after the fact, like it was simply wrong — the same confusion that let critics call Report 9 'wrong' for a scenario it explicitly labeled unlikely, and that lets a measles R0 of 12 in one town and 18 in another be read as a contradiction rather than as two different, correctly measured populations.

lessons.workedExample: A school board reads that 'measles R0 is 15' and sets a 93% vaccination target using 1 - 1/15. A neighboring district, citing a different published study, uses R0 = 18 and targets 94%. Both are defensible: Guerra et al.'s review shows measles R0 estimates genuinely vary this much across real populations because contact rates differ by community density, age structure, and school size — the studies are not simply disagreeing about the same fixed number, they are measuring different populations. A district that instead cited an outlier study reporting R0 = 203.3 and demanded 99.5% coverage would be extrapolating from a low-quality or unusual study far outside the range Delamater et al. found most estimation methods actually support.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this material to see whether a student treats a cited R0 or projection figure as context-dependent evidence rather than a universal constant. A student who says 'measles R0 is 15' without acknowledging the Guerra/Delamater range, or who calls Report 9 'wrong' because the unmitigated scenario didn't occur, is demonstrating the exact confusion this lesson names — and a judge who asks 'R0 relative to what population and contact structure?' is testing for precisely this understanding.

questions.prompt: Why did Guerra et al. (2017) and Delamater et al. (2019) find such wide variation in published measles R0 estimates?

options.text: Measles itself has changed biologically over time, becoming more transmissible
R0 depends on the population's contact structure and the estimation method used, not just the pathogen
Most of the studies they reviewed used incorrect statistical software
R0 is not actually estimable from real-world data

explanations.a: Measles virus transmissibility has not been shown to change substantially; the variation is attributed to context and method, not viral evolution.
explanations.b: Correct: both reviews concluded R0 estimates vary because contact patterns, population settings, and estimation methods differ across studies, not because the true value is unknowable or the pathogen changes.
explanations.c: The papers attributed variation to genuine methodological and contextual differences, not software errors.
explanations.d: R0 is estimable; the point of both reviews is that it is a context-dependent estimate, not that it cannot be measured at all.

questions.prompt: 'Overshoot' in an unmanaged epidemic refers to the fact that:

options.text: Cumulative infections exceed the herd-immunity threshold because infections already in progress keep transmitting past that point
R0 estimates are always overestimated by modelers
Vaccination coverage targets are always set too high
Case counts are undercounted due to testing limits

explanations.a: Correct: because transmission chains already underway don't stop the instant the threshold is crossed, an unmanaged epidemic's final cumulative-infection level runs past the herd-immunity threshold itself.
explanations.b: Overshoot is a dynamical consequence of the SIR equations, not a claim about systematic bias in R0 estimation.
explanations.c: Overshoot describes epidemic dynamics, not a claim about vaccination policy being miscalibrated.
explanations.d: Testing and surveillance undercounting is a separate, real issue but is not what 'overshoot' refers to in this context.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in how the measles R0 range becomes a real-world policy dispute.

items.text: Individual studies estimate measles R0 in different populations using different methods
Guerra et al. (2017) and Delamater et al. (2019) document the wide resulting range of estimates
A policymaker cites a single R0 value to set a vaccination-coverage target
Confusion arises if the chosen R0 is treated as a universal constant rather than a context-dependent estimate

questions.explanation: The variation originates in study-level estimation, gets documented by systematic reviews, and only becomes a practical problem when a single estimate is applied as though it were a fixed, universal property of the pathogen.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its correct description.

right.text: 'If these assumptions hold, this follows' — meant to inform decisions that change the assumptions
Cumulative infections exceeding the herd-immunity threshold in an unmanaged epidemic
The same pathogen yielding different R0 estimates across populations and methods

questions.explanation: These are three distinct sources of public confusion about transmission models: what a projection claims, why unmanaged epidemics overshoot their threshold, and why a single R0 number is not a fixed constant.

lessons.label: Stochastic Transmission Models

sections.heading: From a smooth curve to a random walk
sections.body: The ODE SIR model tracks S, I, and R as continuous quantities and always predicts steady growth when R0 > 1. Real populations are discrete individuals, and infection and recovery are random events, so a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) version treats S, I, R as integers and assigns each possible event a rate: infection fires at rate beta*S*I/N (moving one person S to I), recovery fires at rate gamma*I (moving one person I to R). This randomness from finite, discrete individuals is demographic stochasticity, and it matters most when case counts are small, exactly the regime the smooth ODE trajectory handles worst. It is distinct from environmental stochasticity, randomness driven by external noise such as weather-linked changes in contact behavior or seasonal school terms, which shifts the rates themselves rather than adding sampling noise around a fixed rate. Gillespie's (1977) exact stochastic simulation algorithm, originally developed for coupled chemical reactions, samples true trajectories of this chain: at each step, sum all current event rates, draw the waiting time to the next event from an exponential distribution with that total rate, pick which event occurs with probability proportional to its own rate, update the state, and repeat. Averaging many such runs recovers the ODE trajectory only in the limit of a large population.

sections.heading: Why chains of infection sometimes just die out
sections.body: Because the CTMC is genuinely random, an epidemic that a deterministic model guarantees will grow can instead fizzle out from bad luck in its first few generations. Treating early spread as a branching process, where each case produces a random number of secondary cases averaging R0, the probability q that the whole chain eventually goes extinct satisfies the fixed-point equation q = G(q), where G is the probability-generating function of the offspring distribution; for a roughly Poisson offspring distribution this extinction probability works out to approximately q ~ 1/R0 whenever R0 > 1, with q = 1 (certain extinction) whenever R0 <= 1. A single imported case with R0 = 4 therefore has roughly a 25% chance of never establishing sustained transmission at all, purely from chance, a possibility the ODE model cannot represent since it has no concept of zero and instead treats every fractional infective as capable of transmitting onward forever.

sections.heading: Critical community size and fadeout
sections.body: Bartlett (1957, 1960) used weekly measles case reports from English and Icelandic communities of different sizes to identify a critical community size (CCS): a population threshold, estimated at roughly 250,000 to 300,000 for measles, below which the infected pool stochastically hits zero between epidemic peaks and the disease must be reimported from elsewhere to reappear. Above the CCS, births replenish susceptibles fast enough that some infected individuals almost always persist through the trough between epidemic waves, letting the chain of transmission continue uninterrupted. Below it, small island populations and isolated towns instead show recurring local extinctions punctuated by reintroduction from larger neighboring cities. Deterministic SIR models predict a stable endemic equilibrium at any population size and cannot produce fadeout at all, making CCS a genuinely stochastic phenomenon and a key reason elimination targets are set relative to a population's size and connectivity, not just its vaccination coverage.

lessons.workedExample: Start a Gillespie run with S=999, I=1, R=0, beta=0.3, gamma=0.1 (R0 = beta/gamma = 3). Infection rate = 0.3*999*1/1000 = 0.2997; recovery rate = 0.1*1 = 0.1; total rate = 0.3997. The next event is infection with probability 0.2997/0.3997 = 75%, recovery with probability 0.1/0.3997 = 25%. If recovery fires first, I drops to 0 and the chain is already extinct after one step. That 25% first-step extinction chance lines up with the branching-process approximation q ~ 1/R0 = 1/3 = 33%: both say a sizable chance of fadeout exists even though R0 = 3 comfortably exceeds 1.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees R0 > 1 reported as proof an outbreak 'will happen' is testing whether the student knows deterministic models cannot represent extinction. The strong answer names the branching-process approximation q ~ 1/R0, explains why elimination programs and import-risk assessments require stochastic simulation rather than the mean-field ODE, and can connect Bartlett's critical community size to why some islands or small nations see measles disappear entirely between reintroductions while large cities do not.

questions.prompt: What can the Gillespie algorithm produce that solving the ODE version of the same SIR model cannot?

options.text: Exact stochastic sample paths, including runs where the chain of infection goes extinct
A faster way to compute the same single deterministic trajectory
A numerical estimate of R0 from case data
The equilibrium prevalence of the disease

explanations.a: Correct: Gillespie draws genuine random sample paths of the underlying Markov chain, some of which hit zero infections, a possibility the continuous ODE cannot represent.
explanations.b: Gillespie is not a faster ODE solver; it simulates discrete stochastic events, generally slower per run than integrating the ODE.
explanations.c: R0 is a model input (from beta and gamma), not something the simulation algorithm estimates from data.
explanations.d: Equilibrium prevalence is a deterministic-model concept; stochastic runs can instead go extinct rather than settle at any equilibrium.

questions.prompt: Using the branching-process approximation q ~ 1/R0, a single imported case with R0 = 4 has roughly what probability of fading out without ever causing a sustained outbreak?

options.text: About 75%
About 25%
About 4%
Essentially 0%, since R0 > 1 guarantees growth

explanations.a: This inverts the ratio; q = 1/R0 = 1/4 = 25%, not 75%.
explanations.b: Correct: q ~ 1/R0 = 1/4 = 0.25, a roughly 25% chance of stochastic fadeout despite R0 exceeding 1.
explanations.c: 1/R0 with R0 = 4 gives 0.25, not 0.04; this option confuses the reciprocal with a different quantity.
explanations.d: R0 > 1 only guarantees growth in the deterministic mean-field limit; individual stochastic chains can still go extinct.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of one iteration of the Gillespie exact stochastic simulation algorithm.

items.text: Compute the rate of every possible event (e.g., infection, recovery) given the current state
Draw the waiting time to the next event from an exponential distribution using the summed total rate
Choose which event occurs with probability proportional to its individual rate
Update the state and advance the clock, then repeat

questions.explanation: Rates must be computed first since both the waiting time and the event choice depend on them; the waiting time uses the summed rate, the event choice uses the individual rates, and only then does the state update.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning in stochastic transmission modeling.

right.text: Randomness arising from finite, discrete individuals rather than external noise
Population threshold below which a pathogen fades out between epidemics absent reimportation
Approximately 1/R0 chance that a single introduced case never establishes sustained transmission

questions.explanation: Demographic stochasticity is the randomness source; critical community size (Bartlett, 1957/1960) is the population-scale consequence for endemic persistence; the branching-process result is the early-outbreak consequence for a single introduction.

lessons.label: Network Models of Transmission

sections.heading: Replacing mass action with an explicit contact structure
sections.body: Mass-action mixing assumes every individual is equally likely to contact every other individual, a reasonable approximation for a well-shuffled population but a poor one for sexual-contact networks, hospital referral networks, or friendship networks where some people have far more contacts than others. A network model instead represents each person as a node and each contact capable of transmission as an edge; a person's degree is their number of edges, and the network can be static (fixed contacts, as in a household or school roster) or dynamic (partnerships forming and dissolving over time, as in sexual-contact networks). Transmission can now only travel along actual edges rather than to a randomly re-drawn partner each time step, so the shape of the degree distribution, not just its average, governs how a pathogen spreads and who is reachable from whom.

sections.heading: Degree variance inflates R0
sections.body: Newman (2002) showed that on a configuration-model network with mean degree <k> and second moment <k^2>, the basic reproduction number for an SIR-type process scales as R0 = T*(<k^2>/<k> - 1), where T is the per-edge transmission probability. Because a randomly chosen edge is more likely to lead to a high-degree node than a randomly chosen person is (a size-biased sampling effect sometimes called the friendship paradox), variance in the degree distribution inflates R0 above what the mean degree alone would predict, even when T and <k> are held fixed. This is why a homogeneous mixing model, which effectively assumes every node shares the population's mean degree, systematically underestimates outbreak potential in any real network with a heavy-tailed degree distribution, and why simply reporting an average number of contacts per person understates transmission risk whenever a few individuals have far more contacts than that average.

sections.heading: Bond percolation and the vanishing threshold in scale-free networks
sections.body: Newman (2002) also formalized an equivalence, building on earlier work by Grassberger (1983), between final SIR epidemic size and bond percolation: occupy each edge independently with probability T, and the set of individuals ultimately infected corresponds to the giant connected component of occupied edges. An epidemic takes off exactly when a giant component exists, i.e., above the percolation threshold. Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani (2001) applied this reasoning to scale-free networks, where the degree distribution follows a power law p_k ~ k^-gamma. For gamma <= 3, a range that includes many real social and technological networks, <k^2> diverges as network size grows, driving the epidemic threshold toward zero: an arbitrarily low-transmissibility pathogen can still spread and persist, unlike homogeneous mixing, which always has a nonzero threshold. The practical consequence is that random, coverage-based control (vaccinating a fixed fraction of the population chosen without regard to their degree) cannot drive such a network below threshold as it grows, whereas targeting the small number of highest-degree hub nodes for immunization can, since removing hubs disproportionately shrinks <k^2> and can restore a genuine, nonzero threshold.

lessons.workedExample: Compare two networks with the same mean degree <k> = 4 but different degree variance. Homogeneous network: every node has degree 4, so <k^2> = 16 and R0 = T*(16/4 - 1) = 3T. Heterogeneous network: half the nodes have degree 1 and half have degree 7, giving <k> = 0.5(1) + 0.5(7) = 4 (same mean) but <k^2> = 0.5(1) + 0.5(49) = 25, so R0 = T*(25/4 - 1) = 5.25T. For identical mean degree and identical per-contact transmissibility T, the more variable network produces 75% higher R0 purely from the presence of a few well-connected hubs.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student conflates 'average number of contacts' with the reproduction number. A strong answer explains, using Newman's <k^2>/<k> formula, why two populations with identical mean contact rates can have very different outbreak potential, and cites Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani (2001) to explain why on hub-dominated (scale-free) networks there may be no safe transmission rate at all, making random vaccination coverage targets misleading compared to hub-targeted immunization.

questions.prompt: Per Newman's (2002) formula R0 = T*(<k^2>/<k> - 1), what happens to R0 if degree variance increases while mean degree <k> and transmission probability T stay fixed?

options.text: R0 increases, because <k^2> grows faster than <k>
R0 decreases, since more variable networks have fewer effective transmission paths
R0 is unaffected, since it depends only on the mean degree
R0 becomes undefined once variance is nonzero

explanations.a: Correct: higher degree variance raises <k^2> for a fixed mean, which directly increases the formula's value.
explanations.b: This has the direction backwards; more variable degree distributions increase, not decrease, R0 in this formula.
explanations.c: The formula depends explicitly on <k^2>, the second moment, not just the mean, so variance matters.
explanations.d: The formula is well-defined for any finite <k^2>; it is only degenerate if <k^2> diverges, as in some scale-free cases.

questions.prompt: Per Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani (2001), what happens to the epidemic threshold on a scale-free network (degree exponent gamma <= 3) as the network grows large?

options.text: It rises toward the mass-action threshold
It approaches zero
It stays constant regardless of network size
It becomes undefined only for gamma > 3

explanations.a: This is the opposite finding; scale-free structure lowers, not raises, the threshold relative to homogeneous mixing.
explanations.b: Correct: because <k^2> diverges as network size grows for gamma <= 3, the epidemic threshold vanishes, so even low-transmissibility pathogens can persist.
explanations.c: The threshold changes with network size in this regime; it does not stay fixed.
explanations.d: The threshold problem appears for gamma <= 3, not gamma > 3, where <k^2> remains finite and a nonzero threshold persists.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of mapping an SIR epidemic on a network onto bond percolation.

items.text: Assign each edge a fixed transmission probability T
Occupy each edge independently with probability T
Identify the connected clusters formed by occupied edges
Interpret a giant occupied-edge component as a population-scale epidemic

questions.explanation: The transmission probability must be defined before edges can be randomly occupied; occupied edges must exist before clusters can be identified; only once clusters are found can the giant-component criterion for an epidemic be applied.

questions.prompt: Match each network-epidemiology term to its description.

right.text: A random graph constructed to match a specified degree distribution
The percolation analog of a population-scale outbreak
A high-degree node that disproportionately raises R0 via the <k^2>/<k> term

questions.explanation: The configuration model is the network-generation tool; the giant component is what an epidemic corresponds to under the percolation mapping; hub nodes are the mechanism by which degree variance drives up R0.

lessons.label: Metapopulation and Spatial Spread

sections.heading: Patches coupled by movement
sections.body: A metapopulation model divides a region into discrete patches, such as cities or districts, each running its own local SIR or SEIR dynamics, and couples the patches through movement of individuals or exchange of force of infection, rather than treating the whole region as one well-mixed pool. Within a patch, standard mass-action or age-structured dynamics can apply; between patches, only a fraction of the force of infection or a fraction of individuals is exchanged per unit time. A common coupling form is the gravity model, borrowed from geography: the flux of travelers, and hence transmission coupling, between patches i and j is assumed to scale with the product of their population sizes N_i and N_j and fall off with some function of the distance d_ij between them, mirroring the empirical observation that traffic grows with the size of both endpoints and shrinks with separation, much as Newton's gravitational force scales with the product of two masses and the inverse square of their separation.

sections.heading: Hierarchical traveling waves in English and Welsh measles
sections.body: Grenfell, Bjornstad and Kappey (2001) analyzed weekly measles notifications from around 60 towns and cities across England and Wales from 1944 to 1994, spanning both the pre-vaccination era and the decades after the UK introduced measles vaccination in 1968. Rather than a simple geographic wave radiating outward from a single point, they found hierarchical traveling waves: large cities such as London seeded epidemics that then spread outward to smaller towns with a time lag tied to city size and distance, consistent with gravity-like coupling strongest between large, well-connected population centers rather than simply between geographic neighbors. Rising vaccination coverage restricted this hierarchical pattern but did not eliminate it. Below the critical community size discussed for stochastic fadeout, the smallest towns in their dataset showed no persistent local transmission at all between waves, receiving each epidemic afresh as an import from the urban hierarchy above them, tying the spatial and stochastic pictures of measles dynamics together.

sections.heading: From gravity models to real air-travel networks
sections.body: Modern global-scale models replace assumed gravity-model distances with measured mobility data. GLEAM (the Global Epidemic and Mobility Model), developed by the Vespignani group and described by Balcan et al. (2009), divides the world into thousands of subpopulations built around airport catchment areas, links them using real IATA air-traffic flows plus short-range commuting data, and runs stochastic within-patch SEIR-type dynamics coupled across this empirical network. Because the coupling comes from actual passenger volumes rather than an assumed distance-decay function, two cities thousands of kilometers apart but connected by a busy direct flight route can be modeled as more strongly coupled than two much closer cities with poor transport links, something a pure gravity model with only distance and population as inputs cannot capture. GLEAM was used to project the international spread of the 2009 H1N1 influenza pandemic, informing WHO and public-health agencies in near real time as the outbreak unfolded across dozens of countries within weeks.

lessons.workedExample: Compare gravity-model coupling for two candidate connections from City A (population 1,000,000). City B has population 100,000 and sits 50 km away; using a simple form coupling ~ N_A*N_B / d^2, coupling(A,B) = (1,000,000 x 100,000) / 50^2 = 1x10^11 / 2,500 = 4x10^7. City C has population only 50,000 but sits just 10 km away: coupling(A,C) = (1,000,000 x 50,000) / 10^2 = 5x10^10 / 100 = 5x10^8, about 12 times stronger than A-B despite City C being half the population of City B. Because distance enters squared, proximity can dominate over population size, which is exactly why Grenfell et al. found hierarchical rather than simple concentric-circle spread out of London.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student understands that spatial spread is not simple diffusion outward from an outbreak's origin. The strong answer names the actual empirical dataset (weekly measles notifications, England and Wales, 1944-1994) behind Grenfell, Bjornstad and Kappey's hierarchical-wave finding, explains why gravity coupling depends on both population size and distance rather than distance alone, and can contrast that assumed functional form with GLEAM's use of real air-travel data for global-scale forecasting.

questions.prompt: What spatial pattern did Grenfell, Bjornstad and Kappey (2001) find in weekly measles notifications across England and Wales (1944-1994)?

options.text: Simple concentric circles of spread radiating outward from London
Hierarchical traveling waves, with large cities seeding smaller towns with a time lag
No spatial structure at all; all towns peaked simultaneously
Spread strictly proportional to geographic distance from the coast

explanations.a: The observed pattern was not simple concentric geographic spread; population-size hierarchy mattered as much as distance.
explanations.b: Correct: epidemics were seeded in large cities like London and then propagated outward to smaller towns with a lag tied to both size and distance.
explanations.c: The study specifically documented strong spatial and temporal structure, not simultaneous nationwide peaks.
explanations.d: Coastal distance was not the organizing variable; city-size hierarchy combined with distance was.

questions.prompt: What does GLEAM use to couple its subpopulations, in place of an assumed gravity-model distance function?

options.text: Real air-travel flows and short-range commuting data
A fixed constant coupling identical between every pair of patches
Only straight-line geographic distance between capital cities
Randomized coupling reassigned at each simulation run

explanations.a: Correct: GLEAM, from the Vespignani group as described by Balcan et al. (2009), links airport-catchment subpopulations using measured IATA air-traffic and commuting data.
explanations.b: GLEAM's coupling is structured by real, uneven mobility data, not a uniform constant.
explanations.c: GLEAM uses actual traffic flows between thousands of subpopulations, not just capital-to-capital distances.
explanations.d: The mobility network is built from real data and held fixed for a given scenario, not randomized per run.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in constructing a metapopulation model of spatial spread.

items.text: Divide the region into discrete patches (e.g., cities)
Run local SIR/SEIR dynamics within each patch
Compute inter-patch coupling strengths from a gravity model or measured mobility data
Simulate movement or force-of-infection exchange between patches over time

questions.explanation: Patches must be defined before local dynamics can run within them, coupling strengths must be computed before they can be applied, and the exchange between patches is the final step that produces spatial spread.

questions.prompt: Match each spatial-spread concept to its description.

right.text: Coupling scales with the product of patch populations and falls with distance
Global metapopulation model coupled by real air-travel and commuting data
Large population centers seed smaller ones, with a lag tied to size and distance

questions.explanation: The gravity model is the assumed coupling function; GLEAM is the empirically-driven global implementation; the hierarchical traveling wave is the empirical pattern Grenfell, Bjornstad and Kappey observed that gravity-like coupling reproduces.

lessons.label: Agent-Based and Individual-Based Models

sections.heading: Simulating people, not compartments
sections.body: An agent-based model (ABM), also called an individual-based model, represents each person as a distinct simulated agent with attributes such as age and household, school, and workplace membership, plus a disease state (susceptible, exposed, infectious, recovered) that changes through explicit contacts within those layers rather than through a single population-wide mixing rate. Where a compartmental model lumps everyone of a given disease state together and assumes they behave identically going forward, an ABM tracks each individual's specific history, location, and set of contacts, letting outcomes depend on who exactly someone lives with or sits near at school. This lets an ABM reproduce contact clustering within households, classrooms, and workplaces, and evaluate interventions that target one layer specifically, something a single transmission-rate parameter cannot represent without ad hoc adjustment such as manually shrinking beta by an assumed percentage to mimic school closure.

sections.heading: The pandemic-influenza ABMs
sections.body: Two influential lineages built large synthetic-population ABMs to evaluate pandemic influenza response. Ferguson and colleagues (2005, 2006) at Imperial College constructed spatially explicit models of populations including Great Britain, Thailand, and the United States, with simulated households, schools, workplaces, and communities, to test mitigation strategies such as school closure, case isolation, antiviral treatment, and travel restrictions; the same modeling lineage was later extended for COVID-19 policy advice in early 2020, most visibly in projections of intensive-care demand under different combinations of non-pharmaceutical interventions. Halloran and Longini (2008) built a similarly structured, US-scale synthetic-population ABM, simulating on the order of hundreds of millions of individuals, to evaluate 'targeted layered containment,' combining household-based antiviral prophylaxis, school closure, and social distancing against pandemic influenza, finding that layering several partial measures together outperformed any single intervention applied alone.

sections.heading: What ABMs capture, and what they cost
sections.body: ABMs capture household clustering of secondary cases, contact-driven superspreading and overdispersion, and the differential impact of spatially or socially targeted interventions, all of which compartmental models can only approximate through coarse, population-wide parameter tweaks. The trade-offs are substantial: simulating tens to hundreds of millions of agents across many stochastic replicates is computationally expensive, often requiring dedicated computing clusters and runtimes of hours to days per policy scenario. The models also face an identifiability problem, since many different combinations of household, school, and workplace transmission probabilities can reproduce the same aggregate epidemic curve. Fitting an ABM to case counts alone therefore often leaves its layer-specific parameters underdetermined without additional data, such as contact-tracing or serological studies, to pin them down, meaning two labs can fit the same reported outbreak curve with meaningfully different underlying assumptions about where transmission is actually happening.

lessons.workedExample: Consider a simulated household of four: two adults and two school-age children. The ABM assigns a within-household transmission probability of roughly 15% as the cumulative secondary attack rate over the full infectious period of exposure to an infectious housemate (a typical range for influenza household secondary attack rates), and a much smaller per-contact probability at school, but each child there has dozens of daily classroom contacts. Under a school-closure intervention, the model zeroes out only the school-layer contact rate for all school-age agents while leaving household and community-layer transmission unchanged, letting the simulation show the intervention's effect isolated from the other contact layers, a distinction a single population-wide beta parameter cannot express.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student who used or cited an ABM understands the identifiability problem: many combinations of household, school, and workplace transmission rates can fit the same aggregate case curve, so the specific rates chosen need independent justification (contact-tracing or serology), not just curve-fitting. A strong answer also explains that ABMs exist specifically to evaluate targeted interventions, like school closure, that operate on one contact layer at a time, which a single-beta compartmental model cannot represent.

questions.prompt: What structural feature can an agent-based model represent that a standard compartmental SEIR model cannot without ad hoc adjustment?

options.text: Explicit household, school, and workplace contact layers that can be intervened on separately
A higher basic reproduction number than compartmental models allow
Exact, deterministic prediction of the epidemic's final size
Elimination of all computational cost associated with simulation

explanations.a: Correct: explicit contact layers let an ABM evaluate layer-specific interventions, such as school closure, that a single mixing rate cannot isolate.
explanations.b: R0 is not inherently higher in ABMs; it emerges from the same kind of contact and transmission assumptions as any model.
explanations.c: ABMs are typically stochastic, producing a distribution of outcomes across replicates, not one exact deterministic final size.
explanations.d: ABMs are considerably more computationally expensive than compartmental models, not less.

questions.prompt: What is the identifiability problem in calibrating large agent-based pandemic-influenza models?

options.text: Many different combinations of layer-specific transmission probabilities can reproduce the same aggregate epidemic curve
The models cannot produce an aggregate epidemic curve at all
Household transmission cannot be simulated in any ABM
ABMs always converge to a unique parameter set given enough case data

explanations.a: Correct: without additional data like contact-tracing or serology, multiple household/school/workplace rate combinations fit the same aggregate curve equally well.
explanations.b: ABMs readily produce an aggregate epidemic curve by summing over simulated individuals; that is not the source of the identifiability problem.
explanations.c: Household transmission is a core, well-supported feature of these ABMs; the issue is pinning down its rate uniquely, not simulating it.
explanations.d: The opposite is true: aggregate case counts alone typically underdetermine the layer-specific parameters.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in building and calibrating a synthetic-population pandemic-influenza ABM.

items.text: Construct a synthetic population with explicit households, schools, and workplaces
Assign contact-layer-specific transmission probabilities
Simulate stochastic person-to-person transmission over time
Compare the simulated aggregate epidemic curve to real case data and adjust parameters

questions.explanation: The population structure must exist before layer-specific rates can be assigned, rates must be set before simulation can run, and calibration against real data is necessarily the final step.

questions.prompt: Match each item to its description.

right.text: Imperial College ABM evaluating pandemic-influenza mitigation strategies, later extended for COVID-19 advice
US-scale ABM evaluating targeted layered containment for pandemic influenza
Multiple parameter combinations fitting the same aggregate epidemic curve

questions.explanation: Ferguson and colleagues built the Imperial ABM lineage; Halloran and Longini built the targeted-layered-containment US ABM; the identifiability problem is the calibration challenge both lineages share.

lessons.label: Age- and Contact-Structured Models

sections.heading: WAIFW matrices and the next-generation matrix
sections.body: A who-acquires-infection-from-whom (WAIFW) matrix specifies beta_ij, the transmission rate from age group j to age group i. Historically these entries had to be assumed rather than measured, because serological data on who is immune cannot by itself uniquely determine who infected whom: many different beta_ij matrices can be fit to the same observed age-specific prevalence curve, forcing modelers to impose structural assumptions like proportionate mixing (everyone contacts others in proportion to group size) or strictly assortative mixing (contact concentrated within one's own age group) to make the matrix identifiable at all. The next-generation matrix (NGM) framework, formalized by Diekmann, Heesterbeek and Metz, generalizes R0 to structured populations: build a matrix of expected secondary infections in each age group produced by one infectious individual from each other group, and R0 is that matrix's dominant eigenvalue, the single number summarizing growth potential across all the interacting groups at once.

sections.heading: POLYMOD: measuring contacts directly
sections.body: Mossong et al. (2008) ran the POLYMOD study, collecting paper contact diaries from about 7,290 participants across eight European countries (Belgium, Germany, Finland, Great Britain, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and Poland), recording nearly 98,000 contacts over one assigned day, each logged with the contact's age, setting (home, school, work, leisure, transport), duration, frequency, and whether it involved physical touch. POLYMOD replaced the need to assume a WAIFW structure: contact matrices could now be built directly from measured data and combined with a per-contact transmission probability to construct an empirically grounded next-generation matrix. Because the survey spanned eight countries with different school systems and household sizes, it also let researchers test how much contact structure, and hence model predictions, varies across otherwise broadly similar European settings.

sections.heading: Assortative mixing reshapes vaccination targeting
sections.body: POLYMOD-derived contact matrices consistently show strong age-assortative mixing: contact rates concentrate near the diagonal, meaning children mix overwhelmingly with other children through school, with a smaller secondary concentration between grandparents and grandchildren reflecting family caregiving contact. Because children carry both the highest contact rates and, for many respiratory infections such as influenza and measles, the largest share of transmission, models built on POLYMOD matrices consistently find that vaccinating school-age children produces outsized indirect protection for the elderly, who bear the highest mortality risk but contribute comparatively little to transmission, relative to vaccinating the same number of elderly people directly. This finding, that protecting the group with high mortality is best achieved by immunizing a different group with high contact, underlies child-targeted influenza vaccination policy debates in the United Kingdom and elsewhere, and is the same mixing-pattern logic that motivates cocooning strategies around newborns.

lessons.workedExample: Take a simplified two-group next-generation matrix for children (C) and adults (A): K = [[10, 2], [2, 3]], where K_11 = 10 reflects high child-child contact from POLYMOD-style assortative mixing. The dominant eigenvalue solves (10-lambda)(3-lambda) - 4 = 0, i.e., lambda^2 - 13*lambda + 26 = 0, giving lambda = (13 +/- sqrt(65))/2, so lambda ~ (13 + 8.06)/2 ~ 10.5. R0 ~ 10.5, dominated almost entirely by the K_11 = 10 child-child entry. Because that entry dominates the matrix, reducing it through child vaccination lowers the dominant eigenvalue far more than an equivalent reduction to the smaller adult-adult entry K_22 = 3 would.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student understands that contact patterns, not just contact counts, determine who should be vaccinated. The strong answer explains why vaccinating children protects grandparents more than directly vaccinating an equal number of grandparents would, grounding the claim in POLYMOD's documented age-assortative mixing (Mossong et al., 2008) and the next-generation-matrix logic that R0 is set by the matrix's dominant eigenvalue, not by any single group's contact count in isolation.

questions.prompt: What did the POLYMOD study (Mossong et al., 2008) replace the historical reliance on?

options.text: Assumed WAIFW matrix structures, replaced by contact rates measured via participant diaries
Serological survey data, which POLYMOD showed was unnecessary for any epidemic model
The next-generation matrix framework, which POLYMOD proved mathematically invalid
Vaccination coverage data collected by national health agencies

explanations.a: Correct: POLYMOD measured contact rates directly from diaries across eight countries, removing the need to assume a WAIFW structure.
explanations.b: POLYMOD complements rather than replaces serological data; both remain useful inputs to structured models.
explanations.c: POLYMOD provided empirical inputs to the next-generation-matrix framework; it did not invalidate the framework itself.
explanations.d: POLYMOD measured social contact patterns, not vaccination coverage, which is a separate data source.

questions.prompt: What pattern do POLYMOD-derived contact matrices consistently show across the eight participating countries?

options.text: Strong age-assortative mixing, with contacts concentrated near the diagonal, especially among children
Uniform mixing across all age groups, matching a simple mass-action assumption
Adults contacting only other adults, with children essentially isolated from all age groups
Contact rates that decline with age but show no grouping by age at all

explanations.a: Correct: POLYMOD data consistently show contacts concentrated near the diagonal, with children mixing heavily with other children and a secondary grandparent-grandchild concentration.
explanations.b: Uniform mass-action mixing is exactly what POLYMOD's diary data contradicted; contact rates vary strongly by age pairing.
explanations.c: Children are not isolated; school and household settings generate extensive child-child and child-adult contact.
explanations.d: The data show clear age-pair grouping (assortativity), not a simple monotonic decline with no structure.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in building a next-generation-matrix R0 estimate from POLYMOD-style data.

items.text: Collect empirical contact diaries broken down by participant and contact age
Construct an age-structured contact matrix from the diary data
Combine the contact matrix with a per-contact transmission probability to build the next-generation matrix
Compute the matrix's dominant eigenvalue as R0

questions.explanation: Diaries must be collected before a contact matrix can be built, the contact matrix must exist before it can be combined with transmission probability, and the dominant eigenvalue can only be computed once the next-generation matrix is assembled.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its description.

right.text: Historically assumed transmission-rate structure, underdetermined by serology alone
Contact diary study spanning eight European countries (Mossong et al., 2008)
R0 in an age-structured population

questions.explanation: The WAIFW matrix is the older assumed structure; POLYMOD is the empirical contact-measurement study that grounds it; the dominant eigenvalue of the next-generation matrix is how R0 is recovered once the structured matrix is built.

lessons.label: Heterogeneity and Superspreading

sections.heading: Offspring distributions beyond the population mean
sections.body: R0 is a population average, but the number of secondary cases any individual actually produces, the offspring distribution, can vary enormously even when the mean is fixed, since biological factors (viral load, symptom severity), behavioral factors (number of contacts, adherence to isolation), and setting (a crowded indoor venue versus an outdoor one) all combine to make one infected person very different from another. Lloyd-Smith, Schreiber, Kopp and Getz (2005) modeled each individual's personal reproductive number as a continuous random variable, gamma-distributed with mean R0, which yields a negative-binomial distribution for the realized number of secondary cases, characterized by a dispersion parameter k. Small k means strong overdispersion, most cases infect few or no one while rare individuals infect many, while k approaching infinity recovers the homogeneous Poisson case where everyone contributes roughly equally and individual variation washes out.

sections.heading: The 20/80 rule and measured k values
sections.body: Lloyd-Smith et al. generalized the '20/80 rule' from earlier work on parasite aggregation to infectious-disease transmission: the share of all transmission attributable to the most infectious 20% of cases, which exceeds 80% for strongly overdispersed diseases and is closer to 20% for a homogeneous, Poisson-like disease where transmission is spread evenly. Fitting k to outbreak data, they estimated k ~ 0.16 for SARS-CoV-1 (2003), reflecting its history of dramatic superspreading events in hospitals and apartment complexes such as the Amoy Gardens cluster in Hong Kong, against much lower overdispersion for measles, a disease that spreads efficiently enough that most cases transmit onward. Later work extended the approach to SARS-CoV-2: Endo, Abbott, Kucharski and Funk (2020) estimated k ~ 0.1 from outbreak-size data outside China, implying roughly 10% of cases may drive about 80% of transmission, consistent with documented events at choir practices, meatpacking plants, and cruise ships.

sections.heading: Low k both raises extinction risk and enables explosive events
sections.body: Lloyd-Smith et al. showed low k has a two-sided effect a mean R0 alone cannot capture: for a fixed mean R0 > 1, lower k increases the probability that a newly introduced chain of infection goes stochastically extinct, since most individual cases contribute near-zero secondary infections, while simultaneously raising the risk of an explosive event whenever a high-transmission individual happens to be infected. This combination, frequent fizzling punctuated by rare flare-ups, is why backward contact tracing, identifying who infected a case rather than only who that case infected, becomes a more effective control strategy for overdispersed pathogens than it would be under a homogeneous-Poisson assumption: tracing backward is disproportionately likely to land on one of the rare, highly infectious individuals, and finding that person's other contacts can pre-empt a large cluster before it fully develops.

lessons.workedExample: Take R0 = 2 with k = 0.1, close to reported SARS-CoV-2 estimates. The probability an index case produces zero secondary infections under a negative binomial with mean R0 and dispersion k is (k/(k+R0))^k = (0.1/2.1)^0.1 = 0.0476^0.1. Taking logs, 0.1 x ln(0.0476) = 0.1 x (-3.045) = -0.3045, so the probability is exp(-0.3045) ~ 0.74, about 74%. Compare a homogeneous Poisson process with the same mean R0 = 2: probability of zero secondary infections is e^-2 ~ 13.5%. Despite identical mean R0, the overdispersed process leaves roughly three-quarters of index cases transmitting to no one, while a small minority drive large clusters.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student understands that 'R0 = 2' alone does not tell you extinction risk or superspreading risk, only mean behavior; the dispersion parameter k is what distinguishes those. A strong answer cites specific fitted values (SARS-CoV-1 k ~ 0.16 from Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005; SARS-CoV-2 k ~ 0.1 from Endo et al., 2020) and explains why backward contact tracing outperforms forward tracing precisely because low k means most transmission traces back to a small share of highly infectious individuals worth finding.

questions.prompt: For a fixed mean R0, what does a lower dispersion parameter k indicate about individual transmission?

options.text: Greater variance: most cases infect few or no one while rare individuals infect many
Lower variance: transmission is spread more evenly across cases
A higher mean R0 than reported
That the offspring distribution is Poisson rather than negative binomial

explanations.a: Correct: smaller k means stronger overdispersion in the negative-binomial offspring distribution, concentrating transmission in a minority of cases.
explanations.b: This is backwards; lower k corresponds to higher variance, not lower.
explanations.c: k and R0 are separate parameters; k describes variance around the mean, not the mean itself.
explanations.d: A finite, small k describes a strongly overdispersed negative binomial; the homogeneous Poisson case corresponds to k approaching infinity, not small k.

questions.prompt: Lloyd-Smith et al. (2005) estimated k ~ 0.16 for SARS-CoV-1. What does this low value of k, combined with the 20/80 rule, imply?

options.text: A small fraction of highly infectious cases accounted for most transmission
Transmission was distributed almost equally across all infected individuals
SARS-CoV-1 had an R0 below 1 and could not sustain outbreaks
Contact tracing was ineffective against SARS-CoV-1

explanations.a: Correct: k ~ 0.16 is strongly overdispersed, consistent with the well-documented SARS-CoV-1 superspreading events driving most transmission.
explanations.b: Equal distribution across cases corresponds to large k (near-Poisson), the opposite of the low k reported for SARS-CoV-1.
explanations.c: k describes variance in secondary cases, not the value of R0 itself; SARS-CoV-1 sustained outbreaks with R0 above 1.
explanations.d: Low k is precisely why targeted, backward contact tracing was an effective control strategy for SARS-CoV-1, not an ineffective one.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in estimating a pathogen's dispersion parameter k and using it operationally.

items.text: Collect contact-traced outbreak data on secondary case counts per index case
Fit a negative-binomial offspring distribution to the observed counts
Estimate the dispersion parameter k from the fit
Use k to compute stochastic extinction probability and the 20/80 transmission share

questions.explanation: Secondary-case data must be collected before a distribution can be fit, the fit must be performed before k can be extracted, and only once k is known can extinction probability and the 20/80 share be computed.

questions.prompt: Match each term or estimate to its description.

right.text: Negative-binomial parameter quantifying variation in secondary cases
Share of transmission attributable to the most infectious minority of cases
Estimate from Endo, Abbott, Kucharski and Funk (2020)

questions.explanation: k is the dispersion parameter itself; the 20/80 rule is the generalized statement about transmission concentration it produces; the specific SARS-CoV-2 value of ~0.1 comes from Endo et al.'s 2020 outbreak-size analysis.

lessons.label: Seasonality and Endemic Dynamics

sections.heading: Forcing beta with the school calendar
sections.body: For childhood infections like measles and pertussis, contact rates among children spike during school terms and drop during holidays, so the transmission rate is not constant but seasonally forced: beta(t) = beta0 * (1 + b1 * term(t)), where term(t) is higher during term time and lower during holidays, and b1 sets the amplitude of that seasonal swing relative to the baseline rate beta0. This 'term-time forcing' was formalized in age-structured measles models such as Schenzle (1984), reflecting the recognition that school contact patterns, not weather, drive the dominant seasonal signal for measles transmission in temperate countries, in contrast to some other respiratory infections where humidity or temperature plays a larger direct role in pathogen survival.

sections.heading: Resonance and the biennial cycle
sections.body: An unforced SEIR model with measles-like parameters relaxes toward its endemic equilibrium through damped oscillations with a natural period of roughly one to two years, driven by the same susceptible-depletion-and-replenishment feedback that produces epidemic waves in the first place. When the one-year school-term forcing interacts with that natural period, the system can resonate into a stable period-2 (biennial) cycle: a large epidemic year is followed by a small one, matching the well-documented biennial measles pattern in pre-vaccination England and Wales, where large cities regularly showed a big epidemic year alternating with a much smaller one. Mechanistically, a big epidemic depletes the susceptible pool so heavily that too few susceptibles remain for another big epidemic the next year, and only after roughly two years of new births does the pool refill enough to cross the epidemic threshold again and support the next large outbreak.

sections.heading: From cycles to chaos, and Soper's unfinished problem
sections.body: Soper (1929) built one of the earliest quantitative measles models trying to explain its regular epidemic periodicity, but his simple unforced model produced only damped oscillations settling toward equilibrium, not the sustained cycles seen in real notification data, a gap later termed Soper's periodicity problem, since real measles case reports kept oscillating indefinitely rather than flattening out. Olsen and Schaffer (1990) revisited it with a seasonally forced SEIR model and showed that as forcing amplitude increases, the system passes through a sequence of period-doubling bifurcations into deterministic chaos, arguing that irregular pre-vaccination measles dynamics in some large cities, notably New York, were consistent with low-dimensional chaos rather than simple regular cycles. Later work, including Bolker and Grenfell's, argued that stochastic effects (demographic noise in a finite population) combined with imperfect, non-sinusoidal forcing better explain the same irregular data without requiring true deterministic chaos, an unresolved contrast worth naming as a live modeling disagreement rather than a settled result.

lessons.workedExample: Consider a city of 1,000,000 people with a birth rate replenishing about 2% of the population as new susceptibles per year, and R0 ~ 15 for measles, giving an epidemic threshold susceptible fraction of about 1/R0 ~ 6.7%. Suppose a large epidemic depletes the susceptible fraction down to about 2%. Refilling the gap back up to the 6.7% threshold requires roughly (6.7% - 2%) / 2% per year ~ 2.35 years of births. That arithmetic, susceptible depletion by a big epidemic followed by a roughly two-year refill via births, is the mechanistic reason the resonance between annual school forcing and multi-year susceptible replenishment locks onto a biennial rather than strictly annual cycle.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can explain the biennial cycle mechanistically, through susceptible depletion and replenishment interacting with annual school-term forcing, rather than reciting 'seasonality causes cycles' without a mechanism. A judge may also ask which side of the chaos-versus-noise debate current evidence favors; the strong answer knows Olsen and Schaffer's (1990) own title poses it as a live alternative, and that later stochastic-noise arguments (e.g., Bolker and Grenfell) contest the low-dimensional-chaos interpretation, rather than presenting either side as settled.

questions.prompt: What does term-time forcing tie the seasonal variation in beta(t) to?

options.text: The school calendar, with higher contact rates during term time and lower during holidays
Ambient temperature and humidity fluctuations
Annual vaccination campaign schedules
Birth rate fluctuations across the calendar year

explanations.a: Correct: term-time forcing, as formalized by Schenzle (1984), ties beta(t) to school-term contact spikes and holiday drops among children.
explanations.b: Weather variables are not the mechanism identified for measles' dominant seasonal signal; school contact patterns are.
explanations.c: Term-time forcing predates and is independent of vaccination campaign timing; it describes contact-driven transmission-rate changes.
explanations.d: Birth rate affects the susceptible pool's replenishment over years, not the within-year seasonal forcing of beta(t).

questions.prompt: What pattern arises from resonance between the SEIR model's natural oscillation period and one-year school-term forcing in pre-vaccination measles?

options.text: A stable biennial (large-year, small-year) epidemic cycle
A strictly annual cycle with identical epidemic size every year
Complete elimination of seasonal variation
A cycle with no relationship to susceptible depletion

explanations.a: Correct: resonance between the roughly one-to-two-year natural period and annual forcing locks onto a period-2, biennial cycle, matching documented England and Wales data.
explanations.b: The documented pattern alternates large and small years; it is not a uniform annual repeat.
explanations.c: Resonance amplifies rather than eliminates the seasonal signal, producing the biennial pattern.
explanations.d: The biennial cycle is mechanistically driven by susceptible depletion in the big year and replenishment via births in the following year.

questions.prompt: Order the dynamical route Olsen and Schaffer (1990) described as forcing amplitude increases in a seasonally forced SEIR model.

items.text: Annual (period-1) cycle
Biennial (period-2) cycle
Period-4 cycle
Deterministic chaos

questions.explanation: Olsen and Schaffer (1990) described a sequence of period-doubling bifurcations, from annual to biennial to period-4 and onward, that terminates in deterministic chaos at high forcing amplitude.

questions.prompt: Match each contributor to their role in the seasonality-and-endemic-dynamics literature.

right.text: Early unforced model producing only damped oscillations, leaving the periodicity problem unsolved
Age-structured measles model formalizing term-time forcing
Seasonally forced SEIR model showing a period-doubling route to chaos

questions.explanation: Soper posed the original unsolved periodicity problem; Schenzle supplied the term-time forcing mechanism; Olsen and Schaffer showed that mechanism, at higher amplitude, drives the system into chaos.

lessons.label: Designing Vaccination Programs

sections.heading: From R0 to a coverage target
sections.body: The herd-immunity threshold answers a design question: what fraction of the population must be immune to push Rt below 1? Starting from Rt = R0(1-p) for a perfectly effective vaccine given to a random fraction p, setting Rt = 1 gives the critical coverage pc = 1 - 1/R0. Real vaccines are leaky -- they don't confer perfect immunity -- so the formula gains an efficacy term E: pc = (1 - 1/R0)/E. A vaccine with 90% efficacy against a pathogen with R0 = 6 needs pc = (1 - 1/6)/0.9 = 0.833/0.9 = 0.93, not the 0.83 a perfect vaccine would require. Measles, with R0 commonly cited between 12 and 18 and a highly effective vaccine, still demands roughly 92-95% coverage -- the number every measles outbreak report cites because it sits right at that threshold, and any dip below it reopens the door to sustained chains.

sections.heading: Pulse vaccination and age targeting
sections.body: Continuous routine vaccination struggles to reach every birth cohort fast enough in populations with high birth rates, so programs use pulse vaccination: periodic mass campaigns that vaccinate a wide age band all at once rather than trickling coverage in via routine visits. Agur, Cojocaru, Mazor, Anderson, and Danon (1993) showed mathematically that pulsed campaigns across multiple age cohorts can drive measles below threshold faster than routine dosing alone, which is the logic behind National Immunization Days used in polio eradication and periodic measles catch-up campaigns. Age targeting adds a second lever on top of the pulse timing: because a single birth cohort mixes disproportionately with its own age group, catch-up campaigns aimed at unvaccinated older children and young adults close susceptibility gaps that routine infant dosing alone leaves open for years, which is why school-entry boosters and college-entry MMR requirements are standard policy layers rather than redundant ones.

sections.heading: When partial coverage backfires
sections.body: Coverage below threshold doesn't just fail to eliminate a disease -- for age-severity-linked infections it can make outcomes worse. Rubella is usually mild in children but causes congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) when a pregnant woman is infected in the first trimester, producing deafness, cataracts, heart defects, and other permanent damage in the infant. Vaccinating children reduces circulation, which raises the average age at infection for anyone who stays susceptible; if coverage is too low to reach threshold, more of those late infections land in women of childbearing age. Panagiotopoulos, Antoniadou, and Valassi-Adam (1999) documented exactly this in Greece: rubella vaccination introduced in 1975 at insufficient, inconsistent coverage (roughly 50-60% in the years studied) suppressed transmission enough to shift the average age of infection upward without eliminating it, and CRS cases rose in the following decade rather than falling. Mumps shows an analogous pattern, since complications like orchitis are more common in adult cases, which is why models used to design a catch-up campaign must check the post-intervention age distribution, not just the aggregate incidence.

lessons.workedExample: A school district considers a mumps vaccine with 88% efficacy against a strain with R0 = 5. Critical coverage is pc = (1 - 1/5)/0.88 = 0.8/0.88 = 0.91, so 91% of students need vaccination to push Rt below 1. If the district only reaches 70% coverage, Rt stays above 1 (Rt = R0[1 - E*p] = 5[1 - 0.88*0.70] = 5*0.384 = 1.92), transmission continues, and because circulation is suppressed but not stopped, the average age at infection rises -- shifting mumps cases from children, who mostly recover uneventfully, toward teenagers and young adults, who face a higher rate of orchitis and other complications.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks a vaccination-modeling project for the coverage target and expects the E-adjusted formula, not the bare 1-1/R0 version -- using perfect-vaccine math on a leaky vaccine understates the true target. Judges also probe whether a student understands that partial coverage is not simply 'less good than full coverage': for age-severity-linked diseases like rubella, it can shift the burden onto a more vulnerable age group, a genuinely counterintuitive result that separates students who memorized the formula from those who understand the age-structured mechanism behind it.

questions.prompt: A pathogen has R0 = 6 and a vaccine with 90% efficacy. What is the critical vaccination coverage?

options.text: About 83%, using pc = 1 - 1/R0 and ignoring efficacy
90%, since coverage should just equal vaccine efficacy
100%, since any R0 above 1 requires vaccinating everyone

explanations.a: Correct: 1 - 1/6 = 0.833, and dividing by efficacy 0.9 gives pc = 0.833/0.9 = 0.93, the leaky-vaccine-adjusted threshold.
explanations.b: This is the perfect-vaccine formula; it understates the true coverage needed whenever efficacy is below 100%.
explanations.c: Coverage and efficacy are different quantities: coverage is the fraction of people vaccinated, efficacy is how well the vaccine protects each vaccinated person.
explanations.d: The threshold formula shows coverage needed is well below 100% for most R0 and efficacy combinations; 100% is only required in edge cases like very high R0 with low efficacy.

questions.prompt: Why did rubella vaccination in Greece (documented by Panagiotopoulos et al., 1999) coincide with a rise in congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) cases rather than a fall?

options.text: Coverage was high enough to eliminate rubella in children but not high enough to reach threshold, so the average age at infection rose and more infections landed in women of childbearing age
The vaccine caused CRS directly in vaccinated children
CRS is unrelated to rubella infection timing, so the rise was coincidental
Coverage exceeded the critical threshold, which mathematically always increases severe outcomes temporarily

explanations.a: Correct: below-threshold coverage suppressed but did not eliminate circulation, shifting the average age at infection upward into childbearing years where rubella causes CRS.
explanations.b: The mechanism is epidemiological (shifted age at infection), not a direct vaccine side effect; this misattributes the cause.
