explanations.c: CRS occurs specifically when a pregnant woman contracts rubella, so infection timing relative to age is central to the mechanism, not incidental.
explanations.d: Coverage that reaches or exceeds threshold eliminates transmission entirely, which prevents this age-shift effect rather than causing it; the Greek case involved coverage below threshold.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to derive the leaky-vaccine critical coverage formula pc = (1 - 1/R0)/E.

items.text: Start from Rt = R0(1 - E*p), where p is coverage and E is vaccine efficacy
Set Rt = 1 to find the coverage that sits exactly at the epidemic threshold
Solve for p: 1 = R0(1 - E*p) becomes E*p = 1 - 1/R0
Divide both sides by E to isolate p = (1 - 1/R0)/E

questions.explanation: The derivation starts from the effective-reproduction-number expression that includes efficacy, pins Rt to the threshold value of 1, then does the algebra to isolate coverage.

questions.prompt: Match each vaccination strategy or concept to its description.

right.text: Periodic mass campaigns vaccinating a wide age band at once, used in polio and measles eradication
A vaccine that reduces but does not eliminate susceptibility in each recipient
The minimum immune fraction needed to push Rt below 1
Below-threshold coverage raising the average age at infection, increasing CRS risk

questions.explanation: Each concept plays a distinct role: pulse vaccination is a delivery strategy, leaky-ness is a vaccine property, pc is the coverage target, and the age shift is the mechanism by which under-threshold coverage can worsen severity-linked outcomes.

lessons.label: Non-Pharmaceutical Interventions and Bending the Curve

sections.heading: Every NPI is a knob on effective contact
sections.body: Non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) -- school closure, physical distancing, case isolation, and contact quarantine -- have no biological effect on the pathogen; they work entirely by reducing the contact rate that feeds Rt = R0 * S/N * (fraction of normal contact retained). School closure removes the high-mixing setting where children generate a disproportionate share of contacts; distancing lowers the per-contact transmission probability and the number of contacts per day; isolating symptomatic cases shortens their effective infectious period by removing them from the mixing pool; and quarantining their contacts catches secondary cases before those people can transmit further. A modeler represents each NPI as a multiplier on one or more terms feeding into Rt, which is why NPIs are compared not by how disruptive they feel but by how much they cut that multiplier -- a policy that feels drastic but only trims a peripheral contact setting can move Rt less than a milder measure that targets the highest-mixing venue in the model.

sections.heading: Mitigation, not elimination: the Ferguson framework
sections.body: Ferguson, Cummings, Fraser, Cajka, Cooley, and Burke (2006, Nature) modeled a pandemic-influenza scenario across the US and UK and formalized the distinction between mitigation (slowing spread to reduce peak burden) and suppression (pushing Rt below 1). For a pandemic strain with R0 around 1.8-2.4, no single NPI modeled -- school closure alone, or case isolation alone -- reliably pushed Rt below 1, but their combination substantially delayed and flattened the epidemic peak, cutting hospital demand at the worst moment even though the total number ultimately infected changed comparatively little. This is the origin of 'bending the curve' as a public-health goal distinct from stopping the epidemic outright: buying time for surge capacity and, eventually, vaccine production, rather than eliminating transmission. Their analysis found school closure alone could cut the peak attack rate by up to 40% with little effect on the eventual total infected -- a pure mitigation result, flattening the curve without shrinking it -- while adding household-targeted antiviral prophylaxis to reactive school closure could cut overall clinical attack rates by 40-50%, since drug-based prophylaxis, unlike a contact-only NPI, also removes potential infections rather than just delaying them.

sections.heading: Why imperfect interventions stack multiplicatively
sections.body: Because each NPI acts as an independent fractional reduction on contact or transmission, their combined effect multiplies rather than adds. An intervention cutting contact by 30% paired with one cutting transmission probability by 30% doesn't yield a 60% reduction in Rt -- it yields Rt * 0.7 * 0.7 = Rt * 0.49, a 51% reduction. This multiplicative stacking is precisely why Ferguson et al.'s layered strategy -- combining school closure, household quarantine, and antiviral prophylaxis, each individually insufficient -- outperformed any single measure and is the standard justification for 'layered' pandemic response rather than betting on one intervention alone.

lessons.workedExample: A pandemic influenza strain has R0 = 2.0. School closure is modeled as retaining 75% of normal contact (a 25% reduction), and voluntary case isolation retains 80% of transmission-days (a 20% reduction). Applied together, Rt = 2.0 * 0.75 * 0.80 = 1.2 -- still above threshold, so the epidemic keeps growing, just more slowly than at Rt = 2.0. Adding a third measure, contact quarantine, retaining 85% of remaining transmission (a 15% cut), gives Rt = 1.2 * 0.85 = 1.02, nearly at threshold. This mirrors Ferguson et al.'s (2006) finding that no single plausible NPI reliably suppressed a pandemic strain of this R0, but three layered together approached the threshold.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can explain an NPI's effect mechanistically -- as a specific multiplier on contact rate, transmission probability, or infectious duration -- rather than describing it qualitatively as 'reducing spread.' A strong answer also distinguishes mitigation from suppression: a project claiming an NPI combination 'stopped' an epidemic when its own Rt calculation stays above 1 has confused a flattened, delayed curve with elimination, exactly the distinction Ferguson et al. (2006) formalized.

questions.prompt: An NPI package cuts contact by 20% and a second, independent NPI cuts per-contact transmission probability by 25%. What is the combined effect on Rt relative to baseline?

options.text: Rt is multiplied by 0.80 * 0.75 = 0.60, a 40% reduction
Rt is multiplied by (1 - 0.20 - 0.25) = 0.55, a 45% reduction
Rt is reduced by exactly 45% since the two percentages simply add
The combined effect cannot exceed the larger single-intervention effect of 25%

explanations.a: Correct: independent fractional reductions multiply, so retained contact 0.80 times retained transmission probability 0.75 gives 0.60, a 40% overall reduction.
explanations.b: Simple subtraction of percentages is the additive error; independent multiplicative reductions do not sum this way.
explanations.c: This restates the additive error; the true combined reduction (40%) is smaller than the naive sum (45%) here, though additive errors can also overstate or understate depending on the numbers.
explanations.d: Layered interventions can and typically do exceed any single intervention's effect, which is the entire rationale for combining them.

questions.prompt: Ferguson et al. (2006) modeled pandemic influenza mitigation strategies across the US and UK. Their key finding about single NPIs versus a pandemic strain with R0 around 1.8-2.4 was that:

options.text: No single modeled NPI reliably pushed Rt below 1, but a layered combination substantially flattened and delayed the peak
School closure alone was sufficient to suppress the epidemic in both countries
NPIs had no measurable effect on epidemic peak timing or height
Case isolation alone reduced total infections to near zero

explanations.a: Correct: this is the mitigation-versus-suppression finding at the center of the paper -- combined, imperfect measures delayed and flattened the peak without eliminating transmission.
explanations.b: The paper found single measures insufficient on their own to reliably suppress an epidemic at this R0 range.
explanations.c: NPIs measurably delayed and flattened peaks in the model even though they did not eliminate the epidemic.
explanations.d: Case isolation alone reduced burden but did not drive total infections to near zero in the modeled scenarios.

questions.prompt: Order these NPIs by the specific mechanism each acts on, from the earliest point in a transmission chain to the latest.

items.text: Physical distancing -- reduces the per-contact transmission probability during any given encounter
School/venue closure -- removes a high-mixing contact setting before encounters can occur
Case isolation -- shortens the effective infectious period once a person is already a case
Contact quarantine -- catches secondary cases among a known case's contacts before they can transmit onward

questions.explanation: Closure prevents contacts from occurring at all; distancing reduces transmission risk within contacts that still occur; isolation acts once a person is already infectious; quarantine acts on that person's contacts one step further down the chain.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it means in the mitigation-versus-suppression framework.

right.text: Slowing spread to reduce peak burden without necessarily pushing Rt below 1
Pushing Rt below 1 to actively shrink the epidemic
Delaying and flattening the epidemic peak to protect surge capacity
Combining multiple individually-insufficient interventions so their multiplicative effect approaches or crosses threshold

questions.explanation: Mitigation and suppression are the two strategic goals Ferguson et al. (2006) distinguished; bending the curve is the practical outcome of mitigation, and layering is the tactic that gets a combination of imperfect measures closer to the suppression threshold.

lessons.label: Pandemic Influenza Containment

sections.heading: Containment at the source: two models, one strategy
sections.body: Before a pandemic strain spreads globally, there is a brief window where stopping it at its point of emergence is theoretically possible -- a strategy distinct from the mitigation approach used once global spread has already occurred. Ferguson, Cummings, Cauchemez, Fraser, Riley, Meeyai, Iamsirithaworn, and Burke (2005, Nature) and, independently, Longini, Nizam, Xu, Ungchusak, Hanshaoworakul, Cummings, and Halloran (2005, Science) both modeled this scenario for a hypothetical novel-influenza emergence in rural Thailand, chosen because Southeast Asia was considered the most likely origin region given prior avian-influenza spillover patterns, including the H5N1 cases then circulating in poultry across the region. Both teams modeled a rural setting deliberately, reasoning that a low-density source region gives control measures their best chance of outrunning transmission before an outbreak reaches a major transport hub.

sections.heading: Targeted prophylaxis and the geographic ring
sections.body: Both models tested the same core intervention: geographically targeted antiviral prophylaxis, distributing oseltamivir to everyone within a ring around detected cases, combined with household quarantine and, in some scenarios, school closure or pre-positioned vaccine. Longini et al. found that for a strain with R0 up to about 1.6-2.0, a stockpile of roughly 3 million treatment courses, deployed within about 2-3 weeks of the first detected cases, could contain the outbreak within the source region before it seeded sustained chains elsewhere. Ferguson et al. reached a similar conclusion using a different model structure, reinforcing that containment was feasible in principle but hinged on early detection and fast logistics -- delay past a few weeks let the outbreak outrun the ring. Both papers stressed that the strategy's feasibility fell off sharply as R0 rose above roughly 2, since higher transmissibility meant more parallel chains were already seeded by the time any ring could be drawn around the detected cases.

sections.heading: From modeled containment to real-world R0
sections.body: These 2005 studies motivated national antiviral stockpiling policy, but they modeled a hypothetical strain. When an actual novel H1N1 pandemic emerged in 2009, real-time analyses -- notably Fraser, Donnelly, Cauchemez, and colleagues (2009, Science) -- estimated its R0 at roughly 1.4-1.6, near the lower end of the range the containment models had judged feasible. In practice, by the time the outbreak was recognized as a novel strain it had already spread across multiple countries, so source containment was no longer an option; response shifted to the mitigation strategies described in the companion Ferguson et al. (2006) framework. The 2005 containment models and the 2009 real-time estimate are often read together as a case study in how a strategy validated in simulation can be overtaken by the speed of real-world spread and surveillance lag.

lessons.workedExample: Longini et al. (2005) modeled a Thai district of about 500,000 people with a hypothetical pandemic strain at R0 = 1.9. Their simulation showed that targeted antiviral prophylaxis reaching households and workplaces within a geographic ring of detected cases, deployed within roughly 2 weeks of the outbreak's start and backed by a stockpile of about 3 million courses, contained more than 90% of simulated outbreaks before they exceeded a few hundred cases. Delaying the same response to 4 weeks let the outbreak escape containment in most simulation runs, since by then secondary and tertiary transmission chains had already seeded new geographic clusters outside the ring's reach.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can separate 'containment at source' (Ferguson 2005, Longini 2005 -- stopping a nascent outbreak in one region) from 'mitigation' (Ferguson 2006 -- slowing an already-global pandemic), since conflating the two is a common error. They also check whether a student recognizes the gap between a strategy validated in a simulation with known parameters and the messier real-world 2009 H1N1 response, where surveillance lag -- not model failure -- was the reason containment wasn't attempted.

questions.prompt: According to Longini et al. (2005), what was the approximate stockpile size and deployment window needed for targeted antiviral prophylaxis to contain a nascent pandemic strain at the source in their modeled Thailand scenario?

options.text: About 3 million treatment courses, deployed within roughly 2-3 weeks of the first detected cases
About 300,000 treatment courses, deployed within 6 months
No stockpile was needed; school closure alone was sufficient
About 30 million treatment courses, deployed within 24 hours

explanations.a: Correct: this is the figure the modeled containment strategy relied on -- a moderate stockpile deployed fast, within a few weeks of detection.
explanations.b: This understates both the stockpile size and overstates the acceptable delay; a 6-month window was well past the point the model showed containment failing.
explanations.c: School closure was one of several measures modeled but antiviral prophylaxis targeted to a geographic ring was the core intervention, not a stockpile-free approach.
explanations.d: This overstates the required stockpile size and understates the deployment window well beyond what the model required or what was logistically assumed.

questions.prompt: Real-time analyses of the 2009 H1N1 pandemic (Fraser et al., 2009) estimated its R0 at roughly 1.4-1.6. Why did source containment, as modeled by Ferguson et al. (2005) and Longini et al. (2005), not get attempted against this real strain despite its R0 being within the range the models judged feasible?

options.text: By the time the novel strain was recognized, it had already spread across multiple countries, so the source-containment window had already closed
The real R0 was far higher than any model had considered feasible
Antiviral stockpiles did not exist anywhere in 2009
The 2005 models were later shown to be mathematically invalid

explanations.a: Correct: surveillance lag, not an R0 mismatch or model failure, is why containment shifted to mitigation -- the outbreak was already global by the time it was identified as novel.
explanations.b: The estimated R0 (1.4-1.6) was near the lower end of the range the 2005 containment models had judged feasible, not higher.
explanations.c: Stockpiling policy had been built up partly because of the 2005 modeling studies; the issue was deployment timing relative to spread, not stockpile absence.
explanations.d: The models were not invalidated; their core logic about deployment speed versus outbreak size remained the accepted explanation for why containment became infeasible.

questions.prompt: Order the events in the source-containment story, from modeling study to real-world outcome.

items.text: Ferguson et al. and Longini et al. (2005) model targeted antiviral prophylaxis containing a hypothetical Southeast Asian influenza outbreak
National governments build antiviral stockpiles partly informed by these containment models
A novel H1N1 strain emerges in 2009 and spreads across multiple countries before being identified as pandemic-capable
Fraser et al. (2009) estimate the real strain's R0 at 1.4-1.6 in real time, and response shifts to mitigation rather than source containment

questions.explanation: The 2005 models came first and informed stockpiling policy; the 2009 emergence and its surveillance lag came after, followed by the real-time R0 estimate that confirmed containment was no longer viable.

questions.prompt: Match each study or estimate to its key contribution.

right.text: Modeled containment of a hypothetical Southeast Asian pandemic strain via targeted antivirals, published in Nature
Estimated a stockpile of ~3 million courses and a 2-3 week deployment window for containment, published in Science
Produced a real-time R0 estimate of 1.4-1.6 during the actual 2009 H1N1 pandemic

questions.explanation: Two independent 2005 modeling groups reached compatible conclusions about source containment feasibility, while the 2009 real-time estimate later tested those assumptions against an actual pandemic strain.

lessons.label: Ebola 2014-2016 in West Africa

sections.heading: Real-time R0 and a forecast that overshot
sections.body: The 2014-2016 West African Ebola epidemic in Guinea, Sierra Leone, and Liberia was the first Ebola outbreak large enough to sustain community transmission across national borders, and real-time modeling became central to the response. The WHO Ebola Response Team (2014, New England Journal of Medicine) estimated R0 at roughly 1.5-2.5 across the three countries using case data from the epidemic's first nine months, and projected forward growth that, if unchecked, implied case counts reaching into the hundreds of thousands by early 2015 -- a projection echoed by a widely cited CDC analysis (Meltzer et al., 2014) that modeled up to 1.4 million cases under a no-additional-intervention scenario. The actual epidemic, while devastating at roughly 28,000 cases and 11,000 deaths by its end, fell far short of these unmitigated projections. Guinea, where the outbreak was first identified in December 2013 near the town of Meliandou, saw slower growth than Sierra Leone and Liberia, where explosive urban transmission in Freetown and Monrovia drove most of the case burden through late 2014.

sections.heading: Why the unmitigated forecasts overshot
sections.body: The gap wasn't a modeling error so much as a violation of the unmitigated-growth assumption the projections were built on: they extrapolated the exponential growth rate observed early in the epidemic forward without a declining transmission rate, which is the correct way to illustrate the cost of inaction but a poor forecast once control measures scale up. In practice, safe-burial teams, treatment-unit capacity, contact tracing, and community behavior change expanded far faster than the models' baseline scenarios assumed, bending Rt down well before case counts approached the unmitigated trajectory. The lesson generalizes: an unmitigated-growth projection is a counterfactual meant to motivate response, not a prediction of what will happen once that response arrives. The CDC's Meltzer et al. (2014) report was explicit about this, framing its 1.4-million-case figure as an illustration of the cost of inaction rather than a most-likely outcome, though press coverage often stripped that caveat away when repeating the headline number.

sections.heading: Safe burial and case isolation as the decisive levers
sections.body: Ebola's transmission is unusual in that viral load, and therefore infectiousness, peaks near and after death, and traditional burial practices in the region involved washing and touching the body -- turning funerals into major transmission events. Legrand, Grais, Boelle, Valleron, and Flahault (2007) had built an earlier Ebola transmission model with a distinct funeral-transmission compartment specifically because prior outbreaks showed this route mattered disproportionately. In the 2014-2016 epidemic, campaigns to replace traditional burial with safe, supervised burial teams, combined with faster case isolation in treatment units, are credited as the two interventions with the largest measured effect on bending Rt below 1 in each affected country, ahead of the epidemic's eventual peak.

lessons.workedExample: Using the WHO Ebola Response Team's (2014) R0 estimate of about 2.0 for Sierra Leone at the epidemic's early stage, an unmitigated model with a roughly 2-3 week generation interval projects case counts roughly doubling every few weeks, consistent with the trajectory toward hundreds of thousands of cases used to motivate international response. Contact-tracing and safe-burial data from later in the epidemic showed that once burial-related transmission was sharply reduced, the effective reproduction number in Sierra Leone and Liberia fell below 1 by around late 2014/early 2015 -- months before the unmitigated projection's case counts would have been reached -- illustrating that the forecast's value was as a call to action rather than a prediction of the actual course.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student understands that a headline-grabbing 'projected to reach a million cases' figure is a scenario, not a forecast -- and can explain the specific behavioral change (burial practices, case isolation speed) that made the real trajectory diverge from it. A project that treats the WHO/CDC unmitigated projections as a failed prediction, rather than as a correctly-built counterfactual that helped drive the intervention that falsified it, has missed the central methodological point of real-time outbreak modeling.

questions.prompt: The WHO Ebola Response Team (2014) and a CDC analysis both projected unmitigated case counts far exceeding the roughly 28,000 cases the epidemic ultimately reached. What best explains this gap?

options.text: The projections assumed continued unmitigated exponential growth, but control measures like safe burial and faster case isolation scaled up and bent Rt below 1 before those case counts were reached
The original R0 estimate of 1.5-2.5 was later found to be a measurement error
Ebola stopped spreading on its own once it exhausted susceptible people in the region
The models used the wrong pathogen's transmission parameters entirely

explanations.a: Correct: the unmitigated projections were explicitly built on continued exponential growth; real interventions, especially around burial practices, drove Rt below 1 well before the projected case counts.
explanations.b: The R0 estimate itself was not the source of the gap; the gap came from the no-further-intervention assumption underlying the forward projection, not from a flawed R0 measurement.
explanations.c: Susceptible depletion did not come close to explaining the actual epidemic's end at ~28,000 cases in populations of millions; intervention-driven Rt reduction was the dominant factor.
explanations.d: The models used Ebola-specific parameters drawn from the actual 2014-2016 case data and prior outbreak studies like Legrand et al. (2007); the discrepancy was about assumptions on future intervention, not wrong parameters.

questions.prompt: Why did Legrand et al. (2007) build a distinct 'funeral transmission' compartment into their Ebola model years before the 2014-2016 epidemic?

options.text: Because Ebola viral load and infectiousness peak near and after death, and traditional burial practices involving body contact created a major transmission route in prior outbreaks
Because funerals were the only setting where any Ebola transmission had ever been documented
Because hospital-based transmission was believed to be negligible in all Ebola outbreaks
Because the compartment was required by standard SEIR model structure regardless of the pathogen

explanations.a: Correct: peak infectiousness near death combined with body-contact burial customs made funerals a disproportionately important transmission setting, motivating a dedicated model compartment.
explanations.b: Transmission also occurred via direct contact with symptomatic patients and in healthcare settings; funerals were disproportionately important, not the only route.
explanations.c: Hospital and healthcare-worker transmission was also a recognized and modeled route in Ebola outbreaks, including in Legrand et al.'s framework.
explanations.d: Standard SEIR structure has no funeral compartment by default; this was a deliberate, pathogen-specific addition reflecting Ebola's particular transmission biology.

questions.prompt: Order the events in the West African Ebola epidemic's modeling and response timeline.

items.text: Legrand et al. (2007) build an Ebola transmission model with a funeral-transmission compartment based on prior outbreaks
WHO Ebola Response Team (2014) estimates R0 at roughly 1.5-2.5 from the epidemic's first nine months of case data
Unmitigated projections (WHO and CDC analyses) suggest case counts could reach the hundreds of thousands to over a million absent additional intervention
Safe-burial campaigns and faster case isolation scale up, bending Rt below 1 in each affected country before those projected case counts are reached

questions.explanation: The 2007 model came first and anticipated the funeral-transmission mechanism; the 2014 R0 estimate and projections came next from real epidemic data; the intervention scale-up that falsified the unmitigated projection came last.

questions.prompt: Match each figure or study to what it refers to in the West African Ebola epidemic.

right.text: NEJM paper estimating R0 at roughly 1.5-2.5 and projecting unmitigated growth
Earlier model introducing a distinct funeral-transmission compartment
The epidemic's actual eventual toll, far below unmitigated projections
The two interventions credited with the largest measured effect on bending Rt below 1

questions.explanation: Each item anchors a distinct piece of the case study: the real-time estimate and projection, the earlier mechanistic model, the actual outcome, and the interventions that explain the gap between projection and outcome.

lessons.label: HIV and Long-Wave Epidemics

sections.heading: Why the mean partner number isn't enough
sections.body: Anderson and May's HIV modeling (developed through the late 1980s and collected in their 1991 textbook, Infectious Diseases of Humans) departed from simple homogeneous-mixing models by insisting that sexual-contact networks are risk-structured: people vary enormously in their number of partners, and that variance -- not just the population mean -- drives R0. For a sexually transmitted infection, R0 is proportional to the mean partner-acquisition rate PLUS a term involving the variance of that rate, because a highly connected 'core group' of individuals with many partners both acquires and transmits infection disproportionately often. A population where everyone has close to the same number of partners can have a much lower R0 than one with identical mean partner count but a small core group of very high-activity individuals -- the same intuition Yorke, Hethcote, and Nold (1978) had formalized earlier for gonorrhea's core-group dynamics.

sections.heading: Staged infectiousness over years, not days
sections.body: Unlike influenza or measles, HIV infectiousness is not roughly constant across a short infectious period -- it is sharply staged across years. Acute infection, in the first weeks after exposure, carries viral loads and transmission risk far above the long asymptomatic chronic stage that follows, which can last many years at comparatively low per-act transmission probability; risk rises again as untreated infection progresses toward AIDS and immune control fails. Modeling HIV with a single constant transmission rate, the way SIR treats measles, badly misrepresents the epidemic, because a disproportionate share of onward transmission during the epidemic's early growth phase in a population comes from people in that brief, highly infectious acute window -- a structural feature staged compartmental models (an SI or SEIR variant with separate acute, chronic, and AIDS stages) are built to capture.

sections.heading: Treatment as prevention
sections.body: Because antiretroviral therapy (ART) suppresses viral load, it doesn't just slow disease progression in the treated person -- it sharply cuts their onward transmission risk, turning treatment into a population-level prevention tool. The HPTN 052 trial (Cohen et al., 2011, New England Journal of Medicine) followed serodiscordant couples and found early ART reduced linked HIV transmission by about 96% compared with delayed treatment, the landmark result behind 'Treatment as Prevention' (TasP) policy. In transmission-model terms, TasP works by cutting the per-act or per-partnership transmission probability for treated individuals, which mechanistically lowers R0 the same way case isolation lowers R0 for an acute respiratory infection -- except sustained over years rather than days, which is why HIV epidemics rise and fall on a timescale of decades rather than weeks.

lessons.workedExample: A risk-structured model splits a population into a low-activity group averaging 1 partner/year and a small core group of 5% of people averaging 10 partners/year. The population-wide mean partner rate is only 1.45/year, but because R0 depends on mean plus a variance term, the effective R0 driven mostly by the core group's cross-transmission can exceed 1 even though a homogeneous-mixing model using only the 1.45 mean would predict R0 well below 1 and falsely conclude the epidemic cannot sustain itself. This is exactly the core-group mechanism Anderson and May's HIV framework was built to capture, and it explains why interventions targeting core-group transmission (partner services, PrEP for high-activity groups) have outsized epidemic-level effect compared with population-wide measures of the same intensity.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can explain why HIV epidemiology cannot be reduced to a mean partner count -- the variance-driven core-group mechanism is the specific, non-obvious insight Anderson and May's modeling contributed, and a project that only reports an average number of partners has missed the reason risk-structured models exist at all. Judges also check whether staged infectiousness (acute versus chronic versus AIDS) and treatment-as-prevention are understood as distinct mechanisms rather than folded into one flat 'HIV is hard to model' statement.

questions.prompt: Two populations have the identical mean sexual-partner rate, but Population X has a small high-activity 'core group' while Population Y has nearly uniform partner numbers across everyone. According to risk-structured HIV modeling, what should we expect?

options.text: Population X likely has a higher R0 than Population Y, because R0 depends on the variance in partner numbers, not just the mean
Both populations have identical R0, since R0 depends only on the mean partner rate
Population Y likely has the higher R0, since uniform mixing always maximizes transmission
R0 cannot be compared without knowing the exact viral strain in each population

explanations.a: Correct: this is the core-group insight from Anderson and May's HIV modeling -- variance in partner numbers, concentrated in a core group, raises R0 above what the mean alone would predict.
explanations.b: This is the error risk-structured modeling was built to correct; mean-only models miss the disproportionate transmission driven by a core group.
explanations.c: Uniform mixing does not maximize transmission relative to a variance-concentrated core group at the same mean; the core-group structure tends to raise, not lower, R0.
explanations.d: Partner-number structure, not strain identity, is the variable being compared here; the risk-structuring argument holds across strains with a given per-act transmission probability.

questions.prompt: The HPTN 052 trial (Cohen et al., 2011) found that early antiretroviral therapy (ART) in serodiscordant couples reduced linked HIV transmission by approximately what amount compared with delayed treatment?

options.text: About 96%
About 25%
About 50%
Essentially 0%, since ART only helps the treated individual's own disease progression

explanations.a: Correct: this is the landmark figure behind Treatment as Prevention policy, showing ART's transmission-reducing effect is large, not incidental.
explanations.b: This understates the trial's finding by a wide margin; the effect size was the trial's headline result precisely because it was so large.
explanations.c: This also understates the measured effect; the actual figure was substantially higher.
explanations.d: ART suppresses viral load, which directly reduces onward transmission risk -- the entire basis of Treatment as Prevention as a population-level strategy, not just an individual disease-progression benefit.

questions.prompt: Order HIV infection stages by typical per-act transmission risk, from lowest to highest.

items.text: Chronic asymptomatic infection -- viral load suppressed by the immune system, lasting years
Late-stage/AIDS -- immune control fails and viral load rises again
Acute infection -- the first weeks after exposure, with viral loads and transmission risk far above baseline

questions.explanation: Chronic infection has the lowest sustained transmission risk of the three stages; late-stage disease raises risk again as immune control fails; acute infection carries the highest per-act risk of all, concentrated in a brief early window.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to the researcher(s) or study associated with it.

left.text: Risk-structured HIV modeling with core groups

right.text: Anderson and May
Yorke, Hethcote, and Nold (1978)
Cohen et al., HPTN 052 (2011)

questions.explanation: Anderson and May extended core-group thinking to HIV; Yorke, Hethcote, and Nold had established the core-group concept earlier for gonorrhea; HPTN 052 supplied the trial evidence behind treatment-as-prevention policy.

lessons.label: Vector-Borne and Elimination Modeling

sections.heading: The Ross-Macdonald malaria R0
sections.body: Malaria transmission requires two species -- human and mosquito -- so its R0 cannot come from a simple human-to-human contact model. Ronald Ross won the 1902 Nobel Prize for his 1897-98 discovery that mosquitoes transmit the malaria parasite; that prize recognized the biological finding, not any modeling. Ross's mathematical work on transmission came afterward -- his early transmission modeling developed roughly 1908-1911, in the 1908 Mauritius report and the mathematical appendix to the 1911 second edition of The Prevention of Malaria -- and it was this separate body of modeling that George Macdonald formalized into a full transmission model in 1957, giving the Ross-Macdonald framework still taught today: R0 = (m * a^2 * b * c * p^n) / (-ln(p) * r), where m is the mosquito-to-human density ratio, a is the mosquito biting rate, b and c are the transmission probabilities per bite (mosquito to human and human to mosquito respectively), p is the mosquito's daily survival probability, n is the extrinsic incubation period the parasite needs inside the mosquito, and r is the human recovery rate. The single most consequential term is a^2: because a mosquito must first bite an infectious human and later bite a susceptible human to complete one transmission cycle, the biting rate enters twice, so R0 is far more sensitive to interventions that reduce biting (bed nets, indoor spraying) than the linear terms would suggest.

sections.heading: Mosquito survival is the second lever
sections.body: The p^n term -- survival probability raised to the extrinsic incubation period -- means R0 is extremely sensitive to small changes in daily mosquito mortality, since a mosquito must survive long enough after becoming infected for the parasite to complete development before it can transmit. This is why insecticide-treated bed nets and residual spraying, which primarily shorten mosquito lifespan, have historically been more cost-effective malaria interventions than measures that only reduce biting rate without affecting survival: cutting p by a modest amount can collapse p^n by a much larger factor when n spans 10-14 days, as it typically does for Plasmodium falciparum at tropical temperatures.

sections.heading: Extensions and the elimination bar
sections.body: The same vector-host structure, adapted for a mosquito's biting rate, survival, and vector competence, extends to dengue and Zika, though both add complications the basic Ross-Macdonald form doesn't capture: dengue has four co-circulating serotypes with only temporary cross-immunity, and Zika adds a secondary sexual-transmission route alongside the mosquito-borne one, so both are usually modeled as Ross-Macdonald-derived systems with extra compartments layered on. Whatever the pathogen, the same threshold logic from Lesson 1 of this unit applies: elimination requires pushing R0's effective value below 1, whether that reduction comes from vaccination (as in polio, via the Global Polio Eradication Initiative, and measles, via the Measles & Rubella Initiative, endgame programs) or from vector control that pushes the mosquito-side terms in the Ross-Macdonald formula down far enough that the human-side R0 collapses regardless of how susceptible the human population remains.

lessons.workedExample: A malaria-endemic region has mosquito density m = 4 mosquitoes per human, biting rate a = 0.3 bites/day, transmission probabilities b = c = 0.5, mosquito daily survival p = 0.9, extrinsic incubation n = 12 days, and human recovery rate r = 1/60 (60-day infectious period). R0 = (4 * 0.3^2 * 0.5 * 0.5 * 0.9^12) / (-ln(0.9) * 1/60) is dominated by 0.9^12 ≈ 0.28 and a^2 = 0.09; the numerator is roughly 4*0.09*0.25*0.28 ≈ 0.025, and the denominator (-ln(0.9)=0.105, times 1/60=0.00175) gives R0 ≈ 14. Insecticide-treated nets that cut daily survival to p = 0.8 drop p^12 to about 0.069 -- a 75% reduction from a survival change of only 0.1 -- and recomputing the full formula with p = 0.8 gives R0 ≈ 1.7, collapsing R0 to roughly an eighth of its original value (about 14.5 originally). The drop is even larger than the p^12 term's own 75% reduction implies, because lowering p also increases -ln(p) in the denominator (0.105 at p=0.9 versus 0.223 at p=0.8), compounding the effect there as well, illustrating why survival-targeting interventions punch above their apparent size.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can explain why a^2 (biting rate squared) and p^n (survival to a power) are the two most important terms in the Ross-Macdonald formula, rather than treating all its terms as equally weighted -- this is the specific insight that justifies prioritizing bed nets and residual spraying over interventions that only reduce human-side susceptibility. Judges also check whether a student applying this formula to dengue or Zika understands what the basic framework leaves out (multiple serotypes, sexual transmission) rather than presenting Ross-Macdonald as a universal, unmodified model for every vector-borne disease.

questions.prompt: In the Ross-Macdonald malaria R0 formula, why does a small reduction in mosquito daily survival probability (p) tend to produce a disproportionately large reduction in R0?

options.text: Because p appears raised to the power n (the extrinsic incubation period), so a small drop in p compounds over the ~10-14 days needed for parasite development inside the mosquito
Because p is multiplied by a constant factor of 10 in the formula
Because survival probability has no real effect on R0 in the Ross-Macdonald model
Because human recovery rate r always dominates the formula regardless of mosquito parameters

explanations.a: Correct: the p^n term means survival is raised to a power spanning roughly 10-14 days, so even a modest drop in daily survival compounds into a much larger drop in the mosquito's odds of living long enough to transmit.
explanations.b: There is no such constant multiplier; the sensitivity comes from the exponent structure (p raised to the power n), not a fixed scaling factor.
explanations.c: Survival is one of the most consequential terms in the formula precisely because of the p^n structure; it is not negligible.
explanations.d: r appears in the denominator as a simple linear term and does not dominate the formula's sensitivity the way the a^2 and p^n terms do.

questions.prompt: Why does the mosquito biting rate (a) appear squared in the Ross-Macdonald R0 formula rather than appearing just once?

options.text: Because a single transmission cycle requires the mosquito to bite an infectious human once and a susceptible human again, so the biting rate enters the cycle twice
Because mosquitoes bite exactly twice per day on average, hard-coding a factor of 2
Squaring is a mathematical convention with no biological meaning in this formula
Because human-to-human transmission also requires two bites

explanations.a: Correct: completing one malaria transmission cycle requires two separate biting events -- acquiring the parasite from an infectious human, then delivering it to a susceptible human -- so the per-bite rate a enters the R0 formula twice.
explanations.b: The squaring reflects the two-bite structure of one transmission cycle, not a literal bites-per-day count of two.
explanations.c: The square has a specific biological justification tied to the two-bite transmission cycle; it is not an arbitrary convention.
explanations.d: Malaria has no human-to-human route at all -- transmission is exclusively vector-mediated, which is exactly why the mosquito-side terms, including the squared biting rate, dominate the formula.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of one complete malaria transmission cycle as captured by the Ross-Macdonald model's a^2 term.

items.text: A mosquito bites an infectious human and acquires the parasite
The parasite develops inside the mosquito over the extrinsic incubation period
The mosquito survives long enough to complete that development
The mosquito bites a susceptible human and transmits the parasite

questions.explanation: The cycle begins with an infecting bite, then the parasite develops inside the mosquito over the extrinsic incubation period, which requires the mosquito to survive long enough for that development to complete, and only then can a second bite complete transmission to a new human host.

questions.prompt: Match each vector-borne disease or program to how it relates to the Ross-Macdonald framework.

right.text: The original system the Ross-Macdonald formula was built for
Extended with extra compartments for four co-circulating serotypes and limited cross-immunity
Extended with a secondary sexual-transmission route alongside the mosquito-borne one
Applies the same below-1 R0 elimination threshold, achieved via vaccination rather than vector control

questions.explanation: Malaria is the base case; dengue and Zika are Ross-Macdonald-derived extensions with disease-specific additions; the polio and measles endgame programs apply the identical below-1 threshold logic through a different lever, vaccination rather than vector control.

lessons.label: What Makes a Disease Chronic

sections.heading: A different causal model than an outbreak
sections.body: Acute infectious disease epidemiology assumes a single necessary agent: no measles virus, no measles case. Chronic (non-communicable) disease breaks that assumption. Conditions like heart disease, cancer, chronic respiratory disease, and diabetes persist for months or years, develop gradually, and are not caused by one transmissible pathogen — they arise from an accumulation of genetic, behavioral, and environmental exposures acting over decades. There is no single agent to isolate, culture, or quarantine, so the outbreak-investigation toolkit (find the source, trace contacts, close the restaurant) does not transfer.

sections.heading: Omran's epidemiologic transition
sections.body: In 1971, Abdel Omran proposed the epidemiologic transition theory in the Milbank Memorial Fund Quarterly, describing how a population's leading causes of death shift as it develops. He named three stages: the Age of Pestilence and Famine (infectious disease and malnutrition dominate, life expectancy is low and volatile), the Age of Receding Pandemics (sanitation, nutrition, and early medicine push infectious mortality down), and the Age of Degenerative and Man-Made Diseases (chronic conditions become the dominant killers as populations age and survive infancy and infection). The United States and most industrialized nations completed this transition over the twentieth century. Omran's original three stages describe a one-way march from infectious to chronic disease, but later epidemiologists have refined that picture. Olshansky and Ault proposed a fourth stage, the 'age of delayed degenerative diseases,' in which medical advances push the same chronic conditions to occur later in life rather than eliminating them, extending lifespan without necessarily eliminating disease burden. Many low- and middle-income countries also show a 'double burden of disease': infectious diseases like tuberculosis and malaria persist even as cardiovascular disease and diabetes rise, so the transition's stages overlap rather than replacing one another cleanly.

sections.heading: The 'big four' and why methods must change
sections.body: The World Health Organization groups cardiovascular disease, cancer, chronic respiratory disease, and diabetes as the 'big four' non-communicable diseases, together responsible for over 80% of all premature NCD deaths (deaths before age 70). Because these diseases have long latency, no single necessary cause, and multiple interacting risk factors, epidemiologists studying them rely on decades-long cohort studies and risk-factor epidemiology (comparing exposed and unexposed groups over time) rather than case investigation. A researcher cannot 'trace contacts' for a heart attack; instead they track blood pressure, cholesterol, and smoking status across thousands of people for years.

lessons.workedExample: In 1900, the top three causes of death in the United States were pneumonia/influenza, tuberculosis, and gastrointestinal infections — all acute and infectious, fitting Omran's first two stages. By the 2020s, CDC mortality data show heart disease and cancer alone account for well over a third of all US deaths combined, with essentially no infectious disease in the top ranks outside pandemic years. That flip in a single century is Omran's transition made visible in vital-statistics tables, and it is why a modern epidemiologist studying diabetes needs a cohort followed for twenty years, not a case report filed within a week.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student researching a chronic disease still reaches for infectious-disease framing — asking 'what's the pathogen' or expecting a single trigger — when the honest answer is that no such single cause exists. A strong project explicitly names the causal structure (multifactorial, long-latency, no necessary agent) before proposing a study design, showing the student chose their method because it fits the disease, not out of habit.

questions.prompt: Why can't outbreak-investigation methods (trace the source, find the transmission chain) be directly applied to a disease like type 2 diabetes?

options.text: Diabetes has too low an incidence to study statistically
Diabetes has no single necessary causal agent and develops over a long, multifactorial process
Diabetes is not reportable to health departments
Outbreak methods only work for diseases discovered before 1900

explanations.a: Diabetes is common enough to study easily; incidence is not the limiting factor.
explanations.b: Correct: outbreak methods assume a single transmissible agent and a traceable exposure window, neither of which exists for a multifactorial chronic disease.
explanations.c: Reportability is unrelated to why case-investigation methods fail here.
explanations.d: The historical date of discovery has no bearing on which epidemiologic methods apply.

questions.prompt: Order Omran's three stages of the epidemiologic transition as a population develops.

items.text: Age of Pestilence and Famine
Age of Receding Pandemics
Age of Degenerative and Man-Made Diseases

questions.explanation: Omran (1971) described a shift from famine and infection, through improving sanitation and medicine that reduce pandemic infectious mortality, to a state where chronic degenerative disease dominates the mortality profile.

questions.prompt: Match each 'big four' NCD category to a representative condition within it.

right.text: Heart attack and stroke
Lung or colorectal tumors
COPD and asthma
Type 2 diabetes

questions.explanation: The WHO's four leading NCD categories each cover a cluster of specific conditions; these four together account for over 80% of all premature NCD deaths (deaths before age 70).

questions.prompt: In 1900, the leading causes of US death were dominated by which category, according to the lesson?

options.text: Cardiovascular disease and cancer
Acute infectious disease, such as pneumonia/influenza and tuberculosis
Chronic respiratory disease
Diabetes and metabolic disease

explanations.a: Cardiovascular disease and cancer became dominant later, by the 2020s, not in 1900.
explanations.b: Correct: pneumonia/influenza, tuberculosis, and gastrointestinal infections topped the 1900 US mortality list, consistent with Omran's earlier transition stages.
explanations.c: Chronic respiratory disease was not among the named 1900 leaders in the lesson.
explanations.d: Diabetes mortality became prominent only after the transition to chronic disease dominance.

lessons.label: Multifactorial Causation and the Web of Causation

sections.heading: Rothman's causal pie model
sections.body: In a 1976 American Journal of Epidemiology paper titled 'Causes,' Kenneth Rothman formalized the sufficient-component-cause model, often nicknamed the causal pie. A sufficient cause is a complete causal mechanism — a full pie — that inevitably produces disease once assembled. Each pie is built from component causes, the individual slices; no single slice causes disease alone, but the completed pie does. A component cause that appears in every sufficient-cause pie for a disease is called a necessary cause. This framework lets epidemiologists talk precisely about causes that are neither sufficient nor necessary by themselves, which describes almost every chronic-disease risk factor.

sections.heading: Why chronic disease rarely has a necessary cause
sections.body: Tuberculosis has a necessary cause: without Mycobacterium tuberculosis, there is no TB, even though infection alone is not sufficient (most infected people never develop active disease). Lung cancer looks different. Smoking is a component cause present in many sufficient-cause pies for lung cancer, but it is not necessary — an estimated 10-20% of lung cancer cases occur in people who never smoked, meaning other pies exist that complete without a smoking slice (radon exposure, occupational carcinogens, genetic susceptibility). Because chronic diseases typically have many different sufficient-cause pies built from different combinations of component causes, no single factor is necessary across all of them.

sections.heading: Web of causation vs. the single-pathogen model
sections.body: Infectious-disease epidemiology grew up on Koch's postulates: identify the one organism, show it is necessary, done. In their 1970 textbook Epidemiology: Principles and Methods, Brian MacMahon and Thomas Pugh introduced the term 'web of causation' for chronic disease, picturing genes, environment, and behavior as interlinked strands rather than a single causal arrow. A genetic predisposition might raise susceptibility only in the presence of a particular diet; a behavioral exposure like smoking might matter only alongside an occupational one like asbestos. The web replaces 'find the one cause' with 'map the interacting component causes,' which is exactly what Rothman's pies formalize mathematically. Irving Selikoff and E. Cuyler Hammond's studies of insulation workers gave this a concrete number: asbestos exposure alone raised lung cancer risk several-fold, smoking alone raised it roughly tenfold, but workers exposed to both saw risk climb to somewhere on the order of 50 times baseline — far more than simply adding the two individual effects, showing how two strands of the web can compound each other rather than merely coexist.

lessons.workedExample: Consider two different sufficient-cause pies for heart disease. Pie A might be complete with smoking + hypertension + a genetic lipid-metabolism variant + physical inactivity. Pie B might be complete with type 2 diabetes + obesity + high LDL cholesterol, no smoking involved at all. Neither smoking nor diabetes appears in both pies, so neither is a necessary cause — yet a person can develop heart disease through either route, and public health interventions that block just one slice (say, smoking cessation) still leave Pie B fully intact and able to cause disease on its own.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student states 'smoking causes lung cancer' as though smoking were the single necessary trigger — which cannot be true, since nonsmokers also develop the disease. A strong answer instead frames smoking as a component cause present in many (not all) sufficient-cause pies, explains why removing it lowers population risk without eliminating it, and shows the student understands multifactorial causation rather than reciting a slogan.

questions.prompt: In Rothman's causal pie model, what is a 'component cause'?

options.text: Any factor statistically correlated with the disease, causal or not
One slice of a sufficient-cause pie; on its own it does not produce disease, but combined with other component causes it can complete a mechanism that does
A factor that must be present in every case of the disease
The single strongest risk factor identified in a cohort study

explanations.a: A component cause is a specific causal contributor, not any correlate — correlation without a causal role in a completed pie doesn't qualify.
explanations.b: Correct: component causes are individual slices that combine with others to complete a sufficient cause; none is sufficient alone.
explanations.c: A factor present in every case describes a necessary cause, a stricter and rarer property than being a component cause.
explanations.d: Statistical strength in one cohort does not define the causal-pie concept, which is about mechanistic completion, not effect size.

questions.prompt: Why is smoking NOT considered a necessary cause of lung cancer under the causal pie model, despite being a major risk factor?

options.text: Because smoking rates have declined since the 1960s
Because some lung cancer cases occur via sufficient-cause pies that do not include smoking as a component
Because smoking only causes heart disease, not cancer
Because necessary causes only apply to infectious disease

explanations.a: Declining smoking rates affect incidence, not whether smoking is logically necessary for every case.
explanations.b: Correct: nonsmokers also develop lung cancer through other sufficient-cause pies (radon, occupational exposures, genetic susceptibility), so no pie-completing role is universal.
explanations.c: Smoking is a well-established component cause of lung cancer as well as cardiovascular disease; this option misstates the lesson.
explanations.d: Necessary causes can exist for chronic disease in principle (as with TB's pathogen for infection); the concept isn't infection-exclusive, it just rarely applies to multifactorial NCDs.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps by which a sufficient cause produces disease under the causal pie model.

items.text: Multiple component causes (genetic, behavioral, environmental) are each present in an individual
These component causes accumulate and interact over time
The full set of component causes needed completes a sufficient-cause pie
Disease onset occurs once the pie is complete

questions.explanation: No single component cause triggers disease; the mechanism completes only once enough component causes accumulate to fill an entire sufficient-cause pie, at which point disease results.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

right.text: A complete causal mechanism that inevitably produces disease once assembled
A component cause present in every sufficient-cause pie for the disease
MacMahon and Pugh's model of interlinked genetic, environmental, and behavioral strands replacing a single-pathogen arrow

questions.explanation: Sufficient and necessary causes are precise terms from Rothman's 1976 pie model, while 'web of causation' is MacMahon and Pugh's 1970 conceptual picture of multifactorial chronic-disease causation.

lessons.label: Latency, Induction, and Natural History

sections.heading: Induction period vs. latent period
sections.body: Rothman's causal framework also supplies a vocabulary for time. The induction period is the interval from a causal exposure to the biologic initiation of disease — the moment, invisible to any test, when the first transformed cell or the first arterial lesion appears. The latent period is the interval from that biologic initiation to the point the disease becomes detectable, whether by screening (subclinical detection) or by symptoms (clinical detection). These are distinct clocks: a long induction period means the exposure itself acted decades before disease began; a long latent period means disease was silently present for years before anyone could find it. Confusing the two, or ignoring both, is a common source of bias in chronic-disease research.

sections.heading: Stages of natural history
sections.body: Public health's classic natural-history model, developed by Hugh Leavell and E. Gurney Clark in their prevention framework, divides a chronic disease's course into four stages: susceptibility (risk factors are present but no pathological change has begun), subclinical disease (biological onset has occurred but there are no symptoms — detectable only through screening), clinical disease (symptoms appear and diagnosis typically happens), and outcome (recovery, disability, or death). Each stage maps to a level of prevention: primary prevention acts during susceptibility, secondary prevention (screening) acts during the subclinical window, and tertiary prevention manages the clinical and outcome stages.

sections.heading: Real latencies that break a simple timeline
sections.body: These lags are not academic. Occupational cohorts of asbestos-exposed workers, including Irving Selikoff's studies of insulation workers beginning in the 1960s, found that mesothelioma commonly appears 20 to 40 years after first exposure — a worker exposed in a shipyard can be diagnosed three or four decades later. The British Doctors Study, launched by Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill in 1951, similarly required decades of follow-up before the full scale of the smoking-lung cancer association became clear, because tumors accumulate only after years of sustained exposure. Anyone comparing this year's exposure rate to this year's disease rate for either condition would find little or no association — the true cause sits decades in the past. Not every chronic exposure follows that same multi-decade timeline, though: cohorts of Hiroshima and Nagasaki atomic-bomb survivors showed radiation-induced leukemia peaking only about 5 to 7 years after exposure, while radiation-induced solid tumors such as breast and thyroid cancer did not peak until decades later. The lesson is that induction and latent periods are disease-specific, not a fixed 20-to-40-year rule — a researcher has to look up the expected lag for the specific outcome rather than assume asbestos's timeline applies universally.

lessons.workedExample: A shipyard worker inhales asbestos fibers in 1985. The induction period runs from that exposure until the first malignant mesothelial cells appear, perhaps in the 2000s; the latent period then runs until the tumor is large enough to cause symptoms and get diagnosed, commonly in the 2015-2025 range — a combined 30-to-40-year gap between cause and detection. A researcher studying 2020 mesothelioma cases who looks only at each patient's job or environment in 2020 will find nothing; the causal exposure has to be sought in employment records from the 1980s.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student's study design accounts for lag between exposure and detectable disease. A project that correlates current-year smoking rates with current-year lung cancer incidence, or current air quality with current asthma diagnoses in a slow-developing condition, has made a temporal-mismatch error; the strong answer explicitly lags the exposure data by the expected induction-plus-latent window before testing an association.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes the induction period from the latent period?

options.text: Induction runs from exposure to biologic disease onset; latent runs from biologic onset to detection
They are two names for the same interval
Induction applies only to infectious disease, latent only to chronic disease
Induction is measured in days, latent is always measured in decades

explanations.a: Correct: induction ends when disease biologically begins; latency ends when that disease becomes detectable by screening or symptoms.
explanations.b: They mark different endpoints — biologic onset versus detectability — and are not interchangeable.
explanations.c: Both terms apply generally in epidemiology; the lesson uses them specifically for chronic-disease examples like asbestos and smoking.
explanations.d: Duration is not fixed by definition; both periods can range from short to multi-decade depending on the disease.

questions.prompt: Order the four stages of the natural-history model from earliest to latest.

items.text: Susceptibility (risk factors present, no pathology yet)
Subclinical disease (biologic onset, no symptoms, screen-detectable)
Clinical disease (symptoms appear, typical diagnosis point)
Outcome (recovery, disability, or death)

questions.explanation: Leavell and Clark's natural-history model runs from a pre-pathologic susceptibility stage, through silent subclinical disease, to symptomatic clinical disease, ending in one of the possible outcomes.

questions.prompt: Match each level of prevention to the natural-history stage it targets.

right.text: Susceptibility stage (before pathology begins)
Subclinical stage (screening for silent disease)
Clinical/outcome stage (managing diagnosed disease)

questions.explanation: Prevention levels are defined by which natural-history stage they intervene on: primary before disease starts, secondary during the silent window, tertiary after diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Selikoff's studies of insulation workers found mesothelioma typically appeared how long after first asbestos exposure?

options.text: 20 to 40 years
2 to 4 weeks
6 to 12 months
1 to 2 years

explanations.a: Correct: occupational cohorts found mesothelioma commonly emerging 20-40 years after exposure began, matching the worked example's 1985-to-2015/2025 span.
explanations.b: Weeks is far too short — mesothelioma has one of the longest known latencies of any occupational cancer.
explanations.c: Months is inconsistent with the decades-long latency described for asbestos-related mesothelioma.
explanations.d: A couple of years is still far shorter than the documented decades-long latency for this cancer.

lessons.label: Risk Factors, Markers, and the Causal Continuum

sections.heading: Causal factor, risk marker, or confounded correlate
sections.body: Not everything correlated with disease belongs in the same causal bucket. A causal factor changes disease risk when it is itself changed — lowering blood pressure lowers stroke risk, so blood pressure is causal. A risk marker correlates with disease risk and is useful for identifying who is at higher risk, but changing the marker itself does nothing, because it is not part of the causal mechanism — age is the clearest example: it predicts risk powerfully but cannot be modified to prevent disease. A confounded correlate looks associated only because both it and the disease share an upstream cause; a classic teaching example is that people who carry lighters have higher lung cancer rates, not because lighters cause cancer but because both lighter-carrying and cancer share a common cause, smoking.

sections.heading: Modifiable vs. fixed determinants
sections.body: Chronic-disease risk factors split further into modifiable ones — smoking, blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, diet, physical activity — which are intervention targets, and fixed ones — age, sex, genotype such as BRCA1/2 mutation status — which cannot be changed but are still clinically useful for stratifying who needs more intensive modifiable-factor management or earlier screening. Confusing the two categories leads to wasted intervention effort: no program can 'modify' a patient's age, but a program can absolutely modify their blood pressure. The BRCA1/2 example shows why a fixed marker still matters clinically: a woman carrying a harmful BRCA1 mutation faces roughly a 55-72% lifetime risk of breast cancer (45-69% for BRCA2), versus about 12-13% for the general population. Nobody can 'treat' the mutation itself, but that fixed risk figure is exactly what drives real decisions about earlier and more frequent screening or preventive surgery.

sections.heading: Proximal/behavioral vs. distal/structural determinants
sections.body: Risk factors also sit at different causal distances from the outcome. Proximal determinants are close to the individual — diet, smoking, blood pressure readings. Distal determinants are further upstream, structural forces that shape whether the proximal behaviors are even realistic choices: food access and food deserts, tobacco marketing regulation, neighborhood walkability, income, and healthcare access. A correlation observed at the proximal level, such as 'poor diet correlates with diabetes,' is not automatically an actionable lever if the true driver is a distal structural constraint like food access or income that the individual does not control — treating a distal problem with a purely proximal, individual-behavior intervention often fails.

lessons.workedExample: The Framingham Heart Study, begun in 1948, established that elevated blood pressure and high LDL cholesterol are causal, modifiable risk factors for coronary heart disease: subsequent clinical trials showed that treating hypertension measurably reduces heart attack and stroke incidence, confirming the causal link rather than a mere correlation. The same study also uses age and male sex within the Framingham Risk Score to stratify who needs more aggressive treatment of the modifiable factors — but no clinician tries to 'lower' a patient's age. Age is a risk marker that guides where to intervene; blood pressure is the causal factor actually being intervened on.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student treats every statistically significant correlate in their data as an equally valid target for intervention. A common fair-project error is proposing to 'reduce X' when X is really a risk marker (like age) or a confounded correlate riding on a shared upstream cause — the strong answer identifies which correlates are genuinely causal and modifiable, and flags when the real lever is a distal structural factor rather than the proximal behavior first observed.

questions.prompt: Age reliably predicts chronic disease risk but cannot itself be targeted by an intervention to reduce that risk. What category does age belong to?

options.text: Causal factor
Risk marker
Confounded correlate
Distal structural determinant

explanations.a: A causal factor changes risk when modified; age cannot be modified, so it fails this test despite predicting risk.
explanations.b: Correct: age predicts risk and is useful for stratification, but it is not part of the modifiable causal mechanism itself, which is the definition of a risk marker.
explanations.c: A confounded correlate is associated only via a shared upstream cause with the outcome; age's link to chronic disease is direct biological aging, not confounding.
explanations.d: Distal determinants are structural/environmental (food access, policy); age is an individual, biological, fixed characteristic, not a structural one.

questions.prompt: Match each term to the example that best illustrates it.

right.text: Blood pressure, shown by trials to change heart attack risk when treated
Age or genotype, used to stratify risk but not itself an intervention target
Lighter-carrying appearing linked to lung cancer only because both share smoking as a common cause
Neighborhood food access shaping whether a 'diet choice' is realistically available

questions.explanation: Each category has a distinct causal role: modifiable causal factors respond to intervention, fixed markers stratify without being levers, confounded correlates ride on a shared cause, and distal determinants constrain the feasibility of proximal behaviors.

questions.prompt: Order these determinants from most distal (structural, upstream) to most proximal (closest to the disease outcome).

items.text: Neighborhood food access and income (structural environment)
Individual diet and physical activity (behavior)
Blood pressure and LDL cholesterol (biological risk factor)
Heart disease diagnosis (outcome)

questions.explanation: Structural/distal forces shape behavior, behavior shapes proximal biological risk factors, and those biological factors causally produce the clinical outcome — a chain from upstream to downstream.

questions.prompt: What did the Framingham Heart Study's later clinical trial evidence establish about blood pressure, according to the lesson?

options.text: Blood pressure is only a marker, not a causal factor, for heart disease
Treating hypertension measurably reduced heart attack and stroke incidence, confirming blood pressure as a causal, modifiable factor
Blood pressure correlates with heart disease only because both share age as a confound
Blood pressure cannot be modified through treatment

explanations.a: The lesson describes trial evidence supporting a causal role, not a mere marker role, for blood pressure.
explanations.b: Correct: treatment trials showing reduced heart attack and stroke incidence when hypertension is treated is exactly the evidence that elevates blood pressure from correlate to causal, modifiable factor.
explanations.c: The lesson attributes the association to a direct causal mechanism demonstrated by treatment trials, not to age confounding.
explanations.d: Blood pressure is explicitly described as modifiable through treatment, contradicting this option.

lessons.label: Sick Individuals and Sick Populations

sections.heading: Rose's two questions
sections.body: In his 1985 paper 'Sick Individuals and Sick Populations,' published in the International Journal of Epidemiology, Geoffrey Rose distinguished two questions that sound similar but demand different research designs and yield different answers. 'Why do some individuals get this disease?' — the causes of cases — is answered by comparing sick and healthy individuals within a population, looking for what makes one person different from their neighbor. 'Why does this population have this rate of disease, higher or lower than another population?' — the causes of incidence — is answered by comparing populations against each other, looking at exposures the whole society shares. A factor can explain individual susceptibility without explaining why the population rate differs, and vice versa; both questions are legitimate but they are not the same question.

sections.heading: The prevention paradox
sections.body: Rose also named the prevention paradox: a preventive measure that brings large benefit to a population often brings little benefit to each individual who follows it. Population-wide salt reduction lowers the average blood pressure of an entire society and measurably cuts total strokes, yet any single person cutting salt sees a barely perceptible personal risk reduction, since their starting risk was likely already low. Rose himself put a number on that split: a population-wide reduction of a few grams of salt per day was projected to lower average blood pressure by only a few mmHg per person, yet at the population level that same shift was projected to prevent a meaningful share of strokes and heart attacks — a large aggregate benefit built from a personal change too small for any one person to notice. The paradox is not a flaw in the measure — it is a description of how population-level prevention distributes its benefit thinly across many people rather than concentrating it in a few.

sections.heading: Population-shift vs. high-risk strategy
sections.body: Rose contrasted two prevention strategies. The high-risk strategy screens for and targets individuals with elevated risk factors, offering intensive, tailored intervention to a small tail of the distribution. The population strategy shifts the entire risk-factor distribution — the whole bell curve of blood pressure or cholesterol — modestly downward through broad measures like reformulation or taxation. Rose's key insight was that because the moderate-risk majority is so much larger than the high-risk minority, most future cases of a common chronic disease arise from that large moderate-risk group, even though each person in it faces lower individual odds than someone in the high-risk tail.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a population's blood pressure distribution is such that 90% of people sit in the 'average' range and 10% are classified 'high risk' hypertensive. Even if a high-risk person's individual stroke probability is several times higher than an average-risk person's, the sheer size of the 90% group means it can still contribute more total strokes in absolute numbers than the smaller high-risk 10% does. A high-risk-only screening program that treats just the hypertensive tail therefore leaves the larger share of future strokes, arising from the average-risk majority, essentially unaddressed — which is exactly the case Rose used to argue for population-wide strategies alongside high-risk ones.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student proposing a 'screen and treat the high-risk group' intervention has grappled with Rose's argument that most cases in a common chronic disease come from the much larger moderate-risk majority, not the high-risk tail. The strong answer explains why a population-shift strategy, despite offering each individual only a small expected benefit (the prevention paradox), can prevent more total cases than a high-risk strategy alone, and discusses the real tradeoff of thin-but-broad versus concentrated-but-narrow benefit.

questions.prompt: Rose distinguished 'causes of cases' from 'causes of incidence.' What does 'causes of incidence' ask?

options.text: Why does this specific individual, compared to their neighbor, have the disease?
Why does this population have a higher or lower disease rate than another population?
What treatment cures the disease fastest?
How many component causes exist in a sufficient-cause pie?

explanations.a: That framing is Rose's other question, 'causes of cases,' answered by comparing sick and healthy individuals within one population.
explanations.b: Correct: causes of incidence compares populations against each other to explain differing disease rates, using exposures the whole society shares.
explanations.c: Treatment efficacy is a clinical question unrelated to Rose's population-versus-individual causal distinction.
explanations.d: The causal-pie component-cause count is Rothman's concept, not Rose's incidence-versus-cases distinction.

questions.prompt: What does the 'prevention paradox' describe?

options.text: A measure that benefits the population greatly while offering each individual who follows it only a small personal benefit
A measure that helps individuals but harms the population overall
A statistical error that makes prevention studies unreliable
The fact that prevention only works for infectious disease

explanations.a: Correct: population-wide salt reduction is Rose's example — large aggregate benefit to society, tiny expected benefit to any one already-low-risk individual who adopts it.
explanations.b: The paradox describes population benefit alongside small individual benefit, not population harm.
explanations.c: It is a real description of how benefit distributes, not a methodological flaw or error.
explanations.d: Rose's argument concerns chronic-disease prevention strategy, not a restriction to infectious disease.

questions.prompt: Match each prevention strategy to its defining feature.

right.text: Targets and intensively treats the small high-risk tail of the distribution
Shifts the entire risk-factor distribution modestly downward across everyone

questions.explanation: Rose framed these as complementary but distinct approaches: one concentrates intervention on identified high-risk individuals, the other broadly shifts population-wide exposure levels.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps of Rose's argument for why a high-risk-only strategy under-prevents chronic disease.

items.text: The moderate/average-risk group is far larger in number than the high-risk tail
Even with lower individual probability, the large moderate-risk group produces a large absolute number of cases
A strategy that only screens and treats the high-risk tail leaves most future cases, arising from the moderate-risk majority, unaddressed
A population-wide strategy that shifts the whole distribution is needed to reduce total case burden

questions.explanation: Rose's argument moves from the relative sizes of risk groups, to the absolute case burden each contributes, to the conclusion that high-risk targeting alone under-prevents disease and population-wide shifts are needed.

lessons.label: Lifetime Risk and Long-Horizon Outcome Measures

sections.heading: From snapshot rates to cumulative measures
sections.body: Incidence rate and point prevalence, the Core-level workhorses, capture a snapshot: new cases per unit time, or existing cases at one moment.
