A slow disease that unfolds over decades needs a different kind of measure — one that accumulates. Cumulative incidence is the risk of developing a disease over a defined follow-up window (say, the next 10 years); lifetime risk extends that same logic across an entire lifespan, from birth to old age, answering 'what is the probability this person will ever develop this disease if they live a full life expectancy.' Both are cumulative probabilities, not rates, and both depend heavily on how long the follow-up window is.

sections.heading: Lifetime risk in practice
sections.body: The American Cancer Society's widely cited figure that a woman's lifetime risk of being diagnosed with breast cancer is about 1 in 8 (roughly 12-13%) is a lifetime-risk estimate: it sums age-specific incidence probabilities across every age band from birth through the mid-80s, adjusted for the chance of dying from another cause first. It is a modeled projection assuming average population exposure, not a personal guarantee or a short-term probability, and it shifts over time as age-specific incidence rates or life expectancy change. Reporting '1 in 8' without the lifetime qualifier badly overstates near-term personal risk.

sections.heading: Case-fatality vs. survival
sections.body: Case-fatality is the proportion of diagnosed cases that die from the disease within a defined period, a measure that works cleanly for acute conditions with a short, bounded course. Chronic diseases, whose course can run for decades and whose patients often die of unrelated causes along the way, are instead tracked with relative survival — the proportion of diagnosed patients alive at a follow-up point (commonly 5 years) compared to a demographically matched population without the disease, which factors out mortality unrelated to the disease itself. This long-horizon framing is what lets researchers meaningfully track outcomes for conditions that a same-year case-fatality snapshot would badly misrepresent. US SEER registry data illustrate the range this measure can span: 5-year relative survival for breast cancer is roughly 90% overall, but that figure falls sharply for distant-stage (metastatic) disease at diagnosis, dropping to roughly 30%, showing that a single disease name can carry very different long-horizon outcomes depending on how early the disease was caught — which is exactly the stage-dependent nuance a same-year case-fatality count would erase.

lessons.workedExample: A 50-year-old woman's cumulative incidence of breast cancer over just the next 10 years is on the order of 2%, far below her one-in-eight (about 12.5%) lifetime figure — because the lifetime number pools her risk across every remaining decade of life, from her 50s through her 80s, not just the next ten years. If she were instead evaluated only by a same-year case-fatality-style snapshot, neither number would show up meaningfully at all; it takes a cumulative, multi-decade measure to represent what '1 in 8' is actually describing.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student citing a lifetime-risk statistic (like 1 in 8) understands it as a cumulative probability across an entire lifespan rather than an annual or short-term risk. A common fair-project error is presenting a lifetime figure as if it applied to 'this year' or 'this person right now,' which both overstates near-term risk and reveals the student doesn't understand how the cumulative measure was constructed from age-specific incidence rates.

questions.prompt: What does the American Cancer Society's '1 in 8' lifetime breast cancer risk figure actually represent?

options.text: The chance a woman is diagnosed in any single given year
The cumulative probability of ever being diagnosed, summed across age-specific incidence from birth through the mid-80s
The case-fatality rate for diagnosed breast cancer
The prevalence of breast cancer at a single point in time

explanations.a: An annual/single-year risk is far smaller than the lifetime figure; the lesson's 10-year worked example for a 50-year-old is only about 2%.
explanations.b: Correct: lifetime risk sums age-specific incidence probabilities across a full lifespan, adjusted for competing mortality, which is exactly what produces the 1-in-8 figure.
explanations.c: Case-fatality measures death among diagnosed cases, an entirely different quantity from risk of ever being diagnosed.
explanations.d: Point prevalence is a snapshot of existing cases at one moment, not a cumulative lifetime probability.

questions.prompt: Why do epidemiologists use relative survival rather than case-fatality for most chronic diseases?

options.text: Because chronic diseases have no diagnosed cases to track
Because relative survival factors out mortality unrelated to the disease over a long, multi-year follow-up, which case-fatality's short defined window doesn't handle well for slow diseases
Because case-fatality only applies to cancer
Because relative survival requires no comparison population

explanations.a: Chronic diseases have diagnosed cases; the issue is which metric best represents a decades-long course, not absence of cases.
explanations.b: Correct: relative survival compares diagnosed patients to a matched population without the disease over a long follow-up (commonly 5 years), isolating disease-attributable mortality across a realistic timeframe for chronic disease.
explanations.c: Case-fatality is a general concept applicable beyond cancer; its limitation is fitting a short bounded course, not being cancer-specific.
explanations.d: Relative survival is defined by comparison to a matched population, so it explicitly requires one.

questions.prompt: Match each measure to its definition.

right.text: Risk of developing disease over a defined follow-up window, such as 10 years
Cumulative probability of ever developing disease across an entire lifespan
Proportion of diagnosed cases that die of the disease within a defined period
Proportion of diagnosed patients alive at a follow-up point versus a matched disease-free population

questions.explanation: These four measures form a family of outcome statistics distinguished by their time horizon and by whether they measure risk of disease onset or risk of death after diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to build a lifetime-risk estimate like the 1-in-8 breast cancer figure from age-specific incidence data.

items.text: Obtain age-specific incidence rates for each age band across the lifespan
Adjust each age band for the competing chance of dying from another cause first
Cumulate (sum) the adjusted age-specific probabilities across all age bands, birth through the mid-80s
Report the resulting cumulative probability as the lifetime risk

questions.explanation: Lifetime risk is built by starting from age-specific incidence, adjusting for competing mortality so the estimate isn't inflated by people who wouldn't have lived to develop the disease, then cumulating across the full lifespan.

units.label: Prospective Cohort Studies for Chronic Disease

lessons.label: Anatomy of a Long-Term Prospective Cohort

sections.heading: Baseline enrollment and the exposure-before-outcome guarantee
sections.body: A prospective cohort study begins with a baseline enrollment visit: participants free of the outcome under study complete questionnaires, undergo physical exams, and often donate blood or urine that is frozen for assays years later. Exposure status and covariates are recorded at this baseline moment, then the cohort is followed forward — years or decades — while investigators wait for outcomes to accrue naturally. Because exposure is fixed on paper before anyone has developed the outcome, temporality is built into the design's mechanics rather than reconstructed afterward. This is the operational advantage a chronic-disease researcher is buying: a case-control study asks a person already diagnosed with, say, pancreatic cancer to recall their diet from twenty years earlier, and that recall is contaminated by knowing the diagnosis. A cohort's baseline questionnaire was answered by someone who did not yet know whether they would develop the disease, so there is nothing for illness to distort.

sections.heading: Fixed and dynamic cohorts
sections.body: Cohorts come in two structural flavors. A fixed (or closed) cohort enrolls a defined roster at a single baseline period and admits no new members afterward — the original 1948 Framingham cohort of about 5,200 adults is fixed in this sense; everyone who will ever be in it was enrolled in that first wave. A dynamic (or open) cohort instead allows new, eligible members to enter continuously as time passes and lets others leave when they no longer meet eligibility, so its membership and total person-time keep shifting; occupational cohorts that keep adding newly hired workers, or a hospital registry enrolling every incident patient, are dynamic by nature. The distinction matters for analysis: a fixed cohort's cumulative incidence is straightforward to compute over a shared follow-up window, while a dynamic cohort requires person-time (incidence-rate) methods, since not everyone has the same amount of at-risk time or entered at the same calendar point.

sections.heading: Long latency and multifactorial outcomes
sections.body: Chronic diseases like coronary heart disease, most cancers, and type 2 diabetes typically take one to several decades to develop after the exposures that raise their risk, and their causes are rarely single: diet, smoking, physical activity, blood pressure, and genetics all interact. A case-control study sampling diagnosed cases and healthy controls at one point in time can still estimate an odds ratio, but multi-decade recall of exposure intensity or duration degrades badly, and it can only look backward at outcomes that have already occurred. A prospective cohort, by contrast, can measure dozens of exposures at baseline and repeated follow-up visits, then examine many downstream outcomes from that single measured exposure history — exactly the structure chronic-disease epidemiology needs, since a habit like smoking or a metric like LDL cholesterol plausibly contributes to several diseases at once, not one.

lessons.workedExample: A cohort enrolls 10,000 adults aged 40-59 in 2000, none with cardiovascular disease, and records baseline LDL cholesterol, smoking status, and diet via food-frequency questionnaire. By 2020, 800 have developed coronary heart disease. Because LDL and smoking were measured in 2000, before any case existed, investigators can directly compute incidence in high-LDL versus low-LDL groups and derive relative risk with no recall involved. Contrast a case-control alternative: interviewing the 800 diagnosed patients in 2020 about their diet and smoking in 2000 would rely on twenty-year-old memory, likely biased by knowing they now have heart disease. The same baseline blood samples, banked in 2000, can also later be assayed for a biomarker discovered in 2015 — the cohort answers a question nobody had thought to ask yet.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student's cohort design actually guarantees exposure precedes outcome, or whether the 'baseline' measurement was taken after some participants were already symptomatic — a subtle timing error that quietly reintroduces reverse causation. They also ask whether the cohort is fixed or dynamic and whether the analysis method matches: a fixed cohort analyzed with cumulative incidence is fine, but a dynamic cohort with staggered entry and exit demands person-time incidence rates, and a student who reports a simple percentage without acknowledging unequal follow-up time has likely miscounted the denominator.

questions.prompt: Why does a prospective cohort avoid the recall bias that threatens case-control studies of chronic disease?

options.text: Because exposure is measured at baseline, before any outcome exists, so no one is remembering their past through the lens of a diagnosis
Because cohort studies always enroll far more participants than case-control studies
Because cohort studies use blood samples instead of questionnaires
Because cohort participants are unaware they are in a study

explanations.a: Correct: baseline data is collected before disease status is known, so there is no diagnosis to distort memory.
explanations.b: Sample size is unrelated to recall bias; a small cohort still avoids it because of timing, not scale.
explanations.c: Many cohorts rely heavily on questionnaires (diet, smoking history) at baseline; the protection comes from timing, not the data type.
explanations.d: Awareness of study participation does not cause recall bias; the issue is remembering past exposure after already knowing one's diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of setting up and running a prospective cohort.

items.text: Define eligibility criteria and decide whether the cohort will be fixed or dynamic
Enroll the baseline roster and measure exposure and covariates before any outcome occurs
Follow the cohort forward, admitting new dynamic entrants if applicable
Accrue outcome events over years to decades and analyze using incidence

questions.explanation: A cohort's design choice (fixed vs. dynamic) comes first, then baseline exposure measurement, then forward follow-up, then outcome accrual and incidence analysis.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its description.

right.text: Admits new eligible members and loses others continuously over time
A defined roster enrolled once, with no members added later
The point at which exposure and covariates are recorded, before outcomes occur

questions.explanation: Fixed cohorts close enrollment at one wave, dynamic cohorts allow ongoing entry and exit, and baseline enrollment is where exposure timing is locked in before outcome.

questions.prompt: A researcher wants to study whether decades of dietary patterns contribute to five different chronic diseases (heart disease, stroke, diabetes, certain cancers, and dementia). Why is a single prospective cohort well suited to this, compared to running five separate case-control studies?

options.text: A cohort with baseline diet data can examine multiple downstream outcomes from the same measured exposure, without needing separate recall interviews per disease
Cohort studies are always cheaper and faster to run than case-control studies
Case-control studies cannot compute odds ratios for chronic disease
Only cohort studies are able to enroll more than 1,000 participants

explanations.a: Correct: one baseline exposure measurement can be linked forward to many outcomes, which is exactly the multifactorial, multi-outcome structure chronic disease presents.
explanations.b: Cohorts are typically slower and more expensive than case-control studies, not cheaper or faster; their advantage here is structural, not economic.
explanations.c: Case-control studies routinely compute odds ratios for chronic disease; the issue is decades-long recall accuracy, not an inability to compute a statistic.
explanations.d: Enrollment size is not restricted to cohort designs; large case-control studies exist too.

lessons.label: The Great Longitudinal Cohorts

sections.heading: Framingham and the British Doctors Study: the 1950s founders
sections.body: The Framingham Heart Study enrolled about 5,200 adults aged 30-62 in Framingham, Massachusetts, in 1948, re-examining them roughly every two years under founding investigators including Thomas Dawber. Its defining conceptual contribution arrived in a 1961 paper by Kannel, Dawber, and colleagues, 'Factors of Risk in the Development of Coronary Heart Disease,' which introduced the term 'risk factor' and quantified how hypertension, cholesterol, and smoking each independently raised coronary risk. In Britain, Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill took a different route in 1951: they mailed a smoking-habits questionnaire to essentially the entire registered medical profession, and about 40,000 doctors replied with enough detail to be followed prospectively. The British Doctors Study tracked this cohort for decades, with repeat questionnaires into the 1990s and 2000s, and produced some of the first prospective evidence that cigarette smoking raises lung cancer and coronary death, with mortality rising as reported daily cigarette use increased.

sections.heading: Nurses' Health Study and the Whitehall studies
sections.body: Frank Speizer launched the Nurses' Health Study in 1976, enrolling about 121,700 married female registered nurses aged 30-55 from eleven U.S. states, originally to study oral contraceptives and cancer; repeated mailed questionnaires every two years made it a lasting source of data on diet, hormones, and chronic disease in women, later joined by Nurses' Health Study II in 1989. In Britain, Donald Reid and Geoffrey Rose began the Whitehall Study in 1967, examining roughly 17,000 male civil servants and finding a striking social gradient: men in the lowest employment grade had roughly three times the mortality of men in the highest grade, despite none living in poverty. Michael Marmot's Whitehall II study, begun in 1985 with about 10,308 civil servants of both sexes, extended this and helped establish that psychosocial job strain, not just material deprivation, tracks with cardiovascular risk.

sections.heading: EPIC: cohort science at continental scale
sections.body: The European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC) recruited roughly 521,000 participants across ten European countries during the 1990s, collecting dietary questionnaires and blood samples specifically to study diet and lifestyle against cancer and chronic disease. Its scale lets it detect modest diet-disease associations a few-thousand-person cohort could never resolve, and its cross-national design compares the same exposure-disease relationship across very different diets, from Mediterranean Greece to Scandinavian Denmark. Together these five cohorts share a pattern: none answers one narrow question. Each has been mined for new hypotheses for decades, banking specimens and repeating measurements so a question nobody thought to ask at enrollment can still be answered from data collected before anyone was sick.

lessons.workedExample: The British Doctors Study's early follow-up already showed a dose-response gradient: lung cancer mortality rose in clear steps from nonsmokers up through moderate to heavy smokers, the kind of graded relationship that is one of the Bradford Hill criteria for causation and that a smaller cohort could not have resolved as clearly. Contrast Whitehall I's finding that lowest-grade civil servants died at roughly three times the rate of top-grade administrators over the same follow-up window, despite comparable access to Britain's National Health Service — a result that shifted chronic-disease epidemiology from asking only 'does this substance cause disease' toward asking how socioeconomic position itself gets converted into biology. Neither finding was visible in a single short study; both required tracking the same defined population for years while events accumulated.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask students who cite a landmark cohort to know it as more than a name-drop: what year it started, roughly how large it was, and what its founding question was, because these cohorts are still generating papers decades later on questions their designers never anticipated. A student who says 'Framingham showed smoking causes heart disease' without knowing it began in 1948 with about 5,200 people, or who cannot distinguish Whitehall's social-gradient finding from Framingham's risk-factor finding, has memorized a label rather than understood why sustained follow-up at that scale was necessary to see the effect at all.

questions.prompt: Which 1961 paper is credited with introducing the term 'risk factor' into medical epidemiology?

options.text: Kannel, Dawber, and colleagues' 'Factors of Risk in the Development of Coronary Heart Disease'
Doll and Hill's British Doctors Study report
Marmot's Whitehall II baseline report
Speizer's Nurses' Health Study founding protocol

explanations.a: Correct: this 1961 Framingham paper by Kannel, Dawber, and colleagues coined and quantified 'risk factor' for coronary heart disease.
explanations.b: The British Doctors Study, begun in 1951, established prospective evidence linking smoking to lung cancer and coronary death but did not coin the term 'risk factor'.
explanations.c: Whitehall II began in 1985 and is known for the social-gradient and job-strain findings, not for coining 'risk factor'.
explanations.d: The Nurses' Health Study, founded in 1976, originally studied oral contraceptives and cancer; it did not originate the term.

questions.prompt: Order these cohorts from earliest to latest founding year.

items.text: Framingham Heart Study (1948)
British Doctors Study (1951)
Whitehall I (1967)
Nurses' Health Study (1976)
EPIC (early 1990s)

questions.explanation: Framingham (1948) came first, followed by the British Doctors Study (1951), Whitehall I (1967), the Nurses' Health Study (1976), and EPIC's recruitment beginning in the early 1990s.

questions.prompt: Match each cohort to its approximate scale and signature finding.

right.text: About 121,700 female nurses enrolled in 1976 to study oral contraceptives and later much more
About 5,200 adults enrolled in 1948; source of the term 'risk factor'
About 17,000 male civil servants; found a roughly threefold mortality gradient by employment grade
About 521,000 participants across ten European countries studying diet and cancer

questions.explanation: Each cohort is matched to its founding scale and the finding it is best known for.

questions.prompt: Approximately how many British doctors were followed after Doll and Hill's 1951 mailing, and what did the study find?

options.text: About 40,000 doctors; smoking correlated with a step-wise rise in lung cancer and coronary death
About 121,700 doctors; oral contraceptive use was the primary exposure studied
About 5,200 doctors; hypertension emerged as the primary risk factor
About 10,308 doctors; job strain predicted cardiovascular risk

explanations.a: Correct: roughly 40,000 doctors replied with usable detail, and the study found smoking dose tracked with lung cancer and coronary mortality.
explanations.b: That size and exposure describe the Nurses' Health Study (1976), not the British Doctors Study.
explanations.c: That size and finding describe the Framingham Heart Study (1948), not the British Doctors Study.
explanations.d: That size and finding describe Whitehall II (1985), not the British Doctors Study.

lessons.label: Loss to Follow-Up and Its Biases

sections.heading: Differential versus non-differential loss
sections.body: Every multi-decade cohort loses participants — people move, become too ill to respond, withdraw consent, or simply stop replying to mailed questionnaires. Non-differential loss occurs when the chance of dropping out is unrelated to both exposure and outcome; it shrinks statistical power and widens confidence intervals but does not systematically distort the point estimate. Differential loss is the dangerous kind: when dropout probability depends on exposure status, outcome status, or both, the remaining sample no longer represents the cohort that was enrolled. If, say, smokers who develop early symptoms of heart disease are more likely to drop out of a smoking-and-CHD cohort than symptom-free smokers, the smokers who remain look artificially healthy, and the smoking-CHD association is attenuated toward the null purely by attrition, not because the true effect is smaller.

sections.heading: The rough 5-and-20 rule
sections.body: Clinical epidemiology texts offer a widely used rule of thumb for how worried to be: loss under roughly 5% of the original cohort is unlikely to threaten a study's validity on its own, loss of 20% or more is generally considered a serious threat, and anything in between demands a closer look at whether the losses were differential. The rule is a heuristic, not a formula — a 10% loss concentrated entirely in one exposure arm can do more damage than a 25% loss split evenly across arms — but it gives students a fast gut-check for whether a project's attrition needs a sensitivity analysis before results can be trusted.

sections.heading: Tracing, retention, and bounding the damage
sections.body: Cohorts fight attrition two ways: retention efforts that keep participants actively engaged (periodic contact, address updates, incentives) and passive tracing through vital-records linkage — matching participant identifiers against a national death index or registry so that even someone who stopped answering surveys can still be classified as alive or dead, and often by cause. This recovers outcome status even after a participant is functionally lost to active follow-up. When some loss is unavoidable, investigators run sensitivity analyses that bound the possible damage: best-case and worst-case imputations (assuming all lost-to-follow-up exposed participants did or did not develop the outcome), or inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting, which up-weights remaining participants who resemble those lost. A cohort that reports both its overall retention rate and this kind of bounding analysis gives readers a much stronger basis for trusting the point estimate than one that reports retention alone.

lessons.workedExample: A 20-year cohort of 8,000 participants studying alcohol intake and liver disease retains 7,600 (95%) overall — comfortably under the 5% caution threshold. But broken out by exposure, only 82% of heavy drinkers remain versus 97% of non-drinkers, because heavy drinkers with early liver symptoms disproportionately stopped responding. This 15-point gap is differential loss: the heavy-drinking group that remains under-represents its sickest members, likely attenuating the true alcohol-liver disease association. Investigators cross-check by linking all 400 apparently lost heavy drinkers to the national death registry, recovering cause-of-death for 310 of them, then rerun the analysis first assuming the 90 still-untraceable had the outcome and then assuming none did, reporting both bounds alongside the main estimate.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push past a single reported retention percentage to ask whether loss was broken out by exposure and outcome, because a headline 95% retention rate can hide an 82/97 split that fully explains a weakened result. A student who can only report 'we retained most participants' has not actually ruled out differential attrition as the source of their finding; one who reports retention by arm, explains why it differed, and shows the result survives a best/worst-case bound has demonstrated the estimate is not an artifact of who happened to stay in the study.

questions.prompt: In a cohort studying diet and colorectal cancer, participants who develop early digestive symptoms (which sometimes precede diagnosis) are less likely to complete follow-up surveys than symptom-free participants, regardless of diet group. What kind of loss is this, and what is its likely effect?

options.text: Differential loss tied to outcome status, which can bias the exposure-outcome association
Non-differential loss, since it reduces power but not the point estimate
Selection bias, unrelated to loss to follow-up
This has no effect because dropout is unrelated to diet group

explanations.a: Correct: dropout depending on outcome-related symptoms is still differential loss, even without differing by exposure, and can distort the estimate.
explanations.b: Loss tied to outcome status is differential by definition, not non-differential; it threatens the point estimate, not just power.
explanations.c: This is specifically a loss-to-follow-up mechanism, not a separate category called selection bias.
explanations.d: Being unrelated to diet group does not make the loss harmless; loss tied to the outcome itself can still bias results.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for handling attrition in a long-running cohort.

items.text: Track retention overall and separately by exposure group at study close
Identify whether the loss is differential (depends on exposure or outcome) or non-differential
Use vital-records linkage to recover outcome status for as many lost participants as possible
Run best-case/worst-case sensitivity analysis on any participants still untraceable

questions.explanation: Retention is tracked first, then classified as differential or not, then linkage recovers what status it can, and sensitivity analysis bounds whatever remains unknown.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its description.

right.text: A heuristic: under ~5% loss is low concern, 20%+ is a serious concern
Matching participant IDs to a death index or registry to recover outcome status after active follow-up ends
Up-weighting remaining participants who resemble those who were lost, to correct for attrition
Dropout probability tied to exposure and/or outcome status, which can distort the estimate

questions.explanation: The 5-and-20 rule is a rough threshold, vital-records linkage recovers lost outcome data, inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting corrects statistically, and differential loss is the underlying bias mechanism.

lessons.label: Competing Risks in Long Follow-Up

sections.heading: When one event forecloses another
sections.body: In long cohort follow-up, especially of older or already-ill populations, subjects are often at risk of dying from causes other than the outcome under study before that outcome can occur. A competing risk is exactly this: an event that, once it happens, makes the outcome of interest impossible to ever observe in that person. In a cohort studying time to dementia diagnosis among adults over 70, a participant who dies of a heart attack at age 78 can never subsequently be diagnosed with dementia — death from cardiovascular disease competes with, and forecloses, the dementia outcome. This is different from ordinary censoring (leaving the study, end of follow-up), where the event could still happen later; a competing risk removes the person from the risk set permanently.

sections.heading: Why naive Kaplan-Meier overestimates risk
sections.body: The standard Kaplan-Meier estimator, and the common shortcut of reporting cumulative incidence as '1 minus the Kaplan-Meier survival estimate,' treats competing events as if they were ordinary censoring — as if the person might still develop the outcome later, just outside the observation window. When competing risks are common, this overestimates the true cumulative incidence of the outcome of interest, because it silently redistributes the probability mass of people who died of the competing cause back onto the population still 'at risk,' as though they might yet develop it. In a cohort where a large share of an elderly population dies of cardiovascular disease before ever reaching a dementia diagnosis, naive 1-minus-KM can overstate lifetime dementia risk by a meaningful margin, particularly at longer follow-up times where competing deaths accumulate.

sections.heading: Cause-specific hazards versus the Fine-Gray subdistribution approach
sections.body: Two more careful approaches ask different questions. The cause-specific hazard treats competing-risk deaths as censored and asks: among people still free of any event, what is the instantaneous rate of the outcome of interest? This is the right quantity for etiologic questions about biological mechanism. The cumulative incidence function (CIF), estimated properly, gives the actual proportion of the population expected to experience the outcome by a given time, accounting for the fact that some were removed by the competing event; Fine and Gray's 1999 subdistribution hazard model extends regression to this CIF-based quantity directly. A clinician predicting a patient's real-world probability of dementia by age 85 wants the CIF/Fine-Gray answer; a mechanistic researcher asking whether a gene variant accelerates the biological process of dementia, independent of who dies first, wants the cause-specific hazard.

lessons.workedExample: A cohort of 2,000 adults aged 75 is followed for 10 years to study dementia incidence. Over follow-up, 500 develop dementia and 700 die of other causes (mainly cardiovascular disease) without ever being diagnosed with dementia; 800 remain event-free at 10 years. Naive 1-minus-Kaplan-Meier, treating the 700 deaths as ordinary censoring, estimates roughly 34% ten-year dementia risk. The properly computed cumulative incidence function, which accounts for the fact that those 700 people were permanently removed from the pool who could still develop dementia, estimates closer to 25% — the naive method overstated risk by about nine percentage points because it implicitly assumed the people who died of heart disease were just as likely to eventually get dementia as everyone else.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student analyzing an elderly or multimorbid cohort even recognizes competing risks exist, since reporting 1-minus-Kaplan-Meier cumulative incidence in a population with substantial competing mortality is one of the most common analytic errors in chronic-disease projects — it inflates the headline risk number without the student noticing anything is wrong, because the code runs and produces a plausible-looking curve. A judge asking 'what happened to participants who died of something else before your outcome?' is testing whether the student chose cause-specific or subdistribution hazards deliberately, or simply used whatever survival-analysis function came up first in a search.

questions.prompt: In a cohort of older adults, using 1-minus-Kaplan-Meier to estimate cumulative incidence of dementia while ignoring competing deaths from cardiovascular disease will typically:

options.text: Overestimate the true cumulative incidence of dementia
Underestimate the true cumulative incidence of dementia
Have no effect on the estimate, since Kaplan-Meier already accounts for competing risks
Only affect the cause-specific hazard, not cumulative incidence

explanations.a: Correct: naive 1-minus-KM treats competing deaths as if they might still develop the outcome, inflating cumulative incidence.
explanations.b: The bias runs the opposite direction; naive KM systematically overstates, not understates, cumulative incidence when competing risks are present.
explanations.c: Kaplan-Meier's standard form treats competing events as ordinary censoring, which is exactly the assumption that breaks down with true competing risks.
explanations.d: The bias appears in cumulative incidence estimates specifically; the cause-specific hazard is a different, separately estimated quantity.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning for correctly analyzing a cohort with competing risks.

items.text: Recognize that death from another cause permanently removes a subject from the risk set for the outcome of interest
Decide whether the analytic question is etiologic (cause-specific hazard) or predictive/absolute-risk (cumulative incidence function)
Fit the corresponding model: cause-specific Cox model, or Fine-Gray subdistribution model for the CIF
Interpret the resulting incidence estimate, distinguishing it from what naive 1-minus-Kaplan-Meier would have shown

questions.explanation: Recognizing the competing-risk structure comes first, then choosing the matching question and model, then interpreting results against the naive (and biased) alternative.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its description.

right.text: Treats competing deaths as ordinary censoring and overestimates cumulative incidence
Instantaneous rate of the outcome among those still event-free, treating competing events as censored; answers etiologic questions
Regression model estimating the cumulative incidence function directly, accounting for competing events
An event that, once it occurs, permanently forecloses the outcome of interest

questions.explanation: Naive KM overestimates by mishandling competing deaths, cause-specific hazard answers mechanism questions, Fine-Gray answers absolute-risk questions, and a competing risk is the event that forecloses the outcome.

lessons.label: Immortal Time and Follow-Up Biases

sections.heading: Immortal time: a span where the outcome cannot occur
sections.body: Immortal time bias arises when a period of follow-up during which, by construction, the outcome could not have happened is misassigned to the exposed group, inflating its apparent benefit. The classic setup: a cohort study defines 'exposed' as anyone who ever filled a statin prescription during follow-up, then counts each person's exposure status starting from cohort entry, not from the date they actually started the drug. Anyone who died before they got around to filling that first prescription is, by definition, excluded from the 'exposed' group's death count for the time before their prescription — yet that same stretch of time is still credited to the exposed group as event-free person-time. The exposed group's early follow-up is 'immortal' by definitional accident, not because the drug protected anyone, and the miscounted person-time manufactures a spurious survival advantage.

sections.heading: Healthy-user, healthy-adherer, and prevalent-user biases
sections.body: Related biases arise from who ends up in the 'exposed' or 'adherent' group in the first place. Healthy-user bias: people who take preventive medication as prescribed also tend to eat better, exercise more, and see a doctor regularly, so any comparison of drug-takers to non-takers partly reflects these unmeasured healthy habits rather than the drug itself. Healthy-adherer bias is the same phenomenon isolated within drug-takers: the Coronary Drug Project (1980) found that participants who adhered closely to their assigned placebo — a pill with no active ingredient — still had substantially lower five-year mortality than poor adherers, proving that the act of adherence itself marks healthier, more health-engaged people. Prevalent-user bias occurs when a cohort enrolls people already mid-treatment rather than new starters, so anyone who suffered an early adverse reaction and stopped the drug has already been excluded before the study even began, leaving only survivors of the drug's riskiest early period.

sections.heading: The new-user, time-zero fix
sections.body: Samy Suissa's work on inhaled corticosteroids and mortality in COPD patients is a frequently cited case: several observational studies reported that inhaled steroids reduced mortality substantially, an effect that shrank toward the null once analysts adopted a new-user design — enrolling only patients starting the drug for the first time, with time zero set at the actual prescription date, and defining exposure using only person-time that accrues after that point. The fix is structural, not statistical: align cohort entry (time zero), exposure classification, and eligibility criteria so that no follow-up time is credited to a group before that person could plausibly have experienced the exposure's effect, and treat exposure as time-varying rather than as a fixed label assigned by looking at the whole future.

lessons.workedExample: A cohort study follows 5,000 heart-attack survivors for one year, classifying anyone who ever filled a statin prescription during that year as 'exposed' from day one of follow-up. Patient A fills a statin prescription on day 200 and survives the year; patient B never fills one and dies on day 50. Patient A's first 199 days, when they were not yet taking anything, are counted as statin-exposed person-time, while patient B, who never had the chance to start statins, contributes to the unexposed death count. Re-analyzing with time-varying exposure — crediting patient A's mortality risk to the unexposed group for days 1-199 and the exposed group only from day 200 onward — typically shrinks or eliminates the apparent statin survival benefit, because the immortal early period is no longer misassigned.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe observational drug-benefit claims specifically for immortal time, because it is one of the most reliable ways an entirely spurious protective effect gets published: the bias always favors the exposed group, never the reference group, so a student reporting 'our exposed group had lower mortality' without describing how time zero and exposure timing were defined has likely built the bias into the design rather than found a real effect. The tell of understanding is describing exposure as time-varying from an actual start date, not as a single label assigned by looking at a person's entire follow-up in hindsight.

questions.prompt: A cohort classifies patients as 'statin users' if they ever filled a statin prescription at any point during a year of follow-up, and counts that entire year as exposed time. What bias does this introduce?

options.text: Immortal time bias, because time before the prescription was actually filled is misassigned as exposed, event-free time
Recall bias, because patients may misremember when they started the drug
Loss to follow-up, because some patients stopped taking the drug
Competing risk, because death from another cause prevents the statin outcome

explanations.a: Correct: crediting pre-prescription time to the exposed group creates immortal time that inflates the drug's apparent benefit.
explanations.b: This scenario is about how the cohort classified exposure from records, not about a patient's memory of their own history.
explanations.c: Loss to follow-up concerns dropout from the study, not the timing rule used to define when exposure begins.
explanations.d: Competing risk describes an event that forecloses the outcome; the issue here is a misassigned exposure window, not a foreclosing event.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the new-user, time-zero fix for immortal time bias.

items.text: Restrict the cohort to patients newly starting the drug, excluding prevalent users already mid-treatment
Set time zero at the actual date each patient starts the drug
Treat exposure as time-varying, crediting pre-prescription follow-up to the unexposed group
Compare outcome rates only using correctly time-aligned exposed and unexposed person-time

questions.explanation: The fix starts with restricting to new users, anchors time zero to the actual start date, treats exposure as time-varying, and only then compares correctly aligned person-time.

questions.prompt: Match each bias to its description.

right.text: People who take preventive medication as prescribed also have healthier unmeasured habits overall
Coronary Drug Project (1980) finding that adherence even to placebo predicted lower mortality
Enrolling patients already mid-treatment excludes those who had early adverse reactions and stopped
A period during which the outcome could not occur is misassigned to the exposed group

questions.explanation: Each bias reflects a different mechanism by which the 'exposed' or 'adherent' group ends up looking healthier for reasons unrelated to the treatment itself.

questions.prompt: Observational studies of inhaled corticosteroids in COPD initially reported meaningfully reduced mortality, an effect that shrank after switching to a new-user design with correctly time-varying exposure. What does this best illustrate?

options.text: That immortal time bias inflated the drug's apparent benefit in the original analyses
That inhaled corticosteroids are proven ineffective in all COPD patients
That the drug's benefit was due to a competing risk being ignored
That the original studies had too much loss to follow-up to be valid

explanations.a: Correct: the shrinking effect after adopting a new-user, time-varying design is the signature of immortal time bias having inflated the original estimate.
explanations.b: The change in estimate reflects a methodological correction, not a definitive verdict on the drug's effectiveness for all patients.
explanations.c: Competing risks involve an event foreclosing the outcome, which is a different mechanism from the exposure-timing error described here.
explanations.d: The correction was about how exposure time was assigned, not about how many participants were lost to follow-up.

lessons.label: Nested Case-Control and Case-Cohort Designs

sections.heading: Sampling inside an existing cohort to save money
sections.body: When a cohort has already banked blood or urine at baseline for tens of thousands of participants, running an expensive assay — a genome-wide genotyping panel, a novel biomarker, a detailed pesticide-residue measurement — on every single sample can be financially impossible even years into a well-funded study. A nested case-control design solves this without abandoning the cohort's exposure-before-outcome timing: identify everyone in the cohort who developed the outcome during follow-up (the cases), then sample a smaller comparison group from the cohort (the controls), and assay only those two groups' stored specimens. Exposure was still measured, or is measurable, at baseline, before any outcome existed, so temporality is preserved exactly as in the parent cohort — the savings come purely from not having to assay everyone who never got the disease. This is the same logic large biobank-linked cohorts use whenever a newly discovered biomarker or genetic panel becomes affordable only after the cohort has already aged for years.

sections.heading: Density (risk-set) sampling and what it buys statistically
sections.body: The specific sampling method matters. Density sampling, also called risk-set sampling, selects controls for each case from the set of cohort members still at risk (event-free) at the exact time that case was diagnosed, rather than from the cohort's full membership regardless of timing. This detail is not a technicality: because controls are sampled from the risk set at each case's event time, the resulting odds ratio from a nested case-control analysis is an unbiased estimate of the incidence rate ratio in the full parent cohort — and unlike the classic cumulative-incidence-based case-control odds ratio, this holds regardless of whether the disease is rare, since it derives from the person-time structure of the cohort rather than from approximating a risk ratio.

sections.heading: Case-cohort: one reusable random subcohort
sections.body: A case-cohort study modifies this further: instead of sampling fresh controls for each case, the investigator draws a single random subcohort at baseline, before any outcomes occur, and that same subcohort is compared against cases for every outcome the parent cohort will ever be used to study. This makes case-cohort designs attractive when a cohort is expected to be mined for several diseases over its lifetime, since the subcohort's expensive baseline measurements are made once and reused rather than re-sampled and re-measured per outcome — unlike a nested case-control study run separately for each disease of interest, whose control set must be resampled and reassayed from scratch every time. Both hybrids still depend on the parent cohort having banked usable specimens and recorded baseline covariates carefully enough to support an assay run years or decades later.

lessons.workedExample: A cohort of 60,000 adults gives blood at baseline in 2005; by 2025, 900 develop type 2 diabetes. Genotyping all 60,000 samples for a candidate gene panel would cost far more than the study's budget allows. A nested case-control design uses risk-set sampling: for each of the 900 cases, four controls are drawn from cohort members still diabetes-free at that case's diagnosis date, yielding 3,600 controls — 4,500 genotyped samples instead of 60,000. Because controls were sampled from the risk set at each case's event time, the resulting odds ratio directly estimates the incidence rate ratio for the gene variant, even though diabetes is not a rare outcome in this cohort. A case-cohort version instead genotypes one fixed 3,000-person random subcohort up front, reusable if the same cohort is later mined for cardiovascular disease too.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can explain why density (risk-set) sampling specifically — not just 'we sampled some controls' — is what lets a nested case-control's odds ratio validly estimate the incidence rate ratio, because getting this wrong (say, sampling controls from the entire cohort regardless of when they were still at risk) can bias the estimate, particularly for a common outcome. They also probe whether a student chose case-cohort over nested case-control for the right reason: case-cohort earns its complexity only when the same subcohort will genuinely be reused across multiple outcomes, not as an arbitrary substitute.

questions.prompt: Why does density (risk-set) sampling matter for a nested case-control study's validity?

options.text: It ensures controls are drawn from cohort members still at risk at each case's event time, which makes the odds ratio an unbiased estimate of the incidence rate ratio
It guarantees every cohort member is eventually assayed
It removes the need for a defined baseline cohort
It only matters when the outcome is extremely rare

explanations.a: Correct: sampling controls from the risk set at each case's event time is exactly what makes the resulting odds ratio a valid estimate of the incidence rate ratio.
explanations.b: The entire point of nested case-control sampling is to avoid assaying every cohort member, not to guarantee it.
explanations.c: A nested case-control study depends entirely on an already-established parent cohort; it does not remove that requirement.
explanations.d: Unlike the classic cumulative-incidence case-control odds ratio, the risk-set-sampled odds ratio holds regardless of disease rarity.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of running a nested case-control study with density sampling.

items.text: Identify all cases who developed the outcome during cohort follow-up
For each case, sample controls from cohort members still event-free at that case's diagnosis date
Assay stored baseline specimens only for the cases and sampled controls
Compute the odds ratio, which estimates the incidence rate ratio in the full cohort

questions.explanation: Cases are identified first, controls are then risk-set sampled per case, specimens are assayed only for that subset, and the odds ratio is computed last.

questions.prompt: Match each design or statistic to its description.

right.text: Samples one random subcohort at baseline, reused as the comparison group for every future outcome studied
Approximates the risk ratio only under the rare-disease assumption
Samples controls per case from the risk set at that case's event time; OR estimates the incidence rate ratio regardless of disease rarity

questions.explanation: Nested case-control uses risk-set sampling to validly estimate the rate ratio, case-cohort reuses a fixed subcohort across outcomes, and the classic case-control OR needs the rare-disease approximation.

questions.prompt: A cohort will eventually be mined for both a cancer outcome and, years later, a cardiovascular outcome, and the investigators want to genotype the comparison group only once for both efforts. Which hybrid design fits best, and why?

options.text: Case-cohort, because its single random subcohort selected at baseline can serve as the comparison group for every subsequent outcome
Nested case-control, because risk-set sampling automatically covers every future outcome
A classic case-control study, because it does not require a parent cohort
Either design works identically, since both resample fresh controls per outcome

explanations.a: Correct: the case-cohort design's defining feature is reusing one fixed subcohort across multiple outcomes, which is exactly what avoids re-genotyping controls each time.
explanations.b: Nested case-control sampling is tied to a specific set of cases and must be redone with a fresh control sample for each new outcome studied.
explanations.c: A classic case-control study is not nested in a cohort at all, so it cannot reuse cohort-derived baseline specimens this way.
explanations.d: The two hybrids differ specifically on this point: nested case-control resamples per outcome, while case-cohort does not.

lessons.label: Historical Cohorts and Record Linkage

sections.heading: Occupational cohorts built from employment records
sections.body: A historical (retrospective) cohort reconstructs the entire cohort logic — a defined population, exposure classified before outcome, forward-in-time follow-up — using records that already exist, rather than watching time pass. Occupational cohorts are the classic case: Selikoff, Hammond, and Seidman's 1979 study of asbestos insulation workers used union employment and membership records to assemble a cohort whose asbestos exposure (years worked, job type) was already documented, then linked those workers to mortality records to show sharply elevated deaths from mesothelioma and lung cancer decades after exposure began. Radiation epidemiology's Life Span Study of Japanese atomic bomb survivors similarly reconstructs individual radiation dose from position and shielding at the time of the bombings, then tracks cancer and mortality outcomes across survivors for decades, entirely from records assembled well after exposure occurred but still ordered correctly in time.

sections.heading: Nordic registries and the linkage advantage
sections.body: Denmark, Sweden, Norway, and Finland maintain national registries — civil registration systems assigning every resident a unique personal identifier at birth, linked to hospital discharge, cancer, prescription, and cause-of-death registries — that let researchers assemble a cohort of an entire national birth year or exposure group and follow it for decades essentially for free, since the outcome data was already being collected for administrative purposes. A Danish study can, for instance, identify everyone who filled a particular prescription in the 1990s and link that group to cancer registrations through the present day without ever contacting a single participant. This is enormously cheap follow-up compared to an active prospective cohort's periodic questionnaires and exams, and the registries' near-complete population coverage largely avoids the differential loss to follow-up that plagues actively recruited cohorts.

sections.heading: The tradeoff: data collected for someone else's purpose
sections.body: The appeal of historical cohorts and registry linkage is real, but so is the cost: exposure and covariate data were recorded by employers, hospitals, or pharmacies for administrative or clinical reasons, not to answer the researcher's specific question, so key confounders (smoking status, diet, family history) are often simply missing, and exposure measurement can be crude — an employment record shows years on a job title, not actual asbestos fiber counts inhaled. Electronic health record and insurance claims linkage, increasingly used for chronic disease research, shares this weakness: a prescription claim shows a drug was filled, not that it was taken, and diagnosis codes entered for billing purposes can misclassify disease severity or timing. Historical cohorts trade the cost and duration of prospective follow-up for the risk that the records available were never built with epidemiologic precision in mind.

lessons.workedExample: Selikoff, Hammond, and Seidman's 1979 asbestos study assembled roughly 17,800 asbestos insulation workers from union records covering 1943 to 1976, classifying exposure by years in the trade using employment rosters that already existed, then linked the cohort to death certificates to find lung cancer and mesothelioma deaths several times higher than expected for men of the same age. No participant was prospectively interviewed at trade entry — the entire cohort's exposure history was reconstructed from records built for union administration, not research — yet because employment necessarily preceded any subsequent death, the study still satisfied a cohort's forward-time logic. A modern Danish registry study could similarly track every person prescribed a given diabetes drug since 2000 through the national prescription and cause-of-death registries, at a fraction of the cost of enrolling and actively following the same number of patients for twenty years.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student proposing a historical or registry-based cohort has thought through what the original records were built to capture, because a project that treats an employment roster or a prescription-fill record as equivalent to a purpose-built research questionnaire is likely to under-report a confounder that was simply never recorded, like smoking status in an occupational cohort or actual medication adherence in a claims-based one. The tell of a well-designed historical cohort project is naming which specific covariates were unavailable from the source records and explaining how the analysis compensated, rather than treating cheap decades-long follow-up as a free lunch.

questions.prompt: What is the defining feature that makes a historical (retrospective) cohort still a cohort study, rather than something else?

options.text: Exposure still logically precedes outcome in time, even though both are reconstructed from records after the fact
Participants are contacted and interviewed prospectively
The disease must be rare for the design to work
Controls are sampled from a risk set

explanations.a: Correct: the cohort structure only requires that exposure precede outcome in time, which historical records can still preserve without real-time observation.
explanations.b: A historical cohort specifically does not require prospective contact; it reconstructs the timeline from existing records.
explanations.c: Rare-disease suitability is not what defines a cohort; cohorts, historical or prospective, work regardless of disease rarity.
explanations.d: Risk-set sampling of controls describes a nested case-control study, not a historical cohort.

questions.prompt: Order the construction of an occupational historical cohort like Selikoff's asbestos study.

items.text: Identify a defined population from existing employment or union records
Classify exposure (job type, years worked) using those pre-existing records
Link the cohort to outcome records (death certificates, cancer registries) that extend to the present
Compare mortality or disease rates by exposure level to estimate risk

questions.explanation: The population and its exposure are defined from historical records first, then linked forward to outcome records, and only then compared by exposure level.

questions.prompt: Match each source or system to its description.

right.text: Unique personal identifiers linking hospital, cancer, and prescription data for entire national populations
Union employment records used to reconstruct exposure among insulation workers, linked to mortality
Reconstructs individual dose from position and shielding among Japanese atomic bomb survivors, tracked for decades
Prescription fills or diagnosis codes recorded for billing, not research, used to approximate exposure and outcome

questions.explanation: Each system is matched to what it was originally built to record and how that gets repurposed as cohort data.

questions.prompt: What is the main limitation of using electronic health record or insurance claims data as a historical cohort's exposure and covariate source?

options.text: The data was recorded for billing or clinical purposes, not research, so key confounders may be missing and exposure measurement (e.g., a filled prescription) can be crude
Claims data cannot be linked to mortality outcomes
Claims-based cohorts cannot achieve statistical power
Claims data always overestimates true exposure prevalence

explanations.a: Correct: records built for billing or clinical care were not designed to capture every research-relevant confounder or to measure exposure with research-grade precision.
explanations.b: Claims and EHR data are routinely linked to mortality and other outcome registries; this is not a fundamental limitation.
explanations.c: Claims-based cohorts often have very large sample sizes, giving them strong statistical power; the limitation is data quality, not size.
explanations.d: Claims data (e.g., a filled prescription) is more often an undercount of true use (a filled prescription is not necessarily taken) than a systematic overestimate.

units.label: Risk Factors, Dose-Response, and Exposure Measurement

lessons.label: Measuring Long-Term Exposure

sections.heading: Instruments for exposures that took years to accumulate
sections.body: Chronic disease epidemiology rarely studies a single dose; it studies decades of diet, smoking, or glycemia. Nutritional epidemiology's workhorse is the food-frequency questionnaire (FFQ), pioneered in the modern form by Walter Willett's Harvard group, which asks how often a person ate roughly 130 foods over the past year, then multiplies frequency by a standard portion size to estimate long-run intake. A 24-hour recall, by contrast, captures yesterday's diet in far more accurate detail but says little about a habitual pattern, since diet varies enormously day to day. Cohorts use the FFQ for its low burden and stable exposure-rank, then rely on repeated 24-hour recalls or multi-day diet records to check that the ranking holds up.

sections.heading: Self-report versus biomarkers
sections.body: Every self-report instrument is vulnerable to social-desirability bias and simple forgetting, so chronic epidemiology increasingly validates or replaces self-report with biomarkers. Cotinine, a nicotine metabolite measurable in blood, saliva, or urine, is the standard smoking biomarker, but its roughly 16-20 hour half-life means it reflects exposure over the last one to three days, not a lifetime pack-year history, so it complements rather than replaces self-reported smoking history. Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) works differently: because red blood cells live about 120 days and glucose binds hemoglobin irreversibly, HbA1c integrates average blood glucose over roughly the prior two to three months, making it a genuine medium-term exposure biomarker rather than a snapshot.

sections.heading: Validation, calibration, and the reproducibility problem
sections.body: Before a cohort trusts an FFQ, it validates the instrument against a stronger reference: comparing FFQ-estimated intake to multiple 24-hour recalls, weighed diet records, or objective biomarkers such as doubly labeled water for energy expenditure or urinary nitrogen for protein. Correlation coefficients between FFQ and reference methods for energy-adjusted nutrients typically land around 0.4-0.7, good enough to rank people into intake categories but far from perfect. A separate step, calibration, uses a validation substudy to build a correction equation that adjusts the whole cohort's FFQ estimates toward the reference method's scale. A further complication is that habits change over years: someone's diet or smoking status at baseline may not describe their exposure a decade later, so long cohorts re-administer instruments periodically and must decide whether to model baseline exposure, updated exposure, or cumulative average exposure. The Nurses' Health Study resolves this by cumulative averaging: it re-administers its FFQ roughly every two to four years and averages each participant's successive waves into a single time-varying cumulative-average diet score, so a person's exposure value in the analysis at any given follow-up year reflects their full dietary history to that point rather than a single stale baseline answer or only the most recent update.

lessons.workedExample: The Nurses' Health Study validated its FFQ by comparing it to four one-week diet records collected across a year in a subsample of about 173 nurses. For energy-adjusted protein intake, the correlation between FFQ and diet records was roughly 0.5; for saturated fat, closer to 0.4. Investigators used these validation-study correlations to build calibration equations, then applied them to de-attenuate diet-disease associations estimated from the full cohort's FFQ data, correcting for the fact that a moderate correlation with the reference method understates the true exposure-disease relationship.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a student cite an FFQ-based diet result wants to know whether the student understands that the instrument was validated against something, and against what. The tell of real understanding is naming the reference method (weighed records, recalls, or a biomarker), stating roughly how well the FFQ agreed with it, and acknowledging that self-reported chronic exposures shift over years — not presenting a single questionnaire answer as if it were a lifetime measurement with no error attached.

questions.prompt: Why is HbA1c a better biomarker than a single fasting glucose reading for a chronic-disease cohort studying average glycemic exposure?

options.text: It reflects blood glucose averaged over roughly the prior two to three months because it tracks red blood cell lifespan
It is cheaper to measure than fasting glucose in a large cohort
It reflects glucose exposure only over the past 24 hours
It replaces the need for any dietary self-report instrument

explanations.a: Correct: glucose binds hemoglobin irreversibly and red cells live about 120 days, so HbA1c integrates average glycemia over that window rather than a single moment.
explanations.b: Cost is not what makes it suited to measuring chronic exposure; the biological mechanism of integration over red-cell lifespan is the reason.
explanations.c: That description fits cotinine's short half-life, not HbA1c, which integrates over months.
explanations.d: HbA1c measures glycemia, not diet, so it does not substitute for a dietary instrument like an FFQ.

questions.prompt: A cohort's FFQ shows a correlation of about 0.4-0.7 with weighed diet records in a validation substudy. What does this justify?

options.text: Using the FFQ to rank participants into intake categories, with calibration to correct attenuation in disease associations
Treating the FFQ as measuring true individual intake with no further correction needed
Discarding the FFQ entirely since the correlation is not near 1.0
Concluding the weighed diet record must be flawed since the two methods disagree

explanations.a: Correct: moderate correlation supports ranking exposure and applying a calibration equation built from the validation substudy to de-attenuate downstream associations.
explanations.b: A correlation well below 1.0 means real measurement error exists that must be accounted for, not ignored.
explanations.c: Moderate correlation is exactly the normal, expected result for FFQs and is usable, not a reason to discard the instrument.
explanations.d: The weighed record is the reference method precisely because it is more accurate day-to-day; disagreement reflects FFQ error, not record error.

questions.prompt: Order the steps a cohort takes to validate and calibrate a food-frequency questionnaire.

items.text: Administer the FFQ to estimate habitual annual intake
Collect a reference measure (repeated 24-hour recalls or diet records) in a validation subsample
Compute the correlation between FFQ and reference estimates
Build and apply a calibration equation to correct cohort-wide FFQ estimates toward the reference scale

questions.explanation: Validation requires collecting a reference measure in a subsample, quantifying agreement, and only then building the calibration correction applied to the whole cohort.

questions.prompt: Match each exposure-measurement tool to what it primarily captures.

right.text: Habitual intake pattern over roughly the past year
Detailed intake on one specific recent day
Recent smoking exposure over one to three days
Average glycemia over roughly two to three months

questions.explanation: Each instrument has a distinct exposure window; mismatching a short-window biomarker to a long-term exposure claim (or vice versa) is a common design error.

lessons.label: Measurement Error and Regression Dilution

sections.heading: Random error blurs the true relationship
sections.body: When an exposure is measured with random, non-differential error — noise unrelated to disease status, such as day-to-day fluctuation in blood pressure or imperfect recall of past diet — the measured exposure is a noisy stand-in for the true underlying exposure. This noise does not create a spurious association; instead it flattens a real one. Because people who are misclassified scatter symmetrically around their true value, the exposed and unexposed groups defined by the noisy measurement are less cleanly separated than the groups defined by true exposure, so the measured association is systematically weaker than the true association. Epidemiologists call this attenuation, or bias toward the null, and it is one of the few biases whose direction can be predicted in advance.

sections.heading: MacMahon's regression dilution correction
sections.body: The clearest demonstration is Rory Collins and Stephen MacMahon's regression dilution work on blood pressure and stroke, published in the Lancet's 'Blood pressure, stroke, and coronary heart disease' series in 1990. A single office blood-pressure reading has substantial within-person variability, so the risk gradient estimated using that one measurement understates the association with a person's true 'usual' blood pressure. Using repeat measurements over years within the same cohort, MacMahon's group estimated how much a single reading regresses toward the population mean relative to usual blood pressure, then applied a correction factor to the observed risk ratios. The corrected slope was substantially steeper: a given true difference in usual diastolic pressure was associated with roughly twice the stroke risk difference that the single-measurement analysis had suggested, revealing that prior single-measurement studies had understated the blood pressure-stroke relationship.

sections.heading: Predictable dilution versus unpredictable differential error
sections.body: Regression dilution bias is a special case of non-differential misclassification: because the error does not depend on outcome status, the bias is predictable and correctable if repeat measurements exist to estimate the degree of within-person variability. This stands in sharp contrast to differential misclassification, where measurement error itself depends on disease status — for example, cancer patients recalling past chemical exposure more thoroughly than healthy controls because they have spent time searching for a cause. Differential error can bias an association in either direction, toward or away from the null, and its magnitude cannot be estimated without external validation data, making it far more dangerous to a study's conclusions than the predictable attenuation of random error.

lessons.workedExample: In the MacMahon regression dilution analysis, a single diastolic blood pressure reading of 90 mmHg versus 80 mmHg was associated with about a 1.5-fold difference in stroke risk in uncorrected pooled cohort data. After correcting for regression dilution using repeat measurements to estimate the true usual-pressure difference, the same 10 mmHg difference in usual diastolic pressure corresponded to roughly a 2- to 3-fold difference in stroke risk — the single-measurement estimate had substantially understated the true dose-response slope because within-person variability diluted the apparent gradient.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because 'our correlation was weak so there's no real effect' is a common student error when the true problem is exposure noise, not a null biology. The tell of understanding is distinguishing attenuation from random error — which biases predictably toward the null and can be corrected with repeat measurements — from differential misclassification, which biases unpredictably and demands a different fix (blinding, objective measurement) rather than a statistical correction factor.

questions.prompt: A cohort measures blood pressure once per participant and finds a modest stroke association. What does regression dilution bias imply about the true usual-blood-pressure/stroke relationship?

options.text: The true relationship is likely stronger, because a single reading understates the gradient associated with usual blood pressure
The true relationship is likely weaker, because repeated measurement would introduce more noise
The observed and true relationships must be identical since blood pressure is measured objectively
No conclusion is possible without knowing the direction of differential misclassification

explanations.a: Correct: random within-person variability in a single reading attenuates the observed association toward the null relative to the true usual-exposure relationship, exactly as MacMahon's correction showed.
explanations.b: More repeat measurements reduce, not increase, the noise around a person's usual value, which is why they are used to correct rather than worsen the estimate.
explanations.c: Objective measurement does not eliminate biological within-person variability, which is the source of regression dilution.
explanations.d: This is a case of non-differential (random) error, not differential misclassification, so its direction is predictable, not unknowable.

questions.prompt: Which scenario describes differential misclassification rather than the random error behind regression dilution?

options.text: Cancer patients recall past chemical exposure more thoroughly than healthy controls because they searched for a cause after diagnosis
A single office blood-pressure reading varies from a person's long-term average due to normal day-to-day fluctuation
An FFQ misestimates habitual intake by a similar margin regardless of a participant's future disease status
Instrument calibration drift adds similar noise to every participant's measurement

explanations.a: Correct: recall accuracy here depends on disease status itself, making the error differential, with an unpredictable direction of bias.
explanations.b: This is random, non-differential variability unrelated to outcome — the source of regression dilution, not differential error.
explanations.c: Error unrelated to future disease status is non-differential by definition, even though it is real measurement error.
explanations.d: Uniform drift across all participants is non-differential; it does not depend on who develops the outcome.

questions.prompt: Order the steps MacMahon's group used to correct the blood pressure-stroke association for regression dilution.

items.text: Observe a weaker-than-expected association using single baseline blood-pressure readings
Use repeat measurements within participants over years to estimate within-person variability
Calculate a correction factor for how far a single reading regresses toward the mean relative to usual pressure
Apply the correction to reveal a steeper true dose-response slope between usual pressure and stroke

questions.explanation: The correction requires first observing the diluted association, then using repeat measurements to quantify variability, deriving a correction factor, and finally applying it to recover the true slope.

questions.prompt: Match each type of exposure measurement error to its typical consequence.

right.text: Predictable attenuation toward the null, correctable with repeat-measurement data
Bias in an unpredictable direction, not correctable by a simple statistical factor

questions.explanation: Only non-differential error has a knowable, predictable effect on bias direction; differential error's impact depends on the specific unmeasured relationship between error and outcome.

lessons.label: The Dose-Response Relationship

sections.heading: Monotonic gradients and Hill's biological gradient
sections.body: A dose-response relationship describes how disease risk changes as exposure level rises. The cleanest pattern is monotonic: risk rises steadily with dose and never reverses. The British Doctors Study, followed by Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill starting in 1951, showed lung cancer mortality climbing steadily with pack-years smoked, from roughly baseline in nonsmokers to many times higher in the heaviest smokers, with intermediate categories falling neatly in between. Hill listed 'biological gradient' as one of his nine considerations (in his 1965 address, later called the Bradford Hill criteria) for weighing causation, precisely because a step-wise dose-response pattern is hard to explain by confounding alone — a confounder would need to track dose as tightly as the exposure itself does, which is a demanding coincidence.

sections.heading: Threshold and J/U-shaped curves
sections.body: Not every relationship is monotonic. A threshold relationship shows no detectable risk increase until exposure crosses some level, then rises above it — plausible for toxins the body can fully metabolize or repair below a capacity limit. More strikingly, several chronic-disease exposures show J- or U-shaped curves. Alcohol and cardiovascular disease is the classic contested example: observational cohorts often show light-to-moderate drinkers with lower cardiovascular risk than both abstainers and heavy drinkers, producing a J-shape, though this pattern is now widely suspected to reflect the 'sick quitter' effect, where the abstainer group includes former drinkers who quit due to existing illness. Body-mass-index and mortality shows a similar U-shape, with both very low and very high BMI associated with elevated death rates, complicated by reverse causation from illness-driven weight loss at the low end. Radiation epidemiology supplies dose-response's most rigorously contested threshold debate: the linear-no-threshold (LNT) model, built on the atomic-bomb-survivor Life Span Study, finds measurable excess cancer risk even at doses under roughly 100 mSv, but whether that risk truly extends linearly all the way down to zero or instead flattens below some true threshold where cellular repair keeps pace with damage remains unresolved, and the answer directly shapes radiation-protection dose limits.

sections.heading: Categories versus continuous modeling
sections.body: Studies often report dose-response using quantile categories — quartiles or quintiles of exposure compared against a reference group — because the presentation is simple and requires no assumption about the curve's shape. But cutting a continuous exposure into a handful of bins can obscure or distort the true shape: a threshold hidden inside one quantile disappears, and a genuinely curved relationship gets forced into a stair-step that looks artificially linear or artificially flat. Continuous modeling, which uses every participant's actual exposure value rather than a bin label, preserves more information and can reveal a true nonlinear shape that quantile categories flatten out or misrepresent.

lessons.workedExample: In the British Doctors Study, age-standardized lung cancer death rates per 100,000 person-years rose from about 7 in nonsmokers to roughly 57 in light smokers (1-14 cigarettes/day), 139 in moderate smokers (15-24/day), and 227 in heavy smokers (25+/day) — a clear step-wise gradient across four exposure categories.
