explanations.d: The Cox model leaves h0(t) unspecified regardless of which covariates are added; non-collapsibility is a property of the ratio measure, not of h0(t).

questions.prompt: Order the steps for critically reading a chronic-cohort hazard-ratio result.

items.text: Compare the crude HR to the adjusted HR and note the size of the gap
Check the confidence interval width against the number of events, not just enrolled sample size
Convert the relative HR to an absolute risk difference using the study's baseline incidence
Check whether the paper interprets covariate adjustment coefficients causally (Table 2 fallacy)

questions.explanation: A careful reader moves from the headline relative comparison, to precision, to real-world absolute impact, to checking for a common interpretive error in the same table.

lessons.label: Doll, Hill, and the Smoking-Cancer Case

sections.heading: A case-control study built to catch a rising killer
sections.body: By 1947 British doctors had noticed lung cancer deaths climbing sharply, and the Medical Research Council asked Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill to find out why. Their 1950 BMJ case-control study interviewed roughly 650 lung cancer patients in London hospitals and matched controls with other diseases about their smoking histories. Almost every lung cancer patient turned out to be a smoker, and heavy smokers appeared on the order of 15 to 25 times more likely to have the disease than lifelong non-smokers. A case-control design can be confounded or biased by recall, so Doll and Hill needed a stronger test.

sections.heading: The British Doctors Study confirms it prospectively
sections.body: In 1951 they mailed a smoking-habits questionnaire to essentially all UK-registered doctors and then simply watched who died of what. This prospective cohort — the British Doctors Study — removed the recall problem: smoking status was recorded before disease onset. Their first report, in 1954, already showed lung cancer deaths tracking cigarette consumption. Doll, Peto, Boreham, and Sutherland's 2004 BMJ paper closed out 50 years of follow-up: continuing cigarette smokers died on average about 10 years earlier than never-smokers, though quitting by age 30 recovered nearly all of that loss and quitting by 50 recovered about half.

sections.heading: Hill's causal viewpoints and the industry's counter-move
sections.body: The scale and consistency of these findings pushed Hill to formalize, in his 1965 address 'The Environment and Disease: Association or Causation?', nine viewpoints for judging whether an association is causal — strength, consistency, temporality, biological gradient, and plausibility among them — still taught as the Bradford Hill criteria. The tobacco industry's response, documented in later litigation, was strategic rather than scientific: a leaked 1969 Brown & Williamson memo stated that 'doubt is our product,' since manufacturing uncertainty about a settled body of evidence was cheaper than refuting it.

sections.heading: A field-wide independent check, and a researcher who acted on it
sections.body: Doll and Hill's UK findings did not stand alone: Ernst Wynder and Evarts Graham published a parallel US case-control study in JAMA in 1950, the same year, and found the same pattern in American patients, which mattered because independent replication in a different population and health system is exactly what Hill's 'consistency' viewpoint calls for. The tobacco industry's earliest counter-move predates the 'doubt' memo: a 1954 'Frank Statement to Cigarette Smokers,' placed as a paid ad in hundreds of US newspapers by the major manufacturers, pledged to fund impartial research into smoking's health effects while privately funding work designed to generate uncertainty rather than answers. Doll himself, a smoker, gave up cigarettes around 1950 as the case-control findings emerged and convinced him of the risk — a detail often used to underscore how quickly the evidence became personally, not just statistically, persuasive.

lessons.workedExample: In the 1950 case-control study, of the lung cancer patients interviewed, almost all were smokers, while a meaningfully larger share of the matched controls were non-smokers or light smokers — yielding an odds ratio in the range of 15-25 for heavy smoking. Because a single retrospective study can't rule out recall or selection bias, the 1951 British Doctors Study cohort was the decisive test: doctors reported smoking habits before any disease occurred, and by the 2004 50-year analysis, mortality tracked cigarettes-per-day in a clean dose-response gradient, with continuing smokers losing about a decade of life expectancy on average.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this lesson wants to see the difference between an association strong and consistent enough to act on (RR of 15-25, replicated across a follow-up cohort, with a dose-response gradient) versus a fragile one — and whether the student can name why a prospective cohort answers objections a case-control study can't. It's also a case study in a funded party manufacturing doubt about solid epidemiology, which judges expect students to recognize when they see resistance to their own findings.

questions.prompt: Why did Doll and Hill follow their 1950 case-control study with the 1951 British Doctors cohort?

options.text: To increase the sample size for greater statistical power
To record smoking status before disease onset and remove recall bias
Because the case-control study had found no association
To study female doctors, who were excluded from the first study

explanations.a: Power was a secondary benefit; the core methodological gap being closed was recall bias, not sample size alone.
explanations.b: Correct: a prospective cohort records exposure before outcome, so recalled smoking habits can't be distorted by already having cancer.
explanations.c: The case-control study found a strong association (RR roughly 15-25 for heavy smokers); the cohort was designed to confirm it, not chase a null result.
explanations.d: The British Doctors Study included both sexes, but that wasn't the methodological reason for moving to a cohort design.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the smoking-lung cancer case.

items.text: Doll and Hill publish the 1950 case-control study in BMJ
The British Doctors Study cohort is launched (1951)
Hill publishes his causal viewpoints address (1965)
Doll et al. publish the 50-year follow-up (2004)

questions.explanation: The case-control study came first, prompting the prospective cohort later that year; Hill's causal framework followed as the evidence matured, and the 50-year analysis capped the cohort decades later.

questions.prompt: Match each element of the smoking-cancer case to what it established.

right.text: Initial strong association via retrospective interviews
Prospective confirmation free of recall bias
Quantified roughly a decade of lost life expectancy in continuing smokers
Revealed a strategy of manufacturing doubt rather than contesting evidence

questions.explanation: Each piece of the case plays a distinct role: discovery, confirmation, quantification, and the documented industry response.

questions.prompt: Which of Bradford Hill's 1965 viewpoints does the dose-response gradient in the British Doctors Study most directly support?

options.text: Analogy
Biological gradient
Specificity
Coherence

explanations.a: Analogy refers to reasoning from similar known causal relationships, not a dose-response pattern within this dataset.
explanations.b: Correct: biological gradient asks whether more exposure produces more disease, which is exactly what heavier smoking mapping to higher mortality demonstrates.
explanations.c: Specificity asks whether one exposure maps to one specific disease, which smoking notably violates since it causes many diseases.
explanations.d: Coherence asks whether the association fits with other known biology and lab findings, a separate viewpoint from a dose-response gradient.

lessons.label: Framingham and the Birth of the Risk Factor

sections.heading: A town-wide cohort with no prior hypothesis to test
sections.body: In 1948 the newly formed National Heart Institute enrolled 5,209 adults aged 30-62 from Framingham, Massachusetts, re-examining them every two years to see who developed coronary heart disease and why. Unlike a trial testing one drug, Framingham was an open-ended prospective cohort: it measured blood pressure, cholesterol, weight, smoking, and dozens of other traits, then waited years to see which predicted heart attacks. That patience is what let the study discover predictors nobody had proposed testing in advance, rather than confirming one someone already suspected.

sections.heading: Coining 'risk factor' in 1961
sections.body: William Kannel and colleagues' 1961 paper in the Annals of Internal Medicine, 'Factors of Risk in the Development of Coronary Heart Disease,' used six years of follow-up data to show that elevated cholesterol, high blood pressure, and left ventricular hypertrophy on ECG each independently predicted future coronary events. This paper introduced the term 'risk factor' into medical language and, with later additions of smoking and diabetes, gave clinicians a short list of modifiable targets — instead of treating heart disease as an unpredictable fate, doctors could now screen for it. The concept was later formalized into the multivariable Framingham Risk Score (1998), which combines age, cholesterol, blood pressure, smoking, and sex into a 10-year coronary risk estimate still used in clinics.

sections.heading: A single, largely white town as the whole evidence base
sections.body: Framingham's power came from its depth — decades of repeated measurement on the same people — but its generalizability was limited by its origin: one mostly white, working- and middle-class Massachusetts town in the late 1940s. Risk equations built on it were later shown to misestimate risk in other populations, most notably overestimating coronary risk in some Asian and Hispanic cohorts and underestimating it in some Black cohorts, prompting recalibration efforts like the Pooled Cohort Equations that incorporate more diverse cohorts such as ARIC and the Jackson Heart Study.

sections.heading: Framingham became multigenerational, but stayed one town's descendants
sections.body: Rather than closing out, Framingham grew across generations: in 1971 it enrolled the Offspring Cohort of 5,124 adult children of the original participants and their spouses, and in April 2002 it began recruiting a Third Generation cohort of roughly 4,095 grandchildren, letting researchers study familial aggregation of cardiovascular risk and, later, genetic contributions directly. That design strength is also the limitation's root: even three generations deep, the sample remains descendants of one 1948 Massachusetts town, so the diversity gap the original cohort had is inherited rather than fixed by simply following the same families longer — which is precisely why external cohorts had to be added to correct the risk equations rather than just waiting for more Framingham data.

lessons.workedExample: Kannel's 1961 analysis followed the Framingham cohort for six years and compared coronary event rates across strata of cholesterol and blood pressure. Men in the highest cholesterol stratum developed coronary heart disease at a markedly higher rate than men in the lowest stratum, and the same graded pattern held for blood pressure — each factor added risk independently of the others. That independence is what justified calling them separate 'risk factors' rather than one underlying trait, and it is the logic the later Framingham Risk Score formalizes: multiply out several independently-acting factors to get one 10-year probability.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probing Framingham want to know whether a student understands that discovering a risk factor requires prospective, repeated measurement before disease occurs — not a one-time survey of sick versus healthy people. They also expect students to flag the external-validity problem: a risk score built on one town's demographics can miscalibrate elsewhere, so a project using Framingham-derived risk equations on a different population should say so and cite the recalibration literature.

questions.prompt: What made the Framingham Heart Study able to discover risk factors that hadn't been hypothesized in advance?

options.text: It enrolled an unusually large number of participants
It was a prospective cohort measuring many traits before disease occurred, then following up over years
It randomized participants to different diets
It used genetic sequencing to find novel markers

explanations.a: 5,209 participants is moderate by modern standards; the design's open-ended, repeated-measurement structure mattered more than raw size.
explanations.b: Correct: measuring many traits before outcomes occurred, then tracking who developed disease, let unexpected predictors emerge from the data itself.
explanations.c: Framingham was observational, not a randomized dietary trial.
explanations.d: Genetic sequencing did not exist in usable form in 1948; risk factors were identified from clinical measurements like blood pressure and cholesterol.

questions.prompt: Order these Framingham-related milestones chronologically.

items.text: Framingham Heart Study cohort enrolled (1948)
Kannel et al. coin 'risk factor' in Annals of Internal Medicine
The multivariable Framingham Risk Score is formalized
Pooled Cohort Equations incorporate ARIC and Jackson Heart Study data to address generalizability

questions.explanation: The cohort had to run for years before Kannel's 1961 paper could identify risk factors; the risk score built on that concept came later (1998), and broader recalibration for other populations came after that.

questions.prompt: Match each Framingham element to its contribution.

right.text: Coined 'risk factor' and identified cholesterol, blood pressure, and ECG changes as predictors
Combined multiple risk factors into one 10-year coronary risk estimate
Limited generalizability of the original risk equations
Recalibrated risk estimation using more diverse cohorts

questions.explanation: Each element traces the arc from discovery to clinical tool to correction for a narrow founding population.

lessons.label: Ancel Keys and the Diet-Heart Debate

sections.heading: Seven Countries and the saturated-fat hypothesis
sections.body: Physiologist Ancel Keys launched the Seven Countries Study in 1958, tracking diet and coronary deaths across cohorts in the United States, Finland, Italy, Greece, Yugoslavia, the Netherlands, and Japan. His results, published through the 1960s and 1970s, showed nations with higher average saturated-fat intake had higher coronary mortality, anchoring the diet-heart hypothesis: dietary saturated fat raises blood cholesterol, which drives atherosclerosis and heart attacks. This became the scientific backbone of the 1977 U.S. Dietary Goals and decades of low-fat public health guidance.

sections.heading: The ecological-correlation critique
sections.body: Critics pointed out a structural weakness before Keys even finished: statisticians Jacob Yerushalmy and Herman Hilleboe showed in 1957 that using all 22 countries with available data — rather than the roughly six or seven with the clearest fat-heart correlation — produced a much weaker relationship. This is the ecological-correlation problem: country-level averages can create or exaggerate an association that doesn't hold as cleanly at the individual level, and a researcher choosing which countries to include can inflate an apparent effect. The charge of cherry-picking dogged Keys for the rest of his career, even as later individual-level cohort data lent some support to a saturated-fat-cholesterol link.

sections.heading: The Kearns revelation and the sugar counter-narrative
sections.body: In 2016, historian Cristin Kearns and colleagues published internal Sugar Research Foundation documents in JAMA Internal Medicine showing that in 1965 the trade group paid Harvard researchers Mark Hegsted and Robert McGandy roughly $6,500 (about $48,000 in 2016 dollars), under the oversight of Fredrick Stare, to produce a 1967 New England Journal of Medicine literature review. That review downplayed sugar's role in coronary disease and emphasized fat and cholesterol instead, without disclosing the funding. The revelation reframed decades of dietary guidance as partly shaped by industry money, and fueled the ongoing reappraisal of how strongly saturated fat versus added sugar drives cardiovascular risk.

sections.heading: A lost trial resurfaces and reopens the question again
sections.body: The reappraisal deepened in 2016 when researchers led by Christopher Ramsden recovered and published, in BMJ, the unpublished full dataset from the Minnesota Coronary Experiment — a 1968-1973 randomized trial in nearly 9,400 institutionalized adults that swapped saturated fat for vegetable oil rich in linoleic acid. The recovered data showed the intervention lowered cholesterol as predicted but did not reduce mortality, and possibly increased it in older participants, complicating the simple 'lower cholesterol, lower risk' version of the diet-heart hypothesis that Keys's ecological work had helped popularize. Together with the Kearns revelation, the episode illustrates how incomplete publication, not just weak initial data, can let a hypothesis outrun its evidence for decades.

lessons.workedExample: Yerushalmy and Hilleboe's 1957 reanalysis is the clean demonstration: plotting fat intake against coronary deaths for just six or seven cherry-picked countries produces a striking near-linear line, the image Keys's early work is remembered for. Plotting the same relationship across all 22 countries with data available at the time flattens the correlation considerably, because several countries with moderate fat intake had high coronary death rates and vice versa. The lesson isn't that saturated fat is irrelevant — later prospective cohorts found real, if smaller, associations — but that an ecological correlation built from a hand-picked country list can manufacture a stronger story than the full dataset supports.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this lesson is testing whether a student can separate 'this hypothesis turned out to have some support' from 'this specific piece of early evidence for it was flawed and possibly cherry-picked.' The Kearns revelation raises the sharper question: can the student explain why undisclosed funding is a problem even if the funded conclusion turns out partly correct — because it means the scientific record was shaped by whose interests were funding the literature review, not just the data.

questions.prompt: What was the core statistical problem Yerushalmy and Hilleboe identified in early presentations of the Seven Countries data?

options.text: The sample sizes within each country were too small
Selecting a subset of countries produced a stronger fat-heart correlation than the full 22-country dataset showed
The study measured trans fat instead of saturated fat
Coronary deaths were undercounted in Mediterranean countries

explanations.a: The critique was about country selection, not within-country sample size.
explanations.b: Correct: this is the ecological-correlation and cherry-picking critique — a chosen subset of countries showed a much cleaner correlation than all available countries did.
explanations.c: The hypothesis concerned saturated fat specifically; trans fat measurement wasn't the point of this critique.
explanations.d: Undercounting deaths wasn't the criticism raised; the issue was which countries were included in the comparison, not measurement error in any one country.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the diet-heart debate.

items.text: Keys launches the Seven Countries Study (1958)
Yerushalmy and Hilleboe publish the 22-country reanalysis critique (1957)
Sugar Research Foundation pays Hegsted and McGandy for a literature review (1965)
Kearns publishes the internal-documents exposé in JAMA Internal Medicine (2016)

questions.explanation: Yerushalmy and Hilleboe's critique (1957) actually predates the Seven Countries Study's 1958 launch, aimed at earlier ecological fat-heart data Keys had circulated; the funded review came in 1965, and its funding was exposed decades later in 2016.

questions.prompt: Match each figure or study to their role in the diet-heart debate.

right.text: Proposed the saturated-fat diet-heart hypothesis via the Seven Countries Study
Showed the fat-heart correlation weakens across the full country dataset
Wrote an undisclosed, sugar-industry-funded review downplaying sugar's role
Exposed the industry funding behind that 1967 review in 2016

questions.explanation: The debate spans the original hypothesis, its statistical critique, the funded counter-narrative, and its later exposure.

questions.prompt: Why does undisclosed industry funding of the 1967 review matter, even though later research still finds some saturated-fat and cardiovascular risk association?

options.text: It doesn't matter, since the funded conclusion happened to be defensible
It matters because it shaped which risks the scientific literature emphasized without readers being able to weigh the conflict of interest
It matters only because the payment amount was extremely large
It matters because it proves saturated fat has no relationship to heart disease

explanations.a: Whether a funded conclusion turns out partly right is separate from whether readers should have been able to see the funding source and weigh possible bias.
explanations.b: Correct: the core harm of undisclosed funding is that it distorts the visible evidence base without letting readers account for the conflict of interest.
explanations.c: The dollar amount, roughly $6,500 at the time, was modest; the problem was non-disclosure and its effect on emphasis, not the size of the payment.
explanations.d: The lesson is not that saturated fat is irrelevant; later cohort data found real, smaller associations, so this overstates the conclusion.

lessons.label: The Hormone Replacement Therapy Reversal

sections.heading: Decades of observational data pointing one way
sections.body: Through the 1980s and 1990s, large observational cohorts including the Nurses' Health Study repeatedly found that postmenopausal women taking hormone replacement therapy (HRT) had substantially lower rates of coronary heart disease than non-users — often cited around a 40-50% reduction in risk. Combined with HRT's known effects on lowering LDL cholesterol and raising HDL, this built a strong clinical consensus by the late 1990s that hormone therapy protected the heart, and prescribing rose accordingly.

sections.heading: The Women's Health Initiative reverses the verdict
sections.body: The Women's Health Initiative (WHI) was a large randomized controlled trial designed to test that consensus directly. In 2002, the estrogen-plus-progestin arm was halted early after about 5.2 years of follow-up: Rossouw and colleagues reported in JAMA a hazard ratio of 1.29 for coronary heart disease and 1.26 for breast cancer among hormone users, alongside increased stroke and blood clot risk — the opposite direction from decades of observational data, and strong enough that continuing the trial was judged unethical.

sections.heading: Reconciling the two: healthy-user and timing bias
sections.body: The mismatch is now a textbook case of confounding by indication. Women who chose to take HRT in the observational cohorts tended to be healthier, wealthier, and more health-conscious to begin with — healthy-user bias — and many had already been on hormones for years before entering the cohort, meaning the sickest early users had already dropped out before follow-up began, a form of prevalent-user bias. WHI randomization eliminated both: it enrolled women regardless of prior health behaviors, many starting therapy a decade or more past menopause. Later age-stratified WHI reanalyses suggested the timing hypothesis — that starting HRT close to menopause may carry less cardiac risk than starting it late — but the headline lesson stands: an observational effect this large, this consistent, and this wrong, is why chronic-disease epidemiology treats confounding by indication as a default suspect, not an edge case.

sections.heading: The estrogen-only arm complicates a simple story
sections.body: WHI also ran a separate estrogen-only trial in women who'd had a hysterectomy, stopped in 2004; unlike the combined arm, estrogen-alone was later found to be associated with lower, not higher, breast cancer incidence and mortality compared with placebo, showing that progestin's addition — not estrogen itself — likely drove much of the combined arm's excess breast cancer risk. That split result is a caution against treating 'hormone therapy' as a single exposure: the reversal wasn't uniform across formulations, and prescribing patterns changed dramatically after 2002 as clinicians absorbed a far more conditional, formulation- and timing-dependent picture than the pre-2002 consensus had offered.

lessons.workedExample: Picture two forty-something patients weighing HRT in 1995: one is presented Nurses' Health Study data suggesting roughly 40-50% lower coronary risk on hormones. What that cohort couldn't separate out is that women who both chose HRT and stayed enrolled long enough to be counted also tended to exercise more, see doctors more regularly, and be free of the health problems that would have made a physician hesitant to prescribe hormones in the first place. When the WHI instead randomly assigned roughly equal-risk women to hormones or placebo, that healthy-user advantage vanished from both arms — and the coronary hazard ratio flipped to 1.29, a 29% increase, revealing that the original protective association was substantially confounding, not a true drug effect at that population scale.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is the case a judge reaches for when a project leans on observational cohort data to claim a treatment or exposure effect: the WHI reversal shows precisely how a plausible, well-replicated, biologically-supported observational association (LDL/HDL effects and all) can still be confounded strongly enough to point the wrong direction. A judge wants to hear the student name healthy-user or prevalent-user bias specifically, not just gesture at 'confounding,' and explain why only randomization — not a bigger cohort — could have caught it.

questions.prompt: What did the 2002 WHI trial find for the estrogen-plus-progestin arm, compared to the earlier observational HRT cohorts?

options.text: It confirmed the same roughly 40-50% reduction in coronary risk
It found increased coronary heart disease (HR 1.29) and breast cancer (HR 1.26) risk, reversing the observational finding
It found no effect on any outcome, a null result
It found reduced breast cancer risk but unchanged coronary risk

explanations.a: The trial found the opposite direction of effect on coronary heart disease, not a confirmation.
explanations.b: Correct: the WHI's estrogen-plus-progestin arm was halted for increased coronary heart disease and breast cancer risk, directly reversing the observational cohorts' findings.
explanations.c: The trial found statistically meaningful increased risks, strong enough to halt the arm early — not a null result.
explanations.d: Breast cancer risk also increased (HR 1.26) in the WHI, not decreased.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in reconciling the HRT observational-versus-trial mismatch.

items.text: Observational cohorts like the Nurses' Health Study find HRT users have lower coronary risk
WHI randomizes women to hormone therapy or placebo regardless of prior health habits
WHI coronary results reverse direction, halting the trial arm in 2002
Age-stratified reanalyses propose the timing hypothesis to partly reconcile the two bodies of evidence

questions.explanation: The observational finding came first, the randomized trial was designed to test it, the reversal prompted the halt, and reconciliation via the timing hypothesis followed after.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in the HRT reversal.

right.text: HRT choosers in cohorts were already healthier and more health-conscious
Cohort enrollees who'd used HRT for years had already survived past early risk
Eliminated both biases by assigning therapy independent of prior habits
Proposes risk differs by how soon after menopause therapy starts

questions.explanation: Each concept addresses a distinct piece of why the observational and randomized evidence diverged and how it was partly reconciled.

lessons.label: Barker and the Fetal Origins Hypothesis

sections.heading: Reading disease risk out of century-old birth ledgers
sections.body: David Barker's key insight was archival: Hertfordshire, England had kept detailed health-visitor records of infant weight since the early 1900s. In a 1989 study, Barker and colleagues traced 5,654 men born there between 1911 and 1930 and linked their birth and one-year weights to adult mortality records. Men who weighed 18 pounds or less at one year had roughly two-and-a-half times the ischaemic heart disease mortality of men who weighed 27 pounds or more — a clean inverse gradient between early growth and adult coronary death, decades before any cardiac risk factor would normally be measured.

sections.heading: The thrifty phenotype mechanism
sections.body: To explain this, Barker and diabetologist Hales proposed the thrifty phenotype hypothesis in 1992: a fetus facing poor maternal nutrition redirects limited resources toward brain development at the expense of organs like the pancreas and liver, permanently altering glucose-insulin metabolism to favor fat storage — a useful adaptation if scarcity continues, but a liability if the child later encounters adequate or excess calories. This developmental-programming logic extended the fetal-origins idea, now often called the Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD) framework, to type 2 diabetes and hypertension as well as coronary disease, with low birth weight followed by rapid childhood catch-up growth as a particularly high-risk pattern.

sections.heading: The reversal-paradox critique
sections.body: Critics raised two objections. First, socioeconomic confounding: families with the lowest-birth-weight infants in early-20th-century Hertfordshire were also poorer, more likely to smoke, and exposed to worse adult conditions — any of which independently raises coronary risk, so birth weight could be a marker rather than a cause. Second, statisticians identified what Lucas and colleagues named the 'reversal paradox': because adult body size is itself partly a consequence of birth weight, statistically adjusting birth-weight associations for adult weight or BMI can mathematically flip or distort the apparent effect, making it hard to know how much of the birth-weight association is a modeling artifact rather than biology.

sections.heading: A molecular mechanism, from a different famine
sections.body: Independent evidence for developmental programming came from a very different natural experiment: the Dutch Hunger Winter of 1944-45, when a German blockade cut food supplies to the western Netherlands. Heijmans and colleagues (2008) found that people conceived during that famine still carried, six decades later, altered DNA methylation at the IGF2 growth-regulating gene compared with same-sex siblings conceived before or after it — a molecular trace of prenatal conditions persisting into old age. That epigenetic evidence gives the fetal-origins hypothesis a plausible biological mechanism beyond correlation, even as the Hertfordshire cohort's confounding and reversal-paradox critiques remain unresolved for the coronary-disease and diabetes associations specifically.

lessons.workedExample: In the 1989 Hertfordshire analysis, standardized mortality ratios for ischaemic heart disease fell in a near-linear step pattern across one-year weight bands, from 111 among the lightest infants down to 42 among the heaviest — meaning the lightest-infant group's coronary death rate was roughly 2.6 times the heaviest-infant group's. A critic re-running the same data while adjusting for adult BMI can see that ratio shrink or shift, illustrating the reversal-paradox concern: since adult BMI is downstream of birth weight, adjusting for it partly removes the very pathway (catch-up growth) the hypothesis says matters, so the 'corrected' estimate isn't obviously more correct.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing this lesson wants to see whether a student can hold two things at once: the fetal-origins pattern is real, replicated, and mechanistically plausible via the thrifty phenotype, and it is also vulnerable to socioeconomic confounding and a genuine statistical trap in how it gets adjusted. A project that cites Barker's low-birth-weight-to-adult-disease link should be pressed on whether its own analysis adjusted for a mediator (like adult BMI) in a way that could manufacture or erase the very effect being tested.

questions.prompt: What mechanism does the thrifty phenotype hypothesis propose links low birth weight to adult type 2 diabetes?

options.text: Low birth weight directly damages the heart muscle during gestation
Poor fetal nutrition permanently reprograms glucose-insulin metabolism toward fat storage as an adaptation to scarcity
Low birth weight is caused by maternal diabetes, which is then inherited genetically
Low birth weight infants receive less medical care throughout life

explanations.a: The hypothesis is about metabolic reprogramming, not direct cardiac muscle damage during gestation.
explanations.b: Correct: the thrifty phenotype hypothesis proposes that undernutrition in utero permanently shifts glucose-insulin metabolism to favor fat storage, a liability if later calorie intake is adequate or excessive.
explanations.c: This describes a genetic inheritance pathway, not the developmental-programming mechanism Barker and Hales proposed.
explanations.d: Reduced later medical care is a socioeconomic confounding concern raised by critics, not the mechanism the hypothesis itself proposes.

questions.prompt: Order these developments in the fetal-origins hypothesis.

items.text: Hertfordshire health visitors record infant weights (early 1900s)
Barker links birth/infant weight to adult ischaemic heart disease mortality (1989)
Hales and Barker propose the thrifty phenotype hypothesis (1992)
Lucas and colleagues describe the reversal-paradox critique

questions.explanation: The archival records had to exist before Barker's linkage study; the mechanism was proposed after the epidemiological pattern was found, and the statistical critique of how it's analyzed came later still.

questions.prompt: Match each critique to what it targets in the fetal-origins hypothesis.

right.text: Poverty and its correlates could independently explain both low birth weight and adult disease risk
Adjusting for adult BMI, itself downstream of birth weight, can distort or flip the apparent association

questions.explanation: One critique concerns an unmeasured common cause; the other concerns a statistical artifact from adjusting for a mediator.

lessons.label: Antioxidant and Vitamin Reversals

sections.heading: A plausible mechanism and consistent cohort data
sections.body: Free radicals damage DNA and cell membranes, and antioxidants like beta-carotene and vitamin E neutralize them in a test tube — a clean mechanistic story. Through the 1980s, observational cohorts including the Nurses' Health Study repeatedly found that people with higher dietary or supplemental antioxidant intake had lower rates of cancer and cardiovascular disease. The mechanism was plausible and the epidemiology was consistent across studies, which by the era's own standards looked like a strong case — enough that beta-carotene supplements were widely marketed as cancer prevention before any trial had tested that claim directly.

sections.heading: Two trials reverse the beta-carotene story
sections.body: The Alpha-Tocopherol, Beta-Carotene (ATBC) trial randomized about 29,000 Finnish male smokers to beta-carotene, vitamin E, both, or placebo; its 1994 results showed the beta-carotene group had roughly 18% more lung cancer diagnoses than placebo, not fewer. The Beta-Carotene and Retinol Efficacy Trial (CARET), testing beta-carotene plus retinyl palmitate in smokers and asbestos workers, was stopped about 21 months early in 1996 after an interim analysis found 28% more lung cancers and 17% more deaths in the treated group. Two independent randomized trials, in different at-risk populations, both found the supplement causing the harm it was marketed to prevent. A third large RCT, the Physicians' Health Study (1982-1995, roughly 22,071 male physicians), tested beta-carotene supplementation directly and found neither benefit nor harm — no significant difference in cancer, cardiovascular disease, or overall mortality between the beta-carotene and placebo arms, another null result cutting against the original observational story.

sections.heading: Vitamin E and folate follow the same arc
sections.body: Vitamin E fared little better: the HOPE trial (2000) found no cardiovascular benefit, and its extended follow-up (HOPE-TOO) later suggested a possible increase in heart failure risk among supplement users. Folic acid supplementation trials aimed at colorectal adenoma prevention, including a widely cited 2007 JAMA report, found no protective effect and a signal toward increased risk of advanced adenomas in the folate group. In each case, the pattern is the same: healthy-diet confounding. People who eat more fruits, vegetables, and antioxidant-rich food in the original cohorts also exercise more, smoke less, and see doctors more often — the vitamin was a marker of a health-conscious lifestyle, not its cause, and randomization exposed that once and for all.

sections.heading: The pattern repeats a decade later, in a different cancer
sections.body: The reversal was not a one-time fluke of beta-carotene. The Selenium and Vitamin E Cancer Prevention Trial (SELECT), published in JAMA in 2011, randomized roughly 35,000 men to vitamin E, selenium, both, or placebo to test whether the supplements prevented prostate cancer. Vitamin E alone was associated with a 17% increased risk of prostate cancer compared with placebo — about 76 cases per 1,000 men on vitamin E versus 65 per 1,000 on placebo — despite prior observational and mechanistic support for antioxidant supplementation. Two independent antioxidants — beta-carotene (in ATBC and CARET) and vitamin E (in SELECT) — across two different cancer types, lung and prostate, each independently reversed by randomized trials, is what elevates this from a single failed study to a structural warning about how healthy-user confounding can pervade an entire subfield of nutritional epidemiology.

lessons.workedExample: CARET is the sharpest illustration: researchers enrolled roughly 18,000 smokers and asbestos-exposed workers, randomizing half to daily beta-carotene plus retinyl palmitate and half to placebo. Observational logic predicted fewer lung cancers in the supplement group; instead, an interim safety review found 28% more lung cancer diagnoses and 17% more deaths in that arm, and the trial was halted about 21 months ahead of schedule rather than let participants keep taking a supplement now shown to cause harm. The mechanism proposed to explain the reversal is that beta-carotene metabolites may behave as pro-oxidants rather than antioxidants specifically in the oxidative environment of smokers' lungs.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges reach for this case whenever a project proposes 'nutrient X is linked to lower disease Y in observational studies, so we should supplement it.' It's the cleanest demonstration that a plausible mechanism plus consistent observational associations can still be wrong when the associations are actually tracking an unmeasured healthy-lifestyle confounder — and that only a randomized trial, not a bigger or longer cohort, can catch it. A strong project should preemptively note whether its own nutrient-disease claim has RCT evidence or only cohort evidence.

questions.prompt: What did the CARET trial find when beta-carotene plus retinyl palmitate was tested in smokers and asbestos workers?

options.text: About 28% fewer lung cancer cases, confirming the observational data
No significant difference from placebo
About 28% more lung cancer cases and 17% more deaths, halting the trial early
Reduced lung cancer only among non-smokers in the trial

explanations.a: The trial found more cancers in the treated group, the opposite of the observational prediction.
explanations.b: The difference was significant enough that the trial was stopped about 21 months early on safety grounds, not a null result.
explanations.c: Correct: CARET found roughly 28% more lung cancers and 17% more deaths in the beta-carotene/retinyl palmitate group, reversing the observational expectation.
explanations.d: CARET enrolled smokers and asbestos-exposed workers as its at-risk population; the trial wasn't stratified to show a non-smoker-only benefit.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the antioxidant-vitamin reversal story.

items.text: Observational cohorts link higher antioxidant intake to lower cancer and cardiovascular risk
The ATBC trial finds increased lung cancer with beta-carotene (1994)
CARET is halted early after finding increased lung cancer and deaths (1996)
The HOPE trial finds no cardiovascular benefit from vitamin E (2000)

questions.explanation: The observational associations came first and motivated the trials; ATBC reported its reversal in 1994, CARET's harsher reversal followed in 1996, and the vitamin E null result came several years later.

questions.prompt: Match each trial or study to its key finding.

right.text: Roughly 18% more lung cancer in Finnish male smokers given beta-carotene
Roughly 28% more lung cancer, 17% more deaths; halted early
No cardiovascular benefit from vitamin E
No protection and a signal toward increased advanced adenomas with folic acid

questions.explanation: Each trial independently reversed or nullified an observational antioxidant or vitamin association.

questions.prompt: What best explains why observational cohorts consistently showed antioxidant intake linked to lower disease risk, when randomized trials found no benefit or harm?

options.text: The cohorts measured the wrong antioxidant compounds
People with higher antioxidant intake also tended to have healthier overall lifestyles, confounding the association
The trials used lower doses than the cohorts studied
Antioxidants only work when combined with prescription medication

explanations.a: The compounds studied, like beta-carotene and vitamin E, were consistent between cohort and trial designs; measurement choice isn't the core explanation.
explanations.b: Correct: healthy-diet and lifestyle confounding meant antioxidant intake was a marker for other protective behaviors in the cohorts, an effect randomization removes.
explanations.c: Dose differences aren't the standard explanation offered for this pattern across these trials.
explanations.d: No such medication-interaction explanation is part of the accepted account of this reversal.

lessons.label: Open Debates in Chronic-Disease Epidemiology

sections.heading: Ioannidis and the case against small nutritional associations
sections.body: John Ioannidis has argued for years, including in a 2018 JAMA piece on nutritional epidemiology, that the field routinely reports small relative risks — often in the 1.2 to 1.5 range — from cohort studies loaded with dietary self-report error and unmeasured confounding, then treats them as if they were causal. His broader claim, dating to his widely cited 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False,' is that when an association is weak and the number of plausible confounders and comparisons is large, a nontrivial share of published findings simply won't replicate. This sets up a live methodological question for the whole field: how small a relative risk can observational epidemiology responsibly call causal? The question isn't new — science writer Gary Taubes's 1995 Science article 'Epidemiology Faces Its Limits' reported that editors at the New England Journal of Medicine described a rough editorial rule of thumb of wanting a relative risk of 3 or more before trusting an observational finding, a bar most modern diet and lifestyle associations don't clear.

sections.heading: The alcohol J-curve under genetic scrutiny
sections.body: Decades of observational studies found a J-shaped curve between alcohol intake and cardiovascular risk, with light-to-moderate drinkers appearing healthier than abstainers — but critics noted the 'abstainer' comparison group often included former heavy drinkers who quit due to illness, artificially lowering the apparent health of non-drinkers (sick-quitter or abstainer bias). Holmes and colleagues' 2014 BMJ Mendelian randomization study used a genetic variant (ADH1B rs1229984) that reduces alcohol consumption as a natural randomizer: carriers who drank less for genetic rather than health reasons had lower, not higher, coronary risk across the board, undercutting the idea that moderate drinking itself is protective.

sections.heading: NutriRECS and the limits of small-effect nutrition guidance
sections.body: In 2019 the NutriRECS consortium, led by Bradley Johnston, published Annals of Internal Medicine guidelines concluding there was insufficient evidence to recommend reducing red and processed meat intake, based on a GRADE-style judgment that the underlying cohort associations were low-certainty. The backlash was immediate and unusually public: outside researchers and journals objected that the panel was overriding a broad existing evidence base and noted Johnston's undisclosed prior industry-linked funding history, while three of the panel's own 14 members dissented. Critics also noted the guideline arrived only a few years after the WHO's International Agency for Research on Cancer had classified processed meat as carcinogenic to humans and red meat as probably carcinogenic, based on the same broad category of cohort evidence NutriRECS was now grading as low-certainty — two expert bodies reading similar observational data to strikingly different practical conclusions. The episode crystallizes the chapter's throughline — whether relative risks under roughly 2, the range most modern diet-disease associations fall into, can ever ground causal dietary guidance the way the smoking-cancer relative risks of 15 to 25 once could.

lessons.workedExample: Take the alcohol J-curve concretely: an observational study might report moderate drinkers have a coronary relative risk of about 0.8 compared to abstainers, while heavy drinkers have a relative risk above 1.5. If the abstainer group quietly includes people who quit drinking after a health scare, their elevated baseline risk drops the whole comparison group's health downward, making moderate drinkers look protected by comparison even if alcohol itself does nothing. Holmes's Mendelian randomization sidesteps this: it compares people by a gene variant fixed at conception, unaffected by whether they later quit for health reasons, and found no such protective signal — the genetic evidence points toward the J-curve being substantially an artifact of abstainer bias rather than a real cardioprotective effect.
lessons.judgeFraming: This unit closes the segment because it's exactly the terrain science-fair judges expect students to navigate in their own projects: the studies underlying most modern diet-and-lifestyle claims carry relative risks under 2, well below the 15-to-25-fold signal that made the smoking case unambiguous. A judge wants a student who can state, for their own project's cited evidence, roughly how strong the association is, name the most likely confounder or bias threatening it, and say plainly whether the design available can settle causation — not oversell a weak cohort association as proven.

questions.prompt: What did Holmes et al.'s 2014 Mendelian randomization study find about the alcohol-cardiovascular J-curve?

options.text: It confirmed moderate drinkers have genuinely lower coronary risk than abstainers
Genetically-determined lower alcohol consumption was associated with lower, not higher, coronary risk, undercutting the protective J-curve claim
It found no relationship at all between the ADH1B gene variant and drinking behavior
It showed heavy drinkers have the same coronary risk as abstainers

explanations.a: The genetic evidence pointed the opposite way from the observational J-curve's implied protective effect of moderate drinking.
explanations.b: Correct: carriers of the alcohol-reducing ADH1B variant, who drank less for reasons unrelated to health status, had lower coronary risk, suggesting the observational J-curve reflects abstainer bias rather than true cardioprotection.
explanations.c: The variant was clearly associated with reduced alcohol consumption; that association was the basis of using it as a natural randomizer.
explanations.d: The study's point was about the moderate-versus-abstainer comparison and genetic evidence against protection, not an explicit heavy-drinker equivalence claim.

questions.prompt: Order these developments in the open-debates landscape.

items.text: Observational cohorts establish the alcohol J-curve, with moderate drinkers appearing healthiest
Critics identify abstainer/sick-quitter bias in the comparison group
Holmes et al. publish Mendelian randomization evidence against the protective effect (2014)
NutriRECS publishes its red-meat guideline and triggers public backlash (2019)

questions.explanation: The J-curve was observed first, its bias was identified next, genetic evidence undercutting it followed, and the separate NutriRECS controversy over small-effect meat evidence came in 2019.

questions.prompt: Match each open debate to its central methodological concern.

right.text: Whether small relative risks amid heavy confounding can be treated as causal
Whether the comparison group (abstainers) is biased by prior quitters
Whether GRADE-style low-certainty ratings should override existing dietary guidance

questions.explanation: Each debate targets a distinct weak point in how observational chronic-disease evidence gets interpreted.

questions.prompt: According to this lesson, how do the relative risks typical of modern diet-disease cohort associations compare to the smoking-lung cancer relative risk from earlier in this unit?

options.text: They are roughly the same, both around 15 to 25
Modern diet-disease associations are typically much smaller, often under 2, versus smoking's roughly 15-to-25-fold risk
Modern diet-disease associations are typically larger than the smoking association
The two are not comparable because relative risk cannot be computed for diet studies

explanations.a: The lesson explicitly contrasts the two as very different in magnitude, not similar.
explanations.b: Correct: most modern diet-and-lifestyle cohort associations fall under a relative risk of 2, far weaker than the roughly 15-to-25-fold risk smoking carried for lung cancer.
explanations.c: This reverses the actual comparison; diet associations are described as smaller, not larger.
explanations.d: Relative risk is computable for diet cohort studies; the issue is its typical magnitude and reliability, not whether it can be calculated.

units.label: Advanced Causal Inference for Chronic Disease

lessons.label: Causal Diagrams in Depth

sections.heading: DAGs as the Grammar of Confounding
sections.body: Directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) formalize causal assumptions as pictures: nodes are variables, arrows are direct causal effects, and no arrow can loop back on itself. Judea Pearl built the modern theory in the 1990s on top of Sewall Wright's 1920s path analysis, giving epidemiologists a precise alternative to the vague instruction to adjust for confounders. A backdoor path between exposure and outcome is any path that starts with an arrow into the exposure - it represents a shared cause, meaning confounding, rather than the effect itself. Pearl's backdoor criterion says a variable set Z suffices to estimate the causal effect of X on Y if no member of Z is a descendant of X, and Z blocks every backdoor path between X and Y. Satisfy the backdoor criterion and an observational risk ratio, adjusted for Z, equals the causal effect.

sections.heading: Colliders and the Trap of Over-Adjustment
sections.body: Not every branching point is a confounder. A collider is a variable with two arrowheads pointing into it, as in A to C, B to C. A backdoor path through a collider is already closed - leave it alone. But condition on a collider, or anything downstream of it, and the path opens, manufacturing an association between A and B even when they are truly unrelated. Joseph Berkson identified this mechanism in 1946, showing that restricting a case-control analysis to hospitalized patients can spuriously link two unrelated diseases whenever both raise the odds of admission. Pearl's d-separation rule generalizes this: two variables are independent given a set Z if every connecting path is blocked, either by a non-collider inside Z or by a collider left outside Z. A student who controls for everything measured without checking collider status is not being careful - they are inviting bias in.

sections.heading: Building a Minimal Sufficient Adjustment Set
sections.body: In practice: draw the DAG, enumerate every path connecting exposure and outcome, and sort each path into causal (through mediators, leave open) or backdoor (through common causes, must be blocked). Pick the smallest Z that blocks all backdoor paths while conditioning on no collider and no mediator - software like DAGitty (Textor, Hardt, and Knuppel, 2011) automates this search for graphs too large to check by hand. Two textbook illustrations show what happens when the rule is broken. In the birth-weight paradox, birth weight is a collider of smoking and other causes of low birth weight, such as congenital anomalies; Hernandez-Diaz, Schisterman, and Hernan (2006) showed that stratifying on birth weight alone can make smoking look protective among low-birth-weight infants with no true benefit. In the obesity paradox, Sperrin and colleagues (2016) found collider bias explains only part of the reversed BMI-mortality association seen once a disease cohort is already selected.

lessons.workedExample: Hernandez-Diaz, Schisterman, and Hernan (2006) built a simulated cohort with a known null smoking effect on mortality, generated from a simple DAG: Smoking causes Birth weight, Congenital anomaly causes Birth weight, and Congenital anomaly causes Infant mortality. Smoking and anomaly are independent causes of low birth weight (LBW), and anomaly is the far more lethal one. Marginally, infants of smokers had both higher LBW risk and higher mortality than infants of nonsmokers, as expected. But once the sample was stratified to LBW infants only, the ordering flipped: the relative mortality rate for smokers' LBW infants versus nonsmokers' LBW infants was 0.79, a 21 percent apparent mortality reduction. Nothing protective happened - stratifying on birth weight, a collider, opened a backdoor path through anomaly, which is rare among LBW infants of smokers but common among LBW infants of nonsmokers.
lessons.judgeFraming: A science-fair judge probing a chronic-disease project will ask which variables were adjusted for and why - the tell of DAG literacy is that the answer names a backdoor path, not just variables available in the dataset. Students who cannot distinguish a confounder from a collider tend to over-adjust, throwing every measured covariate into a regression and occasionally conditioning on a downstream collider, which manufactures bias rather than removing it. Judges also probe whether a student can explain a reversed or attenuated association mid-analysis, like an obesity or birth-weight paradox, using the graph rather than hand-waving about complex biology - that distinction separates students who understand causal structure from those pattern-matching a p-value.

questions.prompt: In the DAG where A causes C and B causes C, what kind of variable is C, and what happens if an analysis conditions on it?

options.text: C is a confounder; conditioning on it removes bias between A and B
C is a collider; conditioning on it opens a spurious association between A and B
C is a mediator; conditioning on it blocks part of the true causal effect of A on B
C is unrelated to A and B; conditioning on it has no effect on their association

explanations.a: A confounder has arrows pointing out toward both A and B; here both arrows point into C, which makes it a collider, not a confounder.
explanations.b: Correct: two arrowheads meeting at C make it a collider. The path A-C-B is closed by default, but conditioning on C opens it and creates a spurious A-B association.
explanations.c: A mediator would sit on a causal path such as A causes C causes B; here neither A nor B receives an arrow from C, so C cannot be a mediator.
explanations.d: Conditioning on a collider is exactly the case where a previously blocked path opens, so it does affect the A-B association.

questions.prompt: Hernandez-Diaz, Schisterman, and Hernan (2006) found that among low-birth-weight infants, the relative mortality rate for infants of smokers versus nonsmokers was 0.79. What best explains this apparent protective effect of smoking?

options.text: Smoking has a genuine protective effect on survival for small infants
Birth weight is a collider of smoking and other causes of low birth weight like congenital anomalies; stratifying on it opens a backdoor path that induces the reversal
The dataset was too small to draw any reliable conclusion
Smoking mothers in the sample received systematically better prenatal care, which confounded the result

explanations.a: The paper's entire point is that no protective effect is needed to produce this pattern; it is a structural artifact of stratifying on a collider.
explanations.b: Correct: birth weight receives arrows from both smoking and congenital anomaly, so conditioning on it opens a backdoor path between smoking and the anomaly-driven mortality risk.
explanations.c: The demonstration used a simulated cohort built with a known null smoking effect, not real-world sample size; the paradox is a bias mechanism, not a sample-size problem.
explanations.d: Better prenatal care is a plausible-sounding confounder but is not the mechanism the authors identified; the DAG explanation does not require any such difference in care.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for building a minimal sufficient adjustment set from a DAG.

items.text: Draw the DAG encoding all assumed causal relationships among exposure, outcome, and other variables
Enumerate every path connecting the exposure and the outcome
Classify each path as causal (through mediators) or backdoor (through common causes)
Select the smallest variable set that blocks every backdoor path without conditioning on a collider or mediator

questions.explanation: You cannot classify a path before the graph exists, and you cannot pick an adjustment set before you know which paths need blocking; the order runs from encoding assumptions to enumerating structure to selecting the minimal fix.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

right.text: A path from exposure to outcome that begins with an arrow into the exposure, representing confounding
A variable with two arrowheads pointing into it from two other variables on a path
A rule for choosing an adjustment set that blocks every backdoor path without including descendants of the exposure
Pearl's general graphical rule for reading conditional independence directly off a DAG

questions.explanation: Backdoor paths are the target of adjustment, colliders are the structure that must not be adjusted for, the backdoor criterion is the rule for building a valid set, and d-separation is the general theorem both rest on.

lessons.label: Mendelian Randomization

sections.heading: Genotype as Nature's Randomizer
sections.body: At conception, alleles assort according to Mendel's laws largely independent of the social and behavioral confounders that plague observational epidemiology, and genotype is fixed decades before most chronic disease develops, which rules out reverse causation. Mendelian randomization (MR) exploits this by using a genetic variant robustly linked to a modifiable exposure, such as an LDL-raising allele, as an instrumental variable for that exposure's causal effect on an outcome. Martijn Katan proposed the logic in a 1986 Lancet letter, arguing that apolipoprotein E genotype could test whether low cholesterol truly causes cancer or merely reflects it, without running a trial. The method sat largely dormant until Davey Smith and Ebrahim revived it as a general epidemiologic tool in the early 2000s, and it has since become a standard check on observational chronic-disease findings.

sections.heading: Three Assumptions, One Common Failure
sections.body: MR rests on three instrumental-variable assumptions. Relevance: the variant must be robustly associated with the exposure, checked with an F-statistic, where values below roughly 10 signal a weak instrument. Independence: the variant must be unassociated with confounders of the exposure-outcome relationship, threatened by population stratification. Exclusion restriction: the variant must affect the outcome only through the exposure of interest, not through any other pathway. This last assumption is the one that usually breaks, because a single gene can influence multiple traits at once - a phenomenon called horizontal pleiotropy, distinct from the harmless vertical pleiotropy of a variant acting entirely through the exposure.

sections.heading: Detecting Pleiotropy and Reading Real Verdicts
sections.body: MR-Egger regression (Bowden, Davey Smith, and Burgess, 2015) tests for it directly: across many genetic variants, plot each variant's effect on the outcome against its effect on the exposure. A nonzero intercept signals directional pleiotropy, while the slope still estimates a pleiotropy-adjusted causal effect, at the cost of much lower precision than a standard weighted average. Applied to chronic disease, MR has delivered sharp verdicts. The CRP CHD Genetics Collaboration (2011), pooling 194,418 participants, found CRP-raising variants shifted CRP concentration by up to 30 percent per allele yet showed no association with coronary heart disease, unmasking CRP as a marker rather than a cause. LDL-lowering variants near genes like PCSK9, by contrast, showed each 1 mmol/L of lifetime-lower LDL cutting coronary risk by roughly 54 percent, confirming causality. And Holmes and colleagues (2014), using the alcohol-reducing ADH1B variant in 261,991 people, found genetically lower drinking tied to lower coronary and stroke risk, undercutting claims that moderate drinking protects the heart.

lessons.workedExample: The CRP CHD Genetics Collaboration (2011) pooled 47 studies across 15 countries, 194,418 participants and 46,557 coronary heart disease cases. Four CRP-gene variants shifted circulating CRP by up to 30 percent per allele - strong evidence the instrument satisfied relevance. Yet none of the variants shifted CHD odds. Compare that to Holmes et al. (2014): the ADH1B rs1229984 variant cut weekly alcohol intake by 17.2 percent and raised abstention odds 1.27-fold, and carriers had 10 percent lower odds of coronary heart disease (OR 0.90) and 17 percent lower odds of ischemic stroke (OR 0.83). Same instrumental-variable logic, opposite verdicts: CRP genotype moved the biomarker with zero effect on disease, meaning CRP is a bystander; alcohol genotype moved consumption and disease moved with it, meaning alcohol is causal even in a population whose average intake was already moderate.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probing an MR-based project push on the exclusion restriction specifically, because it is the untestable assumption: a student who can only recite relevance and independence but cannot explain why their chosen variant would affect nothing except the exposure has not actually understood the design. A strong project reports the F-statistic, checks MR-Egger's intercept for directional pleiotropy, and states what a null instrument-outcome association would mean before running the analysis. Citing a case where MR reversed conventional wisdom, such as CRP, signals the student grasps that MR exists precisely to catch observational associations that confounding or reverse causation manufactured.

questions.prompt: Which of the three Mendelian randomization assumptions is most commonly violated by horizontal pleiotropy, and why?

options.text: Relevance, because pleiotropic variants are always weakly associated with the exposure
Independence, because pleiotropy directly causes population stratification
Exclusion restriction, because a pleiotropic variant affects the outcome through pathways other than the exposure
None of the three; pleiotropy only affects statistical power, not bias

explanations.a: Relevance concerns whether the variant predicts the exposure strongly, which is unrelated to how many other traits the variant also influences.
explanations.b: Independence concerns confounders of the exposure-outcome link, such as population stratification, which is a separate threat from pleiotropy.
explanations.c: Correct: exclusion restriction requires the variant to affect the outcome only via the exposure. Horizontal pleiotropy means the variant has an independent path to the outcome, breaking exactly this assumption.
explanations.d: Pleiotropy biases the causal estimate itself, not just its precision, which is why methods like MR-Egger exist to detect and adjust for it.

questions.prompt: The CRP CHD Genetics Collaboration (2011) found CRP-raising variants shifted CRP levels by up to 30 percent per allele but showed no association with coronary heart disease odds. What does this pattern indicate?

options.text: The genetic instrument was too weak to test the hypothesis
CRP is likely a marker of inflammation rather than a cause of coronary heart disease
CRP causes coronary heart disease but only in men
The study lacked statistical power because too few participants were enrolled

explanations.a: A 30 percent per-allele shift in CRP concentration is a strong relevance signal; a weak instrument would show little effect on the exposure itself.
explanations.b: Correct: a strong instrument-exposure association paired with a null instrument-outcome association is the classic MR signature of a non-causal biomarker.
explanations.c: Nothing in the design or result supports a sex-specific causal effect; the study found no CHD association in the pooled analysis.
explanations.d: With 194,418 participants and 46,557 cases, this was one of the largest MR analyses of its era; power was not the limitation.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps of a Mendelian randomization analysis testing whether an exposure causes a chronic disease outcome.

items.text: Select a genetic variant robustly associated with the exposure of interest
Verify relevance using an F-statistic from the variant-exposure association
Test the variant-outcome association as the instrumented estimate of the causal effect
Run MR-Egger or a similar sensitivity analysis to check for directional pleiotropy

questions.explanation: You need a candidate instrument before you can check its strength, you need to confirm strength before trusting the instrumented estimate, and pleiotropy sensitivity analysis is a check applied after the main estimate is in hand.

questions.prompt: Match each Mendelian randomization verdict to the exposure it concerns.

left.text: C-reactive protein (CRP) and coronary heart disease
LDL cholesterol and coronary heart disease

right.text: Genetically lower alcohol intake (via ADH1B) was associated with lower coronary and stroke risk, challenging the moderate-drinking-is-protective claim
Genetic variants shifted the biomarker substantially but showed no association with disease risk, indicating it is a non-causal marker
Lifetime genetically lower exposure was associated with a much larger risk reduction per unit than late-started drug treatment, supporting a cumulative causal effect

questions.explanation: CRP genotype moved the marker with no disease effect; LDL genotype's cumulative lifetime effect exceeded late treatment, consistent with causality; and alcohol genotype linked lower intake to lower cardiovascular risk, undercutting the observational J-curve.

lessons.label: Target Trial Emulation

sections.heading: Writing the Protocol First
sections.body: Miguel Hernan and James Robins argued in a 2016 American Journal of Epidemiology paper, Using Big Data to Emulate a Target Trial, that most flawed observational chronic-disease analyses fail because no one ever wrote down the randomized trial the analysis was implicitly trying to mimic. Their fix: before touching the data, specify a target trial protocol with explicit eligibility criteria, treatment strategies being compared, an assignment procedure, a follow-up period, and an outcome. Only after that protocol exists should an analyst ask which observational data source could emulate each element. The single most important protocol element is time zero: the moment eligibility, treatment assignment, and the start of follow-up all align. In a real trial these three happen at the same visit; in careless observational analyses they routinely do not, and that gap is where bias enters.

sections.heading: Immortal Time and the Prevalent User
sections.body: When treatment status is assessed some time after cohort entry, patients are misclassified as treated for the interval before they actually started, an interval during which they cannot have died or the classification would not exist - this is immortal time bias, and it mechanically favors the treated group. A related error, prevalent-user bias, enrolls patients already partway through treatment, discarding the early period where risk is highest (or where non-adherers drop out) and comparing survivors of that period to new starters. Hernan, Alonso, and colleagues (2008) demonstrated the fix directly: reanalyzing the Nurses' Health Study as a sequence of trials, each starting at the moment a woman initiated hormone therapy, reconciled the study's apparent cardioprotective finding with the null-to-harmful result of the Women's Health Initiative randomized trial once time since initiation was properly aligned.

sections.heading: Clone-Censor-Weight, and the Limits of Emulation
sections.body: When eligible patients' actual treatment strategy is not yet known at time zero, such as whether they will sustain a drug indefinitely or stop within a year, simply classifying patients by their eventual behavior reintroduces the very immortal-time problem the framework exists to avoid, since the future has to happen before the classification can be made. The clone-censor-weight approach solves this without waiting: it clones each eligible patient once per strategy being compared, lets every clone's data accrue identically from time zero, censors a given clone the moment its actual behavior departs from its assigned strategy, and reweights the surviving clones by the inverse probability of remaining uncensored, using their measured history, to correct the selection bias that censoring itself introduces. Target trial emulation is a design discipline, not a statistical fix for missing information: it removes bias caused by misaligned time zero and mismatched treatment classification, but it cannot manufacture an instrument nobody measured, cannot correct for a confounder nobody recorded, and cannot rescue data too coarse to specify eligibility or treatment strategy precisely - a rigorously written protocol applied to poor-quality data still returns a poor estimate.

lessons.workedExample: Hernan, Alonso, Logan, and colleagues (2008, Epidemiology) took the Nurses' Health Study, which had suggested hormone therapy nearly halved coronary heart disease risk, and reanalyzed it as a sequence of trials: each month, eligible women who had just started estrogen-progestin therapy were compared to eligible non-initiators, exactly mirroring how the Women's Health Initiative randomized trial enrolled new initiators. The original whole-cohort analysis, which mixed long-term users with new starters and ignored time since initiation, was distorted by prevalent-user and immortal-time bias. Once emulation aligned time zero to initiation and let risk vary with time since starting therapy, the reconstructed hazard ratios no longer differed significantly from the Women's Health Initiative's trial result, resolving a discrepancy that had confused clinicians for years.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who spots an observational cohort study with a suspiciously strong protective effect will ask exactly one clarifying question: when is time zero, and is it the same moment for eligibility, treatment assignment, and the start of follow-up? A student who cannot answer precisely is very likely carrying immortal-time or prevalent-user bias without knowing it. Judges reward students who state the target trial protocol explicitly before presenting results, and who can also name what emulation cannot fix - an unmeasured confounder does not disappear just because the design discipline improved, and claiming otherwise is itself a red flag of overselling the method.

questions.prompt: A cohort study classifies patients as statin users based on a prescription fill recorded any time in the first two years of follow-up, then compares survival to non-users starting from cohort entry. What bias does this design create?

options.text: Reverse causation, because statins are prescribed after disease onset
Immortal time bias, because patients must survive long enough after entry to be observed filling the prescription and get classified as users
Horizontal pleiotropy, because the prescription affects the outcome through multiple pathways
Berkson's bias, because only hospitalized patients were included

explanations.a: Reverse causation describes disease influencing the exposure measurement itself, which is a different problem from misaligned time zero.
explanations.b: Correct: time between cohort entry and the observed prescription fill is guaranteed survival time misattributed to the user group, inflating its apparent survival advantage.
explanations.c: Pleiotropy is a genetics concept from instrumental variable analysis and does not apply to a prescription-based cohort design.
explanations.d: Berkson's bias concerns selection into a hospitalized sample via a collider, not the timing of exposure classification relative to cohort entry.

questions.prompt: In target trial emulation, why must eligibility, treatment assignment, and the start of follow-up (time zero) all occur at the same moment?

options.text: Because randomized trials require identical calendar dates for every enrolled patient
Because misaligning them creates immortal-time or prevalent-user bias that a randomized trial's design would never produce
Because regulatory agencies require it for drug approval
Because it simplifies the statistical software used for the analysis

explanations.a: Trial patients enroll on different calendar dates; what matters is that each patient's own eligibility, assignment, and follow-up start together.
explanations.b: Correct: a randomized trial assigns treatment at entry by construction, so it cannot generate immortal-time or prevalent-user bias; emulation enforces the same alignment on observational data to close that gap.
explanations.c: Regulatory requirements are not the reason for the design principle; the principle is a bias-avoidance argument that applies regardless of regulatory context.
explanations.d: The alignment is a substantive causal-inference requirement, not a software convenience.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the Hernan-Robins target trial emulation process.

items.text: Write the target trial protocol: eligibility criteria, treatment strategies, assignment, follow-up, and outcome
Identify which observational data source can emulate each protocol element
Align time zero so eligibility, treatment strategy, and follow-up start together for each patient
Analyze the emulated data using an estimator appropriate for the target trial's intention-to-treat or per-protocol contrast

questions.explanation: The protocol must exist before you can ask which data source emulates it, alignment of time zero is a design step that must precede analysis, and the analysis itself comes last.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its description.

right.text: Enrolling patients already partway through treatment, discarding the highest-risk early period and comparing survivors to new starters
A guaranteed event-free interval before exposure classification occurs gets misattributed to the treated group
Duplicating each patient across compared strategies, then censoring and reweighting clones once their behavior deviates from the assigned strategy

questions.explanation: Immortal time bias comes from a delay before exposure classification, prevalent-user bias comes from entering the cohort mid-treatment, and clone-censor-weight is the specific method for handling strategies not yet knowable at time zero.

lessons.label: G-Methods and Time-Varying Treatments

sections.heading: When a Confounder Is Also a Mediator
sections.body: Chronic disease treatments are rarely a single decision; a clinician monitors a patient and adjusts therapy repeatedly, and each adjustment both responds to the patient's evolving state and shapes their future risk. James Robins named this treatment-confounder feedback in a 1986 paper introducing the g-formula: a time-varying variable, such as CD4 count in HIV treatment or blood pressure in hypertension management, is simultaneously a confounder of later treatment decisions and a mediator of the treatment's effect on the outcome. Standard regression has no way to handle a variable that plays both roles at once, which makes sustained, time-varying exposures a structurally different problem from a single point-in-time exposure.

sections.heading: Why Standard Cox Adjustment Fails
sections.body: Adjusting for a time-varying confounder-mediator inside a conventional Cox model blocks part of the treatment's true effect, because the variable sits on the causal pathway between treatment and outcome. But leaving it unadjusted leaves confounding at each treatment decision point unaddressed, since the variable also predicts who gets treated next. Both choices are wrong, and neither can be fixed by picking a different covariate set, because no single-adjustment regression can play both roles correctly at once - this is the same structural trap Robins had earlier described in the healthy worker survivor effect, where workers who become too sick to work are also removed from further occupational exposure, biasing naive comparisons of continuously employed versus retired workers.
