Robins showed the resolution requires estimating the treatment effect as it would occur in a hypothetical world where treatment strategies are fixed in advance for the whole follow-up period, then working out what the observed time-varying confounder-mediator implies about that hypothetical world, rather than conditioning on it directly in an outcome regression.

sections.heading: Marginal Structural Models and the g-Formula
sections.body: Two g-methods solve this. A marginal structural model (MSM) specifies the causal effect of a sustained treatment strategy on the marginal (population-average) outcome distribution, and is fit using inverse probability of treatment weighting: at each time point, patients are weighted by the inverse of their probability of receiving the treatment they actually received, given their treatment and confounder history, which creates a pseudo-population where treatment no longer depends on the time-varying confounders. The parametric g-formula instead directly models the confounder and outcome distributions over time and simulates forward under a fixed treatment strategy. Hernan, Brumback, and Robins (2000) applied the MSM approach to zidovudine and survival in HIV-positive men from the Multicenter AIDS Cohort Study, where CD4 count is both a marker doctors use to start treatment and a consequence of the treatment itself; a standard Cox model adjusted for CD4 count showed zidovudine associated with higher mortality, while the marginal structural Cox model estimated a mortality rate ratio of 0.7, reversing the sign of the naive result.

lessons.workedExample: In the Multicenter AIDS Cohort Study, physicians started zidovudine more often in men whose CD4 count had recently dropped, meaning low CD4 both predicted treatment initiation and independently predicted death. A standard Cox model adjusting for time-updated CD4 count treated CD4 purely as a confounder to control, which also strips out the part of zidovudine's protective effect that operates by raising CD4 count, and it produced a harmful-looking hazard estimate. Hernan, Brumback, and Robins (2000) instead built a marginal structural Cox model, weighting each man's follow-up interval by the inverse probability of the treatment he actually received given his CD4 and treatment history. That model estimated a mortality rate ratio of 0.7 (95 percent confidence interval 0.6 to 1.0) for zidovudine, consistent with a protective effect the naive adjustment had inverted.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe time-varying-treatment projects by asking whether the exposure was measured once or updated over follow-up, and if updated, whether any covariate used for adjustment could itself have been affected by earlier treatment. A student defending a standard regression on a repeatedly-treated chronic disease cohort without naming this feedback problem is exposed immediately, because the judge can point to any covariate on the causal pathway and ask whether adjusting for it removed real treatment effect. Naming inverse probability weighting or the g-formula, and being able to say in one sentence why ordinary adjustment fails here, is the signal that separates a student who ran a regression from one who understood what the regression could not do.

questions.prompt: Why does adjusting for a time-varying confounder in a standard Cox regression fail when treatment is repeatedly reassigned based on that confounder?

options.text: Because Cox regression cannot include any time-varying covariates at all
Because the confounder is also a mediator of treatment's effect, so adjusting for it blocks part of the true causal effect
Because Cox regression requires a normally distributed outcome
Because the sample size becomes too small once time-varying covariates are added

explanations.a: Cox models can technically include time-varying covariates; the problem is not a software limitation but a causal one.
explanations.b: Correct: when a variable is both a confounder of future treatment and an effect of past treatment, standard adjustment removes some of the very effect being estimated.
explanations.c: Cox regression models a hazard function and does not assume a normally distributed outcome; this is not the source of the bias here.
explanations.d: The bias described is structural, arising from the variable's dual role, not from a loss of statistical power.

questions.prompt: Hernan, Brumback, and Robins (2000) found a standard Cox model adjusted for time-updated CD4 count made zidovudine look harmful, while their marginal structural Cox model estimated a mortality rate ratio of 0.7. What explains the difference?

options.text: The marginal structural model used a larger sample of patients
Inverse probability weighting created a pseudo-population where treatment no longer depended on CD4 history, removing confounding without blocking the mediated effect
The standard Cox model made a coding error in defining survival time
The marginal structural model excluded all patients who ever had a low CD4 count

explanations.a: Both models were fit on the same Multicenter AIDS Cohort Study data; sample size was not the differentiator.
explanations.b: Correct: weighting by the inverse probability of the treatment actually received, given confounder and treatment history, breaks the confounder-treatment link in the weighted pseudo-population while leaving the treatment-CD4-outcome pathway intact.
explanations.c: No coding error was involved; the standard model's bias is a well-understood structural consequence of adjusting for a time-varying confounder-mediator.
explanations.d: The marginal structural model retains all patients and instead reweights their contribution to the analysis; it does not exclude anyone based on CD4 count.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for fitting a marginal structural model via inverse probability of treatment weighting.

items.text: Measure treatment and confounder history at each time point for every patient
Estimate, at each time point, each patient's probability of receiving the treatment they actually received, given their history
Weight each patient-interval by the inverse of that estimated probability
Fit the outcome model in the resulting weighted pseudo-population to estimate the marginal treatment effect

questions.explanation: You need the history recorded before you can model treatment probability from it, the probability estimate is required before weights can be constructed, and the weighted pseudo-population is what the final outcome model is fit on.

questions.prompt: Match each g-method concept to its description.

right.text: A time-varying variable that is simultaneously a confounder of future treatment and a consequence of past treatment
A model of the marginal outcome distribution under a sustained treatment strategy, fit using inverse probability weighting
An approach that models the confounder and outcome distributions over time directly and simulates forward under a fixed strategy

questions.explanation: Treatment-confounder feedback is the problem g-methods solve; marginal structural models and the parametric g-formula are the two main solutions, one weighting-based and one simulation-based.

lessons.label: Life-Course Epidemiology

sections.heading: Three Models of How Exposures Accumulate
sections.body: Life-course epidemiology asks not just whether an exposure causes disease but when in a person's life it matters most, and it organizes the answer into three competing models. The critical or sensitive period model holds that an exposure during a narrow developmental window produces effects that later exposure at the same intensity cannot reproduce, with fetal programming as the clearest case: David Barker and Clyde Osmond's 1986 Lancet analysis found English and Welsh districts with higher infant mortality decades earlier, a marker of poor early nutrition, went on to have higher ischemic heart disease mortality, seeding what became the Barker hypothesis, or developmental origins of health and disease. The accumulation-of-risk model instead treats each exposure as adding independently to total risk regardless of timing, so a lifetime of small insults sums like compound interest. The chain-of-risk model sits between them: one exposure raises the probability of a later exposure, which raises disease risk, so the pathway matters as much as any single link.

sections.heading: The Age-Period-Cohort Identification Problem
sections.body: Chronic disease incidence trends are shaped by three time dimensions at once: age (biological aging), period (a calendar-time event affecting everyone alive then, like a new treatment), and birth cohort (a group's shared early-life exposures, like when they took up smoking). The problem is that cohort equals period minus age exactly, so the three effects are perfectly collinear - no regression can separately estimate all three from age, period, and cohort alone without an added assumption or constraint, an identification problem with no purely statistical fix.

sections.heading: Frost's Tuberculosis Cohorts and Why Birth Year Matters
sections.body: Wade Hampton Frost's tuberculosis mortality analysis, found in his papers and published posthumously in 1939, used Massachusetts data from 1880 to 1930 to show that age-specific tuberculosis mortality peaks in cross-sectional data were artifacts of mixing cohorts with very different infection histories; tracking single birth cohorts across time instead revealed mortality declining steadily with age after early exposure, not rising and falling as period snapshots suggested. The same logic explains modern smoking-driven lung cancer trends: because smoking uptake, peak intensity, and cessation differ sharply by the year someone was born, a birth cohort that came of age during peak per-capita cigarette consumption carries elevated lifetime risk that a cohort born decades later, facing a different tobacco-control environment, does not - which is why chronic disease surveillance reports incidence by birth cohort, not only by current age or calendar year.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose lung cancer incidence rises steadily by age in a health system's records, appears to spike in the calendar years 1990 to 2000, and is far higher in people born around 1940 than in those born around 1970. Age alone would predict a smooth rise with no calendar-year spike; a pure period effect, like a new environmental carcinogen released nationwide in 1990, would raise risk for every age and birth cohort simultaneously that decade; a pure cohort effect would show the 1940 birth cohort carrying elevated risk at every age it has passed through, including ages measured well before or after 1990 to 2000. Disentangling which pattern actually holds requires either fixing one dimension by design, such as tracking a single fixed cohort over decades the way Frost did with Massachusetts tuberculosis data, or importing outside information, such as independently known per-capita cigarette sales by birth year, since age, period, and cohort alone cannot be separated from incidence data by regression.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge reviewing a chronic disease trends project will ask whether an observed change in incidence is an age effect, a period effect, or a cohort effect, and a student who answers with a single regression coefficient on all three has revealed they do not know the identification problem exists. Judges also probe timing-of-exposure claims specifically: a project claiming a childhood exposure programs adult disease risk needs to explain why a critical-period model fits better than an accumulation model, using data on exposure timing, not just an association between any early-life measure and any adult outcome, since the three life-course models make different, testable predictions about intervening exposure history.

questions.prompt: Which life-course model best describes Barker and Osmond's 1986 finding, that districts with higher infant mortality decades earlier later had higher ischemic heart disease mortality?

options.text: Accumulation of risk, because infant mortality and heart disease are unrelated independent exposures
Critical or sensitive period, because early-life nutritional conditions were proposed to produce a lasting effect not reproducible by equivalent later-life exposure
Chain of risk, because infant mortality directly causes heart disease through a single mediating step
Age-period-cohort confounding, because the finding is fully explained by calendar-year trends alone

explanations.a: Accumulation of risk would not privilege the early-life period specifically; the Barker hypothesis is explicitly about a developmental window mattering more than equivalent later exposure.
explanations.b: Correct: fetal programming is the textbook critical-period claim, that conditions during a specific developmental window leave a lasting imprint on adult disease risk.
explanations.c: A chain of risk requires one exposure to raise the probability of a later exposure that then causes disease; the Barker hypothesis proposes a more direct developmental mechanism, not a chain of intervening exposures.
explanations.d: The ecological finding used district-level data across birth eras, not a single calendar-year comparison, and calendar trends alone cannot explain a link tied to birth-era nutrition.

questions.prompt: Why can a standard regression not separately estimate age, period, and cohort effects on chronic disease incidence from age, period, and cohort variables alone?

options.text: Because cohort is calculated as period minus age, making the three variables perfectly collinear
Because chronic diseases have multifactorial causes that regression cannot capture
Because incidence data is always too sparse to fit three variables
Because age, period, and cohort effects do not actually exist independently of each other

explanations.a: Correct: cohort equals period minus age by definition, so the three are exactly collinear and no amount of data resolves the identification problem without an outside constraint or assumption.
explanations.b: Multifactorial causation is a separate issue from the specific mathematical identification problem created by the age-period-cohort collinearity.
explanations.c: The problem is structural collinearity, not sample size; even with infinite data the three effects remain unidentified without added assumptions.
explanations.d: Age, period, and cohort effects can each be real and distinct; the problem is that their measured versions are mathematically dependent, not that they are conceptually meaningless.

questions.prompt: Order the historical and conceptual development described in this lesson.

items.text: Frost's posthumously published Massachusetts tuberculosis analysis (1939) shows cross-sectional age-mortality peaks are artifacts of mixing birth cohorts
Barker and Osmond (1986) link district-level infant mortality decades earlier to later ischemic heart disease mortality
Life-course epidemiology formalizes critical-period, accumulation, and chain-of-risk models to interpret such findings
Modern chronic disease surveillance reports incidence by birth cohort to account for the age-period-cohort identification problem

questions.explanation: Frost's cohort method predates and motivates cohort-based thinking, Barker's finding is a later landmark critical-period claim, the three life-course models were formalized to interpret findings like Barker's, and cohort-based surveillance reporting is the applied practice that follows from taking the identification problem seriously.

questions.prompt: Match each life-course model to its defining claim.

right.text: Each exposure adds independently to total disease risk regardless of when in life it occurs
An exposure during a narrow developmental window has a lasting effect that equivalent exposure at another life stage cannot reproduce
One exposure raises the probability of encountering a later exposure, which in turn raises disease risk

questions.explanation: The critical-period model is about timing-specific lasting effects, accumulation is about additive independent exposures, and chain of risk is about exposures linked in a causal sequence.

lessons.label: Triangulation and Bias Analysis

sections.heading: Triangulating Designs With Non-Overlapping Biases
sections.body: No single study design for chronic disease is free of bias, but different designs are typically vulnerable to different biases, and Lawlor, Tilling, and Davey Smith (2016) formalized this into triangulation: deliberately combining an observational cohort, a Mendelian randomization analysis, a target trial emulation, and where available a randomized trial, then asking whether they converge. A cohort study is threatened by unmeasured confounding; an MR analysis of the same question is threatened by pleiotropy instead, a genuinely different failure mode. If confounding were driving the cohort result, there is no reason MR's independent failure mode would happen to reproduce the same answer, so agreement across designs is stronger evidence than any single design alone, while disagreement flags exactly which bias to investigate.

sections.heading: Quantitative Bias Analysis and the E-Value
sections.body: Quantitative bias analysis (QBA) goes further than triangulation's qualitative comparison by assigning numbers to a suspected bias and recalculating the estimate under stated assumptions about an unmeasured confounder's prevalence and strength, turning a footnote about limitations into a testable range. VanderWeele and Ding (2017) introduced a simpler companion measure, the E-value: the minimum strength of association, on the risk ratio scale, that an unmeasured confounder would need to have with both the exposure and the outcome to fully explain away the observed association, given the measured covariates. A large E-value means an unmeasured confounder would have to be implausibly strong to erase the finding; a small E-value means a modest, entirely plausible confounder could do it, which is itself a substantive result rather than a mere caveat.

sections.heading: Negative Controls as Confounding Detectors
sections.body: Lipsitch, Tchetgen Tchetgen, and Cohen (2010) formalized a third check: a negative control outcome is one known to share the exposure's confounding structure but that the exposure cannot plausibly cause, so an association there signals residual confounding rather than a real effect; a negative control exposure is one that shares the outcome's confounding structure but cannot plausibly cause the outcome, serving the same diagnostic role in reverse. A classic example pairs a vaccine exposure with a negative control outcome like unintentional injury: nothing about the vaccine's biology should raise injury risk, so if the same confounding structure - healthier, more health-seeking patients being more likely both to get vaccinated and to be captured in the data as injured or not - produces a spurious association there, it warns that the same structure is probably distorting the vaccine's association with its actual outcome of interest too. If a chronic-disease exposure appears associated with an outcome it has no biological pathway to reach, given otherwise identical confounders, the honest conclusion is that confounding remains uncontrolled everywhere in the analysis, including on the outcome the study actually cares about, and no amount of additional covariate adjustment guarantees otherwise.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose an observational cohort finds a modest chronic-disease exposure associated with a 1.5-fold higher risk of a chronic condition after adjusting for measured confounders. VanderWeele and Ding's E-value formula for a risk ratio of 1.5 works out to about 2.4: an unmeasured confounder would need to be associated with both the exposure and the outcome by a risk ratio of roughly 2.4-fold each, over and above the measured covariates, to fully explain away the finding. A researcher triangulating this result would also run a negative control outcome, a condition sharing the same confounding structure but with no plausible pathway from the exposure, such as an unrelated injury type; if that negative control shows a similar 1.4 to 1.6-fold association, it signals the same confounding structure is likely inflating the real outcome too, undercutting the original 1.5-fold estimate regardless of what the E-value alone would suggest.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges treat a single observational estimate, however large, as necessarily provisional, and reward students who volunteer how strong an unmeasured confounder would have to be to erase their result rather than waiting to be asked. A student who reports an E-value near 1 alongside their effect estimate is telling the judge the finding is fragile; one who reports a large E-value and a negative-control check that came back null is making the strongest case a non-randomized chronic-disease project can make. Judges are also alert to students who triangulate designs that share the same bias, such as two cohort studies with the same confounders, which is not triangulation at all since it duplicates rather than diversifies the vulnerability.

questions.prompt: Why does agreement between a cohort study and a Mendelian randomization analysis of the same exposure-outcome question count as stronger evidence than either study alone?

options.text: Because MR studies always have larger sample sizes than cohort studies
Because the two designs are vulnerable to different, largely unrelated biases, so it is unlikely both would be wrong in the same direction by coincidence
Because Mendelian randomization is immune to all forms of bias
Because cohort studies and MR studies always use the same underlying dataset

explanations.a: Sample size is not the basis for triangulation's logic; some MR analyses are smaller than the cohort studies they are compared against.
explanations.b: Correct: this is the core logic of triangulation as formalized by Lawlor, Tilling, and Davey Smith (2016) - non-overlapping bias structures make coincidental agreement unlikely.
explanations.c: MR has its own major vulnerability, horizontal pleiotropy; it is not bias-free, which is exactly why agreement with a differently-biased design is informative.
explanations.d: Cohort and MR analyses typically draw on different data sources or different aspects of the same source; triangulation's value comes from their differing bias structures, not from using identical data.

questions.prompt: A negative control outcome, one with no plausible causal pathway from the exposure but sharing the exposure's confounding structure, shows a positive association in an observational analysis. What should a researcher conclude?

options.text: The exposure has a previously unknown biological effect on the negative control outcome
Residual confounding is likely present and may also be inflating the association with the outcome of actual interest
The negative control was chosen incorrectly and should simply be discarded
The study has adequate statistical power and no further action is needed

explanations.a: The entire point of choosing a negative control is that no plausible biological pathway exists; a positive association points to a flaw in the analysis, not a real biological discovery.
explanations.b: Correct: Lipsitch, Tchetgen Tchetgen, and Cohen (2010) designed negative controls exactly to detect this - an association where none should exist signals confounding that likely also affects the outcome of interest.
explanations.c: Discarding an inconvenient negative control defeats its diagnostic purpose; a positive result there is itself the finding that needs to be reported and investigated.
explanations.d: A positive negative-control association is a validity problem, not a power problem, and ignoring it would leave the confounding undetected.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a quantitative bias analysis using the E-value.

items.text: Obtain the adjusted effect estimate (e.g., a risk ratio) from the observational analysis
Apply the E-value formula to that risk ratio to find the minimum confounder-exposure and confounder-outcome association needed to explain it away
Compare the resulting E-value to the strength of plausible unmeasured confounders in the study setting
Judge whether the observed association is robust or fragile to unmeasured confounding based on that comparison

questions.explanation: The E-value formula takes the adjusted estimate as its input, the comparison to plausible confounders requires the E-value already computed, and the robustness judgment is the final interpretive step.

questions.prompt: Match each bias-detection tool to its purpose.

right.text: Quantifies the minimum unmeasured confounder strength needed to fully explain away an observed association
Combines multiple study designs with different, non-overlapping sources of bias to see whether they converge
Tests an outcome with no plausible causal pathway from the exposure but the same confounding structure, to detect residual confounding

questions.explanation: Triangulation compares whole designs against each other, the E-value quantifies robustness of a single estimate to unmeasured confounding, and a negative control outcome is a within-study diagnostic for confounding that should not otherwise be there.

lessons.label: Cardiovascular Disease Epidemiology

sections.heading: The modifiable stack behind coronary and stroke risk
sections.body: Coronary heart disease and stroke share a common upstream process: LDL cholesterol infiltrates the arterial wall, is oxidized, and triggers an inflammatory response that builds an atherosclerotic plaque; hypertension raises shear stress and accelerates that same wall injury; smoking adds oxidative damage and promotes clot formation; and diabetes glycates vessel proteins and worsens all three. Framingham Heart Study, begun in Framingham, Massachusetts in 1948, was the cohort that first quantified these as independent, additive risk factors rather than isolated curiosities, and its investigators published the first multivariable coronary risk equation in 1967. INTERHEART (Yusuf et al., 2004), a case-control study spanning 52 countries, showed nine modifiable factors -- abnormal lipids, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, abdominal obesity, psychosocial stress, insufficient fruit and vegetable intake, physical inactivity, and alcohol use -- together accounted for roughly 90% of the population attributable risk for a first myocardial infarction, a strikingly consistent finding across regions and economic settings.

sections.heading: From single factors to calibrated equations
sections.body: Knowing that LDL and blood pressure each raise risk is not the same as predicting an individual's 10-year probability of an event, so epidemiologists built multivariable risk scores. The Framingham risk score combined age, sex, total cholesterol, HDL, systolic blood pressure, smoking, and diabetes status into a point system. The 2013 ACC/AHA Pooled Cohort Equations recalibrated these predictors on more diverse, contemporary US cohorts to estimate 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk and now anchor US statin-initiation guidelines. SCORE2, released by the European Society of Cardiology in 2021, replaced the older SCORE model with region-specific risk charts calibrated to low, moderate, high, and very-high cardiovascular-risk European populations, correcting for the fact that a model built on one population routinely miscalibrates when applied to another.

sections.heading: Mortality decline: prevention or treatment?
sections.body: Age-adjusted CVD mortality in the United States fell by roughly 50-70% between the 1960s and the 2000s, one of public health's largest sustained gains, but epidemiologists still argue over the split between causes. Modeling studies, including the influential IMPACT model applied to US and UK data, split the decline between acute-care and secondary-prevention treatments -- coronary care units, thrombolysis, angioplasty, statins -- and primary prevention: falling smoking rates, better blood pressure control, and dietary shifts in saturated fat and trans fat. Different country-level IMPACT analyses disagree on which side contributes the larger share: the US analysis found treatment and risk-factor change roughly split, while the UK analysis found primary prevention responsible for the larger share. Because these forces act simultaneously and the decline has since plateaued, and even reversed in some younger US subgroups amid rising obesity and diabetes, attribution remains an active, imperfect exercise rather than a settled accounting.

lessons.workedExample: A 55-year-old male smoker with systolic blood pressure 150 mmHg, total cholesterol 240 mg/dL, and HDL 40 mg/dL is entered into the Pooled Cohort Equations, which output a 10-year ASCVD risk of roughly 20%, crossing the 7.5% threshold that triggers a statin discussion under US guidelines. Applying INTERHEART's logic, this single patient carries three of the nine established factors (smoking, hypertension, dyslipidemia); adding diabetes or abdominal obesity would push him further up a population attributable risk curve estimated from nearly 30,000 case-control participants (15,152 cases and 14,820 controls) across 52 countries.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes whether a student can distinguish a risk factor from a risk score: naming that smoking raises MI odds is textbook, but explaining why Framingham-era coefficients need recalibration (as SCORE2 did) before use in a new population, or why a 90% population attributable fraction from INTERHEART does not mean any individual patient's risk is 90% explained, signals real grasp of multivariable epidemiology and its limits when transported across settings and eras.

questions.prompt: INTERHEART (Yusuf et al., 2004) found that its nine modifiable factors together accounted for approximately what share of population attributable risk for a first myocardial infarction?

explanations.a: Correct: across 52 countries, the nine factors together explained roughly 90% of population attributable risk for a first MI.
explanations.b: 50% understates INTERHEART's finding; the study's notable result was how much higher the combined attributable fraction was.
explanations.c: 25% is far below what INTERHEART reported and would undercut the study's central claim about modifiable risk.
explanations.d: 99% overstates the finding; some residual risk (genetic, unmeasured) remained outside the nine factors.

questions.prompt: Why did the 2013 ACC/AHA Pooled Cohort Equations replace the original Framingham risk score for US guideline use?

options.text: Framingham used unreliable lab assays
The Pooled Cohort Equations were recalibrated on more diverse, contemporary cohorts, since a model built on one population can miscalibrate elsewhere
Framingham did not include cholesterol as a predictor
The Pooled Cohort Equations removed smoking as a variable

explanations.a: Framingham's lab methods were not the issue; the concern was demographic representativeness and calibration drift over time.
explanations.b: Correct: risk equations built on one cohort's demographics and era predict poorly when applied to different, more diverse populations, motivating recalibration.
explanations.c: Framingham did include cholesterol; that was not the reason for replacement.
explanations.d: Smoking remained a core predictor in the Pooled Cohort Equations, not a removed variable.

questions.prompt: Order the historical development of cardiovascular risk-prediction tools from earliest to most recent.

items.text: Framingham Heart Study cohort begins (1948)
First Framingham multivariable coronary risk equation published (1967)
INTERHEART case-control study published (2004)
ACC/AHA Pooled Cohort Equations published (2013)
SCORE2 released by the European Society of Cardiology (2021)

questions.explanation: Framingham's cohort (1948) preceded its own risk equation (1967); INTERHEART (2004) then established the modifiable-factor framework globally; the Pooled Cohort Equations (2013) and SCORE2 (2021) are later recalibrations for US and European populations respectively.

questions.prompt: Match each risk tool or study to what it is best known for.

right.text: First identified major CVD risk factors as independent, additive contributors
Case-control study finding nine factors explain ~90% of first-MI risk across 52 countries
2013 US guideline tool estimating 10-year ASCVD risk
2021 European risk charts calibrated to regional risk strata

questions.explanation: Each tool addresses a distinct stage: Framingham established the factors, INTERHEART quantified their combined global attributable risk, and the Pooled Cohort Equations and SCORE2 are region-specific prediction models built on that foundation.

questions.prompt: Modeling studies of the ~50-70% US CVD mortality decline since the 1960s generally attribute the decline to:

options.text: Treatment advances alone, with primary prevention playing no measurable role

A mix of treatment advances (acute care, statins) and primary prevention (smoking decline, blood pressure control), with different country-level IMPACT analyses disagreeing on which side contributes the larger share
Primary prevention alone, since treatment innovations arrived only after the decline had already occurred
An undetermined mix that modeling studies like IMPACT have made no attempt to estimate

explanations.a: Modeling studies such as IMPACT attribute a meaningful share to prevention as well, not to treatment alone.
explanations.b: Correct: IMPACT-style models split the decline between treatment and prevention, but US and UK analyses disagree on which side contributes more, so attribution remains contested rather than settled.
explanations.c: Treatment innovations (CCUs, thrombolysis, statins) are estimated to contribute a substantial share in most analyses, not zero.
explanations.d: IMPACT and similar models have specifically attempted this split, even though the exact proportions -- and which side is larger -- remain debated between country-level analyses.

lessons.label: Cancer Epidemiology

sections.heading: Multistage carcinogenesis and decades of latency
sections.body: Cancer rarely results from a single mutation; the multistage model, formalized statistically by Armitage and Doll (1954) from the strong age-dependence of cancer incidence curves, holds that a cell must accumulate a series of independent mutational hits -- typically affecting oncogenes, tumor suppressors, and DNA repair genes -- before it escapes normal growth control. Because each hit is a rare, roughly random event, the time from first exposure to clinically detectable tumor is commonly measured in decades: lung cancer from smoking typically manifests 20-30 years after habitual exposure begins, and mesothelioma from asbestos can take 30-40 years. This latency is why cohort studies following smokers or asbestos workers only reveal the full excess risk after decades of follow-up, and why an exposure's cancer effect can be substantially underestimated by a study that ends too early.

sections.heading: The established causal agents and the IARC classification
sections.body: The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), part of the World Health Organization, sorts agents into Group 1 (carcinogenic to humans, based on sufficient human evidence), Group 2A (probably carcinogenic), Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic), and Group 3 (not classifiable), having discontinued a former Group 4 (probably not carcinogenic) category. Tobacco smoke is Group 1 and is estimated to cause roughly one-third of all cancer deaths in the United States. Other Group 1 agents illustrate distinct mechanisms: human papillomavirus (HPV), chiefly types 16 and 18, causes nearly all cervical cancer by disrupting p53 and Rb tumor-suppressor function; Helicobacter pylori causes chronic gastric inflammation linked to stomach cancer; hepatitis B virus (HBV) drives a large share of liver cancer, particularly in regions with high perinatal transmission; asbestos fibers cause mesothelioma through chronic pleural irritation; and aflatoxin, a mold toxin found in improperly stored grain and groundnuts, is a potent liver carcinogen that interacts synergistically with HBV.

sections.heading: Why screening looks better than it is: lead-time and length bias
sections.body: Screening trials and observational comparisons are vulnerable to two biases that inflate apparent benefit. Lead-time bias occurs when a screening test simply detects a cancer earlier in its natural history without changing the date of death, making survival time from diagnosis look longer even though the disease course is unaltered. Length bias occurs because screening preferentially catches slow-growing, less aggressive tumors that sit detectable longer, while fast-growing aggressive cancers are more likely to arise and cause symptoms between screening rounds; this makes screen-detected cancers look like a more survivable disease than the true underlying mix. Because of these biases, evaluating screening properly requires randomized trials measuring disease-specific or all-cause mortality, not survival time or 5-year survival percentages, which both biases can inflate without any true reduction in death.

lessons.workedExample: A hypothetical screening program adds five years of lead time to lung cancer detection: a patient truly dies at age 70 regardless of screening, but screening moves diagnosis from age 68 to age 63. Unscreened 5-year survival from diagnosis is 0% (the patient dies just 2 years after diagnosis, well before the 5-year mark), while screened 5-year survival looks like 100% (the patient survives 7 years post-diagnosis, past the 5-year mark), purely from the earlier start clock, with no change in the age of death. Add length bias -- screening catching the indolent tumors that would sit undetected for years anyway -- and the program appears to transform outcomes while true mortality is unchanged, which is why the Mayo Lung Project and later trials switched to mortality endpoints.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes whether a student can tell latency, causal classification, and screening bias apart rather than treating cancer epidemiology as one blob: can the student explain why a 20-30 year lag matters for study design, correctly place an agent in IARC's evidentiary framework instead of just calling it 'a carcinogen,' and -- most diagnostically -- explain why a screening program can raise 5-year survival without saving a single life, which separates students who understand lead-time and length bias from those reciting them as vocabulary.

questions.prompt: Tobacco smoke is classified by IARC as which group, and what share of US cancer deaths does it cause?

options.text: Group 1; roughly one-third of cancer deaths
Group 2A; roughly one-tenth of cancer deaths
Group 1; roughly two-thirds of cancer deaths
Group 2B; roughly one-third of cancer deaths

explanations.a: Correct: tobacco is Group 1, meaning sufficient evidence of human carcinogenicity, and causes roughly one-third of US cancer deaths.
explanations.b: Group 2A is 'probably carcinogenic,' a weaker evidentiary tier than tobacco's Group 1 classification, and understates its death toll.
explanations.c: One-third, not two-thirds, is the standard estimate of tobacco's share of US cancer deaths.
explanations.d: Group 2B is 'possibly carcinogenic'; tobacco has sufficient human evidence and sits in Group 1.

questions.prompt: A screening test detects a slow-growing tumor five years before it would have caused symptoms, but the patient's age at death is unchanged. This apparent survival gain is best described as:

options.text: Length bias, because the survival clock starts earlier without changing the death date
Lead-time bias, because the survival clock starts earlier without changing the death date
Confounding by indication
A true reduction in mortality

explanations.a: Length bias refers to screening preferentially catching slower-growing tumors as a class, not the shifted survival clock for a single earlier diagnosis.
explanations.b: Correct: lead-time bias is exactly this -- moving the diagnosis date earlier inflates survival time from diagnosis without changing the date of death.
explanations.c: Confounding by indication concerns why a treatment was chosen, not the mechanics of survival-time measurement in screening.
explanations.d: Since the age of death is unchanged, there is no true mortality reduction, only an artifact of when the clock starts.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of multistage carcinogenesis reasoning as Armitage and Doll's model frames them, from first exposure to clinical detection.

items.text: Initial carcinogen exposure begins
A cell accumulates a series of independent mutational hits over years to decades
The cell escapes normal growth control and begins clonal expansion
The tumor becomes large enough for clinical detection

questions.explanation: The multistage model requires sequential, independent mutations accumulated over a long latency before a cell escapes control and grows to detectable size, which is why cancer incidence rises steeply with age.

questions.prompt: Match each carcinogen to the cancer it is best established to cause.

right.text: Cervical cancer
Gastric (stomach) cancer
Liver cancer
Mesothelioma

questions.explanation: Each Group 1 agent has a distinct, well-established target organ: HPV disrupts cervical epithelial tumor suppressors, H. pylori drives chronic gastric inflammation, HBV promotes hepatocellular carcinoma, and asbestos fibers cause pleural mesothelioma.

questions.prompt: Why does length bias make screen-detected cancers look more survivable than the true underlying disease mix?

options.text: Because screening preferentially detects slow-growing tumors that remain detectable longer, while fast-growing tumors are more likely to appear between screening rounds
Because screening always improves treatment effectiveness
Because screened patients are, on average, younger than unscreened patients
Because screening tests have higher sensitivity for aggressive tumors specifically

explanations.a: Correct: slow-growing tumors sit in a detectable window longer, so periodic screening catches a disproportionate share of the less aggressive disease, skewing apparent outcomes.
explanations.b: Length bias is a detection artifact, not a claim about treatment effectiveness.
explanations.c: Length bias is about tumor growth rate, not the age distribution of screened versus unscreened patients.
explanations.d: The opposite is true: length bias arises because screening is comparatively worse at catching fast-growing, aggressive tumors between rounds.

lessons.label: Diabetes and Metabolic Disease

sections.heading: Adiposity, inactivity, and diet as drivers
sections.body: Type 2 diabetes epidemiology centers on insulin resistance driven by excess adiposity, particularly visceral fat. Cohort studies use body mass index (BMI) as a cheap population-level adiposity proxy, but waist-hip ratio and waist circumference track visceral fat more directly and predict diabetes risk better at a given BMI, since two people with identical BMI can carry very different amounts of abdominal fat. Physical inactivity independently worsens insulin sensitivity in skeletal muscle, the body's primary site of glucose disposal, while diets high in refined carbohydrates and low in fiber produce sharper glycemic swings that, sustained over years, contribute to beta-cell exhaustion. Metabolic syndrome -- the clustering of abdominal obesity, elevated triglycerides, low HDL, hypertension, and elevated fasting glucose, formalized in criteria from the National Cholesterol Education Program's ATP III report (2001) -- captures this same cluster of insulin-resistance-driven abnormalities as a single diagnosable entity.

sections.heading: Ascertainment: HbA1c versus fasting glucose
sections.body: Diabetes surveillance depends on how cases are ascertained. Fasting plasma glucose and the oral glucose tolerance test were the traditional diagnostic anchors, but glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), which integrates average blood glucose over the roughly 120-day lifespan of a red blood cell, was formally adopted as a diagnostic criterion (threshold 6.5%) by the American Diabetes Association in 2010. HbA1c requires no fasting, is less affected by day-to-day stress or illness, and is the modern standard for both clinical diagnosis and cohort classification, though it can be distorted by conditions that alter red-cell turnover, such as anemia or hemoglobinopathies.

sections.heading: From cohort risk factors to prevention trials
sections.body: Once cohort data established adiposity and inactivity as modifiable diabetes drivers, three trials tested whether intervening on them could prevent disease in high-risk (prediabetic) adults. The Da Qing Impaired Glucose Tolerance and Diabetes Study (Pan et al., 1997), conducted in China, randomized clinics rather than individuals to diet, exercise, or combined intervention and found roughly a 30-46% reduction in diabetes incidence over six years. The Finnish Diabetes Prevention Study (Tuomilehto et al., 2001) individually randomized participants to an intensive lifestyle program targeting weight loss, fat intake, and activity, cutting diabetes incidence by about 58% over roughly 3-4 years of follow-up. The US Diabetes Prevention Program (Diabetes Prevention Program Research Group, 2002) replicated this almost exactly: intensive lifestyle intervention cut incidence by 58% compared with placebo, while metformin alone achieved a 31% reduction, establishing lifestyle change as more effective than first-line pharmacotherapy in this population and anchoring diabetes prevention guidelines worldwide.

lessons.workedExample: In the US Diabetes Prevention Program, prediabetic adults with impaired glucose tolerance were randomized to intensive lifestyle change (goal: 7% weight loss and 150 minutes/week of activity), metformin 850 mg twice daily, or placebo. Over an average 2.8 years of follow-up, the lifestyle arm cut diabetes incidence by 58% relative to placebo, versus 31% for metformin -- meaning lifestyle intervention was nearly twice as effective as the drug, a result that directly traced back to cohort-level associations between adiposity, inactivity, and diabetes risk first established years earlier.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes whether a student can trace the full evidence chain: an observational association (adiposity and inactivity predict diabetes in cohorts) is not proof that intervening on those factors prevents disease -- that step required randomized trials. A student who can name Da Qing, the Finnish DPS, and the US DPP as the trials that closed that gap, and who understands why HbA1c replaced fasting glucose as the modern ascertainment standard, demonstrates they grasp epidemiology as a pipeline from association to intervention, not a single study.

questions.prompt: In the US Diabetes Prevention Program (2002), how did the intensive lifestyle intervention's effect compare to metformin?

options.text: Lifestyle cut incidence by about 58%, versus about 31% for metformin
Lifestyle cut incidence by about 31%, versus about 58% for metformin
Both arms produced identical, roughly 45% reductions
Metformin cut incidence by 58%, and lifestyle showed no significant effect

explanations.a: Correct: lifestyle intervention achieved a 58% relative reduction in diabetes incidence, compared with 31% for metformin, making lifestyle change the more effective arm.
explanations.b: This reverses the actual results; lifestyle outperformed metformin, not the other way around.
explanations.c: The two arms produced clearly different, not identical, reductions -- 58% versus 31%.
explanations.d: Lifestyle intervention was the stronger arm at 58%, and metformin still produced a real, significant 31% reduction.

questions.prompt: Why did HbA1c become the preferred diabetes ascertainment tool over a single fasting glucose measurement?

options.text: It integrates average glucose over roughly 120 days via red blood cell turnover, requires no fasting, and is less affected by day-to-day variation
It is cheaper to measure in every clinical setting
It directly measures insulin resistance in skeletal muscle
It replaced fasting glucose because fasting glucose cannot be measured accurately

explanations.a: Correct: HbA1c reflects the roughly 120-day red blood cell lifespan's worth of average glucose exposure, making it a stable integrated measure that does not require fasting.
explanations.b: Cost was not the driver of HbA1c's adoption; its integrated, fasting-independent measurement properties were.
explanations.c: HbA1c reflects average blood glucose, not a direct measurement of muscle insulin sensitivity.
explanations.d: Fasting glucose remains an accurate, valid measurement; HbA1c was adopted for its stability and convenience, not to replace an unreliable test.

questions.prompt: Order these diabetes prevention trials by publication date, earliest to latest.

items.text: Da Qing Impaired Glucose Tolerance and Diabetes Study (Pan et al.)
Finnish Diabetes Prevention Study (Tuomilehto et al.)
US Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP Research Group)

questions.explanation: Da Qing (1997) was the first of the three prevention trials, followed by the Finnish DPS (2001), then the US DPP (2002), each replicating and extending the prior finding that lifestyle intervention reduces progression to diabetes.

questions.prompt: Match each adiposity or metabolic measure to what it best captures.

right.text: Cheap, population-level overall adiposity proxy
More direct proxy for visceral fat at a given overall body size
Integrated average blood glucose over ~120 days
Cluster of abdominal obesity, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and hyperglycemia as one diagnosable entity

questions.explanation: Each measure serves a different epidemiological purpose: BMI is a coarse population screen, waist-hip ratio isolates visceral adiposity, HbA1c integrates glycemic exposure over months, and metabolic syndrome criteria bundle the insulin-resistance cluster into one label.

lessons.label: Obesity Epidemiology and Its Paradoxes

sections.heading: The BMI-mortality curve is not a straight line
sections.body: When cohort studies plot all-cause mortality against BMI, the result is not a monotonic climb but a J- or U-shape: mortality is lowest in a middle BMI band, roughly 20-25 kg/m2 in most large pooled analyses, rises steeply at very low BMI, and rises more gradually at high BMI. The low end reflects both genuine harm from underweight (frailty, malnutrition) and reverse causation, since occult illness -- undiagnosed cancer, chronic infection, heart failure -- causes weight loss before it causes death, pulling thin, sick people into the low-BMI category and inflating its mortality. The upper end's shallower slope surprised many public-health researchers, since obesity is a well-established risk factor for diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease, yet its mortality signal at moderate obesity levels is less steep than that comorbidity burden alone would predict.

sections.heading: The obesity paradox in heart failure and dialysis
sections.body: In specific patient populations who already have advanced disease -- heart failure and end-stage renal disease on dialysis are the two most studied -- higher BMI is repeatedly associated with lower short- and medium-term mortality, the so-called obesity paradox first widely reported in heart-failure cohorts and in dialysis cohorts in the early 2000s. This inverted relationship, where a factor otherwise known to cause a disease appears protective once the disease is already present, is a hallmark case for teaching selection effects: it is not that obesity truly protects sick patients, but that the way patients enter these cohorts is not random with respect to both BMI and disease severity.

sections.heading: Collider bias and reverse causation as explanations
sections.body: Two mechanisms are usually invoked. Collider bias arises when a study conditions on (restricts its sample to) a variable -- here, having heart failure or being on dialysis -- that is itself a common effect of both obesity and other, unmeasured causes of poor prognosis; conditioning on this collider can induce a spurious inverse association between obesity and mortality within the restricted group even if no true protective effect exists. Reverse causation compounds this: chronic disease itself often causes involuntary weight loss (cachexia) well before death, so among sick patients, the leanest are disproportionately those already dying, making higher BMI look protective by comparison. Together these mean the obesity paradox is widely interpreted as a methodological artifact of studying a selected, already-diseased population rather than evidence that weight gain benefits survival, and it does not extend to primary prevention in the general population.

lessons.workedExample: Consider two groups entering a heart-failure registry: normal-weight patients who developed heart failure primarily from severe, aggressive cardiac disease (few other risk factors needed), and obese patients whose heart failure emerged more gradually from long-term hypertension and diabetes. The obese group may on average have less severe underlying cardiac dysfunction at entry, precisely because obesity alone was often sufficient to trigger disease, while normal-weight patients needed a more severe insult to reach the same registry. This selection difference, not a protective biological effect of fat tissue, can generate the observed inverse BMI-mortality association within the cohort -- a textbook instance of collider bias reinforced by reverse causation, both artifacts of conditioning on an already-diseased sample rather than any survival benefit of weight gain.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes whether a student can explain WHY the obesity paradox appears without concluding that obesity is protective -- the diagnostic failure is a student who reports the paradox as a genuine biological finding rather than naming collider bias and reverse causation as the leading methodological explanations, and who cannot articulate why restricting a sample to an already-diseased population changes the exposure-outcome relationship observed within it.

questions.prompt: In large pooled cohort analyses, the BMI-mortality relationship is best described as:

options.text: A straight line, with mortality rising steadily as BMI rises from the lowest to highest values
A J- or U-shape, with lowest mortality around BMI 20-25 and higher mortality at both low and high extremes
Flat, showing no relationship between BMI and mortality at any level
Inverted, with mortality falling continuously as BMI rises

explanations.a: The relationship is not linear; both very low and very high BMI show elevated mortality relative to the middle range.
explanations.b: Correct: pooled analyses consistently show a J- or U-shaped curve, with the nadir around BMI 20-25 kg/m2.
explanations.c: A flat relationship would contradict the well-documented elevated mortality at both BMI extremes.
explanations.d: Mortality does not fall continuously with rising BMI; it rises again, though more gradually, at higher BMI levels.

questions.prompt: The 'obesity paradox' observed in heart-failure and dialysis cohorts, where higher BMI predicts lower mortality, is best interpreted as:

options.text: Strong evidence that weight gain protects the general population from cardiovascular death
A methodological artifact, largely explained by collider bias and reverse causation (disease-driven weight loss) within an already-diseased, selected cohort
Proof that BMI is an inaccurate measure and should never be used in cohort studies
Evidence that obesity's cardiovascular risks were overstated in prior general-population cohorts

explanations.a: The paradox is observed only within already-diseased, selected populations and does not generalize to primary prevention advice for the general population.
explanations.b: Correct: conditioning on an already-diseased cohort (a collider) plus disease-driven weight loss (reverse causation) are the leading explanations for the inverted association.
explanations.c: BMI's limitations as an adiposity measure are a separate issue; the paradox is chiefly a selection and reverse-causation artifact, not evidence BMI is meaningless.
explanations.d: General-population cohorts' findings on obesity and cardiovascular risk are not undermined by a paradox that arises specifically from conditioning on advanced disease.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning steps that explain how collider bias could produce an inverse BMI-mortality association within a heart-failure cohort.

items.text: Both obesity and other unmeasured factors can independently cause heart failure
A study restricts its sample to only patients who already have heart failure (conditions on the collider)
Within this restricted sample, obese patients disproportionately reached heart failure via obesity alone, while normal-weight patients needed more severe underlying disease
This selection difference can produce a spurious inverse association between BMI and mortality within the cohort

questions.explanation: Collider bias requires first that two causes act on a shared outcome, then that the study conditions on that outcome, which reshapes the apparent relationship between the two original causes within the restricted sample.

questions.prompt: Match each mechanism to its role in explaining the obesity paradox.

right.text: Chronic disease causes weight loss (cachexia) before death, making leanness a marker of severe illness rather than health
Restricting a study to an already-diseased population can induce a spurious association between two of its independent causes

questions.explanation: Reverse causation and collider bias are the two leading explanations specifically for the obesity paradox.

lessons.label: Physical Activity, Diet, and Alcohol

sections.heading: Physical activity: a dose-response curve that plateaus
sections.body: Cohort studies consistently show an inverse dose-response relationship between physical activity and all-cause mortality: each additional increment of activity confers a mortality benefit, but the curve is steepest at the low end, meaning the jump from sedentary to modestly active yields the largest relative gain, while further increases beyond roughly 150-300 minutes per week of moderate activity (the range underlying WHO and US physical activity guidelines) produce progressively smaller additional benefit. This plateau pattern -- large early returns, diminishing later ones -- is a recurring shape in behavioral epidemiology and is the basis for public health messaging that emphasizes moving sedentary people to any activity rather than optimizing already-active people to elite levels.

sections.heading: Dietary patterns and the PREDIMED trial
sections.body: Because diet is a bundle of correlated exposures, nutritional epidemiology increasingly studies whole dietary patterns rather than single nutrients. The Mediterranean diet -- high in olive oil, nuts, vegetables, and fish, low in red meat and refined carbohydrates -- was linked to lower cardiovascular risk in decades of observational cohorts before PREDIMED (Estruch et al., initially published 2013, with a corrected re-analysis in 2018 addressing a randomization irregularity at one site) tested it as a randomized trial in Spain. PREDIMED randomized high-cardiovascular-risk adults to a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil, a Mediterranean diet supplemented with mixed nuts, or a low-fat control diet, and found roughly a 30% relative reduction in major cardiovascular events in both Mediterranean-diet arms, providing rare randomized-trial confirmation of a pattern epidemiologists had inferred from cohorts alone.

sections.heading: Alcohol: from the J-curve to 'no safe level'
sections.body: For decades, cohort studies reported a J-shaped curve between alcohol intake and cardiovascular mortality, with light-to-moderate drinkers showing lower risk than abstainers -- a finding partly explained by the 'sick quitter' problem, where the abstainer comparison group includes former heavy drinkers who quit due to illness, dragging down the abstainer group's apparent health. The 2018 Global Burden of Disease study (Lancet, GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators) reanalyzed alcohol's total health burden across cancer, injury, and cardiovascular outcomes combined, and concluded that the level of consumption minimizing overall health loss was zero, a 'no safe level' finding that reframed decades of J-curve messaging and remains actively debated given the study's reliance on modeled risk curves and self-reported intake.

sections.heading: The shared weakness: self-report
sections.body: All three exposures -- activity, diet, and alcohol -- are still measured predominantly through self-report questionnaires (physical activity recalls, food-frequency questionnaires, alcohol-intake surveys), which suffer from social-desirability bias (underreporting alcohol and overreporting exercise) and simple recall error. This shared measurement weakness is why device-based accelerometry and objective biomarkers are increasingly used to validate or replace self-report in newer cohorts, and why effect sizes from decades-old self-report-only cohorts should be read with some caution about measurement error attenuating or distorting true associations.

lessons.workedExample: PREDIMED enrolled about 7,447 participants at high cardiovascular risk (mostly with diabetes or multiple risk factors, but no baseline cardiovascular disease) and followed them for a median of about 4.8 years. Both Mediterranean-diet arms (olive oil and nuts) showed roughly a 30% relative reduction in the composite endpoint of myocardial infarction, stroke, or cardiovascular death compared with the low-fat control diet -- a result strong enough that the trial was stopped early for efficacy, converting decades of Mediterranean-diet cohort associations into randomized causal evidence.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes whether a student understands that behavioral exposures carry a double burden: first, self-report measurement error that can distort or attenuate true associations, and second, the specific confounding structures within each exposure -- the 'sick quitter' problem inflating alcohol's apparent J-curve, or observational diet associations needing a trial like PREDIMED before they support causal claims. A student who cites PREDIMED's ~30% relative risk reduction and explains why the 2018 GBD alcohol reanalysis overturned the J-curve narrative shows they can track how the same exposure area's evidence base evolved and was revised.

questions.prompt: In PREDIMED, both Mediterranean-diet arms (olive oil and nuts) showed approximately what relative reduction in major cardiovascular events compared with the low-fat control diet?

options.text: About 30%
About 5%
About 70%
No significant reduction

explanations.a: Correct: PREDIMED found roughly a 30% relative reduction in the composite cardiovascular endpoint in both Mediterranean-diet arms.
explanations.b: 5% understates PREDIMED's finding, which was large enough to stop the trial early for efficacy.
explanations.c: 70% overstates the actual reported relative risk reduction from the trial.
explanations.d: The reduction was statistically significant and substantial, not null; that was the trial's headline finding.

questions.prompt: The 'sick quitter' problem helps explain which observed pattern in alcohol epidemiology?

options.text: The apparent J-curve, where the abstainer comparison group includes former heavy drinkers who quit due to illness, making abstainers look less healthy than light drinkers
Why heavy drinkers report the lowest cardiovascular mortality
Why the 2018 GBD study found alcohol has no health effects at any dose
Why physical activity guidelines recommend 150-300 minutes per week

explanations.a: Correct: including former heavy drinkers who quit due to illness within the 'abstainer' group inflates that group's apparent mortality, making light-to-moderate drinkers look artificially protected by comparison.
explanations.b: Heavy drinkers do not show the lowest mortality in these cohorts; light-to-moderate drinkers appeared most protected, which is the pattern being explained.
explanations.c: The 2018 GBD study found the opposite -- that the risk-minimizing consumption level was zero, not that alcohol has no effect.
explanations.d: Physical activity dose-response guidelines are unrelated to the sick-quitter phenomenon, which is specific to alcohol cohort studies.

questions.prompt: Order the evolution of evidence on alcohol and cardiovascular risk.

items.text: Decades of cohort studies report a J-shaped curve: light-to-moderate drinkers show lower cardiovascular risk than abstainers
Researchers identify the 'sick quitter' problem as a likely confounder inflating the abstainer group's apparent risk
The 2018 Global Burden of Disease study reanalyzes total health burden across outcomes and concludes the risk-minimizing consumption level is zero

questions.explanation: The J-curve observation came first from decades of cohort data, the sick-quitter explanation for its likely confounding followed, and the 2018 GBD reanalysis is the more recent revision using a broader combined-outcome framework.

questions.prompt: Match each behavioral exposure area to the specific evidentiary development described in this lesson.

right.text: Dose-response curve with the steepest mortality benefit at low activity levels, plateauing near 150-300 minutes/week
Randomized trial (PREDIMED) confirmed roughly 30% relative cardiovascular risk reduction after decades of cohort association
2018 Global Burden of Disease reanalysis shifted the field from a J-curve to a 'no safe level' conclusion

questions.explanation: Each exposure area followed a distinct evidentiary path: activity shows a plateauing dose-response, Mediterranean diet moved from cohort association to randomized confirmation, and alcohol's evidence base was substantially revised by a combined-outcome reanalysis.

lessons.label: From Risk Factor to Policy

sections.heading: Population attributable fraction as the policy lever
sections.body: The population attributable fraction (PAF) estimates the share of disease burden in a population that would be eliminated if an exposure were removed entirely, combining the exposure's prevalence with its relative risk. PAF, not relative risk alone, is what justifies population-level policy: a modest relative risk affecting nearly everyone (like moderate sodium intake) can carry a larger PAF, and thus a larger policy payoff, than a large relative risk affecting very few people. This is the quantitative bridge between a cohort finding ('smokers have a relative risk of lung cancer around 20-fold that of never-smokers') and a policy question ('how much lung cancer would a smoking ban actually prevent').

sections.heading: Natural experiments testing whether policy worked
sections.body: Because randomizing a whole population to a tax or ban is rarely feasible, policy evaluation leans on natural experiments -- comparing jurisdictions or time periods that adopted a policy against similar ones that did not. Tobacco taxation and clean-indoor-air laws, studied across US states and countries over decades, are consistently associated with reduced smoking prevalence and, with a lag matching cardiovascular disease's shorter latency, reduced acute myocardial infarction hospitalizations shortly after bans take effect -- a pattern documented in numerous before-after and difference-in-differences studies of local smoking bans. Denmark's 2003-2004 industrial trans-fat restriction, one of the first national bans, was followed by studies showing reduced cardiovascular mortality trends relative to comparable countries without such bans, contributing evidence that helped motivate the US FDA's 2015 determination that partially hydrogenated oils were no longer 'generally recognized as safe,' phased out by 2018. Salt-reduction policies, such as the UK's voluntary food-reformulation program beginning in 2003, were followed by measured population sodium-intake declines and modeled reductions in stroke and cardiovascular mortality, though the voluntary, industry-negotiated design makes isolating the policy's independent effect harder than a hard regulatory ban.

sections.heading: Sugar-sweetened beverage taxes and statin thresholds
sections.body: Sugar-sweetened beverage (SSB) taxes, implemented in Mexico (2014) and Berkeley, California (2015) among many others, function as natural experiments repeatedly showing reduced purchases of taxed beverages, with Mexico's tax associated with a roughly 6-12% decline in SSB purchases in the years following implementation, though longer-term effects on obesity and diabetes incidence are harder to isolate given many simultaneous secular trends. Statin primary-prevention thresholds -- the ASCVD risk level at which guidelines recommend starting a statin in someone without existing cardiovascular disease -- illustrate policy running in the other direction, converting an individual multivariable risk equation (the Pooled Cohort Equations) directly into a population-wide treatment rule, which is itself periodically revised as PAF calculations and trial evidence on statin benefit at lower risk thresholds accumulate.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose sodium intake has a modest relative risk for stroke (around 1.2-1.3 per large intake increment) but nearly the entire population is exposed to excess sodium, versus a rare occupational carcinogen with a relative risk of 10 affecting 0.1% of the population. Even though the carcinogen's relative risk is far higher, sodium's PAF can be larger simply because exposure prevalence is so much greater, which is exactly the logic that made population-wide sodium-reduction programs (like the UK's) a more efficient policy lever than any feasible carcinogen-specific occupational regulation -- PAF, not relative risk, tells you where population intervention pays off most.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes whether a student can explain why a modest relative risk can still justify a sweeping policy (the PAF argument), and whether they can name a specific natural experiment -- Denmark's trans-fat ban, Mexico's SSB tax, a local smoking ban -- and describe how its before-after or jurisdictional comparison design let researchers estimate a real-world effect without randomizing an entire population, which is the last link in the chain from cohort risk factor to policy outcome.

questions.prompt: Why can a modest relative risk exposure justify more aggressive population-level policy than a rare exposure with a much larger relative risk?

options.text: Because population attributable fraction depends on both relative risk and exposure prevalence, and a widespread modest exposure can produce a larger PAF than a rare strong one
Because relative risk is always a less reliable statistic than prevalence
Because policy should always target the exposure with the highest relative risk, regardless of prevalence
Because natural experiments can only be conducted on common exposures

explanations.a: Correct: PAF combines relative risk and prevalence, so a common, modestly risky exposure can eliminate more disease burden if removed than a rare, highly risky one.
explanations.b: Relative risk is not inherently less reliable than prevalence; both are needed together to compute the policy-relevant PAF.
explanations.c: Targeting only the highest relative risk while ignoring prevalence is precisely the reasoning error PAF is designed to correct.
explanations.d: Natural experiments can and do study rare exposures too; the PAF argument is about disease burden, not study feasibility.

questions.prompt: Denmark's 2003-2004 restriction on industrial trans fats is an example of which evaluation approach, given that randomizing a whole population to a policy is rarely feasible?

options.text: A natural experiment, comparing outcome trends before and after the policy (and against comparable countries without it)
A randomized controlled trial with individual-level randomization
A case-control study matched on trans-fat exposure
A cross-sectional survey with no comparison group

explanations.a: Correct: policy evaluations like Denmark's ban rely on natural experiments -- comparing before/after trends and similar jurisdictions without the policy -- since individual randomization to a national ban is not feasible.
explanations.b: A national ban cannot randomize individuals; it is evaluated as a natural experiment, not an RCT.
explanations.c: Case-control studies sample by outcome status for individual exposures; a national policy evaluation instead compares population trends across time or place.
explanations.d: A cross-sectional survey without any before-after or comparison-jurisdiction design could not isolate the policy's effect, which is why natural-experiment designs with a comparison group are used.

questions.prompt: Order the steps that connect a cohort risk factor to an evaluated population policy.

items.text: A cohort study establishes an exposure-disease association and its relative risk
Population attributable fraction is calculated by combining that relative risk with exposure prevalence
A policy (tax, ban, reformulation program) is enacted in one jurisdiction or time period
A natural experiment compares outcome trends against a similar jurisdiction or the pre-policy period to estimate the policy's real-world effect

questions.explanation: The chain runs from establishing an association, to quantifying its population-level burden via PAF, to enacting a policy, to evaluating that policy's actual effect through a natural-experiment design.

questions.prompt: Match each policy or program to the exposure it targeted.

left.text: Denmark's 2003-2004 ban (motivating the US FDA's 2015 trans-fat determination)

right.text: Industrial trans fats
Sugar-sweetened beverages
Dietary sodium
Statin primary-prevention initiation

questions.explanation: Each policy targets a distinct chronic-disease exposure identified first through cohort epidemiology: trans fats and cardiovascular mortality, SSBs and metabolic disease, sodium and stroke/cardiovascular risk, and statin thresholds converting individual ASCVD risk equations into population treatment rules.

lessons.label: Populations, Samples, and the Logic of Inference

sections.heading: Parameter versus statistic
sections.body: A target population is every unit a researcher wants to draw conclusions about — every diabetic adult in the United States, say — while a study sample is the smaller group actually measured. A parameter (population mean μ, population proportion p) is a fixed but usually unknowable true value; a statistic (sample mean x̄, sample proportion p̂) is what you compute from the sample and use to estimate it. Inference is the entire logical bridge between the two: you never observe μ directly, you only ever observe x̄ and reason about how close it is likely to be. That reasoning only works if the sample was drawn in a way that gives every population member a known, nonzero chance of selection — probability sampling — rather than being chosen for convenience.

sections.heading: Sampling variability is not sampling error in the colloquial sense
sections.body: Even a perfectly executed random sample will not exactly reproduce the population parameter, because different random draws pull different individuals. This sample-to-sample fluctuation is sampling variability, and it is a mathematical certainty, not a mistake — it shrinks as sample size grows but never vanishes. Confusing sampling variability with sloppy measurement is a common student error: a well-drawn sample of 200 will still disagree with the true population value by some predictable amount, and statistics quantifies exactly how much through the standard error. For a sample proportion, SE = sqrt(p(1-p)/n) — the predictable spread of p̂ around the true p, driven entirely by n. Plugging in p = 0.5 (the most conservative case) gives SE ≈ 7.1 percentage points at n = 50 but only SE ≈ 3.5 points at n = 200: quadrupling the sample size halves the typical sample-to-sample swing, because SE shrinks with the square root of n, not with n itself. That square-root relationship is why sampling variability shrinks but never vanishes — no finite sample eliminates it, it only narrows.

sections.heading: Representativeness is decided at the moment of selection
sections.body: The most consequential decision in any study happens before a single measurement is taken: who gets a chance to be selected. The 1936 Literary Digest poll mailed 10 million straw ballots (about 2.4 million returned) drawn from telephone directories and car-registration lists, then confidently predicted Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt. Roosevelt won with 60.8% of the popular vote. The sampling frame itself was the flaw — in 1936, phone and car owners skewed wealthier and more Republican than the electorate, so no amount of extra mail could fix it. George Gallup, sampling roughly 50,000 people chosen to mirror the electorate's known makeup, called the result correctly. Statistician Jerzy Neyman's 1934 paper formalized why probability-based selection, not sheer sample size, is what licenses generalizing from sample to population.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher wants to know the average resting heart rate of all 14-year-olds in a school district (the target population, true mean μ unknown). She measures a random sample of 150 students and gets a sample mean x̄ = 78 bpm. A second researcher independently draws a different random sample of 150 and gets x̄ = 76 bpm. Both samples were drawn correctly; the 2 bpm gap is ordinary sampling variability, not an error in either study. If instead she had recruited her sample from students already at the nurse's office that week, x̄ might be systematically elevated regardless of sample size — a representativeness failure that no amount of resampling repairs.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can name their target population precisely and explain how their actual sample was drawn, because a mismatch between the two — a sample of volunteers standing in for 'all teenagers,' say — silently limits every conclusion that follows. A student who says 'we can't be sure our sample represents the population because X' shows more statistical maturity than one who reports a p-value without ever stating who the population is, since every subsequent inference inherits whatever selection happened at recruitment.

questions.prompt: Two independent random samples of the same population produce slightly different sample means. What best explains this?

options.text: At least one of the samples must have been measured incorrectly
Ordinary sampling variability, expected even with correct random sampling
The population parameter itself changed between the two samples
Random sampling should always produce identical sample means

explanations.a: Measurement error is possible but not required to explain the gap; random sampling alone produces different statistics from different draws.
