A strong answer states explicitly that Phase I has no control arm and isn't testing efficacy, that Phase II is signal-seeking and underpowered for confirmation, and that only Phase III is designed and powered to be the definitive test — showing the student understands why a promising Phase II result routinely fails to replicate in Phase III.

questions.prompt: In a 3+3 dose-escalation design, if 2 of the first 3 participants at a given dose show dose-limiting toxicity, what happens next?

options.text: Three more participants are added at that same dose to confirm
Escalation stops, and the prior (lower) dose is taken as the maximum tolerated dose
The dose is escalated further to see if toxicity resolves
The trial moves directly to Phase II at that dose

explanations.a: Expanding the cohort to confirm toxicity applies to the case of exactly 1 of 3 showing toxicity, not 2 or more.
explanations.b: Correct: 2 or more toxicities out of 3 (or out of an expanded cohort) means that dose is too high, so the previous, lower dose level is declared the maximum tolerated dose.
explanations.c: Continuing to escalate after 2 of 3 toxicities would violate the safety logic the 3+3 design exists to enforce.
explanations.d: Phase I concludes with a maximum tolerated dose determination; it does not itself decide to advance to Phase II, which is a separate, later decision based on further data.

questions.prompt: Order the phases of clinical trials from earliest to latest in a drug's development.

items.text: Phase I: dose-finding and safety in a small group
Phase II: preliminary efficacy signal in a few hundred patients
Phase III: confirmatory, powered trial against a defined control
Phase IV: post-marketing surveillance in the general population

questions.explanation: Drug development proceeds from safety and dosing, to a signal of efficacy, to a definitive powered confirmatory trial, to real-world surveillance after approval.

questions.prompt: Match each phase to its primary objective.

right.text: Determine the maximum tolerated dose and basic safety, with no control group
Provide the pivotal, powered confirmatory evidence regulators use for approval
Detect rare adverse events in the general prescribing population after approval

questions.explanation: Phase I is about dose and safety; Phase III is the definitive powered trial; Phase IV surveils the drug once it reaches a much larger, more diverse population.

units.label: Statistical Inference: p-values, Confidence Intervals, and Tests

lessons.label: The Logic of Significance Testing

sections.heading: Starting from a straw man
sections.body: Every significance test begins with a null hypothesis (H0), a specific, boring claim you provisionally accept as true even though you suspect it is wrong: the new drug has no effect, the coin is fair, the two groups have equal means. Ronald Fisher formalized this move in Statistical Methods for Research Workers (1925): rather than trying to prove your research hypothesis directly, you assume its opposite and see whether the data make that assumption look absurd. The null is a straw man built specifically to be knocked down by evidence, not a claim anyone believes is likely true.

sections.heading: A ruler for distance from the null
sections.body: To knock it down you need a test statistic, a single number that measures how far the observed data sit from what H0 predicts, in standardized units. A z-statistic for a mean is (sample mean minus hypothesized mean) divided by the standard error; a t-statistic does the same with an estimated standard deviation; a chi-square statistic sums squared standardized deviations across categories. The standardization matters: it converts raw differences, which depend on the units and sample size of the specific study, into a common currency of 'how many standard errors away.' The t-distribution's exact shape depends on degrees of freedom (df), which count how many independent pieces of information remain after estimating the parameters needed for the test; for a two-sample t-test on independent groups with sample sizes n1 and n2, df = n1 + n2 - 2, because one degree of freedom is spent estimating each group's mean before the pooled standard deviation can be computed.

sections.heading: The reference distribution and the reasoning chain
sections.body: The null/reference distribution is the sampling distribution the test statistic would follow across repeated studies if H0 were exactly true and only chance were operating — a standard normal curve, a t-distribution with specific degrees of freedom, a chi-square curve. The full logic chain is: (1) assume H0 true, (2) compute the test statistic from your actual sample, (3) locate that statistic on the reference distribution H0 predicts, (4) ask how far into the tail it falls. A statistic buried in the middle of the distribution is unremarkable under H0; one far in the tail is the kind of result H0 rarely produces, which is the seed of everything a p-value later quantifies.

lessons.workedExample: A trial compares recovery time for a new anti-inflammatory (n=30, mean=5.2 days) against placebo (n=30, mean=6.0 days), pooled SD=1.8 days. H0: true mean difference is 0. The test statistic is t = (6.0-5.2) / (1.8 * sqrt(1/30+1/30)) = 0.8/0.465 ≈ 1.72, with df=58. Under H0, this t-statistic follows a t-distribution centered at 0; a value of 1.72 sits out in the upper tail rather than near the center, which is the raw signal that gets translated into a p-value in the next lesson.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because students routinely skip straight to 'p=0.03, significant' without being able to say what was assumed, what was measured, or against what reference. A judge asking 'what distribution is your test statistic being compared to, and why that one?' is checking whether the student understands the test is a conditional argument (if H0, then this statistic should look like X) rather than a black-box significance button.

questions.prompt: What role does the null hypothesis play in a significance test?

options.text: It is the claim the researcher believes is most likely true
It is a specific default assumption of no effect, provisionally assumed true so the data can be judged against it
It is calculated from the test statistic after the data are collected
It is only needed for chi-square tests, not t-tests

explanations.a: Researchers typically suspect H0 is false; that is why they ran the study. It is a provisional straw man, not their belief.
explanations.b: Correct: H0 is fixed in advance as a specific no-effect claim, assumed true so the observed data can be evaluated against its predictions.
explanations.c: H0 must be specified before analysis; it is not derived from the test statistic, the test statistic is derived using H0.
explanations.d: Every significance test, from z-tests to ANOVA, requires a null hypothesis; it is not chi-square-specific.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in the core significance-testing reasoning chain.

items.text: Assume the null hypothesis is exactly true
Compute a standardized test statistic from the observed sample
Locate that statistic on the reference distribution H0 predicts
Judge how far into the tail the statistic falls

questions.explanation: The chain only works in this order: you must fix H0 first, then compute the statistic from data, then compare it to the distribution H0 implies, then assess extremity.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in a significance test.

right.text: The default no-effect claim assumed true for the argument
A standardized number measuring distance between data and H0's prediction
The distribution the test statistic follows across repeated studies if H0 holds

questions.explanation: H0 supplies the assumption, the test statistic supplies the measurement, and the reference distribution supplies the yardstick for judging that measurement.

lessons.label: What a p-value Is and Is Not

sections.heading: The precise definition
sections.body: A p-value is the probability, calculated ASSUMING the null hypothesis is true, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one actually obtained — formally P(data this extreme or more | H0 true). Every word in that definition is load-bearing. It is a probability about data (or a summary statistic of data), not about hypotheses. It is conditional on H0, meaning the calculation never touches the probability that H0 itself is true or false. And 'at least as extreme' means the p-value sums up the tail area, not just the single point you observed, which is why a two-sided test doubles the one-sided tail: if a test statistic cuts off 0.02 of the area in one tail of the reference distribution, the two-sided p-value counts the matching 0.02 in the opposite tail too, giving p = 0.02 + 0.02 = 0.04.

sections.heading: Four ways students misread it
sections.body: First, a p-value is NOT P(H0 true | data) — that reversed conditional (the probability the null is true given what you saw) is called the inverse-probability fallacy, and computing it actually requires Bayes' theorem plus a prior probability that classical p-values never supply. Second, a p-value is not the probability the effect is due to chance; it says nothing about alternative explanations like confounding or bias. Third, a small p-value is not a measure of effect size or clinical importance — a p=0.001 can come from a tiny, meaningless difference in a huge sample (Lesson 7 develops this). Fourth, p=0.03 does not mean there is a 97% chance the result would replicate; replication probability is a different quantity entirely and depends on the study's power, not just its p-value.

sections.heading: Why 0.05 is a convention, not a law
sections.body: Fisher suggested treating p<0.05 as a convenient threshold for 'worth a second look' in Statistical Methods for Research Workers (1925), explicitly as a rule of thumb, not a boundary derived from any first principle. There is no mathematical reason 0.05 is more correct than 0.01 or 0.10 — it became standard largely through decades of textbook and journal habit, and the American Statistical Association's 2016 statement on p-values explicitly warned against treating it as a bright line separating 'real' from 'not real' effects.

lessons.workedExample: A trial reports p=0.04 for a new supplement's effect on cholesterol. Correct reading: if the supplement truly had zero effect, a difference this large or larger would occur in about 4% of studies of this design by chance alone. Incorrect readings to flag: 'there's a 96% chance the supplement works' (reverses the conditional), 'the effect is real and clinically meaningful' (says nothing about size), and 'this would replicate 96% of the time' (conflates p-value with replication probability, which depends on power).
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask students to state their p-value's meaning in one sentence because the four misreadings are so common that a correct, precise sentence is a strong signal of real understanding. A student who says 'p=0.03 means there's a 3% chance the null is true' has revealed they don't know what was actually computed, even if every number in their poster is otherwise correct.

questions.prompt: A study reports p=0.02 for a treatment effect. What does this value literally represent?

options.text: The probability that the null hypothesis is true
The probability of observing data this extreme or more, assuming the null hypothesis is true
The probability the treatment effect will replicate in a future study
The size of the treatment effect

explanations.a: This reverses the conditional; computing P(H0 true|data) requires Bayes' theorem and a prior, which a classical p-value never uses.
explanations.b: Correct: the p-value is a conditional probability about the data given H0, not a probability about the hypothesis.
explanations.c: Replication probability depends on statistical power and effect size, not on the p-value from a single study alone.
explanations.d: A p-value carries no information about magnitude; a tiny effect and a huge effect can produce the identical p-value under different sample sizes.

questions.prompt: Why is the conventional 0.05 threshold described as 'arbitrary'?

options.text: Because it was derived mathematically from the properties of the normal distribution
Because Fisher proposed it as a convenient rule of thumb, not a principled cutoff, and it became standard through convention rather than proof
Because it only applies to chi-square tests
Because it changes depending on the sample size of the study

explanations.a: No derivation ties 0.05 specifically to any distribution; other thresholds like 0.01 are equally mathematically valid choices.
explanations.b: Correct: Fisher's 1925 suggestion was a convenience, and its dominance since is a matter of adopted habit, reinforced by the 2016 ASA statement warning against treating it as a bright line.
explanations.c: The 0.05 convention is applied across virtually all classical test types, not one specific test.
explanations.d: The threshold itself is fixed by convention; it is the p-value's numeric result, not the threshold, that varies with sample size.

questions.prompt: Match each misreading of a p-value to the concept it wrongly imports.

left.text: 'p=0.03 means 97% chance the null is false'

right.text: Confuses the p-value with a replication probability, which depends on power
Reverses the conditional probability (inverse-probability fallacy)
Confuses statistical significance with effect size

questions.explanation: Each misreading swaps the p-value for a different quantity it was never computed to represent — a hypothesis probability, an effect size, or a replication rate.

lessons.label: Type I and Type II Errors

sections.heading: The 2x2 table of truth versus decision
sections.body: Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson formalized hypothesis testing as a decision problem in a series of papers in 1928 and 1933, crossing the unknown truth (H0 actually true or false) against the decision the test makes (reject or fail to reject H0). That crossing produces four cells. A Type I error is rejecting a true H0 — a false positive, declaring an effect that isn't there. A Type II error is failing to reject a false H0 — a false negative, missing a real effect. The other two cells are correct decisions: correctly retaining a true H0, and correctly rejecting a false one.

sections.heading: Alpha, beta, and the tradeoff between them
sections.body: Alpha (α) is the Type I error rate, the probability of a false positive, set by the researcher before the study — conventionally 0.05, meaning a 5% chance of a false alarm if H0 is really true. Beta (β) is the Type II error rate, the probability of a false negative; 1-β is statistical power, the chance of correctly detecting a real effect (developed further in the power lesson). For a fixed sample size, alpha and beta trade off directly: tightening alpha to 0.01 to guard harder against false positives makes the test more conservative, which mechanically raises beta — the rejection boundary itself moves outward (for a two-sided z-test, the critical value shifts from z=1.96 at α=0.05 to z=2.576 at α=0.01), so real effects now need to clear a higher bar, and more of them get missed. The only way to shrink both simultaneously is to collect more data.

sections.heading: One-sided versus two-sided: spending alpha differently
sections.body: A two-sided test splits alpha across both tails of the reference distribution (e.g., 0.025 in each tail for α=0.05), flagging a result as significant whether the effect runs positive or negative. A one-sided test puts the entire alpha in one tail, which is only justified when a difference in the other direction is genuinely impossible or irrelevant to the question being asked — deciding this after seeing which direction the data went is a well-known way to inflate the true false-positive rate, since a researcher can always find a post hoc reason to call a result one-sided.

lessons.workedExample: A screening test for a rare cancer is evaluated with α=0.05 and the trial is powered at 80% (β=0.20). Out of 1,000 hypothetical trials where the drug truly has no effect, about 50 would show p<0.05 by chance alone (Type I errors). Out of 1,000 hypothetical trials where the drug truly does work, about 200 would fail to reach significance (Type II errors) at that power level, and 800 would correctly detect the effect. Lowering α to 0.01 without adding participants would push that 800 down, since the bar for detection just got higher.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'what did you set alpha to, and what does that choice cost you in beta?' because a project that reports p<0.05 without ever mentioning power is only telling half the error story. A student who can explain why they chose a two-sided test, or why a one-sided test was justified for their specific hypothesis, is demonstrating they understand hypothesis testing as a pre-specified decision rule rather than a post hoc label applied after seeing the data.

questions.prompt: A researcher lowers alpha from 0.05 to 0.01 without increasing sample size. What happens to beta?

options.text: Beta decreases, since the test is now more rigorous overall
Beta increases, because the higher bar for significance makes real effects harder to detect
Beta is unaffected, since alpha and beta are set independently
Beta becomes zero, since Type I errors are now nearly eliminated

explanations.a: Rigor against false positives is not free; it comes at the cost of more false negatives when sample size is held fixed.
explanations.b: Correct: for a fixed sample size, alpha and beta trade off — a stricter threshold for rejecting H0 means real effects must be larger or samples must be bigger to still clear it.
explanations.c: Alpha and beta are linked through the sampling distribution and sample size; changing one while holding sample size fixed moves the other.
explanations.d: Lowering alpha reduces Type I errors but has no direct effect that would drive Type II errors to zero; in fact it typically raises them.

questions.prompt: Order these from the researcher's decision that carries the LOWEST risk of a false conclusion to the HIGHEST, for a fixed sample size, when H0 is actually true.

items.text: Setting alpha = 0.01 (strict threshold)
Setting alpha = 0.05 (conventional threshold)
Setting alpha = 0.10 (lenient threshold)

questions.explanation: When H0 is true, alpha IS the false-positive rate, so a smaller alpha directly means a smaller chance of wrongly rejecting a true null; 0.01 < 0.05 < 0.10.

questions.prompt: Match each cell of the truth-versus-decision table to its label.

left.text: Reject H0 when H0 is actually true
Fail to reject H0 when H0 is actually false
Reject H0 when H0 is actually false

right.text: Type I error (false positive)
Correct decision (power, 1-β)
Type II error (false negative)

questions.explanation: The four-cell table has two error cells (Type I: false alarm, Type II: missed effect) and two correct-decision cells; power is specifically the correct-rejection cell.

lessons.label: Confidence Intervals: Effect Size with Precision

sections.heading: Building the three common intervals
sections.body: A confidence interval pairs a point estimate with a margin of error built from the standard error and a distribution-based multiplier. For a mean: sample mean ± t(critical) × SE, where SE = SD/√n and the t-value comes from the t-distribution at n-1 degrees of freedom. For a proportion: p̂ ± z(critical) × √(p̂(1-p̂)/n), typically using z=1.96 for 95% confidence — 1.96 is the value on the standard normal curve that cuts off 2.5% of the area in each tail (the 97.5th percentile), so leaving the middle 95% of the distribution between -1.96 and +1.96. For a difference between two independent groups: (mean1-mean2) ± t(critical) × SE(difference), where SE(difference) combines both groups' variability, usually as √(SD1²/n1 + SD2²/n2). In every case, a wider interval reflects more uncertainty — smaller samples or more variable data push the multiplier's effect outward.

sections.heading: What '95% confidence' actually means
sections.body: The correct frequentist reading is a statement about the PROCEDURE, not about any single interval: if you repeated the study many times and built a 95% CI the same way each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true population parameter. A single computed interval either does or does not contain the true value — there is no 95% probability attached to that one interval once it's calculated. This is a subtle but real distinction from the informal, and technically incorrect, phrase 'there's a 95% chance the true value is in this interval,' which is a Bayesian-sounding claim that classical (frequentist) confidence intervals do not make.

sections.heading: The CI-test duality, and what a CI shows that a p-value hides
sections.body: A 95% CI and a two-sided test at α=0.05 are mathematically linked: if the CI for a difference excludes the null value (typically zero, or 1 for a ratio), the corresponding p-value is below 0.05, and vice versa. But the CI carries strictly more information than a bare p-value, because its width directly displays precision. Two studies can both report p=0.04 for the same point estimate, yet one has a CI of [1.1, 1.3] and the other [1.01, 8.9] — the first is a precise, tightly bounded effect, the second is a barely-significant result that could plausibly be almost nothing or could be huge. A p-value alone erases that distinction entirely.

lessons.workedExample: A study of a new antihypertensive reports a mean systolic BP reduction of 8 mmHg (SD=15, n=100) versus placebo's 2 mmHg reduction (SD=14, n=100). Difference = 6 mmHg. SE(difference) = √(15²/100+14²/100) ≈ √(2.25+1.96) ≈ 2.05. Using z=1.96 for large n, 95% CI = 6 ± 1.96×2.05 = 6 ± 4.02, or roughly [2.0, 10.0] mmHg. The interval excludes 0, matching a p<0.05 result, but it also shows the true reduction could plausibly be as small as 2 mmHg (clinically marginal) or as large as 10 mmHg (clinically meaningful) — information a p-value alone would not convey.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on 'what's your confidence interval, and what does it tell you beyond the p-value?' because reporting only a p-value is a common way to hide a wide, uninformative estimate behind a single significant-looking number. A student who can correctly explain why '95% confidence' describes the long-run procedure rather than a probability on this one interval, and who reports interval width as a marker of precision, is showing real statistical fluency.

questions.prompt: What does '95% confidence' correctly describe?

options.text: There is a 95% probability the true parameter lies within this specific computed interval
About 95% of intervals built the same way across repeated samples would contain the true parameter
The sample mean falls within the interval 95% of the time
95% of individual data points fall within the interval

explanations.a: This is the common but incorrect Bayesian-sounding reading; a classical CI does not assign a probability to one already-computed interval.
explanations.b: Correct: this is a statement about the long-run performance of the procedure across repeated sampling, not about any single realized interval.
explanations.c: The sample mean is always at the center of its own CI by construction, so this statement is not what confidence describes.
explanations.d: A CI bounds a population parameter like a mean or proportion, not the spread of individual raw data points; that is what a reference range or SD does.

questions.prompt: Two studies report the identical point estimate and both have p=0.04, but Study A's 95% CI is [1.1, 1.3] and Study B's is [1.01, 8.9]. What does this reveal?

options.text: Study A's result is less trustworthy because its interval is narrower
The studies are equally informative since their p-values match
Study A's estimate is much more precise; Study B's effect could plausibly be tiny or huge despite the same p-value
Study B must have had a larger sample size than Study A

explanations.a: A narrower interval reflects more precision, not less trustworthiness; Study A's estimate is the more informative one.
explanations.b: Matching p-values only indicate both crossed the same significance threshold; they say nothing about how precisely each effect was estimated.
explanations.c: Correct: interval width is a direct measure of precision that a bare p-value discards entirely; Study B's wide range spans clinically trivial to very large effects.
explanations.d: A wider interval more often signals a SMALLER or more variable sample, not a larger one; sample size cannot be inferred from this pair alone.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to construct a 95% CI for the difference between two independent group means.

items.text: Compute each group's mean and standard deviation
Compute the difference between the two group means
Compute the standard error of that difference from both groups' variability and sample sizes
Multiply the standard error by the critical t or z value and add/subtract from the difference

questions.explanation: Each step depends on the one before it: the CI's margin of error cannot be computed before the SE, which cannot be computed before the group summary statistics exist.

lessons.label: Choosing the Right Test

sections.heading: Matching test to data type and design
sections.body: The choice of test flows from two questions: what kind of outcome are you measuring, and how many groups, related how? For a continuous outcome compared between two independent groups (drug vs. placebo, different subjects in each), use the unpaired (two-sample) t-test, built on William Sealy Gosset's 1908 work published under the pseudonym 'Student' while at Guinness brewery. For a continuous outcome measured twice on the SAME subjects (before/after, or matched pairs), use the paired t-test, which analyzes the within-subject differences directly rather than treating the two sets as independent. For a categorical/proportion outcome across two groups, use the chi-square test of independence (Karl Pearson, 1900) on the 2x2 table of counts, or Fisher's exact test when expected cell counts are small (conventionally below 5), which Ronald Fisher introduced and popularized through the 'lady tasting tea' example in The Design of Experiments (1935). For a continuous outcome compared across three or more groups, use one-way ANOVA (analysis of variance, Fisher, 1920s), which tests whether at least one group mean differs rather than running many pairwise t-tests. ANOVA's F-statistic is the ratio F = (between-group variance) / (within-group variance): a large F means the groups are more spread out from each other than individual observations are spread out within each group, which is the signal that at least one group mean is genuinely different.

sections.heading: The assumptions each test is quietly leaning on
sections.body: Every parametric test in this family assumes the data are independent observations — each subject contributes information that doesn't leak into another subject's data point, violated by things like repeated measurements analyzed as if independent. T-tests and ANOVA additionally assume the outcome is approximately Normally distributed within each group, or that the sample is large enough for the central limit theorem to make the sampling distribution of the mean approximately Normal regardless. T-tests and ANOVA also assume equal variance across groups (homoscedasticity) — Welch's t-test relaxes this for two groups by adjusting the degrees of freedom when variances differ. Chi-square specifically assumes expected cell counts are large enough (generally ≥5) for its approximation to the true sampling distribution to hold; Fisher's exact test computes the exact probability instead and needs no such approximation, which is exactly why it substitutes for chi-square in small samples.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher tests three fertilizer concentrations (control, low, high) on plant height, with 15 independently potted plants per group. Because there are three independent groups and a continuous outcome, one-way ANOVA is the right first test, not three separate t-tests (control vs. low, control vs. high, low vs. high), which would inflate the overall false-positive rate by running multiple comparisons at α=0.05 each. If ANOVA's overall F-test is significant, a post hoc test (e.g., Tukey's) is then used to identify which specific pairs differ, controlling for the multiple comparisons.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'why this test and not a t-test' or 'did you check your assumptions' because picking the wrong test is one of the most common and most fixable errors in a fair project — running three separate t-tests instead of one ANOVA, or a chi-square on a 2x2 table with a cell count of 2, are both red flags that the student picked a familiar tool rather than the correct one for their data structure.

questions.prompt: A study measures the same 20 patients' blood pressure before and after a 6-week intervention. Which test correctly fits this design?

options.text: Unpaired two-sample t-test
Paired t-test
Chi-square test of independence
One-way ANOVA

explanations.a: An unpaired t-test assumes two independent groups; here the same 20 patients are measured twice, so the before/after values are correlated, not independent.
explanations.b: Correct: the paired t-test analyzes the within-subject before-after differences directly, which correctly accounts for each patient serving as their own control.
explanations.c: Chi-square applies to categorical outcomes across groups, not to a continuous outcome measured twice on the same subjects.
explanations.d: ANOVA is for comparing three or more groups; this design has one group measured at two time points.

questions.prompt: A 2x2 table comparing treatment response has one cell with an expected count of 3. What does this suggest?

options.text: Chi-square is still preferred because it is simpler to compute
Fisher's exact test should be used instead, since chi-square's approximation is unreliable with such small expected counts
ANOVA should replace chi-square for this comparison
The paired t-test is the appropriate substitute

explanations.a: Simplicity does not override validity; chi-square's approximation to the true sampling distribution breaks down when expected counts are this low.
explanations.b: Correct: the conventional rule of thumb is expected counts below 5 call for Fisher's exact test, which computes an exact probability rather than relying on chi-square's large-sample approximation.
explanations.c: ANOVA is for continuous outcomes across groups, not for a 2x2 table of counts.
explanations.d: The paired t-test applies to continuous, related-sample data, not to categorical count data in a contingency table.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to its correct test.

left.text: Continuous outcome, three or more independent groups
Categorical outcome, 2x2 table, adequate cell counts

right.text: Unpaired t-test
One-way ANOVA
Chi-square test of independence

questions.explanation: Test choice depends on outcome type (continuous vs. categorical) and structure (two groups vs. three-plus, independent vs. paired).

lessons.label: Nonparametric Tests and Failed Assumptions

sections.heading: Rank-based alternatives to the t-test and ANOVA
sections.body: When the outcome is clearly not Normally distributed, is ordinal (ranked categories rather than true numbers), or the sample is too small for the central limit theorem to rescue a skewed distribution, rank-based nonparametric tests substitute for their parametric counterparts. The Mann-Whitney U test (Henry Mann and Donald Whitney, 1947) replaces the unpaired t-test: it ranks all observations from both groups together and asks whether one group's ranks are systematically higher, rather than comparing means directly. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Frank Wilcoxon, 1945) replaces the paired t-test the same way, working on the ranks of the within-subject differences. The Kruskal-Wallis test (William Kruskal and W. Allen Wallis, 1952) replaces one-way ANOVA for three or more independent groups, extending the same rank logic across all groups at once. Its test statistic, H, sums each group's squared deviation of average rank from the overall average rank, weighted by group size, and is approximately chi-square distributed under H0, which is what lets the test convert H into a p-value.

sections.heading: Checking the assumptions before you need the substitute
sections.body: Normality is checked visually with a histogram or, more rigorously, a Q-Q plot (where points should track a straight diagonal line if the data are Normal), and formally with the Shapiro-Wilk test, whose null hypothesis is that the data ARE Normally distributed — a small p-value here is evidence AGAINST normality, the opposite direction from most other tests in this unit. Equal variance across groups is checked with Levene's test, whose null hypothesis is that the group variances are equal; a significant Levene's result flags heteroscedasticity, which can be handled either by switching to a nonparametric test or by using Welch's t-test, which does not assume equal variance.

sections.heading: The power cost of switching
sections.body: Nonparametric tests are more robust — they make fewer assumptions and are less distorted by outliers, because ranking compresses an extreme value's influence to just its rank position rather than its raw magnitude. But that robustness has a price: when the data genuinely ARE Normal and the parametric test's assumptions actually hold, the nonparametric equivalent has lower statistical power, meaning it needs a larger sample to detect the same true effect. The commonly cited efficiency figure is that the Wilcoxon/Mann-Whitney family retains about 95% of the t-test's power when data are truly Normal — so the cost is real but modest in that best case, and it only gets more favorable for nonparametric tests as the data depart further from Normality.

lessons.workedExample: A study measures pain scores (a 0-10 ordinal scale, not a true continuous measurement) in 12 patients before and after a physical therapy intervention. A Shapiro-Wilk test on the score differences returns p=0.01, rejecting normality, and the outcome is ordinal besides — both reasons to avoid the paired t-test. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is applied instead: it ranks the absolute differences, keeps track of which direction each ranked difference moved, and sums the ranks for each direction to test whether one direction dominates, without ever assuming the raw pain-score differences are Normally distributed.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because reflexively running a t-test on ordinal survey data or heavily skewed lab measurements is one of the most common statistical missteps at a science fair. A student who can say 'I checked normality with Shapiro-Wilk, it failed, so I used Mann-Whitney instead of a t-test' demonstrates they picked their method based on what the data actually looked like, not on which test they happened to remember.

questions.prompt: A Shapiro-Wilk test on a dataset returns p=0.002. What does this indicate?

options.text: Strong evidence the data ARE Normally distributed, since the null hypothesis of normality was not rejected
Strong evidence AGAINST normality, since the null hypothesis being tested is that the data are Normal
The sample size is too small to run any statistical test
The data have equal variance across groups

explanations.a: A p-value this small leads to REJECTING the null, and Shapiro-Wilk's null is that the data are Normal, so this is evidence against normality, not for it.
explanations.b: Correct: Shapiro-Wilk's null hypothesis is normality, so a small p-value is unusual evidence AGAINST that assumption — the reverse direction from tests like the t-test.
explanations.c: Shapiro-Wilk's result says nothing about whether the sample size is adequate for testing generally; it only evaluates the normality assumption.
explanations.d: Equal variance across groups is evaluated by Levene's test, not by Shapiro-Wilk, which only assesses the shape of a single distribution.

questions.prompt: Data are truly Normally distributed, but a researcher uses the Mann-Whitney U test instead of the t-test anyway. What is the main cost?

options.text: The Mann-Whitney test will produce an invalid, uninterpretable result
Slightly lower statistical power than the t-test, needing a larger sample to detect the same true effect
The test becomes biased toward finding significance even when there is no true effect
No cost at all; the two tests are always mathematically identical

explanations.a: Mann-Whitney remains valid on Normal data; it simply is not the most powerful choice available in that specific case.
explanations.b: Correct: under true normality, Mann-Whitney/Wilcoxon retain roughly 95% of the t-test's power, so the test still works but needs more data to match the t-test's detection ability.
explanations.c: Nonparametric tests do not inflate the false-positive rate; they remain valid, just somewhat less powerful when parametric assumptions genuinely hold.
explanations.d: They coincide in some special cases but are generally different procedures (rank-based vs. mean-based) that can give different p-values on the same data.

questions.prompt: Match each parametric test to its nonparametric, rank-based substitute.

right.text: Mann-Whitney U test
Wilcoxon signed-rank test
Kruskal-Wallis test

questions.explanation: Each nonparametric test mirrors the design of its parametric counterpart — independent two-group, paired two-measurement, or independent three-plus-group — but uses ranks instead of raw values and means.

lessons.label: Statistical vs. Clinical Significance

sections.heading: How sample size decouples 'significant' from 'important'
sections.body: A p-value is driven jointly by effect size AND sample size, and that coupling can pull statistical and clinical significance in opposite directions. Standard error shrinks as sample size grows (SE = SD/√n), so with a large enough n, even a trivially small true difference eventually produces a small p-value — a blood-pressure drug that lowers systolic pressure by a genuinely meaningless 1 mmHg can hit p<0.001 in a trial of 50,000 patients. The mirror problem happens at small n: a real, clinically important effect can fail to reach p<0.05 simply because the study lacked the power to detect it (Lesson 3's Type II error), which is why a 'non-significant' result in an underpowered pilot study should never be read as 'no effect exists.'

sections.heading: Effect-size measures that answer the size question directly
sections.body: Because p-values conflate size and sample size, dedicated effect-size measures exist to report magnitude on its own. Cohen's d, developed by Jacob Cohen and formalized in Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (1988), standardizes a mean difference by pooled SD: d = (mean1-mean2)/pooled SD, with Cohen's own rough benchmarks of 0.2 (small), 0.5 (medium), and 0.8 (large). For binary outcomes, absolute risk difference (ARD = risk in treated group minus risk in control group) reports the raw magnitude directly, and number needed to treat (NNT = 1/ARD), formalized by Laupacis, Sackett, and Roberts (1988), translates that into a clinically intuitive count: how many patients must receive the treatment for one additional patient to benefit. For example, an ARD of 0.05 (a 5-percentage-point drop in event rate) gives NNT = 1/0.05 = 20 — 20 patients need to be treated for one additional patient to avoid the event.

sections.heading: The minimal clinically important difference as the sanity check
sections.body: The minimal clinically important difference (MCID), a concept articulated by Jaeschke, Singer, and Guyatt in a 1989 paper on quality-of-life measures, is the smallest change in an outcome that a patient or clinician would actually consider meaningful, established independently of any particular study's statistics — often through patient-reported thresholds or expert consensus. Comparing a study's confidence interval (Lesson 4) against the MCID is the real test of clinical relevance: if the CI's entire range sits below the MCID, the effect may be statistically real but too small to matter in practice, regardless of how small the p-value is.

lessons.workedExample: A cholesterol drug trial enrolls 40,000 patients and finds LDL drops by 3 mg/dL more than placebo (95% CI: 2.1-3.9 mg/dL, p<0.001). The result is unambiguously statistically significant. But the established MCID for LDL reduction to matter clinically is roughly 30-40 mg/dL in most guideline discussions; a 3 mg/dL drop, even though real and precisely estimated, falls far short. Reporting Cohen's d for this difference (likely around 0.08-0.10, using a typical LDL SD of roughly 30-40 mg/dL) makes the triviality explicit in a way the p-value alone conceals.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on this because 'our result was statistically significant' is the single most overused and least informative sentence at a science fair — it says nothing about whether the effect is big enough to matter. A judge asking 'what's your effect size, and how does it compare to a threshold anyone would call meaningful' is testing whether the student can separate 'detectable' from 'important,' which is exactly the distinction a p-value cannot make on its own.

questions.prompt: A trial with 50,000 participants finds a blood pressure drug lowers systolic pressure by 1 mmHg (p<0.001). What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The result is both statistically and clinically significant, since p<0.001 is a very small p-value
The result is statistically significant but likely not clinically significant, since 1 mmHg is a trivial change
The result is neither statistically nor clinically significant
The small p-value proves the effect is large

explanations.a: A very small p-value here mainly reflects the enormous sample size shrinking the standard error, not that the effect itself is large or meaningful.
explanations.b: Correct: at n=50,000, even a clinically trivial 1 mmHg difference can produce a tiny p-value; statistical and clinical significance have decoupled.
explanations.c: The result IS statistically significant by the p<0.001 criterion; the issue is that statistical significance alone says nothing about clinical importance.
explanations.d: A p-value is not a magnitude measure; a tiny effect in a huge sample and a huge effect in a small sample can produce the same p-value.

questions.prompt: What does the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) provide that a p-value cannot?

options.text: A more precise estimate of the sample's standard error
An externally established threshold for what magnitude of change patients or clinicians would consider meaningful, independent of any one study's statistics
An alternative way to compute the same p-value using a different formula
A guarantee that a statistically significant result is also true

explanations.a: MCID is about clinical relevance of magnitude, not about the precision of a standard error calculation.
explanations.b: Correct: MCID is set independently, often via patient-reported thresholds or consensus, giving a magnitude benchmark that a p-value's yes/no significance test does not provide.
explanations.c: MCID and the p-value answer different questions (how big vs. how surprising under H0) and are not alternative computations of the same thing.
explanations.d: Neither MCID nor a p-value guarantees a result is 'true'; both are tools for interpreting an estimate, not proof of underlying truth.

questions.prompt: Match each effect-size measure to what it quantifies.

right.text: A mean difference standardized by pooled SD
The raw difference in event risk between treated and control groups
How many patients must be treated for one additional patient to benefit, equal to 1/ARD

questions.explanation: Cohen's d applies to continuous outcomes in SD units; ARD and NNT both apply to binary outcomes, with NNT being the reciprocal of ARD expressed as a patient count.

units.label: Power, Sample Size, and Study Planning

lessons.label: What Statistical Power Means

sections.heading: Power Is 1 Minus Beta
sections.body: Every hypothesis test carries two ways to be wrong. Alpha (type I error) is the chance of rejecting a true null hypothesis — a false positive, conventionally capped at 0.05. Beta (type II error) is the chance of failing to reject a false null — a false negative, missing a real effect. Power is defined as 1 minus beta: the probability the study correctly detects an effect that truly exists, at the effect size the trial was built to find. The field-standard convention is alpha = 0.05 and power = 0.80 (beta = 0.20), meaning a trial designed this way accepts a 1-in-5 chance of missing a real effect of the specified size. Many modern pivotal trials, especially in oncology and cardiovascular medicine, now target 90% power given the cost and ethical weight of a false negative in a confirmatory trial.

sections.heading: The Four-Way Lock
sections.body: Alpha, power, effect size, and sample size (n) are algebraically bound together in every sample-size formula: fix any three and the fourth is determined. Demand more power at the same alpha and effect size, and n must rise. Shrink the effect size you insist on detecting, and n must rise sharply to compensate. Tighten alpha (say from 0.05 to 0.01, a more conservative false-positive threshold), and power falls unless n also rises. Investigators cannot get a cheap, small, highly powered trial that reliably detects a tiny effect — the four quantities trade off, and a proposal that promises all four simultaneously without raising n should be checked.

sections.heading: What an Underpowered Trial Actually Costs
sections.body: Freiman, Chalmers, Smith, and Kuebler's 1978 review in the New England Journal of Medicine examined 71 published randomized trials that reported "no significant difference" and found most had under 30% power to detect even a 25% relative risk reduction — meaning a negative result was statistically uninformative, not evidence of no effect. Underpowered trials also raise an ethical problem: enrolling patients in research that has little realistic chance of answering its own question exposes them to risk and burden for a study that cannot deliver a reliable answer, which most research-ethics frameworks treat as a violation of equipoise. Underpowered studies also distort the published literature, since the few that happen to reach significance by chance get published while true small effects go undetected.

lessons.workedExample: Raising power from 80% to 90% at a fixed alpha = 0.05 (two-sided) and fixed effect size requires roughly 34% more sample size. The sample-size formula scales with (z_alpha/2 + z_beta)^2. At 80% power, z_beta = 0.84, giving (1.96+0.84)^2 = 7.85. At 90% power, z_beta = 1.28, giving (1.96+1.28)^2 = 10.51. The ratio, 10.51/7.85 ≈ 1.34, is exactly why a funder asked to bump a trial from 80% to 90% power should expect roughly a third more patients, not a token increase — the relationship is fixed by the formula, not negotiable by adding a few extra enrollees.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe power specifically when a project reports a "no significant difference" result, because that phrase is only informative if the study had adequate power to detect a meaningful effect in the first place. The tell of real understanding is a student who can state the power their design actually achieved (not just that they ran a t-test) and distinguish "we found no effect" from "we couldn't have found one even if it existed."

questions.prompt: A trial is designed with alpha = 0.05 and power = 80%. What is beta?

explanations.a: 0.05 is alpha, the type I error rate, not beta.
explanations.b: Correct: power = 1 − beta, so beta = 1 − 0.80 = 0.20, the accepted chance of missing a true effect.
explanations.c: 0.80 is the power itself, not beta.
explanations.d: 0.95 is 1 − alpha (the confidence level), not beta.

questions.prompt: Freiman et al. (1978) reviewed 71 published "negative" randomized trials and found that most:

options.text: Had adequate power (≥80%) to detect a clinically meaningful effect
Had well under 30% power to detect even a 25% relative risk reduction
Used no significance testing at all
Had power exceeding 95%, making the null result highly reliable

explanations.a: The opposite was true — most of the reviewed trials were badly underpowered.
explanations.b: Correct: most had under 30% power for a 25% relative risk reduction, meaning their negative results were largely uninformative.
explanations.c: The trials did use significance testing; the problem was inadequate power behind those tests, not the absence of testing.
explanations.d: Power was far below 95% in most of the reviewed trials, which was exactly Freiman and colleagues' concern.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a basic a priori power analysis.

items.text: Choose alpha (type I error tolerance) and the desired power
Estimate the smallest clinically meaningful effect size to detect
Estimate the outcome's variability from pilot or prior data
Solve the sample-size formula for n

questions.explanation: Design choices (alpha, power) come first, then the effect size and variance the study needs to be sensitive to, and only then can the formula be solved for n.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

right.text: Probability of a false positive: rejecting a true null hypothesis
Probability of a false negative: failing to reject a false null hypothesis
Probability of correctly detecting a true effect (1 − beta)

questions.explanation: Alpha and beta are the two error rates a test can commit; power is defined directly from beta as the complementary correct-detection probability.

lessons.label: Effect Size and the Minimal Clinically Important Difference

sections.heading: Standardized vs. Raw Effect Size
sections.body: A raw effect size is stated in the outcome's own units — a 5 mmHg drop in blood pressure, a 2-point change on a symptom scale — and is what clinicians and patients intuitively understand. A standardized effect size strips out the units so effects can be compared across studies and instruments. The most common is Cohen's d, the mean difference between groups divided by the pooled standard deviation: d = (mean1 − mean2) / pooled SD. Cohen (1988) proposed rough conventions — d ≈ 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large — as a rule of thumb for fields lacking an established minimal important difference, not as a substitute for a clinically grounded number.

sections.heading: Powering for the MCID, Not the Best Case
sections.body: Jaeschke, Singer, and Guyatt's 1989 paper formalized the minimal clinically important difference (MCID): the smallest change in an outcome that patients themselves would perceive as beneficial, enough to justify a change in management despite its side effects and cost. Anchor-based methods estimate it by comparing score changes to an external reference, such as a patient's own global rating of improvement; distribution-based methods instead express it as a fraction of the outcome's standard deviation, commonly around 0.5 SD as a rough default. Concrete, field-specific anchor-based MCIDs exist and are preferred over the generic 0.5 SD default when available — published examples include a 10 mm change on the 100 mm visual analog pain scale and a 100 mL improvement in FEV1 for COPD trials. Powering a trial for the MCID rather than for the largest effect a pilot happened to show keeps the sample size honest — powering for an inflated "best case" effect produces a deceptively small, cheap-looking n that is unlikely to be adequate for the real, more modest effect a treatment actually delivers.

sections.heading: Pinning Down Variance
sections.body: Every sample-size formula also needs an estimate of the outcome's variance, which typically comes from pilot data or a published trial in a similar population. Pilot standard deviations from small samples are themselves noisy estimates, so guidance is to use the upper end of a confidence interval around the pilot SD, or a larger published trial's SD, rather than the point estimate. That upper bound comes from the chi-square distribution: for a pilot of n patients (df = n − 1) and sample SD s, the (1 − alpha) upper confidence limit on the variance is (n − 1)s^2 / chi-square_{1-alpha/2, df}, where chi-square_{1-alpha/2, df} is the LOWER-tail critical value. For a pilot of n = 20 (df = 19) with s = 15, the 95% upper limit on the variance is 19 × 225 / 8.91 ≈ 480, an upper SD bound of about 22 rather than the pilot's point estimate of 15 — a meaningfully larger, more conservative number to power against. Underestimating variance is one of the most common ways a trial ends up quietly underpowered despite a seemingly careful calculation.

lessons.workedExample: A pilot study (n=20) on a fatigue intervention finds an outcome standard deviation of 15 points on a fatigue scale, and a patient-panel anchor-based process sets the MCID at 5 points. Standardized effect size: d = 5/15 ≈ 0.33, a small-to-medium effect. Contrast this with an earlier open-label report that showed a 12-point improvement: d = 12/15 = 0.8, a large effect that would justify a much smaller trial. Powering for the 12-point figure instead of the 5-point MCID would leave the confirmatory trial badly underpowered for the true, more modest effect a controlled comparison is likely to reveal.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a project's effect size is the MCID or a number quietly cherry-picked from the most favorable pilot result, because powering for an inflated effect is one of the most common ways a science-fair "statistically significant" result turns out to be an underpowered fluke that will not replicate. A student who can justify their effect size against an anchor-based or distribution-based MCID, rather than against whatever number made the sample size look achievable, is demonstrating real understanding.

questions.prompt: Cohen's d is calculated by dividing the raw mean difference by:

options.text: The sample size
The pooled standard deviation
Alpha
The power

explanations.a: Sample size does not enter the formula for Cohen's d.
explanations.b: Correct: d = (mean1 − mean2) / pooled SD, which is why d is unitless and comparable across studies.
explanations.c: Alpha is the significance threshold, unrelated to computing d.
explanations.d: Power is a downstream consequence of d, n, and alpha — not an input to computing d itself.

questions.prompt: Why prefer the minimal clinically important difference over the largest effect a pilot happened to suggest when choosing what to power a trial for?

options.text: Because larger effects always make trials more expensive to run
Because powering for an inflated effect risks the trial being underpowered for the true, more modest effect
Because regulators legally require the MCID be used in every trial
Because the MCID is always simpler to calculate than a raw effect size

explanations.a: Cost is not the core reasoning; the issue is statistical validity of the resulting design.
explanations.b: Correct: an effect size that is too large gives a falsely small, cheap-looking n that is likely inadequate once the real effect turns out to be smaller.
explanations.c: There is no blanket legal requirement to use the MCID; it is a methodological best practice, not a mandate.
explanations.d: MCID estimation via anchor- or distribution-based methods can be more, not less, involved than computing a raw difference.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to arrive at the effect size used in a sample-size calculation.

items.text: Determine the minimal clinically important difference via anchor- or distribution-based methods
Gather pilot data or published estimates of the outcome's variance
Convert the MCID and variance into a standardized effect size (Cohen's d) if needed
Plug the effect size and variance into the sample-size formula

questions.explanation: The clinically meaningful difference is set first from patient-centered evidence, variance is estimated separately, the two combine into a standardized effect size, and only then is the formula solved.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its description.

right.text: Ties the minimal important difference to an external reference like patient global rating of change
Expresses the minimal important difference as a fraction of the outcome's standard deviation
Standardizes a raw mean difference by dividing by the pooled standard deviation

questions.explanation: Anchor-based methods use an external clinical reference; distribution-based methods use the outcome's own spread; Cohen's d is the general-purpose standardized effect size formula.

lessons.label: Calculating Sample Size for Means and Proportions

sections.heading: Two-Group Means: The Formula and a Shortcut
sections.body: For a continuous outcome compared between two equal-size groups, the per-group sample size is n = 2(z_alpha/2 + z_beta)^2 * sigma^2 / delta^2, where sigma is the outcome's standard deviation and delta is the difference to detect. Lehr's (1992) quick rule collapses this to n ≈ 16/d^2 per group, where d is the standardized effect size (Cohen's d), specifically for the common design of alpha = 0.05 two-sided and 80% power — a fast sanity check before running the full formula. Both formulas assume equal-size groups; for unequal allocation at a k:1 ratio (say, twice as many patients on the experimental arm as on control), the required total sample size grows by a factor of (k+1)/(2k) relative to a balanced design with the same per-group formula, so an unbalanced design that is easier to recruit for still costs more total participants for the same power.

sections.heading: Two-Group Proportions Share the Same Bones
sections.body: For a binary outcome, comparing two proportions p1 and p2 uses a structurally similar formula: n per group ≈ [z_alpha/2 * sqrt(2*p̄(1−p̄)) + z_beta * sqrt(p1(1−p1) + p2(1−p2))]^2 / (p1 − p2)^2, where p̄ is the average of the two proportions. It looks more complicated because a proportion's variance, p(1−p), depends on the proportion itself rather than being a separately estimated sigma, but the skeleton is identical: a squared error-rate term in the numerator, the squared absolute difference in the denominator. For small samples, Fleiss's continuity-corrected version adds a small extra term to this formula to better approximate the exact binomial test; it costs a slightly larger n than the uncorrected formula above, which is the standard first-pass estimate.

sections.heading: The Inverse-Square Law of Sample Size
sections.body: Both formulas share the same structural consequence: n scales inversely with the SQUARE of the effect size (delta or d) and directly with the outcome's variance. Halving the detectable difference does not double the required n — it roughly quadruples it, because delta appears squared in the denominator. This is why trials chasing small absolute effects (a 2% versus a 4% risk reduction) need four times the participants of an otherwise identical trial, and why cardiovascular prevention trials aimed at modest risk reductions in a common condition can require tens of thousands of patients even though a proof-of-concept study of the same drug needed only dozens. The same squared relationship makes power itself comparatively cheap to buy: because z_beta enters the formula only linearly while delta enters squared, raising power from 80% to 90% (z_beta from 0.84 to 1.28) increases n by roughly a third, far less than the fourfold cost of halving the detectable effect.

lessons.workedExample: Using Lehr's rule, a pilot suggests a medium standardized effect, d = 0.5, for a continuous outcome at alpha = 0.05 two-sided, 80% power: n ≈ 16/0.5^2 = 16/0.25 = 64 per group, 128 total. If the true effect turns out to be half as large, d = 0.25, then n ≈ 16/0.0625 = 256 per group — exactly four times as many, not twice — which is the inverse-square law showing up numerically rather than abstractly. For a two-proportion comparison — p1 = 0.30 versus p2 = 0.20, alpha = 0.05 two-sided, 80% power — p̄ = 0.25, so n ≈ [1.96×sqrt(2×0.25×0.75) + 0.84×sqrt(0.30×0.70 + 0.20×0.80)]^2 / (0.30 − 0.20)^2 ≈ (1.20 + 0.51)^2 / 0.01 ≈ 293, rounding up to 294 per group — the same skeleton as the means formula, just built from proportion variances instead of a separately estimated sigma.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this formula because students often describe a small achieved sample size as "a little underpowered" when the real shortfall, given the inverse-square relationship, is much larger than intuition suggests. A student who can say "we could only detect an effect twice as big as planned, meaning our achieved power for the true effect size was far below 80%, not just slightly below it" is demonstrating they understand the formula's structure, not just its existence.

questions.prompt: If the true effect size a study wants to detect is halved, with alpha and power held constant, the required sample size roughly:

options.text: Doubles
Quadruples
Stays the same
Is halved

explanations.a: Doubling would be the case if n scaled linearly with 1/delta, but it scales with 1/delta^2.
explanations.b: Correct: because n is proportional to 1/delta^2, halving delta multiplies n by 2^2 = 4.
explanations.c: n is highly sensitive to the effect size through the squared term; it does not stay constant.
explanations.d: A smaller effect size requires MORE sample size to detect, not less.

questions.prompt: Lehr's quick rule, n ≈ 16/d^2 per group, applies specifically to:

options.text: A two-sample comparison of means at alpha = 0.05 two-sided and 80% power
Any combination of alpha and power
Proportions only, never continuous outcomes
Event-driven survival analysis

explanations.a: Correct: the constant 16 bakes in (z_0.025 + z_0.80)^2 ≈ 7.85, doubled for a two-group comparison, specific to that alpha/power combination.
explanations.b: Changing alpha or power changes the constant; 16 is not universal across all settings.
explanations.c: Lehr's rule is for continuous outcomes compared via standardized effect size, not proportions.
explanations.d: Survival analysis uses event-count formulas like Schoenfeld's, not this means-comparison shortcut.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to compute required n using the two-sample means formula.

items.text: Fix alpha and desired power, and look up z_alpha/2 and z_beta
Estimate the outcome's standard deviation and the minimal detectable difference
Compute the standardized effect size d = difference / SD
Solve n = 2(z_alpha/2 + z_beta)^2 / d^2 per group

questions.explanation: The z-values depend only on design choices and come first; the difference and SD are empirical inputs; combining them gives d; only then can the formula be solved.

questions.prompt: Match each change to its effect on the required sample size, holding everything else fixed.

left.text: Increasing the effect size to detect

right.text: Decreases required n
Increases required n (more noise to overcome)
Increases required n (stricter false-positive threshold, for fixed power)

questions.explanation: A bigger target effect is easier to detect and needs fewer participants; more variance and a stricter alpha both make detection harder and require more.

lessons.label: Sizing Survival and Rare-Event Trials

sections.heading: Power Depends on Events, Not Patients
sections.body: In time-to-event trials analyzed with a log-rank test or Cox proportional-hazards model — cancer recurrence, cardiovascular death, transplant rejection — statistical power depends on the NUMBER OF EVENTS observed, not the number of patients enrolled. Schoenfeld's (1983) formula gives the required event count for a two-arm trial with equal allocation: d = 4(z_alpha/2 + z_beta)^2 / (ln HR)^2, where HR is the hazard ratio the trial is powered to detect. A trial can enroll ten thousand patients, but if very few of them experience the event of interest, the study remains statistically uninformative regardless of its headline enrollment number. Both the log-rank test and Schoenfeld's formula rest on the proportional-hazards assumption: that the ratio of event rates between arms stays constant over the whole follow-up period, rather than the treatment effect emerging late or fading early. When hazards are non-proportional — a treatment that only kicks in after several months, for instance — a single hazard ratio and event count calculated up front can understate the events actually needed, and the trial may need a weighted log-rank test or a pre-specified analysis at a fixed time point instead. Competing risks, where patients can experience a different terminal event (such as death from another cause) that removes them from being at risk for the outcome of interest, similarly complicate both the event-rate estimate and the standard Cox model, and are common in cancer trials where the disease itself and its treatment both carry other mortality risk.

sections.heading: Why Trials Get Event-Driven, Not Calendar-Driven
sections.body: Because power tracks events rather than headcount, oncology and cardiovascular-outcomes trials are commonly designed as "event-driven": an independent data monitoring committee tracks the accumulating event count and locks the primary analysis once the pre-specified target is reached, rather than on a fixed calendar date. A low-event-rate population (say a prevention trial in relatively healthy people) can enroll thousands of patients and still take years longer to reach its event target than a high-risk population would, even with identical enrollment numbers.

sections.heading: Accrual and Follow-Up Jointly Set Enrollment
sections.body: Translating a target event count into an actual enrollment number requires estimating the control-arm event rate over the study's total observation time, then dividing the required events by that rate to get total patient-years needed. Patient-years, in turn, come from two levers: the accrual period (how fast patients are recruited) and the follow-up duration (how long each patient is observed after enrollment). Slower accrual or a shorter follow-up window means each patient contributes less at-risk time, so investigators must either enroll more patients or extend the trial's calendar length to accumulate the same number of patient-years and, ultimately, the same number of events.

lessons.workedExample: A cardiovascular-outcomes trial targets 90% power to detect a hazard ratio of 0.80 at alpha = 0.05 two-sided. With z_0.975 = 1.96, z_0.90 = 1.28, and ln(0.80) = −0.223: d = 4(1.96+1.28)^2 / (0.223)^2 = 4(10.51)/0.0498 ≈ 844 events required. If the control arm's annual event rate is 5%, the trial needs roughly 844/0.05 ≈ 16,880 patient-years, split across an accrual period (recruiting patients over, say, three years) and a minimum follow-up (observing each patient for at least another two to three years) — which is exactly why such trials commonly enroll tens of thousands of patients over a multi-year accrual-plus-follow-up window.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe survival-design projects because students frequently report enrolled patient count as if it alone determines the study's power, missing that a trial with too few observed events is uninformative no matter how large the enrolled cohort looks on paper. The tell of real understanding is a student who states the target event count from a formula like Schoenfeld's, and can explain how accrual rate and follow-up duration together determine whether that target is reachable within a feasible trial length.

questions.prompt: In a survival-analysis trial using the log-rank test or a Cox model, statistical power is driven primarily by:

options.text: The total number of patients enrolled
The total number of events observed
The number of study sites
The length of the informed consent form

explanations.a: Enrollment alone does not determine power; a large cohort with few events is still underpowered.
explanations.b: Correct: power in time-to-event analysis is a function of the number of events observed, per Schoenfeld's formula.
explanations.c: Number of sites affects logistics and accrual speed but is not itself the driver of statistical power.
explanations.d: Consent form length has no bearing on statistical power.

questions.prompt: Schoenfeld's (1983) formula computes the required:

options.text: Number of patients to enroll
Number of events needed to achieve target power for a given hazard ratio
Length of the accrual period in months
Hazard ratio itself, given a fixed sample size

explanations.a: Patient enrollment is derived afterward from the event count and the estimated event rate, not computed directly by this formula.
explanations.b: Correct: Schoenfeld's formula solves for the number of events, d, needed given alpha, power, and the target hazard ratio.
explanations.c: Accrual period is a separate planning step that converts required patient-years into a recruitment timeline.
explanations.d: The hazard ratio is an input to the formula (the effect size to detect), not its output.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to size an event-driven survival trial.

items.text: Use Schoenfeld's formula with alpha, power, and the target hazard ratio to get required events
Estimate the control-arm event rate over the planned follow-up period
Convert required events into required patient-years using the event rate
Split patient-years into an accrual period and a follow-up period to set total enrollment and trial duration

questions.explanation: The target event count is fixed first by the effect size and power, then translated into patient-years via the expected event rate, then into an actual enrollment and calendar plan.

questions.prompt: Match each factor to its effect on an event-driven trial's design.

right.text: Increases the patient-years needed to accumulate enough events
Increases each patient's at-risk time, reducing the number of patients needed
Shortens the calendar time to reach full enrollment, without changing the number of events needed per patient

questions.explanation: Event rate and follow-up duration change how many patient-years are needed per event; accrual speed changes only how quickly enrollment itself is completed.

lessons.label: Attrition, Non-Adherence, and Inflating n

sections.heading: Inflating for Loss to Follow-Up
sections.body: Every sample-size formula assumes complete outcome data on every enrolled participant, which no real trial achieves. Lachin's (1981) inflation approach corrects for this directly: if the expected dropout rate is R, the enrollment target becomes n' = n / (1 − R), so that after the anticipated loss, the number who actually complete the trial with analyzable data still meets the originally planned power. A 15% expected loss to follow-up means dividing the computed n by 0.85, inflating the enrollment target by roughly 18% — a correction that is easy to skip and, when skipped, is one of the most common reasons a well-calculated trial finishes underpowered. This inflation assumes uniform dropout: the same rate in both arms, missing at random with respect to treatment, so the only cost is fewer analyzable patients and the power loss Lachin's formula corrects for. Differential dropout — where one arm loses patients faster than the other, often because a more burdensome or less tolerable treatment drives its own attrition — is a separate and more serious problem: it can bias the effect estimate itself, not just shrink the analyzable sample, because the patients who drop out are systematically different from those who remain. A single pooled inflation factor does not detect or correct for this; investigators need to examine dropout rates by arm and consider sensitivity analyses when they diverge.

sections.heading: Non-Adherence Dilutes the Effect, Not Just the Headcount
sections.body: Even patients who remain in a trial through its end may not receive the treatment as assigned. Crossovers occur when control-arm patients gain access to the active treatment; drop-ins or contamination occur when patients obtain a similar intervention outside the protocol. Because intention-to-treat analysis — the standard, bias-protecting approach — keeps every patient analyzed in their original randomized arm regardless of what they actually took, non-adherence shrinks the observed difference between arms toward zero relative to the true biological effect. This dilution silently drains the trial's actual achieved power even when enrollment hits its numerical target exactly, because the enrollment inflation formula fixes the analyzable-patient problem but does nothing about a shrunken effect size.

sections.heading: Two Separate Problems, Two Separate Fixes
sections.body: Attrition and dilution require distinct corrections. Inflating enrollment addresses "not enough analyzable patients"; it does not restore an effect size that non-adherence has diluted. Addressing dilution instead requires either improving adherence directly — commonly through a run-in period that excludes patients unlikely to comply before they are ever randomized — or explicitly powering the study for a smaller, diluted effect size rather than the full biological effect the intervention would show under perfect adherence. A trial that hits its enrollment target but ignores dilution can still land underpowered for the effect it is realistically able to observe.

lessons.workedExample: A team calculates n = 200 per arm for 80% power to detect their target effect. Anticipating 20% loss to follow-up, they inflate the target to 200 / (1 − 0.20) = 250 per arm, 500 total, so roughly 200 analyzable participants per arm remain even after dropout. Separately, if 10% of control-arm patients are expected to cross over to active treatment, a true 10-point mean difference might be diluted toward an observed 9-point difference (10 × (1 − 0.10) = 9 under the simple linear dilution model) — meaning the original n = 200 calculation, built on the undiluted 10-point effect, still understates the sample actually needed once dilution, not just dropout, is accounted for.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe attrition and adherence assumptions because a trial that recruits its full planned enrollment but never separately budgeted for dropout and crossover will silently under-deliver power, even though its headline numbers look complete. The tell of understanding is a project that states both a dropout-inflated enrollment target and a separate acknowledgment that non-adherence dilutes the detectable effect — not just a single inflated headcount presented as if it solved both problems.

questions.prompt: A trial computes it needs n = 100 per arm and expects 20% loss to follow-up. Using Lachin's simple inflation, the target enrollment per arm is approximately:

explanations.a: 100 ignores the expected dropout entirely.
explanations.b: 120 would result from simply adding 20% rather than dividing by (1 − 0.20).
explanations.d: 150 overcorrects; the inflation factor for 20% dropout is 1/0.80 = 1.25, not 1.5.

questions.prompt: Treatment dilution from crossovers and drop-ins primarily:

options.text: Increases the effective sample size available for analysis
Shrinks the observed between-arm difference toward zero, lowering achieved power
Has no effect on power as long as intention-to-treat analysis is used
Only matters in survival trials, not trials with continuous outcomes

explanations.a: Dilution affects the size of the observed effect, not the count of analyzable participants.
explanations.b: Correct: because intention-to-treat keeps diluted, crossed-over patients in their original arm, the true effect gets blurred toward the null, lowering the study's actual achieved power.
explanations.c: Intention-to-treat is exactly what preserves the dilution in the analysis rather than removing it — it protects against bias but does not undo the power loss.
explanations.d: Dilution from non-adherence applies to any outcome type, continuous or time-to-event, whenever assigned treatment is not what patients actually receive.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for planning around attrition and non-adherence.

items.text: Estimate the base sample size for the target effect and power
Estimate expected loss to follow-up and inflate enrollment accordingly
Estimate expected crossover or non-adherence and its likely dilution of the effect
Decide whether to add a run-in period, enroll further, or power for the diluted effect

questions.explanation: The base calculation comes first, dropout inflation corrects the analyzable-patient count next, and only after estimating dilution can the team decide how to address the separate loss of effect size.

questions.prompt: Match each issue to its correction.

right.text: Reduces analyzable participants; corrected by inflating enrollment (e.g., dividing n by 1 minus the dropout rate)
Dilutes the observed treatment effect toward the null; corrected by powering for a smaller effect or improving adherence
Screens out likely non-adherent participants before randomization to reduce future dilution

questions.explanation: Dropout and dilution are distinct threats to power, and a run-in period is a design tool aimed specifically at preventing dilution rather than dropout.

lessons.label: Multiplicity and the Alpha Budget

sections.heading: Family-Wise Error Inflation
sections.body: Testing at alpha = 0.05 means a single test has a 5% chance of a false positive if the null is true. But a trial rarely runs just one test — multiple endpoints, subgroup analyses, and repeated interim looks at accumulating data are all additional tests, and each one adds its own 5% chance of a spurious "significant" finding. The probability that AT LEAST ONE of several independent tests comes back falsely significant, the family-wise error rate (FWER), is approximately 1 − (1 − alpha)^k for k tests. At alpha = 0.05 and k = 10 tests, FWER ≈ 1 − 0.95^10 ≈ 0.40 — a 40% chance of a false positive turning up somewhere in the results, even if nothing real is happening.

sections.heading: Bonferroni and Hierarchical Alternatives
sections.body: The simplest correction, the Bonferroni method, divides alpha by the number of tests (alpha/k per test) to hold the family-wise rate near its nominal level, but it is conservative and costs real power, especially when the endpoints are correlated rather than independent. Modern trials increasingly use hierarchical, or gatekeeping, testing instead: hypotheses are pre-specified in a fixed order — primary endpoint, then a key secondary endpoint, then the next — and each is tested at the FULL alpha but only if the hypothesis before it in the sequence was significant. No per-test correction is needed because the family's whole 0.05 is spent once, along a pre-planned gated path, rather than divided across independent tests.

sections.heading: Subgroups and Interim Looks Spend From the Same Budget
sections.body: Unplanned subgroup analyses — by age, sex, dose, or any other slice — and repeated interim looks at accumulating trial data are additional implicit multiple comparisons that draw from the same alpha budget.
