The ISIS-2 (1988) aspirin and streptokinase trial famously reported that patients born under the astrological signs Gemini or Libra appeared to derive no benefit, a deliberately absurd example the investigators used to illustrate how a large enough number of subgroup slices will produce spurious "significant" findings purely by chance. The corrective discipline is to pre-allocate the total alpha across every planned primary, secondary, and interim comparison in a Statistical Analysis Plan finalized before the data are unblinded, rather than testing everything at the full 0.05 and reporting only whichever comparison happened to cross the threshold. For repeated interim looks specifically, the standard control mechanism is an alpha-spending function: rather than testing at the full 0.05 at every look, the total alpha is spent gradually across a pre-specified number of looks according to a chosen schedule. The Pocock (1977) boundary spends alpha roughly evenly across looks, giving a constant, easier-to-cross threshold but leaving less for the final analysis; O'Brien-Fleming (1979) instead spends very little alpha early and reserves most of it for later looks, so early interim analyses need an extremely strong signal to stop the trial while the final analysis stays close to the full nominal alpha. Group-sequential designs pre-specify the spending function and number of looks before unblinding, the same discipline the Statistical Analysis Plan already requires for subgroups and secondary endpoints.

lessons.workedExample: A trial pre-specifies one primary and four secondary endpoints. Testing all five at alpha = 0.05 each gives a family-wise error rate of approximately 1 − 0.95^5 ≈ 0.23, a 23% chance that at least one secondary endpoint shows a spurious "significant" result by chance alone. Applying Bonferroni, each of the five is instead tested at 0.05/5 = 0.01, holding the family-wise rate back near 5%. Alternatively, using hierarchical gatekeeping, the team tests the primary endpoint first at the full 0.05; only if it is significant do they test secondary endpoint 1 at the full 0.05, then secondary endpoint 2, and so on down the pre-specified order — no division of alpha required.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe multiplicity because a project reporting "endpoint 3 of 8 was significant, p = .04" with no correction and no pre-specified order is exactly the pattern that manufactures false discoveries out of noise. The tell of real understanding is a pre-specified analysis order or a corrected alpha threshold stated before the data were unblinded, not a correction chosen after seeing which comparison happened to cross 0.05.

questions.prompt: Testing 10 independent hypotheses each at alpha = 0.05, the approximate family-wise error rate (chance of at least one false positive) is closest to:

explanations.a: 5% is the per-test alpha, not the family-wise rate across 10 tests.
explanations.b: 10% would understate the compounding effect of running 10 separate tests.
explanations.c: Correct: 1 − 0.95^10 ≈ 1 − 0.60 = 0.40, roughly a 40% chance of at least one false positive.
explanations.d: 95% would require far more than 10 tests at this alpha to approach.

questions.prompt: The Bonferroni correction controls the family-wise error rate by:

options.text: Increasing alpha for each individual test
Dividing alpha by the number of tests being performed
Testing only the primary endpoint and ignoring the rest
Requiring a larger effect size for every comparison

explanations.a: Increasing alpha per test would make the multiplicity problem worse, not better.
explanations.b: Correct: each of k tests is evaluated at alpha/k, holding the overall family-wise rate near the nominal level.
explanations.c: Bonferroni still tests every pre-specified hypothesis; it adjusts the threshold, not the count of tests run.
explanations.d: Bonferroni changes the significance threshold (alpha), not the effect size being tested for.

questions.prompt: In hierarchical (gatekeeping) testing, a secondary endpoint may be tested at the full pre-specified alpha only if:

options.text: It was selected as interesting after looking at the results
The hypothesis immediately before it in the pre-specified sequence was significant
The trial's sample size was doubled
A separate Bonferroni correction is also applied to it

explanations.a: Choosing endpoints after seeing results is exactly the unplanned-comparison problem gatekeeping is designed to prevent.
explanations.b: Correct: gatekeeping tests hypotheses in a fixed, pre-specified order, and each step is only opened if the prior step in the chain was significant.
explanations.c: Sample size is unrelated to whether a gated hypothesis unlocks; it depends on the outcome of the prior test in the sequence.
explanations.d: Gatekeeping is an alternative to Bonferroni, not a supplement to it — no additional per-test division of alpha is needed.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a pre-specified multiplicity-control plan.

items.text: Enumerate all planned endpoints, subgroups, and interim looks before unblinding
Choose a multiplicity method (Bonferroni or hierarchical gatekeeping) and pre-specify its order or thresholds
Write the plan into the Statistical Analysis Plan before the trial is unblinded
Test hypotheses according to the pre-specified order or thresholds after unblinding

questions.explanation: Every comparison must be enumerated and a method chosen before the plan is locked in writing, and only after unblinding are the actual tests run against that pre-committed structure.

questions.prompt: Match each item to its description.

right.text: Divides alpha evenly across all planned tests; simple but conservative
Tests endpoints in a pre-specified order, each at full alpha, gated by the significance of the prior test
Deliberately absurd subgroup used to illustrate how enough slices of data produce spurious significant findings by chance

questions.explanation: Bonferroni and gatekeeping are two competing solutions to the same multiplicity problem that the ISIS-2 example was designed to dramatize.

units.label: Analyzing Trial Data: Survival, Regression, and Estimands

lessons.label: Time-to-Event Data and Censoring

sections.heading: When the outcome is a clock, not a checkbox
sections.body: Many trials do not ask whether an event happened but when: time to death, relapse, graft failure, or disease progression. This is time-to-event (survival) data, and it has a structure ordinary continuous or binary outcomes lack — the trial ends before every participant has had the event. A cancer trial enrolling patients over three years and following them for two more will contain patients who enrolled late and are still alive at the analysis date, patients who dropped out, and patients who died. Treating 'still alive at last contact' as either a failure or a missing value both throw away real information: the patient did survive for some known duration, even though the final outcome is unknown.

sections.heading: Right-censoring: information, not missingness
sections.body: When a patient's event time is only known to be greater than some observed follow-up time, that observation is right-censored — common causes are the study ending, loss to follow-up, or an unrelated withdrawal. The key statistical move, formalized in Kaplan and Meier's 1958 paper, is to treat censored time as a genuine contribution: the patient is counted as event-free (at risk) for every moment they were observed, then removed from the risk set at the censoring point rather than being scored as a failure or deleted outright. Deleting censored subjects biases estimates toward whoever happens to have short follow-up; scoring them as failures biases the treatment arm that enrolled later or was followed more closely. Right-censoring is only one pattern in a broader family: left-censoring occurs when an event is known to have happened before observation began but the exact time is unknown, and interval-censoring occurs when the event is known only to fall between two observation times — a disease-onset date known only to lie between two clinic visits is interval-censored, while a study that enrolls patients only after diagnosis and never observes time before enrollment introduces left-truncation. Trial follow-up data are overwhelmingly right-censored, but the name specifically distinguishes it from these other mechanisms.

sections.heading: Survival, hazard, and why the mean fails
sections.body: The survival function S(t) gives the probability of being event-free past time t. Its derivative-based counterpart, the hazard function h(t), gives the instantaneous event rate among those still at risk at time t — hazard is a rate per unit time, survival is a cumulative probability, and confusing the two is the single most common conceptual error in reading trial results. Because a meaningful fraction of participants may never experience the event during follow-up, the mean survival time is often mathematically undefined or unreliably estimated from the tail of the curve. Median survival — the time at which S(t) first drops to 0.50 — is the standard headline summary precisely because it depends only on the observed portion of the curve, unlike the mean, which requires extrapolating past the last observation.

lessons.workedExample: A 24-month trial enrolls 200 relapsed-leukemia patients on a staggered basis. By the analysis date, 90 have died, 20 were lost to follow-up at various points, and 90 are alive and still being followed. All 110 non-death observations are right-censored: a patient followed 14 months before being lost contributes 14 event-free months to the risk sets, then exits. If the true median survival is 18 months, a naive analysis that dropped the 110 censored patients would estimate median survival from only the 90 deaths — understating survival, since patients who died fastest are automatically the ones with complete data, while long survivors are disproportionately the ones still being followed and therefore censored.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a Kaplan-Meier curve or a reported median survival on a poster will ask what happened to participants who never had the event — if the presenter cannot explain right-censoring, the follow-up mechanism, or why the mean was not reported, it signals the analysis was copied from software output rather than understood. The pointed follow-up is: 'were your dropout rates similar across arms?' — differential censoring (e.g., sicker patients on one arm quitting the study) can fabricate an apparent treatment effect.

questions.prompt: A patient enrolls in a 3-year survival trial and is alive and event-free when the study ends at 3 years. How should this observation be handled?

options.text: Excluded from the analysis since the outcome is unknown
Counted as a treatment failure at 3 years
Right-censored at 3 years, contributing event-free time up to that point
Imputed using the trial's average survival time

explanations.a: Excluding the patient discards real information — they are known to have survived at least 3 years.
explanations.b: Scoring event-free survivors as failures systematically understates survival.
explanations.c: Correct: right-censoring keeps the patient in every risk set up to 3 years without assuming what happens after.
explanations.d: Imputing from the average sidesteps the actual observed follow-up time and is not how censoring is handled.

questions.prompt: Why is median survival reported instead of mean survival when a trial has heavy censoring?

options.text: The median is always a smaller, more conservative number
The mean requires extrapolating past the longest observed follow-up, which the data cannot support when many patients are censored
Regulators require medians by law
The mean cannot be computed for any continuous variable

explanations.a: The median is not systematically smaller; the reasoning is about estimability, not conservatism.
explanations.b: Correct: with censoring, the survival curve's tail beyond the last event is unknown, so the mean (the full area under the curve) is often undefined or unstable, while the median only needs the curve down to 50%.
explanations.c: There is no such blanket legal requirement; the choice is statistical.
explanations.d: Means are computable for continuous variables in general — the issue is specific to censored survival data.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

right.text: Instantaneous event rate among those still at risk
Cumulative probability of being event-free past time t
An event time known only to exceed the observed follow-up

questions.explanation: Survival is a cumulative probability, hazard is a rate, and right-censoring is a form of partial information rather than a missing value.

questions.prompt: Order the events for a single patient who is lost to follow-up partway through a survival trial.

items.text: Patient enrolls and enters the risk set
Patient is followed and remains event-free for several months
Contact is lost; last known event-free time is recorded
Patient is right-censored and removed from later risk sets

questions.explanation: The patient contributes event-free time up until the point contact is lost, at which point they are censored rather than scored as a failure.

lessons.label: The Kaplan-Meier Estimator

sections.heading: Building the curve from risk sets
sections.body: Kaplan and Meier's 1958 paper, 'Nonparametric Estimation from Incomplete Observations,' gave trials a way to estimate S(t) without assuming any particular shape for survival — no exponential, no Weibull, just the data. The method walks through the distinct times at which events actually occurred. At each event time t_i, it computes the conditional probability of surviving that instant: (number at risk minus number of events) divided by number at risk. The overall survival estimate at any time is the running product of these conditional probabilities across every event time up to and including t — hence the estimator's other name, the product-limit estimator. Censored patients are removed from the risk set at their censoring time but never counted as events, exactly implementing the principle from the previous lesson.

sections.heading: Why the curve is a staircase
sections.body: Because the estimate only changes at observed event times, the Kaplan-Meier curve is a step function: flat between events, then dropping vertically at each event time by an amount proportional to how many at-risk patients failed there. A drop from 10 at-risk patients with 1 event is a smaller step than a drop from 10 at-risk with 3 events. Reading the curve, the y-axis at any x gives the estimated probability of remaining event-free past that time; the point where the curve crosses 0.50 (interpolated if it lands between events) is the median survival. If the curve never reaches 0.50 because follow-up ended first, median survival is reported as 'not reached' — itself a meaningful, favorable result, not a data failure.

sections.heading: Reading the tick marks
sections.body: Kaplan-Meier plots conventionally show small vertical tick marks on the curve at times when a patient was censored rather than experiencing the event. These marks matter for two reasons: they show where the risk set is shrinking for reasons other than events, and a cluster of censoring ticks just before the curve would otherwise have dropped is a red flag — it can mean patients were withdrawn right before an anticipated bad outcome, or that follow-up simply thinned out, either of which widens the confidence interval on the tail of the curve and makes late-curve claims (e.g., 'survival at 5 years') less trustworthy than early-curve claims. A number-at-risk table printed beneath the x-axis, showing how many patients remain at each time point, is the standard way trials disclose this shrinkage transparently.

lessons.workedExample: Ten patients enter a trial. At month 3, 1 of the 10 at-risk dies: conditional survival = 9/10 = 0.90, so S(3) = 0.90. Two patients are censored at month 4 (no drop, but risk set falls to 7). At month 6, 2 of the remaining 7 at-risk die: conditional survival = 5/7 ≈ 0.714, so S(6) = 0.90 × 0.714 ≈ 0.643. If no further deaths occur before the study ends and the curve never falls to 0.50, the report reads 'median survival not reached, S(6 months) = 0.643.' The number-at-risk row would show 10, then 7 (after censoring), then 5.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can read the actual mechanics off a Kaplan-Meier plot rather than reciting 'it shows survival over time.' A strong answer traces a specific drop to a specific number of events at a specific risk-set size, explains why the curve is flat between events, and flags when a late-curve estimate is unstable because the number-at-risk has thinned to single digits — a caution students who only memorize the shape rarely offer.

questions.prompt: Why does the Kaplan-Meier curve only drop at observed event times rather than declining smoothly?

options.text: Because it is a nonparametric estimator built directly from the discrete event times in the data, with no assumed underlying distribution
Because censored patients are averaged into a smooth interpolation
Because the method assumes an exponential distribution between events
Because software rounds continuous time into monthly bins

explanations.a: Correct: the estimator is the running product of conditional survival probabilities computed only at times where an event was actually observed, producing a step function.
explanations.b: Censoring shrinks the risk set but does not smooth or interpolate the curve.
explanations.c: Kaplan-Meier is nonparametric precisely because it makes no distributional assumption like exponential survival.
explanations.d: The step behavior comes from the estimator's definition, not from time binning.

questions.prompt: A Kaplan-Meier curve never crosses 0.50 by the end of follow-up. What is the correct way to report median survival?

options.text: Report the survival probability at the last observed time as if it were the median
Extrapolate the curve's slope forward to estimate when it would reach 0.50
Report median survival as 'not reached'
Substitute the mean survival time instead

explanations.a: That number is a survival probability at a fixed time, not a median survival time, and reporting it as such misrepresents the estimate.
explanations.b: Extrapolating beyond the data is not supported by the nonparametric method and is not standard practice.
explanations.c: Correct: when the curve never reaches 0.50 within observed follow-up, the honest and standard report is 'median survival not reached.'
explanations.d: The mean has the same undefined-tail problem as the median once the curve does not reach a landmark within follow-up, often worse.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in constructing a Kaplan-Meier estimate at a given event time.

items.text: Identify the number of patients at risk just before the event time
Count the number of events occurring exactly at that time
Compute the conditional survival probability for that time point
Multiply this conditional probability by the running product from all earlier event times

questions.explanation: Kaplan-Meier is a product of conditional survival probabilities, each computed from the risk set and event count at that specific time.

questions.prompt: Match each Kaplan-Meier plot feature to what it represents.

left.text: A vertical tick mark on the curve
A vertical drop in the curve
The number-at-risk row beneath the x-axis

right.text: An event (or cluster of events) occurring at that time
A censored observation at that time
How many patients remain under observation at each time point

questions.explanation: Ticks mark censoring, drops mark events, and the at-risk table discloses how thin the data get over time.

lessons.label: Comparing Survival: the Log-Rank Test and Hazard Ratio

sections.heading: Testing whole curves, not single points
sections.body: Once two Kaplan-Meier curves are drawn for a treatment and control arm, the natural question is whether they differ, and a t-test comparing means will not work because means are often undefined under censoring. The log-rank test, developed by Nathan Mantel in 1966 and given its now-standard form by Richard and Julia Peto in 1972, instead compares curves across their entire span. At every distinct event time in the pooled data, it computes the number of events expected in each arm under the null hypothesis that both arms share the same hazard, given how many patients from each arm were at risk at that moment. Summing the observed-minus-expected events across all event times, then squaring and standardizing, yields a chi-square statistic. The test's strength is that it weights every event time equally and needs no assumption about the shape of the hazard over time — its weakness is exactly that: it can miss a real difference concentrated early or late if the curves cross, since gains in one period cancel losses in another.

sections.heading: The hazard ratio as the effect size
sections.body: The log-rank test gives a p-value but no effect size. The hazard ratio (HR), typically estimated alongside it (formally via Cox regression, covered next lesson), summarizes the relative instantaneous event rate: HR = h_treatment(t) / h_control(t). An HR of 0.70 means that at any moment during follow-up, a treated patient who has survived event-free to that moment has 70% of the control arm's instantaneous risk of the event — a 30% relative reduction in hazard, not in absolute risk and not in cumulative risk over the whole trial.

sections.heading: Hazard ratio versus risk ratio: a routinely confused pair
sections.body: A risk ratio (or relative risk) compares cumulative probabilities of the event by a fixed time point — e.g., the proportion who died by 5 years in each arm. A hazard ratio compares instantaneous rates continuously over the whole follow-up period and, unlike a risk ratio, is not simply 'how many events happened' but 'how fast are they happening, conditional on still being at risk.' The two numbers are not interchangeable and can diverge substantially when the hazard ratio is not constant over time (e.g., a drug with an early surgical risk but long-term benefit) or when the risk ratio's time point is chosen well after most events have already occurred, compressing the remaining at-risk population. Reporting an HR from a Cox model as though it were a risk ratio overstates precision about absolute benefit that the hazard ratio was never designed to convey.

lessons.workedExample: A trial randomizes 400 patients to a new anticoagulant versus standard care and follows them for stroke. The log-rank test comparing the two Kaplan-Meier curves yields chi-square = 6.8, p = 0.009 — the curves differ significantly across the full follow-up period. The accompanying hazard ratio is 0.65 (95% CI 0.48-0.88): at any instant, treated patients who remain event-free have 65% of the control arm's instantaneous stroke hazard. Separately, cumulative stroke incidence by 3 years is 8% on treatment versus 12% on control — a risk ratio of about 0.67, numerically close here but conceptually a different quantity, since it only compares the two fixed endpoints rather than the whole time course.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use this pair of concepts to separate students who ran a statistical test from students who understand what it tested. A common trap is asking a presenter to state, in one sentence, what their hazard ratio means for an individual patient — a correct answer references instantaneous rate and conditional survival, not 'patients on treatment were 35% less likely to have the event,' which describes a risk ratio. Judges also probe whether a nonsignificant log-rank p-value with visibly crossing curves was investigated further, since log-rank can under-power exactly that pattern.

questions.prompt: A trial reports HR = 0.65 for stroke. What does this value mean?

options.text: Treated patients have 65% lower cumulative stroke risk by the end of the trial
At any moment, event-free treated patients have 65% of the control arm's instantaneous stroke hazard
65% of treated patients avoided stroke entirely
The absolute risk reduction is 65 percentage points
The treatment reduced deaths by 65% in the first year only

explanations.a: That describes a risk ratio at a fixed endpoint, not a hazard ratio, which is an instantaneous rate comparison.
explanations.b: Correct: the hazard ratio compares instantaneous event rates among those still at risk, continuously across follow-up.
explanations.c: This confuses the hazard ratio with an absolute proportion of patients avoiding the event.
explanations.d: Absolute risk reduction is a percentage-point difference in cumulative risk, a wholly different quantity from a hazard ratio.
explanations.e: Nothing in an HR restricts its interpretation to the first year; it applies across the modeled follow-up unless proportional hazards is violated.

questions.prompt: Two Kaplan-Meier curves cross partway through follow-up, with one arm better early and the other better late. What is the main limitation of the log-rank test here?

options.text: The log-rank test cannot be computed at all when curves cross
It weights all event times equally, so early and late differences in opposite directions can cancel and mask a real pattern
It requires the curves to start at the same value
It only works when there is no censoring

explanations.a: The test is still computable; it simply may lose power to detect the pattern.
explanations.b: Correct: because it sums observed-minus-expected across all event times with equal weight, opposing effects in different periods can offset each other.
explanations.c: Both curves start at 1.0 by construction (all patients event-free at time zero); this is not the issue.
explanations.d: The log-rank test is explicitly built to handle censored data; that is one of its main purposes.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to what it actually measures.

right.text: Ratio of instantaneous event rates over continuous follow-up
Ratio of cumulative event probabilities by a fixed time point
Whether two entire survival curves differ, summed across all event times

questions.explanation: HR is instantaneous and continuous, risk ratio is cumulative and fixed-time, and the log-rank statistic tests the whole curve rather than producing an effect size.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a log-rank test comparing two arms.

items.text: Pool all distinct event times from both arms
At each event time, compute the expected number of events per arm under the null of equal hazards
Sum the observed-minus-expected events across all event times
Standardize the sum into a chi-square statistic and obtain a p-value

questions.explanation: The log-rank test accumulates the discrepancy between observed and null-expected events at every event time, then converts that sum into a formal test statistic.

lessons.label: Cox Proportional Hazards Regression

sections.heading: Modeling hazard with covariates
sections.body: David Cox's 1972 paper 'Regression Models and Life-Tables' introduced a way to estimate the effect of treatment on survival while simultaneously adjusting for other variables — age, baseline severity, comorbidity count — without having to specify the underlying shape of the hazard function over time. The Cox model writes the hazard for an individual as h(t) = h0(t) × exp(β1x1 + β2x2 + ...), where h0(t) is an unspecified 'baseline hazard' that can vary freely with time, and each exp(βi) is the hazard ratio associated with a one-unit change in covariate xi, holding the others fixed. Because h0(t) cancels out of the ratio between any two individuals' hazards, Cox regression is described as semi-parametric: it makes no assumption about the baseline hazard's shape but does assume the covariate effects are constant multipliers of it. This lets a trial report, for example, an HR of 0.72 for treatment 'adjusted for age and baseline ECOG performance status' in a single coefficient, rather than needing separate curves for every covariate combination.

sections.heading: The proportional-hazards assumption
sections.body: The model's core assumption is that the hazard ratio between any two groups (or per unit of a continuous covariate) stays constant over the entire follow-up period — the two arms' hazards may differ, but their ratio does not change with time. Two standard diagnostics check this. A log-log plot (log of negative log survival, log(-log S(t)), plotted against log(t) for each group) should produce roughly parallel curves if proportional hazards holds; converging, diverging, or crossing curves suggest a violation. Schoenfeld residuals, one per covariate per event time, provide a more formal test: under proportional hazards these residuals should show no trend over time, and a statistically significant slope (tested, e.g., via the approach formalized by Grambsch and Therneau in 1994) flags a time-varying effect.

sections.heading: What to do when it fails
sections.body: When proportional hazards is violated — a common real pattern is a surgical or treatment-related early hazard that reverses into a later benefit — reporting one single pooled hazard ratio for the whole follow-up period is misleading, since it averages two opposite effects into a number that describes neither period accurately. Standard remedies include splitting follow-up into time intervals with separate hazard ratios per interval (a time-varying coefficient), stratifying the baseline hazard by the offending covariate so it is no longer assumed to be shared, or switching to restricted mean survival time, a model-free summary that avoids the proportionality assumption altogether by measuring area under the survival curve up to a fixed horizon.

sections.heading: Interpreting adjustment
sections.body: An adjusted HR answers a different question than an unadjusted (crude) HR: it estimates the treatment effect holding the listed covariates fixed, which matters when those covariates are imbalanced between arms despite randomization or when the trial is observational rather than randomized. In a well-randomized trial, adjustment mainly tightens the confidence interval by explaining some of the outcome variance; in an observational comparison, adjustment (and its limits — only measured confounders can be adjusted for) is often the entire basis for any causal claim.

lessons.workedExample: A trial of an experimental valve replacement enrolls 500 patients and fits a Cox model for mortality with treatment, age, and baseline ejection fraction as covariates. The adjusted HR for treatment is 0.68 (95% CI 0.52-0.89), meaning that among patients of the same age and ejection fraction, treated patients have 68% of the control arm's instantaneous mortality hazard at any follow-up time. A log-log plot shows the two treatment curves diverging sharply in the first 30 days (surgical risk) before running roughly parallel afterward — a Schoenfeld residual test confirms a significant time trend for treatment (p = 0.01), so the team reports separate 0-30-day and post-30-day hazard ratios instead of the single pooled 0.68.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a Cox model on a poster will ask two things in sequence: what does the adjusted hazard ratio control for and why, and has proportional hazards actually been checked. Presenters who report an adjusted HR without naming the covariates, or who never mention checking the assumption, signal they ran default software output rather than diagnosing the model — and a judge who spots visibly crossing survival curves alongside a single reported HR will treat that HR as suspect until asked about directly.

questions.prompt: What does the baseline hazard h0(t) represent in a Cox proportional hazards model?

options.text: The hazard for a patient with all covariates equal to zero, with an unspecified shape over time
The average hazard across the whole trial, assumed constant
The hazard ratio between treatment and control
A parametric exponential hazard fit to the control arm only

explanations.a: Correct: h0(t) is the hazard when all covariates are zero, and the model leaves its shape over time completely unspecified — this is what makes Cox regression semi-parametric.
explanations.b: The baseline hazard is explicitly allowed to vary with time, not assumed constant.
explanations.c: The hazard ratio comes from the exp(β) terms, not from h0(t) itself.
explanations.d: Cox regression avoids assuming any parametric form like exponential for the baseline hazard; that is its defining feature.

questions.prompt: A Schoenfeld residual test shows a significant time trend for the treatment covariate. What does this indicate?

options.text: The sample size is too small to fit a Cox model
The proportional-hazards assumption is violated for treatment, so a single HR may not describe the whole follow-up period well
The log-rank test should be used instead, since Cox regression has failed
Censoring was handled incorrectly
The hazard ratio must be exactly 1.0

explanations.a: Schoenfeld residuals test an assumption about the model's structure, not sample size adequacy directly.
explanations.b: Correct: a significant trend in Schoenfeld residuals over time means the treatment's hazard ratio is not constant, i.e., proportional hazards does not hold for that covariate.
explanations.c: The log-rank test has the same limitation regarding time-varying effects and is not a fix; time-varying coefficients or stratification are the standard remedies.
explanations.d: This diagnostic is about the constancy of hazard ratios over time, unrelated to how censoring was coded.
explanations.e: A time trend says nothing about the HR's average value, only that it is not constant.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for diagnosing and responding to a proportional-hazards violation.

items.text: Fit the Cox model and obtain a pooled hazard ratio
Check log-log survival plots or Schoenfeld residuals for a time trend
Confirm the trend is statistically significant, indicating non-proportional hazards
Refit using time-varying coefficients or stratification instead of a single pooled HR

questions.explanation: You first fit the standard model, then diagnose whether its core assumption holds, then adapt the model if it does not.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in Cox regression.

right.text: The hazard ratio associated with that covariate
A visual check for parallel curves across groups
A formal per-covariate test for a time trend in the hazard ratio

questions.explanation: exp(β) gives the effect size, while the log-log plot and Schoenfeld residuals are two ways of checking the proportional-hazards assumption behind it.

lessons.label: Linear and Logistic Regression for Trial Data

sections.heading: Two regressions for two kinds of outcome
sections.body: Not every trial outcome is time-to-event. When the outcome is continuous — blood pressure change, a symptom score, weight loss in kilograms — linear regression models it as a weighted sum of covariates plus normally distributed error: Y = β0 + β1(treatment) + β2(age) + ... + ε, and β1 is directly interpretable as the mean difference in Y attributable to treatment, holding the other covariates fixed. When the outcome is binary — remission yes/no, treatment success yes/no — linear regression breaks down because predicted probabilities can fall outside 0 to 1 and the constant-variance assumption fails. Logistic regression instead models the log-odds of the outcome, logit(p) = β0 + β1(treatment) + ..., so exp(β1) is an odds ratio: the multiplicative change in the odds of the outcome associated with treatment, holding other covariates fixed.

sections.heading: Odds ratios are not risk ratios
sections.body: An odds ratio compares odds (p/(1-p)) across groups, not probabilities directly, and the two diverge as the outcome becomes more common — for a rare outcome (say, under 10%) an odds ratio closely approximates a risk ratio, but for a common outcome (a 40% or 60% event rate) an odds ratio can look considerably more extreme than the corresponding risk ratio, a distortion that has led to real cases of exaggerated trial claims in press coverage. This mirrors the hazard-ratio-versus-risk-ratio confusion from survival analysis: each regression family's native effect measure (mean difference, hazard ratio, odds ratio) is a distinct quantity from cumulative risk, and readers should ask which one a headline number actually is.

sections.heading: Adjustment and interaction terms
sections.body: Both regression types support multivariable adjustment: including a prognostic baseline covariate (disease severity at randomization, site, prior treatment history) tends to increase statistical power in a randomized trial by explaining outcome variance the arms didn't otherwise separate on, even though randomization already balances confounders on average. An interaction term — adding a treatment-by-covariate product term such as treatment × sex — tests effect modification: whether the treatment effect itself differs across levels of that covariate. A significant interaction means the single overall treatment effect is misleading and subgroup-specific effects should be reported instead; a nonsignificant interaction does not prove the effect is uniform, only that the trial lacked power to detect heterogeneity, since interaction tests characteristically need several times the sample size of the main effect to reach the same power.

lessons.workedExample: A trial of a new antihypertensive fits linear regression for systolic blood pressure change, adjusting for baseline BP and age: the treatment coefficient is -8.2 mmHg (95% CI -11.0 to -5.4), meaning treated patients dropped 8.2 mmHg more than controls on average, holding baseline BP and age fixed. A secondary binary outcome, 'BP controlled below 130/80 at 12 weeks,' is analyzed with logistic regression: OR = 2.1 (95% CI 1.4-3.2), meaning the odds of control are 2.1 times higher on treatment. Because the control rate is 55% in the trial (a common outcome, not rare), this OR of 2.1 corresponds to a smaller risk ratio of roughly 1.3 — reporting '2.1 times more likely to be controlled' without noting this gap would overstate the everyday-language impact of the finding.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a presenter reporting an odds ratio can say, without hedging, whether their outcome was common or rare in the trial — because that single fact determines whether the OR can be loosely read as a risk ratio or not. A second common probe is the interaction term: if subgroup results are shown on a poster without a formal interaction test, a judge will ask whether the subgroup difference was pre-specified and formally tested, since eyeballing subgroups for 'the drug worked better in women' without an interaction p-value is a classic source of false subgroup claims.

questions.prompt: Why can't linear regression be used directly for a binary trial outcome like remission yes/no?

options.text: Binary outcomes cannot be coded numerically
Predicted values can fall outside the 0-1 probability range and the model's error-variance assumptions fail
Linear regression cannot include a treatment covariate
Binary outcomes require Cox regression instead

explanations.a: Binary outcomes are routinely coded 0/1; that is not the obstacle.
explanations.b: Correct: linear regression can predict probabilities below 0 or above 1 and assumes constant-variance normal errors, both of which are violated by a binary outcome, which is why logistic regression is used instead.
explanations.c: Linear regression can include any covariate, including treatment; the issue is the outcome type, not the predictors.
explanations.d: Cox regression is for time-to-event outcomes, not binary outcomes in general; logistic regression is the standard tool here.

questions.prompt: A trial reports OR = 2.1 for a binary outcome with a 55% event rate in controls. What is the most accurate statement?

options.text: The risk ratio is also approximately 2.1, since OR and risk ratio are always equal
Because the outcome is common, the OR of 2.1 likely overstates the corresponding risk ratio
OR cannot be computed when the event rate exceeds 50%
The odds ratio is invalid because the outcome should have used Cox regression

explanations.a: OR and risk ratio only converge for rare outcomes; at a 55% control rate they diverge meaningfully.
explanations.b: Correct: with a common outcome, the odds ratio amplifies the apparent effect relative to the risk ratio, since odds grow nonlinearly as probability moves away from the extremes.
explanations.c: Odds ratios are well-defined for any probability strictly between 0 and 1, including above 50%.
explanations.d: Cox regression is for time-to-event data; a binary yes/no outcome at a fixed follow-up point is exactly what logistic regression is designed for.

questions.prompt: A trial tests a treatment × sex interaction term and finds it nonsignificant (p = 0.40). What is the correct conclusion?

options.text: The treatment effect is proven identical in men and women
The trial found no evidence of effect modification by sex, but this does not rule out heterogeneity the trial was underpowered to detect
The main treatment effect is therefore invalid
Subgroup analysis should be abandoned entirely for this trial

explanations.a: A nonsignificant interaction is not proof of equality; interaction tests are notoriously underpowered relative to main-effect tests.
explanations.b: Correct: absence of evidence for an interaction is not evidence of absence, especially given the larger sample sizes interaction tests typically require.
explanations.c: The interaction test result has no bearing on the validity of the main treatment effect estimate.
explanations.d: The nonsignificant interaction says nothing about whether other subgroup questions were worth pre-specifying; it does not invalidate subgroup analysis as a method.

questions.prompt: Match each regression concept to its description.

right.text: Mean difference in the continuous outcome associated with the covariate
Odds ratio associated with the covariate
Test for whether the treatment effect differs across levels of another covariate

questions.explanation: Linear regression coefficients are mean differences, logistic regression's exponentiated coefficients are odds ratios, and interaction terms formally test effect modification.

lessons.label: Analysis Populations: ITT, Per-Protocol, and Estimands

sections.heading: Three ways to define who counts
sections.body: After randomization, real trials always have some non-adherence: patients who stop the drug, switch arms, or never start it. How the analysis handles these patients defines the analysis population. Intention-to-treat (ITT) analyzes every randomized patient in the arm they were assigned to, regardless of what they actually took — this preserves the balance randomization created between arms on both measured and unmeasured factors, and is the standard primary analysis for superiority trials because it protects against bias from differential dropout. Per-protocol analysis includes only patients who adhered to the assigned regimen as specified, which can better estimate the biological effect of actually taking the drug but reintroduces confounding, since the reasons patients stop treatment (side effects, worsening disease, recovery) are rarely random. As-treated analysis groups patients by what they actually received rather than what they were assigned, which fully abandons the protection of randomization and is the most bias-prone of the three.

sections.heading: Why the choice changes the answer
sections.body: A well-known and cautionary illustration is the Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial (CAST), which stopped early in 1989 when the antiarrhythmic drugs under study were found by ITT analysis to increase mortality despite successfully suppressing arrhythmias, the very outcome doctors expected to translate into survival benefit — a per-protocol or as-treated analysis restricted to patients who tolerated the drug could plausibly have hidden this harm by dropping exactly the patients who were doing poorly on it. This is the general pattern: per-protocol analyses tend to make treatments look more favorable than ITT because the patients who drop out are disproportionately those doing badly, whichever arm they are in.

sections.heading: The estimand framework and missing data
sections.body: Because 'the treatment effect' can mean different things depending on how intercurrent events (treatment discontinuation, rescue medication, death before the endpoint) are handled, the ICH E9(R1) addendum (2019) formalized the estimand framework: before analysis, a trial must state precisely what question is being answered — the population, the outcome, how intercurrent events are handled (e.g., treatment-policy strategy, ignoring subsequent treatment changes, versus hypothetical strategy, asking what would have happened had discontinuation not occurred), and the summary measure. This forces ITT-versus-per-protocol from an afterthought into an upfront, pre-specified design choice. Missing outcome data compounds the same problem: last observation carried forward (LOCF), which substitutes a patient's last observed value for missing later ones, was historically common but assumes flat trajectories after dropout, an assumption rarely defensible and now discouraged by regulators. Multiple imputation, formalized by Rubin in 1987, instead generates several plausible completed datasets reflecting the uncertainty about the missing values, analyzes each, and pools the results — properly propagating that uncertainty into the final confidence interval rather than pretending the missing data never happened.

lessons.workedExample: A weight-loss drug trial randomizes 300 patients; by week 24, 40 have discontinued treatment (20 per arm) due to side effects or lack of effect. An ITT analysis, using each patient's last available weight (with missing data handled by multiple imputation rather than LOCF), finds a between-arm difference of 3.1 kg. A per-protocol analysis restricted to the 260 adherent completers finds a larger difference of 4.5 kg — because dropouts, who are disproportionately non-responders, are excluded from the per-protocol comparison, inflating the apparent effect relative to what a patient prescribed the drug in practice would experience.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will ask which analysis population was the pre-specified primary analysis, because reporting only the more favorable per-protocol number, or switching from ITT to per-protocol after seeing the data, is a recognized way trials overstate effects. A sharper judge will ask how missing data were handled — an answer of 'we just used the last measurement we had' (LOCF) without acknowledging its flat-trajectory assumption signals the presenter has not engaged with why regulators moved away from it.

questions.prompt: Why is intention-to-treat the standard primary analysis for superiority trials rather than per-protocol?

options.text: ITT always produces larger, more impressive effect sizes
ITT preserves the balance randomization created, while per-protocol reintroduces confounding by excluding non-adherent patients non-randomly
Per-protocol analysis is not statistically valid under any circumstances
ITT requires no adjustment for baseline covariates

explanations.a: ITT effects are typically smaller, not larger, than per-protocol effects, since it includes non-adherent patients who dilute the apparent effect.
explanations.b: Correct: because who drops out is rarely random, excluding them (as per-protocol does) breaks the confounding control randomization provided.
explanations.c: Per-protocol analysis is valid as a secondary or supportive analysis; the issue is using it as the sole primary analysis due to its confounding risk.
explanations.d: ITT and covariate adjustment are separate design choices; ITT concerns which patients are included, not whether covariates are used.

questions.prompt: What historically common method for handling missing follow-up data is now discouraged because it assumes a patient's outcome stays flat after they drop out?

options.text: Multiple imputation
Complete-case analysis
Last observation carried forward (LOCF)
Intention-to-treat analysis

explanations.a: Multiple imputation models uncertainty about missing values rather than assuming a flat trajectory; it is the more modern, favored approach.
explanations.b: Complete-case analysis drops missing patients rather than assuming their trajectory is flat; it has its own biases but not this specific one.
explanations.c: Correct: LOCF substitutes the last observed value forward, implicitly assuming no further change occurred, which is rarely realistic and is now discouraged by regulators.
explanations.d: ITT is a population-definition principle, not a specific method for imputing missing values.

questions.prompt: Order the elements the ICH E9(R1) estimand framework requires a trial to pre-specify before analysis.

items.text: Define the target population and outcome of interest
Specify how intercurrent events like treatment discontinuation will be handled
State the summary measure (e.g., mean difference, hazard ratio)
Conduct the pre-specified primary analysis

questions.explanation: The estimand framework requires the question to be fully defined, including intercurrent-event handling, before the analysis is run, rather than deciding after seeing the data.

questions.prompt: Match each analysis population to its defining rule.

right.text: Analyzed by assigned arm regardless of actual adherence
Analyzed only among patients who adhered to the assigned regimen
Analyzed by what treatment patients actually received

questions.explanation: The three populations differ in how they treat non-adherence, with ITT alone preserving randomization's balance.

lessons.label: Interim Analysis, Data Monitoring, and Stopping Rules

sections.heading: The multiple-testing problem of looking early
sections.body: Large trials often check results before final follow-up completes, but each additional look at accumulating data is another opportunity for a false-positive result, since a 0.05 significance threshold applied repeatedly inflates the overall Type I error well past 5%. Group-sequential designs solve this by pre-specifying a fixed number of interim looks and spending the total error budget across them according to a boundary. The O'Brien-Fleming boundary, from a 1979 paper by Peter O'Brien and Thomas Fleming, sets an extremely strict significance threshold at early looks (often requiring p under 0.001 to stop) that relaxes toward the nominal 0.05 only at the final analysis — this conserves most of the error budget for the end, so an early stop reflects an unusually strong signal rather than noise. Lan and DeMets' 1983 alpha-spending function generalized this into a flexible framework that does not require the number or exact timing of looks to be fixed in advance, spending a chosen fraction of total alpha as a continuous function of information accrued so far.

sections.heading: Who watches the data
sections.body: An independent Data and Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB), composed of clinicians, statisticians, and ethicists with no stake in the trial's outcome, reviews unblinded interim results against the pre-specified stopping boundaries — investigators and sponsors typically remain blinded throughout, since their design decisions or enrollment behavior could otherwise be influenced by knowing which arm is ahead. The DSMB can recommend stopping for benefit, when the treatment effect crosses the efficacy boundary early enough to make continuing unethical to the control arm; for harm, when the treatment arm is doing significantly worse, as happened with CAST's 1989 early termination once antiarrhythmic drugs were shown by interim monitoring to increase mortality; or for futility, when interim data make it improbable the trial can reach a significant result even with full enrollment, via a conditional power calculation.

sections.heading: Early stopping tends to overstate the effect
sections.body: A trial stopped early for benefit crosses its efficacy boundary at a moment when, by definition, the observed effect estimate is unusually large relative to its own confidence interval — that is precisely why it crossed the boundary at that particular look rather than a later one. Averaged across many trials, effect estimates from early-stopped trials are systematically larger than the true effect would show with full follow-up, a well-documented regression-to-the-mean-like phenomenon; meta-analyses that pool such trials without adjustment can therefore overstate benefit, which is why some statisticians argue for bias-corrected estimates when a trial stops early.

sections.heading: Reading a non-inferiority margin
sections.body: Non-inferiority trials do not test whether a new treatment is better, but whether it is not unacceptably worse than an active control, typically because the new option offers some other advantage (cost, side-effect profile, dosing convenience). The non-inferiority margin is a pre-specified maximum acceptable difference, chosen to preserve a defensible fraction of the active control's known historical benefit over placebo — if the new treatment's confidence interval stays entirely within that margin of the control, non-inferiority is declared. A margin set too wide can pass a genuinely worse treatment; the margin must be justified from prior placebo-controlled evidence, not chosen after seeing the trial's own results.

lessons.workedExample: A cardiovascular outcomes trial plans three interim looks plus a final analysis, using an O'Brien-Fleming boundary that requires p < 0.0001 at the first look, p < 0.004 at the second, p < 0.023 at the third, and p < 0.041 at the final look to preserve overall alpha at 0.05. At the second interim look, the DSMB observes p = 0.002 favoring treatment — this crosses the boundary, and the DSMB recommends stopping for benefit. A separate non-inferiority trial of a new antibiotic sets its margin at 10 percentage points, based on the active control's established 25-point advantage over placebo in prior trials (preserving well over half of that effect); the new drug's 95% CI for the difference in cure rates is entirely within 10 points of the control, so non-inferiority is declared.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a presenter citing an early-stopped trial understands that the reported effect size is likely inflated relative to what full follow-up would have shown — citing a dramatic early-stopped result as if it were a stable final estimate is a common overreach. For non-inferiority claims specifically, judges ask where the margin came from and whether it was justified by prior placebo-controlled data or simply picked to make the new treatment pass, since an unjustified or overly generous margin can smuggle a worse treatment through as 'non-inferior.'

questions.prompt: Why does repeatedly testing a trial's data at multiple interim looks require a stricter significance threshold at each look than a single final analysis would?

options.text: Because each additional look inflates the overall Type I error rate if the same 0.05 threshold is reused every time
Because interim data are always less accurate than final data
Because DSMBs require extra statistical margin for their own error
Because sample size shrinks at each interim look

explanations.a: Correct: each look is a fresh opportunity for a false positive, so spending the error budget unevenly (strict early, relaxed at the end) keeps the cumulative false-positive rate at the intended level.
explanations.b: Interim data are just as accurate as final data would be at that sample size; the issue is repeated testing, not data quality.
explanations.c: The stricter threshold is a statistical correction for multiple testing, not a buffer for DSMB error.
explanations.d: Sample size accrues, it does not shrink, over the course of a trial with interim looks.

questions.prompt: A trial stops early for benefit at an interim look. What is the expected relationship between the reported effect size and the true effect?

options.text: The reported effect is unbiased and equal to the true effect on average
The reported effect tends to be systematically larger than the true effect, because stopping happened at a moment of an unusually large observed effect
The reported effect tends to be systematically smaller than the true effect
There is no relationship, since interim and final analyses use different patients

explanations.a: Stopping precisely because the boundary was crossed builds in a selection effect that biases the estimate upward, not an unbiased one.
explanations.b: Correct: crossing an efficacy boundary requires an unusually favorable observed effect at that specific look, which systematically inflates reported effects from early-stopped trials.
explanations.c: The bias runs in the favorable direction, since only unusually large effects trigger early stopping for benefit.
explanations.d: Interim and final analyses use the same accumulating patient cohort, not separate groups; the bias comes from the stopping rule itself.

questions.prompt: In a non-inferiority trial, what must the non-inferiority margin be justified by?

options.text: Whatever difference makes the new trial's own results pass
Prior placebo-controlled evidence establishing the active control's benefit, so the margin preserves a defensible fraction of that benefit
The trial's observed standard deviation only
Regulatory convention with no need for prior evidence

explanations.a: Choosing the margin after seeing results defeats its purpose and can let a genuinely worse treatment pass; margins must be pre-specified.
explanations.b: Correct: the margin should be grounded in the active control's known historical advantage over placebo, ensuring a 'non-inferior' result still preserves meaningful benefit over doing nothing.
explanations.c: Standard deviation informs sample-size and power calculations, but the margin itself is a clinical-relevance judgment tied to the control's known effect.
explanations.d: Margins require justification from prior evidence; they are not simply a matter of convention.

questions.prompt: Match each stopping reason to its trigger.

right.text: Treatment crosses the pre-specified efficacy boundary early
Treatment arm shows significantly worse outcomes than control
Conditional power calculations show reaching significance is highly improbable even with full enrollment

questions.explanation: A DSMB can recommend stopping for three distinct reasons, each with its own statistical trigger.

questions.prompt: Order the components of a group-sequential monitoring plan as they are set up and used.

items.text: Pre-specify the number of interim looks and choose a boundary (e.g., O'Brien-Fleming)
Allocate the total alpha budget unevenly across looks, strict early and relaxed at the end
DSMB reviews unblinded interim data against the boundary at each look
DSMB recommends continuing, or stopping for benefit, harm, or futility

questions.explanation: The boundary and alpha-spending plan must be fixed before the trial starts, then applied by the DSMB at each scheduled interim review.

units.label: Landmark Trials and the Statistics Wars

lessons.label: James Lind and the Origins of the Controlled Trial

sections.heading: Six pairs, six treatments
sections.body: In May 1747, aboard HMS Salisbury, ship's surgeon James Lind selected twelve sailors sick with scurvy whose cases were, in his words, 'as similar as I could have them.' He put all twelve on the same base diet and then split them into six pairs, each pair getting a different daily addition: a quart of cider; twenty-five drops of elixir vitriol (dilute sulfuric acid) three times a day; two spoonfuls of vinegar three times a day; half a pint of seawater; two oranges and one lemon daily; or an electuary of garlic, mustard seed, horseradish, balsam of Peru, and gum myrrh. Within six days, the two sailors on citrus were fit for duty; one of them went on to nurse the others. Same starting population, same background diet, one variable changed per pair, groups compared concurrently — this is the earliest well-documented controlled clinical comparison in medicine.

sections.heading: What it lacked
sections.body: Lind's design had no randomization: he does not describe how sailors were assigned to pairs, leaving room for unconscious selection bias. Groups held only two men each, with no formal statistics to rule out chance. And Lind muted his own finding — his 1753 'A Treatise of the Scurvy' buried the citrus result among lengthy reviews of rival theories and did not recommend citrus as a clear, isolated cure, hedging toward broader dietary reform instead.

sections.heading: A 48-year gap to adoption
sections.body: Despite the dramatic six-day result, the Royal Navy did not act for decades. Only in 1795, after sustained advocacy by physician Gilbert Blane, did the Navy make citrus juice a mandatory ration on its ships. The merchant marine waited even longer, until the Merchant Shipping Act of 1867. The delay reflects a pattern that recurs throughout this unit: cost, supply logistics for a global fleet, and competing theories of disease causation can stall even a striking, correctly interpreted result for generations.

lessons.workedExample: Lind's six arms, one pair each: (1) cider, one quart/day; (2) elixir vitriol, 25 drops three times/day; (3) vinegar, two spoonfuls three times/day; (4) seawater, half a pint/day; (5) two oranges plus one lemon/day; (6) an electuary of garlic, mustard seed, horseradish, balsam of Peru, and myrrh, three times/day. All twelve men ate the same shipboard diet otherwise. By day six, the citrus pair had recovered enough for duty; every other arm showed no comparable improvement. The comparison isolates one variable (the added treatment) against a shared background — the logical core of a controlled trial — even though the sample (n=2 per arm) is far too small to rule out chance, and assignment was not randomized.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this lesson to see whether a student can separate 'controlled' from 'randomized' and 'blinded' — three distinct design features students routinely conflate. A strong answer explains precisely what Lind's concurrent, single-variable comparison achieved (control) and precisely what it didn't (unbiased allocation, adequate power, a p-value), and can explain why a compelling result doesn't guarantee fast adoption — the 1747-to-1795 gap is a concrete case of the evidence-to-practice lag judges expect students to name, not just gesture at.

questions.prompt: What specifically made Lind's 1747 comparison 'controlled' even though it had no randomization?

options.text: All six pairs shared the same starting condition and background diet, differing only in the one added treatment
The sample size was large enough to rule out chance
Lind was blinded to which sailors received which treatment
He calculated a p-value comparing the six arms

explanations.a: Correct: holding the background conditions constant and varying one treatment per concurrent group is the essence of a controlled comparison, independent of randomization or statistics.
explanations.b: The opposite is true — two sailors per arm is a very small sample, one of the trial's real limitations.
explanations.c: Lind selected and assigned the sailors himself with no blinding described; blinding is a separate design feature entirely absent here.
explanations.d: No formal statistical test existed in the 1747 write-up; the conclusion rested on the visibly dramatic six-day recovery, not a computed probability.

questions.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.

items.text: Lind runs the twelve-sailor comparison aboard HMS Salisbury
Lind publishes A Treatise of the Scurvy
The Royal Navy makes citrus juice a mandatory ration
The Merchant Shipping Act requires citrus for merchant sailors

questions.explanation: The trial (1747) preceded its own publication (1753), which preceded Royal Navy adoption (1795, after Gilbert Blane's advocacy), which preceded the merchant marine's much later mandate (1867).

questions.prompt: Match each treatment arm to what the pair actually received.

right.text: Two oranges and one lemon daily
25 drops of dilute sulfuric acid, three times daily
Half a pint of seawater daily
A paste of garlic, mustard seed, horseradish, balsam of Peru, and myrrh

questions.explanation: Each of the six pairs received one distinct addition to the shared shipboard diet; these four (plus cider and vinegar) made up the full comparison.

questions.prompt: Why didn't the Royal Navy adopt citrus rations immediately after Lind's clear 1747 result?

options.text: Lind's own 1753 treatise hedged the finding, and cost, supply logistics, and rival disease theories delayed institutional action for decades
Because the trial actually found citrus had no effect
Because scurvy was rare and not considered a serious naval problem
Because Lind never published his results

explanations.a: Correct: Lind muted his own conclusion in the 1753 treatise, and the Navy faced real logistical and theoretical barriers before Gilbert Blane's advocacy led to the 1795 mandate.
explanations.b: The citrus pair recovered dramatically within six days; the trial result itself was clear.
explanations.c: Scurvy was a major cause of death and incapacitation in the 18th-century Navy, which is exactly why a fix mattered.
explanations.d: Lind published A Treatise of the Scurvy in 1753; the problem was how he framed the finding within it, not whether he published at all.

lessons.label: The First Modern Randomized Trial: MRC Streptomycin, 1948

sections.heading: Why alternation wasn't enough
sections.body: By the 1940s, some trials already assigned every other patient to treatment versus control — an 'alternation' scheme. But alternation is predictable: a clinician who knows the next patient is slated for the control arm can consciously or unconsciously steer a sicker or milder patient toward that slot, quietly unbalancing the groups. Streptomycin, isolated from Streptomyces griseus in 1943, was scarce and expensive in postwar Britain, and the Medical Research Council had only enough to treat a limited number of tuberculosis patients — a rationing problem that Austin Bradford Hill turned into a scientific opportunity. The trial was overseen by the MRC Tuberculosis Trials Committee, with physician Philip D'Arcy Hart running the day-to-day ward organization and patient selection while Hill designed the statistical scheme — a division between clinical management and methodological design that itself modeled how a rigorous trial could be organized.

sections.heading: Random numbers, sealed envelopes
sections.body: Hill had statisticians generate a treatment-allocation schedule from a table of random numbers, sealed into opaque, numbered envelopes at a central office and labeled only with a hospital name and sequence number. Ward staff opened the next envelope only after a patient's eligibility had already been confirmed and recorded, so no one could see or infer the assignment in advance — allocation concealment layered on top of random generation. This two-part mechanism, generate randomly and conceal from whoever enrolls, is what distinguishes the trial from earlier alternation designs, which randomized nothing and concealed nothing.

sections.heading: Result and legacy
sections.body: 107 patients with acute progressive bilateral pulmonary tuberculosis were enrolled: 55 to streptomycin plus bed rest, 52 to bed rest alone, the era's standard care. Published in the British Medical Journal in 1948 as 'Streptomycin treatment of pulmonary tuberculosis,' the trial found four deaths among the 55 streptomycin patients in the first six months versus fourteen among the 52 controls — a difference (chi-square 7.38, p between .01 and .001) too large to attribute to chance. X-rays were also read by an independent panel unaware of treatment assignment, adding a form of outcome-assessment blinding. The combination — random allocation, concealment, and blinded assessment — became the template for the modern randomized controlled trial, and Hill is widely credited as its architect. Patients were not told they were part of a randomized comparison, reflecting the informed-consent norms of the era rather than modern trial ethics. The 1948 result did not end the search for TB treatment: it set the template for the 1950 MRC trial combining streptomycin with para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS), which established combination therapy as the standard needed to prevent the drug resistance that streptomycin alone often produced.

lessons.workedExample: Picture the coordinating office: a statistician draws a random-number sequence and types it onto slips, one per envelope, sealed and numbered 1 through 107, sent to participating hospitals in batches. A physician confirms a new patient meets the TB criteria, then — only at that point — opens the next-numbered envelope to learn whether the patient goes onto streptomycin or bed rest alone. Because the envelope is opened after enrollment is locked in, the physician cannot pick a healthier patient for one arm. At six months: 4 of 55 streptomycin patients had died versus 14 of 52 controls, a result strong enough (p between .01 and .001) that chance alone was an implausible explanation.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this lesson to check whether a student can name the actual mechanism of randomization rather than just the word — generating an unbiased schedule is only half of it; concealing that schedule from whoever enrolls patients is the other half, and a design missing either half (like plain alternation) is vulnerable to selection bias. A student who can explain why sealed, sequentially numbered envelopes defeat foreknowledge — and can cite the trial's actual mortality numbers rather than a vague 'it worked' — is demonstrating real methodological understanding, not just historical trivia.

questions.prompt: Why was every-other-patient 'alternation' allocation considered inferior to Bradford Hill's random-number method?

options.text: Alternation is predictable, so a clinician could anticipate the next assignment and selectively steer certain patients toward it
Alternation produces unequal group sizes, while randomization guarantees exactly equal groups
Alternation cannot be used with sealed envelopes
Alternation requires more patients than randomization to reach significance

explanations.a: Correct: because alternation follows a known pattern, foreknowledge of the next assignment opens the door to conscious or unconscious selection bias in who gets enrolled when.
explanations.b: Group sizes can be unequal or equal under either scheme; the core problem with alternation is predictability, not group balance.
explanations.c: Sealed envelopes are simply one implementation method; the objection to alternation is about predictability, not envelope compatibility.
explanations.d: Sample size requirements depend on effect size and variability, not on whether allocation is alternated or randomized.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the MRC trial's allocation-concealment mechanism.

items.text: Statisticians generate a treatment schedule from a table of random numbers
Numbered, sealed envelopes are prepared and sent to hospitals
A patient's TB diagnosis and eligibility are confirmed and recorded
The next-numbered envelope is opened to reveal the patient's assignment

questions.explanation: The schedule is generated and sealed before any patient arrives; only after eligibility is locked in is the envelope opened, which is exactly what prevents foreknowledge from biasing enrollment.

questions.prompt: Match each trial feature to what it accomplished.

left.text: Independent panel reading x-rays blind to assignment

right.text: Generates an unbiased sequence of treatment assignments
Conceals the upcoming assignment from whoever enrolls the next patient
Prevents assessment bias when judging patient outcomes

questions.explanation: Randomization, allocation concealment, and blinded outcome assessment are three separate safeguards, each defeating a different source of bias.

questions.prompt: In the trial's first six months, how did mortality compare between arms?

options.text: 4 of 55 streptomycin patients died versus 14 of 52 controls
14 of 55 streptomycin patients died versus 4 of 52 controls
Mortality was identical in both arms
All streptomycin patients survived and all controls died

explanations.a: Correct: 4 of 55 streptomycin patients died versus 14 of 52 controls in the first six months, a difference judged too large to be chance (p between .01 and .001).
explanations.b: This reverses the actual result — streptomycin patients had the lower death count, not the higher one.
explanations.c: The mortality difference was substantial and statistically significant, not identical.
explanations.d: Both arms had deaths; the result was a large reduction, not a complete absence of death in either group.

lessons.label: The Salk Polio Vaccine Field Trial, 1954

sections.heading: 1.8 million 'Polio Pioneers'
sections.body: Starting April 26, 1954, at Franklin Sherman Elementary School in McLean, Virginia, the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis enrolled roughly 1.8 million children in the largest field trial in history to that point to test Jonas Salk's killed-virus polio vaccine. The evaluation, led by biostatistician Thomas Francis Jr., ran two designs simultaneously in different areas because state health officials and parent groups disagreed about the ethics of withholding vaccine from children during a raging epidemic.

sections.heading: Two designs, one trial
sections.body: In one set of areas, 623,972 children were randomized in a double-blind, placebo-controlled design — neither families nor the administering doctors knew who received vaccine versus an inert saline placebo, and neither did the evaluators scoring outcomes. In other areas, over a million more children participated as 'observed controls': only second-graders were offered the vaccine, while first- and third-graders, who had not consented to vaccination, served as an unrandomized comparison group by virtue of their grade alone. This observed-control arm existed because some local officials balked at randomizing children to a placebo when a promising vaccine was available, but it meant the comparison groups differed by more than vaccination status — grade, and whatever correlates with it, could confound the result.

sections.heading: The verdict and the lesson
sections.body: Announced April 12, 1955, results showed 428 cases of paralytic polio among the 749,236 children in the randomized placebo-control areas versus 585 cases among the 1,080,680 children in the observed-control areas — different populations, different case rates, not directly comparable head-to-head. Francis's team concluded the vaccine was 80-90% effective against paralytic polio. The randomized arm gave a cleaner causal estimate than the observed-control arm, because randomization balanced unmeasured factors (household exposure, prior infection, socioeconomic status) that grade alone could not. The trial cemented double-blind placebo-controlled randomization as the gold standard precisely because officials could see, side by side, how much cleaner its answer was than the alternative they had been forced to run in parallel.

lessons.workedExample: Consider a hypothetical school district using the observed-control design: all second-graders are offered the vaccine, while first- and third-graders are left unvaccinated as the comparison. If wealthier families disproportionately enroll their second-graders (better access to the school nurse's clinic day) and wealthier households also have less crowded housing and thus lower polio exposure, the vaccinated group would look healthier partly because of income and crowding, not vaccine efficacy alone — a confound randomization would have neutralized by scattering those factors evenly across both arms. The real trial's parallel randomized arm, using an inert placebo and blinding, avoided exactly this problem.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this trial because it is the clearest large-scale illustration of why randomization matters beyond having a comparison group at all: the observed-control design still had a comparison, but grade-level assignment let confounders ride along with vaccination status. A student who can explain specifically what randomization added over the observed-control arm — balancing unmeasured confounders, not just 'being more scientific' — shows real grasp of the concept rather than reciting that RCTs are 'the gold standard.'

questions.prompt: Why did some areas of the 1954 trial use an unrandomized 'observed control' design instead of randomizing all children to vaccine or placebo?

options.text: Some state officials and parent groups objected to the ethics of withholding vaccine via placebo during an active epidemic
There wasn't enough vaccine to randomize more children
Randomization was not yet a known statistical technique in 1954
Thomas Francis Jr. preferred the observed-control design scientifically

explanations.a: Correct: local objections to placebo-controlled randomization in children during an epidemic led some areas to use the grade-based observed-control design instead.
explanations.b: Vaccine supply was not the stated reason for the split design; the issue was ethical and political objections to placebo use.
explanations.c: Randomization was already established methodology by 1954, following trials like the 1948 MRC streptomycin trial.
explanations.d: Francis led the evaluation of both designs but the observed-control design existed because of local resistance to randomization, not his scientific preference.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the 1954-1955 Salk trial timeline.

items.text: Trial begins at Franklin Sherman Elementary School
Randomized double-blind arm and observed-control arm run in parallel across different areas
Thomas Francis Jr.'s team compiles and analyzes case counts from both designs
Results are announced: vaccine judged 80-90% effective

questions.explanation: The trial launched April 26, 1954, ran its two parallel designs through the school year, and the evaluation team announced findings on April 12, 1955.

questions.prompt: Match each trial design to its defining feature.

right.text: Children randomly assigned to vaccine or inert placebo, blinded to families and evaluators
Second-graders offered vaccine; first- and third-graders serve as unrandomized comparison by grade

questions.explanation: The two designs ran in different areas simultaneously because officials could not agree on the ethics of placebo-controlled randomization.

questions.prompt: Why is the randomized arm's effectiveness estimate considered more trustworthy than the observed-control arm's, even though both had comparison groups?

options.text: Randomization balances unmeasured confounders like exposure and socioeconomic status across arms, which grade-based assignment cannot do
The randomized arm enrolled more total children than the observed-control arm
The observed-control arm used a placebo while the randomized arm did not
