The randomized arm's results were announced first

explanations.a: Correct: random assignment scatters both measured and unmeasured confounders evenly across arms, something grade-based selection into the observed-control groups cannot guarantee.
explanations.b: The observed-control areas actually included more children (over a million) than the randomized placebo-control areas (623,972 assigned).
explanations.c: It's the reverse: the randomized arm used blinded placebo control; the observed-control arm had no placebo at all.
explanations.d: Both sets of results were compiled and announced together in April 1955; timing of announcement isn't what makes one estimate more trustworthy.

lessons.label: Trials That Overturned Practice — and Warned Us

sections.heading: ISIS-2: proof, and a joke about proof
sections.body: The 1988 Second International Study of Infarct Survival (ISIS-2) randomized 17,187 patients with suspected acute myocardial infarction to streptokinase, aspirin, both, or neither. Aspirin alone cut five-week vascular mortality from 11.8% to 9.4% (a 23% odds reduction); streptokinase alone cut it from 12.0% to 9.2% (25%); the combination reduced it by 42%. Cheap daily aspirin, previously untested at this scale for heart attack, became standard emergency care almost overnight. But the paper is equally famous for a deliberate joke: the authors ran a subgroup analysis by the patient's astrological birth sign and found that aspirin appeared to slightly harm patients born under Gemini or Libra — a statistically 'significant' result with zero biological basis, included specifically to demonstrate how easily chance subgroup findings mimic real effects when you slice a large trial into enough small pieces.

sections.heading: CAST: a plausible mechanism, killed by data
sections.body: Doctors reasoned that since irregular heartbeats (ventricular ectopy) after a heart attack predicted sudden death, drugs that suppressed those ectopic beats should reduce death. The Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial (CAST) tested this on the antiarrhythmics encainide and flecainide starting in 1987. The Data and Safety Monitoring Board halted those arms in April 1989: encainide and flecainide patients had over twice the total mortality of placebo patients (56 of 730 versus a much lower placebo rate; relative risk 2.5) and more than three times the rate of arrhythmic death (relative risk 3.6). A biologically sound-sounding mechanism had produced the opposite of its intended effect, and only a randomized trial with real mortality as the endpoint — not just ectopic-beat counts — caught it.

sections.heading: WHI: decades of observational data, reversed
sections.body: Observational studies like the Nurses' Health Study had long suggested hormone replacement therapy (HRT) protected postmenopausal women against heart disease, and it became routine care. The Women's Health Initiative, a randomized trial of estrogen plus progestin, was stopped early in 2002 after roughly 5.2 years of follow-up (originally planned to run to 2005) when the data showed increased breast cancer, coronary heart disease, stroke, and blood clots outweighing the benefits, which included fewer hip fractures and less colorectal cancer. The reversal illustrates a recurring theme across all three trials: observational associations and even mechanistic plausibility can mislead, and only randomization, run to completion or stopped early by a monitoring board watching real harm, resolves the question honestly.

lessons.workedExample: In ISIS-2, splitting 17,187 patients by twelve astrological signs creates small subgroups where random noise can look like a real effect purely by chance — run enough subgroup comparisons and roughly one in twenty will cross the p<0.05 threshold even if nothing is actually different. The Gemini/Libra 'harm' signal was exactly this: a chance finding from slicing a large, genuinely positive overall result (23% mortality reduction) into small enough pieces. The authors published it deliberately, as a built-in warning label against over-trusting any single subgroup result — including ones that look far more medically plausible than star sign.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe these three trials because each teaches a distinct, exam-worthy failure mode: ISIS-2's astrology joke exposes data-dredging and multiple-comparisons risk in subgroup analysis; CAST shows that a plausible surrogate endpoint (suppressing ectopic beats) can diverge from the outcome that actually matters (survival); WHI shows observational confounding can persist for decades until a randomized trial corrects it. A student who cites the specific trial that matches the specific failure mode — not just 'randomized trials are better' — is showing they understand why each one became a landmark.

questions.prompt: Why did the ISIS-2 authors deliberately include a subgroup analysis by astrological sign in their published results?

options.text: To illustrate, using an implausible variable, how subgroup analyses can produce spurious 'significant' findings by chance
Because they genuinely believed birth sign affected aspirin's cardiac benefit
Because a journal editor required an astrology section for all cardiology papers
To distract readers from the trial's disappointing overall result

explanations.a: Correct: the astrology subgroup was included specifically to warn readers that slicing a trial into many small subgroups can manufacture 'significant' but meaningless findings.
explanations.b: The authors used birth sign precisely because it has no plausible biological link to aspirin's effect, making the spurious result obvious.
explanations.c: There was no such general editorial requirement; this was a deliberate methodological point negotiated between the ISIS-2 authors and the journal.
explanations.d: ISIS-2's overall result was strongly positive (23-25% mortality reductions), not disappointing, so there was nothing to distract from.

questions.prompt: Order these trials by publication year.

items.text: ISIS-2 (aspirin and streptokinase for MI)
CAST (antiarrhythmics after MI)
Women's Health Initiative (hormone replacement therapy)

questions.explanation: ISIS-2 published in 1988, CAST's encainide/flecainide arms were halted and reported in 1989, and the WHI hormone trial was stopped and reported in 2002.

questions.prompt: Match each trial to the specific lesson it demonstrates.

right.text: Subgroup analyses can manufacture spurious significant findings from chance alone
A plausible surrogate marker (suppressing ectopic beats) does not guarantee the outcome that matters (survival)
Long-standing observational associations can be overturned by a randomized trial

questions.explanation: Each trial is a landmark for a distinct methodological failure mode: data-dredging, surrogate-endpoint mismatch, and observational confounding.

questions.prompt: What was the key reason CAST's Data and Safety Monitoring Board halted the encainide and flecainide arms in 1989?

options.text: Patients on those drugs had roughly 2.5 times the total mortality of placebo patients
The drugs were too expensive to continue supplying
Ectopic beats were not being suppressed as expected
Patients were dropping out of the trial at an unusually high rate

explanations.a: Correct: encainide and flecainide patients showed a relative risk of about 2.5 for total mortality and 3.6 for arrhythmic death compared to placebo, prompting the board to stop those arms.
explanations.b: Cost was not the stated reason for halting the trial; the drugs were in fact suppressing ectopic beats as intended.
explanations.c: The drugs were suppressing the ectopic beats as designed; the problem was that despite this, mortality rose rather than fell.
explanations.d: The trial was halted because of the mortality signal identified by the monitoring board, not because of dropout rates.

lessons.label: The p-value Controversy: Fisher vs. Neyman-Pearson

sections.heading: Fisher's significance testing
sections.body: In his 1925 'Statistical Methods for Research Workers,' Ronald Fisher proposed the p-value as a continuous measure of evidence against a single null hypothesis: how surprising is this data if nothing is going on? Fisher suggested p<0.05 as a convenient, informal threshold for calling a result 'significant' enough to warrant attention — never intended as a rigid accept/reject rule, and never paired with a specified alternative hypothesis or a pre-set error rate. For Fisher, a p-value was evidence to weigh in context, potentially alongside replication, not a verdict.

sections.heading: Neyman-Pearson's decision framework
sections.body: Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson built a different, decision-theoretic framework starting in 1928-1933: specify both a null and an alternative hypothesis in advance, fix a Type I error rate (alpha, the chance of a false positive) and consider Type II error (beta, a false negative, and its complement, power), then apply a fixed decision rule — reject or fail to reject — without interpreting the p-value's exact size afterward. This framework is about long-run error control across many decisions, not the evidential weight of any single result.

sections.heading: An incoherent hybrid, and the 2016 ASA statement
sections.body: What gets taught and practiced today is neither pure Fisher nor pure Neyman-Pearson but an unacknowledged hybrid: researchers set alpha=0.05 in advance (Neyman-Pearson's language) but then report and interpret the exact p-value's magnitude as graded evidence (Fisher's usage), and rarely specify power or an alternative hypothesis with Neyman-Pearson's rigor. Statisticians, notably Gerd Gigerenzer, have described this blend as internally inconsistent — it borrows the ritual of a bright-line cutoff from one framework and the intuitive language of 'strength of evidence' from the other, without either framework's full logic. In 2016 the American Statistical Association, in a statement authored by Ronald Wasserstein and Nicole Lazar, formally warned against common misuses: a p-value does not measure the probability the null hypothesis is true, does not measure the size or importance of an effect, and 'p<0.05' alone should not be treated as a complete basis for a scientific conclusion.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher runs a trial, gets p=0.03, and declares 'a significant effect, strong evidence the drug works.' Under strict Neyman-Pearson logic, having pre-set alpha=0.05, the correct statement is only a binary one: reject the null, full stop — the exact value 0.03 versus 0.049 carries no extra meaning within that framework. Under strict Fisher logic, p=0.03 is graded evidence against the null in this one dataset, but Fisher never licensed the language of a fixed 'significant/not significant' decision rule with a pre-registered alpha. The researcher's sentence borrows the decisiveness of Neyman-Pearson and the evidential language of Fisher simultaneously — the exact hybrid the ASA's 2016 statement targeted.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this history because 'p<0.05' is the single most misused phrase at a science fair, and knowing that it descends from two incompatible frameworks — one about long-run decision error rates, one about evidential weight in a single dataset — lets a student explain precisely what a p-value can and cannot claim. A strong answer can state, without hedging, that a p-value is not the probability the null hypothesis is true and is not a measure of effect size, and can trace why 0.05 became a convention rather than a law of nature.

questions.prompt: What is the core difference between Fisher's approach to significance testing and Neyman-Pearson's?

options.text: Fisher treated the p-value as graded evidence against a single null hypothesis; Neyman-Pearson built a pre-specified decision rule controlling long-run error rates between two hypotheses
Fisher required a pre-set alpha level; Neyman-Pearson did not use any error rate at all
Fisher's method only applies to randomized trials; Neyman-Pearson's applies only to observational studies
There is no meaningful difference; they are the same framework under different names

explanations.a: Correct: Fisher's p-value is a continuous measure of evidence against one null hypothesis, while Neyman-Pearson's framework specifies both hypotheses in advance and applies a fixed decision rule controlling Type I and Type II error rates.
explanations.b: This reverses it — the pre-set alpha and formal error-rate control belong to Neyman-Pearson, not Fisher, whose p-value was an informal, continuous evidence measure.
explanations.c: Neither framework is restricted to a particular study design; both are general statistical inference frameworks applicable across designs.
explanations.d: The two frameworks differ substantially in logic and purpose, which is exactly why their unacknowledged combination is criticized as incoherent.

questions.prompt: Order these developments in the p-value's history.

items.text: Fisher proposes the p-value and the informal p<0.05 convention
Neyman and Pearson develop the decision-theoretic hypothesis-testing framework
Textbooks and practice blend elements of both into an unacknowledged hybrid
The American Statistical Association issues a formal statement warning against p-value misuse

questions.explanation: Fisher's 1925 proposal came first, Neyman-Pearson's framework followed in 1928-1933, the hybrid emerged through mid-20th-century textbooks and practice, and the ASA's corrective statement came in 2016.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to the framework it belongs to.

left.text: p-value as graded evidence against one null hypothesis
Pre-specified alternative hypothesis and fixed alpha/beta error rates
2016 statement warning p-values don't measure effect size or the null's probability

right.text: Fisher's significance testing
Neyman-Pearson hypothesis testing
American Statistical Association

questions.explanation: Each concept traces to a distinct source: Fisher's evidential p-value, Neyman-Pearson's decision framework, and the ASA's 2016 corrective statement.

questions.prompt: According to the ASA's 2016 statement, which of these is a correct description of what a p-value measures?

options.text: How surprising the observed data (or more extreme data) would be if the null hypothesis were true
The probability that the null hypothesis is true
The size or practical importance of the observed effect
The probability that the result will replicate in a future study

explanations.a: Correct: a p-value is a statement about the compatibility of the data with the null hypothesis, not a statement about the hypothesis itself or the effect's importance.
explanations.b: The ASA statement explicitly warns that a p-value does not equal the probability the null hypothesis is true; this is one of the most common misinterpretations.
explanations.c: Effect size and importance are separate quantities from statistical significance; a very small, unimportant effect can still produce a small p-value with a large enough sample.
explanations.d: A p-value from one study says nothing directly about whether a future study will replicate the finding.

lessons.label: The Replication Crisis and Open Science

sections.heading: Ioannidis: why most findings might be false
sections.body: In 2005, John Ioannidis published 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False' in PLOS Medicine, arguing mathematically that a finding's chance of being true depends not just on its p-value but on the field's typical effect sizes, study power, number of tested relationships, and flexibility in study design and analysis — and that in fields with small effects, small samples, and many tested hypotheses, most 'significant' results should be expected to be false positives even when every individual analysis was performed correctly. The paper was theoretical, but it named the conditions that make a literature untrustworthy before anyone had systematically measured how bad the problem actually was.

sections.heading: p-hacking and HARKing
sections.body: Two specific practices supply the flexibility Ioannidis warned about. P-hacking is trying multiple analyses, subgroups, or stopping points until one crosses p<0.05, then reporting only that one. HARKing — Hypothesizing After the Results are Known, a term Norbert Kerr coined in 1998 — is presenting a post-hoc finding in a paper as though it had been the study's original, pre-specified hypothesis, which hides how many other hypotheses were quietly tested and discarded first. Both practices are usually not fraud; they are what researcher degrees of freedom look like when nothing forces a decision to be locked in before the data arrive.

sections.heading: Measuring the damage, and open-science fixes
sections.body: The Open Science Collaboration's 2015 paper in Science attempted to directly replicate 100 psychology studies: 97% of the originals had reported statistically significant results, but only 36% of the replications did, and replicated effect sizes averaged about half the size of the originals. The fix that has gained the most traction is pre-registration: publicly time-stamping a study's hypotheses, design, and analysis plan before data collection, so p-hacking and HARKing become visible by comparison against the registered plan. Registered reports go further, having a journal accept a study for publication based on its pre-registered design alone, before results are known, removing the incentive to fish for significance. Chris Chambers pioneered the format at the journal Cortex starting in 2013, and the Center for Open Science, co-founded by Brian Nosek, has pushed pre-registration infrastructure across fields since. A live, unresolved debate continues over whether frequentist reforms like pre-registration are sufficient or whether Bayesian methods, which update a degree of belief rather than testing a single null hypothesis, address the underlying problem more directly.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher tests whether a supplement affects memory, measuring ten different memory subtests. Nine show no effect; one crosses p<0.05. Reported alone, that one result looks like a real, pre-planned finding — classic HARKing if the paper frames it as the original hypothesis, classic p-hacking if the choice to report only that subtest was made after seeing all ten results. A pre-registration filed before data collection, naming the primary outcome subtest in advance, would have made this selective reporting visible to any reader who checked the registration against the published paper — exactly the transparency mechanism the open-science movement built in response to findings like Ioannidis's 2005 argument and the Open Science Collaboration's 2015 result.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this lesson because 'my results were statistically significant' is not, by itself, evidence of a real effect once a judge knows how many silent researcher degrees of freedom typically sit behind a single reported p-value. A student who can name p-hacking and HARKing specifically, cite the Open Science Collaboration's 36% replication rate, and explain how pre-registration closes the gap by locking in the analysis plan before results exist is demonstrating exactly the methodological literacy a rigorous project requires.

questions.prompt: What did Ioannidis's 2005 paper argue determines whether a published 'significant' finding is likely to be true?

options.text: Not the p-value alone, but factors like study power, effect size, number of hypotheses tested, and analytic flexibility in the field
Only whether the p-value was below 0.05
Only the total number of citations the paper later received
Only whether the study was randomized

explanations.a: Correct: Ioannidis's argument combined power, effect size, the number of hypotheses tested (including unreported ones), and flexibility in design and analysis to estimate a finding's likely truth.
explanations.b: His whole point was that p<0.05 alone is insufficient information; the same p-value implies very different truth probabilities depending on power and how many hypotheses were tested.
explanations.c: Citation count is not part of Ioannidis's mathematical argument about a finding's probability of being true.
explanations.d: The argument applied broadly across study designs, not narrowly to randomization status.

questions.prompt: Order these milestones in the replication-crisis timeline.

items.text: Norbert Kerr names and describes HARKing
Ioannidis publishes 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False'
Chris Chambers launches registered reports at Cortex
The Open Science Collaboration reports its 100-study replication results

questions.explanation: Kerr's HARKing paper appeared in 1998, Ioannidis's argument in 2005, registered reports at Cortex began in 2013, and the Open Science Collaboration's replication results were published in 2015.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

right.text: Trying multiple analyses or stopping points until one crosses significance, then reporting only that one
Presenting a post-hoc finding as though it were the study's original hypothesis
Publicly time-stamping a study's hypotheses and analysis plan before data collection
A journal accepts a study for publication based on its design, before results are known

questions.explanation: P-hacking and HARKing are the problems; pre-registration and registered reports are the two open-science responses, differing in whether the journal commits to publication in advance.

questions.prompt: In the Open Science Collaboration's 2015 replication study of 100 psychology studies, what fraction of replications reproduced a statistically significant result, compared to the originals?

options.text: 36% of replications were significant, versus 97% of the original studies
97% of replications were significant, versus 36% of the original studies
Both the originals and replications were significant about 90% of the time
Only 5% of either the originals or replications were significant

explanations.a: Correct: 97% of the original studies reported significant results, but only 36% of the direct replications did, with replicated effect sizes averaging about half the original magnitude.
explanations.b: This reverses the actual figures; the drop was from the originals' 97% down to the replications' 36%, not the other way around.
explanations.c: The whole point of the study was the large gap between original and replication significance rates, not near-parity.
explanations.d: Both figures are far higher than 5%; the originals were significant nearly universally (97%), and just over a third of replications were.

units.label: Advanced Designs and Reading Real Trials

lessons.label: Bayesian Inference and Bayesian Trials

sections.heading: Updating belief: prior, likelihood, posterior
sections.body: Bayes' theorem combines what was believed before seeing data (the prior) with what the data say (the likelihood) to produce an updated belief (the posterior): posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior. In a trial with a binary response, a convenient choice is a Beta prior on the response rate, because it combines algebraically with a binomial likelihood to give a Beta posterior — no simulation required. A flat Beta(1,1) prior treats all response rates as equally plausible before the trial starts; as patients respond, the posterior sharpens around the observed rate. This differs fundamentally from the frequentist machinery taught earlier: a p-value asks how surprising the data would be if the null hypothesis were exactly true, while a Bayesian posterior directly answers 'given this prior and this data, how probable is each possible treatment effect?'

sections.heading: Credible intervals and the posterior probability of benefit
sections.body: A 95% credible interval is the range containing 95% of the posterior probability — it can be interpreted directly as 'there is a 95% chance the true effect lies here,' which is exactly the statement students often mistakenly apply to a frequentist confidence interval. A confidence interval instead makes a claim about the procedure: if the trial were repeated many times, 95% of such intervals would contain the true fixed parameter, but any single interval either does or does not. Bayesian trials commonly report the posterior probability of benefit directly, e.g., P(treatment effect > 0 | data), which maps onto the clinical question a physician actually asks far more naturally than a p-value does.

sections.heading: Adaptive stopping without alpha-spending
sections.body: Frequentist group-sequential trials must pre-specify a fixed number of interim looks and spend a shrinking error budget at each one (O'Brien-Fleming-style boundaries) because repeatedly testing the same accumulating data inflates the false-positive rate. Bayesian inference is not subject to this penalty in the same way: because it conditions only on the data actually observed (the likelihood principle), a trial can check the posterior probability of benefit as often as desired and stop whenever a pre-specified threshold is crossed, without a formal alpha-spending correction. This does not make Bayesian designs free of false-positive risk in practice — regulators still require the design's frequentist operating characteristics (its type I error and power under repeated simulation) to be checked before approval, which the FDA's 2010 guidance on Bayesian statistics in medical device trials made explicit.

lessons.workedExample: A phase II trial of a new drug uses a flat Beta(1,1) prior on response rate. After 30 patients, 18 respond. The posterior is Beta(1+18, 1+12) = Beta(19,13), with posterior mean 19/32 ≈ 0.59. Historical controls respond at 40%. Integrating the Beta(19,13) density above 0.40 gives a posterior probability of roughly 99% (≈98.6%) that the true response rate exceeds the historical rate — a direct, interpretable statement the trial team can act on, in contrast to a p-value from a one-sided binomial test against the same 40% benchmark.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can state, in one sentence, what a credible interval means and how that differs from a confidence interval — many students recite the Bayesian definition for both, which is the single most common conceptual slip in this area. A second probe is whether adaptive Bayesian stopping is understood as depending on conditioning on observed data rather than being 'exempt' from false-positive concerns; a student who claims Bayesian trials never need error-rate checking has overclaimed, since regulators still require simulated operating characteristics.

questions.prompt: A 95% Bayesian credible interval for a treatment effect is best interpreted as:

options.text: If the trial were repeated many times, 95% of such intervals would contain the true effect
Given the prior and the observed data, there is a 95% probability the true effect lies in this interval
95% of individual patients will show this effect
The p-value for the null hypothesis is 0.05

explanations.a: That is the frequentist confidence-interval interpretation, a statement about the long-run behavior of the procedure, not about this specific interval.
explanations.b: Correct: a credible interval is a direct probability statement about the parameter, conditional on the prior and the observed data.
explanations.c: Credible intervals describe uncertainty about a population-level parameter, not the distribution of outcomes across individual patients.
explanations.d: A credible interval is not a p-value or a hypothesis-test threshold; it summarizes the posterior distribution.

questions.prompt: Why can a Bayesian adaptive trial check its posterior probability of benefit at many interim looks without a formal alpha-spending correction?

options.text: Bayesian trials are exempt from any false-positive risk
Bayesian inference conditions only on the data actually observed, per the likelihood principle, rather than on a hypothetical space of repeated looks
Bayesian trials always enroll fewer patients than frequentist ones
Regulators do not require any operating-characteristic checks for Bayesian designs

explanations.a: False-positive risk is not eliminated; it is instead assessed via simulated operating characteristics rather than an alpha-spending formula.
explanations.b: Correct: because inference depends on the observed data alone rather than the sampling distribution of repeated tests, looking at the data repeatedly does not distort inference the way it does under repeated frequentist testing.
explanations.c: Sample size depends on the specific design and effect size, not on the inference framework alone.
explanations.d: Regulatory guidance, including the FDA's 2010 Bayesian guidance for device trials, still requires simulated frequentist operating characteristics.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of Bayesian updating in a trial analysis.

items.text: Specify a prior distribution for the parameter of interest
Collect trial data and form the likelihood
Combine prior and likelihood to obtain the posterior distribution
Summarize the posterior as a credible interval or a posterior probability of benefit

questions.explanation: Bayes' theorem requires a prior specified before the data are seen; the likelihood from the data updates that prior into a posterior, which is then summarized for decision-making.

questions.prompt: Match each Bayesian term to its role in a trial analysis.

right.text: Belief about the parameter before data are observed
How probable the observed data are under each possible parameter value
Updated belief combining prior and data
A range holding a stated probability of the posterior distribution

questions.explanation: Prior and likelihood are the two inputs to Bayes' theorem; the posterior is their combination, and the credible interval is a direct summary of that posterior.

lessons.label: Adaptive, Group-Sequential, and Platform Trials

sections.heading: Re-estimating sample size and shifting allocation mid-trial
sections.body: A group-sequential trial with planned interim looks can also adapt beyond simply stopping early. Sample-size re-estimation adjusts the planned enrollment at an interim analysis when a nuisance parameter (event rate, outcome variance) turns out different from the design assumption; a blinded re-estimation, which recalculates only from pooled variance without unblinding treatment assignment, preserves the trial's type I error without needing a statistical penalty. Response-adaptive randomization (RAR) goes further, shifting the allocation ratio across arms as data accumulate so that more future patients are assigned to whichever arm is currently performing better, rather than holding a fixed ratio for the whole trial. RAR trades some statistical efficiency and analytical simplicity for an ethical gain: fewer patients are randomized to an arm the accumulating data suggest is inferior.

sections.heading: Basket, umbrella, and platform master protocols
sections.body: Three related designs test multiple hypotheses under one administrative and statistical framework, called a master protocol. A basket trial tests one targeted therapy across several disease types that share a molecular feature — the 2015 vemurafenib basket trial (Hyman et al.) tested a single BRAF-V600E inhibitor across many BRAF-mutant cancer types in one protocol. An umbrella trial tests several targeted therapies within a single disease, assigning each patient to a drug matched to their biomarker subtype, as in the Lung-MAP umbrella trial for squamous non-small-cell lung cancer. A platform trial goes further still: it is a perpetual master protocol with a shared control arm, into which new treatment arms can be added and underperforming arms dropped over the trial's lifetime without stopping the whole enterprise.

sections.heading: RECOVERY and I-SPY 2 in practice
sections.body: The RECOVERY platform trial, launched in the UK in March 2020, tested multiple candidate COVID-19 treatments against a shared standard-of-care control under one protocol. Its dexamethasone comparison, reported in June 2020, randomized 2,104 hospitalized patients to low-dose dexamethasone versus 4,321 to usual care; the drug reduced 28-day mortality by about one-third in ventilated patients and about one-fifth in patients on supplemental oxygen, with no benefit in patients not requiring oxygen. I-SPY 2, an ongoing breast-cancer platform trial, uses Bayesian response-adaptive randomization within biomarker subgroups: a drug 'graduates' from the platform once its Bayesian predictive probability of success in a confirmatory phase III trial crosses a pre-set threshold, or is dropped for futility, letting new agents rotate through the same infrastructure and shared control.

lessons.workedExample: In RECOVERY's dexamethasone comparison, the ventilated-patient subgroup showed a mortality rate ratio of about 0.65 versus usual care, and the oxygen-only subgroup showed about 0.80, while patients not needing any respiratory support showed no mortality difference. This graded result — benefit scaling with baseline severity — is exactly the kind of subgroup pattern a platform trial's large shared control arm and pooled infrastructure make statistically feasible to detect quickly during a live pandemic, compared to running three separate single-arm trials from scratch.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can distinguish a platform trial's efficiency (shared control, perpetually rotating arms) from its main statistical risk: because the control arm accrues over a long calendar period, standard of care or patient population can drift, so a treatment arm added later is not being compared against a truly contemporaneous control unless the analysis accounts for time period. A second probe is whether the student can correctly place a named real trial into basket, umbrella, or platform rather than using the terms interchangeably.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes response-adaptive randomization (RAR) from a standard fixed-ratio randomized trial?

options.text: RAR shifts the allocation ratio toward better-performing arms as data accumulate
RAR assigns every patient to the same arm after the first interim look
RAR eliminates the need for a control arm
RAR is only used in single-arm trials

explanations.a: Correct: RAR updates the allocation probabilities over time so more patients go to arms showing better accumulating results, unlike a fixed ratio held for the whole trial.
explanations.b: RAR shifts probabilities gradually; it does not assign every remaining patient to one arm after a single look.
explanations.c: RAR still requires comparison arms, including typically a control, to judge which arm is performing better.
explanations.d: RAR is a multi-arm concept; a single-arm trial has no allocation ratio to adapt.

questions.prompt: In RECOVERY's dexamethasone comparison, which patient subgroup showed no mortality benefit?

options.text: Patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation
Patients on supplemental oxygen but not ventilated
Patients requiring no supplemental oxygen
All subgroups showed an identical benefit

explanations.a: Ventilated patients showed the largest benefit, roughly a one-third mortality reduction.
explanations.b: Oxygen-only patients showed a smaller but real benefit, roughly a one-fifth mortality reduction.
explanations.c: Correct: patients not requiring any supplemental oxygen showed no mortality difference from dexamethasone.
explanations.d: The benefit was graded by baseline severity, not identical across subgroups.

questions.prompt: Order the operational steps of a platform trial using a shared control arm.

items.text: New candidate treatment arm is added to the existing master protocol
Patients are randomized between the new arm and the ongoing shared control
Interim analysis compares the new arm's accumulating results against control
Arm is dropped for futility or graduates for confirmatory testing

questions.explanation: A platform trial adds arms into an already-running shared-control structure, randomizes against that control, monitors interim results, and then drops or graduates the arm based on those results.

questions.prompt: Match each master-protocol design to a real trial that used it.

right.text: Vemurafenib tested across BRAF-mutant cancer types
Lung-MAP, matching biomarker subtypes to targeted drugs in one lung cancer type
RECOVERY, a perpetual shared-control protocol for COVID-19 treatments

questions.explanation: Basket trials test one drug across diseases sharing a molecular feature, umbrella trials test several drugs within one disease by biomarker, and platform trials run a perpetual shared-control structure across rotating arms.

lessons.label: Meta-Analysis and Systematic Review

sections.heading: Pooling effects: fixed-effect versus random-effects models
sections.body: A meta-analysis combines effect estimates from multiple studies into one pooled estimate, weighting each study by the precision of its own estimate (inverse-variance weighting). The fixed-effect model assumes every included study is estimating the exact same underlying true effect, with observed differences between studies attributed purely to sampling error; this model gives large studies nearly all the weight. The random-effects model, formalized by DerSimonian and Laird in 1986, instead assumes each study estimates its own true effect drawn from a distribution of related-but-different true effects, adding a between-study variance component (tau-squared) on top of within-study sampling error. Random-effects pooled estimates are typically similar in the point estimate but have wider confidence intervals, because they explicitly acknowledge that studies conducted in different populations, doses, or settings are not all measuring identical quantities.

sections.heading: Quantifying heterogeneity: Cochran's Q and I-squared
sections.body: Cochran's Q is a chi-squared test asking whether observed between-study variation exceeds what sampling error alone would predict; it is a formal significance test but has notoriously low power when few studies are pooled, so a non-significant Q does not prove homogeneity. The I-squared statistic, introduced by Higgins and Thompson in 2002, reframes the same information as a percentage: I-squared = 100 times (Q minus degrees of freedom) divided by Q, describing the proportion of total variability across studies attributable to real heterogeneity rather than chance. A widely used rough guide from Higgins et al.'s 2003 BMJ paper treats I-squared near 25% as low, 50% as moderate, and 75% as high heterogeneity, though these bands are guidance, not thresholds.

sections.heading: Publication bias and the PRISMA standard
sections.body: A funnel plot graphs each study's effect estimate against its precision; in the absence of bias it should look like a symmetric inverted funnel, since small imprecise studies scatter widely while large precise studies cluster near the pooled effect. Asymmetry — commonly a gap where small studies with null or unfavorable results should be but are not, because they were never published — suggests publication bias. Egger's 1997 regression test for funnel-plot asymmetry formalizes this visual check statistically. Systematic reviews are expected to follow the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) reporting standard, first published in 2009 and updated in 2020, which specifies a flow diagram tracking records from initial database search through duplicate removal, screening, full-text eligibility assessment, and final inclusion.

lessons.workedExample: A meta-analysis pools 8 RCTs of an antihypertensive drug. Cochran's Q = 15.4 with 7 degrees of freedom (8 studies minus 1), giving I-squared = 100 times (15.4 minus 7) divided by 15.4, or about 54.5% — moderate heterogeneity, favoring a random-effects model over fixed-effect. The funnel plot shows a visible gap in the lower-left region where small studies with null or harmful results would be expected but are absent, and Egger's test returns p = 0.03, statistically confirming the asymmetry a reviewer would otherwise only eyeball.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student picks fixed- versus random-effects based on genuine clinical and methodological similarity across studies rather than mechanically by which test 'passes,' since Cochran's Q is underpowered with few studies. They also probe whether I-squared is correctly described as a proportion of variability, not a measure of effect size, and whether a claimed 'the literature agrees' conclusion is backed by a funnel plot or Egger's test check for publication bias rather than just counting positive studies.

questions.prompt: An I-squared of 80% for a pooled set of trials means:

options.text: 80% of the pooled effect size is due to bias
80% of the total variability across study estimates is attributable to real heterogeneity rather than chance
80% of patients responded to treatment
The pooled effect is statistically significant at p < 0.20

explanations.a: I-squared quantifies heterogeneity in effect estimates across studies, not bias or the size of the pooled effect itself.
explanations.b: Correct: I-squared is the percentage of total variation across studies explained by real between-study differences rather than sampling error.
explanations.c: I-squared says nothing about the magnitude of clinical response; it is a property of how consistent the study estimates are with each other.
explanations.d: I-squared is unrelated to a significance threshold or p-value for the pooled effect.

questions.prompt: Why would a reviewer choose a random-effects model over a fixed-effect model for a set of pooled trials?

options.text: Random-effects always gives a narrower confidence interval, which looks more precise
The included studies differ meaningfully in population, dose, or setting, suggesting true effects vary across studies rather than being identical
Random-effects requires fewer studies to run
Fixed-effect models cannot be computed when there are more than five studies
Random-effects removes the need for inverse-variance weighting

explanations.a: Random-effects models typically produce wider, not narrower, confidence intervals because they add between-study variance to the estimate.
explanations.b: Correct: when studies plausibly estimate different true effects due to clinical or methodological diversity, random-effects is the more defensible model.
explanations.c: Model choice depends on study similarity, not the number of studies available.
explanations.d: Fixed-effect models can be computed for any number of studies; there is no such cutoff.
explanations.e: Both models use inverse-variance weighting; random-effects adds a between-study variance term on top of it.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of a PRISMA-style systematic review flow diagram.

items.text: Records identified through database searching
Duplicate records removed
Records screened by title and abstract
Full-text articles assessed for eligibility
Studies included in the quantitative synthesis (meta-analysis)

questions.explanation: PRISMA tracks records from the initial search through deduplication, title/abstract screening, full-text eligibility review, and finally the studies retained for pooling.

questions.prompt: Match each tool or statistic to what it assesses in a meta-analysis.

right.text: Significance test for whether heterogeneity exceeds chance
Percentage of variability due to real heterogeneity
Visual check of effect size against precision for asymmetry
Regression test formalizing funnel-plot asymmetry

questions.explanation: Q and I-squared both quantify heterogeneity, one as a test and one as a proportion, while the funnel plot and Egger's test both target publication bias, one visually and one statistically.

lessons.label: Beyond the RCT: Causal Inference from Observational Data

sections.heading: Propensity scores: matching and weighting on measured confounders
sections.body: When randomization is infeasible or unethical — a suspected teratogen cannot ethically be assigned to pregnant volunteers — researchers try to reconstruct a fair comparison from observational data. The propensity score, introduced by Rosenbaum and Rubin in 1983, is the estimated probability that a person received the treatment given their measured covariates (age, comorbidities, disease severity, and so on), typically from a logistic regression. Propensity-score matching pairs treated and untreated individuals with similar scores; propensity-score weighting (inverse probability of treatment weighting, IPTW) instead reweights the whole sample so that, on average, the weighted treated and untreated groups look balanced on measured covariates, mimicking what randomization would have produced — but only for the covariates that were actually measured and entered into the model.

sections.heading: Instrumental variables and Mendelian randomization
sections.body: An instrumental variable is a factor associated with the treatment but affecting the outcome only through the treatment, and not sharing any common cause with the outcome — a condition called the exclusion restriction. Mendelian randomization exploits genetic variants as instruments: because alleles are assigned essentially at random at conception, a gene variant that raises LDL cholesterol but has no other plausible effect on heart disease can substitute for an experiment nature never ran, letting researchers estimate the causal effect of lifetime LDL exposure without a trial. The exclusion restriction is the design's weak point — a gene variant that affects the outcome through a second pathway (pleiotropy) violates it and reintroduces confounding through the instrument itself.

sections.heading: Target-trial emulation and the residual-confounding caveat
sections.body: Hernán and Robins formalized a discipline in 2016 called target-trial emulation: before touching observational data, explicitly write the protocol of the hypothetical randomized trial you wish you could run — eligibility criteria, treatment strategies compared, assignment time zero, outcome, follow-up duration, and analysis plan — then emulate each element as closely as possible in the observational data, which avoids classic errors like immortal-time bias (crediting survival time to a treatment before it was actually started). Even with a well-designed target-trial emulation, propensity matching, or an instrument, observational estimates remain vulnerable to residual confounding: bias from confounders that were never measured. The clearest historical warning is hormone replacement therapy — observational cohorts (including the Nurses' Health Study) suggested HRT reduced coronary heart disease risk, but the 2002 Women's Health Initiative randomized trial found an increased risk, a discrepancy later attributed largely to confounding by indication and the 'healthy-user' pattern among women who chose HRT.

lessons.workedExample: An observational cohort compares statin users to non-users for cardiovascular mortality. Before matching, statin users are on average younger and have fewer comorbidities than non-users (standardized mean difference for age = 0.35, a large imbalance). After 1:1 propensity-score matching within a caliper of 0.02 on the logit scale, the standardized mean difference for age drops to 0.02, indicating good balance on measured covariates. The matched analysis reports a hazard ratio of 0.75 (95% CI 0.65-0.85) for statin use. This balances everything the propensity model measured, but says nothing about unmeasured factors like diet or exercise habits that could still differ between statin users and non-users and bias the hazard ratio.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can state plainly that propensity scores, instrumental variables, and target-trial emulation only address confounders that were actually measured or instrumented — never invoke these methods as if they fully substitute for randomization. The HRT-versus-WHI discrepancy is the standard example judges reach for: a student who cites an observational effect estimate should be ready to name what confounders were controlled, what plausibly was not, and why an RCT (if one exists) is the stronger evidence.

questions.prompt: A study uses propensity-score matching and achieves excellent balance on all measured covariates. What can still bias the treatment effect estimate?

options.text: Nothing; matching on the propensity score fully replicates randomization
Residual confounding from variables that were never measured or included in the propensity model
The fact that propensity scores can only be used with binary outcomes
Matching always increases the sample size beyond what randomization would give

explanations.a: Propensity-score matching balances only the covariates entered into the model; it cannot balance what was never measured, unlike true randomization.
explanations.b: Correct: unmeasured confounders remain a threat regardless of how well the measured covariates are balanced.
explanations.c: Propensity scores can be used with binary, continuous, or time-to-event outcomes; that is not the limitation here.
explanations.d: Matching typically discards unmatched individuals, which usually reduces rather than increases the analyzed sample size.

questions.prompt: For a genetic variant to serve as a valid instrumental variable for an exposure, it must satisfy the exclusion restriction, meaning:

options.text: The variant must directly cause the outcome through a pathway other than the exposure
The variant must affect the outcome only through its effect on the exposure, with no other pathway
The variant must be measured after the outcome occurs
The variant must be associated with the outcome but not with the exposure

explanations.a: A variant with a direct second pathway to the outcome (pleiotropy) violates the exclusion restriction rather than satisfying it.
explanations.b: Correct: the exclusion restriction requires the instrument's only route to the outcome to run through the exposure being studied.
explanations.c: Timing of measurement is not what defines the exclusion restriction; genetic variants are fixed at conception regardless.
explanations.d: A valid instrument must be associated with the exposure, not disconnected from it; being associated with the outcome only through the exposure is the requirement.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of target-trial emulation as formalized by Hernán and Robins.

items.text: Specify eligibility criteria for the hypothetical trial
Define the treatment strategies being compared
Specify assignment time zero and outcome/follow-up
Specify the analysis plan
Emulate each protocol element using the observational data

questions.explanation: Target-trial emulation requires writing the full hypothetical trial protocol first, then matching the observational data analysis to that protocol element by element, rather than starting from whatever the data happen to contain.

questions.prompt: Match each causal-inference method to its defining feature.

right.text: Reweights the sample to balance measured covariates between groups
Uses a factor linked to treatment but not to the outcome except through treatment
Explicitly specifies a hypothetical RCT protocol before analyzing observational data

questions.explanation: Each method addresses confounding differently: reweighting on measured covariates, exploiting an external instrument, or disciplining the whole analysis by a pre-specified trial protocol.

lessons.label: Critically Appraising a Trial Paper

sections.heading: Reading the CONSORT flow diagram
sections.body: The CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) statement, most recently updated by Schulz and colleagues in 2010, requires published RCTs to include a flow diagram tracking participants through the whole trial: how many were assessed for eligibility, how many were excluded and why, how many were randomized to each arm, how many were lost to follow-up or discontinued the intervention, and how many were ultimately analyzed. This diagram is often more informative than the abstract, because uneven attrition between arms — say, twice as many dropouts in the treatment arm as in control — signals a threat to the trial's internal validity that no amount of statistical significance in the reported result can fix, since the people who dropped out are systematically different from those who stayed.

sections.heading: Cochrane RoB 2 and GRADE certainty
sections.body: The Cochrane risk-of-bias tool, in its 2019 revision (RoB 2, Sterne et al.), rates each trial on five domains: the randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result, each judged low risk, some concerns, or high risk. GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation, Guyatt et al., 2008) then rates certainty in a body of evidence as high, moderate, low, or very low: randomized trials start at high certainty and are downgraded for risk of bias, inconsistency across studies, indirectness to the question at hand, imprecision, or suspected publication bias, while observational studies start low but can be upgraded for a large or dose-dependent effect — GRADE's own thresholds treat a relative risk of 2 or more (or 0.5 or less) as large enough to upgrade certainty by one level, and a relative risk of 5 or more (or 0.2 or less) as large enough to upgrade it by two levels, so 'large effect' is a checkable number, not a judgment call.

sections.heading: Spotting spin and selective outcome reporting
sections.body: Spin is language that distorts how results are interpreted without technically misstating a number — for instance, emphasizing a significant secondary outcome in the abstract's conclusion while downplaying a non-significant primary outcome. Boutron and colleagues' 2010 study in JAMA, which reviewed RCT reports with a non-significant primary outcome, found spin was rare in trial titles but common in the abstract's conclusion and the discussion section of the main text, present in roughly half to three in five of the reports it examined. Selective outcome reporting is the related, more concrete problem of comparing the outcomes specified in a trial's prospective registration (such as ClinicalTrials.gov) against what the published paper actually reports and emphasizes; a mismatch — a new outcome appearing, or the pre-registered primary outcome quietly demoted to secondary — is a documented, checkable red flag rather than a matter of opinion.

lessons.workedExample: A trial's ClinicalTrials.gov registration lists all-cause mortality at 12 months as the primary outcome; the result is non-significant (p = 0.12). The published abstract instead leads with a secondary outcome, hospital readmission, significant at p = 0.03, and concludes the drug 'significantly improves outcomes.' The CONSORT flow diagram shows 12% attrition in the treatment arm versus 4% in control. A careful reader flags three things at once: the primary-outcome demotion versus the registry (spin), the uneven attrition (a missing-outcome-data risk under RoB 2), and would apply GRADE downgrades for risk of bias and imprecision before treating the readmission finding as reliable.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student defending a cited trial can name the pre-registered primary outcome and say whether it matches what the abstract emphasizes, whether attrition was balanced across arms in the CONSORT diagram, and which RoB 2 domain would flag a specific problem in the paper. Reciting 'it was randomized, so it's unbiased' without having looked at the flow diagram or the registration record is the single most common failure judges are trained to catch.

questions.prompt: Why is the CONSORT flow diagram often more revealing than a trial's abstract?

options.text: It reports the p-value for the primary outcome
It shows exclusions, randomization counts, and attrition by arm, which can reveal threats to validity a significant result alone would hide
It replaces the need for a statistical analysis
It only appears in observational studies, not RCTs

explanations.a: The flow diagram tracks participant counts through the trial stages; the p-value is reported elsewhere in the results.
explanations.b: Correct: uneven attrition or heavy exclusion, visible only in the flow diagram, can undermine a trial's conclusions regardless of a significant headline result.
explanations.c: The flow diagram documents participant flow; it does not substitute for the statistical analysis of outcomes.
explanations.d: CONSORT's flow diagram is specifically for randomized trials, not observational studies.

questions.prompt: A trial's registered primary outcome was non-significant, but the abstract's conclusion emphasizes a significant secondary outcome instead. This is best described as:

options.text: A valid interim analysis
Spin, since the interpretation is shaped to feature the favorable secondary result over the registered primary result
Evidence of a Type II error
Standard GRADE upgrading

explanations.a: Nothing here describes an interim look at the data; it describes how the completed trial's results were framed in the abstract.
explanations.b: Correct: shifting emphasis to a favorable secondary outcome while the registered primary outcome was non-significant is the textbook definition of spin.
explanations.c: A Type II error is a failure to detect a true effect; this scenario is about how results were reported, not a statistical error rate.
explanations.d: GRADE upgrading applies to observational studies showing large effects; it has nothing to do with which outcome an abstract emphasizes.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of critically appraising a published trial paper.

items.text: Check the trial's prospective registration for the pre-specified primary outcome
Compare the registered primary outcome to what the abstract emphasizes
Examine the CONSORT flow diagram for exclusions and attrition by arm
Apply the Cochrane RoB 2 domains to rate risk of bias
Assign a GRADE certainty rating to the body of evidence

questions.explanation: Appraisal starts with the pre-registered plan, checks it against what was published, examines participant flow, rates domain-specific bias, and finally summarizes overall certainty.

questions.prompt: Match each appraisal tool to what it evaluates.

right.text: Participant flow: eligibility, randomization, attrition, analysis
Domain-by-domain risk-of-bias rating for one trial
Overall certainty rating across a body of evidence
Detects selective outcome reporting or spin

questions.explanation: Each tool targets a different appraisal question: participant flow, trial-level bias, evidence-body certainty, and reporting fidelity against the pre-registered plan.

lessons.label: Designing a Rigorous Science-Fair Experiment

sections.heading: Randomization, controls, and blinding at student scale
sections.body: The same design principles that protect a phase III drug trial protect a science-fair project, just at a smaller scale. Randomization means assigning experimental units to conditions by a chance procedure — drawing lots, a random-number generator — rather than by convenience (all the biggest plants get fertilizer, all the healthiest mice get the new diet), which prevents a systematic difference between groups from masquerading as a treatment effect. A control condition establishes what happens without the intervention, so any change can be attributed to the treatment rather than to time, growth, or measurement drift alone. Blinding — keeping the experimenter or the person taking measurements unaware of which unit received which condition — guards against unconscious bias in how ambiguous results get scored, and is achievable even in a school project by having someone uninvolved in treatment assignment do the measuring.

sections.heading: Power calculations and pre-registration
sections.body: Before collecting a single data point, a rigorous design specifies the smallest effect size worth detecting, then calculates the sample size needed to detect it with adequate power — conventionally 80% power at a two-sided alpha of 0.05, following Cohen's 1988 guidelines. A common rule-of-thumb approximation for a two-sample t-test is n is approximately 16 divided by the squared effect size (Cohen's d) per group; skipping this step is why so many student projects run with 3 to 5 replicates per condition, far too few to reliably detect anything but a huge effect. Pre-registering the hypothesis, sample size, and planned statistical test — writing them down before seeing the data, even informally in a lab notebook dated before data collection — closes off the temptation to change the analysis after the fact.

sections.heading: Choosing the right test and avoiding pseudoreplication or p-hacking
sections.body: Pseudoreplication, a term formalized by Hurlbert in a widely cited 1984 paper, is treating repeated measurements from the same experimental unit as if they were independent replicates — measuring 20 leaves from one plant does not give an n of 20, because all 20 measurements share that one plant's unmeasured quirks; the true unit of replication is the plant. P-hacking, documented systematically by Simmons, Nelson, and Simonsohn in a 2011 paper, is the practice of trying multiple outcomes, subgroups, or statistical tests until one crosses p < 0.05, then reporting only that result as if it were the single planned analysis — pre-registration is the direct defense against it. The correct statistical test follows from the data structure decided at design time: a two-group continuous comparison calls for a t-test, more than two groups an ANOVA, and categorical outcomes a chi-square test — chosen before the data are seen, not selected afterward because it produces the smallest p-value.

lessons.workedExample: A student tests a fertilizer using 5 treated plants and 5 control plants, but takes 20 leaf-size measurements per plant and analyzes all 200 measurements as independent data points. This is pseudoreplication (Hurlbert, 1984): the true sample size is 5 plants per group, not 200 leaves. Averaging to one value per plant first, the honest n is 5 and 5. A power calculation for detecting a large effect (Cohen's d = 0.8) at alpha = 0.05, power = 0.80 requires roughly 25 plants per group using the n ≈ 16/d² approximation — showing the 5-plant design is underpowered by a factor of five before a single measurement is taken.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges routinely ask 'what was your n, and is that biological replicates or repeated measurements on the same unit?' — a student who cannot separate the two has usually pseudoreplicated. They also ask whether the statistical test and hypothesis were decided before or after looking at the data; a rigorous answer points to a dated pre-registration or lab notebook entry, while 'I tried a few tests and this one was significant' is the fastest way to lose credibility with a judge trained to spot p-hacking.

questions.prompt: A student measures leaf size 20 times on each of 5 treated plants and analyzes all 100 measurements as independent data points. What is the statistical problem?

options.text: Pseudoreplication: the true unit of replication is the plant (n=5), not each leaf measurement
Underpowering, because 100 measurements is too small a sample
P-hacking, because multiple tests were run
Nothing; 100 independent measurements is a valid sample size

explanations.a: Correct: repeated measurements on the same plant share that plant's unmeasured characteristics and are not statistically independent, so the real n is the number of plants, not the number of measurements.
explanations.b: The problem is not that 100 is too few; it is that treating correlated measurements as independent inflates the apparent sample size and understates uncertainty.
explanations.c: P-hacking involves trying multiple analyses to find significance, not the structure of the measurements themselves.
explanations.d: 100 leaf measurements from 5 plants are not independent data points; this is the pseudoreplication error, not a valid large sample.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of pre-registering a hypothesis and analysis plan before collecting data?

options.text: To guarantee the study will find a significant result
To prevent selecting or switching outcomes and tests after seeing the data, which inflates false-positive results
To reduce the number of replicates needed
To eliminate the need for a control group

explanations.a: Pre-registration does not affect whether an effect exists; it only prevents post-hoc selection of favorable analyses from real data.
explanations.b: Correct: fixing the outcome, test, and hypothesis in advance closes off the researcher-degrees-of-freedom problem that produces p-hacked false positives.
explanations.c: Pre-registration is unrelated to statistical power or the number of replicates needed to detect an effect.
explanations.d: A control group is a separate design requirement; pre-registration does not substitute for it.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of designing a rigorous student experiment, before any data is collected.

items.text: State the hypothesis and define the unit of replication
Calculate the sample size needed for adequate power
Pre-register the hypothesis, sample size, and planned statistical test
Randomize units to conditions and, where possible, blind measurement
Collect data and analyze using the pre-specified test

questions.explanation: A rigorous design fixes the hypothesis and replication unit first, sizes the study to detect the target effect, locks in the plan by pre-registering it, then randomizes and blinds before any data collection begins.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

right.text: Treating non-independent repeated measurements as if they were independent replicates
Trying multiple tests or outcomes until one reaches significance, then reporting only that one
The probability of detecting a true effect of a given size, given the sample size and alpha
Fixing the hypothesis, sample size, and analysis plan before data collection

questions.explanation: Pseudoreplication and p-hacking are the two classic student traps this lesson targets, while power and pre-registration are the design safeguards that prevent them.

units.label: Foundations: Prevention Strategy and the Surveillance Enterprise

lessons.label: What Public Health Surveillance Is — and Isn't

sections.heading: The Langmuir definition and the loop it describes
sections.body: Alexander Langmuir, the CDC epidemiologist who founded the Epidemic Intelligence Service in 1951, gave surveillance its modern meaning: not watching people, but watching disease. His successors Thacker and Berkelman refined it in 1988 into the definition still taught today: the ongoing, systematic collection, analysis, and interpretation of health data essential to planning, implementing, and evaluating public health practice, closely integrated with timely dissemination to those who need to know. The last clause is the hinge. Data that sits in a database is not surveillance; surveillance is a loop — collect, analyze, interpret, disseminate, act — that only closes when someone uses the finding to change what public health does next, which then generates new data to collect.

sections.heading: Not research, not a one-off investigation
sections.body: Research tests a defined hypothesis, has a start and end date, and usually requires informed consent and institutional review board oversight because its goal is generalizable knowledge. Surveillance has no end date, exists specifically to trigger action rather than publish a finding, and is typically classified as public health practice rather than research, which is why routine case reporting does not require individual consent. An outbreak investigation is different still: it is a discrete, time-limited response — an epidemiologist sent to answer 'what is causing this cluster' — often triggered BY a surveillance signal but not itself a surveillance system.

sections.heading: Four purposes a system has to justify
sections.body: A working system earns its cost against four jobs, and each has a real system built specifically to do it. Detecting events means recognizing an outbreak early enough to intervene: the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System's (NNDSS) routine case counts were what first flagged the 2015-2016 spread of Zika virus into the continental United States, turning scattered travel-related reports into a recognized event worth an emergency response. Monitoring trends means tracking whether a disease is rising, falling, or seasonal over years, not flagging a single spike: West Nile virus surveillance tracks dead-bird reports and mosquito-trap infection rates every summer to show whether that season's transmission is running above or below prior years' baseline, well before any human case is confirmed. Evaluating programs means asking whether an intervention already paid for actually worked: measles case surveillance before and after the introduction of routine childhood MMR vaccination showed U.S. incidence fall by more than 99 percent, the kind of before-after comparison that only a continuously running system, not a one-time study, can produce. Setting priorities means deciding which of many competing health problems gets the next dollar, using exactly this kind of trend and burden data to justify one program's budget over another's. A system that only counts cases without feeding any of these four uses is data collection, not surveillance.

lessons.workedExample: On June 5, 1981, the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report published a short notice: five cases of Pneumocystis pneumonia, an infection normally seen only in severely immunosuppressed patients, among previously healthy young gay men in Los Angeles. This was not a designed study — it was a passive surveillance-style report from clinicians who found the pattern unusual enough to flag. The notice triggered an outbreak investigation, which snowballed into the recognition of AIDS and, eventually, decades of hypothesis-driven HIV research. One event moved through all three categories in sequence: a surveillance signal, an investigation, and only then research.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this distinction because student projects routinely mislabel a one-time data pull as 'surveillance' or claim a screening program is 'research' to dodge consent requirements. A judge who asks 'is this ongoing, and who acts on it' is checking whether the student understands that surveillance is defined by its continuous loop and its action mandate, not by the fact that health data was collected.

questions.prompt: What makes a data-collection effort 'surveillance' rather than a one-time research study, under the Langmuir/Thacker-Berkelman definition?

options.text: It uses a larger sample size than typical research
It is ongoing and its findings are disseminated to trigger public health action
It requires informed consent from every participant
It is conducted exclusively by government employees

explanations.a: Sample size is not part of the definition; a small sentinel network is still surveillance.
explanations.b: Correct: the definition requires continuous operation plus timely dissemination that feeds action — the surveillance-to-action loop.
explanations.c: The opposite is usually true: surveillance is public health practice and is typically exempt from the consent and IRB requirements that govern research.
explanations.d: Private labs and clinicians report into surveillance systems constantly; government staff analyze and act on the data but are not the sole collectors.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the surveillance-to-action loop.

items.text: Collect health data from clinicians, labs, or other reporters
Analyze the data for patterns or anomalies
Interpret what the pattern means for public health
Disseminate findings to those who need to know
Act, generating new data that re-enters the loop

questions.explanation: Each stage depends on the one before it, and action feeds back into new collection, which is why surveillance is described as a loop rather than a linear process.

questions.prompt: Match each activity to its category.

left.text: A state health department's year-round notifiable disease reporting system
A CDC officer sent to find the source of a single restaurant's Salmonella cluster
A randomized trial testing whether a new drug lowers blood pressure

right.text: Surveillance
Outbreak investigation
Research

questions.explanation: Surveillance is continuous and system-wide; an outbreak investigation is a discrete response to one signal; research tests a hypothesis for generalizable knowledge.

lessons.label: The Levels of Prevention

sections.heading: Leavell and Clark's natural history of disease
sections.body: In 1953, Hugh Leavell and E. Gurney Clark proposed that every disease moves through a natural history: a prepathogenesis period where risk factors accumulate in a susceptible host, followed by a pathogenesis period running from subclinical biological onset through clinical disease to an outcome — recovery, disability, or death. They mapped intervention onto this timeline as primary prevention (acting before pathogenesis begins), secondary prevention (acting once disease exists but before symptoms force a diagnosis — early diagnosis and prompt treatment), and tertiary prevention (limiting disability and rehabilitating after clinical disease is established). Their 1965 revision is still the framework taught in every introductory epidemiology course.

sections.heading: Primordial prevention: the level added later
sections.body: Leavell and Clark's model started one disease-case at a time, at the individual host. In 1978, WHO epidemiologist Toma Strasser proposed a level upstream of primary prevention: primordial prevention, which stops a risk factor from becoming common in a population in the first place, rather than intervening once individuals already carry it. The canonical case is Finland's North Karelia Project, launched in 1972 after the province recorded the world's highest recorded rate of cardiovascular disease deaths: rather than screening individuals for high cholesterol, the program worked with communities, food producers, and dairy farmers to shift the population's diet away from saturated fat and reduce smoking rates region-wide. Over the following 25 years, coronary heart disease mortality among North Karelia's working-age men fell by roughly 67 percent, from about 690 to 100 deaths per 100,000 annually — a population-level shift in exposure that never required identifying who was personally 'at risk.' A soda tax that keeps a population's average sugar intake lower for an entire generation follows the same logic; it never asks whether any one person is 'at risk.'

sections.heading: Four levels, one disease, and why upstream changes strategy
sections.body: Take cervical cancer. Primordial: comprehensive sex education and tobacco control policy shift population-level HPV exposure and cofactor risk before any individual is assessed. Primary: HPV vaccination (available since 2006) prevents infection in a vaccinated individual. Secondary: Pap smear and HPV testing catch precancerous cervical changes while still asymptomatic and highly treatable. Tertiary: chemotherapy, surgery, and rehabilitation manage disease already present, limiting death and disability. Surveillance underlies every level — tracking risk-factor prevalence for primordial, vaccine coverage for primary, screening uptake and detection rates for secondary, and survival or recurrence for tertiary — but the strategy shifts from cheap, population-wide, and years-before-onset (upstream) to expensive, individual, and after damage is done (downstream).

lessons.workedExample: A school district considers two interventions against teen vaping: (1) a city ordinance raising the tobacco/vape purchase age and taxing e-liquid, versus (2) a nicotine-cessation clinic for students already diagnosed with dependence. The ordinance is primordial — it shifts population exposure before any individual becomes a user, costs little per capita, and its effect shows up as a lower prevalence rate in the school's substance-use surveillance data over years. The cessation clinic is tertiary — it is expensive per student, requires an existing diagnosis, and its effect shows up as individual case outcomes, not population trends. Both are legitimate, but a judge would expect a student to name which one their project is actually testing.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the levels because student projects frequently propose a screening tool and call it 'prevention' without specifying which level, which hides whether the project intervenes before or after biological onset. Naming primordial, primary, secondary, or tertiary forces a student to state exactly where on the natural-history timeline their intervention acts and what outcome measure that implies — incidence for primary, detection rate for secondary, survival or disability for tertiary.

questions.prompt: A mammography program screens asymptomatic women to catch breast cancer before symptoms appear. Which level of prevention is this?

options.text: Primordial prevention
Primary prevention
Secondary prevention
Tertiary prevention

explanations.a: Primordial prevention would act on population-level risk factors before any individual disease process begins, not detect existing disease.
explanations.b: Primary prevention stops the disease process from starting at all (e.g., a preventive vaccine), not detect it once present.
explanations.c: Correct: secondary prevention is early diagnosis of disease that already exists but is still preclinical, exactly what mammography screening does.
explanations.d: Tertiary prevention manages disability and complications after clinical disease is diagnosed, which is downstream of a screening catch.

questions.prompt: Order these stages of Leavell and Clark's natural history of disease from earliest to latest.

items.text: Risk factors accumulate in a susceptible host (prepathogenesis)
Subclinical biological onset of disease
Clinical disease with recognizable symptoms
Outcome: recovery, disability, or death

questions.explanation: The natural history runs from risk accumulation before disease exists, through silent biological onset, to symptomatic disease, to a final outcome — the timeline the four prevention levels are mapped onto.

questions.prompt: Match each intervention to its level of prevention.

left.text: A sugar-sweetened beverage tax applied city-wide
A Pap smear detecting precancerous cervical cells
Cardiac rehabilitation after a heart attack

right.text: Primordial prevention
Primary prevention
Secondary prevention
Tertiary prevention

questions.explanation: The tax shifts population risk-factor exposure before disease begins (primordial); the vaccine prevents infection in an individual (primary); the Pap smear catches disease early (secondary); rehab limits disability after disease is established (tertiary).

lessons.label: Population vs High-Risk Prevention Strategies

sections.heading: Rose's two strategies
