questions.prompt: Using the Lincoln-Petersen capture-recapture estimator N = (n1 × n2) / m, if source 1 finds 100 cases, source 2 finds 80 cases, and 20 cases appear on both lists, what is the estimated true total?

explanations.a: Correct: N = (100 × 80) / 20 = 400, meaning source 1 alone (100 cases) was capturing only a quarter of the true burden, and even the union of both sources (100+80-20=160 unique cases) reached only 40% of it.
explanations.b: 180 is simply the sum of the two source counts, which double-counts overlapping cases and ignores the capture-recapture logic entirely.
explanations.c: 100 is just source 1's count alone; it ignores what the overlap with source 2 implies about undercounting.
explanations.d: 20 is the overlap count m itself, not the estimated total population produced by the formula.

questions.prompt: Match each CDC surveillance attribute to its definition.

right.text: Proportion of true cases the system actually detects
Speed from the event occurring to an actionable report
How accurately reported cases reflect the true population by person, place, and time

questions.explanation: These three attributes each capture a distinct dimension of system performance: detection completeness, speed, and demographic/geographic accuracy.

lessons.label: When Should a Population Be Screened? Wilson-Jungner

sections.heading: Ten criteria, not one accurate test
sections.body: In 1968 James Maxwell Glover Wilson and Gunnar Jungner wrote WHO Public Health Papers No. 34, laying out ten principles a condition and a test must both satisfy before mass screening is justified. The condition must be an important health problem with a recognizable latent or early symptomatic stage, and its natural history must be adequately understood. The test must be suitable and acceptable to the population being screened. Critically, an accepted treatment must exist, facilities for diagnosis and treatment must be available, and there must be an agreed policy on whom to treat as patients — screening for a disease with no downstream care pathway just manufactures anxiety. Finally, case-finding should be a continuing process, not a once-and-for-all project, and its cost must be economically balanced against total medical expenditure. Sensitivity and specificity, the Core module's focus, satisfy only criteria five and six; the other eight are about the health system around the test. The paradigm case that shaped this thinking was newborn screening for phenylketonuria: Robert Guthrie's simple 1963 bacterial-inhibition blood-spot test could be run on every newborn, and because a strict low-phenylalanine diet started early prevents the intellectual disability the condition otherwise causes, PKU cleanly satisfied every one of the ten criteria years before Wilson and Jungner wrote them down.

sections.heading: Why 'accurate' is not the bar
sections.body: A highly accurate test for a condition with no effective treatment still fails Wilson-Jungner, because detecting it changes nothing but the patient's knowledge of it — and can cause harm through anxiety, labeling, and unnecessary follow-up procedures. This is why population screening for some conditions remains controversial even with excellent tests: the science of detection outran the science of what to do with a positive result.

sections.heading: Modern additions since 1968
sections.body: Andermann and colleagues, writing in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization in 2008, revisited Wilson-Jungner for the genomic era and synthesized emerging criteria the original ten did not anticipate: informed choice and consent (screening is not automatically beneficial to every individual the way treatment of symptomatic disease is), confidentiality protections for genetic and other sensitive results, and formal quality assurance and monitoring of the program itself, not just the test's laboratory performance. These additions reflect decades of experience showing that a program can satisfy the original ten criteria on paper and still cause net harm if uptake, follow-up, and equity of access are not actively managed.

lessons.workedExample: A biotech pitches a school science fair on a saliva test for a rare neurodegenerative condition that is 98% sensitive and 97% specific. Applying Wilson-Jungner: criterion 2 (accepted treatment) fails — there is no disease-modifying therapy, only supportive care available regardless of when diagnosed. Criterion 4 (recognizable latent stage) is shaky — the natural history from a positive test to symptom onset is not well characterized. Even though criteria 5 and 6 (suitable, acceptable test) are strong, the program should not launch: detecting the condition years early changes no clinical decision and may only burden the patient with unusable knowledge, which is exactly the harm the ten criteria were built to prevent.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe Wilson-Jungner because students conflate 'we built an accurate test' with 'we should screen the population.' A student who can only defend a proposed screening program by pointing to sensitivity and specificity is missing eight of ten criteria; a strong answer names which specific criterion (treatment availability, natural history, program continuity) their proposal satisfies or violates, showing the accuracy of a test was never the whole question.

questions.prompt: A test is 99% sensitive and 99% specific for a condition with no available treatment. Under Wilson-Jungner, mass screening for it is:

options.text: Justified, since a highly accurate test is the main requirement
Not justified, because there is no accepted treatment for those identified
Justified, because early knowledge always benefits the patient
Not justified, because the test's specificity is too low

explanations.a: Test accuracy satisfies only two of the ten criteria; without an accepted treatment, screening fails criterion 2 regardless of how accurate the test is.
explanations.b: Correct: Wilson-Jungner requires an accepted treatment and available treatment facilities before mass screening is justified, not just an accurate test.
explanations.c: Wilson-Jungner explicitly rejects this assumption — detecting a condition that cannot be treated can cause harm (anxiety, labeling) without any offsetting clinical benefit.
explanations.d: 99% specificity is very high; the criterion violated here is the absence of treatment, not test performance.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in applying the Wilson-Jungner framework to a proposed new screening program.

items.text: Confirm the condition is an important health problem with a known natural history
Confirm a suitable, acceptable test exists
Confirm an accepted treatment and treatment facilities are available
Establish an agreed policy on whom to treat and a plan for continuing, quality-assured case-finding

questions.explanation: The framework starts with the disease itself, moves to the test, then to what happens after a positive result, and finally to running the program as an ongoing, monitored system rather than a one-time effort.

questions.prompt: Match each Wilson-Jungner element to what it is judging.

left.text: 'There should be a recognizable latent or early symptomatic stage'
'There should be an accepted treatment for patients with recognized disease'

right.text: The disease's natural history
What happens after diagnosis
Individual autonomy over a decision that isn't automatically beneficial
Program sustainability, not a one-off effort

questions.explanation: The ten original criteria span the disease, the test, and the treatment pathway; the 2008 additions extend the framework to consent, equity, and ongoing program quality that the 1968 version did not address.

lessons.label: Lead-Time and Length-Time Bias

sections.heading: Lead-time bias: moving the finish line, not the death
sections.body: Five-year survival — the share of diagnosed patients alive five years later — looks like the natural way to judge whether screening helps. It is not, because screening changes WHEN a clock starts without necessarily changing WHEN a patient dies. If a cancer would have caused death at age 60 either way, and screening finds it at age 52 instead of age 55 (the age it would have caused symptoms), the patient's 'survival since diagnosis' jumps from 5 years to 8 years even though they die on the exact same day. That three-year gap between early detection and the point symptoms would otherwise have appeared is the lead time, and inflating survival by it without saving a single life is lead-time bias. It is the single most common reason a screening program looks like it works in observational data before a proper trial is run.

sections.heading: Length-time bias: catching the slow ones
sections.body: Screening is not a random sample of a disease's timeline — it is a snapshot that disproportionately catches slow-growing cases, because they spend a long preclinical window detectable but symptom-free, while fast, aggressive cases race through that window and present with symptoms between screening rounds (interval cases). Marvin Zelen and Manning Feinleib formalized this in their 1969 Biometrika paper 'On the Theory of Screening for Chronic Diseases,' introducing a stable-disease model showing that screen-detected cases are systematically biased toward longer sojourn times — and slow-growing disease has better prognosis to begin with, independent of any treatment benefit. So a screening program can report excellent survival among its detected cases purely by selectively finding the tumors that were never going to be aggressive.

sections.heading: Mortality is the honest endpoint
sections.body: Both biases inflate survival without inflating benefit, which is why randomized trials measuring disease-specific or all-cause mortality in the full invited population — not survival among the diagnosed — are the standard a program must clear before it is adopted. The National Lung Screening Trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2011, is the model: it randomized over 53,000 current and former heavy smokers to low-dose CT versus chest X-ray and reported a 20% relative reduction in lung cancer mortality for CT, a comparison immune to both lead-time and length-time bias precisely because both arms were screened on the same schedule and the outcome was death, not survival-since-diagnosis. A program that instead advertised CT's higher 5-year survival among its screen-detected cases, without the randomized mortality comparison, would have been reporting exactly the inflated number this lesson warns against.

lessons.workedExample: Two towns each have 1,000 people with the same lethal cancer, all of whom die at exactly age 70 regardless of when diagnosed (no treatment benefit). Town A screens and catches cases at age 62; town B waits for symptoms at age 68. Town A's 5-year survival looks fantastic (patients diagnosed at 62 are alive at 67, well past 5 years) while town B's looks worse (diagnosed at 68, everyone dies just 2 years later at age 70, short of the 5-year post-diagnosis mark, giving 0% five-year survival). Both towns have identical mortality — everyone dies at 70 — but town A's survival statistic makes screening look life-saving. Only comparing age-70 mortality rates between the two towns reveals there was no benefit at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because 'our screening program raised 5-year survival from X% to Y%' is the single most common flawed claim in student epidemiology projects. A student who understands lead-time and length-time bias will instead ask for a mortality comparison from a randomized or well-matched cohort, and can explain in the two-town or Zelen-Feinleib framing why survival alone cannot distinguish real benefit from an artifact of earlier detection or a favorable case mix.

questions.prompt: A new screening program shows diagnosed patients living 8 years post-diagnosis on average, up from 5 years before screening began — but disease-specific mortality in the population is unchanged. What best explains this?

options.text: The screening program is working; survival is the correct endpoint
Lead-time bias — diagnosis moved earlier without moving the date of death
The test's specificity improved
The disease became less lethal during the study period

explanations.a: Unchanged mortality is the tell that survival improved only because the diagnosis clock started earlier, not because fewer people died.
explanations.b: Correct: if mortality is flat while survival-since-diagnosis rises, the extra years are lead time added to the front of the disease course, not extra years of life.
explanations.c: Specificity affects false positives, not the relationship between diagnosis timing and death timing.
explanations.d: Nothing here indicates a biological change in lethality; unchanged mortality with rising survival is the signature of lead-time bias, not a genuinely less lethal disease.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning that explains why length-time bias inflates screen-detected survival.

items.text: Slow-growing tumors spend a long time in a detectable, symptom-free preclinical window
A periodic screening round is much more likely to catch a case during that long window
Fast-growing tumors have a short window and often appear as interval cases between screens instead
Screen-detected cases are therefore enriched for slow-growing, better-prognosis disease

questions.explanation: The bias arises because screening's chance of catching a case scales with how long that case sits in the detectable window, which systematically favors slower disease over faster disease.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its description.

right.text: Earlier diagnosis inflates survival time without delaying death
Screening preferentially detects slow-growing, better-prognosis cases
Formalized the stable-disease model explaining preferential detection of long-sojourn cases
The honest endpoint that both biases fail to distort

questions.explanation: Lead time is about when the clock starts; length bias is about which cases get caught at all; mortality is immune to both because it is anchored to death, not to the diagnosis date.

lessons.label: Overdiagnosis and Overtreatment

sections.heading: The extreme case of length bias
sections.body: Length-time bias says screening preferentially catches slow-growing disease. Overdiagnosis is the limiting case: detection of disease that was never going to progress to cause symptoms or death within the patient's lifetime at all. It is not a false positive — the histology is real, the cells genuinely meet the pathological definition of cancer — but the patient was better off never knowing, because treatment now begins with no possible mortality benefit and full exposure to surgical, hormonal, or psychological harm. This distinguishes overdiagnosis from a false positive, where the test result itself is simply wrong; here the result is right and the finding is still net-harmful.

sections.heading: How epidemiologists estimate it
sections.body: Because no test at the individual level can tell an indolent cancer from a lethal one, overdiagnosis is estimated at the population level, chiefly through excess-incidence methods: compare cumulative cancer incidence in a screened population against a matched unscreened population over enough years that any lead time has fully played out, and mortality has not shifted; the persistent gap in incidence is the overdiagnosis estimate. The reservoir this excess draws from is visible directly in autopsy studies. Harach and colleagues, in a 1985 Finnish autopsy series published in Cancer, sectioned the thyroids of 101 people who died of unrelated causes and found occult papillary carcinoma in 35.6% of them — a hidden reservoir of thyroid cancer nobody knew they had. Bell and colleagues' 2015 systematic review of prostate autopsy studies found latent prostate cancer prevalence rising from about 5% under age 30 to 59% over age 79, in men who died of something else entirely.

sections.heading: South Korea's thyroid-cancer epidemic
sections.body: Ahn, Kim, and Welch documented the clearest field demonstration in a 2014 New England Journal of Medicine paper: after South Korea rolled out widespread ultrasound screening, thyroid-cancer diagnoses rose roughly 15-fold from 1993 to 2011, yet thyroid-cancer mortality stayed essentially flat the entire time — the signature of tapping the autopsy-scale reservoir rather than catching cancers that would otherwise have killed.

sections.heading: Overtreatment follows automatically
sections.body: Because an overdiagnosed case cannot be identified as such at the time, essentially all overdiagnosed patients are treated, converting a detection artifact into surgery, radiation, or lifelong hormone therapy with only downside risk. A thyroidectomy carries real chances of permanent hypoparathyroidism or recurrent laryngeal nerve injury affecting the voice; radical prostatectomy carries substantial risk of permanent erectile dysfunction and urinary incontinence. For a patient whose cancer was never going to progress, every one of those harms is pure loss with no offsetting survival gain, which is why overdiagnosis is counted as a harm of screening itself, not merely a statistical curiosity.

lessons.workedExample: A country introduces universal thyroid ultrasound screening. Before screening, thyroid cancer incidence is 5 per 100,000 per year and mortality is 0.5 per 100,000 per year. Ten years after screening starts, incidence has risen to 75 per 100,000 (a 15-fold jump, mirroring the real South Korean pattern) but mortality is still 0.5 per 100,000. Since the autopsy literature shows roughly a third of adults harbor occult papillary thyroid carcinoma that would never surface clinically, the unchanged mortality alongside the incidence spike indicates the program is mostly finding members of that pre-existing reservoir, not preventing thyroid-cancer deaths — and most of the newly diagnosed patients will still undergo thyroidectomy.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe overdiagnosis because 'we increased cancer detection' sounds like unambiguous good news to most students, and distinguishing it from a genuine mortality benefit requires the harder argument that flat mortality alongside rising incidence is itself the evidence of harm, not success. A strong answer cites the incidence-versus-mortality divergence pattern (as in the Korean data) rather than simply asserting overdiagnosis exists.

questions.prompt: Which pattern in population data is the classic signature of overdiagnosis following a new screening program?

options.text: Incidence and mortality both rise together
Incidence rises sharply while mortality stays flat
Incidence stays flat while mortality falls
Both incidence and mortality fall together

explanations.a: If both rose together it would suggest the program is finding cases that were always going to become clinically apparent, not a reservoir of indolent disease.
explanations.b: Correct: this is exactly the pattern Ahn, Kim, and Welch (2014) documented in South Korea — roughly a 15-fold incidence rise with flat mortality — indicating the excess diagnoses were not going to cause death.
explanations.c: A mortality fall with flat incidence would suggest a treatment or prevention improvement, not overdiagnosis.
explanations.d: Both falling would suggest the disease itself is becoming less common or less lethal, not that screening is uncovering a hidden reservoir.

questions.prompt: Order the logic of the excess-incidence method for estimating overdiagnosis.

items.text: Identify a screened population and a comparable unscreened population
Wait long enough for any lead time to fully play out in both groups
Compare cumulative incidence between the two groups over that period
Attribute the persistent incidence gap to overdiagnosis

questions.explanation: The method needs a comparison group and enough follow-up time that any remaining incidence gap can no longer be explained by lead time, leaving overdiagnosis as the remaining explanation.

questions.prompt: Match each finding to its source.

left.text: 35.6% occult papillary thyroid carcinoma in autopsies of people who died of other causes
Latent prostate cancer prevalence rising from about 5% (under 30) to 59% (over 79) at autopsy
~15-fold rise in thyroid cancer incidence with flat mortality after screening rollout

right.text: Harach et al. (1985), Finnish autopsy series
Bell et al. (2015) systematic review of autopsy studies
Ahn, Kim, and Welch (2014), South Korea

questions.explanation: The autopsy studies establish the size of the hidden reservoir of indolent disease; the Korean incidence-mortality divergence shows that reservoir being tapped in real time by a screening program.

lessons.label: Evaluating Screening Program Performance

sections.heading: Metrics beyond sensitivity and specificity
sections.body: A test's sensitivity and specificity are fixed properties measured in a lab or validation study; a program's performance is a different, moving target measured in the field. Coverage (or uptake) is the share of the eligible population actually screened in a given cycle — a program with a superb test but 30% coverage protects far fewer people than a mediocre test at 80% coverage. Detection rate is the number of cases found per thousand screened, used to check the program is finding roughly the expected disease burden. Recall rate is the share of screened people called back for further workup after an abnormal result; a program with a high recall rate but low detection rate is generating a lot of false-positive anxiety and cost for little benefit, while one with too low a recall rate risks under-calling true disease. Interval cancers — cases diagnosed clinically in the gap between one negative screen and the next scheduled one — are the sharpest field check on real-world sensitivity, since they reveal what the program actually missed, not what a validation study predicted it would miss.

sections.heading: Organized versus opportunistic screening
sections.body: Organized screening invites a defined eligible population on a set schedule, tracks who attended, applies uniform quality standards to every reader and machine, and can therefore report all four metrics above. Opportunistic screening happens whenever a clinician or patient decides to order a test during an unrelated visit, with no population denominator, no systematic recall, and no way to compute a true coverage or interval-cancer rate, because no one knows who was eligible but never tested. The Nordic countries and the UK moved cervical and breast screening to organized, invitation-based programs specifically because opportunistic screening reliably reached the same motivated, already health-engaged patients repeatedly while missing higher-risk populations entirely — the inverse care law. Smith-Bindman and colleagues documented the practical cost of the more opportunistic US approach in a 2003 JAMA comparison: recall rates in the largely opportunistic US system ran roughly twice as high as the UK's organized NHS Breast Screening Programme, driving substantially more negative biopsies without finding more large, clinically important cancers — extra harm from recall variability that a tightly quality-controlled organized program is built to suppress.

sections.heading: Why a randomized mortality trial still sits above all of this
sections.body: None of these program metrics proves the program saves lives; they only prove it is running as designed. The Health Insurance Plan of New York trial, begun in 1963, and the Swedish Two-County Trial led by Tabár beginning in 1977, are the reference standard because they randomized whole populations to invitation or no invitation and followed mortality — the only design immune to both lead-time and length-time bias, which no program-metric audit can rule out on its own.

lessons.workedExample: A national breast screening program reports: coverage 72% of eligible women, detection rate 6 cancers per 1,000 screened, recall rate 4%, and 1.2 interval cancers per 1,000 women-years between rounds. A neighboring opportunistic system has no coverage figure at all (unknown denominator), a recall rate of 11% because radiologists individually vary their thresholds, and cannot compute an interval-cancer rate because it does not track who was screened and when. Even though both programs might use an identical mammography machine, the organized program's lower recall rate suggests better-calibrated reading, and only the organized program can be audited for whether it is missing disease between rounds.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe program metrics because a student who reports only 'our test is 95% sensitive' has described the test, not the program that would deploy it — and a judge who asks about coverage, recall rate, or interval cancers is checking whether the student can separate 'is the test good' from 'is the program working,' since a great test embedded in a low-coverage or high-recall program can still fail the population it serves.

questions.prompt: A program has excellent test sensitivity but only 35% of the eligible population attends screening. Which metric captures this specific shortfall?

options.text: Detection rate
Coverage
Interval cancer rate
Specificity

explanations.a: Detection rate measures cases found per thousand screened, not what share of the eligible population was screened at all.
explanations.b: Correct: coverage (uptake) is the share of the eligible population actually screened, and it is a program-level property independent of how good the test itself is.
explanations.c: Interval cancers measure what the program misses between rounds among those who WERE screened, not attendance.
explanations.d: Specificity is an intrinsic test property; it does not change based on how many eligible people show up.

questions.prompt: Order these from a property intrinsic to the test to a property that requires a full randomized program evaluation.

items.text: Sensitivity and specificity, measured in a validation study
Coverage and recall rate, measured from program records
Interval cancer rate, measured by tracking screen-negative patients over time
Mortality reduction, measured in a randomized trial like the Swedish Two-County Trial

questions.explanation: Each step requires more infrastructure and more time than the last: test properties need only a validation study, program metrics need operational tracking, and only a randomized trial with mortality follow-up can prove the program saves lives.

questions.prompt: Match each screening model or trial to its description.

left.text: Health Insurance Plan of New York trial (begun 1963)

right.text: Invitation-based, defined eligible population, trackable coverage and interval-cancer rates
Ad hoc testing during unrelated visits, no denominator, cannot compute coverage
Randomized whole populations to invitation vs. no invitation and followed mortality

questions.explanation: Organized programs can report the full set of performance metrics because they track a defined population; opportunistic screening cannot; and randomized mortality trials remain the only design that proves benefit independent of program-metric or bias concerns.

lessons.label: Vaccination Coverage and Program Monitoring

sections.heading: Two ways to measure reach
sections.body: Coverage — the share of a target population that has received a vaccine — is tracked through two complementary channels. Administrative data divides doses given (reported by clinics and vaccination teams) by the estimated target population, which is fast and cheap but drifts when the denominator (often a census projection) is wrong. Household coverage surveys, such as the Demographic and Health Surveys and UNICEF's Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys, sample actual households and ask about vaccination history or check records directly, correcting for denominator error at the cost of being slower and more expensive to run. The WHO/UNICEF Estimates of National Immunization Coverage (WUENIC) reconcile both streams every year across roughly 195 countries and 14 antigens, using expert judgment to resolve disagreements between what clinics report and what surveys find. In wealthier countries, immunization information systems (IIS) — state or regional registries that log each dose against an individual child — support the same function at finer geographic resolution than a national survey ever could.

sections.heading: A national average can hide a local outbreak
sections.body: National coverage is a mean, and a mean can look reassuring while concealing exactly the variance that matters for transmission, because unvaccinated people rarely distribute themselves randomly — they cluster by school, neighborhood, or community, often along religious, philosophical, or geographic lines that correlate with exemption policy. In the United States, national kindergarten MMR coverage sits around 91-93%, yet the 2019 measles outbreak centered on Orthodox Jewish communities in Brooklyn and Rockland County, New York happened inside pockets far below that figure: Rockland County's overall child vaccination rate was 72.9% as of April 2019, and one Waldorf school within it was at 56%, while an affected Brooklyn neighborhood had been under 80% before emergency vaccination campaigns pushed it to roughly 91%. A registry that only reports the state or national number would have missed the risk entirely; the outbreak was findable only by mapping coverage down to the school and zip-code level.

sections.heading: Aiming above the threshold, not at it
sections.body: Because clustering is the norm rather than the exception, and because measles' basic reproduction number of roughly 12-18 pushes its herd-protection threshold to about 92-95% (the derivation of that threshold from R0 belongs to transmission modeling), a program that targets exactly the national threshold on average will still leave pockets below it. The operational goal is therefore to monitor coverage at the smallest geographic and institutional unit the data allows and push every identified pocket above threshold, not just the national mean.

lessons.workedExample: A state health department sees a comforting 94% statewide MMR coverage figure, within the 92-95% herd-protection range for measles. Drilling into its immunization registry by county and school district reveals three private-school clusters at 58%, 65%, and 71% coverage — invisible in the state average because they are small relative to the state's total child population but internally cohesive enough (students interact daily within the school) to sustain a measles chain of transmission once one imported case arrives, exactly as happened with the 56% coverage Waldorf school in Rockland County in 2019. The registry-level view, not the statewide figure, is what would flag these schools for a targeted catch-up vaccination campaign before an outbreak, not after.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because a student who reports only a national or state coverage percentage has not actually assessed outbreak risk — a judge asking 'what is coverage at the school or neighborhood level, and how would you find pockets below threshold' is checking whether the student understands that averages conceal exactly the geographic clustering that determines whether a chain of transmission can sustain itself.

questions.prompt: A state reports 94% MMR coverage, within the herd-protection range, yet still experiences a school-based measles outbreak. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The vaccine's efficacy dropped that year
Unvaccinated children are clustered in specific schools or communities well below the state average
The state average was calculated incorrectly
Measles' reproduction number fell below the threshold

explanations.a: Vaccine efficacy for MMR is stable and high; a single-year outbreak with a state average above threshold is not explained by an efficacy drop.
explanations.b: Correct: unvaccinated individuals cluster geographically and institutionally, so a state average within threshold can still contain specific schools or neighborhoods well below it, exactly as in Rockland County (72.9% overall, one school at 56%) in 2019.
explanations.c: The scenario does not indicate a calculation error; state averages are simply insensitive to sub-population clustering by construction.
explanations.d: R0 is a property of the pathogen's transmissibility, not something that changes based on local outbreaks; a falling R0 would lower risk, not explain an outbreak.

questions.prompt: Order the steps a health department would take to find a hidden vaccination pocket before it causes an outbreak.

items.text: Reconcile administrative dose reports with survey or registry data at the national or state level
Disaggregate coverage down to county, school, or neighborhood level
Identify units falling below the herd-protection threshold despite a reassuring overall average
Target a catch-up vaccination campaign at those specific units

questions.explanation: Coverage monitoring only catches clustering if it moves from a single aggregate number down to finer geographic units, then acts on the units that fall short rather than the average that looks fine.

questions.prompt: Match each source or system to its role in coverage monitoring.

right.text: Fast and cheap but sensitive to denominator (census projection) error
Slower, sampled directly from households, corrects denominator error
Annual WHO/UNICEF reconciliation of administrative and survey data across ~195 countries
Individual-level dose tracking enabling fine-grained pocket detection

questions.explanation: Each system trades off speed, cost, and resolution differently, which is why programs use several in combination rather than relying on any single national figure.

lessons.label: Measuring Vaccine Effectiveness in the Field

sections.heading: Efficacy in a trial, effectiveness in the world
sections.body: Efficacy is the risk reduction measured in a randomized controlled trial under tightly controlled conditions — a defined dose schedule, a healthy and closely monitored trial population, and standardized outcome ascertainment. Effectiveness is the risk reduction observed once the vaccine is deployed into a messy real population: patients who skip a booster, cold-chain failures, waning immunity over seasons, and a case mix that includes people the original trial excluded, such as the frail elderly or the immunocompromised. Effectiveness is usually lower than trial efficacy, and monitoring it every season is essential because a vaccine's real-world performance can shift as circulating strains drift away from the ones the vaccine targeted — an annual concern for influenza vaccines in particular. The 2014-2015 US flu season is the clearest cautionary case: overall vaccine effectiveness came in at just 19%, because more than 80% of circulating H3N2 viruses had drifted away from the A/Texas/50/2012 strain the vaccine had been built to match, a mismatch CDC could only quantify because test-negative surveillance was running that season and every season around it.

sections.heading: The test-negative design
sections.body: Running a new randomized trial every season to measure effectiveness is neither ethical nor practical once a vaccine is recommended for everyone, so field epidemiologists rely on observational designs instead. The test-negative design has become the standard for both seasonal influenza and COVID-19: patients presenting to clinics or hospitals with a defined set of respiratory symptoms are all swabbed and tested; those who test positive for the target pathogen become cases, and those who test negative — who sought care for a similar-looking illness but do not have the target pathogen — become the controls. Vaccine effectiveness is then estimated by comparing vaccination rates between the two groups. Because both groups are drawn from people who chose to seek care with similar symptoms, the design largely cancels out confounding by health-care-seeking behavior and reduces misclassification of who was truly infected, two problems that plague a traditional case-control design using community controls who never sought care at all.

sections.heading: Confounders the design must still fight
sections.body: Test-negative studies remain vulnerable to healthy-vaccinee bias, where people who seek vaccination are systematically healthier or more health-conscious than those who do not, inflating apparent effectiveness — a systematic review found roughly 83% of influenza VE studies carried a high risk of this and related confounding by indication, where sicker, higher-risk patients are vaccinated preferentially, which can bias effectiveness in either direction. Differential testing — vaccinated patients being tested less aggressively, or clinicians ordering different test types for vaccinated versus unvaccinated patients — can also distort the case/control split if not standardized across all enrolled patients regardless of vaccination status.

lessons.workedExample: A health network enrolls every patient hospitalized with acute respiratory illness during flu season and tests all of them with the same PCR panel. Of 400 patients who test positive for influenza (cases), 60 were vaccinated (340 unvaccinated); of 800 who test negative (controls, sick with something else), 320 were vaccinated (480 unvaccinated). The odds of vaccination are 60/340 = 0.18 among cases versus 320/480 = 0.67 among controls, giving an odds ratio of about 0.26. VE = (1 - OR) x 100% comes out to roughly 74%, meaning vaccinated patients had substantially lower odds of being an influenza case among all people sick enough to be hospitalized with respiratory symptoms that season.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because students often cite a single trial-reported efficacy number as if it applies unchanged forever, and a judge asking 'how would you know if effectiveness dropped this season' is checking whether the student can name the test-negative design, explain why it controls for care-seeking behavior better than community controls, and name at least one confounder (healthy-vaccinee bias, differential testing) it still has to address rather than assuming an observational estimate is automatically unbiased.

questions.prompt: In a test-negative design study of influenza vaccine effectiveness, who serves as the control group?

options.text: Healthy people randomly sampled from the community
Patients who sought care with similar symptoms but tested negative for influenza
Patients who tested positive but had mild symptoms
Unvaccinated patients matched by age only

explanations.a: Community controls are used in a traditional case-control design, not the test-negative design, and they introduce more confounding by care-seeking behavior.
explanations.b: Correct: test-negative controls are patients who sought care for a similar illness but tested negative for the target pathogen, which keeps cases and controls similar in health-care-seeking behavior.
explanations.c: Test-positive patients of any severity are cases, not controls, in this design.
explanations.d: Matching only on age does not describe the test-negative design's defining feature, which is selecting controls from the same symptomatic, care-seeking population as the cases.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a test-negative vaccine effectiveness study.

items.text: Enroll all patients presenting with the defined symptom set at participating clinics
Test every enrolled patient with the same diagnostic method
Classify test-positive patients as cases and test-negative patients as controls
Compare vaccination rates between cases and controls to estimate VE

questions.explanation: The design's bias reduction depends on testing everyone the same way before splitting them into cases and controls by test result, not by vaccination status.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its description.

right.text: Risk reduction measured in a randomized trial's controlled conditions
Risk reduction observed once deployed in the real, mixed population
Vaccinated people are systematically healthier, inflating apparent VE
Sicker, higher-risk patients are preferentially vaccinated, biasing VE in either direction

questions.explanation: Efficacy and effectiveness differ by setting; healthy-vaccinee bias and confounding by indication are two distinct ways real-world vaccination status correlates with underlying health risk rather than the vaccine itself.

lessons.label: Vaccine Safety Surveillance

sections.heading: Passive systems: cast a wide net, expect noise
sections.body: The Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS), co-run by the CDC and FDA since 1990, accepts reports from anyone — clinicians, patients, manufacturers — describing any health event after any vaccine, with no requirement that the vaccine actually caused it. This is a deliberate design choice: passive reporting is cheap to run and catches rare events a trial could never be powered to detect, but it cannot by itself distinguish a true signal from coincidence, because plenty of unrelated illnesses will occur shortly after vaccination purely by chance in a population of millions. VAERS is a hypothesis-generating tripwire, not a hypothesis-testing system; a spike in reports triggers investigation elsewhere, it does not itself establish causation.

sections.heading: Active systems that can actually test a hypothesis
sections.body: The Vaccine Safety Datalink (VSD), a CDC collaboration with large healthcare organizations begun in 1990, links electronic health records across millions of enrollees, letting epidemiologists run real analytic studies — comparing vaccinated and unvaccinated patients, or the same patient's risk in a defined time window after vaccination versus outside it — instead of just counting spontaneous reports. The self-controlled case series design, widely used in this setting, compares each patient's own event rate during a biologically plausible risk window after vaccination against that same patient's rate at other times, which cancels out any confounder that does not change over the observation period, such as underlying chronic disease.

sections.heading: RotaShield: the system working as designed
sections.body: RotaShield, the first licensed rotavirus vaccine, was approved in August 1998. Between September 1998 and July 1999, VAERS received 15 reports of intussusception (a bowel obstruction) in infants who had recently received it — an unusually tight cluster for a rare event. That passive signal triggered a case-control study, which found an approximately 37-fold increased risk of intussusception 3 to 7 days after the first dose, translating to an excess risk of roughly 1 case per 10,000 vaccinated infants. On October 22, 1999, the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices voted to stop recommending RotaShield, and the manufacturer withdrew it that same month — a textbook passive-to-active handoff from tripwire to confirmed causal signal to withdrawal in about a year.

sections.heading: Why most spikes are false alarms
sections.body: Most VAERS clusters do not replicate under active-system scrutiny, because a passive system with millions of reports will always generate coincidental clustering by chance alone; the discipline is treating every VAERS signal as a lead to test in VSD or a similar system, never as a conclusion on its own.

lessons.workedExample: A new vaccine is rolled out nationally and VAERS logs 40 reports of a rare autoimmune condition in the first six months, more than expected by background rate alone. Investigators turn to the Vaccine Safety Datalink and run a self-controlled case series: for every patient in the VSD population who develops the condition, they compare that patient's own risk in the 42 days after vaccination against their risk in a control window a year earlier or later. If the rate ratio comes back near 1.0, the VAERS cluster is judged coincidental — background cases that happened to follow vaccination by chance in a large population — and no action is taken, in contrast to RotaShield's confirmed 37-fold ratio, which was far too large to be coincidence.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because students often treat a VAERS report count as proof of harm, and a judge asking 'is that number more than you'd expect by chance, and has it been tested in an active system' is checking whether the student understands passive surveillance generates hypotheses while active systems like the Vaccine Safety Datalink test them — RotaShield is the reference case precisely because that handoff happened correctly and quickly.

questions.prompt: A spike in VAERS reports for a rare condition after a new vaccine, by itself, establishes:

options.text: That the vaccine causes the condition
A signal worth investigating in an active surveillance system, not causation
Nothing, because VAERS data should be ignored entirely
That the vaccine should be withdrawn immediately

explanations.a: VAERS accepts reports with no requirement that the vaccine caused the event, so a spike alone cannot establish causation; that requires a controlled comparison.
explanations.b: Correct: VAERS is a hypothesis-generating tripwire; a spike triggers investigation in an active system like the Vaccine Safety Datalink, which is exactly how the RotaShield signal was confirmed.
explanations.c: VAERS is not ignored; it is precisely the tripwire that caught the RotaShield signal from just 15 reports, which then warranted formal investigation.
explanations.d: Withdrawal followed the RotaShield case-control study confirming an approximately 37-fold risk increase, not the initial VAERS reports alone.

questions.prompt: Order the actual sequence of the RotaShield intussusception investigation.

items.text: RotaShield is licensed and enters routine use (1998)
15 intussusception reports accumulate in VAERS over about ten months
A case-control study finds an approximately 37-fold increased risk 3-7 days post-dose
ACIP votes to stop recommending the vaccine and it is withdrawn (October 1999)

questions.explanation: The sequence moves from licensure, to a passive-system signal, to active-system confirmation of a causal association, to the policy action that signal justified.

questions.prompt: Match each system or design to its role in vaccine safety surveillance.

right.text: Passive spontaneous reporting; generates hypotheses, cannot confirm causation alone
Active system linking health records across millions of enrollees to test hypotheses
Compares each patient's own event rate in a risk window vs. other times, canceling stable confounders

questions.explanation: Passive and active systems play complementary roles: VAERS casts a wide, noisy net across the whole vaccinated population, while VSD and designs like the self-controlled case series can actually test whether a VAERS-flagged signal holds up under a controlled comparison.

units.label: Health Disparities, Social Determinants, and Equity

lessons.label: Determinants of Health: The Layered Model

sections.heading: The rainbow: four layers around the person
sections.body: Dahlgren and Whitehead's 1991 'rainbow' model arranges the causes of health outcomes as concentric layers around an individual core of fixed traits (age, sex, genetics). The next layer is individual lifestyle factors (diet, smoking, activity), which is itself shaped by the layer around it: social and community networks — family, peer groups, neighborhood ties. Beyond that sit living and working conditions: agriculture and food supply, education, the work environment, unemployment, water and sanitation, and access to health services. The outermost layer is general socioeconomic, cultural, and environmental conditions — the laws, markets, and policies that set the shape of everything inside them. The point of drawing it as nested rings rather than a list is that upstream layers constrain what is even possible in the layers closer to the person: a lifestyle 'choice' like eating fresh vegetables is bounded by whether affordable groceries exist in the neighborhood, which is bounded by housing and zoning policy.

sections.heading: Disparity, inequality, inequity: three words, three claims
sections.body: These terms get used interchangeably but make different claims. A health disparity is simply a measurable difference in an outcome between groups — descriptive, no judgment implied. A health inequality is a disparity that is systematic and socially patterned rather than random. A health inequity, following Margaret Whitehead's 1992 formulation, is a subset of inequalities judged to be avoidable, unnecessary, and unfair — differences that arise from unjust social arrangements rather than free choice or biology. A three-year gap in life expectancy between two random hospitals might be a disparity with no clear pattern; the same gap tracking consistently with neighborhood income is an inequality; if that gap traces back to decades of discriminatory lending that could have been prevented, it is an inequity.

sections.heading: Causes of the causes
sections.body: Michael Marmot's phrase 'causes of the causes' names the layered model's core insight for epidemiology: proximate risk factors like smoking, hypertension, or missed vaccinations are themselves outcomes of upstream social conditions — income, education, housing, discrimination. Treating only the proximate cause without touching the upstream layer leaves the mechanism that produced it intact, so a new proximate risk factor tends to fill the gap. Marmot chaired the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health, whose 2008 report 'Closing the Gap in a Generation' documented life-expectancy gaps of well over a decade between neighborhoods only a few miles apart within the same city — evidence that the upstream layer, not biology, was doing most of the work.

lessons.workedExample: A town has two neighborhoods with a 12-percentage-point gap in childhood asthma rates. A clinician might treat this as a disparity driven by indoor allergens (individual lifestyle layer). A public-health team using the rainbow model traces it further: the high-asthma neighborhood sits along a zoned industrial corridor (living/working conditions layer) because 1950s zoning ordinances (general socioeconomic/environmental layer) routed heavy trucking and factories away from wealthier districts. The lifestyle-layer intervention (better inhalers) treats the proximate cause; only a zoning or emissions intervention touches the cause of the cause — and only the latter, if the pattern is judged avoidable and unjust, counts as addressing an inequity rather than just a disparity.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can locate their intervention within the rainbow model and defend why they chose that layer. A project that measures a disparity, calls it an inequity without checking whether it is avoidable and unjust, and proposes an individual-layer fix (a pamphlet) for a structural-layer cause (housing policy) reveals the student hasn't distinguished description from moral claim, or symptom from upstream driver — the two most common gaps in disparities projects.

questions.prompt: A study finds two ethnic groups differ in diabetes rates, but the pattern is inconsistent across cities and doesn't track with any social variable the researchers measured. Which term best fits this finding alone?

options.text: Health disparity
Health inequality
Health inequity
Fundamental cause

explanations.a: Correct: disparity is the neutral, descriptive term for any measured difference, with no claim yet about social patterning or fairness.
explanations.b: Inequality implies a systematic social pattern, which this finding explicitly lacks.
explanations.c: Inequity requires judging the gap avoidable and unjust; that judgment needs more than an unexplained difference.
explanations.d: Fundamental cause is a theory about why disparities persist across diseases, not a term for a single measured gap.

questions.prompt: Order these from the Dahlgren-Whitehead model's innermost layer to its outermost layer.

items.text: Fixed individual traits (age, sex, genetics)
Individual lifestyle factors
Social and community networks
Living and working conditions
General socioeconomic, cultural, and environmental conditions

questions.explanation: The rainbow model nests layers from the fixed individual core outward through lifestyle, social networks, and material conditions, to the broadest societal conditions that bound everything inside.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its correct description.

right.text: An avoidable, unjust gap arising from unfair social arrangements
Upstream social conditions that generate proximate risk factors
A systematic, socially patterned difference not yet judged as unjust

questions.explanation: Inequity adds a moral/avoidability claim on top of inequality's social patterning; 'causes of the causes' is Marmot's term for the upstream layer that produces proximate risks.

questions.prompt: A researcher fixes a lead-poisoning disparity in children by handing out water filters, without touching the aging lead pipe infrastructure that only serves low-income blocks. In rainbow-model terms, this intervention targets which layer relative to the problem's origin?

options.text: It targets the same outer layer where the problem originates
It targets an inner layer while the cause sits in an outer layer
It targets an outer layer while the cause sits in an inner layer
Layers are irrelevant once a fix reduces exposure

explanations.a: The pipe infrastructure is an outer, living/working-conditions-level cause; filters are an inner-layer, individual-level response, not a same-layer fix.
explanations.b: Correct: water filters act at the individual/lifestyle layer while the aging pipe infrastructure sits in the living-and-working-conditions layer — a cause-of-the-cause left untouched.
explanations.c: This reverses the direction: the fix is the inner-layer action, and the infrastructure cause is the outer layer.
explanations.d: The model's whole point is that which layer an intervention hits changes whether it addresses the origin or only the symptom.

lessons.label: The Social Gradient in Health

sections.heading: The Whitehall studies
sections.body: Starting in 1967, Donald Reid and Geoffrey Rose followed roughly 17,000 male British civil servants across employment grades — from top administrators down to unskilled messengers and porters — in what became known as Whitehall I. All participants worked for the same employer, had job security, and access to the UK's National Health Service, ruling out the crudest explanation (no insurance, no doctor) for any health gap. Yet over ten years of follow-up, mortality tracked employment grade in a stepwise pattern: the lowest grade had roughly three times the mortality rate of the highest grade, with intermediate grades falling in between rather than clustering near either extreme. Cardiovascular disease accounted for a large share of the gap. Whitehall II, begun in 1985 by Michael Marmot with over 10,000 participants including women for the first time, extended the design and probed psychosocial mechanisms, notably the demand-control model: jobs combining high demands with low personal control over one's work predicted worse cardiovascular outcomes independent of grade.

sections.heading: A gradient, not a cliff
sections.body: The critical finding is that health did not divide people into two camps of 'poor and sick' versus 'everyone else fine.' Every step down the civil-service hierarchy carried a health cost, including the step from the second-highest to the highest grade — men just below the top still fared worse than men at the very top. This rules out a simple poverty-threshold explanation, where only material deprivation below some cutoff matters, and points instead toward relative social position itself — status, autonomy, and psychosocial stress — as a driver operating across the whole distribution.

sections.heading: Why a gradient changes prevention strategy
sections.body: Geoffrey Rose's population-strategy argument follows directly from gradient findings: because risk is distributed continuously across the whole population rather than concentrated in a poor minority, interventions aimed only at the worst-off will miss most of the burden, which sits in the large middle of the distribution. Rose laid out this logic in his 1985 paper 'Sick Individuals and Sick Populations,' introducing what he called the prevention paradox: a measure that brings large benefit to the population as a whole often offers little to each participating individual, which is why population-wide strategies can look unrewarding person by person even while shifting the whole distribution's risk. A gradient implies shifting the whole population's exposure to the underlying social conditions, not just rescuing a targeted subgroup.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a hospital tracks 10-year cardiovascular mortality by the six Whitehall employment grades and finds rates of 12% (lowest grade), 9.5%, 7.5%, 6%, 5%, and 4% (highest grade) — a smooth step-down rather than a jump only at the bottom, with the lowest grade at roughly three times the mortality of the highest. A poverty-threshold model predicts the bottom one or two grades should look distinctly worse than everyone else clustered together; the actual data show the second-from-top grade (5%) still notably exceeds the top grade (4%), even though both groups are securely employed professionals. That residual gap between comfortable-but-not-highest grades is the signature of a true gradient and is what pushed Whitehall researchers toward psychosocial explanations like job control rather than material deprivation alone.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probing a disparities project ask whether the student's data show a gradient or a threshold, because the two imply different fixes. A student who finds a stepwise pattern across five income quintiles but proposes an intervention aimed only at quintile one has designed a response to a threshold problem for a gradient finding — the tell that they analyzed the shape of their own data rather than assuming poverty is binary.

questions.prompt: What made the Whitehall I finding hard to explain by lack of health insurance or access to care?

options.text: All participants were British civil servants with job security and NHS access, yet mortality still tracked grade
The study only included people already diagnosed with heart disease
Participants paid out of pocket for all care, so access was equal by definition
The gradient only appeared in the lowest-income countries studied

explanations.a: Correct: uniform employer, job security, and NHS access for all grades removed the most obvious access-to-care explanation, isolating grade itself as the driver.
explanations.b: Whitehall I followed a general cohort of civil servants over time, not a pre-diagnosed patient sample.
explanations.c: The UK's National Health Service, not out-of-pocket payment, covered participants — that is precisely why access differences couldn't explain the gap.
explanations.d: Whitehall I was a single-country UK cohort of civil servants, not a cross-country comparison.

questions.prompt: Whitehall I found that men in the lowest employment grade had mortality roughly how many times that of men in the highest grade?

options.text: About 1.2 times
About 3 times
About 10 times
Mortality was statistically identical across grades

explanations.a: This understates the gap; the actual ratio was much larger than a marginal difference.
explanations.b: Correct: the lowest grade showed roughly threefold the mortality of the highest grade over the ten-year follow-up.
explanations.c: This overstates the gap well beyond what Whitehall I reported.
explanations.d: The entire point of the study is that mortality was not identical — it stepped down across every grade.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning that leads from the Whitehall findings to Rose's population-strategy conclusion.

items.text: Mortality steps down across every employment grade, not just at the bottom
This rules out a poverty-threshold model where only the poorest matter
Most of the population's health risk therefore sits in the broad middle of the distribution, not a small extreme
Effective prevention must shift the whole population's exposure, not just target the worst-off subgroup

questions.explanation: The stepwise gradient rules out a threshold model, which relocates most of the risk burden to the population middle, which in turn implies Rose's population-wide prevention strategy.

questions.prompt: Match each Whitehall study feature to its description.

right.text: Begun 1967, ~17,000 male civil servants, found threefold gradient in mortality by grade
Begun 1985, over 10,000 participants including women, probed psychosocial mechanisms
High job demands with low personal control predicts worse cardiovascular outcomes

questions.explanation: Whitehall I established the gradient itself; Whitehall II extended the cohort to women and tested psychosocial mechanisms such as the demand-control model of workplace stress.

lessons.label: Fundamental Cause Theory and Why Disparities Persist

sections.heading: Link and Phelan's 1995 claim
sections.body: Sociologists Bruce Link and Jo Phelan published 'Social Conditions as Fundamental Causes of Disease' in the Journal of Health and Social Behavior in 1995, arguing that socioeconomic status (SES) is not just one risk factor among many but a 'fundamental cause' that produces disparities in disease outcomes regardless of which specific mechanism happens to be dominant at a given moment in history. Their claim rests on four features: SES shapes access to flexible resources — money, knowledge, prestige, power, and beneficial social connections — that can be deployed to avoid risks or minimize the consequences of disease; SES influences multiple disease outcomes through multiple pathways at once, not a single risk factor; SES involves access to resources that help avoid the health consequences of disease once it occurs, not just avoiding exposure; and, crucially, this association is reproduced over time even as the specific mechanisms linking SES to health change entirely.

sections.heading: Why eliminating one risk factor doesn't close the gap
sections.body: The theory's sharpest prediction is that removing any single proximate risk factor will not eliminate the SES–health association, because people with more resources simply redeploy them toward whatever risk becomes newly relevant. Historically, when infectious disease dominated mortality, SES groups differed in access to clean water and sanitation; as chronic disease became dominant, the gap re-emerged through differential smoking cessation, diet, and access to statins and cancer screening. A frequently cited illustration: as public-health campaigns reduced smoking, cessation happened first and fastest among higher-SES groups, so the smoking-attributable mortality gap between rich and poor widened even as overall smoking prevalence fell nationally — the resource (money, knowledge, freedom to quit without job-related stress) simply migrated to a new battlefront.

sections.heading: Contrast with purely behavioral explanations
sections.body: A purely behavioral or proximate model treats smoking, poor diet, or missed screenings as the causes of disparities, implying that education campaigns targeting behavior should close the gap. Fundamental cause theory predicts such campaigns will succeed unevenly, widening rather than closing disparities, because the resources needed to act on new health information are themselves unequally distributed. HPV vaccination shows the same pattern through a different mechanism: uptake climbed fastest among adolescents whose parents had more education and easier access to routine pediatric care, so vaccine-preventable disparities in cervical and other HPV-related cancers widened for a period even as national vaccination coverage rose overall — a second illustration that new preventive tools reliably reach resource-rich groups first.

lessons.workedExample: Consider colorectal cancer screening uptake after national guidelines began recommending routine colonoscopy. A behavioral model predicts uptake should rise roughly in step with public awareness, closing existing gaps as information spreads equally. Fundamental cause theory predicts the opposite pattern and is the one actually observed in US data: higher-SES groups, with better insurance coverage, more flexible work schedules to take a day off, and stronger patient-provider relationships, adopted screening first and fastest, while lower-SES groups lagged — so colorectal cancer mortality disparities by education and income widened for a period even as overall screening rates and overall mortality improved nationally.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use fundamental cause theory to test whether a student's intervention will survive contact with reality. A project that eliminates one risk factor (say, secondhand smoke exposure) and claims this will close a health disparity is vulnerable to the question: what happens to the disparity once this specific mechanism is gone — does the resource gap simply find a new pathway? A student who can name the next likely mechanism, or propose intervening on the resource gap itself rather than one symptom, demonstrates they understand disparities as structurally reproduced rather than as one fixable behavior.

questions.prompt: According to Link and Phelan's 1995 fundamental cause theory, why does eliminating one specific disease risk factor typically fail to close the SES-health gap?

options.text: Because SES groups have genetically different susceptibility to disease
Because higher-SES groups redeploy their flexible resources toward whatever risk becomes newly relevant
Because public health campaigns are legally required to target only high-SES groups first
Because lower-SES groups experience no change in disease risk over time
Because fundamental cause theory only applies to infectious disease, not chronic disease

explanations.a: Fundamental cause theory is a social, not genetic, explanation — it locates the mechanism in resource access, not biology.
explanations.b: Correct: money, knowledge, power, prestige, and connections are flexible resources that migrate to whatever mechanism currently drives disease, reproducing the gap under a new guise.
explanations.c: No such legal targeting requirement exists; the pattern arises from unequal resource access, not policy design.
explanations.d: Lower-SES groups' risk does change, often improving in absolute terms — the theory concerns the persistence of the relative gap, not stagnation.
explanations.e: The theory's central claim is that it applies across historical shifts from infectious to chronic disease dominance, which is why it predicts persistence rather than a one-time association.

questions.prompt: Order the sequence fundamental cause theory predicts when a new health-protective technology or information becomes available.

items.text: A new risk-reducing technology, treatment, or information becomes available
Higher-SES groups adopt it first using money, knowledge, and flexible time
The disparity in this specific outcome widens even as overall population rates improve
Lower-SES groups eventually gain access, and the gap shifts to the next available mechanism

questions.explanation: Fundamental cause theory predicts uneven early adoption by resource-rich groups, a temporary widening of the disparity, and eventual migration of the gap to whatever mechanism becomes newly relevant, rather than a one-time closure.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its role in fundamental cause theory.

right.text: Money, knowledge, power, prestige, and social connections that can be redeployed to any risk
SES affects health through many mechanisms simultaneously, not one single risk factor
The SES-health association persists even as the dominant disease mechanism changes historically
Interventions must eliminate all four resources simultaneously to have any effect

questions.explanation: Link and Phelan's four defining features are flexible resources, multiple simultaneous pathways, resource use after disease onset, and persistence of the association across historical shifts in disease mechanism; r4 is not one of these features.

lessons.label: Measuring Disparities

sections.heading: Absolute versus relative gaps
sections.body: The simplest way to quantify a disparity is an absolute gap — the arithmetic difference between two group rates, in the same units as the outcome (percentage points, deaths per 100,000). The relative gap is the ratio of the two rates instead. These can tell very different stories about the same data. If disease A falls from 40% to 20% in a high-SES group and from 80% to 60% in a low-SES group, the absolute gap stays constant at 40 points, but the relative gap rises from 2.0 to 3.0 — the low-SES group's rate is now three times the high-SES group's, rather than twice it, even though the point gap hasn't moved. Reporting only one measure can make a program look like it is closing disparities (absolute gap flat or shrinking) while the other measure says it is widening them (relative gap growing), which is exactly the pattern epidemiologists see repeatedly as overall disease rates decline.

sections.heading: Whole-distribution measures: SII, RII, and the concentration index
sections.body: Comparing only the top and bottom groups wastes information and is sensitive to how the groups are cut. The slope index of inequality (SII) instead regresses the health outcome against a cumulative ranking of the entire population by socioeconomic position (e.g., every person is ranked 0 to 1 by income percentile), producing an absolute measure of the gradient's steepness across the whole distribution, not just the extremes. The relative index of inequality (RII) is the SII divided by the population mean, giving a relative version comparable across outcomes with different baseline rates. The concentration index, widely used in WHO health-equity monitoring, is built from a concentration curve — cumulative share of the health variable plotted against cumulative share of the population ranked by SES — and ranges from -1 to 1, with 0 indicating no socioeconomic gradient at all.

sections.heading: The reference group problem
sections.body: Every disparity measure requires choosing a comparison point: the population average, the best-off subgroup, or a fixed historical baseline. Comparing every group to the single best-off subgroup (as US Healthy People targets often do) tends to produce larger, more alarming gaps than comparing each group to the population mean, because the best-off group is, by definition, an extreme rather than typical value. For example, a state with an infant mortality rate of 6 per 1,000 births looks only modestly above a national average of 5.4 per 1,000, but about 71% worse than the single best-performing state's rate of 3.5 per 1,000 — the same underlying rate, reported against two different reference points, yields two very different headlines.

lessons.workedExample: A county's infant mortality rate falls from 10 to 5 per 1,000 births in its wealthiest quintile and from 20 to 12 per 1,000 in its poorest quintile over a decade. The absolute gap shrinks from 10 to 7 per 1,000 — a real improvement by that measure. But the relative gap rises from 2.0 (20/10) to 2.4 (12/5) — the poorest quintile's rate is now proportionally further from the wealthiest than before. A press release citing only the absolute gap would claim progress on equity; a health department computing the relative index of inequality across all five quintiles, not just the extremes, would flag that the underlying gradient steepened even as every group's raw rate improved.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student reports both absolute and relative measures and can explain why they diverge, because citing a single favorable number is the most common way disparities projects overstate progress. A student who shows only that a gap shrank in percentage points, without checking the ratio, has not actually established that equity improved — the tell of rigor is recomputing both directions and explaining the divergence rather than picking whichever number supports the desired conclusion.

questions.prompt: A disease's absolute gap between two groups shrinks over ten years while the relative gap (ratio) grows over the same period. What pattern in the underlying rates produces this?

options.text: The higher-rate group's absolute drop was larger than the lower-rate group's, narrowing the point gap, while its proportional decline was smaller, widening the ratio between them
Both group rates rose by the same percentage points
The two group rates became numerically identical
This combination of trends is mathematically impossible

explanations.a: Correct: the higher-rate (disadvantaged) group's absolute drop is larger than the lower-rate group's, which narrows the point gap, while its proportional decline is smaller than the lower-rate group's, which widens the ratio between them — exactly the pattern in the worked example above, where the poorest quintile fell 20 to 12 (a bigger point drop but a smaller percentage drop) and the wealthiest fell 10 to 5.
explanations.b: Rising rates in both groups by the same amount would keep the absolute gap constant, not shrinking, and would not necessarily change the ratio in this direction.
explanations.c: Identical rates would produce a relative gap of 1.0 and an absolute gap of 0, not a growing relative gap.
explanations.d: This divergence is a well-documented, mathematically ordinary pattern seen whenever overall disease rates decline across groups with different baselines.

questions.prompt: Why do epidemiologists prefer the slope index of inequality (SII) over a simple top-versus-bottom group comparison?

options.text: SII uses the entire population's ranked distribution, not just two extreme groups, and is less sensitive to how groups are cut
SII does not require any socioeconomic ranking data at all
SII is always numerically identical to the relative gap
SII can only be computed for exactly two groups

explanations.a: Correct: SII regresses the outcome against the full cumulative socioeconomic ranking, capturing the whole gradient rather than only the extremes and their arbitrary cutpoints.
explanations.b: SII is built directly from a socioeconomic ranking of the population, so it requires exactly that kind of data.
explanations.c: SII is an absolute measure; the relative index of inequality (RII) is its relative counterpart, and the two are generally not numerically identical.
explanations.d: SII's advantage is precisely that it works across the full distribution, not just two groups.

questions.prompt: Match each disparity measure to its description.

right.text: Arithmetic difference between two group rates, same units as the outcome
Ratio of two group rates
Built from a curve of cumulative health share against cumulative population share ranked by SES; ranges -1 to 1

questions.explanation: Absolute and relative gaps are the two simplest two-group measures; the concentration index generalizes this to the whole ranked population using a Lorenz-like curve.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to compute a slope index of inequality (SII) for a health outcome across an entire population.

items.text: Rank every individual in the population by socioeconomic position, from lowest to highest
Convert each person's rank into a cumulative population share (0 to 1)
Regress the health outcome against this cumulative rank across the whole population
Read the regression slope as the absolute gradient from the most to least disadvantaged

questions.explanation: SII requires first ranking and rescaling the whole population by SES before regressing the outcome against that ranking, so the resulting slope reflects the full distribution rather than two arbitrary groups.

lessons.label: Structural and Life-Course Determinants

sections.heading: Redlining and the HOLC maps
sections.body: In the 1930s, the federal Home Owners' Loan Corporation (HOLC) produced 'residential security' maps for major US cities, grading neighborhoods from A (green, 'best') down to D (red, 'hazardous') to guide mortgage lending. Grade D neighborhoods were overwhelmingly ones with Black and immigrant residents, regardless of the actual condition of housing stock or residents' income; the practice became known as redlining. Banks and the Federal Housing Administration used these grades for decades to deny mortgages and investment in redlined areas, which locked residents out of homeownership-based wealth building for generations and starved those neighborhoods of infrastructure investment. Studies using the original HOLC maps against present-day health data find that formerly redlined neighborhoods still show measurably worse outcomes today — higher rates of asthma emergency visits, hypertension, and elevated summer heat exposure from fewer trees and more paved surface — an eighty-plus-year-old administrative decision still legible in current health surveillance data.

sections.heading: Weathering: cumulative wear from chronic adversity
sections.body: Arline Geronimus proposed the weathering hypothesis in 1992: chronic exposure to social and economic adversity, including discrimination, produces cumulative physiological wear that accelerates biological aging, independent of any single acute stressor. Evidence includes elevated allostatic load — a composite biomarker score built from measures such as cortisol, blood pressure, waist-to-hip ratio, and cholesterol that together index cumulative stress-system strain — among Black Americans at a given age compared to white Americans; Geronimus's later work also found Black women with shorter telomere length than white women at the same age, a cellular marker consistent with faster biological aging. A documented crossover in birth outcomes adds a second line of evidence: adverse outcomes for Black mothers do not improve with maternal age the way they do for white mothers, and can worsen — the opposite of the typical pattern where older, more established mothers fare better.

sections.heading: Life-course models and Krieger's ecosocial embodiment
sections.body: Epidemiologists distinguish two life-course models of how early exposures produce later disease: the critical-period model, where exposure during a specific developmental window (e.g., prenatal) has lasting effects regardless of what happens afterward, versus the accumulation model, where each exposure across life adds independently to risk. Nancy Krieger's ecosocial theory, developed from the mid-1990s onward, frames the unifying mechanism as embodiment: the idea that people literally, biologically incorporate the material and social conditions of their environment across the life course and across generations, integrating economic, political, and discriminatory exposures into a single framework rather than treating societal, community, and individual levels as separate.

lessons.workedExample: A research team overlays a city's original 1930s HOLC map with a current CDC PLACES dataset on adult asthma prevalence by census tract.
