Crucially, the Levin formula only produces a meaningful PAF if the RR plugged in reflects a genuinely causal, unconfounded effect — if unmeasured confounding inflates the RR, the resulting PAF overstates how much disease elimination of the exposure would actually prevent, so a defensible PAF claim requires defending the causal RR estimate, not just the arithmetic.

sections.heading: Prevented fractions and population impact numbers
sections.body: For protective exposures — vaccination, seatbelts, statins — the mirror-image metric is the prevented fraction: the share of cases that did NOT occur among the exposed (or population) because the protective factor was present, calculated the same way but with RR < 1 and interpreted as cases averted rather than cases caused. Multiplying PAF or prevented fraction by the total case count converts a fraction into a population impact number — an estimate like 'roughly 480,000 U.S. deaths per year are attributable to cigarette smoking' (a CDC estimate) — the form health agencies actually use to argue for or defend an intervention's real-world reach.

lessons.workedExample: Historical case-control data on smoking and lung cancer gave an RR near 20 for smokers versus nonsmokers, with smoking prevalence around p=0.20 in the population. PAF = 0.20(20-1) / [0.20(19)+1] = 3.8/4.8 ≈ 0.79, meaning about 79% of lung cancer cases in that population are attributable to smoking — close to the roughly 80-90% figure health agencies commonly cite. Notice what drives that number: if prevalence fell to p=0.05 with RR unchanged, PAF drops to 0.95/1.95 ≈ 49%, dropping by nearly 40% in relative terms, even though smoking is exactly as dangerous to each smoker as before. The burden estimate tracks prevalence as much as toxicity.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe PAF because it exposes a common student error: assuming the exposure with the highest RR is automatically the best public-health target. A judge will ask a student defending an intervention to state the exposure prevalence they used, not just the RR, and to show the Levin formula rather than quoting a borrowed PAF from a different population — PAF is not a fixed property of an exposure, it moves whenever prevalence moves.

questions.prompt: Exposure A has RR=30 and 1% prevalence. Exposure B has RR=1.8 and 55% prevalence. Which statement is most likely true?

options.text: Exposure A must have the larger PAF because its RR is much higher
Exposure B could have the larger PAF despite its much lower RR
PAF cannot be compared between exposures with different RRs
Both exposures have identical PAF since RR times prevalence is undefined

explanations.a: PAF depends on prevalence as well as RR; a rare exposure with a huge RR can still yield a small population fraction.
explanations.b: Correct: PAF = p(RR-1)/[p(RR-1)+1]. Plugging in gives A ≈ 0.225 and B ≈ 0.306, so the common, weaker exposure has the larger population impact.
explanations.c: PAF is directly comparable across exposures using the same Levin formula; the comparison is exactly what the formula is for.
explanations.d: RR and prevalence combine multiplicatively inside a defined formula, not into an undefined quantity.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to compute a population attributable fraction using Levin's formula.

items.text: Estimate the relative risk (RR) linking exposure to disease
Estimate the exposure prevalence (p) in the target population
Compute p(RR-1) using those two values
Divide p(RR-1) by [p(RR-1) + 1] to get PAF

questions.explanation: Levin's formula needs both inputs (RR and prevalence) before the algebra; the numerator is built first, then normalized by the denominator to yield a fraction between 0 and 1.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

right.text: Absolute incidence difference between exposed and unexposed groups
Share of all population cases removable by eliminating a causal exposure
Share of cases avoided because a protective exposure was present

questions.explanation: AR is an absolute rate difference confined to the exposed group; PAF scales that idea to the whole population for harmful exposures; prevented fraction is the analogous quantity for protective ones.

questions.prompt: A city eliminates a low-RR but very common environmental exposure and case counts drop by half. This is best explained by:

options.text: A calculation error, since low RR exposures cannot meaningfully affect population burden
High prevalence inflating the PAF despite the modest RR
The exposure must have actually had RR near 20, not a low value
PAF only applies to occupational exposures, so this scenario is invalid

explanations.a: Low RR does not preclude large population impact; prevalence is an equal partner in the PAF formula.
explanations.b: Correct: PAF rises with prevalence even at modest RR, exactly the mechanism illustrated by the smoking worked example when prevalence changed.
explanations.c: The scenario is consistent with a modest RR combined with high prevalence; inferring a higher RR is unnecessary and unsupported.
explanations.d: PAF applies to any exposure-disease pair with an estimable RR and prevalence, not a restricted category.

lessons.label: Summary Measures of Population Health

sections.heading: Weighting deaths by how early they occur
sections.body: A death count alone treats a death at 90 the same as a death at 20, which is misleading when comparing causes: heart disease kills mostly older people while injury and overdose kill disproportionately young ones. Years of potential life lost (YPLL) fixes an endpoint — commonly age 75 — and sums (endpoint minus age at death) across every death from a cause. A death at 20 contributes 55 YPLL; a death at 70 contributes only 5. The CDC has long used YPLL-to-75 to argue that unintentional injury and drug overdose deserve more public-health attention than raw mortality rankings suggest, since both cluster in younger age groups.

sections.heading: DALYs: folding disability into the same currency as death
sections.body: The disability-adjusted life year (DALY), developed for the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study led by Christopher Murray and Alan Lopez for the WHO and World Bank starting in the early 1990s, extends the YPLL logic to nonfatal illness. DALY = YLL + YLD: years of life lost to premature death, plus years lived with disability. In the incidence-based approach GBD uses, YLD = (number of incident cases) x (a disability weight between 0, perfect health, and 1, equivalent to death) x (average duration of the case, in years); equivalently, a prevalence-based approach multiplies prevalent cases by the disability weight alone, since prevalence already folds in duration. Disability weights were derived from large population surveys asking respondents to compare pairs of health states — the GBD 2010 revision alone drew on roughly 30,000 respondents across several countries — turning subjective severity judgments into a number that can be added to mortality data.

sections.heading: QALYs, HALE, and the value judgments underneath
sections.body: The quality-adjusted life year (QALY) runs the same idea in reverse for cost-effectiveness analysis: it counts years GAINED at a given quality-of-life weight (1 = full health) rather than years lost, and underlies thresholds like the UK's NICE guideline of roughly £20,000-30,000 per QALY gained. The original 1990s GBD DALY also applied age-weighting (valuing a year of life lived in young adulthood more than one in infancy or old age) and time discounting (typically 3% per year, shrinking the value of years far in the future or past); both were dropped in the GBD 2010 revision after criticism that they were normative choices dressed up as neutral math — Sudhir Anand and Kara Hanson's influential 1997 critique argued these were ethical value judgments smuggled into a supposedly objective metric, a critique the GBD collaboration eventually accepted by removing both weightings. In the GBD 2019 rankings, neonatal disorders is the single leading cause of DALYs worldwide, ahead of ischemic heart disease and stroke — even though ischemic heart disease remains the leading cause of deaths in absolute terms — illustrating how a burden ranking built this way, with its age-at-death weighting, can differ from a ranking built on death counts alone: deaths in newborns each carry far more lost years than deaths at the older ages typical of heart disease. HALE (health-adjusted life expectancy), introduced by WHO around 2000, compresses mortality and morbidity into one life-expectancy-style number for cross-country comparison.

lessons.workedExample: A disease causes 100 deaths at an average age of 40, against a standard life expectancy of 80 — YLL = 100 x (80-40) = 4,000 years. The same disease produces 1,000 new (incident) cases of a chronic complication rated at disability weight 0.2, each lasting an average of 5 years — using the incidence-based YLD formula, YLD = 1,000 x 0.2 x 5 = 1,000 years. Total DALY burden = YLL + YLD = 5,000. Notice that YLL dominates here (4,000 of 5,000); a disease that instead killed few people but disabled many for decades — like some chronic mental illness — could invert that ratio, which is exactly why GBD reports both components separately, not just the DALY total.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can distinguish burden (DALYs, which count years LOST and are used to rank diseases for research and funding priority) from benefit (QALYs, which count years GAINED and are used to judge whether a specific intervention is worth its cost), and whether they can name at least one buried value judgment — a disability weight, an age-weight, a discount rate — that makes DALY totals a policy choice, not a raw fact.

questions.prompt: Two diseases cause identical numbers of deaths at identical ages. Disease X leaves many survivors with severe long-term disability; Disease Y leaves almost none. Which statement is correct?

options.text: X and Y have identical DALY burdens because YLL is the same for both
X has a higher DALY burden than Y, driven by a larger YLD component
Y has a higher DALY burden because it has fewer confounding disability weights
DALYs cannot be computed unless disability duration is infinite

explanations.a: YLL is identical, but DALY = YLL + YLD, and X's larger disabled survivor population adds substantial YLD that Y lacks.
explanations.b: Correct: with YLL held equal, the disease producing more long-term disability adds more YLD, raising its total DALY burden above Y's.
explanations.c: Fewer disability weights does not raise burden; Y's smaller YLD component lowers, not raises, its DALY total relative to X.
explanations.d: YLD is computed from a specific case count, disability weight, and duration, not from infinite duration.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to compute a DALY total for a disease in a population, using the incidence-based approach.

items.text: Sum (standard life expectancy minus age at death) across all deaths to get YLL
Identify incident nonfatal cases and their associated disability weight
Multiply incident cases by disability weight and average duration to get YLD
Add YLL and YLD to obtain total DALYs

questions.explanation: YLL and YLD are computed independently from mortality and morbidity data respectively, and only combined into the single DALY figure at the final step.

questions.prompt: Match each summary measure to what it is used for.

right.text: Weighting deaths by age to highlight premature mortality causes
Ranking disease burden by combining lost years and disabled years
Judging whether a specific intervention's benefit is worth its cost
A single cross-country life-expectancy-style summary of population health

questions.explanation: YPLL and DALY both prioritize causes of ill health at the population level; QALY evaluates interventions economically; HALE compresses mortality and morbidity into one comparable expectancy figure.

lessons.label: Evaluating Interventions Without Randomization: Interrupted Time Series

sections.heading: Modeling a break in the trend, not just a before/after average
sections.body: Many public-health policies — smoking bans, soda taxes, speed limits — cannot ethically or practically be randomized, but they still turn on at a known date, which an interrupted time-series (ITS) design exploits. Rather than comparing one before-average to one after-average (which ignores any trend already underway), ITS fits a segmented regression across the whole series: outcome = b0 + b1(time) + b2(intervention indicator) + b3(time since intervention). Here b1 is the pre-existing secular trend, b2 is the immediate jump or drop in level right at the intervention, and b3 is the change in slope afterward — did the trend itself bend, not just the level. Separating these three terms is what lets ITS claim an effect beyond whatever was already happening.

sections.heading: Two real policy evaluations
sections.body: Scotland's smoke-free legislation took effect in March 2006; Pell et al. (2008, New England Journal of Medicine) applied an interrupted-time-series-style analysis to hospital admissions for acute coronary syndrome and found a 17% relative decline in the year after the ban, over and above the modest secular downward trend already present before it. Mexico's 2014 tax on sugar-sweetened beverages was evaluated by Colchero et al. (2016, BMJ) using household purchase data: taxed-drink purchases fell about 6% on average across the tax's first year, rising to roughly 12% by December of that same first year, relative to the projected pre-tax trend. Berkeley, California's 2015 soda tax showed a similar pattern in Falbe et al. (2016, American Journal of Public Health), with sugar-sweetened beverage consumption in lower-income neighborhoods dropping roughly 21% post-tax.

sections.heading: What can fool an ITS
sections.body: Two threats dominate. Co-interventions are other changes that land near the same date — a mass-media campaign, a recession, an unrelated policy — and get credited to the intervention being studied; Scotland's ban, for instance, coincided with a period of generally declining smoking prevalence that the regression's pre-period trend term is designed to net out, but only if enough pre-period points exist to estimate that trend reliably (methodologists like Wagner et al., 2002, generally recommend at least eight to twelve points per segment). Regression to the mean is the second threat: if a policy is enacted specifically because an outcome had just spiked, some of the subsequent drop would have happened anyway as the outcome reverted toward its usual level, with or without the policy.

lessons.workedExample: Before Scotland's March 2006 smoking ban, acute coronary syndrome admissions were declining at a steady secular rate (b1 slope, negative but small) for several prior years. Fitting the segmented model to the extended series, the fitted b2 term captures an abrupt level drop right at the March 2006 boundary and the model's projected 'no-ban' trend line — simply extending the pre-ban slope forward — predicts noticeably more admissions than were actually observed a year later. The gap between that counterfactual projection and the observed count is where the reported 17% relative reduction comes from; it is not simply comparing the average admission rate in 2005 to the average in 2007.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe ITS because students often collapse it into a simple before/after comparison, which cannot distinguish a real policy effect from a trend that was already declining. A strong answer names the level-change term (b2) and slope-change term (b3) separately, states how many pre-period points were used to estimate the counterfactual trend, and can name at least one plausible co-intervention that might explain part of the observed change instead of the policy itself.

questions.prompt: In the segmented regression Y = b0 + b1(time) + b2(intervention) + b3(time-after), which coefficient captures whether the RATE of change itself was altered by the policy, as opposed to a one-time jump?

options.text: b1, the pre-intervention trend
b2, the intervention indicator
b3, the change in slope after intervention
b0, the intercept

explanations.a: b1 describes the trend that already existed before the intervention, not any change caused by it.
explanations.b: b2 captures an immediate level shift right at the intervention point, not an ongoing change in the trend's rate.
explanations.c: Correct: b3 is added specifically to let the slope bend after the intervention, separate from any immediate level jump.
explanations.d: b0 is simply the regression intercept and carries no information about a policy-driven change.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in building and interpreting an interrupted time-series analysis of a policy.

items.text: Collect a time series with enough pre-intervention points to estimate the secular trend
Fit the segmented regression with level and slope terms at the known intervention date
Project the pre-intervention trend forward as the no-policy counterfactual
Compare observed post-intervention values to the counterfactual, checking for plausible co-interventions

questions.explanation: The counterfactual can only be projected after the trend is estimated from sufficient pre-period data, and the resulting gap is only credited to the policy once other explanations are ruled out.

questions.prompt: Match each ITS concept to its description.

right.text: A different event near the same date that could explain part of the observed change
An outcome reverting toward its usual value after being unusually high when the policy began
An abrupt shift in the outcome right at the intervention point
A change in the outcome's ongoing rate of change after the intervention

questions.explanation: Co-interventions and regression to the mean are threats to validity that mimic a policy effect; level and slope changes are the two things the regression itself is built to separate.

lessons.label: Difference-in-Differences and Natural Experiments

sections.heading: Subtracting away the trend you'd have seen anyway
sections.body: An interrupted time series has no comparison group, so any trend affecting everyone at once — a recession, a national campaign — can be mistaken for a policy's effect. Difference-in-differences (DiD) fixes this by adding an untreated comparison group and taking two differences: the before-after change in the treated group, minus the before-after change in the comparison group. Whatever changed for everyone cancels out in the subtraction, leaving (in principle) just the treatment's effect. The entire design rests on the parallel trends assumption: absent the treatment, the treated group would have moved in the same direction and by the same amount as the comparison group. That assumption cannot be tested in the post-treatment period, but it can be supported by showing the two groups tracked each other closely in the years before treatment. The standard robustness check is the placebo, or event-study, test: re-estimate the model as if the treatment had occurred at each pre-treatment period in turn, and confirm none of those false 'effects' differs significantly from zero — a significant pre-trend break signals that parallel trends is unlikely to hold and that the post-treatment estimate is suspect.

sections.heading: Synthetic control when there's no natural comparison group
sections.body: Sometimes only one unit is treated and no single untreated unit is a convincing match. Abadie and Gardeazabal (2003) introduced the synthetic control method for exactly this case, and Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller (2010) applied it to California's Proposition 99, a 1988 tobacco tax and control law: instead of picking one comparison state, they built a weighted combination of other states, chosen so the resulting 'synthetic California' matched California's actual pre-1988 cigarette sales trajectory as closely as possible. After 1988, California's real per-capita cigarette sales fell increasingly below the synthetic control's trajectory, opening a gap of roughly 20-30 packs per capita by the late 1990s, attributed to Prop 99.

sections.heading: Natural experiments: policy variation as if randomly assigned
sections.body: A natural experiment exploits variation that policy or circumstance created for reasons unrelated to the outcome being studied, letting researchers treat it as quasi-random. State-by-state variation in whether and when states expanded Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act after 2014 has been used this way, with DiD comparisons between expansion and non-expansion states estimating effects on insurance coverage, access to care, and mortality. Card and Krueger's 1994 minimum-wage study, comparing fast-food employment in New Jersey (which raised its minimum wage) to neighboring Pennsylvania (which didn't), is the methodological template most often cited outside health economics for the same DiD logic applied to a policy border.

lessons.workedExample: A state taxes cigarettes; smoking prevalence there falls from 25% to 18% (a 7-point drop) over the following two years. A neighboring, untaxed state's prevalence falls from 24% to 22% over the same period (a 2-point drop) — reflecting a broader secular decline in smoking unrelated to either state's tax policy. DiD = (-7) - (-2) = -5 percentage points, the portion of the treated state's decline attributable to the tax itself once the shared secular trend is subtracted out. If the two states' prevalence had instead been diverging for years before the tax, that pre-trend would undercut the parallel trends assumption and the -5 point estimate could not be trusted.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe DiD because students often report only the treated group's before-after change and skip the comparison group entirely, which cannot distinguish a policy effect from a trend everyone was already on. A strong defense states the parallel trends assumption explicitly, shows pre-treatment trend lines for both groups as evidence, and — for a single treated unit — explains why a synthetic control built from multiple donor units is preferred over picking one ad hoc comparison.

questions.prompt: Why is the parallel trends assumption central to difference-in-differences, and how would you support it?

options.text: It guarantees causality by definition and needs no supporting evidence
It is untestable in the post period but supportable by showing similar pre-treatment trends in both groups
It only matters when sample sizes are small
It requires the two groups to have identical outcome levels before treatment

explanations.a: No assumption guarantees causality automatically; parallel trends is a strong, unverifiable-in-the-future assumption that still needs supporting evidence.
explanations.b: Correct: the counterfactual post-treatment path of the treated group cannot be observed, so researchers instead show the treated and comparison groups moved together before treatment as indirect support.
explanations.c: Parallel trends matters at any sample size; it is about the comparability of trajectories, not statistical power.
explanations.d: DiD only requires similar TRENDS (rate of change) before treatment, not identical starting LEVELS — a constant gap in levels is fine since the design differences it away.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in building a synthetic control estimate for a single treated unit.

items.text: Assemble a pool of untreated donor units with relevant pre-treatment data
Choose weights on the donor units that best match the treated unit's pre-treatment trajectory
Construct the synthetic control as that weighted combination going forward in time
Compare the treated unit's post-treatment path to the synthetic control's path

questions.explanation: The donor pool and matching weights must be fixed using only pre-treatment data before the synthetic trajectory can be extended forward and compared to what actually happened.

questions.prompt: Match each method or example to what it illustrates.

right.text: Subtracting a comparison group's change from a treated group's change
A weighted combination of untreated units used when no single comparison unit fits
The tobacco-control policy evaluated by Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller (2010)
A minimum-wage natural experiment comparing neighboring states

questions.explanation: DiD and synthetic control are the general methods; Prop 99 and the New Jersey-Pennsylvania minimum wage study are the specific applications each is best known for.

lessons.label: Community and Stepped-Wedge Trials

sections.heading: Randomizing places instead of people
sections.body: Some interventions cannot be assigned to individuals at all — a whole town either has fluoridated water or it doesn't — and others would leak across arms if assigned individually, since people in the same clinic or school talk to each other and share norms (contamination). Cluster, or community-randomized, trials solve both problems by randomizing whole groups: towns, clinics, schools. Grand Rapids, Michigan became the first city in the world to fluoridate its public water supply, in January 1945, with nearby Muskegon serving as an unfluoridated comparison city; follow-up studies over the following decade found dental caries rates among children born after fluoridation began fell by roughly 60% relative to the unfluoridated comparison population — the trial that established water fluoridation as public-health policy.

sections.heading: A later, more rigorous community trial
sections.body: The Community Intervention Trial for Smoking Cessation (COMMIT), funded by the National Cancer Institute and run from 1988 to 1993, randomized 11 matched pairs of communities across the United States and Canada, one member of each pair to an intensive multi-channel smoking-cessation intervention and the other to usual care. The trial found a meaningful effect among light-to-moderate smokers but no significant effect on heavy smokers, a result that reshaped how cessation programs targeted their resources afterward. Both trials illustrate the tradeoff at the heart of community-randomized designs: they answer a policy-relevant question no individual-level trial could, at the cost of a much smaller number of independently randomized units.

sections.heading: Design effect, and the stepped-wedge alternative
sections.body: People within the same cluster tend to resemble each other — shared water supply, shared social norms — which is captured by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), typically small (0.01-0.05) in community trials but still consequential. This inflates required sample size by the design effect, 1 + (m-1) x ICC, where m is the average cluster size; a cluster trial needs that many more total individuals than an individually randomized trial of the same statistical power. When withholding a believed-beneficial intervention from any cluster is unethical, or rollout must be staggered for logistical reasons, the stepped-wedge design offers an alternative: every cluster eventually receives the intervention, but in a randomized order over sequential time steps, so each cluster serves as its own control before its crossover and as a comparison for clusters not yet switched. This design forces a different analysis method than a parallel-arm cluster trial: because every cluster contributes both untreated and treated periods, the standard approach uses mixed-effects or generalized estimating equation (GEE) models that account simultaneously for within-cluster correlation and for any underlying calendar-time trend, so a real intervention effect isn't confused with secular change happening across all clusters as time passes.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose an individually randomized trial of a school hand-hygiene program would need 200 students per arm for adequate power. Randomizing by classroom instead, with average cluster size m=50 students and ICC=0.02, gives a design effect of 1 + (50-1)(0.02) = 1 + 0.98 = 1.98. The cluster trial therefore needs roughly 200 x 1.98 ≈ 396 students per arm — nearly double — which at 50 students per classroom works out to about 8 classrooms per arm. Ignoring the design effect and simply dividing 200 by 50 to get 4 classrooms would leave the trial badly underpowered.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this topic because students often treat a cluster trial's participant count as if it came from an individually randomized study, ignoring that clustered individuals are not statistically independent. A strong answer names the ICC, computes or at least states the design effect formula, and can explain why a stepped-wedge design might be chosen over a parallel-arm cluster trial when it is unethical or impractical to permanently withhold the intervention from any site.

questions.prompt: Why does an individually randomized sample-size calculation understate the number of participants needed for a cluster-randomized trial?

options.text: Because clusters always have higher dropout rates than individuals
Because individuals within the same cluster are correlated, reducing the effective sample size, which the design effect corrects for
Because cluster trials always test weaker interventions
Because randomization is impossible at the cluster level

explanations.a: Dropout is a separate, real concern in trial design but is not the reason cluster and individual sample-size formulas differ.
explanations.b: Correct: shared cluster-level factors correlate individuals' outcomes (measured by the ICC), so each additional person adds less new information than in an individually randomized trial, requiring the design-effect inflation.
explanations.c: Intervention strength is unrelated to why the sample-size formula differs between individual and cluster randomization.
explanations.d: Cluster-level randomization is entirely feasible and is exactly what community trials like Grand Rapids-Muskegon and COMMIT used.

questions.prompt: Order the rollout logic of a stepped-wedge trial from design to completion.

items.text: Enroll all clusters while none yet receive the intervention
Randomly assign each cluster a time step at which it will cross over
Roll the intervention out to one group of clusters per step, in the assigned random order
Continue until every cluster has received the intervention
Analyze outcomes using each cluster's own pre-crossover period as within-cluster control data

questions.explanation: Stepped-wedge trials start with a common untreated baseline, roll out in a randomized staggered order, and finish with every cluster treated, which is what lets each cluster contribute both control and treated data.

questions.prompt: Match each term or trial to its description.

right.text: Measures how similar individuals within the same cluster tend to be
The sample-size inflation factor, 1 + (m-1) x ICC, needed for cluster designs
The first water fluoridation trial, comparing a fluoridated city to an unfluoridated one
An 11-matched-pair community trial of a smoking-cessation program

questions.explanation: ICC quantifies within-cluster similarity, the design effect converts that into a required sample-size multiplier, and the two named trials are the landmark examples of community-level randomization.

lessons.label: Modern Surveillance Analytics

sections.heading: Automated aberration detection
sections.body: Modern surveillance systems don't wait for a human to eyeball a graph; they run statistical algorithms continuously against incoming case counts and flag departures from an expected baseline. CUSUM (cumulative sum) charts, adapted from industrial quality control (Page, 1954), sum small deviations from baseline over successive time points, which makes them sensitive to a sustained shift that is too small to trigger a single-day alarm but adds up over days. The Farrington algorithm (Farrington et al., 1996, developed for what is now the UK Health Security Agency) instead fits a quasi-Poisson regression to several years of historical baseline data for the same time of year, applies a 2/3 power transformation to stabilize variance, and generates an upper alert threshold; it remains a backbone of European infectious-disease surveillance. The CDC's Early Aberration Reporting System (EARS), built after the 2001 anthrax attacks for syndromic surveillance, uses simpler moving-average-based methods (its C1, C2, C3 algorithms) designed to work even without much historical baseline data — useful for a brand-new data stream.

sections.heading: Nowcasting reporting delays
sections.body: Raw daily case or death counts systematically undercount the most recent days, because reports take time to reach a central database — a lag that makes a real, ongoing rise look like a decline if read naively. Nowcasting corrects for this by modeling the historical pattern of how each day's eventual total fills in over subsequent days or weeks, then using that pattern to project what the still-incomplete recent counts will eventually reach. The technique became widely visible during the COVID-19 pandemic, when health agencies needed a defensible estimate of the true, most-recent trajectory rather than an artifact of incomplete reporting.

sections.heading: Genomic surveillance and the pitfalls of high-frequency proxies
sections.body: Sequencing pathogen samples lets surveillance track how a pathogen is evolving, not just how much of it is circulating; the UK's COG-UK consortium sequenced a large share of the world's SARS-CoV-2 genomes during 2020-21, feeding open platforms like GISAID and Nextstrain (built by Bedford and Neher) that enabled early detection of variants such as Alpha and Delta. But high-frequency digital signals carry a documented failure mode: Google Flu Trends, launched in 2008 to estimate flu activity from search queries, was shown by Lazer et al. (2014, Science, 'The Parable of Google Flu') to have overestimated flu prevalence by roughly 140% at the peak of the 2012-13 season, partly because Google's own changing search-suggestion algorithm altered the very search behavior the model depended on — a caution that fast proxy signals drift and need continual validation against slower, confirmed case data, not a one-time calibration.

lessons.workedExample: An emergency department's expected daily count of gastrointestinal-illness visits, from several prior years of baseline data, is about 20 visits with day-to-day variation of roughly ±5. On three consecutive days the observed counts are 28, 30, and 32 — each single day is elevated but not wildly outside normal variation on its own. A CUSUM chart accumulates each day's deviation above baseline (roughly +8, +10, +12) rather than resetting after each day; the running total crosses the alert threshold on day three even though no single day would have triggered a simple fixed-threshold alarm, catching the sustained cluster earlier than eyeballing daily counts would.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this topic because a student who says 'we flagged an outbreak when cases exceeded a threshold' hasn't shown they understand that the threshold has to come from a model of expected baseline, including seasonality and trend, not an arbitrary fixed number. A strong answer names a specific algorithm (CUSUM, Farrington, EARS) and, when digital proxy data is involved, cites the Google Flu Trends failure as evidence that fast signals must be validated against confirmed case data rather than trusted at face value.

questions.prompt: Why did Google Flu Trends fail to accurately estimate flu prevalence during the 2012-13 season?

options.text: It used a fixed threshold instead of a modeled seasonal baseline
It relied on search-query patterns that drifted as Google's own search-suggestion algorithm changed, decoupling the signal from true flu activity
It lacked any historical data to compare against
It only tracked genomic sequences, not case counts
It was never validated against any confirmed case data at any point

explanations.a: Google Flu Trends' failure mode was about its input data drifting, not about using a fixed alert threshold like a simple surveillance chart.
explanations.b: Correct: Lazer et al. (2014) documented that changes in Google's own algorithm altered user search behavior, breaking the assumed stable relationship between searches and true flu prevalence, causing roughly 140% overestimation at the 2012-13 peak.
explanations.c: It was trained on historical search and case data; the problem was that the relationship it learned stopped holding, not an absence of historical data.
explanations.d: Google Flu Trends used search-query volume, not genomic sequencing, which is a separate surveillance method.
explanations.e: It was compared against CDC case data, which is precisely how the overestimation was discovered and documented.

questions.prompt: Order the steps a CUSUM-based aberration detector performs to flag a possible outbreak.

items.text: Establish an expected baseline count and its normal variability from historical data
Compute each new day's deviation from that expected baseline
Accumulate deviations across consecutive days rather than resetting daily
Trigger an alert once the cumulative sum crosses a preset threshold

questions.explanation: CUSUM's defining feature is accumulating small deviations over time instead of judging each day in isolation, which is what lets it catch a sustained shift before any single day looks alarming.

questions.prompt: Match each surveillance method or tool to what it does.

right.text: Regression-based baseline modeling with a variance-stabilizing transform, used across European surveillance
Statistically correcting recent counts for reporting-delay undercounting
Open phylogenetic platform for tracking pathogen variant spread
Simpler moving-average detection methods usable without much historical baseline

questions.explanation: Farrington and EARS are both aberration-detection algorithms but differ in how much historical baseline they require; nowcasting and Nextstrain address reporting delay and genomic tracking respectively, distinct problems from case-count aberration detection.

lessons.label: Anatomy of a Public-Health Win: Tobacco Control

sections.heading: The signal: a rising death rate with no obvious cause
sections.body: In the 1930s and 1940s, clinicians in the US and UK noticed lung cancer deaths climbing steeply among men, a disease once rare enough that some doctors had never seen a case. Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill's 1950 British Medical Journal case-control study of London hospital patients found heavy smokers roughly 50 times more likely to have lung cancer than nonsmokers; they then launched the British Doctors Study, a prospective cohort enrolling roughly 40,000 UK physicians beginning in 1951 and following their smoking habits and mortality for decades, which by 1956 confirmed the dose-response relationship in living data. The US Surgeon General's 1964 report, led by Luther Terry, synthesized over 7,000 studies and declared smoking a cause of lung cancer, converting a statistical association into a policy mandate.

sections.heading: The intervention: MPOWER as a coordinated package
sections.body: WHO's 2008 MPOWER framework names six proven levers: Monitor tobacco use, Protect people from smoke, Offer help to quit, Warn about dangers, Enforce ad bans, and Raise taxes. Excise taxes work through price elasticity: a roughly 10% price increase reduces overall consumption by about 4%, with youth uptake even more price-sensitive. Smoke-free indoor air laws produce fast cardiac payoffs — Helena, Montana's 2002 ordinance was followed by a documented drop in acute myocardial infarction admissions during the law's six months in effect, a decline that reversed when a court suspended it (Sargent et al., 2004). Canada became the first country to mandate graphic warning labels in 2000. WHO estimates that MPOWER-style tobacco-control policies implemented worldwide since the framework's 2008 launch have collectively helped avert tens of millions of premature deaths, evidence that the package's effect scales far beyond any single country's rollout.

sections.heading: The outcome: prevalence falls, mortality lags for decades
sections.body: US adult smoking prevalence fell from about 42% in 1965 to roughly 11% by 2021 (CDC), tracking the cumulative rollout of taxes, clean-air laws, and counter-marketing. But lung cancer mortality did not fall in lockstep: because cancer risk depends on decades of cumulative exposure, male lung cancer death rates kept climbing until they peaked around 1990, only then beginning a sustained decline as the cohorts who quit or never started aged into the population. This lag is the central lesson — a successful prevention program shows up in behavior data almost immediately but in mortality data only after a latency of a generation.

lessons.workedExample: A student tracks two curves for US men from 1965 to 2010: CDC smoking prevalence (self-reported, annual) and CDC WONDER lung cancer mortality rate (age-adjusted, annual). Prevalence declines steadily starting in the mid-1960s. Mortality keeps rising for another 25 years, peaking near 1990 at roughly 90 per 100,000, before declining. Plotting both on one time axis and marking the ~20-25 year gap between the prevalence turn and the mortality turn is the single graphic that makes the exposure-to-outcome latency concrete instead of abstract.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this lag because it is the single most common source of a wrong causal claim in a chronic-disease science-fair project: a student who overlays a policy's launch year directly against a mortality curve and expects an immediate bend will either misread a decades-long latency as 'no effect' or, worse, credit a recent policy for a mortality decline that was actually set in motion a generation earlier. A judge who asks 'why does mortality keep rising for 20 years after prevalence starts falling?' is testing whether the student understands induction period, not just correlation.

questions.prompt: US male lung cancer mortality kept rising for roughly two decades after smoking prevalence began its sustained decline in the mid-1960s. Why?

options.text: Because tobacco taxes were not raised until after 1990
Because cancer risk reflects decades of cumulative prior exposure, so mortality lags behind changes in current smoking behavior
Because the Surgeon General's 1964 report was not statistically significant
Because lung cancer surveillance data were not collected before 1990

explanations.a: Taxes are one MPOWER lever among several, but the lag exists regardless of tax timing because it reflects biological latency, not policy sequencing.
explanations.b: Correct: lung cancer in a population reflects cumulative smoking exposure accumulated over decades, so a drop in current smoking rates only shows up in mortality after that latency period.
explanations.c: The 1964 report synthesized thousands of studies and was considered conclusive at the time; statistical significance is not the reason for the mortality lag.
explanations.d: CDC WONDER mortality data extend back well before 1990; the lag is real and appears in the actual data, not a gap in data availability.

questions.prompt: Order the events in the tobacco-control case from earliest surveillance signal to final population-level outcome.

items.text: Doll and Hill's 1950 case-control study links smoking to lung cancer
US Surgeon General's 1964 report declares smoking a cause of lung cancer
MPOWER-style taxes, smoke-free laws, and warning labels roll out
Adult smoking prevalence falls from ~42% to ~11%
Male lung cancer mortality peaks around 1990, then declines

questions.explanation: The surveillance signal (1950 study) preceded the policy mandate (1964 report), which preceded the interventions, which drove the behavior change (prevalence), which only after a latency drove the mortality outcome.

questions.prompt: Match each MPOWER-style intervention to the mechanism by which it reduces smoking.

right.text: Raises the price, reducing consumption via price elasticity of demand
Reduces secondhand exposure and cues to smoke in shared indoor spaces
Increases perceived risk at the point of purchase or use

questions.explanation: Each MPOWER lever targets a different point in the causal chain from availability and cue to perceived risk, which is why the package works better than any single lever alone.

lessons.label: Eliminating Cervical Cancer: Screening Meets Vaccination

sections.heading: Secondary prevention: from Pap smears to HPV DNA testing
sections.body: George Papanicolaou's mid-20th-century cytology smear let clinicians catch precancerous cervical changes before they became invasive cancer, and routine Pap screening drove US cervical cancer mortality down for decades — a textbook secondary-prevention win. But cytology reads a cell's appearance, not its cause, and can miss precancer or trigger unnecessary follow-up. Because more than 90% of cervical cancers are driven by persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), primary HPV DNA testing — detecting the virus itself — now outperforms cytology at finding disease earlier. The US Preventive Services Task Force's 2018 guidelines allow primary HPV testing alone every five years for ages 30-65 as an alternative to Pap smears every three years, reflecting this shift from looking at cells to looking for the cause.

sections.heading: Primary prevention: Australia's vaccination program
sections.body: Gardasil, the first HPV vaccine, was approved in 2006 after clinical trials found it close to 100% effective at preventing persistent infection and precancerous lesions caused by the vaccine-targeted HPV types in women with no prior exposure to those types. Australia became one of the first countries to launch a national, school-based HPV vaccination program, starting with girls in 2007 and extending to boys in 2013, and achieved roughly 80% coverage among eligible girls within a few years of rollout. Brotherton and colleagues (2011) documented a sharp drop in high-grade cervical abnormalities among vaccination-eligible young women within a few years of rollout — an early, direct surveillance signal that the vaccine was working at the population level, not just in trials. Modelling by Hall and colleagues (2019, Lancet Public Health) projected Australia could reduce cervical cancer to below the WHO elimination threshold by around 2028, making it a likely first country to effectively eliminate the disease as a public health problem.

sections.heading: Combining layers: the WHO 90-70-90 targets
sections.body: WHO's 2020 Global Strategy to Accelerate the Elimination of Cervical Cancer sets three targets to be reached by 2030: 90% of girls fully vaccinated against HPV by age 15; 70% of women screened with a high-performance test (such as HPV DNA testing) by age 35 and again by 45; and 90% of women identified with cervical disease receiving treatment. Elimination is defined quantitatively as incidence falling below 4 cases per 100,000 women-years. The 90-70-90 framework is deliberately layered — no single intervention reaches elimination alone, since vaccination protects the unexposed, screening catches infections and lesions already present in unvaccinated or older cohorts, and treatment closes the loop for those who screen positive.

lessons.workedExample: A student compares two hypothetical Australian birth cohorts using published surveillance patterns: women born before 1997, who aged out of the school vaccination program and rely mainly on Pap/HPV screening, versus the first fully vaccination-eligible cohort born around 1997-2000, who received HPV vaccination as adolescents before likely HPV exposure. Following Brotherton et al.'s design, the student would compare rates of high-grade cervical abnormalities (a screening-detected precursor) between the two cohorts at matched ages, expecting the vaccinated cohort's rate to be substantially lower, then note that the observed drop confirms prevention happened before disease could progress, not merely that screening caught more cases.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe whether a student can explain why vaccination and screening are not redundant. A common error is treating HPV vaccination as making screening obsolete, or treating screening as sufficient on its own; the tell of real understanding is the layered-defense argument — vaccination prevents infection in people not yet exposed, while screening remains essential for anyone vaccinated after sexual debut, unvaccinated, or infected with a HPV type outside vaccine coverage, and treatment protects those who screen positive regardless of vaccination status.

questions.prompt: Why does WHO's elimination strategy require both HPV vaccination and screening targets rather than vaccination alone?

options.text: Because vaccination protects future infections but does not treat or detect existing infections and precancerous lesions in already-exposed or unvaccinated women
Because the HPV vaccine has been shown to be ineffective in real-world settings
Because screening is cheaper than vaccination and was kept only for budget reasons
Because WHO targets are set independently of each other with no epidemiological rationale

explanations.a: Correct: vaccination is primary prevention for the not-yet-exposed, while screening (secondary prevention) is needed to catch disease already present in unvaccinated, older, or already-exposed populations.
explanations.b: Brotherton et al. (2011) and subsequent Australian data showed the vaccine working at the population level; ineffectiveness is not the reason screening remains part of the strategy.
explanations.c: Cost is not the epidemiological rationale; screening is retained because it addresses a population vaccination cannot reach in time.
explanations.d: The 90-70-90 targets are explicitly layered to cover different points in the disease's natural history, not set independently.

questions.prompt: Order these developments in the cervical cancer prevention case from earliest to most recent.

items.text: Papanicolaou cytology (Pap smear) screening becomes routine
Gardasil HPV vaccine approved (2006)
Australia launches national school-based HPV vaccination (2007)
USPSTF allows primary HPV DNA testing alone every 5 years (2018)
WHO sets 90-70-90 elimination targets for 2030 (2020)

questions.explanation: Cytology-based screening predates the vaccine era; the vaccine's approval and Australia's rollout came next, followed by the shift toward HPV DNA primary screening, and finally the global elimination targets that combine both strategies.

questions.prompt: Match each component of the WHO 90-70-90 strategy to what it targets.

left.text: 70% screened with a high-performance test by 35 and 45
90% of women with cervical disease treated

right.text: Primary prevention: stopping HPV infection before exposure
Secondary prevention: detecting infection or precancer already present
Tertiary step: closing the loop for those who screen positive

questions.explanation: The three targets map onto three distinct stages of the disease's natural history, which is why elimination requires all three together.

lessons.label: Designing a Population-Level Science-Fair Project

sections.heading: Picking a data source and a question it can actually answer
sections.body: Three open surveillance sources dominate student projects for good reason: CDC WONDER (US mortality and natality records, queryable by state, year, and cause), BRFSS (the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System, an annual state-level telephone survey of self-reported health behaviors like smoking and physical activity), and Our World in Data (curated, sourced global time series on disease burden, vaccination, and risk factors). The first design decision is incidence versus prevalence: incidence (new cases over a time window) suits questions about what is currently driving a trend, such as a policy's effect on new smokers; prevalence (existing cases at a point in time) suits questions about total population burden, such as how many adults currently have diabetes. Picking the wrong one for the question — for instance, using prevalence to claim a policy caused a recent change, when prevalence reflects years of accumulated cases — is a common, avoidable design error.

sections.heading: Ecological and before-after designs, and their shared trap
sections.body: Most feasible student projects are ecological studies: comparing units — states, countries, counties — rather than individuals, because that is the resolution BRFSS and CDC WONDER actually provide. A before-after design compares one unit's outcome before and after an event, such as a state's cardiac admission rate before and after a smoke-free law, mirroring Sargent et al.'s 2004 Helena study design. Both designs share a well-known trap: the ecological fallacy, formalized by Robinson (1950), which is the error of inferring an individual-level relationship from a group-level correlation. If states with higher tobacco taxes have lower lung cancer rates, that does not prove any individual who faced a higher tax was personally less likely to get cancer — the correlation could be confounded by state-level differences in income, healthcare access, or baseline smoking culture that a group-level comparison cannot separate out.

sections.heading: Pre-specifying the analysis before looking at the data
sections.body: A credible population-level project states its hypothesis, comparison groups, and outcome measure before pulling the data, not after — otherwise it is easy to try several variables, several time windows, or several state groupings until one produces a striking-looking correlation, a form of p-hacking that a project write-up should explicitly guard against. Concretely: write down the exposure (e.g., state cigarette excise tax per pack), the outcome (e.g., BRFSS current-smoking prevalence), the comparison (e.g., high-tax vs. low-tax states, or the same states before and after a tax hike), and the expected direction, before opening the dataset.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to test whether state soda taxes reduce obesity. Pre-specified plan: exposure = presence of a city or state sugar-sweetened-beverage tax (e.g., Philadelphia's 2017 tax); outcome = BRFSS self-reported obesity prevalence; comparison = the taxed jurisdiction's rate in the two years before versus two years after the tax, ideally against a similar untaxed jurisdiction as a control. The student must flag, in the write-up, that this is ecological (jurisdiction-level) data — a resident's own soda consumption and weight were never linked to the same tax record — so any observed drop supports a population-level association, not a proof that any specific taxed individual drank less soda and lost weight.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe ecological-fallacy awareness because it is the fastest way to tell a student who understands surveillance-data limits from one who is pattern-matching a correlation to a headline. A student who says 'states with X law have lower Y rate, therefore the law reduces individual risk' without acknowledging the group-to-individual leap has made exactly the inferential error Robinson (1950) named; a student who explicitly states the design is ecological and names the confounders it cannot rule out is demonstrating the judgment a real applied epidemiologist needs before recommending policy from aggregate data.

questions.prompt: A student finds that US states with higher cigarette taxes have lower lung cancer rates, using CDC WONDER state-level data, and concludes 'a higher tax causes any given individual smoker to be less likely to develop lung cancer.' What is the flaw?

options.text: CDC WONDER does not contain mortality data, so the comparison is impossible
The claim commits the ecological fallacy: inferring an individual-level effect from a state-level (group) correlation
Lung cancer incidence cannot be studied using any government data source
Cigarette taxes have never been shown to reduce consumption at any level

explanations.a: CDC WONDER does provide queryable US mortality data by state and cause; that is not the flaw here.
explanations.b: Correct: the data compare states (groups), not individuals, so the group-level correlation cannot be used to infer what happened to any specific individual smoker — this is the ecological fallacy Robinson named in 1950.
explanations.c: Government surveillance sources like CDC WONDER and BRFSS are designed for exactly this kind of population-level study; the issue is the individual-level conclusion drawn from group-level data, not the data source itself.
explanations.d: Tax-driven consumption effects are well documented at the population level; the flaw is the leap to an individual-level causal claim, not a claim that taxes have no effect at all.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of designing a population-level science-fair project correctly.

items.text: Choose incidence or prevalence based on the question being asked
Pre-specify exposure, outcome, comparison groups, and expected direction
Pull the data from CDC WONDER, BRFSS, or Our World in Data
Analyze the pre-specified comparison and report results, flagging the ecological design

questions.explanation: The framing decisions (incidence/prevalence, and pre-specifying the analysis) must come before the data is pulled and analyzed, or the project risks p-hacking and an unacknowledged ecological-fallacy leap.

questions.prompt: Match each data source to what it actually provides.

right.text: US mortality and natality records queryable by state, year, and cause
Annual state-level telephone survey of self-reported health behaviors
Curated, sourced global time series on disease burden and risk factors

questions.explanation: Choosing the right source depends on knowing exactly what unit and variable it records — mortality records, self-reported behavior, or global aggregate trends.

lessons.label: Communicating Risk and Reading a Public-Health Report

sections.heading: Absolute versus relative risk, and the missing denominator
sections.body: A headline reading 'drug X doubles your risk of condition Y' describes relative risk — the ratio between two rates — and hides the absolute risk, the actual baseline probability being doubled. If a condition's baseline risk is 1 in 10,000, doubling it means 2 in 10,000: a change most people would consider small, even though '100% increased risk' sounds alarming. The denominator problem compounds this: a report stating '500 cases this month' is meaningless for comparing places or times unless paired with the population size and time window it was counted over, turning a raw count into a rate. A student reading any public-health report should first ask what the denominator was, and whether the headline number is absolute or relative.

sections.heading: Number needed to screen and the honest cost of prevention
sections.body: Number needed to screen (NNS) or treat (NNT) answers a different, more useful question: how many people must go through an intervention for one to benefit? A widely cited Cochrane review (Gøtzsche and Jørgensen, 2013) estimated that for every 2,000 women invited to mammography screening over ten years, one death is prevented, while about ten healthy women are overdiagnosed and treated unnecessarily for a cancer that would never have caused harm. A similar trade-off shows up for statins used in primary cardiovascular prevention, where commonly cited estimates put the NNT on the order of 100 to 200 people treated over five years to prevent one heart attack or stroke, alongside a much larger group who take a daily pill for a benefit they were never going to receive. Reporting only 'screening saves lives' without the NNS and the overdiagnosis cost hides the real trade-off a population — and an individual deciding whether to be screened — is actually making.

sections.heading: Framing effects and surveillance artifacts
sections.body: Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman's 1981 'Asian disease problem' showed that describing an identical outcome as '200 of 600 will be saved' versus '400 of 600 will die' shifts people's choices, even though the underlying numbers are the same — evidence that how a risk is framed, not just its size, drives public response. Reports can also mistake a surveillance artifact for a real disease change: Ahn and colleagues (2014, New England Journal of Medicine) documented South Korea's thyroid cancer incidence rising roughly 15-fold from 1993 to 2011 while thyroid cancer mortality stayed essentially flat — the 'epidemic' tracked the introduction of widespread ultrasound screening, not a true rise in disease, a pattern known as overdiagnosis.

lessons.workedExample: A local news report states: 'New cases of Condition Z rose 300% in our county this year.' A careful reader checks: was the denominator constant (same population size), was the definition of a case unchanged, and did testing volume change? Suppose the county opened a new free screening clinic that roughly quadrupled the number of people tested. If the underlying prevalence of Z in the population is unchanged but testing roughly quadrupled, a 300% rise in detected cases is exactly what more testing predicts even with zero real change in disease — the same artifact pattern as Ahn et al.'s thyroid cancer finding, just at local-news scale instead of national-registry scale.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe risk communication because it is where a scientifically correct project can still mislead a reader through presentation choices alone. A student who reports only relative risk, only a raw case count without its denominator, or a rising-incidence finding without ruling out a change in testing volume has produced a technically defensible but practically misleading result; the tell of genuine rigor is when a student proactively reports absolute risk alongside relative risk, states the NNS or NNT where relevant, and explicitly checks whether a change in surveillance intensity — not disease reality — could explain an observed trend.

questions.prompt: South Korea's thyroid cancer incidence rose roughly 15-fold from 1993 to 2011 while thyroid cancer mortality stayed essentially flat (Ahn et al., 2014). What does this pattern most likely indicate?

options.text: A genuine 15-fold increase in the true rate of thyroid cancer in the population
Overdiagnosis: increased ultrasound screening detected many indolent cases that would never have caused death, inflating incidence without changing mortality
A change in the definition of death used in mortality reporting
A data entry error in the national cancer registry

explanations.a: If true disease incidence had risen 15-fold, mortality would be expected to rise as well, at least with some lag; a flat mortality rate argues against a true 15-fold increase in dangerous disease.
explanations.b: Correct: this is the classic overdiagnosis signature — incidence rises sharply because more screening finds more (often indolent) disease, while mortality stays flat because the additional detected cases were not going to cause death.
explanations.c: The mortality definition is not what changed; the incidence side of the pattern (driven by screening volume) is what shifted, and mortality data tracked deaths using consistent criteria.
explanations.d: The pattern is a well-documented, published epidemiological finding (Ahn et al., 2014, NEJM) attributable to screening intensity, not a data entry artifact.

questions.prompt: Order the questions a careful reader should ask when a report claims cases of a disease 'rose sharply this year.'

items.text: What was the denominator (population size and time window) behind the reported numbers?
Did the case definition stay the same across the comparison period?
Did testing or screening volume change over the same period?
Only after ruling out the above, consider whether disease incidence truly changed

questions.explanation: Denominator, case definition, and testing volume must be checked before concluding a raw rise in reported cases reflects a true rise in disease, since any of the three can produce an apparent increase on its own.

questions.prompt: Match each risk-communication concept to what it captures.

right.text: The ratio between two rates, e.g. risk doubling
The actual baseline probability of the outcome
How many people must be screened for one to benefit

questions.explanation: A relative-risk figure alone can sound dramatic while the absolute risk stays small, and NNS translates both into the practical cost of delivering the intervention to a whole population.

lessons.label: The Field in Practice: Careers and the Public-Health System

sections.heading: The disease detectives: EIS and applied field epidemiology
sections.body: The CDC's Epidemic Intelligence Service (EIS) was founded in 1951 by Alexander Langmuir, motivated by Cold War fears that the Korean War could bring biological warfare and by the recognition that the US had no standing corps of field investigators to detect an outbreak fast. EIS officers, nicknamed 'disease detectives,' enter a two-year fellowship where they are dispatched on short notice to investigate outbreaks anywhere in the country or world, applying the same case-definition, line-list, and epi-curve tools taught in outbreak-investigation training to real, unfolding events. The model proved durable enough that other countries built equivalents, and EIS alumni have gone on to lead major public-health institutions, making the fellowship as much a career pipeline as an emergency-response unit.

sections.heading: The layered system: local, state, federal, and global
sections.body: Applied epidemiology in the US runs through a nested chain: local and county health departments are usually the first to receive a report of a reportable disease (from a clinician or lab), state health departments aggregate and analyze reports across jurisdictions and can request CDC support, and the CDC coordinates federal surveillance, sets case definitions, and deploys EIS officers for large or novel outbreaks. Above the national level, the World Health Organization (WHO, founded 1948) coordinates global surveillance and issues international guidance, while regional bodies do parallel work — the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), established in 2005 in the wake of SARS, plays that role for the European Union. Data and authority flow up this chain, and case definitions and resources flow back down it.

sections.heading: From analyst to policy, and where student skills map to real jobs
sections.body: The core workflow that turns a number into a decision is: surveillance data collection, epidemiologic analysis (rates, trends, case-control or cohort comparisons), risk assessment, a policy recommendation, implementation, and program evaluation — which feeds back into surveillance, closing the loop. Every step in this chain corresponds to a real job title: a field epidemiologist or EIS officer runs the outbreak investigation, a biostatistician builds the statistical model behind the risk estimate, a public-health analyst turns state or CDC WONDER data into the dashboards that inform local policy, and a global-health officer at WHO or a national ministry translates that analysis into a program like a vaccination campaign. A student who has framed a hypothesis, pulled BRFSS or CDC WONDER data, and pre-specified an analysis has already practiced the first three steps of this exact pipeline.

lessons.workedExample: Trace a real reportable-disease event through the chain: a clinician diagnoses a cluster of unusual illness and reports it to the county health department (local); the county cannot determine the source and escalates to the state health department, which requests CDC's Epidemic Intelligence Service for field support (state to federal); the deployed EIS officer runs a case-control study to identify the exposure, consistent with the outbreak-investigation framework of case definition, line list, and epi curve; the finding becomes a state policy recommendation (e.g., a food recall or a facility closure); and post-recommendation surveillance data are then evaluated to confirm the intervention actually reduced new cases, closing the loop.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about the surveillance-to-policy pipeline and the EIS model because they want to know whether a student sees their project as an isolated exercise or as a scaled-down version of a real system with real institutions and real jobs behind it. A student who can name where their own analysis would sit in the local-state-federal-global chain, and who understands that EIS-style field epidemiology exists precisely because Langmuir judged in 1951 that outbreak response could not wait for ad hoc staffing, demonstrates they grasp public health as an operating system, not a set of facts to memorize.

questions.prompt: Why was the CDC's Epidemic Intelligence Service (EIS) created in 1951?

options.text: To replace state health departments with a single federal reporting system
Because Alexander Langmuir judged the US lacked a standing corps of trained investigators to detect outbreaks quickly, amid Cold War fears of biological warfare during the Korean War
To provide biostatistics training for hospital administrators
As a response to the WHO's founding in 1948

explanations.a: EIS supplements and supports state and local health departments during investigations; it did not replace the layered local-state-federal reporting structure.
explanations.b: Correct: Langmuir founded EIS in 1951 specifically to build rapid-response outbreak investigation capacity, motivated by Korean War-era biological warfare concerns and the absence of trained field investigators.
explanations.c: EIS trains field epidemiologists in outbreak investigation, not primarily biostatistics for hospital administration.
explanations.d: EIS was a US national response driven by wartime biological-threat concerns, not a direct response to WHO's 1948 founding, which is a separate global institution.

questions.prompt: Order the surveillance-to-policy pipeline from first step to last.

items.text: Surveillance data collection
Epidemiologic analysis (rates, trends, comparisons)
Risk assessment
Policy recommendation and implementation
Program evaluation, feeding back into surveillance

questions.explanation: Data must be collected and analyzed before risk can be assessed and a recommendation made, and evaluation closes the loop by feeding new surveillance data back into the system.

questions.prompt: Match each level of the public-health system to its typical role.

right.text: First to receive a reportable-disease report from a clinician or lab
Aggregates reports across jurisdictions, can request federal (CDC) support
Coordinates global or regional surveillance and issues international guidance

questions.explanation: Each tier of the system has a distinct scope, from first-contact reporting locally to guidance-setting at the global or regional level.
